Phoning Home starts out simple enough.  Find resources, craft items, and defend yourself.  Then it gets a little complicated.  Find ANI, craft items (for two), and defend both of you.  After that, it gets insane.  Take care of ANI, carry her over rough terrain, use a lot of your resources on her, tell her to stay or follow (maybe she'll listen or maybe not), craft items (again, for two), and she'll make pull your hair out.  Despite all of that, the story is engaging, the maps are fairly large, and there is much to explore.
Pros:
Graphics are very well done
A great story-line
A mystery unfolds as you play the game
Very challenging
The developers are actively updating and answering questions
Cons:
ANI slows down the game to a crawl
Thrusters are hard to control
The island hopping level, some of the portals are deliberately hidden from view
There are places where you can get stuck
After it's said and done, the story-line is solid and this mystery had me guessing all the way up to the end.  I enjoyed finding resources and crafting items to fix something or to complete a task.  This game kept me busy for awhile and that's what it's really about.
Unfortunately, ANI slows this game down considerably.  She moves much to slow and she doesn't always do what you tell her.  At one point, you both have to climb up a mountain to fix some radio antennas.  The first pathway is in front of you and easy to climb.  The other two are substantially harder to find.  The paths are not marked at all and what looks like a path may be a dead end.  This happens quite often.  However, it was only after a couple of play-throughs before I realized that the portals, more often than not, drop you off where you need to go, that's my fault.
I encountered a few bugs while playing this game too.  The most notable was when I had to jump into a pit using the kinetic damper to break my fall... the ground was not visible.  I loaded my most resent save and that fixed the problem.  I also encountered a couple of trigger errors, but I sent my saved game to the developers and they fixed it.  I'm fairly certain that most, if not all, of the trigger errors that I encountered have been fixed, so that may not be an issue anymore.
At the time of this review, Phoning Home was selling for $19.99.  Is it worth it?  Let's be honest.  There were times that I wanted to quit and play something else, but I stuck with it and learned much about the eccentricities of this game.  What's the bottom line?  Did I have fun?  Yes, yes I did, so... Yes it's worth it.

The positive view on this is, that these problems are easily fixable with a little bit effort from the game design and programming department and are NOT totally screwed up mechanics you can't fix in years. Therefore I think, the game can be really enjoyable when these details are improved.
For what I've seen the world isn't really "alien" from a visual standpoint - at least the first area could play on earth - but the developers worked with landmarks to guide you through the open world and I never was stuck. Actually sometimes I saw something interesting in the distance (but couldn't exactly tell what it was...some kind of alien structure?) and the game created this feeling of "I want to know what's going on here" which not many games are able to do for me.
For my further play-trough I hope that the game focuses on creating a good feeling, excitement for exploration and NOT stretching the crafting-mechanics too much to extend the play-time. Salt and Sanctuary is probably going to be one of the few games I actually end up replaying. It's very much like a Souls game, but it's also got a great metrodvania feel. Pros and cons are as follows:

Typically tight controls
Great art style that emphasizes colors and shading when it needs to(Except for those faces)
A lot to explore
A large amount of customization for such a small game
Rewarding when taking down bosses or getting through tough areas
Meh:
Not as difficult as it could have been. It's typically balanced, but it's not going to challenge you to be pushed to your limits. It definitely rewards patience, but bosses and enemies become predictable very quickly, lowering the difficulty of the game. Some parts will still feel difficult, but it's not overbearing, in my opinion.
Cons:
Stun lock. Enemies will knock you down and start chaining attacks, giving no time for recovery and feeling cheap
Starts to drag a little towards the end. The world felt a little worn, but it's still great to explore. Just a little more variety would have been appreciated.
It's a good game. Great even. It's really enjoyable, and it's probably going to end up being one of those indie game gems. It's a solid 9/10.

I tried, o how i tried to love this game. 500 + hours of Dark Souls 1/2/3 games, loved every minute of getting wrecked in them. This game however, tries so hard to be Dark Souls, that it forgets what makes the Souls games awesome, a FAIR challenge.
In this game, rolling is busted and hardly works, there's no stat to increase HP, the controls are clunky and fail to give the player the required fast and crisp input to complete the gimmicky bosses and over-used platforming sections. Not to mention that most of the deaths in this game come from either missing a jump, and dying, or getting hit off a ledge and dying that way. Thats not fun at all, there are hardly any fun 1v1 enemy encounters, it's constantly throwing multiple enemies at you that stunlock you, or send you flying, becuase if anything touches you, you GO ♥♥♥♥ING FLYING OFF THE SCREEN. Most enemies can 2 shot you, if there's 2 enemies on the screen, be sure as hell they will combo you around the screen like a ♥♥♥♥ing Super Smash game.
The main problem with this game is that there are too many arbitrary and artifical ways they make the game harder. "Here, fight this boss on a series of crumbling ledges that also periodically shoot fire at you" this is the definition of a gimmicky boss, sure it takes some skill, but the amount of trial and error required to get passed some of these poorly designed encounters, leaves the player feeling frustrated even after a win. Everytime i beat a boss in a DS game for the 1st time, i was so happy at what i had just accomplished, knowing i just completed a difficult, but fair fight (barring some cheesy♥♥♥♥♥bosses in DS2 of course). Another issue is that the game also reduces your total amount of HP everytime you are hit, another artifical way to increase the difficulty, even with the ring which helps reduce the amount of HP lost from taking those hits, its still completely unnecesary. It just feels like the devs made the game to make players feel bad, "hope you like fighting on ledges that 1 misstep and your dead while 5 enemies are constantly chasing you and archers are launching arrows at your face! isnt it great how hard our game is!?" Its like the game just laughs at you and doesn't respect the player like a Souls game, which always builds up the players skills, making every new area a fun new challenge that's teaching you the ropes at the same time as kicking your♥♥♥♥♥
In the end, i think if there was far less crushingly difficult platforming and less ledges/cliffs/holes in the ground, i would have maybe stuck it out (The controls certainly don't help). But im sick of trying my best in a given section, only to have a trash mob enemy hit me once, and throw me flying off a ledge to my death. The Souls-like mechanics are well done in some places, the way Salt(Souls) work, fat rolling, weapon/armour variation and  the tech tree is OK for what it is, the atmosphere is nice as well, but the game severly lacks the balance from a Souls game. That is to say, the balance of difficulty vs frustration, which is what keeps the player playing, that feeling of "Man, i got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked, but i totally made some mistakes, and i can do better", not "Hey this boss will 2 shot me no matter what happens unless I play perfectly for the next 5 mins" and "Why am i fighting 5 enemies on a bunch of narrow platforms, this is cheap and makes me feel bad!".
Im a patient man, having just finished casually speedrunning DS3, beating Doom on Nightmare (which was hard as ♥♥♥♥, but so fun!), but this game will test the patience of any gamer i can think of. Be wary of this game, as it will crush your soul so hard, youll boot up a Kane and Lynch game while cutting yourself for reprieve.

I know what you're thinking: Holy crap, this game looks really stupid!
Well, it is stupid, but it's also fun.  In most cases, video game bowling sucks (I've never been a fan of REAL bowling, either), but this game has a nice twist to it.  While rolling your ball down the lane, you can somewhat control it and when doing so, you can grab different positive and negative items.
Positive items help YOU, whereas negative items hurt your opponent, which can be a real person or the AI.  This adds a whole new dynamic to the game and turns what could've been a real flop into something quite entertaining.
There are achievements (if that means a whole lot to you) and a "normal" bowling mode, just in case you don't want to deal with crazy game items.  I don't know WHY you'd want to do that, but it's there.
You can play against a real person if you want.  This is restricted to local gameplay on ONE PC, so you can't bowl against anyone online.

This game was absolutely top of the line in its original form back in the day. It's not top of the line today.
It's still the old game, with old gameplay, old bugs, old clunky animations, old audio. It's clearly not a game of today. But damn, compare it to the original! Quite amazing how the game plays _exactly_ the same, just .. prettier.
It felt good being back in Adelpha again!
There are some bugs though. I can't remember jumping and swimming worked as bad as it did in this remake. Sometimes animations would get stuck and you'd be unable to move at all. Save often! Fortunately, the lengthy Gamasaav buildup is shortered, and an autosave feature is present which saves often. I had to use it a couple of times, fortunately without losing much, if any, progress.
Considering how the world is so prettyfied, I feel they could've done a better job at NPC models. They have dorky faces and weird eyes. It's not just because they're aliens. It just seems off the way it is now. Another thing is pickups. there was hardly any vegetation in the original game. And while it looks pretty well done, it makes it quite hard to spot drops and other items that can be picked up. The HUD helps, as it did in the original. But because the vegetation now blocks a lot, it seems to me the HUD might help a little more.
If you're unknown to Outcast and you can forgive the old-style gameplay and occasion bugs, you have an amazing world to get aquinted, to with a great story being told in an accessible game.

As a big fan of the original Outcast I immediately jumped at the opportunity to re-visit Adelpha and some old friends.
After halfway finishing the game I must say I am mostly pleased, but also somewhat disappointed.
The renewed graphics look beautiful, for the most part. The soundtrack is still, in my opinion, one of the most notable of its kind. The story, while mostly stereotypical for its kind, still manages to completely grasp me thanks to wonderful and varied characters.
But the controls are (still?) extremely frustrating. Jumping especially is nerve-wracking, precise jumps take a lot of time (and luck). The AI of the enemies is laughable, they run in circles (and often directly into your crosshair).
All in all would I recommend
? Yes, I would, mostly for the strengths of the original (characters, world, soundtrack). Although I will admit that even as a fan I would not pay full price (34,99€ for me) just for updated graphics. If you see it in a sale and like SciFi (even if it's cheesy at times) give it a try.

Prospekt is a simplistic, yet very nice use of the Source Engine, but seemingly only using Half-Life 2 assets, minimally with custom ones. Unlike most i've talked to that have played this game, I don't have a problem with this, since it is supposed to be part of the Half-Life 2 story and previous games. If you're unfamiliar with the collaboration back in 1999 between Valve and Gearbox Software, the game, "Half-Life: Opposing Force", it is esentially made to take place at the exact same time that Half-Life takes place, just in the view of United States Marine, Adrian Shephard. This game is a continuation of that game, with the same character, Corporal Shephard. The game does create familiarity with those that have played Half-Life 2, with things extremely simular to Nova Prospekt, and the Citadel. Bottomline, the usage of the the familiar assets, creates a more inviting environment for those that might not be familiar with anything past that.
Now, many of the complaints i've heard about this game, most especially, that the puzzles are very easily solved, and the game as a whole is too short. Sure, that's not wrong, but the puzzles does have a bit of fun to them in trying to figure it out, with how simplistic or complex it could be. About it being short, yes, it took me less than 2 hours to complete it, and I did it in one day. I really don't have a problem with that, as it does open the door for replay value, because you know it won't take long to do; The game could also be replayed while listening to the Developer Commentary, from Mr. Richard Seabrook himself.
The way I see it, yes, the game is short, and looks a little lazy due to it being a reusage of assets, and being simple, but like I said, it's fun to figure out the puzzles the first time, and has some replay value. But, me, as a huge Half-Life fan, who has played every game more than once or twice...or maybe more...had fun with this little game, because it does feel simular and is very close to what you'd imagine Valve would do themselves. I honestly think that as long as you've got an open mind, and some time, you could enjoy this game, especially if you're a Half-Life fan.

This game is a great mix of my favorite elements. I enjoy RPG's with collecting and crafting as well as match 3 type puzzle games. This is like the hybrid of my dreams. I have not played another form of this (though my GF has been trying to convince me to play the mobile version but I do not like to play games on my iPhone). I'm about half way through the early chapters and it's very engaging. The first 10 missions were very easy (too easy IMHO) but it did build my confidence with how to use the skills, allocate the heroes, and really choose a good allies for the more challenging missions.
The graphics are very cute for a puzzle game- nothing spectacular but not grainy and blurry either. Pixels look good on my PC and it loads very fast. I enjoy the graphic configuration feature which pops up every time you start the game. It allows you to select your screen resolutions & graphics quality. This makes a big difference if you only have a small tablet PC like I do.
There is far more strategy involved in this vs. a regular Match 3 like BeJeweled. Here the heroes you use make a huge difference in how well the battle's go. It is exceptionally like Pokemon and I think adults who like Pokemon will love this game if they enjoy puzzlers. I enjoy the ability to fuse and enhance the heroes - this provides a level of customization you can apply to any hero you favor- and it's RPG based. I'm a leisurely player and don't rush through - I go back and replay older missions to get extra items to fuse with and I pay attention to the Heroes/allies information.
Overall any gamer who enjoys games like Puzzle Quest and Puzzle Chronicles or other Match 3 games and RPG"s must pick this up - it's addictive once you pass the early missions which are too easy. There is only one save file - but that's ok for me as the game is priced at a good point. It's something you could pick up and do in a boring lecture or when you have time at work - unlike some RPG's which are tough to engage in without allocated time.

As lootbox simulators go, this one is definitely above par and in some ways has completely perfected the lootbox genre - no wonder it was considered GOTY. Starting with lootboxes that are actual trash, you work your way up the hierarchy of boxes to obtain better and better in game items, and consequentially better and better boxes of loot. I enjoyed how items looked like low quality jpegs of things that are box-like in nature. These items can be equiped by the player and it is refreshing that any number of items can be equiped and they don't seem to affect gameplay OR aesthetics (unlike so many lootbox simulators where the items obtained drastically affect the aesthetics of the player character!)
One huge criticism of the game is that lootboxes never contained additional lootboxes. I don't know how companies can still be getting away with this in 2017 - if you're going to sell lootboxes, some of those lootboxes better contain other boxes that contain loot but also have an additional probability of yet more boxes.
An unusual positive in this lootbox simulator - it contains a small video game for those who aren't in it simply for the thrill of the box or get too tired of winning. The video game resemblies the classic game Snake, except that instead of a snake you are a dolphin and there are also portals in what is clearly a industry insider reference to the cult-classic, lootboxless failure Portal. Needless to say I stuck to opening my boxes.

The concept of Evolve really intrigued me last year.  However, when 2K implemented the worst DLC system known to man kind in a PAID 60 DOLLAR GAME I wouldn't touch it with a 300 foot pole.
Well, 2K has decided to go with Turtle Rock's original plan to have a F2P title.  This, currently, is the BEST f2p system I have ever seen implemented in any game.  I am VERY careful about f2p titles, because so many are "pay to win".  Well, (in it's current state) there are absolutely ZERO ways to buy currency or advance in any way.  It is all through in game unlocks.  However, if you own the game prior you will unlock most of the characters and monsters.  I actually purchased the game from a key site for 6 bucks after playing about an hour I loved it so much.  But back to the F2P system.  You play matches to unlock in game currency to in turn purchase characters and skins with.  After doing the 2 tutorials you will unlock one monster and one character right off the bat.  There is also a free rotation weekly like most f2p games.  I am sure that 2K and TR will add a shop with real money at some point, but even then there is no "OP" pay to win class.  All of them are quite balanced.  Now on to the gameplay.
This is a 150% different game.  I was extremely skeptical after first hearing about the new move to f2p but it is clear TR took the games flaws and really worked on fixing them.  First off, they added a "dome" ability for every class.  This recharges in match and can trap the monster in an impenetrable dome for a small amount of time.  This makes combat MUCH more fast paced and fun.  Instead of hunting the monster for half the game this makes it way more approachable.  They have also removed half the maps and only have 4 extremely well crafted arena type levels.  Along with this only Hunt is the current playable game mode, which is the best and most competetive as to not split up the community.  Now, graphics.
The graphics have had a huuuuuuge overhaul and are absolutely GORGEOUS, I have a GTX 1070 and can max everything and have a steady 140 fps on my 144 hz display.
All in all, this is an absolutely unprecedented move by a AAA publisher and I really hope this game takes off as I am having the time of my life.  I am so thankful Turtle Rock had the opportunity to make the game the way THEY wanted it to be made.
Go ahead, give it a go.  After all, it is free :)

As a game developer in a big company myself, my advice is that you put more thoughts into the first-30-minute player experience. Right now, it's not fluid & missing on many fronts.
Issues encountered:
===============
1. The support of controller is incomplete. I've an official microsoft windows controller, and I had to go to the option menu to activate the controller support.
2. The tutorial and control hint only support keyboard and mouse. For controller user, the experience is disorienting.
3. The 'compass' has no background overlay. As a result, against the clear blue sky, it's practically invisible. This leads to frustration.
4. For the inventory menu, the tool tips only work with the mouse via hovering. This requires a re-design to accommodate the controller.
5. As the control scheme is unorthodox and has no tutorial support, I experimented with it and led to constant loss of health and death. Drop on fire? Minus health, Jump too high and fall? Minus health. How to heal myself? Unknown. Go easy on players who try to explore your game, like putting a few health packs in the inventory.
6. Spend the most part of the first 30 minutes exploring a grassy landscape and collecting thing. It's not exactly engaging. The first 30 minutes need to be more tightly scripted, engaging the players constantly with events and plot development. Give the players a reason to continue.

** Pure Unbridled Fun **
Old digitized actor fighting games tended to have a lot of things in common - they looked ridiculous, were expensive to make & play, and weren't very fun.
Streets of Fury EX is what you get if you only left in the ridiculous, focused on fun, and actually made a good game.
Pick from a large cast of people, many obviously average individuals hamming it up on camera, hit the streets and beat the crap out of a huge number of people in the most over-the-top ways possible, all while maintaining a fun, free-style combo system that's surprisingly deep and satisfying.
Reminding me a lot of Guardian Heroes with it's three-lane combat and the ability to continue to juggle the limp bodies of your defeated enemies until they explode (yup) this is a cooperative brawling game with the options that should make anyone who loves fun happy.
Want to learn a character or blow off steam?  Set it to Easy and enjoy 99 continues.  If you every want to enable friendly fire, this is the mode to do it in.
Want more of a challenge?  Set it Normal; you'll need a basic understanding of the core mechanics to survive.
Know the game really well?  Set it to hard -- only people with solid knowledge of the game's mechanics can complete the campaigns.
The range of characters go from a Streetfighter/Art of Fighting type, to a dry-humping Frenchman with dreadlocks that hurls a barrage of VHS tapes but they've all got different styles, strengths and the ability to string together fantastic combos.
Don't let the silliness fool you; the game's mechanics are surprisingly deep with a super meter (for Fury attacks), Guard meters (broken through repeated hits), parries (which stun enemies when times right), and Stamina (used for Special attacks) plus a less-broken Combo Breaker counter if you're hit too many times.
Each character has 3 basic attack buttons (normal, launcher, special) and each button provides a string of 4 different attack patterns, each with different uses.
Game play is centered around stringing together combos and juggling enemies so you don't get overwhelmed, using normal attacks to give your Stamina time to recharge and then launching into Furries for limited invulnerability.  Each type of enemy (except bosses) have a limited moveset but special properties, and stages are well designed, switching up the action from simple beat-downs on a large mob to dealing with smaller numbers of special-property enemies that require utilizing the mechanics taught earlier to deal with.  (Example:  Super-armour enemies with a very slow guard-breaking attack that need hit-and-run tactics, or aggressive enemies that are better dealt with via parry)  The game also rewards bold tactics, such as using the Parry to thwart a small area-afffect guard-breaking blast.
Throw in Survival, Challenges (which really test how well you've learned mechanics) and you have a very solid fighter that other more serious fighters wish they were.

Phoning Home
Released
ION LANDS
ION LANDS
3D Adventure
7th of February, 2017
Singleplayer
When I first saw screenshots of this title, I was expecting it to be just another cute robot-themed game that’s geared predominantly towards a younger audience. Phoning Home’s mechanized protagonist sure looks a lot like WALL-E at first glance yet the similarities end there. ION is a far more resourceful robot and even braver than most Star Wars droids. Between repairing his crash-landed ship, protecting his fragile friend ANI and contacting his homeworld, the players will guide our hero through an equally fascinating and perilous journey.  Hard to believe that such a polished and refreshingly authentic game, is the Steam debut of a dev team that has had no previous experience on the platform. I guess I became almost numb from so much mediocrity within recent indie games, that I forgot Steam can still offer a surprise every now and then.
While ION’s forte certainly ain’t combat, he’s more than capable of outsmarting his few (but deadly) foes on this new strange planet he’s stranded on. Even more tragically, the subsequent crash not only left ION without the means of communicating with his base of operations but also separated him from ANI, another robot and his only palpable friend since the AI guiding him along the way is hardly the company he so desperately needs. So “phoning home” is a priority, but ensuring ANI’s structural integrity is also paramount. A complex but still intuitive crafting system, plays a central role within the title’s gameplay since players shall have to produce everything from the repair modules, ship components and even fuel for the robots to press forward. Using the individual thrusters may help speed up the resource gathering and exploration parts a lot, but they shall take a toll on ION and particularly on ANI.
Fortunately, the developer understood the frustration most gamers have when trying to protect a non-combatant ally and thus, ANI can be ordered to stop or follow at the players' discretion. Enemies aren’t in large supply but whether we’re talking of giant golems, abstract lava creatures or flying dinosaurs (pterosaurs), ION is far better off simply avoiding them than to engage directly. Especially with the intial weapon that is just a pipe. So Phoning Home feels more natural as you roam the faily large open levels in search for new basic resources from which you shall craft more complex ones. It doesn’t drag on or imply any degree of boredom, but I was still annoyed by the constant backtracking to the crash site. At least dynamic weather effects plus day/night cycles are also implemented and the game itself is beautifully textured and designed. Fields filled with benign life forms such as huge butterflies or flowers are a stark contrast to the barren wastelands you shall also explore. From volcanic to arctic landscapes and even abandoned structures in the desert that clearly point out to previous civilizations. If you didn’t have a near constant companion with you, it would have really been a bleak exploration game, such as Lifeless Planet.
Phoning Home manages to simulate the stress and perils of being stranded in a foreign place, but since out protagonist never loses hope and even manages to escape, the game most certainly has the happy ending it deserves. From a graphical perspective, eye candy’s aplenty and the sounds + voice acting are also of high quality and diversified enough. The slow-pace given by ION’s own lack of speed is a game design choice which might not be very popular but still doesn’t warrant the far too many negative reviews this title has been receiving. Achievements (including ones that imply you must never heal) and Trading Cards sweeten the deal but the price tag might still be a bit too high. If that’s the case for you, wait for a Steam Sale or bundle and you won’t regret purchasing and playing Phoning Home. Come for the exploration and crafting and stay for the story. ION and ANI depend on you!

There is certainly fun to be had here for lovers of the Beat 'em Up genre. It's not to be taken too seriously and it's "cheap production value" and classic Mortal Kombat-esque sprites is part of the charm. The game play shows similarities to Phantom Breaker: Battle Ground (input a command to switch planes) and various fighting games in terms of combat. There are tons of playable characters, including the Nostalgia Critic and Benzaie from
that are unlocked as you perform combos to increase your Security Level.
Combat wise, you have a variety of "Mash X" string combos that change based on the direction you are holding. The Y button provides various launchers that also function based on the direction you're holding. The B button actions like the Smash Bros games as well, providing different special moves like travel attacks, slide kicks and dragon punches. The game doesn't tell you this, but doing the down B attack (or the B attack) in the air can sometimes do a sort of dive kick, which can be handy in dealing damage and continuing combos. Finally, there are "fury" moves which act like supers from a fighting game. Both you and enemies can block and be guard crushed, and after being attacked too much, either of you can perform an unblockable counter (even as you're dying!), though, enemies don't do it too often.
You can string these moves together, in silly, spammy, but bombastic combos. However, some enemies can resist being stunlocked/interuppted and perform a powerful attack that will set you up to take more damage or be juggled. I can't quite always say the game is fair. One the one hand, you can batter the enemies in an almost Dynasty Warriors style fashion, and it takes learning of the enemy behaviors to really maximize your dominance. On the other hand, you can easily get stun locked and juggled to oblivion, especially by some of the more annoying enemies like the "Drop kicking cornrow F**ker" or "nunchuck slinging b**ches". There are many places I dread in the first act (which I can't beat the last boss on :( ) because I'm expecting to loose 3/4th of my health to a handful of enemies.  (though, some playable characters might handle them better than others, you have to unlock them though).
These unfair moments hold me from seriously suggesthing this game. I had fun with it, and not a terrible buy at sale, but I don't recommend it if you're looking for a good brawler that you want to finish. Maybe get it on sale to experience for an hour or so, or spend hours getting good at it, which seems preposterous for it's corny nature.

Battle/levelup/team:
the leveling and skill system is very simple.
You started out with 25 diamonds in the beginning, which give you the ability to summon a “fearsome” hero and to join your team.
You can then pick other units dropped from battle to join your team as you progress.
Each unit has its own special and attack skills that triggered by matching the right colors of the gems.
Each time after winning a battle, the chosen heroes in your team will get a chance to level up.
In a few occasion after accumulating enough XP, your whole team will level up too.
Battle system get very complicated as you progress further and unlock new chapters.
In later missions especially battle against the legendary dragons, one shot from the dragons will be sufficient to kill your team. It’s very important to have your leader fully evolved and the right heroes summoned to help you out.

Even my heavy RPG games have never elicited this response from me.  I hope that once I finish this game I will have the capacity to remember to come update this review with some better insight and what will probably be more abounding laudation.
In short, This game is well worth the price for a one of a kind experience.  If it's on sale you have even less of an excuse to not own it.

Full disclosure:  I bought the game on sale for 8.75 euros, and a bit over a half an hour is more than enough to tell me this needs refunding. I need to go review one of the games I liked after this so I don't only have negative reviews on my account.
Now, the review:
To be frank, the text this game's store page presents (reviews, and that "The Long Dark is a thoughtful, exploration-survival experience..." bit) is hilarious to read after playing about a half hour of this game. Let me describe to you my extremely immersive, realistic, "thoughtful" experience:
Character wakes up.  The first action I can take is to tap a button in a specific pattern while watching a guy grip a shard of glass with his (bare?) hand the size of a combat knife blade and pull it entirely through and out of his palm and react like he got stung by a hornet.
Our hero then burns himself on a small (burning twig-branch from the crash) fire he's a good foot away from.  He's freezing to death next to this, and several other fires, none of which can apparently warm him, and none of which can be used to light a stick on fire to use to quickly start a campfire. Our hero instead gathers wood amongst the snow.
He builds a fire in a cave, which warms him, but alas, he is thirsty. Clearly the "thoughtful" thing to do is build another fire that needs its own matches and tinder (if only we had another campfire to get a burning branch from...) He builds this fire directly in thick snow (which would more likely than not put the fire out or make it intensely smoky).  Our hero click this fire, selects a number of liters, and the gods kindly provide snowmelt for him, conveniently in plastic containers that we had no sign of having before.
Did I mention the fires each have a slow loading bar during which you get to sit and do nothing while watching it steadily tick by?
This was not a good way to start this game's experience.  I know some people enjoy this game, but I presume they either just enjoy grinding and aren't paying attention to the surroundings enough to realize how silly this all is, OR they're not taking the game seriously and just want to go punch wolves.  If this was shown as a silly game from the get-go that eventually gets intimidating, this could have gotten a pass, I guess.  I wouldn't have bought it in the first place.  But no. "The Long Dark is a thoughtful, exploration-survival experience," we're told.  Not cool with me.
I don't mean to sound bitter, I really don't.  I had high hopes for this game. What was revealed about the rest of the game (supposed half-hour time passage for a single cardboard box, unreasonable meal requirements for the calories someone freezing would need...) was just icing on the cake.
If the devs feel this is overcritical or unfair, I am completely open to being contacted for discussion.  What I was shown in the opening minutes was just enough to tell me this wasn't worth the ~9 euro risk of playing past the refund period.

Don't let all the negative reviews about this game ruin your fun. Get it on sale if you are nervous. My son and I just beat the game 100% clear today, and we enjoyed pretty much every minute. The 3-Dness of it takes some getting used to, but the game is mostly 2-D, if that makes sense. Remember that "3D" level of contra? yeah, kinda like that, you get used to it. We loved this game. My 5 year old will write the rest (Father will ask questions, and he types out the answer) "What did you think of Trine 3?" It was good.  The reviews were wrong, it is not bad.
It's categorically worse than the previous two games (which were great). 3D mechanics aren't great, and it has a lot of bugs.

It's not as good as the first two games, but considering they were great games this still makes for a reasonably well made game.
The transition to a 3D environment does nothing to help this game. The platforming is much more difficult because it's harder to figure out where you are and where you will land. And the developers cut down on the amount of abilities you have to basically one per character. This is most evident with the wizard which can now only conjure up one box and move objects. This means that the puzzles are much more simple and tranversing the terrain is not nearly as fun. It basically boils down to putting down one box with your wizard and using your archer to grapple up to it and jump on the platform. And it makes the combat annoying as well, because it's very easy to miss your target because of the skewed camera angles which you can't switch.
The transition to 3D also greatly expanded the budget, which means the developer ran into difficulties halfway through and had to finish up the game. So what we received is half of the game which was originally intended to be made. And it shows in the story, because it really feels you're only halfway through once you're done, maybe not even that.
That being said it's still a solid game and the biggest problem with Trine 3 is that it comes after 2 extremely well made games which already showcased how to do things properly. If this were a new IP it would have been much better received. If you're willing to take this game as it is you'll enjoy your time with it, so I am going to recommend it (if you get it at a reasonable discount).

Definitely one of my new favorite games and easily the best platformer i've ever played. I went into this game expecting an homage to dark souls and i got that and so much more. the combat system, the salt used for levelling up and upgrading equipment, the sparse story told through item descriptions and npc interactions...it's jsut so lovely and perfect. the many sanctuaries around the world that can be upgraded with various npcs that provide various services as well as area bonuses. like dark souls, salt and sanctuary has something like covenants (called creeds) that you can level up in and collect bonuses from. the skill tree is massive and reminds me of path of exile's humungous skill tree. regardless of your starting class, salt and sanctuary allows you to create a fully customizable character that can be proficient in anything. i really like the branding system. i've only found 2 'brands' so far, but one allows me to use certain obelisks to reverse gravity in certain areas and walk on the ceiling. the other allows me to jump off walls. i'm sure there are more out there and i'm curious to see how they help me progress through the world. the 2D platforming nature of salt and sanctuary combines with the branding system to allow for more vertical gameplay than dark souls could pull off. i also really like the way you can unlock shortcuts between the sanctuaries and that there are even little hidden checkpoints that act like sanctuaries and restore your health/potions while on the way to certain bosses. the 2D nature also gives a certain advantage to the bosses in that they only have to attack in one of 2 directions. it adds a certain level of challenge to not being able to dodge left or right, but only forward and back. the many different weapons have their own attack patterns that add some depth to the combat and the fact that you can transmute them into other, potentially more powerful weapons is pretty amazing.
all in all, i can honestly say that i like this game as much as the souls games. if you like dark souls and platformers, don't wait-just get it. the only downside to this game is that there's no multiplayer. but there's local co-op, which is almost as good.

The Outsider in particular I think will survive in gaming memory for quite some time. And this isn't to say anything about the gameplay, which is incredibly smooth, intuitive, and engaging. It seems like there's dozens of ways to get through any given level, and though the game only has three endings, your choices affect the enemies, so it still feels like every kill-or-spare decision matters. There's never a down moment in this game. It never drags, and there are never places where you become complacent because you've learned all the enemies' tricks. It's the perfect pace and the perfect length for the gameplay it offers. 10/10, would definitely recommend, especially with the sequel coming out this year.

I...have a hard time hitting the "recommended" button. But I'm going to anyway.
First off, this is more of a kinetic novel than a proper Visual Novel. The sprites and backgrounds are more limited than you'd expect from the genre, and there are only really choices at the end.
The art is pretty good. It gives personality to all of the characters with rather elaborate yet simplistic designs and wonderful backgrounds.
And it functions as it should. No technical issues.
However, there ARE problems, mostly in regards to the story itself (which is what you rate when you review games like this anyway):
1) The script is hideously anachronistic. I get that it's supposed to be a fictional world and you have magic and such existing in the game, but there are references to things that really shouldn't exist given the technological level present in the story. The author seemed more focused on telling a specific story than dealing with the small details. If references to French Fries in what's implied to be an ancient Asian country (and I mean actually ancient. There's proof in the game that it takes place thousands of years in the past) ruin your suspension of disbelief, it's not for you.
2) It's DEPRESSING. I'm going to come right out and say it that there's no good ending to the game. There's a "True" ending, but it's depressing as hell. Of course this isn't by itself a bad thing, as there are plenty of games with depressing plots that are VERY good. But it doesn't STOP being depressing. Seriously it needs a fifth ending. I even have ideas as to where and when in the narrative it should be, but hey not my game so yeah. And that leads into...
3) Really the choices don't feel like they matter. All you're really doing is choosing the best way for the main characters' lives to suck. If they even last that long. I mean I hesitate hinting at this kind of stuff in a review but this is seriously a turn off for some people, and if I met the author I'd chastise them for not fully taking advantage of the medium to give a wider variety of endings, so that the player feels satisfied.
4) The villain is horrible. We don't really get to know him, but we're supposed to feel bad for him. Literally every single piece of misery the characters undergo is entirely his fault. There is ONE part of ONE ending when a bit of misery is NOT his fault, and it feels so forced as to have only been added in to make the main characters' lives, again, suck. He's also a terrible leader, strategist, and tactician, and really should have been assassinated at some point in the story.
But the kicker? He never does. And what happens with him in the True End infuriated me and ALMOST got me to click that "No" under "Do you recommend this game?"
So you're probably wondering why I didn't.
Well...it made me care. I like Miyon. I like Gai. I like Sasa. I like Zoluu. The humor regarding Neek was entertaining (even if it did, anachronistically, involve comics). The characters were complex and multifaceted, with tiny bits of nuance given their limited time (which is a running theme in the story, that people are more complicated than you see on the surface)
I wanted MORE from them. And I was inspired to work on some of my own writing.
So, for the price, I'd say I got a lot of value out of it. But I hold out hope the writer can improve.

I'm usually hesitant about buying short games, but something about this one caught my eye as I was looking at a list of games on sale. Best decision I've made in a long time, and a much better use of my money than most things I waste it on.

Cursed Sight is relatively brief as visual novels go, but manages to tell a captivating story in the few hours it has to its name. The story follows Gai, who is 10 years old, and has just been sold into slavery. He becomes the servant of a temple in East Taria, a generic Asian country, and the personal attendant of Miyon, a young girl perpetually clad in a veil. The reason for that is the titular Cursed Sight: Miyon cannot look directly at someone without causing their death. In an exchange of sorts, Miyon received the power of prophecy: through ritual, she can see the future. Anything further than those details constitutes a rather extreme spoiler, considering the brief length of the game.
The game's arguably biggest flaw, such as it is, is its divisive protagonist. Gai is one of those rare children in fiction who acts his age, and as a result is kind-of a brat. Self-centered, constantly sarcastic, and hopelessly blunt, Gai makes for a narrator character with a keenly defined personality. That personality, however, can be rather offputting. Gai does develop some over the course of the novel, but his self-centered nature and sarcasm never go away. If that's going to turn you away from the story's strong points, so be it.
The second biggest "flaw" is not a flaw so much as a natural consequence of how the game was designed. If you go into visual novels hoping to make a lot fo plot-altering decisions, this isn't one of those games. There are a handful of endings, all branching off from clearly designated route splits, while otherwise the player is on-rails, acting as Gai, not a generic player cipher who would be more malleable.
Also, have to give points to the developer for giving the game a "timeline" feature of sorts to make it easy to jump to the branching points that do exist. A lot of visual novels would be greatly improved by such a mechanic, so seeing such a small one pull it off is encouraging.
The art that exists is well-done, while the music falls squarely under the category of "effective but forgettable". The characters are relatively well developed given the limited time allotted by the game. While it may not be the most lengthy or complex experience on the visual novel market, Cursed Sight tells its story well enough and memorably enough to be worth giving a chance. Check it out.

This is the most fun I've ever had with a beat 'em up.
Streets of Fury EX certainly doesn't have the ambiance of Dungeons & Dragons: Chronicles of Mystara, or the soundtrack of Streets of Rage, or the visuals of Capcom's Alien vs Predator.
But what the game lacks in artistic and techincal prowess, it makes up for with its zany humour, large cast of playable characters, and awesome gameplay depth.
Each character feels very unique, and though a few can feel underpowered, they're still interesting in their own right. The combo system is super flexible - way more than I ever expected! Worth mentioning as well, a few internet and fighting game community figures are playable characters! Most of them are popular in France (this is a French game after all), like Mr Quaraté, Yamato and Bob Lennon, but you'll probably recognize Benzaie from the That Guy With The Glasses website. A friend of mine and I tripped across this while looking for hilariously bad games on XBox Indies.  We started off laughing our asses off at the character sprites that looked like they were made by a few friends getting together on a Saturday with a camera or reading the bizarre character bios and backstories.  But then we found ourselves genuinely hooked on the combo happy multiplayer.  After finishing the demo we actually ponied up for the full version and played it all weekend.
Fast forward to 2016 when I noticed Streets of Fury EX randomly on Steam.  I wasted no time picking it up (and immediately  notifying my friend from before).  This "EX" version is largely the same as the XBox version, but it adds more content and higher resolution assets.
The game itself is a beat em up that takes a lot of queues from Guardian Heroes on the Sega Saturn.  You and your opponents shift between three vertical planes.  You'll be tasked with punching out scores of bad guys using one of a roster of characters that all look pretty much like normal people in their street clothes.  But just like Guardian Heroes you can easily pull off ridiculous combos by stringing together elaborate-but-easy-to-pull-off moves.  Lots of launching, air combos, juggling, and crowd controlling AOEs.  Inputs are simple and once you have the basics down you can be racking up combos in the hundreds in no time.  With up to 4 players going at it at the same time, things can get absolutely bananas.
So the gameplay is fun (though not necessarily perfectly balanced) but the presentation is definitely what got its hooks in me.  It's all very low budget and none of the "actors" look particularly menacing.  Bosses are usually just regular mobs that are scaled bigger or tinted a different color.  This may all sound unimpressive but it adds to the game's charm: it's clearly a low budget effort from a small team, but the game emulates the fun of Guardian Heroes exceptionally well.  The game can eventually get repetitive with a limited number of backgrounds and characters, but I say for those that know what they're getting into it's a hugely fun time.

Oneshot is one of the most intriguing Adventure/Puzzle games I have ever played. Like Undertale, the game has a unique way of interacting with the player in both gameplay and story. And while the game is pretty short, taking me only 4 hours for my first play through, the story and characters stayed in my thoughts days after my playthrough of it.
In Oneshot, you guide a child named Niko on his quest to restore a world's long dead sun and hopefully return him home. The story is well told with great characters and writing that makes you care about the world and it's inevitable fate. The game does a great job at involving the player
Overall, the story and characters are strong and it was enjoyable all the way through.
The gameplay of Oneshot focused mainly on puzzles and exploration. Like most adventure games, a lot of the puzzles involves using or combining items in order to move on. All of these puzzles are simple and makes logical sense.
These puzzles really impressed me and I have to applaud the developers for their excellent use of these elements.
From the great story and interesting puzzles Oneshot is a fun and unique experience. If you were a fan of Undertale, I would highly recommend that you play this game. It is truly a very unique and unforgettable experience.

I would give this game something between a thumbs up and a thumbs down because I do like some aspects of the game.  However, they force me to make a black & white choice and I choose "No Way".  The graphics are pretty good, the basic gameplay is OK but there are a lot of issues:
1.  There are places on the maps you can get stuck and not be able to get out of AND you cannot kill yourself to continue playing the game!  You have to leave the game altogether and rejoin (if you can).
2.  There is no way to kick or ban a player on your own server DURING the game ...you have to wait for the game to be over!  This is the ONLY thing you can do to protect yourself and it isn't even in-the-moment or real-time!
3.  Rampant cheating via engineered hacking/aimbot/God-mode programs ruin any opportunity for the expectation of fair play.  I feel as though I have left more games than I have finished because of these jerks.  I wish them all a horrible painful death in the real world.  They have collectively stolen the money we have invested in this game and Steam does nothing to stop it.  Indeed, the cheaters occasionally talk about such things and defend their own actions on the Discussion channels and you never see a Steam moderator step in and take any action.  They have left us to the wolves.
4.  The "game-view" or "sight-view" (what you see vs. what the enemy sees) is really screwed up.  I can be inside a tunnel with no view of the enemy yet he can see me and kill me.  How is that fair?  My arms and legs aren't hanging out, I am OUT OF SIGHT and even this is no defense.  Being out-of-sight is not even considered stealthy in a game that is BUILT on concept of stealth?
5.  There is no way to configure your own server for "Pistols-Only", "No Pistols" or anything else that would allow different styles of play or game modes for variety.  Every server and every map is largely identical with few deviations.  It quickly  becomes boring.
6.  Character movement and control is full of inconsistencies... in some places you cannot go prone for no aparent reason.  Where you can go prone, while you are crawling on your belly you may encounter a flat board or step in the ground.  Crawling across this change in terrain causes you to STAND UP!  Instant death in many circumstances.  Other places with boards or terrain changes this doesn't happen and you pass right through them.  In some places you cannot go prone, but if you hit "Crouch" it instantly goes prone instead.  VERY inconsistent on a portion of the game that SHOULD be rock-solid in its second version.
7.  Cheaters/hackers/banned players can just make up a new name and continue playing.  How does this help the integrity of the game?  There is no way to stop them and the game LETS them get away with it for as long as they want.
The game was fun when I first started but now is only occasionally fun and the more I play the more frustrated I get.  There are far too many problems, not enough players, too many cheaters and there is NO support from the developer or this provider so I have decided to stop buying ANY more games like this.  Little quality control or standards seem to be applied and the user pays the price.

Lovely planet is a fiendishly difficult first person shooter puzzle platformer, designed with speedrunners in mind.
I went into it expecting expecting a pretty hard challenge, but I had to grind later levels A LOT. So, if you strive to get 100% achievements in your games, think twice about getting that one.
Options:
Seems like game was designed for gamepad first, which shows in simplicity of options menu. But it does seems to have everything that is required, so no harm done there.
Visuals:
Game was designed to look like a PS2 era cel-shaded game, which devs successfully pull off.
Some visual could be better redesigned or cut out to better suit game for speedrunning purposes, but it looks like adding some unnecessary details was a deliberate choice on developer side.
Overall very solid in this part.
Sound:
Music is nice, though maybe unremarkable. Sound effects are alright, if a bit annoying after some time.
Looks like less polish went into this part.
Story:
Not much story to speak of. Developers didn't want players to concentrate on the story, so they put all flavor text in japanese and spread it around the levels.
Controls and Gameplay:
I played game with mouse and keyboard, so your results may vary.
Game boasts pretty tight and responsive controls. Your character moves, shoots, and changes direction very fast, allowing for some pretty cool movement.
Game starts pretty slow, but picks up the pace very fast, and keeps throwing new mechanics at you, not being afraid to combine them for very difficult sections.
This is the meat of the game. Sound and looks are superficial, and there is next to none story. But difficult levels will put your skills of as an FPS player to the test.
Overall: if you are not afraid of the challenge, you can pick this one up. Otherwise - steer away clear.

Also the voice we hear a lot about Shepard's memories feels sometimes absurd as it didn't reveal almost nothing relevant about the gameplay or the in-game story plot, it was kind of annoying too and I only can think that the purpose of it was to engage the gamers and ask for a sequel of the story, which I have my doubts and personally I wouldn't like to play nor even purchase the sequel -If sometime comes out-, after I played this one.
In conclusion I can say my overall feeling is just OK, but I really feel this product would have been better launched as a free mod instead of a retail game on its own. I'd say the balance between price and enjoyment, nevertheless is quite subjective, in my opinion that balance is not right at all, I mean here we have a very expensive product and really a very random modification for HL2. So it's not very worthy to purchase or spend some money on this one.... You know BM really worth’s what you play for it but this one not at all. And even the fantastic and very immersive Cry of Fear would be worthy to pay for it but even that great master piece is absolutely free.
Also I have this very annoying "A.I. Disable" bug that made me began some chapters from scratch more than once!!!! And as far as I know the developer couldn't fix it properly yet. So be warned about that.
So finally I can say, being an experienced mod gamer -I've played more than 200 mods in my personal record and review more than 150- This could have been better released as a free mod rather than have to spend some money on it. So my advice to his developer is just to learn from this experience and if he wants to launch some more products please do it in the big HL2 modding community, you could definitely would learn a lot from it and even be a better designer.

As a die-hard HL-fanboy I had to have this one ... Bought it with -50% and didn't regret it! First of all: I think the problem most people have with this game is the price-tag ... Other mods (worse mods) don't get that much hate, cause they're for free - just my theory. Now to the hard facts ... Spoiler alert!
PROS:
- Adrian "Mothereffin" Shephard (best sidekick in the HL-universe besides Alyx imo)
- You instantly get the typical HL-feeling
- Music is great, especially the cues are really well placed
- Sound is really neat (no wonder cause mostly original from HL2)
- New soundeffects and voice overs are very well done - voice actors did a good job
- Graphics ... no complaints here - great lighting/shadows/effects (sometimes a little bit too dark, flashlight is essential)
- Great atmosphere overall (maybe because of the darkness haha joking aside: great (!) atmosphere)
- Cool story bits here and there, especially cool link to the original OF (audio flashbacks)
- Some cool little puzzles (unfortunately most of them are at the beginning of the game)
- Nice enemy encounters, good variation, nice flow to the game
- GMAN jump scare ... got me hooked at the beginning
- Xen! (Spoiler?)
- Nice twist in Leveldesign later in the game... The earth looks cool from space (Spoiler?)
- The orbital sector-idea was fresh
- Some nice little easter-eggs... I spotted an Aperture Science logo in close proximity to a portal, that was neat!
- Drunk garden gnomes! (Easter-egg spoiler?)
- Nice little details here and there
- No technical problems at all, game ran smoothly till the end (played it October 2016)
- Artistic feel to the game, you can sense the dedication of the developer (Cheers to Richard at this point! Respect!)
- Well its Adrian Shephard so... he's cool
- And don't forget the GMAN... he's also cool
CONS:
- Leveldesign is too straight forward, you often have the feeling that you're running through a pipe with nothing happening
- Some parts feel a bit unimaginative, just run and gun ...
- Major game design flaws: You get overwhelmed with health-items very often and enemies spawn like rats - feels like a railshooter sometimes
- It's called Prospekt, but as far as I'm concerned it was waaaaaay too little Nova Prospekt and too much of Combine vanilla
- Did I say too little prison-action? Well it's worth 2 cons imo, because that's really bothering me
- Wasted potential: No prisoners (except two or three dead Vortigaunts), no prison daily routine, no sight of Gordon Freeman (although what I know it starts when Gordon is also in Nova Prospekt)
- No real P.C.V. (maybe with update)
- Enemy A.I. felt a bit dumber than in HL2
- Story felt a bit meaningless at the end ("bossfight" was more confusing than challenging)
- Crowbar as the melee weapon? WTF? Why no pipe wrench? Strange, strange ...
- No new weapons... at all (at least I expected new skins for standard weapons from HL2)
- Way too little headcrab/zombie-action... if I remember correctly, there's only one zombie in the entire game, besides soldier-zombies
- The dominant colors in this game are orange and blue... and I mean DOMINANT, just look at the screens
- Way too many electrical lights, no sunshine at all in the game (not really a CON but ...)
- Too many assets from HL2 (I get it, it's a mod - but at least new skins would be great!)
- I really don't get the stealth bonus maps ... there's no real stealth mechanic in my opinion ... just Pac-Man in first person
- Once again: It's called Prospekt and for me there wasn't enough Prospekt
So my conclusion is: If you're a HL-fan, just buy it ... support a dedicated/passionate developer and it's more of the universe you love (even if it's not canon... just pretend it is)! If you're just interested because it looks cool and stuff ... play Half-Life 2, HL2: Episode 1 and 2, then Half-Life 1, HL: Opposing Force and Blue Shift and if you don't have enough with that go buy a copy of Prospekt!

Second Contact is the product of a developer who loved their game so much that they wouldn’t take no for an answer. After a failed Kickstarter to fund a full and proper remake, Appeal went ahead and did it anyway.
The original Outcast was a pain to get working right on modern hardware, so Appeal revamped the engine and Outcast v1.1 was born. Not only looking better, the 1.1 revamp added further drawing distances, controller support, achievements, cards, and other Steam-centric features. This revamp was to pave the way for a full and proper remake.
But it didn’t happen.
The new sales could not outweigh the monumental costs of a true and proper remake. Despite the setback, Appeal forged ahead and partnered with publisher Bigben to make Second Contact a reality.
And here we are today.
Second Contact is a painstaking recreation of the original ported into the Unity engine. Fans of the original will note several points when they fire it up. First is the intro. No longer an animated sequence, we now have a flash animation of the story. Disappointing? Yes. Necessary? Also yes. The only available video is painfully low res, and you can’t just wrap sugar around a turd and call it candy.
Next up you will find the audio is the same, this is a blessing and a curse. I was not looking forward to some low-rent voice actor either mimicking David Gasman’s Cutter Slade or straying completely from him, so I was happy to hear the original sound. Well, almost.
It seems the original voice files are either of very low quality, or missing completely and had to be re-sampled. The clipping and artifacting of the sound bytes can be difficult to endure, especially when you still have the amazing Lennie Moore soundtrack in glorious hi-def. This could be mitigated through volume sliders, if Second Contact had any.
The next contention to be made is the dearth of options in the video and audio department. Only the basics are available, and Appeal has promised to address this. Unity can be a finicky engine to get running smoothly for some hardware, SLI users for example, but Appeal is currently working hard on the first patch. Looking back at the love that Outcast v1.1 received, this is surely only the beginning.
Appeal has also taken some creative license in the worlds recreation. Okaar for instance no longer has its leafy autumn feel, it now wears Shamazaar’s trappings instead. I have yet to complete the remake, so I can’t comment on more at this time, but if I had to guess - I'd say this is all part of the same problem.
Many of these issues that people are taking with this remake seem to stem from one thing – a lack of money. If that were not the case, could they have re-recorded all the dialogue, re-created the intro sequence in CG, and taken the time to reinvigorate the biomes of Outcast? Absolutely. Would they have lost the magic in the process? Possibly. Would it make it a better game? No, absolutely not.
Some of the things that make Outcast such an endearing memory are the janky movement, jumping, and general traversal of the landscape. Like Resident Evil’s tank controls, these features are part of the charm. Appeal has painstakingly recreated this experience for a reason. You are meant to explore, converse, and wrap yourself in the beauty of Outcast’s world. Turning the game into a first person shooter would completely trample that experience and had they done so back in 1999, no one would be remembering it fondly today.
This is a worthy remake, despite the people that don’t seem to get it. It doesn’t replace the original, and it's not meant to. Second Contact is a revisit to that place you got lost in years ago. Stop comparing and just enjoy the ride.

The concept of Evolve really intrigued me last year.  However, when 2K implemented the worst DLC system known to man kind in a PAID 60 DOLLAR GAME I wouldn't touch it with a 300 foot pole.
Well, 2K has decided to go with Turtle Rock's original plan to have a F2P title.  This, currently, is the BEST f2p system I have ever seen implemented in any game.  I am VERY careful about f2p titles, because so many are "pay to win".  Well, (in it's current state) there are absolutely ZERO ways to buy currency or advance in any way.  It is all through in game unlocks.  However, if you own the game prior you will unlock most of the characters and monsters.  I actually purchased the game from a key site for 6 bucks after playing about an hour I loved it so much.  But back to the F2P system.  You play matches to unlock in game currency to in turn purchase characters and skins with.  After doing the 2 tutorials you will unlock one monster and one character right off the bat.  There is also a free rotation weekly like most f2p games.  I am sure that 2K and TR will add a shop with real money at some point, but even then there is no "OP" pay to win class.  All of them are quite balanced.  Now on to the gameplay.
This is a 150% different game.  I was extremely skeptical after first hearing about the new move to f2p but it is clear TR took the games flaws and really worked on fixing them.  First off, they added a "dome" ability for every class.  This recharges in match and can trap the monster in an impenetrable dome for a small amount of time.  This makes combat MUCH more fast paced and fun.  Instead of hunting the monster for half the game this makes it way more approachable.  They have also removed half the maps and only have 4 extremely well crafted arena type levels.  Along with this only Hunt is the current playable game mode, which is the best and most competetive as to not split up the community.  Now, graphics.
The graphics have had a huuuuuuge overhaul and are absolutely GORGEOUS, I have a GTX 1070 and can max everything and have a steady 140 fps on my 144 hz display.
All in all, this is an absolutely unprecedented move by a AAA publisher and I really hope this game takes off as I am having the time of my life.  I am so thankful Turtle Rock had the opportunity to make the game the way THEY wanted it to be made.
Go ahead, give it a go.  After all, it is free :)

But, there appears to have been more effort put into this than into some Steam games that expect to be taken seriously. (The creators of which expect them to be taken seriously. Y'know what I meant.)
The "build the game to drive players to the cash store with glitter and cattle prods" design trend has gotten very old, and deserves the poke in the eye with a shiny, lootbox-skinned stick that this little game gives it. So, thumbs up for that. And all flippancy aside, things like the name of the first tier of lootboxes may be cheap laughs (along with the previously mentioned sarcastic snorts), but I'll take 'em. I can use all the laughs I can get!

This review will have 2 parts: joke review and serious review
First, the joke review (which is a not recommended):
Great game; it recreates the loot box controversy well.
HOWEVER; I cannot recommend it. Why? Because if this game wants to be a perfect satire, it has to cost $60. If it isn't $60 and has exploitative lootboxes it is meaningless.
11/10 GOTY IGN
And now my actual thoughts:
I Can't Believe It's Not Gambling (ICBING) is a satirical game about lootboxes in videogames and how ridiculous the increase of monetization of customers has been. The goal is to open lootboxes with a fake currency and collecting skins for your lootboxes. To earn more cash you have to play a snake clone called Not BF2 where you play as a whale collecting lootboxes (looks like it's pisstaking actual designs, I recognise the Overwatch one). Earning coins is easy enough with this minigame but when you're done you get to open more lootboxes. Which after a while becomes addictive. You open box after box, celebrate when you see a legendary colour dropping only to be disappointed when you get another damn repeat. Selling the skins makes up for a bit of the cost, but of course if you get common after common you'll have to resort to Not BF2 to earn more.
My main complaint is that the devs could have done a bit more with earning coins. To be a bit more realistic playing it could give next to nothing unless you grind like mad, and you could "pay" for more coins. A simple buy currency button that guilt trips you whenever you click it. Something like that. (and by a button I mean clicking it gives you coins without a enter card number interface at all)
However the best part about ICBING is that it might POSSIBLY be an exit drug should someone with a real gambling addiction gets into lootboxes. By buying the game that person might be able to use this to fulfil the urge while seeking help. Which is what it is at the end of the day. ICBING is hilarious, but it should be a reminder that publishers are attempting to get more dolla dolla bills by exploiting a common human weakness, and that is a major♥♥♥♥♥♥move. And shows that when the AAA games industry crashes, we should have no sympathy.
As for how good it is as a game, it's a dollar, and even though this game isn't winning any awards anytime soon, it's decent fun for that price.
Recommended.

OneShot is an Story-Driven puzzle adventure game made in RPGMaker
Originally released in 2014 as a freeware experimental game with it's main draw being the one shot mechanic, Closing the game would kill the main character and render the game permanently unplayable, unless you had a little technical know-how to completely clear the games data.
The game was expanded upon and later released onto Steam on December 9th 2016. The expanded version adds new story elements, upgrades graphics, simplifies menu's and also removes the one shot mechanic, closing the game now just makes a quick save, however the game does try to make you feel bad for doing so, but it also doesn't seem to mean much in the long run.
Oneshot begins with a small Neko like character named Niko waking up in a strange dark house, after solving a few simple puzzles Niko will find a large lightbulb that just suddenly begins to glow in his hands, after some more wandering around  he comes across a robot who informs him that this strange world's sun went missing some time ago, and in the all consuming darkness the world started to slowly come to an end, but all is not lost, because the lightbulb that Niko found is the new sun, and Niko is the messiah who will save the world with the god of this world's guidance, aka you! Niko can communicate directly with the player to help him in his pilgrimage to to return the worlds sun.
The main gameplay loop of oneshot is exploring the dystopian appocalyptc world solving puzzles and trying to figure out how to progress further on your journey. Most puzzles are standard advenure game deals, combine items, interacting with certain items, but occassionally Niko will come across computer terminals, interacting with these computer terminals will let you interact with The Entity, another god-like being who seems to know more than he's letting on,  the entity will give you anwers to certain puzzles, usually by interacting with you outside of the game, there aren't very many of these fourth wall breaking puzzles in the game, but the ones that are here range from pretty basic to kind of mind-blowing in the second half. The game is fairly easy throughout in fact I ended up having the hardest times with puzzles in the first main area.
If I were to describe Oneshot in two words, they would be 'adorably sad'. The game has a gloomy hopeless tone, many characters you meet seem to be of the impression that the world is beyond or not even worth saving and most of them  seem to have accepted that they're going to die. That being sadid Main character Niko is an adorable bundle of joy who wants to save the world even if he isn't really cut out for the job. Despite the game's grim tone I would normally liken to Dark Souls, the game isn't shy of having a few more humorous moments.
The story does leave many unanswered questions by it's end however  the developers hint that in the future we may get an update that adds more story content and answers the unanswered questions, as the game is currently however it is certainly a complete story, you could play it now and be perfectly satisfied..
Oneshot is definitely worth your time, if your a little apprehensive about parting with your money for the steam version, give the free version a try first, just remember.

I recommend this game to anyone with a friend or two, and a love for solving puzzles however the hell they deem fit. This game, and the Trine series at large, have a wonderful take on solving puzzles, which is one of a surprisingly freeing laissez faire, they leave you an entire kit of tools at your disposal, and ask you to use them as you see fit, and as a result me and my good friend broke a lot of the puzzles in what were clearly unintended solutions, having a blast doing so.
This game is also rocking the pretty in a big bad way, if you're anything like me, you'll find yourself stopping at various points just to admire the scenery or the unusual flora and fauna that populate it. Even the things that really aren't there to be interacted with at all have a certain care in their design you rarely see even in large budget games.
Two things though, this game is short, shorter feeling than the others in the series, even, so if you're looknig for 60 hours, this isn't for you, and it ended abruptly and unsatisfyingly, leaving it feeling like half a game. I get the feeling there was the intention to do more, but it got held over for another game, These are pretty bad sticking points, but they don't make the overall product not a worthwhile experience.
I feel I should also address the 3D perspective issue that a lot of people seem to have. Some of the anger I've seen over this I feel can be attested to just the series deviating from it's expected status quo by eschewing the 2D puzzle feel, and I didn't consider it much harder to control, and never really felt myself losing grip on where I was in the depth of field, but I could see a genuine case being made against it, as occasionally there were some frustrating moments with sliding something onto a switch or panel in three-dimensional space. It allowed for the inclusion of some pretty cool puzzles as well though, like moving Zoya's rope around posts and the like to tie things together, and still felt mostly very well thought out.
Overall even though it has it's problems and it just kind of ends, I still had a really good time playing, and I wouldn't want to rob anyone of that by not recommending it.
