A decent indie title bogged down by largely beginner mistakes.
The premise and presentation is interesting. You play as an explorer robot named ION who crashlands on a planet that is rich with resoures and you need to survive and find a way to phone home(roll credits). The game certainly has personality, the character designs are pretty neat, a cross between Wall-E, Star Wars and ET most of the time. Your ship has a personality that brings a lot of Portal characters to mind and while not entirely original, it is one of the better takes on the humorless, business centered, arrogant robot companion archetypes and he is one of the games highlights. Especially when you find and repair another ship with a completely opposite personality and the 2 starts bickering. The companion robot, ANI whom you find later is a bit cliche'd. A feminine talkatative and somewhat impish robot who instantly falls in love with you. imagine if Wall-E was female and EVA male and that's pretty much their releationship. except ION is silent. At least they have an in-game excuse for this in that his speech chip is supposedly damaged, but still. Seeing ANI make several attempts at romanticising someone who can't even respond was initially cute, but after a while it became almost sad. overall, pretty good setup and characters.
Now the gameplay is a mixed bag.  it IS a survival game so crafting and maintenance galore. the game isn't too stingy with crafting items and you do have a compass that shows you nearby items. ION isn't too hard to maintain either, even though he has 3 needs, fuel for rocket thrusters, power for sprinting, using weapons and staying alive and hull damage, maintaining them isn't too hard, they last a decent amount of time and items for restoring them are fairly abundant. i haven't had any issues there yet. however, when you find ANI, you not only have to repair her when damaged(no power or fuel needs, thank god) but she does corrode and you do need to make coatings for her to prevent that. and you want to because if she corrodes, her movement slows to a crawl and to my knowledge you can't undo corrision! and she doesn't do enough to warrant your attention. she can fight, but other than that, she is basically an escort mission. she can't teleport to you if she falls too far back, if a sandstorm appears. you need to find shelter or constantly craft coatings for her and you need her to progress. why can't she find random crafting items for you, perhaps give you fuel or power or teleport closer if she gets too far away, just something to make her more self reliant. how could she ever think she could even survive on the planet, if she was smart she would have stayed on her ship.
Combat is fairly basic, fire a relatively slow moving projectile at usually slow moving enemies, movement is pretty good overall, the thruster is a bit wonky as it only seems to add upward momentum, aka don't use it if sliding because you will keep your momentum, a forward thruster would be great could have speed up the slow walking too. which reminds me, the walking is slow. it feels like the world is large and characters slow specifically to pad out the gameplay. note to indie devs, don't do that. most pc gamers already have a library filled with unfinished games due to a lack of time to play them. a short and sweet game is much better than a long sluggish one. fortunately, the devs are aware and have increased sprint speed slightly, but ideally there should be an upgrade or a forward thruster that significantly speeds you up.
The gameplay has a good framework but isn't handled as well as it should. i'd love to see a sequel or a redux where all of these issues are fixed because there really is a good survival game hidden in there somewhere.
as far as graphics and audio go, there's no issues. i've heard people complain about it being hard to run, i'm rocking a gtx 1080 and playing at 4K max with a near locked 60fps so i don't see any issues. but i'm also rocking the 2nd best video card right now period so. graphics themselves are well polished. not the best of the bunch, but art is quite coherent and some particles really impress. sound effects are also very pleasant, impressively so for an indie title. now graphics options are fairly basic. so is input options. gamepad support is shoehorned in there and just kinda works. it plays best with M\K.
I think in summary, this is a potential indie gem that has it's appeal already, but a few dumb decisions, especially mid game, holds it back. Fortunately, the beginning 2 hours is a good taste of what the game has to offer so you can safely refund quite fast if you don't quite feel like it's up your alley. The devs have done a good job listening to feedback and patching, but i think a redux of sorts is needed to really leverage the game's potential. it's a recommend from me, but a cautious  one. I nonetheless wish the devs good luck in the future, i think they have potential

I can't recommend this game in it's current condition. There's a decent game in there somewhere, but it has serious balancing and control problems that make it a frustrating experience, especially in the later stages of the game. Lack of a map means you'll spend a lot of time wandering around the desert section looking for the single trail which leads to the top of each of the 3 mountains where the mission goals are located. Insufficient crafting materials that do not respawn means that you'll spend a lot of time trying to find essential items in the large levels going only by the jumble of monotone icons on the HUD. Nightime lasts far too long and I found myself simply waiting in cover (to protect the robot companion with which you are lumbered and which has all the durability of a dead slug) until daybreak. The single greatest problem is that you have to keep your robot companion in perfect shape through the entire game because you won't find out until it's too late that if it's armor or corrosion levels drop below certain levels they cannot be brought back up to 100%. The companion's speed decreases as corrosion levels increase so it lags further and further behind which means you can't keep a close eye on it's health while trying to find enough crafting materials for the both of you. You'll need a lot of those crafting materials due to the constant attacks by the various nasties the game world contains and for which your defensive measures are totally inadequate.
Since I've reached the point where I have to mostly carry the companion, I'm just going to leave the game unfinished and check periodically to see if they've fixed the problems. I'd like to finish the game but I have zero desire to start a new game. The story just isn't that interesting.

I was so excited for this release. I am a die hard outcast 1.1 fan, I even hold the world record speedrun time for the game. To hear that this was coming out was a dream come true. I bought it right away and started playing. What I found was less than satisfying. The audio imports are identical, the zones are accurate to the original and very beautiful to look at. But the beauty of the game does not compensate for how ABSOLUTELY CLUNKY IT IS.
Movement is awful. Cutter Slade handles like a drunk elephant. He will not sprint unless in a perfect and unobstructed straight line, he decides do dodge roll if and when he wants to with little prompting. The dodge roll only seems to roll me off of a surface into water or roll me straight into enemy fire. Useless to be honest. If I walk by an object or person that can be interacted with, even a door- cutter slade will slow down, look at the object or person and circle around it like magnetic attraction until he is a safe distance away from it then proceeds to run again.
Climbing is basically absent compared to the original, rarely does he climb to a surface i'd like him too, especially because jumping is the worst. Very clunky an uncomfortable to control. Many times I want to jump onto a boat or back onto land and instead Cutter decides he would rather dive headfirst into the dock.
The bugs in this game are almost endearingly and quantifiably similar to the original game, weird things happen like floating NPC's that I can no longer speak to, or reloading a save game only to find out it has caused and irreversible bug that does not allow further gameplay because an NPC will not appear. Etc. Etc. What a joy.
UI is decent, however controls are not customizable you are stuck with what you have and it is very limited.
Combat is very close to the original and a quite like it, there is an element of free look 'over the shoulder' that is nice.
I will continue to play this game, because it does yield some good things, but to be honest what hinders it the most (and an incredible amount) is the lack of control you have over your movement compared to the original game. In conclusion, this game is 2 steps forward, 3 steps back. I would love to see updates to many many things. I will spend most of my time back on Outcast 1.1.
(p.s., the beautiful autumnal feel of Okaar is scrapped for an identical tropical feel to shamazaar.)

EDIT: changed review to 'thumbs up'. Enjoy it too much. For some critizism (still true), see the rest of the post.
The original Outcast is one of the best three games I ever played.
This new version is still fun and deserves some good reviews. I would vote 'neutral' if possible. But the overall impression is they took out some 'magic' and replaced it with issues. What I mean is:
1.) Controls. The original controls were *responsive*. You changed between normel and combat mode seemlessly and it felt natural. Combat was fun. Now when you change movement direction in normal mode, Cutter is breaking, then slowly turning and accelerating towards the new direction. It feels odd and can be your death in combat. It feels like the controls are working against you. They introduced a roll to counter that, but it doesn't work reliably and isn't fun.
2.) Collision. You'll get stuck a lot. In some cases you can't even jump on small plateaus (30 cm). If jumping against an (invisible) wall, your jump height may be reduced to 10cm probably because of friction with the wall or whatever. Invisible collision boxes hinder you to  reach objects right in front of you.
3.) Your Twon Ha cannot jump anymore. So you'll always have to take the stairs in Shamazar even if you own one.
4.) Your Twon Ha is green on the map (instead of yellow like any other animal) just like any Talan, making it impossible to find. New map has improved alot, though. The 'scan map' effect is replaced by a sorry excuse effect. Takes -1000 from magic.
5.) The Shamaz healing spell effect looks like a fire magic particle effect right from the asset store. If doesn't follow you. In the Original it was a fun mini game to let the 'healing cloud' catch you. This is now gone. Does take away some magic.
6.) Talans look like humans now. Does take away some magic. But they have lipsync, which is cool. Though does not work 10% of the time.
7.) Conversations don't have an animated camera anymore, all is static now. Takes a lot of magic away.
8.) The 'dead body collision' bug is still in there.
9.) Accurate jumping is almost impossible. You'll have to jump much earlier than you might expect or you'll fall. Feels wrong.
10.) Melee combat doesn't work anymore. At least against a garmor. Didn't test against Talans.
I know the team switched to a new platform (Unity) and many bugs may be just because they don't use it correctly or didn't find a work around for it's issues. Some bugs might be because they probably use lots of premade assets from the store and didn't care to tweak them accordingly. Right now the game feels unpolished. I really hope they find the time and money to improve it.
Good luck guys!

My overall rating for Cursed Sight: 88/100
Another visual novel from the creator Invertmouse, this time set in medieval fantasy of two kingdoms, who are struggling for control over the world and the key to solve this is a cursed sight of one priestess named Miyon. Lets see in detail, what went good and what should be better.
GAMEPLAY
+ Nice timing of chapters
+ Animations
+ Multiple endings
- Some cruel moments
Chapters were timed perfectly, story was a bit cliché, but originally processed, what I count as a great plus for this title, due in time, when everything was discovered, original presentation is a key how to achieve a players attention. Also animations were fine, I am glad, that also multiple endings were positive feature, not just self-purpose.
But the moment with rabbit was very cruel and disturbing. I know, this was the purpose, but I think it might be avoided. Just personal opinion. :-D
CHARACTERS
+ Gai
+ Miyon
+ Sasa
+ Queen Hydrianne
o King Lok
- West Tarians
Gai was funny, but also I liked his saracsm, as a kid who was torn from his world and sent to slavery. Miyon was a typical spoiled brat, but when you went under her mask, you saw, what was the true reason behind her behaviours. I liked Sasa from the very start, she was as catalysator of other relationships and a mentor who would everyone desire to have. Positive character was also Queen Hydrianne, I think that is how a leader should behave.
King lok was neutral, I understand his pose, yet, the potential was not fully achieved. But West Tarians had their potentials a bit wasted, especially Gai's sister's companion, who was changing his appearance and poses too quickly and a bit cheaply.
VISUALS
+ Shoujo style
I liked, that this style was chosen, it fitted perfectly for the set-up and story. Nothing to complain here about.
SOUNDTRACK
+ Fitting the stiuation
+ Atmospheric
Efe Tozan did a great work composing those songs, I liked them and some of them I listen to even today. Songs were changing accordingly to the situation and atmosphere. Thumbs up here.
SUMMARY
Cursed sight has a rich story and no superheroes, what allows players to join them and enjoy, what authors presented to us. Even players out of this genre might find this novel interesting, as story is not disturbing, drawings are decent and atmosphere brilliant.
Recommended, also with extras.

Music was also great it made me feel the mood perfectly. I just wish the story was a bit longer but nonetheless all in all, Cursed Sight is a great VN.

(Excuse my english, i am no native, but i felt this review is better written in english, hope it helps!)
The first thing if have to say, that i dont like the direct comparism to the Souls Series. Its more often called "2D Dark Souls" then its called by its real name. Yes, its true that the game takes a lot of things from the Souls Franchise and its easy to see and say where the inspiritation came from. But it mixes it up with its own unique ideas wich make this game very special.

The 2D perspective and the controlls give this game the possiblity to use jump'n run mechanics and also some metroid or castlevania elements mixed up with pretty well working combat system wich wants to figured out by the player. The combat is challenging as it is in the Souls Series but it has its own flow coming from the faster movement of the players characer. The list of weapons and armor is large, there is a huge skill tree, many possibilites to build yor character.
The worlds in this game look amazing and beatiful, very detailed you can see that the devs loved what they did. There is a very unique vibe that you can feel while playing the game. Its all dark and sad, but in the same moment this sadness is broken up by the funny design they have choosen for your character and the npcs. The worlds dont equal each other and so do the bosses. There are various enemies, wich are all well designed mostly feel well placed and not just put there just to be there.
There are not many downsides for this game. In some situations the game is a bit unfair, cause you will die without having the chance to escape or win the fight. It takes some time to figure out the Sanctuary, Creed and weapon enforcement mechanics. Escpecially the Sanctuary/Creed thingy is a bit confusing. But thats all.
To put it in a nutshell: If you are a Souls-Fan like i am, you will love this game, if you like well planed and lovely designed 2D metroidvania games, you will love this game. If you like challenging hack'n slay with tactical combat, you will also love this game.

So I randomly stumbled across this when I was done with Dark Souls 3, and I was feeling a bit empty inside since I had few interesting things to play. Some fights can be a bit irritating, as large enemies have a tendency to push you back a lot, and even block you off from certain areas. My main irritation so far has been the boss fights, as the ones I've done so far (6 or 7) have been kind of lackluster. They start out with a set of moves, and progressively as the fight goes on, they just become faster. I'd much rather have phases in the fight, rather than linear difficulty progression, and adding new moves when you reach said phase would make it a lot more interesting.
That being said, I can definitely recommend this game if you enjoy combat-heavy metroidvania games, and liking the Souls series doesn't hurt.

This was a pleasant surprise in every sense of the word.
When you look at this, you probably want to laugh at how ridiculous this looks, yet how intriguing at its game play. In fact, I only bought this game because a friend of mine showed it to me one day. When he got me and a couple other friends together for a game, I was left impressed and amused. Naturally, I got curious enough to want to get the game now.
What can be said about this? Well you really cannot do any worse for $10. For $10, you get two campaign modes, five levels each, a good cast of playable characters with their own combo strings to discover, four player cooperative and competitive play, a few other games modes thrown in for good measure, you get enough to justify the price, yet it feels like a huge treat to me.
Maybe I'm being too favorable to it, so let me make it simple:
-Do you enjoy beat em ups?
-Do you enjoy fighting games?
-Do you still find digitized sprites to be charming?
-Do you plan on getting some friends together for some games?
-Do you enjoy something that's simple to figure out yet complex to master?
-Do you grow tired of beat em ups with RPG stats like I have?
You will find enjoyment in this game. I never regretted it, and there is a good chance that neither will you.

Imagine you're in North West England, it's late at night and it's freezing cold in the middle of winter. The pubs have all closed so there's animals wandering around mindlessly. Make sure you dress warmly and grab the nearest knife you can find  because every living thing wants to fight you. Suddenly someone or I should say some THING approaches you barking like a wild dog, what do you do? Well if you don't have a knife you're buggered and should get out of there asap, but assuming you have a knife scream "COME EEED" go in for a good old scrap and make sure to stab them multiple times.
After you've roughed them up you're probably going to bleeding pretty badly, so take your shirt off and use it to bandage the wound. Under normal circustances I'd tell you to go to the hospital, but since the conservative government keeps making cuts to the NHS I wouldn't recommend it.
Make sure to take all their stuff and make your way to the nearest dump you call home. Take a load off, reflect on all of your great accomplishments you've made that night and end your day with a dodgy meal with undercooked meat riddled with parasites. Medicine is scarce because of the NHS so you'll have to try and make yourself better with some shifty looking mushrooms and a nice cup of tea.
The next day you'll wake up feeling like death and the cycle begins all over again.

Overall, I recommend playing OneShot. While it didn't resonate with me like "Undertale" did (which I admit is a tall order), it was a pleasant experience with a unique game mechanic and a relaxing athmosphere. Given that it cost me the same amout as a movie ticket, it game me five hours of good entertainment. So, I cosider it well worth the price.
The drawback to the game was that it requires the player to become invested with the story and have the characters resonate with them or it falls flat. Which they didn't for me. While they weren't badly written or annoying, there just wasn't enough to the characters to make them compelling and they all lacked a defined identity. I could see all of the elements there, but they either weren't given enough time to connect or their identities didn't extend beyond the character's appearance. In the later parts of the game, the bizzare character appearances were jarring and seemed completely out of place versus everything that I've exerienced up to that point. The characters designs were more grounded and defined by the area, but the later part of the game just seemed to turn to random objects as character heads. Finally, I found that the main character Niko, was bordering on saccharine. I understand why it was designed that way as Niko was supposed to be a child and they were following a "chibi" art-style, but there were times where the maple-syrup was laid on a bit thick (see what I did there).
On the other hand, the game has an enjoyable, striking, and simple art-style. I enjoyed the world and the design of everything within in. The bold colours, the play of light and dark, and the designs of buildings, characters, and the cut scenes were warm and welcoming. I certainly applaud the designers for that. I also enjoyed the simple music and sound effects. They were effective for what they were to represent and pleasant to listen to. I enjoyed the primarily piano score as it was relaxing and soothing at many times. The music also helped to convey the feelings of the scene effectively without being heavy-handed. I also enjoyed the climax of the game as it was a unique meta-game moment that I haven't experienced before. While I find digging through game files as annoying at times, this was tolerable and the ending was an effective and memorable idea.

------------------------------
You should note that since the devs fell short of their initial kickstarter goal, some corners have been cut for the release of this product. There's no doubt that they'll keep improving it further with patches in due time, so take into account dates of reviews when reading them.
Review:
Outcast is a game of fancy concepts. The game is full of interesting ideas that truly reflect its own era and the type of innovativeness games used to strive for before the entire industry turned into "familiar makes money".
This game does Bioware/Bethesda style dialog and story telling in a 3D RPG (In 1999!) where your choices affect the local's opinions of you and their attitude. What you say to them has an effect, what you do them or others has an effect. You'll need to tread carefully and diplomatically if you don't want to be left alone and scolded by everyone.
During the opening of the game you'll be told the backstory to this small field trip. It's done in stylized minimalistic animation. The original had a full 3D animation, but it looks dated now so I guess they opted for this instead. Some may not like it, but don't get put off by it. It works.
When you start the game proper you will be thrust into a sort of tutorial area. The game is EXTREMELY story heavy, so if you have the time, do listen all the things they will tell you about the world. You will also need to complete 4 tutorial challenges, which are short and easy. You'll also receive gear and a saving crystal. This item can be used at nearly anytime to save your game, but if you use it near enemies, they might hear you save the game and come rushing towards you with guns blazing. This is simply one of my favorite concepts in the game.
After tutorial you will be thrust into the world proper, but I won't spoil anymore! Find out for yourself. Now, onto technical review:
The game is absolutely gorgeus. Hell, even the original is still gorgeus but this just takes that and makes it even better! I love it. The soundtrack, in 1999, was unusual because it was recorded by a real live orchestra! They kept that in this remaster and it still sounds amazing. Other sound affects, as well as dialog, is directly ripped. Unfortunately, I don't think they had access to the old lossless soundfiles, which makes all speeches sound a bit dated. But honestly, that's just nitpicking. It didn't bother me at all while playing.
The options menu is barebones. You can pretty much change gameplay settings, language, difficulty, controls and quality of graphics (with only 1 setting for graphics). For me this wasn't a problem, but the lack of audio settings and console controller remapping is definitely an issue. I think this will be fixed in a patch later on. Speaking of audio, there is no surround sound. Definitely patch stuff.
I've played the game with an Xbox controller. It feels good, a little odd. Buttons are weird, but workable. The camera is a bit wonky but nothing that detracts from the experience too much.
Movement is slightly clunky. Sometimes surfaces you feel like you should be able to move on might only allow you to go in one direction, among some other oddities. This is probably due to porting the original game code to a new engine. Which, by the way, might mean that some age old bugs are still around. It's very likely that the devs will release a patch soon which will address some more popular issues.
Overall, this game is very good. If you're used to modern video games you might have a harder time adjusting, but if you want to experience the 90's with a shiny new skin, this game is all you need. It is still a very good RPG, story and mechanics wise, which is a testament of the uniqueness of this game and it's ability to stand up to time.
I applaud the devs for doing this despite the failed kickstarter, and hell, I am really happy that they succeeded with doing this and I'm so happy that I may finally finish what I started as a kid while admiring the gorgeus world of Adelpha. The patches will only make it even better.
Here's hoping for a sequel!

Ok, so I got like zero game time in on this, however I got nearly 20 hours on the Outcast 1.1 and probably 50+ on the original that I still have on disc including the box.
With that said, I know what to expect game wise. I've played it over and over enough times and love this game. I came obviously for the graphic improvements, sound, updated controls, and obviously a newer interface. Let's review that shall we?
Graphics are stunning. I don't care what anyone says regarding some low res textures for the interiors mostly. That was obvious in the original and while I don't think they are trying to pay a homage to that here, the game is primarily outdoors so the interiors should never be distracting enough like that. They do have enough little details littered about inside and there is zero load time. You literally walk in and out of a structure as you please. Aside from that gripe that others may have mentioned, the characters detail, shading, and animations are all solid. I'm highly satisified with them all around and think a lot of people are going to be blown away the second you leave the starting snow region.
Sound is an interesting one. The game had amazing sound to begin with. From the sound of walking and crunching the snow, to the splash of the water when you swim around, it's almost like you are there. I don't however feel like they truly updated it in HD/HQ though. It's like the exact same files were used. Again, I'm not sure that is a bad thing because the original to this day has some amazing sound effects that compete with whatever is out. Even the voice acting seems to have been carried over. Again, because I had no problems with the original, I have zero problems here.
The controls I am still getting used to as you can tell by my barely anything game time. I'm almost thinking the original still had tighter controls. Mostly because they introduced a new dodge feature now and I feel like I keep accidently activating it when I'm using the introduced sprint feature. Again, these can be things I'll probably get used to but as of now, the original without these extra moves seemed a lot easier to control. Otherwise, the game is still a 3rd person action adventure where you freely move the protagnist anywhere the hell you want.
The interface. Probably the second most welcoming introduction to compliment the new graphics. The way you can review your inventory, dialague with the locals, and activate the save feature have been hella improved. I can't find anything wrong here.
Final word. If were ever a fan or slightly had interest in the original Outcast, this is really a no brainer. If you ever got pretty far in the original and maybe got tired of it or thought something was too difficult, why not give it a shot in this day and age? Surprisingly, the gameplay which has not changed since 1999 remains competitive with current modern games. I mean it didn't win 100s of awards back in 1999 for nothing. It's a fun action adventure with plenty to do and see. I'm stoked to see the other worlds because I think any fan of the original had his favorite world as you can describe them as the  snow region, city region, jungle, farmlands, volcanic, and waterworld. My favorite being the waterworld :)
Highly recommended.

I am a huge fan of fan projects that are focused on single player. As they usually produce the most interesting results. I've played a ton of them and I always try and look for the positives. I'm not against paying for a mod, but there's a level of quality to be expected with a price tag attached. Prospekt does not meet these expectations. In a lot of ways it feels like someone's first mod. The attention to detail is too low, there are no major changes to the game design. The game has nothing that pulls you into it, let alone justifies its $10 MSRP price tag.
The level design is amateurish at best. At worst you're fighting the poor lighting that the game gives you. It's either
or puzzle elements that are drenched in darkness. Whilst there can definitely be dark moments, the fact that the game is so dark makes me think the developer doesn't know how to properly light Source engine levels. The exceeding brightness of
also lends credibility to this theory. The level design itself is fairly linear. None of it is notable except being a lot of big rooms... typically full of nothing. Enemy engagements aren't great, either. The transition between areas are... a ton of vents. In fact if you love vents and disembodied voices communicating to you, then this game comes highly recommended.
The game graphically looks fine other than the lighting issues, but that's mostly because it's using the stock Half-Life 2 textures with a filter that greatly increases the color saturation, which looks odd. The contrast appears to be tweaked a bit as well but it's hard for me to tell. They changed the HUD's font to some really ugly large font. I'm not a fan but it's a pretty minor change anyways.
At this point I'm starting to ramble, but honestly this game didn't impress me whatsoever. I read the forums and the developer seemed dedicated to improving it and I commend that, but I find it hard to justify money on this. Best of luck with your future endeavors. May luck bless you... but it has abandoned you here IMO.

This is an unofficial sequel to Half-Life: Opposing Force, set during the events of HL2. So, as you can see the reviews for this game are mixed. I'll talk about that in a little bit. For now, I'll explain why I love the game.
It's more action-packed, fun and thrilling gunplay just like Half-Life 2. There are quite a few mods out there that do a poor job of matching up to the source material, but this one pays its homage to HL2 while forging its own path, a rare balance I have trouble finding in mods/spinoffs.
As far as the story goes, you're playing as Corporal Adrian Shepard, in an alternate reality where he's freed by the Vortigaunts to help defeat the Combine's forces in Nova Prospekt. You play through the prison and beyond, without spoilers, you go somewhere VERY cool.
Let it be known that this is a serious challenge. Playing on Hard, I'd say it's probably 2x as hard as HL2 on Hard. There are some parts of the game where I had to use 100% of my ammo to survive, and then there are parts when I had way more than enough. There were times when I had to hide behind cover and wait to be pushed to surivive.
The Summer 2016 update that was pushed added some interesting stealth levels where the goal is to get to the end without getting detected. I think it's awesome that Richard, the developer, doesn't let having a finished product prevent him from adding new content.
About the length of the game, it is a bit short, only about 3 + 1/2 hours, but I felt like it was a good length. Some people would prefer to get it on sale. I myself got it on sale, and I think $5 is a steal for this. If you need to play it right now, $10 isn't a price you'll regret.
Now, onto the game's controversial reputation. A lot of people had unrealistically high expectations at launch, because quite a few video game news sites toted that the mod was official. It's not. You can read Richard's full reasoning behind the reputation via this reddit post:
I think he tried his best and succeeded. Give his game a try, it's not almost flawless like HL2, but it's still a 9/10 title. If it's not for you, that's fine. By getting it, you've witnessed someone else's piece of art, and you can check it out again anytime.

Bought. Played around, reasonably enjoyed it.
Then I accidentally broke progression during an early objective, which prevented me from getting a vital item. And the game autosaved afterwards. With no way to backtrak and get the item.
Then the game's autosave somehow got messed up and every time I died I fell through the world.
Refunded; game is full-release and should not have easily encountered progression-breaking or save-breaking bugs.

+ Visually the game looks amazing with very large open environments with a lot of detail. The world feels massive compared to the size of your character.
+ The story is pretty good. You play as a robot (who's eyes look similar to WALL-E), who crash landed on a foreign alien planet. Your goal is to look for resources and build parts to repair your ship and escape although your mission changes as you discover more.
+ Lots to explore with many large landscapes and environments
+ The crafting system is great, and very easy to understand. You go out find resources, and once you find a resource others of the same type will be displayed on the compass. Once you have the right amounts you can build various things to extend your fuel, power, health, or important parts for the ship.
+ Good voice acting
- The pacing is EXTREMELY slow. The map is huge, and your small bot moves so slowly even while sprinting. I feel like the game developers wanted to intentionally drag out the length of the game.
- Resources are very limited and scarce (I don't believe they respawn), they are also scattered throughout each area in very small amounts. This means you will have to spend a ton of time going around the map gathering. Combined with the problems mentioned above, this becomes a bit tedius.
- Without warning, you will take heavy damage if go anywhere close to the edge of the map or the ravine's filled with lava. Even if you are no where near the lava and are just exploring climbing rocks, you may suddenly lose most of your health. It's also hard to heal early on considering how limited the resources are.
[Suggestion to Developers: If the Sprint speed was ~2x faster than what it is now, I would have enjoyed the game to a far greater extent]

Video review and game-play on YouTube:
Phoning Home was an interesting little game with a rich soundtrack and great voice acting.  I enjoyed the game-play, and found ION's ability progression quite nice.  All in all, this is a great game and I can recommend it in the current state.  It could use some polish here and there, and I hope the developers listen to players suggestions.
PROS:
Right from the start screen, you can tell the sound track for this game is fantastic.  I thoroughly enjoyed the ambient music, ambient background noise, sound effects, and voice acting.  Witty banter and engaging dialogue kept the story flowing and really drew me into this beautiful world.  I truly kept wondering what was going to happen next.  I feel like the core of a good adventure game should be an interesting story, and this game nailed it.
The game looks great.  The scenery is beautiful.  It looks like the developers put a lot of work into making the game feel immersive and impressive.  The world feels large and the sense of scale of a little robot walking around the terrors of the world is striking.
Game-play was enjoyable.  I enjoyed the gathering, crafting, and general mechanics of this game.  Controls feel responsive and I had no crashes, bugs, or other technical issues.
CONS:
There are parts of the game where if you don't have what you need, then you can get stuck and have to reload.  I had to reload 3 times at one point because I didn't have a certain flower before jumping down into a canyon.
Not a huge fan of the AI pathing for ANI.  She kept falling off a cliff at one point on her own which became very frustrating.  Feel like that could be refined.
The thrusting cool-down time felt just a tad bit too long.  I think the game would pace a bit better if I didn't have to wait 2-3 seconds between each jump.
Gathering resources is fun most of the time, but can also be a bit tiresome.  I feel a lot of games of this type suffer from this mechanic however.

Fair warning,
is a
game! This does not make it a bad game, however. It’s actually a great game. It’s a visual novel with only two opportunities to make choices and four endings so most of the time is spent reading. I put the game on auto and read it while eating dinner, it was very relaxing; a digital book with gorgeous artwork.
The
is about Gai, a young boy from West Taria whose parents have just sold him into slavery to the neighboring kingdom of East Taria. He begins working at the grand temple and soon meets Miyon, the girl with the aforementioned cursed sight. With the ability to predict the future and sometimes change it, Miyon has lived a sheltered life as the kingdom’s treasure and works for the king. You also meet Sasa, a local dancer and friend to Miyon who soon take you under her wing and acts as a surrogate mother to you and the young Miyon. The story advances ten years and war breaks out between the two lands of Taria. What happens next is a series of life-changing events for Gai and Miyon as well as the kingdoms.
Along with this gripping story about life, loss and self discovery is
filled with vibrant colors and emotions. Each smile and frown on the characters help drive the story along and pull you even more as the incredibly well written story captivates you. The music in Cursed Sight adds the finishing touch in the immersion as you follow along on the characters’ journeys.
I highly recommend buying
if you enjoy visual novels. The game may take very sad turns but it’s a testament to
that it jerks your emotions around and even after finishing the game leave you speechless. I was very moved by this game and believe that you will be as well.

Being a slave isn’t the best career option available, in my personal opinion. Being a slave to a eccentric, somewhat abusive girl who can change fate and can kill you by simply looking at you with her eyes might be an even worse option. That is the predicament Gai, a ten-year-old boy, finds himself in after being sold by his West Tarian family to a temple in East Taria. Gai quickly realizes how bad his situation is when the girl in question is referred to as “The Treasure of the Nation.”
Cursed Sight, from developer InvertMouse opens with a quick introduction to Gai, and the temple in East Taria where he will be serving “The Treasure of the Nation,” named Miyon. Miyon possesses an ability known as the Cursed Sight. It gives her the power to affect the future, at the cost of her energy, which is of great use to King Lok, the king of East Taria. It also causes anyone who makes eye contact with her eyes  to die. For that reason, she must always wear a veil over her eyes, to protect those around her. On top of all of that, she is also about ten years old, the same age as Gai, and extremely stubborn. Needless to say, the two children don’t get along very well, which is problematic for Gai who could very well be executed if he displeases Miyon to the point that it angers the King Lok.
Gai is a treat of a character. At the start of the story, he is only ten years old, and is written as such. He whines, and complains, and gets flustered and embarrassed. Sometimes he acts selfish, and lets his anger get the better of him. Miyon is the same way, and acts as one would expect a ten-year-old girl who is used to only ordering slaves around to act. Now, it wouldn’t be much fun to read about two kids fighting all the time. I could just go visit my younger sisters if I wanted to see that. This is where Sasa plays a huge role. Being older than Gai and Miyon, she acts as a motherly figure to the two, stopping their fighting, making them talk to each other, and just being there for the both of them when times are tough. She is the perfect counter-weight to the two children, and Gai’s crush on her is so childlike, it reminds me of my childhood crushes.
The first half of the VN allow us to get to know the characters very well. The days flow by naturally, with no explicitly stated time progression which allows Cursed Sight to avoid the rapid, sudden character development scenes that plague many VNs (A sudden development to a character that happens in an unrealistic amount of time is what I am referring to. The main example of this is the protagonist and female falling in love over the course of a week in a common route). The story, after building the characters up in a methodical manner, starts moving forward in the second half of the VN. King Lok declares war on West Taria and begins using Miyon’s powers to his benefit. This begins to take a toll on Miyon, tiring her out more easily, and even worse for her well-being and safety, her powers begin declining. Gai, now willingly helping Miyon with Sasa’s encouragement is extremely worried about her, and begins looking for ways to help her.
The story, especially in the second half, is powerful, but still does not ignore the characters, keeping the fun, enjoyable character interaction that I came to love in the first half of the VN. Despite that, things do get pretty heavy later on, and the choices that you must make can be difficult. It is absolutely worth getting every ending though, as care and effort was put into each one. The true ending is phenomenal and easily one of the best endings to any OELVN I have read.
The art of Cursed Sight is very high quality, and professional. The backgrounds are vibrant, and the characters show so much personality through the art. When a character smiles, their happiness shows. It isn’t simply a drawn smile, its a facial expression of happiness (which is even more impressive for Miyon whose face we only ever see half of). What I think I loved even more than that was the aging of the characters. The VN does feature a time skip, and the character portraits age appropriately. Its a fantastic touch, one I’d like to see more VNs with a time skip or long time progression do.
I really only have one area I feel the need to be nit picky on with Cursed Sight. The writing style can be confusing at times, and this is mostly due to the presentation of the writing. Like most VNs Cursed Sight features a text box, but it reads more like a book/novel rather than a VN. The portrait and name of the person speaking do not appear when there is dialogue. Instead, it works like a book, with the quoted dialogue being followed by, “said Miyon” or “she said sadly”. At times, I found myself getting lost trying to figure out who was speaking, though this is more due to my fast reading pace than it not being stated.
Cursed Sight is a fantastic, tightly bound narrative that will pull on the heartstrings more than once. It features fun, enjoyable characters, with great production values, and a wonderful story. It is a bit on the shorter side, clocking in for me at a bit under 2 hours, but it’s very focused on telling its story, and does not add too many fluff scenes just to pad out the length. I highly recommend Cursed Sight for any OELVN fans, and VN fans alike.

Salt and Sanctuary is a clone of Dark Souls. If you've played all three, you'll be instantly familier with the mechanics and overall game world. This is in no way a bad thing, as the game is fantastically polished and overall, more fun then Dark Souls III, so far. Here's why:
If you are a Souls junkie, this is an insta-buy.

Salt and Sanctuary is a 2D action adventure game that is basically like a hybrid of Dark Souls gameplay with a bit of Castlevania sprinkled in. It is a bit of a Metroidvania game but like Dark Souls it has no minimap and the difficulty is hard enough that you will die plenty.
The game's art style may seem iffy when starting the game; it's a bit sketchy and looks a little like a flash game, but make no mistake - the game itself is absolutely massive. It's easily the size of your typical Castlevania game and the slower paced gameplay makes it seem even larger. Considering the size and scope of the game which rivals Dark Souls series, it's a bargain even at the non-sale price.
The gameplay has about the same pacing as Dark Souls in its combat, and it also has the ability to block, and roll, amongst other things. However, a minor qualm is that sometimes enemy attacks aren't telegraphed that well in advance, making them hard to dodge in time. Besides that, though, it does one of the best approximations of Souls combat in 2D and features a ton of different types of builds.
The amount of platforming in the game is more significant than souls, which I suppose makes up for the fact that you can't really fall off ledges in a 2D game unless there is a lot of platforming. I think they went a little overboard with it, falls probably killed me more times than actual enemies, unless you count enemies hitting you off ledges as being "killed" by one.
The amount of lore in the game is quite nice and the game is more text heavy than your typical action indie game, with each inventory item having a ton of lore and even the level up screen having segments of legendary tomes. But, like Dark Souls, it doesn't interrupt the game unless you wish to read the lore. The lore itself, however, is quite solid.
This game is basically what that cheap Dark Souls ripoff Slashy Souls SHOULD have been. An amazing version of Souls in 2D that pretty much has everything a fan of dark action games should want.
Overall the game is fun and the people who will get the most kick out of it are those who have played the Souls series and are looking for more similar gameplay. However, anyone looking for an extremely fun Metroidvania should also give it a try.

I'm going to just be straight out with this, but I've read several reviews before I decided I wanted to get this game (props to my cousin for buying this game for me), but a lot of people seem to give this game a thumbs down for a several reasons that I feel like doesn't justify it so. Just so you know, this is probably going to be a lengthy review/rant.
First of, I can understand that for some people, they can find this pretty boring because of all the walking needed to be done. But what do you expect from an exploration/survival kind of game. It's very similar to The Forest, but it's very much less so because theres no cannibals and you can only do so much in the cold. The description literally says "There are no zombies -- only you, the cold, and all the threats Mother Nature can muster." If theres not enough action for you, like the lack in wolves, then increase the difficulty. So, I think people are just expecting too much from these kinds of games.
I see a lot of people complain about the tutorial in the campaign being garbage because it tells you to open up or do something without actually directing you on where or how to. I never find this a REAL problem for most games because well.. theres a thing called key bindings. If you don't know how to open up the menu or how to interact with things, you just press esc, go to options, and look at the key bindings and it will tell you what buttons on your keyboard/controller will do. It's that simple. And I dont understand why people give games bad reviews because of something like that. Same with if you don't like what the buttons do, you can just change it to something youre more comfortable with.
As for a little add on to this complaint, by the way, I'm sorry, I've never really had a problem with my hunger/thirst. I have had problems with my fatigue, and how fast time can go by for the entire day, but it's never been a big issue to me. 10 mins to break a branch into 3 sticks is very quite unrealistic, but I also don't really notice it put a dent in my time exploring or doing important things. Also, maybe it's a bit too early for me to say, but I find plenty of resources in the campaign so I'm never out of food or drinks.
Some frustrations I actually did have in the game's campaign so far, is the lack of real weapons. While I do find plenty of resources in the beginning, they aren't enough for me to give as points for trust. So it's difficult to achieve any kind of hints a person will give on good items. In the beginning, your only weapon will be pebbles and man is the aiming and throwing actually quite difficult to understand. Realistically, it wouldn't be that easy to hit something from a distance, but regardless I do find that part difficult. And I know other reviewers have mentioned the poor aiming system.
I've only played about 8 hours of the game and I've only touched the campaign. But if any of you are planning to get the game, it's wise to take into account of my review. And other people's as well, positive AND negative. Like, literally filter the tags. I can't say that I love this game, but I like it so far.

Sniper: Ghost Warrior 2 is a first person shooter that focuses on stealth and sniping and presents itself with quite a couple of improvements over the 2011-released prequel.
The story is stereotypical modern first person shooter bla bla. Terrorists try to obtain a weapon of mass destruction and you have to stop them before they get the chance to use it... so, really exciting stuff there. While the story is as generic as it can be, the storytelling and the dialogues, combined with the actual gameplay, work out surprisingly well and keep things going without every really boring you to death.
S:GW2 is based on the CryEngine 3 (the same engine used for Crysis 3) and while the original game already looked fairly decent, S:GW2 made an even bigger step forward towards visual quality. The texture detail, lighting and level design of the different locations made me stand still and just look around for a bit more than once.
Along with the enhanced visuals, the gameplay mechanics also greatly improved. The AI in the prequel was a horrible pain as enemies would spot you through walls or over a distance of hundreds of meters. Thankfully, the AI was completely re-done for S:GW2, so enemies behave like they should and also show some actual intelligence as, depending on the area, they will try to flank you from all sides or hide behind cover. Additionally, if you break the line of sight or hide in foliage, they will start searching for you.
Each of the 'hotspot' areas in the levels provide you with one or more overwatch spots from which you can safely identify your targets and take them out either one by one, 2 with one bullet if they stand in line or even an entire group if you shoot a grenade on one of the enemy's belts. Alternatively, you can also get closer and take them out either with your knife or your silenced sidearm and if you want to be a real Ghost, you just sneak past them so they will never know you were there.
As the enviroments change, you will have to utilize your thermal or night vision to progress safely and spot your enemies. While this is a nice gimmick and the night vision is often required in really dark areas, I barely used the thermal vision, though it can help spot enemies that blend into the enviroment or are covered by obstacles. The visions are also pretty much the only gadgets you have and while you get C4 charges during certain key points in the game, it feels somewhat lame to not be able to place Claymore mines and lure enemies into them. Or just blow them up with frag grenades.
While the prequel had some action-heavy levels where you actually went head-on towards your enemies and mowed them down with your combat rifles, S:GW2 doesn't feature something like that at all. You have to stick with your sniper rifle as your primary weapon at all times and while the game actually is called 'Sniper', I feel like this strict sniper rifle-only thing killed a bit of the gameplay dynamic and possible replayability of the game as it eliminates the option for the player to replay a level and, instead of silently sniping the enemies, just going nuts with an assault rifle and pumping bullets into everything that moves.
I tried to be as stealthy as possible, so the base campaign took me around 6.5 hours to beat. The Siberian Strike DLC, which consists of 3 fairly lengthy levels, added another 2.5 hours on top of it. While a couple people seem to be still playing the multiplayer mode, I can't comment on that as I was never able to join a server and gave up after dozens of tries and a couple attempts to fix it.
All in all, S:GW2 is a huge improvement over the sequel and seeing what turds City Interactive has produced in the past (prior to S:GW), it's good to see that they can do something decent for a change. If they keep up this level of quality, I might eventually start looking forward to their upcoming games again.
If you're looking for a decent and good-looking sniper experience, make sure to give S:GW 2 a shot (A shot - get it? Because it's a sniper game... hahahaha. Ah, nevermind).

As you can see by my username I really love Outcast. I played the original back when it came out in 1999 and it was my absolute favorite games of all time. Nothing came close to the great world that Outcast built up. Everything in it had some kind of internal logic and sense to it and the more you learned about the world and it's lore, the more intriguing it got. Also the soundtrack is still absolutely fantastic (performed by the moscow symphony orchestra).
Now I have played this new version to little to really expand on all the good and bad of this remake so I might have to add those later. The game does give a mixed impression when it comes to the technial department and I hope that does not scare away new players. The graphics on the environments looks really good (the moving clouds and sky in shamazaar looks amazing), but the characters and animations are not as great, and the general feeling of controling things are quite stiff.
Outcast is not about fast twitch controls though, it is about the great world that will suck you in the more you play it. If you are new to Outcast I really recommend to try to look past the somewhat rough edges and give it a real chance. I am convinced you will not regret it.
From playing this little so far one thing that still awes me is the AI. The AI at the time was groundbreaking, but it still has features that not even new games have. You can ask other NPC:s for the location of other NPC:s and they will tell you where they saw them last, or even point at them if they are close. They will also not want to gossip about other NPC:s if that NPC actually is near them and if you talk to a Talan other Talans will often stop and eavesdrop etc. You can also affect the world in many ways (cut of supply of things like food or taxes to make the soldiers weak and lose morale etc) and travel wherever you want from the start of the game. There is a great sense of dynamic in the world. (I do however dislike that you can now see how strong the enemies are etc by a stat in your inventory  or the strength of their morale or food supply etc, putting numbers and stat on things always makes things feel less alive so I prefer these stats to be hidden and you have to ask other Talans for the status of the enemy forces)
If I have to say something really negative it is actually outside the game. The trailer for the game is absolutely abysmal. It is not only extremely generic to the max, and bland and focuses only on action parts, but it gives off a total wrong wibe of what the game is actually like. This is not a stupid action game, this is a great adventure game with a deep world and interesting lore you can explore.
Also on a sitenote, for some reason there are big ugly markers on the enemies in this verison of the game (like ? markers above enemy soldiers who are suspecting things etc) that are really ugly and distracting. I really recommend to turn these off in the options.
All in all Outcast is still a fantastic unique game that everyone should experience. It might be a little hard to get in to at first, but it will grow on you more and more as you play it, and by the time you have finished it and stopped playing you will surely have many fond memories of the world as if it was an actual place you had visited, which few games manages to do. I really hope the Outcast saga can get a continuation in a sequel at some point because it really deserves it.

So, as an Outcast fan, I have been waiting for this day since I first read the news that the Appeal team regained this IP.
And as this day has come, I have to say I am very disssappointed with the result.
They have literally taken the old game code, and just brushed up the graphics a bit. And did a bad job in doing so. If this remake was released in 2004, it would've been an awesome job. But now, it's no good at all.
Let's start with the intro movie. The comic book style they went with is obviously a decision based on costs. There's hardly any animation in the characters, and defenitely absolute zero facial expression. The vortex in the end kind of looks like how my 6 year old  cousin would draw a tornado. But.. the intro is not the game, I think to myself. If they invested all this time and effort into it, the game itself should be great.
But then you start. You realise from the camera panning and the textures going through eachother when Cutter wakes up on that stretcher, that this is litterally the old game code with some slightly brushed up graphics on top of it.
You start walking around a bit and than you notice that that doesn't work the same anymore. I'm making side-rolls constantly because i can't press left or right while running. since that now makes you do a roll to the side. I start opening in game menu's and controlls, and that's something you can either like or dislike, but in my opinion, it looked better in the old version.
But at this point I'm not ready to give up. I do Jan's tests, of which I can still do 3 of them without even talking to Jan, and I enter the daoka to go to Shamazaar. Since I know I'm gonna need some helidium (or green and red crystals as they're now called), I figure I shoot the spiders that are very close to the shamazaar daoka. I again realise, this isn't a remake. More of a re-skin, as the same old bug where you can't shoot a spider when there's also another dead spider, and the live spider kind of seems to stay underneath the dead one.
I then start making my way towards the village, when I notice there's absolutely no animation in the rice fields. It's just texture going on top of another texture. Nothing more than that. Again, acceptable if we would live in 2004, but last time I checked we're near the end of 2017.
I'm now starting to think about what kind of team has put this together. I know the old founders of appeal, Yves Grolet and Yann Robert, were involved. And I'm not really sure if Franck Sauer was actually involved in this remake. But this really feels like they did this just with the 2, or 3 of them. Forgetting that they are not graphics artist, that they are not animation specialists... So I decide to lookup the current Appeal studio on linkedIn. And I find a company with 4 employees, three of which I can see: Yves, Yann and and a third guy who looks like he worked parttime on this remake, as he is also a teacher at a local university. So it does look like this was no more than 4 people. To do literally everything.
Now, I don't know how small their budget was, and if they were able to work on this full-time. But honestly, if Outcast was my original creation, I would have been ashamed to release this.
On a positive note, I like that they stuck to the original voice over. that's what the Ulukai and the talan should sound like, and anything new I would not have liked.
Summary:
Game Control: worse than the original
Graphics: Better than the original, but at a level you would've expected in 2004.
Sound/Music: Original voices, so that's good. Orchestral recordings (one of the best video game soundtracks of all time if you ask me) are good, but could've been remastered as well.
Usually, I would ask for a refund. But as I do sincerely hope they learn from this, and I do want them to finally start working on a sequel, I will not. I still feel like the Outcast IP has loads of potential. And I want to see future games in the outcast universe. But I do hope, that if they do start on an actual outcast 2, they start hiring some talented people. This really feels like the product of a bunch of (older) guys who are stuck in their ways and do not want to move to the modern world.
So, if you've never heard of Outcast, keep walking. Nothing to see here.
If you've played the original, buy it. Support the team for their effort, and hope they will start on a sequel.

So I played InvertMouse's free VN Without Within here on Steam, and at the time I gave it a weak recommendation only because it was free and short. Now that I've gotten a sampling of a longer VN that's paid for from InvertMouse, I'm sad to say that it's not much better.
So, the good things. Art and music are fantastic, as well as certain choice aspects (providing a branching screen where we can go back to important decisions instead of saving all the time), as well as a switch in narrative at one point in the story.  The concept itself is fascinating, and some of the scenes were great, However, that brings us to...
...the writing. The events that take place were really interesting, but the writing handled them very poorly, with very weak linkages. Characters that we are supposed to feel for suffer from poor development, making it hard to empathize in certain scenes. Motivations that drive key political players (and the overarching war in Taria) get thrown out the window (as well as logic) in several endings of the game, making for a baffiling conclusion to various routes. The writing is at times incredibly bulky, often with really, really bad word choices or phrases that kill any immersion with the story, as well as making me really, really dislike our main character Gai.
Indeed...out of all the characters in the story, he frustrated me the most. The story is supposed to show that he has grown up, but 90% of the story shows absolutely no indication of that, and when we do see a more mature Gai, it's in one or two endings and is not nearly as smooth and cohesive as I think the writer intended it to be. A lot of things are just thrown into the route to be taken as word, when it would have worked way better had it been shown through development (this goes for all character development and relationship development...don't get me started on the love story).
I think this story really suffers from being short. If the writer had taken time to write more to flesh it out, it would have been stronger and able to stand up on its own. Sure, it would have taken longer to read, but I think, as evidenced by this and Without Within, the writer has difficulty making short stories and would benefit more writing something longer. It just seems he or she has trouble balancing the fine line between condensing the story and still writing believable characters and interactions. It's a shame, because I truly think the concept behind the story is fantastic.

A very (bitter)sweet  and touching experience - if you are into games that will make you laugh and cry in equal measure (more of the latter towards the end) then this title is definitely for you.
Observations:
- this is NOT a dating sim but an interactive story. Every choice leads to a different ending.
- the art is pretty and tasteful though fairly simple.
- The writing is decent although it gets out of the setting character sometimes  (references to chainsaw hands in a medieval China-like country? I almost expected to find the Necronomicon next). The MC feels and talks more like a modern teenager than any peasant servant has any right to.
- Length- ~3 hours.
- Got it on sale for £2.49, Probably would not pay more for the length so wait for at least 50%.
- No true happy endings and the 'best' one almost made me cry. Very touching and sentimental.
Overall, 7/10. +1 if you love drama and getting your heart strings tugged.

I honestly did not expect much from a vn made by InvertMouse, after playing their free short novel, "Without Within" (also on steam). However by the end of it my opinion is completely changed. The story is unique, in a historical oriental style; it tells a great tale of adventure, drama and romance.. The length is modest, I managed to finish it entirely within less than 3 hours. And in those 3 hours it has given me a final ending which I would remember for a good 3 months or so.. Truthfully speaking, achieving the final ending requires you to play throughout the other 3 endings first, and these endings aren't all particularly pleasant.. HOWEVER they do add to the final effect of relief and bliss which the finale gives so yes they are crucial, don't skip them. The plot development was nice, overall it was a solid story. I wouldn't say it to be too good if it weren't for the feeling that reading EVERY ending will give you. The story telling style however is in a modern style, which may make it feel out of place but for me personally it made things more enjoyable.The art is one of the best I've seen in a visual novel, vivid and vibrant colors affecting the mood and tone of things. I cannot say the same for the music however, sweet-sounding it is it does seem kind of out place at times.
Overall, this visual novel is something to keep you occupied for a short amount time. It is very friendly to first timers and tells a great story. I am not saying that it is an extremely good story, but overall with its endings and final ending, it is a conclusive, well-written and enjoyable legend.. (or feels trip if you see it that way)
I would rate it an 8.7/10, great score for a great game.

The fundamental question behind the concept of fate is as old as storytelling itself. Do we truly forge our own path through the causality of the universe, or are we beholden to some kind of unknowable higher order? And if the universe is set on a specific course,
?
is a visual novel developed and written by
, it was released in August 2015 following a successful Kickstarter campaign earlier the same year. It's 45000 words long with four different endings and took me a bit more than three hours for 100% completion.
The story is set in a fictional medieval far-east-inspired nation where a select few people are born with the gift (or curse, depending on how you look at it) of fate magic. One of the central characters, a young girl named Miyon, can influence the tides of fate in her nation's favor, but everyone who looks into her eyes is
. Enter the protagonist of the story, Gai, a young boy
. He gets assigned to do various household chores in the temple where Miyon is held.
First things first: I really liked this VN and I have no regrets at all about reading it. It has high-quality artwork and a fitting soundtrack – neither is deeply unique or special compared to other VNs, but they go together well to form a very cohesive whole, and I have to appreciate
when I see one. It packs everything you'd expect from a modern VN, including auto and skip modes as well as copious amounts of save slots. As always, the multiplatform support is something that I personally greatly appreciate.
The story is an interesting beast, the premise sounds generic enough at first but the plot does itself a huge favor by avoiding romance-themed routes and most of the clichés that typically come with them, focusing on
instead. The plot is beautifully rich and engaging, the events of the story could easily fill out twice or thrice the word count, and if there is one otherwise common problem that
deftly avoids, it's boredom. The introduction is short and sweet, the conflict comes swiftly, and there was never any moment where I felt like I wanted to stop reading.
Regrettably, the riptide of dramatic events is also the biggest problem I had with
. It has been said that a story needs a rhythm, an ebb and flow, to not push its readers away. If there's one thing for me that would have turned my somewhat shaky recommendation into a firmer one, it would have been
. Even though the story only features one explicit time skip, it feels like too much character development happens off screen. To its credit, the novel still manages to make the
of Gai's and Miyon's interactions from
to
pretty believable, but if it had had more slice-of-life segments where the characters just simply talk to one another, learn about each other and clarify
and where they stand on various issues, I think that would have worked wonders to sell me more forcefully on the relationships portrayed in the dramatic scenes. Additionally, a minority of the endings also seemed unduly rushed.
I'm not sure whether I can put my finger on all of
's strengths, and it's hard to summarize what a new reader should expect from the story. Romance is hinted at, but not really explored. Political intrigue
, but not really explored either. The worldbuilding is
, but too coarse to really be able to make up your own stories in the setting. But perhaps the most glaring issue I had was with the weird colloquialisms and anachronisms sprinkled throughout the script (the worst offender: a quip about chainsaws) that are probably intended to be charming, but just come across as out of place.
I'm doing a pretty terrible job recommending a VN I liked, aren't I?
Let's loop back to something I liked about the story: I like being surprised (I have a bit of a soft spot for genre subversions), and a very positive surprise I got from
was the way it handles its main characters.
With many stories you get the impression that the setting shapes itself around the protagonist, hiding all sorts of plot conveniences
well enough to fool most casual readers, and in the end everyone gets what they deserve because that's how stories tend to work. Gai starts out in a position of complete and utter helplessness (and in hindsight the start of the VN does a great job at portraying the mindset of a ten year old boy who just had the belief strongly reinforced that, in the grand scheme of things, nothing he values is safe and nothing he does matters), and you'd expect a "hero's journey" style rise to glory as he overcomes his inner demons. But then that doesn't happen at all, Gai and Miyon simply keep being normal people with normal issues, tossed here and there by circumstance like plastic bags in the wind, and when you reach your first ending, chances are you won't find it satisfyingly fulfilling but rather just
. It seems that for someone imbued with fate magic, Miyon has tragically little control over her own fate – a bittersweet irony and one of the literary masterstrokes that make me like
as much as I do.
I'd love to go into more detail here, but more than that I want to give you the chance to read
spoiler-free. There's certainly enough in there to be worth a read, and unless you dislike fantasy as a genre (or you think that every fantasy protagonist needs to follow the "hero's journey" and be virtuous and just at all times), you
won't be disappointed.

A 2D Souls game with some not great design choices. This game is not a roguelike or roguelite. It is a clearly Souls inspired game, even stated by the developer.
Good
Animations are satisfying.
Visceral and fun combat.
Nice atmosphere.
Bad
Enemies can grab you from different planes and from across ledges, notably the beginning wolves.
It has the DaS 2 equivalent of lifegems, making it a bit too easy to get health back.
It's not clear how to tell if someone is an enemy or an NPC due to the art style. Not the most important thing, but it's annoying.
The inventory isn't very clear on how weapons and shields work. You have two slots for either a weapon or a shield on either side of the inventory, but equiping a weapon on either side will only let you use one of those weapons if you're two handing.
No obvious equip load indicator, so no way to know what's too heavy on sight, something Souls does right.
No obvious armor or weapon stats, so no way to know what's good or bad on sight, something that, again, Souls does right.
No normal enemy life bars, which is just a QOL thing, but still.
The UI is just clunky and doesn't flow well.
It's a more rough Souls, basically. I personally didn't like it, but hey, you might.

is the third game in a series of physics-based puzzle platformers.
Like its predecessors, it features three heroes who are zapped to a magical land by a mysterious artifact and forced to do its bidding. Each of the three (a wizard, a burglar, and a knight) has its own special abilities which can be used or combined to manipulate the environment in the necessary way to advance. The heroes can each be swapped out at will by a single player, or controlled separately by multiple players.
Unlike its predecessors, Trine 3 allows players to move three-dimensionally, and adds some Crash Bandicoot-style depth-oriented platforming areas as well as some area arena battles. Overall, this works well, and adds a new dimension to the game, figuratively as well as literally. However, there's often no clear indication of things' depth relative to each other, which can become frustrating from time to time. Character progression has been eliminated, with each hero now possessing a static set of abilities from beginning to end - optional pickups are now used to unlock extra play areas instead of new player abilities. This is a good thing - it simplifies gameplay, as well as removing the possibility of becoming overpowered and just coasting through everything. Possibly as an additional result of this, I felt like the puzzles were more streamlined and less finicky than in previous Trines. Again, I feel like this is a benefit - I spent less time frustrated because I couldn't get some rock or piece of wood oriented
, and more time solving new puzzles.
With respect to graphics and sound, the latest installment continues to provide what I've come to expect from the series: highly polished, often psychedelic visuals that lend a dreamy quality to the playing experience, perfectly matched by a top-notch fantasy soundtrack and great audio effects.
The story is engaging but not excessively complex, and ends rather abruptly, with the intimation that there will be more to come in future installments. I spent about 7 hours playing through the game as a single player, including exploring all of the optional challenges - I expect that, as with previous Trines, gameplay is both more difficult (
) and has more replay value with multiple players.
Gamepad support was a bit finicky - the game seemed somewhat schizophrenic about whether it wanted to see my Steam controller as an xbox gamepad or not on any given launch. I ended up binding the keyboard/mouse controls in Steam instead - they were totally sufficient as such, and the extra grip buttons were nice for e.g. levitating things inward/outward.

Phoning Home is an atmospheric story-driven exploration survival game. You play as a mute robot named ION, and you crash land on an alien planet. With the guidance of the ship’s AI, you must find a way to phone home for help. Not long into your mission, you come across another robot named ANI. The two of you must work together as strange alien life emerges, and the planet itself defies the laws of nature. I find the story interesting, and I definitely get that Wall-E meets E.T. vibe, but with a different tone for the narrative.
The majority of the game is essentially a walking simulator. Exploration is often necessary in order to find the resources you need to craft the tools you’ll need to survive. You’ll also need to guide, carry, maintain, and protect another robot ANI. I wish I could have just left her somewhere, but she requires upkeep. As far as walking simulators go, the game is enjoyable for the first couple hours, until I hit a large desert area From that point on I became so incredibly bored and frustrated trying to reach the objectives.
After finally repairing the first tower, a storm came, and she said to go ahead and explore, and that she would catch up after the storm ended, so I did. The storm lifted, but she never followed, so I was unable to progress without losing a ton of progress (that I wasn’t willing to repeat). Autosaves occurred after I had gotten a fair ways away, so I couldn’t find my way back up again. After my initial frustrations with finding my way up in the first place, and ANI not following like she said she would, I did my best to finish up the mission without her, but couldn’t,  so I gave up. In hindsight, I should have manually saved more frequently, but I also think having to manually save often hurts the immersion. I think more options from autosaves to load might have helped a lot.
I played the game for a bit over 5 hours, and the last 3 hours of that time I wanted to stop playing. The game has a solid start, but it grew tiresome. I would have liked to have seen how the story progressed, but unfortunately, I felt so discouraged that I lost the will to continue.
Phoning Home looks amazing, sounds great, and has an intriguing story. I’m sure some people will enjoy it, and I’m happy for those who do. However, I cannot recommend Phoning Home, as I did not enjoy a large portion of the experience. Simply put, I was just not having fun with it enough to want to see it through. It’s not very often that I don’t want to finish a game, but this is one of those times. After walking around for what felt like forever hoping to find the correct path among hundreds of pseudo paths took simply its toll. My boredom and frustration claimed victor, and I stopped playing.
