While there are a lot of things that I really like about Phoning Home, there is one thing that keeps it from being as good as it could have been.
If I had to classify Phoning Home I would say that it is a single player story-driven crafting survival game. The main element of the game is exploring the environment, overcoming obstacles and either avoiding or killing enemies. Phoning Home plays like most exploration games except that it adds a crafting mechanic. As you explore you will encounter materials which you use to craft things like health and fuel or more permanent upgrades for you character. These mechanics work surprisingly well together and create an experience where it feels like you are trying to survive on a strange planet.
The story is also surprisingly strong. The game kind of reminds me of WALL-E but with a different tone. The story and characters are interesting and I want to see how the story ends. The graphics/visuals are also very good for an indie developer.
Phoning Home's big issue though is that it relies a little too much on backtracking at times. You need to be frugal with resources or you are going to have troubles. Even if you are frugal you will likely have to revisit areas in order to collect resources that you need. Since the game limits how much of each material that you can hold, you can only do so much stocking up on a resource. This leads to situations where you need a resource and have to waste time roaming around looking for that material.
Controllers also don't seem to work at this point. When using the right stick to control the camera it feels like the camera is stuck in slow motion. While the game works fine with the keyboard and mouse I hope this issue with controllers is fixed soon since the game would play better with a controller than a keyboard and mouse.
If you don't really care for crafting games or story-driven games, Phoning Home is probably not going to be for you. If you like the idea of adding a crafting mechanic to a story-driven game though I think you could enjoy Phoning Home quite a bit.

A solid, surprisingly deep beat-em-up. Battles are in 2D, but take place on multiple "planes" that you can jump between at will, much like Guardian Heroes. Combat is heavily based on a wide variety of devastating "Fury" moves like upheaving bursts of fire, powerful area-of-effect clearing blasts, and excessive punch combos.
The most notable point is that despite the gameplay, the game's graphics and art direction are hilarious: it's a hilarious parody of games like Pit Fighter and early Mortal Kombat, but seemingly much more self-aware and in on the joke, which works well with the game's atmosphere. It works extremely well as a "parody" of the genre, but doesn't skimp on the gameplay as a result, as the battles are a bit more involved than the average beat-em-up, what with the wide variety of moves.
The only real issue is the lack of online co-op. Aside from that, if you're a fan of beat-em-ups and the early 90's digitized photo graphics aesthetic, and like beat-em-ups that aren't just button mashing, don't hesitate to pick this up.

This game isn't an official Opposing Force sequel, but this is the closest we'll get to it, at least for now. Playing as Adrian Shephard again is a breath of fresh air, as most HL2 mods center Gordon Freeman as the main protagonist. With the game still updating (with some impressive new levels and models coming along the way as seen from posts and streams), it has shown many improvements from how the original product turned out to be.
The music is amazing, has that certain thrill when you enter battle against the Combine forces. Voice acting wise, it is mostly good, but could use a little work on some dialogue. Graphics wise, there has been some good improvement to the lighting and some atmosphere, but still remaining true to Half Life's style. The game comes with some custom models you can notice in some locations throughout your journey, but easy to miss if you are focused on the action. Unfortunately as of right now, the game lacks the important aspect seen with the rest of the Half Life setting: The story. Every Half Life fan enjoys the story within the games, but this game has yet to have a complete narrative story.
Overall, this game is probably worth the money when on sale. However, once the newer stuff comes along, it'll be worth playing again. For now, I am looking forward in the future to play this game some more, and I wish luck to Rich to further make this game the best experience for every Half Life fan out there. Give the Creator of this game all your support, he is going to need it!

Not exactly, but Sam "Serious" Stone has similarly funny one-liners (albeit much fewer) when he blows up an alien attempting to kill him. In the cutscenes you can also notice he is full of muscles and that he also wears sunglasses. This was Croteam's own hero with which they wanted to conquer the FPS genre back in 2001.
The idea was to tone down the gameplay we got to know in Duke Nukem. Duke could use some items which were strategically important at select locations. Also, we frequently searched for objects such as keycards. And remember that heights also became important? That with our jetpack secrets became accessible?
Sam makes it way simpler: he shoots first then asks questions later. We go from one room to another and only when we killed everybody can we proceed. Sometimes we have to activate levers but these are rare occasions. With Sam it really is all about shooting and increasing our score for each level. Greater difficulty settings yield us increased multipliers. We do not even have to reload our weapons (a similarity with Doom).
Well, yes. We hunt for artifacts in Egypt (sometime in the future) to make sure we can kill the leader of the enemy race invading Earth. We know we failed but Sam was able to use a special device to travel back in time to correct our mistake. Although  the entire first game takes place in Egypt the locales vary from tombs and city-like areas to deserts and at one point we even find ourselves in the sewers. Don't expect an interesting story and dozens of cutscenes here, though.
The 3rd iteration of Croteam's Serious Engine was used to completely redo the original game. Screenshots and comparison videos speak for themselves: the game has better looking, crispier textures and each alien was completely remodelled to look better. A later version of the engine was used to make the 3rd episode in the series. It does its job properly without changing the core gameplay which is just as fast and dynamic as it was in the original version.
This is how you remaster your software. You make it look better, sound louder and neglect annoying DLCs (I am looking at you, Painkiller). If you are a newcomer to this franchise perhaps Serious Sam 3 should be your first purchase (after all, it is a prequel to the story). However, if you played this 15 years ago when you were a kid it's high time you included it in your library of digital games.

It's still good ol' Outcast, and it's still great. Might be a bit on the pricy side, but what you get is pretty great.
The graphics are suitably Outcast. It will not blow you away with its shine or glimmer, but it is consistent in its art direction and delivery. The opening scene showers you in particle physics and it looks pretty great, in my opinion.
I expect it to run fairly OK on most machines.
Sound is ripped straight from Outcast, with a few new additions, and thats not a bad thing. The original sounds are strange and fantastic, it suits the world it's in.
Do expect somewhat lowfi audio though, the orignal game came out in the 90's after all.
Gameplay is also pretty much the same, but a somewhat reworked camera makes it better and equal at the same time. It's not worse off, nor automatically better either. It does jerk around abit when aiming and walking down a slope.
I'm not sure I like the addition of explenation of the different names of places, things and beings. I liked the way you had to figure this out on your own in the original, even if it didn't take much to figure it out. It just breaks the immersion seeing an explenation of what the Yods are in parentheses next to the word.
Jumping is still very odd, and will not sit right with most people, even if the animation has been reworked.
Animations for Cutter Slade have been reworked, they look better for the most part but syncing the animation with the audio is a slight issue. Melee combat looks odd and should either be ignored by players or need another rework by the devs.
The options menu is pretty much the worst part of this game, and probably the only real problem the game has at launch. Other gripes people have with the game can be forgiven as a relic kept from the original game, mostly nitpicks to be honest.
But the options menu is terrible.
It has three tabs, "Main", "Keyboard" and "Graphics".
The "Main" tab does contain a lot of options. Voice and text language, game options (health and difficulty), some camera options (invert Y axis, sensitivity), crosshair position, targeting assistance and the likes.
The "Keyboard" tab you'd expect to contain all the key binding you'd be able to bind, but no. It has some of the keys, but blenty missing.
This might be a problem with the fact they now fully support gamepads and has a console release. Chop it down to poor PC port, somewhat.
The "Graphics" tab contains the barebones of graphics settings. You can change resolution, fullscreen on or off, vertical sync on or off, and "Quality" ranging from "normal" to "very high".
No texture filtering options, no texture quality options, no FOV option, no particle quality option, no shadow quality option, you name it.
The "Quality" option seems to not impact performance at all, and seems to only changes the shadow quality.
Not only is the graphics options barebones, there is no audio options to speak of.
I expect them to update the options menu at a later date, or at least I hope they will.
Back to the great stuff. The game loads really fast, it might only take a couple seconds to load from level to level, or from a save, or just booting up the game in general. It's fast, really fast.
The UI has been reworked, and it's a step up from the original. The original was far from bad, but this new one is more inline with how we expect modern UI's to look and work. It's simple and to the point.
Did I mention the music is great? Well, it's the same soundtrack from the original, so it's bound to be fantastic.
The game only takes up about 8.5 GB of harddrive space. In a time where games take upwards of 50 to over 100 GB, it's refreshing to see a game that doesn't need that much space.
TL:DR
It's a great remake, but a tad bit pricy.

Okay, so highly anticipated Outcast - Second Contact finally arrived.
I backed their kickstarter campaign (unsuccesful though), and now, after about 2 years of development, the game has finally arrived.
As a hardcore Outcast fan (the game is in my top3 along with Drakan and Dark Earth... weird list, huh? =) , I've experienced some negativity, when I discovered, that some aspects of the original game were changed. I'd prefer things exactly as they were, but maybe with a bit updated graphics.
But they've changed a lot - from movement system to combat. Everything became a bit more casual - probably, to attract new audience. Now there are blue annitations next to local words in dialogues, like Yods, Fae Rhan, Mon, Essence and other stuff of Outcast mythology. Movement now include different sneaking mechanics and weird rolls. And yes, there's stamina and sprint (which is def a good change). There are a few bugs, like involuntary locking on some objects or jumping on slopes, which now do wierd stuff.
Obviously, touching the original concepts was a dangerous act, I'm sure a lot of fans will start to stink, as they always do. Personally for me, these changes are not THAT important, since the original spirit of Outcast is still there. And some new mechanics are even fun, since I've passed original Outcast about 20 times in the last 18 years, so something new is a good thing.
Summarizing. The game is still great, and I totally recommend it to old players and new players alike. But. There's more important thing.
As Outcast fan I've been waiting for Outcast 2 for most of my life. And now, after 18 years, it can actually happen! If this game is successful enough. And I feel obligated to help this to happen. And, if you liked Outcast back in 1999, I think you should support this project.
My opinion only.

OneShot is a short, puzzle-adventure game that doesn't take more than 4 hours to complete. It's a fun little game that will do things to you, the player, that you won't be expecting.  I'd compare it to Pony Island and Undertale into how it messes with you, though I won't delve further into details for spoilers.  However, my main gripe with this game is that it seems to crash a lot on my computer.  My computer drive crashes between location transitions for some reason, which quickly became irritating to me since every time the game crashed, I lost quite a good chunk of my progress and had to start all over again.  I'm not sure if this is just a problem with my computer, and it didn't happen all the time, but it's noteworthy enough in my opinion to mention.
I would reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys puzzle adventure games and who enjoy self-aware video games, however only when it's on sale.  I feel the 10 dollar price tag is a bit steep for a 4 hour game.

Cursed Sight is the first visual novel I've purchased here on Steam, so I dove in without any idea what to expect.
While it offers an interesting plot and the art itself is beautiful, I'm mainly unsatisfied with how the script is written. Several technical errors were found in the narrative, and the overall tone and language don't fit. In fact, I've come to dislike the main character, Gai, due to the way he is portrayed.
Other problems:
1. There are areas in the novel that became boring and uninteresting that I've skipped several parts just to get to the end.

And now for my actual review.
As i said before I loved the story. I loved that the game wasn't a cliche "the main character is a morally perfect goody two shoes." But you CAN be that way if you choose.
.There are a few seperete endings to the game that I don't really feel like going into now but if you do get the game I am sure that you will want to discover them just as much as I did.
Gameplay wise this is the best game I have ever played. It was incredibly smooth no matter what I did. Be it Jumping from roof to roof or killing a guy, or just simply walking along. I found the stealth aspect to be very well done and to never be a problem or hinderince to the game. There are many ways to take down your target with different outcomes both in the moment and in the ending of the game. For anyone looking for a good stealth game with satisying combat this is a game you will probably enjoy.
The characters really had me hooked. I even became attached to a maid in the hub world of the game due to her quirky attitude. The enviornment for the game is great as well. It is set in a steam punkesq world where everything uses gears and odd and interesting tech to run. The setting itself is in a victorian Londan world with tall but easily climable buildings and great places to hide.
The gadgets, ooooohhhhhh the gadgets. I cant even begin to explain how good these were. They were so well done and worked in such great ways and could be used in a ton of inovative ways. However you will never be without your trusty knife and crossbow.
I only have 3 problems with the game. And one isn't truly that bad. The first and worst one is that you are essentially punished for using all the cool gadgets given to you. Use them too much to kill too many people and you get the "bad" ending. Why give us all these neat little toys and then say "No don't use that."? It is really bothersom. The secound issue I have with the game is the AI. It is sometimes dissapointing. You could be hiding on the other side of a bush from a guard with you head completly expossed and they wont notice you at all. Or you could be walking down a street in broad daylight and the guards wouldn't show even the faintest signs of curriosity. My third and final problem is the sound track. It's great in the moment don't get me wrong. However I struggle now even after just playing the game to recall even a bit of any of the songs.
Overall I would say this game is sitting at a 9/10 to an 8/10 for me and is my personal favorite game of all time.

Trine 3 is a decent game. Not an amazing game like the previous titles in the series, but solid nevertheless.
The visuals are great - the game further improves upon the style used in previous installations, and the now-varying camera angle permits for even prettier views.
Gameplay is OK - on one hand, the hero abilities differ from Trine 1/2, but there seems sense to that:
- The Thief's hook is replaced by a rope that clings onto specific movable and immovable objects. While this grants less movement freedom than the hook, aiming hook at arbitrary surfaces with a third-person camera would undoubtedly be a complete mess, and the rope is given it's own features (tying objects together and/or tying around corners and objects).
- The Wizard only summons boxes now. A bit of a shame, of course, but then, summoning planks would imply rotating planks, and that would require more buttons for a rather clumsy result (try building a house of cards in Tabletop Simulator, for example).
Regardless, the game makes decent use of old and new mechanics to create a bunch of little puzzles with multiple solutions.
Audio is great, featuring an OST by the same amazing Ari Pulkkinen that did the music for the previous titles of the game.
Online multiplayer is good. Has a few quirks, but remains playable, and in my experience does not have any major issues. The only thing to mention here is that the levels are the same regardless of the number of the players, so playing together only opens new ways of completing puzzles and levels through cooperation.
On the obvious downside, the game is pretty short. That's a thing.
, there's a thing that places it aside of other shorter-than-expected games - it has a level editor and Steam Workshop support.
And not just any level editor, but the same level editor that was used to make levels in the actual game - you can do anything that you see in the game with it. And publish it on workshop. And play it with people online.
So you could make a bunch of custom levels. Or modify the standard levels to make them harder (be that obstacles or puzzles). Or use scripting to just mess with things and make something that works completely differently.
There's an
on the editor too.
Having seen many games, I think this is a very important thing long-term.
All things said, I consider this a worthy title for a collection,

I got this game in a humble bundle. I was looking at it for quite a while, because I knew it had a "story" mode and the thing that always put me off survival games is the pointlessness in it all. I just don't have the time any more to aimlessly wander around trying to survive as long as I can. It often gets boring after a while. So, I'll focus my review on the Wintermute mode.
Wintermute is an episodic story mode with survival elements...that after having played 10 hours of it now falls unfortunately flat on its face. The graphics are nice, the story is ok, the characters are unfortunately absolutely boring, the setting is, however, interesting, but there's too much playtime with too little development to keep it that way. The first few in-game days are basically a tutorial. Gather this, gather that, sleep, treat wounds, escape. Then the game opens up a bit and lets you basically do whatever you want, but in order to progress the story, you have to go to certain areas and do certain things for the people you find there. It was already annoying in episode 1, but episode 2 is just a pointless exercise in futility. Why, for the love of god, would you create a story-driven mode and then just have your character walk 500 miles in every direction to get simple things? Srsly, the trek from the cabin to the dam was already long enough, but then you have to go back...and then you have to travel TWICE that distance to another part of the game world 0o
Out of my 10 hours I've spent most of my time walking, and I know that travel is an important aspect of a survival game, but in a story mode you could at least construct the story in a certain way that you don't have to go backtracking 20 times, but instead you go forward. I mean, the whole premise is ridiculous. You're looking for your friend, who might be dying, dead or who could die at any moment, and is possibly being hunted by people and wild animals, but instead you're wasting WEEKS helping people you don't even know, so they let you in on a little secret that is necessary to progress. I kind of understood it in Ep 1, but Ep 2 is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Will figured out the solution to the problem on his own a long time ago already, why is he still staying doing menial tasks for some♥♥♥♥♥♥ "Hey, get me 10kgs of deer meat!" Well, ladi♥♥♥♥ing da, you want me to waste bullets on deer I don't need, and then you want me to slog 10 kgs of deer meat back to you, which overburden me, which means I'm unable to run. Oh, and did I mention the wolves, which are everywhere and are attracted by scent and sound and will aggressively stalk and attack you?
I've read through a walkthrough now to see how much bs I still need to do in order to finally progress in the game, and it's just not worth my time anymore, sorry :/ Especially since the game has several more episodes "planned", which don't even have a release date. So, basically, the game calls itself finished, but it is not, which is reason enough alone to give it a bad review.
The whole survival aspect itself is entertaining, but also pretty basic. Apart from the wildlife there shouldn't be too much threat to you. And there's no long-term progression it seems. However, there are quite a few items you need in the game, which will quickly overburden your character. A hunting knife here, a hatchet there, a steel cutter, a lamp, a flare gun, an actual gun. You can either decide to leave most of it in base and be unprepared when you need them, or you carry it all with you and tire yourself out quickly, while not being able to sprint long and fast or at all. Gotta say, I'm not a big fan of it, despite my initial intrigue. Makes me a bit sad.

For someone like me who likes a good Sniper shot from miles away, waiting several seconds up to a minute just for one good shot is okay, everyone else can stop reading here and leave.

The music is great, hands down the best part of the game. Kudos to the music guy Calum Bowen.
The game itself... isn't all that great.
The graphics need some more baking, even for a budget Katamari Damacy / Nobi Nobi tribute.
There are some lazy-looking particle effects and there are great differences in the level of graphic detail during gameplay (the tiny purple stars and Japanese phrases vs. the huge featureless terrain), which gives the game a heterogeneous look (in a bad way).
There are hours of content, but the level design is haphazard and at times unintuitive. I would have rather had a shorter game with levels that had more care put into them.
Also, for those looking for a competitive game, I hope hacked leaderboards don't stop you from enjoying a game (at the time of writing, this game has them). Being about shooting while moving, it's also sorely missing a crosshair, which should have at least been included as an option.
If you choose to play it, here's two pieces of advice:
1. Turn the SFX off. The SFX consist of lazy, tacky sounds that don't do the music any justice. You lose the tell for the apples being tossed, but it's still worth the awesome (uninterrupted) music.
2. If you find the shooting enemies annoying, know that you can kill them by hitting any of their bullets (bug or feature?).
Overall, I still think it's a decent game, just not for $6. I'd say grab it on sale if you know what you're getting into, and even then only bother if you like the OST.

Some of the voice acting is well done, and the recycled voice work from Half Life: Opposing Force was surprisingly nice to hear. But everything else about this game disappointed me. Even my love for all things Half Life couldn’t get me to properly finish it.

I've been meaning to give this game a try before Dishonored 2 came out.  When Bethesda announced that for a limited time you could get this game free with a preorder of Dishonored 2, I pounced on the offer. This game is really fun! The main appeal of it to me was its dynamic story; it can play out with a lighter tone or a very dark tone depending on how many people you kill.
You have a plethora of different ways to kill the enemy, as well as ways to take them down in a nonlethal manner. You can sneak up on them and put a knife in their throat, or you can put them in a chokehold and knock them out. You can blast them in the face with a shotgun, or put them to sleep with a tranq dart. You can summon a swarm of rats and watch them LITERALLY DEVOUR your enemies... or you can stick to the shadows and slip by the enemies entirely. The amount of tactical freedom in this game was staggering, both with how to dispatch your enemies and how to move through the level.
I'm trying to keep this spoiler free, but as a warning if you want the game to play out in a happier way, I highly, HIGHLY recommend you play as nonlethal as possible for the first half of the game (first 3-4 main missions). From what I could tell, the tone of the story was largely determined in that time. I'm rather disappointed with how depressing my story ended up; you are given a warning at the beginning of the game about the consequences of playing highly lethal, but I didn't take it seriously enough. I unleashed utter carnage in the first few missions and killed all of the main targets. After the first few missions I already started to see the negative effects that my actions were having on the story. I decided I needed to change my ways: the whole second half of the game I played very nonlethal, sparing all the main targets and inflicting very few casualties. But it was too late, and the story went spiralling down despite my best efforts to turn things around.
All in all I loved my time in the world of Dishonored, and am REALLY pumped for the second installment!

A buggy, unfinished and disappointing mess. The dev team clearly ran out of budget at some point and/or bit more than they could chew.
The game looks pretty and shiny, but the style just doesn't work as well in a 3D plane; the environments, while breathtaking, feel messy, cramped, and I'm often left wondering what's in the foreground and what's in the background, leading me to misjudge the depth of a jump and die more times than I'd care to admit.

Level progression is completely non-existent in this installment, consequently, there's practically zero motivation to go around getting all the collectibles like there was in the previous games. Characters have been streamlined, retaining their basic starting skills but missing the extra abilities that made it possible and fun to improvise around the different puzzles that the game threw at you.
Perhaps the most disappointing aspect about this whole thing is the way they handled the story; the game ends right when the first act would usually wrap up in a traditional three act narrative. It comes out of nowhere, goes nowhere, and not much gets explained. Even as someone who didn't care much for how the plot panned out, it was very jarring to see.
Other complaints include horrible lip syncing (no seriously, their mouths would start moving literally 30 seconds before anything was said), ugly character models (Zoya looks like she's been tweaking out with her eyes bulging out all the time and Pontius' model is way too realistically modeled to fit the style), and way too many bugs to even begin to list (luckily, none have been game breaking for me). Ironically, the bugs are what made this enjoyable to play, so I don't know if more QA would've made this better or worse to go through. With two friends tagging along, it was hilarious to see all the ways this fell apart as we tried to cheese our way through the puzzles.
If you're looking at this and thinking about buying it, play Trine 1 and 2 first. If you have and want more, buy this one only if it's on sale and you have people to suffer through it with you.

The game looks, plays, and feels like Call of Duty, except the only weapon you get to use is a sniper rifle. There are several different kinds of sniper rifles (MSR, M24, M82A1, etc.), but the only other weapon you have to use is a suppressed pistol, firing which feels like shooting a BB gun. The voice acting is horribly bad, and I do mean BAD. The game is almost played for you unless you are playing on the hardest difficulty. Everything is spelled out for you almost exactly, including where to go, who to kill and in what order, and where every last enemy is. On that note, enemies are lifeless. You might as well be shooting at mannequins. They will randomly spew out different phrases in Russian(?), from, I believe, a pool of set quotes. This being an FPS I'm not too surprised. The game also 'borrows' tricks and gimmicks from Call of Duty 4 rather frequently... I won't give any spoilers though.
Despite all this, environments are verdant and, though linear, well-designed as far as visuals go. The sniper aspect is, though somewhat inaccurate, challenging enough; firing a shot at the wrong time will have several automatic rifles firing in your direction, a bit pulse-pounding, but this is easily avoided, because, even though bullets can fly straight through enemies and hit a piece of metal behind them, resulting in a loud 'pang' sound, this will still not alert them. In fact I'm sure the only way to get detected is to stand in their direct line of sight, and even then it takes a few seconds for them to notice you. It's also apparent that you are playing as a perfectly weightless man, because you cannot hear your footsteps at all - I'm serious, they are completely silent. Because of this, you can sprint up behing an enemy and stab him with no difficulty at all.
Definitely one of my less enjoyed shooters, but at least the sniping is a bit (and I do mean a VERY SMALL BIT) more realistic than Call of Duty.

I played EVOLVE's beta before it released and didn't purchase it. Now Evolve Stage 2 releases after layers and layers of DLC and poor business choices as a free to play title.
All the characters are unlockable through in-game progression which is a great change. The problem is the mistrust the company has gathered from its previous practices isn't gone for me personally.
The game is still fundamentally poorly balanced, but it does the best it can in this uneven 4v1 format. The biggest issues are the diverse set of characters and monsters which in many cases don't synergize well, the player down/revive system and the extremely poor gameplay pacing.
Characters often are missing tools still to deal with certain monsters, like the kraken who likes to stay airborn or the wraith who simply sends AI clones at hunters at the press of the button and stalls out games. Beause of the lack of useful controlling abilities in many matchups the game becomes some sort of strange, lopsided damage race between the hunters dealing damage and the monster just trying to down all the players quickly one-by-one.
Downed players can only use their pistol to shoot or self heal if they're medic. Most fights devolve into the monster body camping the player they down because the hunters either lose damage output or important tools to allow them to keep fighting. The game is very punishing to anyone who doesn't manage their jetpack fuel and the game does a poor job of explaining this core concept.

The changes made thus farr in Stage 2 have caused the game to determined by a number of small skirmishes that happen far more frequently. While the game timer might have been cut in half, the typical game length has been decresaed significantly while actually increasing the number of fights in a game.
I stopped playing Evolve on the Gorgon patch because of dwindling numbers, and back then the game was often decided in 1-2 fights in a typical game. Either the monsters expertly evaded the hunters and hit level 3 or got a good jump on the enemy team at level 2, or the humans would locate and desimate the monster early. While it was certainly possible for the match to go a different direction, this was the typical flow of gameplay in an Evolve match.
In this update, monsters are far less vulnerable stage 1 and due to change dome mechanics often can escape the first dome. During this fight, the players are aiming to get through the monsters armor (that builds and regens much more quickly than ever before) while the monster is aiming to knock players down, build up strikes, and low the dome time before running off again to rebuild armor and hopefully evolve. After that, players seek to keep up with the monster in a chase and if the players can track down the monster before it evolves again they will typically gain an extremely large lead over the monster.
Due to moving a skill point from level 3 to level 1, Stage 2 is now a very large power spike for the monster. While prior to Stage 2 I would of said that the monsters and heros are even at Stage 2, if the monster manages to get to stage 2 at full health, it has the a noticable advantage.
Overall, these changes serve to make Evolve a quicker and more engaging experience and I believe are a positive direction for the game to take.

First things first, in my opinion this game should not be compared to Dark Souls.
As someone who beat all Dark Souls games multiple times, I see why people compare it to Dark Souls and I have to say, that some facts are pretty identical to Miyazakis masterpiece (lets forget Dark Souls 2 for a moment). But this game feels more like a 2D brawler, like Streets of Rage or to be more precise, because of the higher difficulty level, like the old Shinobi or Ninja Gaiden games.

The game has a stunning artwork. Everything looks like a painting. The animations are fluid and the combat system is "inspired" by Dark Souls (damn, looks like this comparison is just too fitting...), means you have a fast depleting stamina bar wich is used for every action taken and a even faster depleting healthbar, if you are not carefull enough. And it
deplete, because the bosses are difficult, have mostly two or more phases and are just freaking awesomely designed. For example an early boss,
looks just terrifyingly epic and has some pretty beautiful and deadly attacks.
The weapons you will use have different move patterns, wich needs to be mastered. But for me, here ends the similarities between Dark Souls and Salt and Sanctuary.
Salt and Santuary plays like a 2D plattformer, stuck into a great RPG-corset. And the battlesystem reminds me somewhat of Devil May Cry, with its fast and light attacks and the heavy but slow attacks and of course the aerial combos. Yes, right - aerial combos. You can knock your enemies up in the air and follow them with some hits and a final blow to the ground, wich is a good way to deal damage while avoiding it.
By the way, wich needs some explanation too is, that if you want to play a sorcerer or cleric:
When you cast spells, your stamina bar will loose some maximum stamina, wich represents fatigue. So you need some "blue health pots" (they are different for each faction) to restore your maximum value.
And lets not forget that this game is a metroidvania, too. You will find items and equipment wich will help you find new ways, even in the starting area, after you have departed for round about 3 hours. So prepare for some backtracking, if you want to reveal all the secrets of the island.

To be honest, this game looks like Dark Souls, feels like Dark Souls, but it plays totally different compared to Dark Souls.
The World itself, with its melancholic feel and artwork wants to be explored. The weapons and skills wants to be mastered. The epic bosses want to be defeated. This game breaths and lives the vibe of the Souls-Games, but it has it own ideas and tweaks to be its own game. If you like the Souls-Games and need a new fix, this will greatly sufficient.
Even if I have not yet completed the game, I am sure that I will remind this game as "Salt and Sanctuary" and not as "the 2D Dark Souls game".
(Edit: After exactly 15 hours of play time I have beaten the game, and it is pretty awesome. The ending will left you want to play more and thankfully there is NG+.Still I need to say, that the last few bosses were much to easy, at least for my build, wich contained heavy armor and a two-handed mace)

an energetic sidescroller beat-em-up which not so much riffs on Dark Souls as rips out its teeth and installs its own glinting replacements in its jaws. they're good replacements. shiny and chrome. in spite of the radically different inputs, I'd say the biggest difference from Dark Souls is just that enemies tend to have small movesets, and those tend to be more intuitive, which I really liked; after enough hours of wildly thrashing skeletons in Souls games, you start to wish enemies were a little easier to learn, a little more predictable. S+S takes great care in that, with enemy telegraphs feeling more like what you'd see in a Castlevania. it tightens things up for a less fridgeperson-speed game.
apart from that, it's 2D Dark Souls, right down to the interface. if you don't like Dark Souls, maybe you'll like it in 2D more. if you do like Dark Souls, you'll enjoy rediscovering it in 2D, and maybe being slightly baffled at -just how far- they go to make their game feel just like it.

I highly recommend this visual novel. While it's "short" enough to finish in a single sitting (about 2 hours to reach every ending if you make use of strategically placed saves or the scene skip system), this works to the game's advantage, as it rarely feels like the story is stagnating as it can in stories that focus on the slice-of-life elements that are often found in longer visual novels.
The pacing is a bit awkward near the beginning, but the majority of the game is very well-written. The only "flaw" I noticed in the game was that two major plot points are so heavily foreshadowed that genre-savvy readers can tell what will happen long in advance, but this isn't always a bad thing.
Fair warning: there is no unambiguously happy ending to this game. All 4 endings involve bad things happening, and even the "Final" ending unlocked from completing the other 3 can be seen as a sad ending.
Another quick thing to note is that while there are elements of romance in this game, it is not a romance-focused visual novel. There are no "character routes" that change who the main character is interested in. If being able to choose the protagonist's love interest is what you're looking for, this may not be the right game.
Bottom line: If you're looking for a visual novel with a well-written and serious story that won't require weeks of reading to finish, this is a good choice.

I'm a big visual novel fan, and I was initially hesitant on purchasing this visual novel due to it being outside of my eastern-origin visual novel comfort zone, but I went against my gut instinct and bought it anyway. After playing the game and achieving all 4 endings I am still not sure about my feelings towards the game.
The beginning of the novel started out at a nice pace, providing insights into the world that Gai was from and the society he was being thrown into. The narration, background art, and music was all stunning during the first 20 minutes of the game, and had me completely hooked.
Unfortunately once the character Sasa was introduced I felt as though I could slowly tell where the story was going, and some of the major plot points became predictable. Suddenly the music and background art became repetitive, and the narration had turned into something more light hearted, with some sort of slapstick humor occurring every other scene.
By the middle of the game I felt like I was reading something entirely different than what I had originally enjoyed. Miyon, who had been a very interesting character to me from the start, became a hollow tsundere, and Gai seemed to become more immature and annoying despite 8 years passing since the beginning of the game. Each ending felt rushed, and I was disappointed with the "true ending" which was only unlocked after viewing the other 3.
Despite everything I have said I would recommend this game to someone new to visual novels, or trying to get into the genre. It is an easy read, and few choices have to be made during the game. I found the concept of "cursed sight" to be enjoyable, but the execution of it was not quite to my tastes. Overall I would give this game a 5/10.

This game is a parody of old school beat-em-up games. A really good parody!
Seriously, on my first playthrough I couldn't stop smiling or laughing even when i tried. If you played this kind of games in the 90s you'll know what I'm talking about when you play this one :P
Anyway, the fighting mechanics are solid; in fact they are better than most old beat-em-ups. There are a lot of  playable/unlockable characters with unique personalities and fighting styles. And, for the most part, their animations are very smooth. The gameplay can be a bit repetitive, but very polished and challenging.
I wish they included more female characters and female enemy npcs. In fact, I wish they had a bigger variety of unique enemies as a whole, especially when it comes to the bosses. Still, by combining different enemy types on each level the game will push you to keep coming up with new strategies.
The one thing that failed to impress me is the level design. Levels are kind repetitive and flat. In the old-school fighting games you were fighting on moving trains, inside buildings, inside elevators, on beaches, in gardens, etc. There were bystanders, destructible barrels and boxes, power-ups and weapons that you could pick up. Not here unfortunately. Most of the time in Streets of Fury you are fighting either in the streets, parking garages, or the subway platform, but the textures and colors are so similar for each location that it feels like you are on the same stage over and over.
Despite the shortcomings, Streets of Fury EX is a great game. Well worth the $10 price. I really want a sequel. (But please improve level design!)

The main pros and cons about this game are quite known by now, therefore I'll make this quick:
+ atmosphere (graphics, soundtrack)
+ coop
- length
- no skill tree
As for me, the missing skill tree is indeed the greatest con, especially when compared to Trine 2 - it yielded a whole load of different solutions for the puzzles, like e.g. conjuring up a plank with Amadeus or use Pontius' shield to cross a gap, to describe a simple case (and Zoya's anti-gravity bubble was a whole new dimension entirely). Of course, in Trine 3 it would not have been possible to include Trine 2's system due to Trine 3's length (taking my time, I 100%-ed the game with a friend in ~8 hours of play-time compared to 25 hours for Trine 2), as the developers simply couldn't have hidden enough of those trinkets you had to collect.
The main novelty - 3D gameplay - was nice to see but just raised too many problems, on the one hand with the controls, on the other hand for the devs as the level design became too expensive, prohibiting a longer game.
The coop experience was good as usual for Trine games; we faced quite a few technical problems (mostly related to poor ping between my friend and myself) but eventually managed to complete the game. At this point, I want to emphasise Frozenbyte's great support team - I had a discussion with one of them, who came up with possible solutions, always replying to my emails within one or two days at most. Apart from multiplayer, I didn't experience any bugs.
Storywise, I liked that the game included a little bit of backstory for both the Trine and the three heroes, the latter being told in short levels parallel to the main story which focused on one character at the time.
In conclusion, I can recommend the game for people who completed (and liked) the first two installments, perhaps not at the full prize of 22€ (for that it does feel too short), but perhaps if it drops to at least 15€ in a sale. That said, I really hope to see a Trine 4 some day in the future, perhaps going back to 2.5D gameplay...

I've been meaning to give this game a try before Dishonored 2 came out.  When Bethesda announced that for a limited time you could get this game free with a preorder of Dishonored 2, I pounced on the offer. This game is really fun! The main appeal of it to me was its dynamic story; it can play out with a lighter tone or a very dark tone depending on how many people you kill.
You have a plethora of different ways to kill the enemy, as well as ways to take them down in a nonlethal manner. You can sneak up on them and put a knife in their throat, or you can put them in a chokehold and knock them out. You can blast them in the face with a shotgun, or put them to sleep with a tranq dart. You can summon a swarm of rats and watch them LITERALLY DEVOUR your enemies... or you can stick to the shadows and slip by the enemies entirely. The amount of tactical freedom in this game was staggering, both with how to dispatch your enemies and how to move through the level.
I'm trying to keep this spoiler free, but as a warning if you want the game to play out in a happier way, I highly, HIGHLY recommend you play as nonlethal as possible for the first half of the game (first 3-4 main missions). From what I could tell, the tone of the story was largely determined in that time. I'm rather disappointed with how depressing my story ended up; you are given a warning at the beginning of the game about the consequences of playing highly lethal, but I didn't take it seriously enough. I unleashed utter carnage in the first few missions and killed all of the main targets. After the first few missions I already started to see the negative effects that my actions were having on the story. I decided I needed to change my ways: the whole second half of the game I played very nonlethal, sparing all the main targets and inflicting very few casualties. But it was too late, and the story went spiralling down despite my best efforts to turn things around.
All in all I loved my time in the world of Dishonored, and am REALLY pumped for the second installment!

Although I got this game for free in the BundleStars giveaway, I am planning on buying the game for friends. This game is incredible for people who have played FPS games for a while on PC. You can truly test your movement, aiming, timing and puzzle skills because believe it or not, this game's got it all.
The game is split up into five worlds, with a varying amount of levels in each world. You'll be getting around 90 levels with individual leaderboards for Global, Friends and Your own scores. If you have a group of friends who love to be competitive, you could have a semi-multiplayer experience, with that one guy getting like 2 seconds ahead of everyone else's times and nobody knowing how.
The idea of the game is to shoot the red box people, which the game refers to as 'baddies'. Once all of them have been defeated, you need to walk into a purple pole to submit your time. The major point of this game for me is how although there is a set out route for general play, there are many shortcuts that you can find. Some are massive whereas some may only shave 0.5 seconds. It's a gold mine for competitive players who want to best their friends. The only rules in this game are that you start at
and you need to reach
having defeated the baddies.
For not even £5, this game is worth it. I don't know how people who class themselves as 'casual' fps players would handle this game, as World 4 and 5 get pretty intense and can also get quite frustrating.
The game has a 3 Star rating system. The three stars are Blue, Green and Yellow/Gold which are obtained through:
Blue - Shooting all the baddies and completing the level.
Green - Clearing the level quickly.
Yellow/Gold - And achieving 100% accuracy.
Although you can achieve all 3 stars in one run, you
need to in order to 100% the level. You can run through it with bad accuracy in order to get a good time for green, then run it again much slower to achieve the yellow/gold star for accuracy.
If I'm not mistaken, when you get a time on the leaderboard and you didn't get all the stars, next to your name you will have a square. However if you get all the stars, your square will be a star shape instead, showing everyone who sees you on the leaderboard as having achieved 100% accuracy along with your good time.
Even if you were casually picking up this game, it's a good way to improve at many things you would need to improve at other FPS.

This game had promise, but never really lived up to it.
The NPCs exist mainly to send you to your next McGuffin - there's no real sense of life from the NPCs, or any feeling that they have a life that exists when you're not looking.
Many things are alluded to, but never actually expanded upon. The mile-wide-inch-deep phrase comes to mind, here.
The breaking of the fourth wall never really makes sense from a narrative standpoint - it feels as if the developers realized they could make a pop-up prompt with text in it, and really wanted to have it wear out its welcome. The dialogue accompanying the window prompts is poorly written. It's reminiscent of someone trying to sound mysterious or imposing, without knowing how to actually accomplish that.
Puzzles are arbitarily placed - they feel like they're there simply for the sake of having a puzzle to impede your progress.
There's no opportunity to bond with the main character. We're force-fed cutscenes about how sad she is, how she had a dream, etc., but we're never given anything more. Her interactions with NPCs (as rare as they are) are flat and add nothing to her as a character.
If you simply want a game that has puzzles placed throughout it, this game is probably for you.
If you want a game that has meaningful dialogue, intelligent narrative, and a sense of something *more*, look somewhere else.

Sniper: Ghost Warrior 2 is many things and the thing that attracted me was the sniping aspect of the game, as the name suggests. Let me explain: this game does look a lot better than its predecessor and that's thanks to Cryengine 3. That being said, most other aspects of this game are average at best. Voice acting is okay...nothing spectacular and the same goes for AI. The story is not really engaging and there is virtually no character development.
Now for the part you're waiting to hear about: the sniping. Few games capture the true feel of sniping (here I'm speculating, having never been a sniper or anything of the sort) as this game does. When you approach a combat situatuon there are several things you must consider: 1.) Your surroundings. Are you exposed or hidden? Do you have a good grasp of the area or are you working on limited information? 2.) Your heartbeat. This effects your shots. To be the most accurate, you must wait for your heartbeat to lower or you will have major bobbing of the scope. 3.) Distance and wind direction. On the lower difficulties, the game will assist you with this aspect. I play on the hardest, this means no assist. You must assess the range and power of the wind and take your shot accordingly. This is where the game shines in my opinion.
Of course, you can just shoot without taking these things into consideration but this retracts from the game I think. Sniper: Ghost Warrior wants you to think like a sniper and if you do, you will be rewarded with the satisfaction of making that perfect shot.

I played EVOLVE's beta before it released and didn't purchase it. Now Evolve Stage 2 releases after layers and layers of DLC and poor business choices as a free to play title.
All the characters are unlockable through in-game progression which is a great change. The problem is the mistrust the company has gathered from its previous practices isn't gone for me personally.
The game is still fundamentally poorly balanced, but it does the best it can in this uneven 4v1 format. The biggest issues are the diverse set of characters and monsters which in many cases don't synergize well, the player down/revive system and the extremely poor gameplay pacing.
Characters often are missing tools still to deal with certain monsters, like the kraken who likes to stay airborn or the wraith who simply sends AI clones at hunters at the press of the button and stalls out games. Beause of the lack of useful controlling abilities in many matchups the game becomes some sort of strange, lopsided damage race between the hunters dealing damage and the monster just trying to down all the players quickly one-by-one.
Downed players can only use their pistol to shoot or self heal if they're medic. Most fights devolve into the monster body camping the player they down because the hunters either lose damage output or important tools to allow them to keep fighting. The game is very punishing to anyone who doesn't manage their jetpack fuel and the game does a poor job of explaining this core concept.
The pacing of the game is improved because of the dome update, but teams are still punished by monsters who get away by basically wasting their time. The only thing to do inbetween fights is use tracking skills and manage your jetpack fuel. There are no secondary objectives in the game worth pursuing. Monsters are encouraged to avoid the hunters until later, so many matches start with several minutes of chasing.
I think the game's concept is poorly executed and  the game's pricing and egregious DLC practices in the past leave a sour taste.
I salute the devs for making that decision. So many good games have died just because out of stubborness. Cheers and to a hopefully bright future!

The changes made thus farr in Stage 2 have caused the game to determined by a number of small skirmishes that happen far more frequently. While the game timer might have been cut in half, the typical game length has been decresaed significantly while actually increasing the number of fights in a game.
I stopped playing Evolve on the Gorgon patch because of dwindling numbers, and back then the game was often decided in 1-2 fights in a typical game. Either the monsters expertly evaded the hunters and hit level 3 or got a good jump on the enemy team at level 2, or the humans would locate and desimate the monster early. While it was certainly possible for the match to go a different direction, this was the typical flow of gameplay in an Evolve match.
In this update, monsters are far less vulnerable stage 1 and due to change dome mechanics often can escape the first dome. During this fight, the players are aiming to get through the monsters armor (that builds and regens much more quickly than ever before) while the monster is aiming to knock players down, build up strikes, and low the dome time before running off again to rebuild armor and hopefully evolve. After that, players seek to keep up with the monster in a chase and if the players can track down the monster before it evolves again they will typically gain an extremely large lead over the monster.
Due to moving a skill point from level 3 to level 1, Stage 2 is now a very large power spike for the monster. While prior to Stage 2 I would of said that the monsters and heros are even at Stage 2, if the monster manages to get to stage 2 at full health, it has the a noticable advantage.
Overall, these changes serve to make Evolve a quicker and more engaging experience and I believe are a positive direction for the game to take.

Out of the morass of Early Access suvival games that glut the market surges The Long Dark; its success attributable to focused design.  Simplicitly is the game's strength as it allows the developers to add depth to the handful of existing mechanics.  On the higher difficulties of sandbox/survival mode merely getting through the days with enough food and warmth is a challenge.  Killing a wolf or a bear an even greater achievement.  Where modern AAA games are centered aroud wish-fulfillment and overpowered player characters, the Long Dark offers a brutal challenge to those looking for one (consider it the Gothic 2 NOTR of survival games).
Although Unity isn't the greatest of engines the aesthetics make up for a lack of graphical fidelity.  It's a watercolor world that is often bleak but still adds just enough to keep things visually interesting.  The world itself is vast with interconnected regions of varying difficulty -- even the small connecting regions have their share of unique landscapes and hazards.  There is also a narrative story mode broken down into episodes but I honestly got bored mid-way through the second.  The real fun is to be had in sandbox, ramping up the difficulty to see how long you can survive against an increasingly hostile world.

I enjoyed reading this visual novel greatly, read it all in one sitting glued to the screen. The novel is very kinetic, with there only being two places where you make a choice, and each choice leads to a different ending, so if you would rather a less kinetic novel, this one probably isn't for you. That aside, onto pros and cons.
Pro's
+The character design was pretty good.
+Miyon is a very endearing character, IMO.
+The overall story was good, but I had a few qualms I have with specific scenes.
+The characters are generally likeable.
+The endings, again aside from a minor qualm with a specific scene, are very good.
+It is clean, no echhi at all. This may be a con for you.
Cons
-Gai uses a lot of modern slang, objects, and imagery in his thoughts and dialogue, it can be a bit jarring given the setting and one of the endings highlights how out of place it is.
-Gai will often crack jokes at the worst times possible, this could ruin immersion in a few scenes, the most notable in particular (ENDING SPOILER) when
-I found myself disagreeing with how a couple of the endings played out, but that is a minor qualm because my disagreement could be in the minority.
-It is too short for me, taking only about 3 hours to get all the endings. That may not be a con to you.
-It is clean, no echhi at all. This may be a pro for you, as it is for me.
All this aside, had the last visual novel I read not been eden*, I would probably have fallen madly in love with this one, as it stands, I merely enjoyed it greatly.

This game gives off such a mixed bag of emotions its insane really. It explores levels of emotion and ties between people that is rarely explored by devs, VN authors or anything at all, the reason for this is that its easy to mess up when going into these sorts of topics, i cant say what they are because they are spoilers.
So Cursed Sight is a bit janky at the start, you may or may not be annoyed as the protagonist starts as a 10 year old, as you can imagine the life of a 10 year old is simple, we dont have much experience and we are a bit immature and indecisive at that age and that is reflected rather well. Pacing issues crop up a lot at the start, mainly for the first thirty minutes while they try and set the foundations down, this is the maining area of improvement id say because its very short, three hours to finish all endings is very short and the longer you know the charecters the more impacting the endings will be.
On the topic of the endings ill say that two are out right stunning, in a good way. Its because the author can string so many emotions into a set of around 500 words and it can be interpreted in so many ways, its the kind of ending that will be left lingering in your head for weeks as you try to fully compile the various effects and outcomes.
That is where this game indirectly elevates itself from a standard issue VN to a masterpiece, you oddly get many hours out of this because of how much you think about it outside of the game, while its short it somehow becomes longer after its finished.
Many animes and VNs have tried to do something like this, we are talking about stuff like Clannad or From the New World.
On the other parts the artstyle and the general artwork is very good and the interface works as it should. The music fits the scenarios very well but its not too memoriable.
In the VN market this is 100% a sleeper hit. I look forward to the future works from this dev because they have set the bar very high for themselves now.

At the end of the day I wish I could recommend Garshasp: The Monster Slayer but there are just too many things that stop me from doing so. This is by far the shortest game I've ever played. The whole game is under 2 hours and that is with cutscenes and the credits. I noticed it was made by a rather small team and I do applaud them for finishing this game.
The visuals are poorly made, especially for a game in 2011. It looks worse than the first God of War game, which is what inspired (to say the least) this game and that came out all the way back in 2005. Even compared to other games released around the same time frame 2009-2011 it still looks very dated. There are quite a few tehnical bugs that needed to be ironed out. There were lots of times when my character model got stuck in the air, couldn't move or I could see thru the map. Also I'm not a huge fan of the character design. The eyes and head looks very odd compared to the rest of the body.
As far as gameplay goes the hack and slash is decent. There are 2 weapons in the game and it's lucky that you start off with the best. Enemies can be grabbed to finish them off and bosses have quick time events set up as their finishers. The sword starts to get pretty boring due to the highly limited combos and abilities and the new mace type weapon you discover later on is just too slow of the enemies and doesn't pack as much of a punch (this is because the sword will be a much higher level at that point).
Breaking up the action are some very basic puzzles and platforming. The puzzles I liked. They were not intrusive, pretty easy and it was a breath of fresh air from the combat. The platforming however is terrible. This is because of the camera angles selected (you cannot swing the camera around as it is locked in place) and because of the unresponsive jump controlls when hanging on a ledge. There's also another section where you slide down the wall which I'm not a fan of to be honest.
The sound is serviceable. The narator does a good job and the effects are what you'd expect. The soundtrack has one memorable track - the theme.
When it comes to the story this game does a really bad job at it. The narator tells you a bit so that you have a faint ideea of what's going on but really all that happens in the game is that the big bad guy kills your brother and goes back home with the magic stick he stole. You chase after him. That's it... No character development, no backstory and just a few hints about the regions you're visiting from the narator.
Overall this would have been much better received if it fixed the platforming issues, worked out the technicall problems and told an actual story. The combat needs a lot more added to it as it is very basic right now.

So basically your a just a sorcerer's apprentice, but you're the only person available who can save the Kingdom. How successful your spells are depends on how much "juice" you have. Most of the time if you're low you can borrow juice from other characters, but at a cost. HOWEVER this game depends more on your ability as a player to unravel the court intrigue. You use the intrigue to advance your own ambitions and there's alot of different options for how the story ends.
Pros:
-Good length.
-Well written characters. I think this is the strongest point of the game. You don't learn alot about the characters, BUT they're utilized REALLY well. They advance the plot and put the focus on your character.
-Court intrigue is cleverly done. Lot's of clues and misdirections, keeps you guessing what's really going on here.
-Juice mechanics and how magic works. Wizard magic Vs Sorcerer magic.
-Good summaries of the information you uncovered when you're talking to other people.
Cons:
-Some of your decisions go no where, gives you a lazy answer and asks you to choose again.
-Mistakes! Sometimes it gives you information you didn't actually acquire.
-I found Fergie (your companion) kinda pointless. Mainly exists to give you more juice, but there's so much more that could have been done with her. For example: There's a part where you follow her glowing foot prints. That was really cool, but the rest of the time you just feed her.
-Sometimes it doesn't let you solve a problem and just gives the answer. I want to puzzle this out for myself, not be given all the answers because I picked the right thing at random.
-It can drag in places.
Final verdict:
-It's not a bad CYOA, but it does drag on and vex me. There's just too many decisions that seem to go no where. And at other times information is given too freely. I think it's one of the weaker CYOA.

I'm an avid customer of Fantasy esque Choice of Game titles and because of this I would like to think that I have a fair grasp on what is enjoyable (in my opinion) and what is not.
The overarching story is grand but not so involved that it outshines the smaller aspects.
The writing itself is predominantly flawless (in terms of grammar) and most importantly it is witty, humorous and entertaining.
The mystery that the plot hinges on is expertly unraveled throughout the game and keeps you on your toes enough so that you can never be sure exactly who is behind it until the later chapters.
It also does a great job at expressing the characters to the point where you feel like you understand them and their motives without learning their entire life story.
Above all, I feel like the choices you make during the game significantly impact the story and the possible achievements confirm this. With every playthrough where you make differing choices your story will change, sometimes slightly and other times it will differ wildly.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the genre.

It's not often these days, unfortunately, that an entirely new, original series will start on a strong and striking note in the gaming mainstream. Many of the best games around today (in the mainstream), it is sad to admit, are reboots and reimagined sequels to established franchises. However, trust Bethesda to deliver a new and exciting addition to the scene with all the trimmings of any other big-budget competitor.
This is a stunning game and it's enormous! And when I hear a game is enormous, I usually imagine an endless sand-box world to explore, which can sometimes not really be that good a thing. Dishonored resists this temptation and opts for a more linear sequence of smaller sandboxes, not disimilar to games like the later Splinter Cell entries. Dishonored of course is first person view, which works for it, but it's just as sneaky. Or you can go for straight up shoot-em-up action if you like. It's up to you.
One of the best things about this game is you can be good at it. And when I say good I mean superhero good. Check YouTube user kekkoSoNicSyNdIcAtE for examples of this. I've never played a game that relies on talent and learning ones craft this much since Street Fighter II. The type of stuff you can pull off will amaze you doing it as much as a person watching it.
The world you are thrown into is diseased, dank, Lovecraftian and dirty and it's so immersive that I could have sworn I came out of it with a layer of grime on me that I couldn't shake for days. The DLC campaigns are superb as well, markedly different to the main game and contribute interestingly to the story and experience as a whole. Most surprisingly as well, considering this game is made by Bethesda who are infamous for designing and writing great games that are hindered with silly little mistakes and flaws, I didn't encounter one singular bug.
Worth every penny.

Abundant with Japanese text and whimsically oversized bric-a-brac, the nonsense world of Lovely Planet could easily be mistaken for the
latest project from Katamari creator Keita Takahashi. Indeed, as a homage to the Japanese director’s work it is reverential to the point of plagiarism, complete with his trademark pastel colours, a nefariously catchy soundtrack and a font lifted straight from Noby Noby Boy. As it turns out, this initial ruse is just the first of the many traps and pranks that developer Quicktequila has gleefully threaded throughout Lovely Planet, constituting a debut effort that loves nothing more than to make a complete fool of the player time and time again. Be it a slyly hidden enemy or that moment when, mid jump, a fatal patch of goo conveniently slips right under your feet moments before you touch the ground, one thing’s for sure: Lovely Planet doesn’t let you get comfy.
It’s not that the game’s particularly complicated. On the contrary, Lovely Planet is about as rudimentary a first person shooter as you’re likely to find in 2014, its blocky geometry and utter dismissal of narrative ambitions rounding off what is essentially a back to basics re-evaluation of the genre. Restricting the player’s abilities to running, jumping and shooting, the game thrusts the mechanical core of first-person shooters to the centre of the agenda, cutting straight to the pavlovian delight of squeezing a digital trigger and amplifying it through increasingly frantic and difficult challenges. Unlike most modern video games which introduce perks, upgrades and additional abilities as the game unfolds, Lovely Planet equips the player with all the tools they’ll need at the get go, consecrating the player’s raw skill as the sole means and measure of their progress. As such, there’s no back doors when it comes to the more challenging levels – it’s a case of get good or give up. This axiom holds true not just across the game’s hundred or so stages but also at the level of individual enemy encounters. Players scarcely have more than a few milliseconds in which to eliminate targets and in later sections of the game, each of these small victories is swiftly interrupted by another incoming missile or deviously placed obstacle. Such hostility affords very little room for improvisation, fostering a highly prescriptive style of play in which just one correct approach to each level seems possible: some levels might as well include a driving line of the likes seen in Forza or Gran Turismo given the dearth of wiggle room available. Thus, Lovely Planet often plays like a puzzle game, the player fumbling towards each level’s “solution” – jump there, shoot that enemy first, then dodge that bullet, etc – through trial and error.
It is in this sense that this cutesy, ostensibly kid-friendly shooter is actually a close relative of Dark Souls, both games offering experiences characterised by copious rehearsal and meticulous execution, not to mention crippling difficulty. But where the layers of complexity in Dark Souls afford the player a certain amount of agency – be it through the choice of weapons, experience point allocation or class selection – Lovely Planet is significantly more restrictive. In some ways this works to the game’s advantage: with just one variable to consider, it’s always clear to the player that their own physical ability is the only barrier to success, making for a more accessible experience than navigating the many esoteric and ambiguous systems which notoriously turn newcomers off Dark Souls. By the same token, however, Lovely Planet is also a less mentally stimulating affair. From Software’s game teaches the virtues of patience and critical play, prompting players to continually question and re-evaluate their approach in response to the situation at hand, cautiously attending to a multitude of competing factors. They become unstuck not through brute force repetition but by examining every angle of the problem until something clicks, reaching a bespoke solution all their own. In Lovely Planet however, there is little mystery about how a level should be beaten, with enemies often approaching you head on or placed helpfully within your immediate line of sight. Thus, the player’s only option then is to run through the level over and over, until finally they perform each step of the developer’s dance with absolute precision. As with real life choreography, the end product is often breathtaking, and with enough practice the player can find themselves pirouetting through levels, dispatching foes with delicate touch of a virtuoso. But such flawless runs are possible only after long sessions of arduous repetition, and at the point when the player’s interaction with the game has become entirely automated. Simply put: where Dark Souls is a mindful experience, Lovely Planet is often a mindless one.
As difficult and repetitious as Lovely Planet gets however, rarely is it frustrating. It’s hard to hold a grudge against a game so whimsical,
especially when it delivers even the most nefarious of its tricks with such stone-faced innocence. Indeed, it’s the wealth of charm exuded throughout Lovely Planet in tandem with its highly simplified mechanics that solidify it as a thoroughly accessible introduction to the “masocore” genre, capturing the cathartic rush of accomplishment that draws players to such punishing games while avoiding the usual dark imagery and reams of potentially overwhelming minutiae. Indeed, it’s dichotomies like this that define Lovely Planet – the balance of frustration and satisfaction, the interplay of skill and memory, the cuddly visuals disguising hardcore difficulty – and hence amount to an inevitably polarising experience. While the ecstatic hit of finishing a particularly tricky level is certainly satisfying, whether such fleeting contentment is worth all the preceding effort will vary from player to player, as will the entertainment value of a experience which relies so much upon repetition. Still, players will undergo a very palpable sense of growth, able to pull of feats of skill seemingly impossible when just starting out. Whether or not this transformation carries any meaning outside of the game itself is debatable, but more important is the feeling it evokes, coating Lovely Planet with a sugary sweet sprinkling of gratification that some will find hard to resist.

IMHO, this is the best "Go Straight" beat-em-up after Streets of Rage Remake, but that has the advantage of already having a template, music, sprites, etc to work from. Streets of Fury, however, has a far better combo system! Seriously, the amount of variety and personalisation of the combos is a joy. It's also taken a leaf or two from the Saturn/XBLA classic Guardian Heroes, which is probably the other member of the "Best Scrolling Beat-em-ups Trilogy".
Yeah, the graphics can look a bit dodgy a first glance - but look at the animation! The more you look at and play with the characters, the work more you see has gone into making some excellent game mechanics. The music's great, there's loads of interesting and diverse characters, 4-player co-op/versus, unlockables, a couple of fun modes, etc and from what I hear, there's more content in the pipeline... This won't convert people who hate the genre, but there's definitely something quite pure and essentially videogamey about a game like this that a lot of people will enjoy - definitely recommended.
