Garshasp really wants to be the God of War. He's even been practicing Kratos' trademark scowl of perpetual anger.
Unfortunately for him he's a little like that friend who thinks they're a brilliant singer, only you'd rather force macaroni noodles inside your ears than listen to them belt out off-key renditions of what at some point where probably real songs but have morphed into unimaginable abominations through a voice you can't seem to escape. Garshasp is clumsy at his best of times, broken at his worsts, and always as entirely unpleasant as his almost reptilian face which firmly states that no, we are not and will never be friends (he's kind of an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like that).
The Monster Slayer is an action game that plays like a bunch of awkward breakdancers trying to murder each other but somehow only managing to land a hit every third try. Garshasp's movements are flashy, but annoyingly slow and prone to completely breaking the already poor hit detection, with hits and characters clipping through each other constantly as everyone flails around madly until they run smack into one of the omnipresent and aggressively restrictive invisible walls.
Even when combat is "working" it's still essentially broken, with your character being entirely overpowered and enemies only being a threat so much as their outrageously large health bar threatens to put you to sleep as you monotonously mash the same buttons waiting for them to eventually die. The fixed camera is as pleasant and functional as a handicam held by someone who has had a few too many drinks, either obscuring platforms, breaking the environment, or causing you to puke as it stutters around erratically.
And naturally there are the moments when the game simply gets a little fed up with having to even partially function and decides it's going to chop your framerate in half, or freeze up during an important jump, or just crash entirely because damn it being a game is hard and Garshasp has had enough of it! Frankly I've had quite enough of him as well.
Please don't call. Forget this ever happens. I'll be busy with drowning myself in booze hoping I can do the same.

h1] Great God of War clone on PC!![/h1]
Garshasp is an Indie Game developed in Iran by a small group of people. It tells the story of Garshasp , an ancient persian warrior who wants to avenge his brother's death by an evil warlord. This is a by the numbers hack and slash game not afraid of showing it's God of War influences. In fact , David Jaffe had an indirect role in the development of this game.
The game is 5 hours long in average. I've got yet to see if it has any new game plus mode or extra features once you beat it. However , it can take up to 10 hours or more to complete all achievements the game includes.
When it comes to performance and pc specific features. For an Indie game , I would say it does the job. It includes a launcher where you can toggle some settings like texture quality , vsync , HDR and a couple more. Also you can include any resolution previously set with Nvidia Control Panel in case you want to downsample the game.
It has some glitches and stuttering /FPS drops from time to time (specially when there are many enemies on screen) but nothing too alarming or gamebreaking. I've had yet to have a CTD.
As a sidenote , the game includes dubbing to many languages (you can even play in Persian for extra epichness) but I haven't seen any subtitles option.
Graphically speaking , it looks like a cross between a PS2 and a Seventh Gen title. Better looking than PS2 era God of War titles , but nothing special. The music and artstyle are really good though and the fit the mood of the game.
All in all I believe this is a title worth recomending. We need some more hack and slash games on PC and games like this one and Marlow Briggs will always be welcomed on the platform. I would say this game is a steal for 5 USD or less : AA production and very entertaining.

If you're reading this, then you probably already know that the controls in this game are convoluted and imprecise, and that the art style is a bit strange (Garshap, in the cut scenes,
).  You probably also know about the cheestastic writing and voice-overs. None of that bothers me. I can live with it all and, while I'm not familiar with the Persian legend upon which this is based, Garshasp has a Cimmerian feel to it. Being a Conan fan, all of that cheesy goodness works in the game's favor for me.
But, oh man, that camera. That insanely bad camera that goes where it wants, when it wants and, over which, you have zero amount of control.  It's actually a bunch of static cameras placed in odd locations without any thought as to how that placement will affect gameplay, and there is no logic to it. This isn't a racing game, and I'm not watching a replay, so why not have it over my shoulder, like any other action game?  Why am I sometimes running toward the camera? This isn't Crash Bandicoot 2, and I don't see a polar bear chasing me, so what gives? You're seriously telling me this didn't bother anyone while they were building the game?
But even that isn't a deal breaker for me; I've played plenty of games with poor cameras, and I'm sure I'll play plenty more. No, the deal breaker for me is that the developers don't care about the player. Period. This is evident at the first boss, who crashes through a wall in front of you (one of the few times the camera is actually behind you, where it should be). He
Yet, after the battle, the game
(presumably hoping you won't notice the GIGANTIC HOLE IN THE WALL) and won't allow you to walk through it. Why? Because the developers have decided they want you to climb the ladder behind you instead.
Nope, sorry. Forget this game; life is far too short. God bless anyone for sticking with it as long as they did. This "developers vs players" ideal is just poor design, plain and simple. This ill-will could have been avoided by simply having the wall collapse behind the boss when he crashed through it, but apparently it wasn't important.  Instead, it's a slap in the face to people who paid for the game, and if the developers are sticking their collective middle finger up at me this early, I'm not sticking around long enough to see how bad it gets later. Not recommended.

Well, butter my biscuits, if you'd have told me that Evolve will ever have more than 100 players playing again at the same time, I would've called you a witch and burned you on the stake. This is a story about how Evolve, a game that was deemed a massive failure, managed to turn it all around with one decision that boosted their players LITERALLY hundredfold, going from 80 to 8000 within the first hours it launched.
Evolve is a great game. I've always said that, it's why I bought the game, it's why I've tried playing it here and there even though I knew it was already dead and people jumped ship. The only shortcoming it had was in terms of pricing. Granted, you need to say that this was likely pushed by the publisher, not the developers themselves, at a time where microtransactions were getting inreasingly popular in games, and publishers kept wanting to know "How high can we go?" Well, turns out that Evolve was the prime example of "too high", because their massive pricing for both the game and the two(!) Season Passes.
Gameplay-wise, you could argue that the game is repetitive, but that's hardly an argument these days when MOBAs and the like are so popular, because repetition is not actually a bad quality, it's just something that some people dislike. You can argue about balance all you want, but at the end of the day it's a sheer impossible task to balance a 1v4 asymmetrical multiplayer game, that has over 100 different combinations of hunter and monster matchups, each with their own abilities. But, we're not here to really talk about much of the gameplay, because the game's been out for a while and everyone that hasn't lived under a rock for the past year has had the possibility to look up some footage of the game and whatnot. What we're here today is to discuss why this game went from zero to hero.
Free to play. That's a decision that no company makes lightly, because the sheer amount of difference in numbers it can make is astounding, both in the amount of people playing, and in the amount of money you can make. Free to play titles are inherently different from bought titles, as one would assume, the main difference being that they're free. So, straight up, no 60 bucks needed to jump into the game, just download the game and you're good to go. The actual amazing thing is, that they decided to make ALL of their content available with in-game currency. That's right, none of the content that was previously behind a paywall is locked away, which means that you've got this absolutely great game all to yourself.
But where's the catch? Well, actually, there is none. I know, right? At least right now, there is literally no downside to playing the game, as there is actually, factually no "Pay to win" content in the game, because you cannot buy in-game currency with real-life money AT ALL. That's right, this is the most free to play game that will ever exist. I'm aware this is likely a temporary situation to see how things will work out, and given that it's a beta, a lot of things can change, but as long as they only ADD a real-life money option and do NOT take away the ability to unlock everything by play, I can hardly find any reason to not play the game. Unless, of course, you don't like it.
Granted, it's free to play, which means you now follow a free weekly rotation of hunters and monsters until you unlock yourself some stuff, but other than the fact that it might be a little grindy, nothing's stopping you from getting the full game experience. Unlike, you know, before. Where it cost like more than 100 bucks to get everything in the game.

TL;DR:
An excellent 2D game inspired by the Souls and Castlevania series as many mentioned already.
Melee is fun and viceral, magic melts faces and is satisfying once you get used to the aiming system, and I didn't try archery yet so I can't say anything about it.
As the game progresses, some abilities are unlocked that are used to access areas which weren't accessible beforehand.
Dodging isn't as bad as some people say, it is just different than what we're used to from Souls game, especially about timing and "pushing then dodge" mechanic.
Music has a lot of electric guitar in it, so this can be a plus if you like that.
Atmosphere is gloomy which fits game's theme well.
Difficulty is overall well balanced in my opinion, as challenge seemed to steadily increase with gameplay experience, making areas and bosses feel evenly difficult (actual difficulty vs perception of it).
Weapon ranges can be visually tricky at times since they hit farther than the tip of the weapon. Range is actually determined by the "slash" visual effect rather than weapon's length itself. Just need to gauge distance accordingly.
No voice acting. That would have been a nice additional touch, but considering Ska Studios' size, it is understandable.  In the other hand, might as well have none at all than having laughable voice acting some triple-A developpers dare to feed us with.
Price tag is very reasonable for the game's high quality.
Overall, a nice game that is worth buying. Should appeal to people who were craving for a new Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, and/or fans of Souls series that also like platformers like Metroid/Castlevania.

What a beautifully crafted game. After years of playing first person shooters with the same mechanics, playing a game so thoughtfully made is such a treat.
I bought this early access and had tons of fun messing around with the survival mode. Now that the game has been officially released with the campaign, the update offers even more in terms of plots, survival and exploration.
The graphics are simple, but simple is all you need to convey the quiet, haunting and bleak nature of the cold.
The landscapes and dynamic weather offers a constantly changing environment that will affect your gameplay. Packs of roving wolves in the campaign force you to change tactics or routes, and the temptation that abandoned buildings offer you is too good to pass up as you are forced to scavenge for anything usable.
The campaign so far has been excellent. I spent countless hours in the first episode, meeting the old lady's demands. I spent hours building reserves in key areas so that I had safe places awaiting me should I require detours. And after having met all of her demands, I happily grabbed her daughter's resources and rappelled down the mountain.
I evaded death at every corner, staving off hunger by eating scraps and lighting fires in blizzards. Finding caves in -25 degree weather made playing this game a taut survival. I've never been so happy to find lumps of coal before.
And then when I finally emerge out of the caves, after having limped forward on sprained ankles with hypothermia, I'm greeted with the scene of a bear attacking an old man who yells at me to shoot it.
BANG.
Credits roll.
WTF?
...........
Episode 2......
!!!!!!!!!!
The survival modes I found fun and challenging. The bleak landscape offers small clues here and there about useful items. The developers made available certain abandoned areas that literally beg to be explored. When I was out in blizzards, I was constantly intrigued as to what I would find if I continued further. At times I was rewarded with unique items, others, with death. Plan appropriately.
The atmosphere in the game is excellent. Walking around, searching through rubble in the abandoned dam was creepy as well with all sorts of ambient noises. Stumbling through a blizzard only to come across an abandoned building was interesting in what it might potentially offer.
What I loved most about this game was the balance between reality, a certain demise if needs weren't met with the sprinkling of hidden loot across the maps.
An incredibly fun and lifelike game that is unpretentious in its reality. Makes me want to leave the city and live in the wild on my own.
Worth the retail price.

Trine 3 is the first in Trine series to be featuring a platformer in 3D. It's beautiful, as usual, and as to be expected from Frozenbytes. The scenery is breathtaking, and given that this is 3D makes it even better. And the soundtracks, of course, Akki really is a leading example how a composer should've been -- nothing less than magnificent. Soundtrack is included in Trine 3 folder as 192 kbps files (quite disappointing though they're not lossless, but better than nothing).
The next point... gameplay, unfortunately for gameplay... is very lacking. Try using Zoya's arrow in battle, you'll be flabberglasted. The platformer essence is still there, although nerfed in many ways. In battle it's Pontius' chance here to shine, though, the other two are quite useless. Oh and the grappling hook experience is quite atrocious unlike when it was still 2D-platformer. Quite possibly this is major negative points that many players hate. Game length is also very short. To be quite honest, despite the missing features and cliffhanger ending, I still think it's a decent game.
While it's less than ideal, I have seen the efforts of Frozenbyte to patch and improve the game despite their hard situations. I guess not many developers would have done so if they had been in FB's situation.
For Trine 4, I hope they can incorporate back the older features like tech trees/skills like before.
Still, I prefer to recommend the game, for me to give them negative would hurt the developer unnecessarily. I think they've heard the feedback from us playerbase loud enough, and they'll try to amend it. Remember how they treated older Trines and gave updates many times? Let's give them a chance.
Looking forward to Trine 4.

While the addition of the third dimension can be a hassle at times, Trine 3 is another great game in my opinion. Not as good as either of it's predecessors but still mostly enjoyable. The game is great. Still has same enchanting visuals and narrative as before.  It does feel a bit less polished in 3D movement, but it is still very delightful. In my opinion it has all the charm of previous installations and I'm glad developers tried something new - so few do experiment with their franchises. The main "board" screen with level selection felt appropriate, and the book flipping mechanic in some of the later levels was pretty and cool. Side missions felt like a little delicious extra on top of main campaign. All in all I enjoyed trine 3 a bunch, and can easily recommend it to other people, just be aware that due to budget constraints main story wasn't finish so don't expect nice wrap up there.
I also feel that other reviewers are being unjust, declaring that game is:
* buggy - obviously this may vary, but it hasn't been true in my case, I haven't encountered any issues. Game runs smoothly from techincal side. It seems to require kb+m to setup controls, but after that is completely playeable with the controller.
* short - yes the story was cut short, which I think devs were upfront about. But it is still full 6+ hours of single player campaign and missions, that's longer than some AAA titles these days.
* need to collect trineangles to unlock levels - uh, I'm not really sure what the idea is, but you have to really mess up to be forced to redo any levels. If you don't try to rush them down like a speed run - collecting enough trineangles is easy even on the first go.

It's a shame the devs ran out of money to finish the game, because the 3D Platforming feels really good, and the game looks just as trine should.  I really hope an expansion wrapping up the story comes along, and rather than tearing this game to shreds, I think we should try and support the devs as much as we can.

An interesting game if a bit shallow. Not so much roleplaying as you are pegged into the role of what passes for a 20 somthing year old in today's world. The "game" is well put together if a bit bland and it's blandness might speak to some going through a similar situation. Overall 6 out of 10.

Unless I'm mistaken, this short interactive novel would appear to have been made with Twine (the free and easy-to-use software program, not a sturdy piece of string). As Twine projects go, it's a little spiffier and more ambitious than most, though not exactly by a landslide.
It has no sound, only the occasional lovingly hand-drawn illustration, and opts for the bog-standard blue links to indicate where you can click next to progress/make choices (though in all fairness this may have been a well-thought-out aesthetic decision, rather than just default laziness). The story it tells is relatable if unexceptional, and there's absolutely nothing wrong with the author's command of the written word (always a nice thing in text adventures, I'm sure you'll agree). The font is perhaps a tad on the small side - especially if you have a small monitor - and almost entirely devoid of frills, but it gets the job done. There's a couple of minor spelling errors, but nothing you'd fail an essay over. And it has self-deprecating Morrissey and Joy Division references, which is certainly never a bad thing in my book.
One definite negative is that it doesn't appear to have a save function. I mean, yes, it's short - under thirty minutes kind of short - but a save would still be preferable. And there isn't a HUGE amount of agency, but perhaps enough to make it replayable, should your first run-through of the storyline prove sufficiently intriguing. I personally gave it a quick second spam-through, and it does have some decidedly divergent paths, should you find the possibilities compelling enough (I didn't, but then again, I'm no longer in my twenties, and largely lost interest in the perils of the "dating world" some time ago).
The biggest issue for many, I suspect, will be the price. Is it worth three dollars? Honestly, I think the dev was pretty brave to ask ANY price for what is on offer here, much less more than 99c. My advice were they a friend would have been to chuck this one up for free, solidify your "audience", and make the next one longer and as cheap as you can possibly make it on Steam (i.e. 99c)!
There's certainly nothing overtly incompetent or hate-worthy here...on the whole, a rather "nice first effort" indeed. "Underwhelming" is perhaps the nastiest insult you could throw its way. I certainly wouldn't recommend it at full price to anyone bar the most ferociously Twine-curious, and would advise even sale-hunters to keep their expectations low. (Unless you're recently single and feel like a touch of the straw which broke the camel's back: an optimistic view of relationships this sure-as♥♥♥♥♥♥ain't, so if you're looking for that extra little push over the brink, this may well be the product to do it.)
Verdict: 6.5/10.

20something is a touching interative fiction game that cuts to heart of the world of dating and intimacy for a young man in his early twenties. Scenes are told through a highly relatable stream of consciousness, humorously interwoven with 'bad but good' action movies, 'bad but good' parties and 'bad but good' dates. Amongst the soul searching and eerily familiar romantic encounters, the story also touches on mental health issues and alcohol abuse, two topics young men often feel unable to talk about in healthy and productive ways, and are helpful to see represented in media. If you're are a fan of interactive fiction or indeed anyone who has navigated the perils of online dating, fumbling encounters or long awkward moments, then I highly recommend this game.

There is nothing a player should relish more in Dishonored than the opportunity to stare down the barrel of a loaded gun. Facing the very real, very quick possibility of being shot opens up a vast, bloody rainbow of possibilities, and there’s very little that the imagination can conceive of that Dishonored does not provide the tools to achieve. You could stop time, and simply step out of the way. Or even better, stop time, possess the shooter, and walk him into the path of his own bullet. You could stop the bullet itself, load it you’re your own gun, and shoot back before your enemy reloads. You could teleport behind the enemy and shove a blade through his last meal. Or strap a bomb to his back before he even realizes the bullet missed.
To don the mask of Corvo Attano--a master assassin--is to invite a freedom of ingenuity the likes of which, one console generation and an actual Thief reboot later, remains an elusive, rare thing. Dishonored is a game that felt ahead of the curve three years ago, and only just now feels right at home. That just barely excuses just how little work went into improving Corvo’s second go-around.
There is certainly an argument to be made that Dishonored didn’t really need anything new to get a re-release. To those who will be taking their first voyage into Dunwall, Dishonored will be a revelation. On paper, it’s little more than a simple revenge tale: The Empress of a far away, sea-faring, steampunk kingdom has been assassinated, and you, her royal protector, has been framed for the murder. While rotting in jail, you're visited by a Satanic figure called The Outsider. He gives you supernatural powers, which will help you exact vengeance and liberate Dunwall from the usurpers who rule in the Empress’ stead.
The devil is in the details. This isn’t just an Assassin’s Creed situation of moving to the proper vantage point to make a kill, escaping and awaiting further orders after the coast is clear. Every murder and every mercy affects the world, brings fear or hope to the populace, feast or famine, peace or disease. While it is possible to barge through Dunwall, slaying everything in your path with extreme prejudice, you’ll find the task at hand becoming a bleak ordeal. It becomes a story of desperate public servants shattering under the weight of an unyielding zombie plague with no cure, of a frightened populace that shrieks at the sight of your mask, where recovery is impossible, with a new pile of corpses replacing the twice-killed ones faster than they can be removed.
Dishonored isn’t quite an open world game, but the streets, alleyways, and decadent mansions are so dense with traversable nooks and paths the relative linearity of the stages is completely obscured. It also helps that there isn’t a side mission in the entire game that doesn’t serve a greater purpose rather than just to fill empty space. The focus, instead, is in making the world feel lived in, practical, and used. Unlike most steampunk, Dunwall doesn’t feel sterile, like a brand new appliance that just happens to have people living in it, but like a real city that has seen life, death, crime and providence. The city runs on its whaling industry, and the evidence of how its affected life is virtually everywhere. These are all important lessons in world-building many a developer has yet to truly learn, making Dishonored look like even more of a step forward. It’s a game with flaws, for sure. The final third of the game is rather bland and flavorless compared to all the little captivating touches that grace the rest. The DLC switches gears from Corvo to rival assassin Daud, and it’s a very different feel, though on average, it’s not necessarily better (though the trippy and introspective second episode, The Brigmore Witches, fares better than the rather procedural and dry Knife of Dunwall). Still, the main event is a marvel of unique, engrossing game design.
What I´m left with here is the best PC version of Dishonored that money can buy--and make no mistakes, that still makes this the best version of a fantastic game—but as a re-release on systems far more capable than their predecessors, this is a perfunctory release that doesn’t justify the price tag except out of sheer convenience. There’s no in between here; there’s either every reason to pick up this version if you've never played Dishonored, or no reason whatsoever if you've donned Corvo's mask before.
~cmaexi 15.06.2016

For a first time effort, Richard Seabrook has done an incredible job with creating a compelling game.
While it wasn't perfect, no-one's first game ever is. But I am impressed with the quality of this venture, and sincerely look forward to his next projects.
PROS:
* Music. One thing I love is how fitting the music is for the situation. Whether you're trying not to be found, or whether you are breaching a Combine base, the music just feels so right for the situation.
* Backstory. I'd never really played Opposing Force, and was going in blind with who Shepherd would be. But after playing this game, and seeing his flashbacks to his life before this, I feel like I've known him for as long as I have Gordon Freeman.
* Execution and engagement. Not everybody can make a good game, but Richard Seabrook is not one of those people. I was invested the whole time, and never once thought about getting up and taking a break.
CONS:
* Missing captions. It's hard to tell what exactly the flashback sequences are saying, and the blaring siren doesn't help, either.
* Contrast. Early on, the game was way too dark to make anything out, and later, it was just so brightly lit, I thought my retinas would melt.
* More hints on where to go. The game, while beautifully made, is not exactly well laid out. I remember hunting for a vent for about twenty minutes trying to dodge antlions, before realizing that it was on the wall, requiring some climbing.
Overall, this is an incredible mod to an already amazing game, and I guarantee it won't be a purchase you'll soon regret.

I am putting a thumbs up on this game but there are some issues.
1. OK, first of all this is not worth $10 at least at this point, when you consider the free mods out there with high replay value. But I will not compare this to free mods. If this game is on sale, pick it up if it's at $5 or less, the way it is right now.
2. There are differences between Freeman and Shephard. To be a true Opposing Force sequel, Shephard must start off with the wrench and not the crowbar. I mean, that's just basics.
3. The game is very repetitive. Combine computers everywhere, pushing the same button to open door after door of combine soldiers. It's a prison, I get it. Prisons are built very much in this way, and Nova Prospekt is probably no different. However, teleporting to different areas, such as Xen (which only lasted 5 minutes) should bring about some surprises. This game does not.
4. The Valve support and greenlight convinced me to buy this game. I would have probably skipped on it knowing what I know now. Talking as if this is some sort of Opposing Force sequel is a good way to get someone to buy this game, but when you play it, you realize that it does not give you the feeling that it really is a sequel or even related to Opposing Force at all. The voice acting does barely OK, however there is more pointless trash talking than actual Half-Life semantics going back and forth.
The game's soundtrack, overall level design (besides the massive amounts of combine computers), and trading cards save the game from getting no review at all from me. The soundtrack is awesome, and fits well within the gameplay. The overall cubemap design is decent, minus the lack of creative mechanics within the map design (such as repetitive computer buttons from room to room). Also, as I am writing this review, trading cards are available and I hope they come frequent considering the price of this HL2 mod rehash. I will reboot a new game on this at least once a year to acquire trading cards simply because I bought the game, and that's about it. If and when this game sees some available achievements, the replay value of Prospekt will grow.

I highly recommend this game to any Half-Life fan with a few hours to kill.
Praise:
- Well-designed and creative environments. The author does a good job of balancing the need for interesting combat arenas with creating the feeling that these are real, working facilities. There's also a surprising amount of new assets.
- The vast majority of the game is spent fighting Combine Overwatch troops, who I personally find more interesting than any other enemy type in the game.
- Conforms to established Half-Life canon in all respects, as far as I can tell.
- Balanced combat challenges mixed with occasional environmental puzzles. Lots of big, set-piece encounters. I was playing on easy, and I only died once (due to my own stupidity). Some of the larger battles would be quite murderously difficult on Hard, so there should be a good challenge if you like that sort of thing.
- Weapons and ammo are fed to the player with great care, forcing you to vary your weapon use. This keeps things interesting.
Criticism:
- Voice acting is adequate at best. The Combine radio messages and the Vortigaunt dialogue is actually well-done. The problem lies with the periodic audio flashbacks where Shepard remembers times with his fellow Marines before Black Mesa. Before starting to play Sniper Ghost Warrior 2, my expectations were very high. I was expecting it to at least match the original game in terms of gameplay features. Unfortunately it failed to do this, and ultimately failed to meet the standards of the Cry Engine 3 (one of the most powerful engines currently available).
Similar to the way I felt before and after I started playing the game, I’ll start with the good things and move on to the bad things and finish with the best part.
Sniper Ghost Warrior 2 does the sniping aspect very well.  There aren’t too many FPS games out there that focus on sniping, or at least, there aren’t any out there that have this much depth to sniping. The developers have done a superb job at creating a realistic sniping experience. Various measurements need to be taken before lining up the perfect shot and different locations mean different adjustments. Distance, wind, and even the curve of the bullet need to be taken into consideration. This makes sniping enemies very enjoyable and varied, depending on conditions.
The developer, City Interactive seemed to have focused perhaps
on the sniping aspects of the game, because that’s about all that’s good about it :/ I’ve noticed a lack of gameplay features that were present in the previous game such as, grapple hooking your way to high places, picking up enemy firearms, using throwing knives to take out enemies. The gameplay revolves completely around using your sniper rifle to well……..snipe, and using your P220 pistol if things get up close and personal. The P220 features in all three of the chapters as a sidearm, but the primary sniper rifle changes depending on what chapter you’re playing. Apart from finding the occasional enemy Dragunov rifle, you have no other weapons to find or interact with.  This seriously upset me.
Level design is another issue with Sniper Ghost Warrior 2. The levels are detailed, but I feel this is just a way of disguising how painstakingly linear they are. Each chapter has you following a set path with a few open vistas to shoot enemies from a far. The vistas do offer fairly detailed locations to find and shoot enemies, but ultimately they just serve as complex shooting galleries and you never actually get to explore them. The levels are also too small. I find myself disappointed whenever I round a corner, only to realise that I’m in an even smaller house than the last one I was in. I was really hoping for a more open ended level design, but City Interactive has decided to play it safe and keep things way too simple.
Lastly, I’ll talk about the multiplayer. This is the most surprising part about Sniper Ghost Warrior 2. It’s actually a decent addition to the game. I was highly expecting an equally lack luster experience online as I did with my campaign experience, but it turned out better than expected. Sniping is really the only feature in multiplayer, but it’s easier to enjoy due to the lack of a forced story or other cheesy scripted events. The multiplayer levels are really well designed, plenty of places to hide, plenty of choices for rifles to use, and plenty of intensity that should have been more common in the single player. Looking around the maps for enemies is a long and tiring process, but once you find one and line up the perfect shot, it’s all worth it. Hearing the bullet whizz past your head as another sniper takes shots at you, forcing you to relocate before it’s too late, that’s an awesome feeling too. It’s a nice break from the normal run and gun shooters out there, where the SMG class is king. In this case, less is more.
Overall I did enjoy Sniper Ghost Warrior 2. While it didn’t meet my expectations, it still does sniping better than any other game I’ve played. I can see myself continuing to play the multiplayer, while waiting for the DirectX 11 patch to be released. I might get 10 more hours out of it if I’m lucky. If you’re a sucker for FPS games like me, this will be worth your time. If not, then you won’t be missing much.

I usually don't buy early access games, and while this game did not do anything to make me more inclined to look closer at other early access titles in the future it is certainly an entertaining game all things considered and a recommended buy.
If you were the kind of player who focused on building beautiful structures and cities rather than elaborate trade routes and combat strategy in previous city-building games, Stonehearth is for you. The art is adorable and you'll feel immersed in the daily lives of your "hearthlings". With practice you can build beautiful structures and the online community has created tons of downloadable blueprints if you are not artistically inclined. It is wonderful to see your small settlement grow, and depending on your chosen game mode it can feel very rewarding to finally overcome the struggles of providing food, shelter, and protection, and see your village flourish.
I say village, because while the game doesn't seem like it it can run quite sluggishly even on higher end rigs when villager count starts ticking over a certain amount. The developers seem active enough but two years in early access is a bit worrying. The game has a few game-breaking bugs, and even though they can be worked around to some extent they are annoying for sure. The building mode takes a bit to get used to, and one of the many current bugs can make it difficult to build larger structures. Hopefully, the developers will not abandon this game - it has great potential, and in time it may become one of the golden titles of its genre.

The Long Dark, developed by Hiterland Studio, is an exclusive single-player experience. It is a very lonely, challenging, first person survival game. Wandering a large, forlorn and en-wintered area of northern Canada in first-person, your existence is reduced to a daily quest to survive the elements. Everything you do presents a potential risk/reward dicotomy; simply travelling from one safe shelter to another can become a life or death proposition.
The sound and graphics quality are excellent and create a very emotional atmosphere. The art is georgeous. Its style seems influenced by comicesque, mid 20th century graphic-novels; yet it portrays the game themes well, never undermining the premise of the 'reality simulator' genere. There are occassional grapics and physics glitches, but they are infrequent. The game is very stable and robust in its current version. It continues to receive excellent patching and upgrades from the developers.
The player interface is minimalist, in keeping with the 'survival sim' theme. Inventory and other stats are easily navigated. Hunting game is well simulated using scavaged primitive tools, or (if you are lucky) a crappy old iron sights rifle. As expected, combat (with wolves, bears and - recently - moose) is not a 'twitch-fest'; it is designed as an environmental event - albeit one that requires some button mashing and invokes a fair degree of stress! Creature behaviour is well modeled, however the AI of 'fleeing' animals does need some attention.
The game has a VERY well developed free-play 'survival' mode. Despite no missions or NPC intergration, every day you will have to set new goals to obtain food, shelter and warmth. At the highest difficulty settings you will need to push hard just to stay alive, let alone thrive! Cold, hunger and injuries are a constant menace. Crafting is 'realistic', consuming significant time, energy and relevant resources. This realism makes starting a fire or even repairing clothes a task worth contemplating! Mistakes are unforgiving and death is permenant!
The Story Mode is in development, with two parts released at this time. It explores the background leading to the Long Dark, the collapse of the local communities and the relationship between the two protagonists (Will and Astrid). NPCs are incorporated into the storyline for relevant narrative, however voice acting is pretty sparse. Expect this aspect of the game to undergo significant further development.
Overall, The Long Dark offers a great single-player experience. It is a very sold survival simulator, set in a beutiful and interesting environment. The care and thought put into its development is a real tribute to Hinterland. If you enjoy personal goal-setting, exploring and extreme, viseral survival challenges you will love TLD.

So, I just finished this game and.. It wasn't that good.
Firstly, the game is more-or-less built to be played with a controller. The camera-work is neat and all, but it moves around in such a way that just doesn't feel natural with keyboard/mouse. Which is weird, as it wasn't released on console (...According to Wikipedia) and it still has "save-points" and the like, which are(/were) typically signs of a console game.
I played the game over three sessions, the first two of which lasted only half an hour/quarter of an hour, simply because I got bored of the game. The button-mashing was too much and the combat wasn't that great. Only in the last session did I "truck through" and play for a whopping hour and a half, and then the game was done.
The combat is nothing to speak of, with just a handful of combos (of which 'block+jump', 'block+interact', 'block+light-attack' and 'block+heavy-attack' being the majority) and a few (quite satisfying!) finisher-moves, that boiled down to either weird QTEs (which were, at times, notoriously hard to pull off because the game'd be too quick to register your first "command" and then you'd fail the QTE) or automatic KO's.
The bosses are, at first, interesting - but their moveset is way too easy to figure out, and then they become ludicrously easy.
The graphics are subpar, with a lot of visual artifacts. Animations are, at times, pretty wonky and there are places where it's possible to see through the terrain.
The camera moves by itself, which is probably for the best w.r.t. the graphics of the game.
The "levels" were very linear, although there are secrets (health-increasing bitbobs) that can be found by "exploring" a few hidden crannies here and there. The checkpoints seemed spread out quite generously, except for the few places where a mistake in your platforming would mean death.
Speaking of the platforming, it was fairly dull and easy - with the controls being the major reason of dying.
The story is okay-ish, but I could not stand the voice-work and the constantly repeating "combat track", although the three/five-ish instrumentals were pretty decent, they certainly lacked variety.
As an aside: The achievements seem fairly buggy. They (seemingly) only "count" your latest playthrough, as I got the "complete the game with no gameovers" achievement, although I know I died at points (but maybe that's just me not dying enough to not have a "continue"? I didn't see any indication of this, though). I also got the "Kill both Vlamboor without getting hit" achievement, but didn't get "Kill Vlamboor without getting hit". Who knows?
All in all, I wouldn't recommend this game. It's dull and subpar. Sure, if you _really_ need to kill three hours, but then, there's plenty of other indie games out there that are better. The legend of Garshasp deserves better than this game.

As odd as it may seem, I actually thought I'd really like this game. I don't mind games that are lacking in quality, as long as they provide a good time. Unfortunately, this one soured rather quickly. For those of you out there who were planning on playing this with a controller, it's...extraordinarily hard to get used to. Left stick rolls, right stick/directional pad moves, etc. This was odd, but doable, so I learned it and continued on (though it didn't get easier). I found myself enjoying the level, despite being able to spam one attack that kills the majority of enemies in one hit, taking most of the challenge out of the fighting. The narrator sounds cheesy, Garshasp himself doesn't look human in cutscenes (seriously, look at community screenshots, it's kind of an inside joke), but the environments are nice, and the game sets up what could have been a decent action title.
There are those who like this game, and I definitely see why. I enjoyed it up until the infamous "wall falling" sequence in level one, where the game teaches you how to slide down a wall with a dagger whilst avoiding patches of wall that will dislodge you. This was fun--until I was instant-killed by a boulder that fell on my head after a 0.02 second window of it appearing on the screen. Obviously, trial-and-error is part of gaming, so I tried again, going different routes and speeding up his falling to avoid the boulder. About 20 tries (no joke) later, I had tried everything (going left, right, center, speeding up, slowing down, avoiding boulders, etc.), and even when I thought I'd passed it, the game instant-killed me despite seeing no boulder on the screen or imperfection in the wall. I'm not sure if it was a glitch, if there was a boulder that just didn't appear on screen, or what it was, but my journey with Garshasp ends here.
This is my first "not recommended" review, and it comes with regret. I wanted to like this game, and I enjoyed it up until the Invisible Instant-Death. You may very well enjoy this, especially if you have a soft spot for "bad" games, but be forewarned that many people cannot even get it to work. Check the latest issues in the Community section--some people can't get it to load at all (I couldn't until I messed around with the game's files and launched the application from the .exe file, for example), some people only get a title screen, etc. Also, if you'd like to try it but don't want to pay full price, check the bundle websites. Garshasp shows up in bundles quite a bit, which is where I got my copy.
Check this game out if you want to, but definitely do your research before purchasing.

EDIT:
I managed to make it work. You have to
1, Reinstall Physix (from redist folder)
2, Resinstall Flash (from redist folder)
3, Restart the computer
4, Run it as administrator (Don't have to run it with XP compatibility, I could run it as Win 7 compatible)
Optional:
5, Run GarshaspConfig and choose the keymap tab and select xbox360 profile (if you have an XInput compatible gamepad), otherwise the sticks will be switched.
It's also recommended to set the graphics to low for the wall sliding section, so it's easier to see the barriers (there are 2 barrier types: light and dark; light does little damage).
So after you have been through this, what we have is still a bad game, with boring combat and bad leveldesign.

I managed to complete Dishonored, all of the optional content and even replay certain missions again, in less than 10 hours. For a game that at the time cost between £30-40, this game really is not value for money.
The game itself starts off strong, seemingly offering a variety of paths, both in how to complete your mission and how to play the game.
You play as Corvo, the bodyguard to the Empress of a steam punky like empire who's main source of fuel is whale oil. Shortly after returning home from a mission, the Empress is assassinated (good work bodyguard), and her daughter and heir abducted. It turns out the assassins hired to kill the Empress and kidnap her daughter were hired by a triumvirate of high ranking members of the Empire who frame you for the crime.
Naturally, you escape and try to avenge the Empress, save the Empress' daughter and clear your name.
Storywise, the game is pretty solid, a little clichéd if you want to be overly critical, but nothing majorly is wrong with the story.
To me however, the story is the strongest thing going for the game.
Most missions can be completed in a variety of ways, ranging from killing people, which effects the game's ending, rendering them unconcious, which also effects the game's ending, or sneaking past them entirely. You can even choose to spear all the traitors who framed you, fancy that.
However, the game's combat is notably easy. You are given a pretty impressive arsenal of weapons, that means even if you are caught out of stealth, you can defend yourself more than admirably, or simply run off. Furthermore, the leveling system allows you to purchase spells, that only increase your level of power, from having people consumed by rats, to blinking silently around the map.
If you are really bad at the combat, constantly getting caught while hiding and can't get the hang of the spells there is one final tactic you can employ. Running. And I don't mean "I'll run away, lose them and come back." you can literally just sprint past enemies, most of which are armed with swords and you seem to be faster than them anyway, from start to finish. I found, even on the last mission, that I could simply run through enemies who took so long to notice me I was half way down the corridor by the time they began chase, and almost out of sight by the time they started running.
The endings also seem a bit generic, but I shan't get into them for that would be a massive spoiler.

It's not often that I find a game that can manage to be simple in form yet as gripping and emotional as OneShot effortlessly manages to be. A game that is both bleek yet comforting, brief yet nostalgic; it shows a rarity that few indie games, and even games in general, possess - a seamless mix of effort, passion and talent. I'm not going to spoil anything but after beating the game and experiencing the vast number of emotions the game made me feel, the end left me a shivering mess with what path the game took. The aesthetic is perfectly realised, with a consistently nostalgic atmosphere that reflects the story of a dying world incredibly well. There is an absolutely genius meta aspect of this game, which both drives home the connection between the player and the world of the game, as well as the connection between the player and the game's protagonist, "Niko", which is the catalyst for an emotional aspect of the game that was unlike anything I've ever experienced. As far as problems with the game go, there really are not many. However, excuse my nitpicking as I try to name some of them. The biggest one that comes to mind is that, as the title implies, you only have one shot to play the game, meaning that you can only complete the game once (unless of course you have experience with tampering with in-game files). While this makes for an incredible emotional experience, especially by the end of the game, you are left emotionally drained and unsatisfied, though it more has to do being unsatisfied with the choices you've made than the game itself. True, I could also be seeing this as a problem because it left me an emotional wreck by the time it had ended, but I feel like it may have been the games intention.
All-in-all, absolutely beautiful story realised near-perfectly by the people behind it. If you're interested in a story and aren't looking for a game that doesn't rely upon gameplay (as, frankly, there is very very little), then you just might love this game as much as I did. I'm gonna be thinking about this game for a long while and will definitely find some way to replay it.

The first Sniper: Ghost Warrior had many flaws, and despite them, I loved the game. Hoping for a complete overhaul, I purchased the sequel. I'll start with the good. The graphics look very good. Definitely a huge improvement over the first game. The change in the game's engine was an upgrade as well, but at the same time, the awkward movement is the first of many flaws of this game. As some people pointed out, when you scope in, the background around the scope zooms in as well as the scope. Not really a big deal to some, but for most of the players who take notice in detail like this and enjoy the closest simulation to sniping as you can get, it was a very big downfall of the whole game, as well as unrealistic. As there are some parts in the game where stealth is implemented, which was a nice change from the first, but about 90% of it was: run here, shoot these guys, run here, "wait for them to pass", run, shoot, etc. Very repetitive, which was another large downfall in the first game. One of the biggest turn-offs with this game, just like the first, was the story. For one, it was super short, and could be completed in a couple hours. Second, it was horribly generic. Your typical action-packed FPS that tries to use explosions to make it look better. Sure, the kill-cams and bullet-cams are sweet, but are used to make it look better than it is. Overall, I liked it. For $30, it was a good game, but I probably wouldn't recommend it to someone who is looking for a semi-realistic sniping experience, but possibly to someone who doesn't play games a whole lot, or just doesn't care about the little details. Like the first, I love both games due to the attempt at a sniping experience, but at the same time, they could have done way better.

One thing is certain: Sniper Ghost Warrior 2 is certainly more enjoyable than its predecessor. But is it that much better if you look closer ? No, but there are a few things that have been improved.
First of all, the game now runs on the CryEngine 3. It's definitely visible as the game looks more vibrant and detailed, but faces are still a bit low poly. And the environments, while they look frequently beautiful, are still not open. The game lets you walk in only one direction, so, like the first one, it's still linear. Not a big deal at all, but it would've been cooler if you had the chance to kill people from more than one location.
Another improvement is that it's more stealthy. In the first one there were a few moments where you had to kill (waves of) enemies using regular weapons, which was a bit odd considering the fact that it's a sniper game and it's called Sniper Ghost Warrior. SGW2 fixes that problem. You still get to switch to your handgun, but there are no other weapons besides that one and your trusty sniper rifle. Firefights are more intense because of that. Now, intense might not be the right word for it, because they aren't really, but you get the feeling you're playing as a real sniper. And while kills aren't as satisfying as sniping someone in Sniper Elite V2 it still does a good job of mixing up the action with some slow motion bullet kills. Even if they're not that spectacular.
The game consists of three acts, with several missions in each act. Missions will take somewhere between 10-30 minutes, and most of us will finish the game within 5,5 hours. It's not overly long and therefore stays enjoyable all the way through.
If you're into sniper games, like me, SGW2 might be worth your time and money. It all depends on how much of a fan you are. Still, if I had to choose between this game and Sniper Elite V2, Sniper Elite would win without a doubt. That doesn't mean it's bad, but it does mean there's still room for improvement.

I think it's refreshing to play a survival game that does not revolve around zombies, or huge abandoned cities that are filled with the same dull grey and brown color pallets, but instead we are treated with a realistic portrayal of man vs nature. Not only that, but the scenario of the game is pretty unique, one that has not really been explored enough, or at least given proper raw representation of what it is to be trapped in a cold environment, surrounded by snow and dangerous wild life. It does, in my opinion, a fantastic job of putting the player in a such a brutal situation where common logic dictates their means of staying alive.
The Long Dark has come such a long way from its Early Access days, a development process that did indeed take time to iron out all of the bugs, mechanics, A.I., graphics and continued to grow and become a staple in the survival genre. It is really a remarkable achievement of both love and care from the fine people at Hinterland Studios for bringing us a product that was honestly necessary for this genre to evolve. It was clearly stagnating and wasn't really going anywhere, since the majority of survival games had pretty major flaws to them and only a handful were able to blend both the mechanics and atmosphere to give the sense of urgency and, most importantly, fun.
You are given the choice to either play the story mode of the game or simply go out in the wilderness and survive as long as you can. Whatever you choose, the gameplay remains the same. Make sure you stay warm, make sure you're fed and hydrated, make sure you are rested, and, of course, make sure you don't die. Sounds simple enough, but the beauty of The Long Dark lies in its presentation. Everything from the environments to the sound design are amazing. The maps are so large and, because of this, the game promotes exploration as means of obtaining resources for survival. As hard as the game can be, even stressful at times since you are constantly trying to find shelter, fighting against the weather and avoiding predators, it does have its moments of pure relaxation when you are walking down the road with the sun hitting your face while the calmness of the area around you gives the sense of hope.
From what I have playes so far, I can say for sure that The Long Dark is perhaps the greatest survival game ever made, managing to set the bar really high for any future survival game. With an emphasis on atmosphere and exploration, Hinterland have beautifully crafted a brilliant game that awakens your nature inside and force you to make your critical decisions and mistakes. It's cold, it's scary, it's beautiful and it's going to keep you coming back for more. I highly recommend The Long Dark!

Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power is unfortunately quite the divisive title. This most recent addition to the Trine franchise attempts to breach new ground in terms of innovative gameplay, and while respectable in concept is flawed in implementation. Trine 3 can be described as a concept piece with a limited budget. It would seem that the visuals took the cake in regards to the budget, and in doing so failed to incorporate what makes the Trine franchise so enjoyable in it's previous iterations.
First of all the mechanics of the game received a complete downgrade, from the lackluster puzzles to the touchy combat, and the greatest offender - the platforming. Gone are the collectible items of Trine 1, gone are the unique skills of the three heroes in Trine 2. Each hero has been given one sole ability, from the Wizard's one box, to the Knights glide and the Thief's hook swing. This negates much of what made platforming such an enjoyable experience - the variety and complexity of how to traverse the terrain. In fact, the simplicity of movement was very important, and with the "3D" visuals one would need a sharper eye and the ability to perceive depth and distance more accurately.

Secondly, Trine 3 unfortunately manages to completely bypass any semblance of an original tracklist, and instead makes use of remixed music from both the previous titles. This is something that I can often look beyond, but as the previous Trine games have always delivered incredibly original, exceptional and beautiful music that I was saddened to see Trine 3 without it's own unique musical flair.
Thirdly, Trine 3 was surprisingly bereft of a story. It's narration was scattered, and it's length incredibly short. The focus this time around was on the origins of the Trine, and throughout the narrative we gain little insight (if just slightly enough), on the Trine, the other artifacts, and our heroes antagonist - Sarek. Perhaps if the developers had taken this story to it's conclusion... perhaps if they had continued with another mission or two? Rebuild the Trine this game, not the next. Give us a climax to the events of the game, not a complete cutoff halfway through.
Now, perhaps the title's saving grace would be the fantastic visuals. The new "look" boasts some magnificient visuals and artwork as well as reasonably well designed and animated character and object models. Most importantly, the absolutely stunning game level backdrops are quite the treat. Looking beyond the surface layer is where the gorgeous visuals truly shine. With Trine's attempt at 3D gameplay, much was done to develop the world in terms of it's landscape, from the rivers and oceans, mountains and canyons, castles and villages. Unique perspectives, angles and the like really add to the overall achievement in artistic design and direction.
In the end, Trine 3 is definitely a worthwhile casual product for those who truly love the Trine franchise. The dominant achievement would definitely be the excellent visuals, but the lack of mechanics and narration should (and rightly so), drive off all newcomers. I recommend Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power, but only to a degree. In the end it's best to stick to the superior Trine & Trine 2, respectively.

You like Dark Souls? You like metroidvanias? Then you'll like Salt and Sanctuary.
The game is basically Dark Souls in 2D. I know a lot of games are compared to Dark Souls without reasons nowadays but this one takes a lot (by that I mean A LOT!) of ideas from DS (which isn't a bad thing since souls games are very good games).
Pros:
- Gorgeous atmosphere and artstyle
- Nice music
- Rewards exploration
- Huge skill tree like in Path of Exile
- You can build your character as you like. Starting with a mage doesn't mean you'll never wear heavy armors nor shoot any crossbow.
- Works really well with kb/m
- The game is challenging and forces you to take care of your suroundings (lots of traps, which you can use at your advantage!, damn slimes that hides into the trees to fall on you,...)
- Quite open with some variations in the level (like the forest where you have to carefully jump from tree to tree to avoid falling to your death)
The gameplay is very satisfying too. You have one normal attack, one heavy attack + a falling attack when you use heavy attack while jumping. You can switch between two loadouts (I'm a mage so I have my weapon + my magic wand on one, and a shield instead of the wand on the other), you can roll, block and jump.
Cons (I didn't find real issues for the moment so all of these are nitpicky):
- The mouse cursor isn't locked to the game window (I use DualMonitorTools to fix that)

Best local co op fun I've had in a while.  I've been playing this with my friend for a while on his PS4, and I'm psyched to finally have it on Steam for myself.
The game is a 2D Dark Souls, in essence. There are even some things that the game does even better than Dark Souls IMO. The staple Souls attributes are here, 'bonfires', 'estus flasks', 'covenants', etc. The famous 'lose all your currency when you die' is here too, and now enemies actually acquire your currency (salt) and become stronger instead of just dropping it (although I believe Bloodborne did this as well).
If you know Dark Souls, you'll probably know that even though this sounds like hell, it's a fun experience that is full of intense gameplay and hopefully some character building trial and error moments.
100% recommend this game if you have someone to local co op with (I don't think it has online co op). Couch Co Op is fading away, and this is the most fun I've had in a local Co Op RPG for a long time.
Even if you don't, you will be very familiar with this game and most likely enjoy the experience if you like Dark Souls. If you haven't even played Dark Souls, this is a nice place to start experiencing that type of game, as $18 is a steal for this much content.

I am unable to give this game a proper rating as it shouldn't be treated as such. The game is 'bad', yet hilarious (well, not quite, but you get the idea).
This game is NOT a "game". It's a protest against AAA games and their companies, much like what DLC Quest was. Except, you will not enjoy the actual "Game" that is offered; you will instead be continuously opening loot boxes. And for what? A sense of "Pride and Accomplishment"? There is no reason this game is 'good' other than that it's pure genius at poking fun at recent AAA releases. Very well done, MES.
This game is a satirical parody of AAA games and their methods (in this case, the new "loot box" craze) to try and squeeze more money out of player's pockets. The execution of this game is perfect; you WILL spend more time opening boxes than playing the "Game". The "Game" itself is garbage. You'll play the first level maybe 10 times and by the end stages you're only playing the next tier once just to see what's changed. The only reason to 'play' is so you can open the next tier of loot boxes, so you can then try and get lucky, and then get more coins so you can open the next tier. That's it. That's all this game is. It represents how evermore, games are integrating excuses to gamble, to the point where the gambling aspect is of a higher quality than the game itself. Once again, bravo MES. This game is parody gold.
- Runs on anything, probably even your phone (oooh, how about an iOS or Android port?)
- The level of your account is equal to the amount of loot boxes you have opened and is irrespective of the "Game" itself; a very clever "screw you" to the future of gaming.
- Less than a dollar for a couple of giggles, as well as a powerful and daunting insight into the future of the video game industry.
- Less than an hour of playtime to reach the final "stage".
- Add the option for multiple save games, as well as a difficulty setting, which allows the following tiers:
- "Owner" - Easy
- "Sponsored" - Medium
- "Lucky" - Hard
- "Realistic" - Very Hard
- The only difference between all of these difficulties is the chance of the rarity of items dropping.
I felt a sense of pride and accomplishment across this rollercoaster of a game. BoTW got nothing on this amazing game that should have been game of the year.

404Sight is a great adrenaline fuelled parkour game. The game uses one very interesting mechanic which i something I haven't experienced before. The game is based around momentum. When you first start out it's a bland white / grey path and however once the action key is pressed a green path appears. Running on said green path grants speed to the player, However along the way there are red pads which slow you down and can make you restart to the previous checkpoint if it depletes your whole speed bar. You can boost with the speed bars and jump as well. It's a shame to see a game so good not be recognised. When asking friends if they had heard of it they simply said, no! The game is really fun. You want to get the perfect runs so you play through the levels over and over and over again until you feel like you've gotten a good idea of the map which 9 times out of 10 you don't because you forget one simple spot which slips you up.
All in all I love this game the upbeat music(which I forgot to mention)complements the gameplay nicely.
I would recommend this game to anyone who wants a free to play game when they are bored of playing vastly open world mmorpg's

This game is the first game I have endorsed because I thought the effort put in was well worth my time to express how I feel about this mod.
Pros.
1. The Aesthetic. MAN! The design of the levels and a lot of the effects and particles used are WAY COOL! Really pretty game! Animations were unique and well done.
2. The game play hit head on with what you would feel in any other Half-Life game. This game is a lot more challenging however and a lot of people disliked that but I loved it!

Cons.
1. Now there's really only one or two that I can think of, and it was the voice acting for the combine. More HL1 inspired weapons maybe? (A little ambitious but sounds SUPER cool :P)
More enriched gameplay and integrated levels would be REALLY nice. I thought the soldier dialog from bootcamp was a really nice touch and would like to see more of that kind of integration.
Overall 8.5/10 on the game and I have and will continue to recommend this mod and I am very excited to see where it goes!

So. Here we are. 2 years later from my first review of "Evolve Stage 2". At first, this was a positive review, about how it was free, and you might as well give it a chance. About how this free to play update gave this game a new light, a new life.
It's dead. They killed it.
So, lets start from the beginning, shall we? Back before it was "Stage 2", back before the game was out of beta or alpha. Back when I was 12 on an airplane, reading a Game Informer magazine.
Like I said, I was 12, on an airplane, reading an issue of "Game Informer". I don't remember anything else in the issue other then maybe something about a new CoD coming out, and the first coverage I saw of Evolve. The cover of the magazine is what instantly grabbed me, if I'm remembering right, it was the signature logo of Evolve, the infamous monster footprint (I think, I don't own this copy of the magazine anymore, but I'm pretty sure at least). And of course, the EVOLVE logo itself. When I saw the footprint and the logo, I knew I had stumbled upon something special. I open the magazine and flipped to the 3 pages that Evolve was being featured on. I'd be reading those same 3 pages for the rest of my flight. It amazed me, to say the least. I'd never been aware of this asymmetrical type of gameplay before, where it was 4 vs 1. But what stook out the most to me, was being able to play the monster. I'd always wanted that, to be able to play as the big baddy in a game, but I never thought it would happen (for some reason, I was a stupid 12 year old). But, here it was, in front of me, my dream game. I would be able to play as a big, bad, awesome monster. But, I was also interested in the hunters, they looked super cool as well, wielding a lightning gun, a harpoon cannon, and orbital bombardment device. Sure, it was the monster that got me most excited, but I was pretty excited to play these hunters as well, searching through a dence forest to find a giant killing machine. I wanted to see this game, I wanted to play this game, I needed this game.
It was a long flight.
Let's fast forward to, lets say... 8-9 months later.
I had watched countless video's on Evolve, trying to scrap up any info I could on it. I got amazingly hyped at the reveal of the Kraken, and the next 4 hunters joining the fray (Hyde, Maggie, Bucket, and Laz). My hype train for the game was not only off the rails, but now heading off a cliff to be eaten by a Goliath. And when they announced that the alpha was coming soon, and if you wanted to get in you had to sign up for it, you know that I was one of the first to be on that sign up page. I got in (I think I cheered out loud when I got the confirmation e-mail). Soon after that, there I was, controller in hand, xbox on, and the download of the Evolve Alpha Build was complete. It was the most fun I'd ever had my entire life up to that point. I won't go into details, but I loved it... a lot. I was in love with this game. When the alpha was done I still craved more, all I could think about was this game. Anyone or anything mentioning the words "goliath" or "evolve" or even just "monster" made my mind go straight to this game, this amazing game. Not to long after that, the beta came out. And, of course, I played it. I needed this game to come out. I followed anything on Evolve, and watched every video I could find, watched every lets play, every stream, every trailer 3 times over. And then it came out.
And that's when my love of this game started slowly fading.
I played the full release non stop for a week. Dominating hunters while playing the monster, or hunting down and killing the monster with my friends, or alone. Heh, this one time, my friends and I were playing against this monster, and he left, so I sneakily left the game and joined it to play as the monster against my friends. They really hated me for that, but I won in the end so it was worth it. Once my week of non stop Evolve-ing was over, I started playing it less and less, like any game. It had nothing to do with me getting bored or annoyed, I just had other things I needed to do at the time. But, soon enough, I started to pick out a lot of problems from my, "perfect", game. "Why do these really bad skins cost so much?" "Why is Wraith so stupidly overpowered?" "Why do I have to pay a lot REAL money to buy these hunters and monsters?" It was slowly becoming clear to me what this game really was. A big cash grab. Ok, maybe that's a bit harsh, but it kinda was, even if Turtle Rock didn't intend it. It was truely sad for me, seeing these big red stains on my perfect white carpet that was Evolve. I started to see more and more; more things that should be changed, or not there in the first place. I started to watch less and less videos on the game, I started to tune out of Evolve live streams, I no longer cared who the next hunters or monsters were going to be. And, eventually, I stopped playing Evolve all together; forgetting the 12 year old kid on that plane ever existed. It was the end of Evolve for me. It was time to move on.
And then, 2 years later... I looked up Evolve on steam.
"Stage two?" I remeber saying out loud to myself. I was leaving the house at the time, so I didn't have much time to investigate, but, I did have time to quickly check what this "Stage 2" meant.
I clicked on the Evolve icon and scrolled down a bit. "Install now" is what was in place of the $59.99 price tag. I was shocked, I scrolled down more to read the update. It detailed that the game was now free, and had a boat-load of new tweaked and new features. I was interested. I didn't find myself excited, no where close to how 12 year old me felt on that plane, but I was interested. Like I said, I didn't have time to really investigate, so I turned my computer off and headed out, leaving my mind to speculate what this new free to play update would bring to my once beloved game.
When I got home, I went to the Evolve news section on steam to see what this new update would bring. It said that it would bring a faster paced hunt, all hunters would be able to trap the monster now, and that they would continue to add new hunters and monsters into the game (an empty promise). There were a lot more features, but this review is getting real long, so I'm just gonna move on. I was a little hesitent on some hesitant on some of these features, but I didn't think much of it. More importantly, it would breath new life into the game, and that's all I cared about at the time. I felt the craving again, the craving to feast on the puny hunters, to evolve and dominate. And to play with my friends again, to hunt and destroy the monster. I was excited now. I downloaded the game and started playing the tutorial again, feeling that urge to play this game again. This game that I devoted so much of my time to, so much of my attention to. It felt good to be playing it again.
That didn't last long.
Sooner or later, the same thing happened as before, with the first version (legacy). I started to see the problems, to ask why some things were how they were, and not being changed. Lobbies were broken, and not being fixed, monsters were able to crush the hunters with ease because hunters barley did any damage anymore, for some reason. The new dome system was a joke, if the monsters heath decreased past 2 bars, the dome would just go down, why not just stick with a one minute timer, like in legacy? The gameplay, for me at least, was to fast now. It didn't feel like a hunt for the monsters or the hunters, more like a game of tag, in which when you tagged the other player, you had a brawl for a bit until someone gets hurt. It was dull. Lifeless. Boring.
And then, 2K made TRS stop working on Evolve.
It's done now. 2K took what little life the game had left and finished it. Like a dying animal.
And maybe, like with a dying animal... it was for the best.
I don't reccomend this. I'm just gonna let it die.

This is one of my favorite games. A game with very pleasing graphics. A cutesy art style and, for the most part, solid mechanics. I have put plenty of hours and after getting passed the issues it is a very fun game.
Some good things:
1.)The AI influences eachothers happiness. This was a new feature from when I got it but it makes it really fun to have to manage everyone.
2.)AI's have personality. Each AI has a little trait on their character sheet that changes how they interact with other citizens and work. Some are pessimistic which make your citizens less happy when they talk to others(stated in first point), others yearn to do certain proffesions, making it a good idea to want to have them work as that proffesion; Even if he/she has not so great stats.
3.)Building homes and such is really easy. Select the floor tool and mark a section. Put some walls. Maybe put another floor. Then a roof, and add some doors and some windows. Placing furniture and such is also a breeze, just select it from the menu and place it down.
4.)Township - Most city building games just want you to grow a large city (sim city, city skyline, etc.). Stonehearth gives people a goal to shoot for. They give you an objective to work towards, enemies to defend against, and stories to partake in.
Now somethings I don't like:
1.)The AI is a bit stupid. I don't know how many times I have had to destroy a building and replace it just because one of the AI got stuck in a corner or something. I built this storage section in this mountain and one of my people got stuck on this 1x1 tile in mid air. I had to manually pull him out. Also, when mining, even with a ladder to the top of a ledge (if I am trying to clear out an area) they will start from the bottom or if it's really tall. They won't mine all of it before going to the next level and so I have to build a ladder just so they can get what they missed.
2.)Bugs - Hopefully they will be fixed but a lot of the times, I get to a point where I have to restart from a fresh game just because in my current save, they AI stop doing anything. After a couple quick google searches you can find that this is a prevalent issue among players.
3.)Building - It has its ups and downs. An up is that the tools are really easy to use. The downs is that if you want to make a custom building (placing it block for block). It won't work with the other tools. If you make a custom floor and wall, then the roof tool won't work with what you built so you have to make it yourself. I once made a floor that went up a couple of steps and entered into a balcony. I had to make a custom wall so that the balcony wasn't included inside and the wall cut the two sections in half. After I did this, the roof tool couldn't find where the wall was and refused to place it on the walls.
4.)Building and AIs - Building just has a bunch of issues for me (biggest mechanic I found interest in). Sometimes, if you place parts of a building, like mentioned in point 4, the AI might not finish it. They will build other buildings but not the one I made first. It can get really really annoying if I want them to finish that first so that my city doesn't look ugly with all the scafolding and what not.
5.)Mining - Mining can be difficult. If you want to make a cave city then it takes a really long time to get the citizens to mine everything perfectly the way you want it. Sometimes they just wont mine it. Othertimes because you can't see how far you have them mining, they will mine to far and you can't place tiles back that you mined. So you will forever have sections of land that are different form the rest of the land.
All in all though it is actually a really good game. The management that the game requires of you is extremely fun and not too dificult to where it requires you to sell your soul in order to further progress. Finding a way to progress can be a bit difficult but almost guaranteed, you won't have anyone die unless you stop paying attention to them. If you decide to not start with a farmer as the desert people(Raaya's Children?), getting food is harder than as the forest people(it's been a while). Though that just makes the game more fun in my opinion. Though, again, it isn't to hard to where it's impossible to recover from a mistake.
