Serious Sam HD: The First Encounter is a 3D first person shooter in the style of the original doom. That means insane amounts of enemies, extremely fast and tight gunplay, coupled with a story that only exists to throw more enemies at you in increasingly insane waves.
Serious sam's story isn't important at all, its there to justify the gameplay. While this might be a turn off for some who only enjoy games with rich or decent story, Serious sam is the kind of game where all its chips are placed squarely on combat. But, the basic set up is simple. Mental, an evil space emperor is attacking earth, earth sends Sam "serious" stone back in time to find a way to stop mental, but mental sends his forces back in time to kill you as well. The game takes place in ey olde egypt, but outside of the level design and a few names, don't expect to interact with anything egyptian.
Where this game shines is its combat, from beginning to end every fight is a bloodbath. The game spaces out what guns you get throughout the game, keeping combat fresh by constantly rewarding your progresss with a new murder tool. By the end of the game you'll be carrying more guns than you might think you need, but you will need every last one, because every gun is wildly different from each other, and adds a new layer of depth each time you grab one. Combine this with the steady introduction of new enemies, combining them with previous enemies in gradually harder and harder encounters, along with fantastic level design. The engine serious sam was made on is optimized for massive numbers of enemies on screen, so your not fighting ten, or fifteen enemies at once, you'll regularly be facing upwards of fifty to one hundred enemies all at once.
You also can't take that much damage. Exactly like the original doom, you have health, and armour, which can go to one hundred, but can be increased to two hundred with the use of rare pick ups. You don't regenerate health, its up to you to keep healthy by avoiding the bullet hell levels of projectiles coming your way and avoiding the charging hordes of melee monsters. It will test your reflexes, it will test your ability to prioritize and plan on the fly, and it will give you the most satisfying feeling after coming out of some of the most difficult encounters one can plow through.
The only downsides to this game are minor, but might turn off some. Its graphics are pretty lack luster, it doesn't look amazing in any way and the level aesthetic is pretty bland outside the blanket "egyptian" theme. The small amounts of dialog in the game all come from sam, who only spouts one-liners. Personally I'm not a fan of his voice actor, but then again it adds to the charm in a way, as everything but the combat has this feeling of cheapness. While it doesn't look great, it never looks terrible, unless you get outside the map and your running along an endless, flat expanse of nothingness.
Serious sam is a spiritual successor to the original doom games, taking every element of their gameplay and putting it in a 3D enviroment. Its fast, its difficult, and its extremely fun from beginning to end. If your looking for a story your looking in the wrong place, but if your someone who enjoys a first person shooter with difficult, varied combat, or misses the old school doom but wants it in 3D, I'd recommend this and its sequel.

A nice otome with great visuals and good voice acting. The plot has similarities among routes, and the focus is on the relationship between MC and the love interest. The only recurring characters are Soshi and Kagemitsu. Romance is definitely the selling point and while there is some angst, it's dealt with quickly. The setting is well developed and enjoyable, the Westernization of Japan is approached believably.
Each route was about 1 hour and a half long for me, and 8 hours were enough to complete every guy's happy ending and force skip to get the normal ending. It will probably take longer than that if you are in it for the VA. Each route is about 14 chapters. Getting the happy endings is extremely easy, the choices to make are clear. Skipping becomes super fast once you set the speed to 'summary' and force it to all.
I was positively surprised by MC. Depending on the route she's self aware, proactive and in general very likeable. She has clearly defined tastes and strengths. She made me really happy compared to the terrible MCs that populate otomes.
There isn't a description of the guys' personalities, so I'll just write a few spoiler-free lines about them:
There is an overarching narrative, and my suggested route order would be Kei > Kagemitsu > Sera > Tanba. Kei's route works as standalone, the other three have a common theme explored in different ways. I skipped half of Soshi's route because incest is one of my squicks, but I would play it either first or last. You do see a lot of Soshi in all the other routes, by the way, so I didn't feel like I missed out.
In short, it's a light read with good production value, but the price is hardly justifiable despite the full voice acting because of the lack of depth. It's definitely an enjoyable game if you keep in mind it's a mobile port.

Yup, that's right, this is another RPG Maker game. And that's not a bad thing, per se (just take a look at the most brilliant To the Moon), but there are so many bad RPG Maker games out there that nowadays, it makes you cautious.
Stargazer starts out with a very straightforward premise. A young man named Zach loves astronomy. So much so, that he spends most of his nights out in the forest looking up at the stars. His nickname, predictably enough, is the Gazer. Until one day, a star falls from the heavens, and Zach hurries over to the crater. Except it's not just a lump of red hot rock, it's a blonde young woman called Aura. Nicknamed Star. The town is ruled by an evil old man called the Chancellor, and of course, he's after the star. So the pair decide to flee and tour the world, visiting all the summits they can to go look at the stars from an elevated height. To do so, they smuggle aboard a pirate ship.
Sorry, just give me a second, I'm having Stardust flashbacks.
As gameplay goes, it's nothing to write home about, pretty straight forward turn based JRPG style. You equip your characters with gear of varying stats, and everyone takes a turn to whack at the baddies, whether that's badgers, bears or foxes. So far, I've only recruited the Star, the Gazer, and the Detective, but I hear there are few more, that your characters interact, and you can even have weddings in your party.  When you take a look at the cards, however, there's something profoundly disturbing: they're all white.  And they all have blue eyes.
So far, there's been very little to grab me, to be honest. For starters, the premise is such a huge déjà vu, but the developer adds insult to injury by sending you on a series of fetch quests in the first hour. The fetch quests are a bit grating, as they reinforce inane stereotypes. You play as Aura and she runs into a young girl who immediately wants to recruit her into her club, the Princess Butterflies. And of course, surprise, surprise, the girls are at war with the boys who keep slinging mud and teasing them. The girls' response? To steal a "prized item" from the boys' hideout and to capture the leader and kiss him. I don't even know where to start, there are so many things wrong. Predictably enough, Aura gets into a heap of trouble, arousing the suspicions of townsfolk after being specifically told to lie low. I'll grudgingly admit that without this, the game would lack impetus, but I can't help but wonder if there could've been another way to get this storyline moving. The Chancellor's goons tracking Zach and Aura from the crash site to his home, perhaps?
As it is, the game doesn't have any major game breaking flaws, but it's a series of small and not so small offenses that are its downfall. All in all, I didn't *hate* my time with Stargazer, but with some many other wonderful games waiting for me in Backlog, however, odds are I won't be returning to it.

Similar to the critically acclaimed Undertale, Oneshot is a beautifully crafted game that is designed to make you have feels, no matter what way you play. With a point and click style of puzzle game play and a cast of lovable characters, this game drags you into the depths of the world it has introduced, breaking the fourth wall and hammering you with first person knowledge only you, not the character you "play as", can experience. It's up to you how to play and what cohice you make, but no matter what, you will come out of Oneshot feeling sad, guilty, and yet overwhelmingly satisfied... for the most part. But the slight dissatisfaction is intentional, and completely shattering. I absolutely love this game from top to bottom, and it was worth every penny, even if its a small, ~5 hour game.

OneShot works, it just does. At first I was a bit reluctant, having such a high rated game feel so... same-y. And don't get me wrong, I love story driven games and RPGMaker projects, but you end up expecting /something else/ if everyone is talking about it. Kinda like Undertale I guess (but as someone mentioned before, this is NOT UT). And well, there's this one thing that blew my socks away at the very begining, one really effective fourth-wall-breaking moment, but... I had actually spoiled myself that bit in the one review that convinced me to give this game a shot.
So, I kept playing, loving the music, the characters, the lore, the art. Oh, the beautiful art. And the whole enviroment is so charming. There's also the several fourth-wall-breaking puzzles that I was honestly impressed by, but I still had my doubts.
And then, the Thing happened... the game really started for me.
I was amazed. Not only by the sheer amount of coding it must've taken to achieve /that/, but most of all it was the way the game made you feel you were part of everything too. Kind of like OFF, by Mortis Ghost, but in a much less depressing way. I finished my first playthrough right before the new year, and honestly I couldn't have asked for a better closure. The second playthrough is just as fun as the second one, if not more because you know so much more now, and there's also the easter eggs here and there. Oh, and George? She's a great character. High fives to the writer for that, you know what you did.
Give it a shot, but remember, you've only got one.

I know it's popular right now to say that a game is "the Dark Souls of this genre." Well this is one of those real legit uses. It's a Lord of the Fallen level shameless homage, just transplanted into a 2D platforming Metroidvania world. You have sanctuaries that act as bonfires, resting at them replenishes health, stamina and item usage but respawns enemies. You have salt instead of souls (though the level system is a bit more unique, each level gives you a point to put into a skill tree instead of directly increasing stats). You can hit a button to switch between one-hand or two-handing a weapon, dodge, have equipped weight limits, can parry into a big counterhit, build as a rogue or warrior or wizard or cleric or whatever. Yadda yadda. What's impressive is that they took all of these features and transplanted them into 2D in a way that works. There are things like Covenants to join, but abandoning one will mark you as a sinner, there are upgrade paths for weapons that require finding obscure materials, there are shortcuts to unlock and annoying fast enemies and poison status effects and the ability to leave messages for other players, it's all here. Plus local co-op.
You probably already know if you like Souls-like games by now, and if you do, then get this because it's a good one, and oddly cute in its mimicry but no less brutal or compelling with some messed up monster design and serious challenge. A little brother to the real series and just at the right price. About my only complaint is the sketchy art style sometimes looks a little too rough in an un-stylized way, and there's some heavy overuse of tilesets. Remember how every area in a Souls game looks basically unique? Not so here. Quite a lot of identikit caves and castle halls. But then that's really just window dressing after all.

Stonehearth is truly an amazing game, I have been following it for a while because I have loved the style of a town builder since I was a kid.  I finally decided to purchase it and I do not regret it one bit.  Stonehearth does really well and I was instantly addicted.  A little about the game:  when you start out you get a randomly generated crew of workers, whom you can later on assign roles (like blacksmith, farmer, etc) and you get to choose a randomly generated section of land to start out.  You gather, build, and defend your village from monsters.  All in all, would highly recommend.

I totally recommend this game if you enjoy town building games. Compared to other games in similar fashion you also get random events and intruders and need to protect your town. You can even design your own buildings fairly easily. The game is als not very hard to learn. Get a stable food source, get some soldiers (Footmen) to protect your town, trade and let your mason/carpenter/blacksmith/engineer craft things.
This game has a very cute voxel design and I really like it. It runs very stable for most of the time but once you reach 20 Hearthlings (which is max btw, hope it gets increased in the future) it can happen that the game slows down a bit, but restarting the game usually solved that for me.
I do sometimes get error messages of which I am not sure why they happen or what causes them as I see nothing wrong. I only really had two game breaking bugs where one time the hud was not working correctly and the other where my footmen would fight enemies and neither would take damage resulting in an endless fight. Again restarting the game solved both of these bugs.
I can only recommend this game and I am excited for what else the devs plan for the game in the future.

This is a nice little puzzle game about controlling two walker drones to reach the cargo lift and the end of each area. The puzzles gradually build in difficulty and complexity, and there wasn't a moment where I felt like I was missing a detail about a puzzle mechanic. If I ever felt lost, it was because I wasn't thinking hard enough. And the story was engaging as well, with a fair bit of humor to it. Even the ending was nice, if a bti cheesy.
There was one annoying little bit around 5/6ths of the way in wherein the fact that the warp places you a few tile-lengths away from the exit meant that you sometimes fell into the plasma below. This tested my patience but, thankfully, this only happened on one puzzle. There was also another weird glitch I observed which would sometimes prevent one bot from walking onto the lift (by having it fall through into the plasma below) when the other bot was on it, but restarting the game seems to fix it for now, so it wasn't as bad.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game. It is a fun little puzzler with a nice sense of humor and great style.

Factotum 90 has only 30 levels, but still manages (just) to pack in enough old school charm and moments of head scratching to satisfy your average 3D puzzle fan. The singleplayer co-op, and by that I mean you alternate control between two robots on a splitscreen, works well thanks to thoughtful and clear puzzle layouts allied to very good controls. There's no pixel perfect nonsense or split-second time constraints here. If anything, I'd say the game errs slightly on the easy side, but that's preferable IMO to getting frustrated. Oh, and achievement hunters will be happy to know it's a simple one to complete 100%. There's an achievement for finishing the last level, and 12 for pressing buttons, pulling levers and exploding bombs x number of times. One thing I would like to have seen is an option to toggle off the music, but that's the only real negative I have. Maybe couch coop and even online coop would have given it broader appeal.
Overall it's a fairly solid 7/10 and definitely worth the sub-£5 price tag.

I'm loving this little hidden gem puzzle game that I picked up in the winter sale.  If there was ever a hidden gem, I think this is it.  Terrific game, fun puzzles, fun atmosphere, good production qualities.  I'm about 2 hours in now and have had a great time with this so far.

Control a pair of robots to solve puzzles in this single-player cooperative game with coherent vision and excellent voice acting.
In Factotum 90, you solve puzzles with two little robots in an attempt to repair your damaged space ship.  The screen is split down the middle, with a camera focused on each robot, and you can switch between robot controls at any time.  It's impossible to avoid thinking of Portal when seeing the clean level design, buttons, and ballast boxes... and that's high praise in my book.  Guiding you on your quest though this future-70s ship is another crewmember stuck in a different part of the vessel.  Primary game content took me about four hours to complete.
+ puzzle design (challenging without ever being obtuse)
+ puzzle progression (tests build on each other)
+ cute robots that chatter when passing near each other
+ good voice acting
- missed opportunity to make a Weighted Companion Cube reference ('Beautified Ballast Box?)
- the two main interactions (picking up box, scanning terminal) are two different buttons, when they probably should be one.  Especially considering that a stretch of the game has no terminals and there are no reminders of what that infrequently-used button was.  Someone who plays the game stretched out over a longer period may forget a control in the meantime.

Serious Sam is a game about killing as many enemies as possible before they overwhelm you. The game throws so many enemies at you at once, it's easy to become fatigued by the sheer amount. This game is intense. Hearing the galloping of hooves or the sound of the earth shaking while mooing sounds follow shortly after will scare you for life.
The graphics look beautiful in the Serious Sam 3 engine. Killing monsters has never looked so amazing. The blood splattering on my face looked almost realistic. After I'd slaughtered everything, it was truly a treat to observe the scenery.
Sam loves to comment on events that take place sometimes. He doesn't comment on everything, just the new events that take place. Such as: encountering a new enemy for the first time.
Serious Sam: The First Encounter HD consists of one theme, 13 levels and two secret levels. The theme is Ancient Egypt. This game took me 7 hours to complete on normal difficulty. This is an old school shooter where the only goal is to get from A to B as you blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up, without dying, while trying to find all the secrets. The story is simple and is given to by text as you advance through each level. You don't have to read the story, but I found it interesting even if it is basic. If you love Doom, you will love this game.
The gameplay is very fun. However, the game does become repetitive after a while as the game does very little to mix things up. This game loves to trap you in tight corridors while spawning enemies around you. It does it quite often. It becomes very predictable. The game loves to trick you by placing traps around each level. To bait you, they love to activate them after you collect health and ammo. Do you see that heart over there? IT'S A TRAP! I did become bored after three hours of blowing up enemies as it all began to feel the same. I began to think: "Ok... I've been blowing up these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s for ages! When can I advance to find something new?"
The levels are very well designed. Nothing feels cluttered or wasted. Everything has been well placed and thought out. The enemies are incredibly varied. Each enemy is designed for a specific purpose. One enemy will sprint towards you, whilst another will bombard you with fire from above. But they were merely a distraction. Three more powerful enemies will charge through the weaker ones and strike you. There are 17 different enemies in this game.
The sound is a bit iffy sometimes. It's subpar compared to everything else. It doesn't sound top notch. This makes it obvious that they didn't have a high budget when they were making this game. After all, they were on the verge of bankruptcy at the time. Serious Sam saved the studio. However, they could have remade them for the HD edition.
There are ten weapons. Each with their own strengths and weaknesses. You will use all of them as ammo is fairly scarce. Especially when battling hordes of enemies. The mini gun and XL2 Lasergun feel very powerful to wield. I loved spraying bullets at the enemies as they charged towards me. It feels very nice. However, the Schofield .45 and the 12 Gauge Pump-Action Shotgun are useless after you pickup the Double Barrel Coach Gun and the M1A2 Thompson as there are simply too many enemies in the later levels for them to be useful. They're too weak.

There have been things removed from the HD remake of Serious Sam: The First Encounter due to issues regarding the engine. Such as: the inverted-gravity effect in The First Encounter has been removed and Harpies can no longer carry Beheaded Kamikazes.
The online multiplayer has been improved, but unfortunately no one is online. Score-match has been removed.
Presentation: 7/10
Graphics: 8/10
Sound: 7/10
Gameplay: 7/10
Multiplayer: DEAD. RIP.
Final Verdict: 7/10
Overall, it is a good game. But, I recommend you get it on sale if you do chose to purchase it. Recommended to the people who love Doom, Wolfenstein, Painkiller, Quake, Bulletstorm, Shadow Warrior, SiN Gold, and Turok.

I do recommend this game, but not to everybody, as there are people that will find its faults weigh heavier than the fun of this game.
First, I admit to have played the previous two installments and was especially enchanted by the looks of part two. When I heard the announcement of the game developers to shift from a 2D to a 3D style sidescrolling puzzle-platformer, I was very eager for the inital reviews, and, to put it mildly, was shocked. The gameplay was said to render the game barely playable, and bugs would appear at any corner. So I waited for some time, and after only half a year the game was featured in a pretty cheap bundle, so this was the opportunity to pick it up and get my personal opinion. And boy, do I regret not having bought the game sooner (even though I probably woudn't have had the time to play it, just to make sales look nicer for what is in my opinion a very talented game development studio).
Yes, the new 3D style has a couple of downfalls, as you will misjudge some jumps or opponent locations. But seriously, I couldn't care less, because the art design and the music make more than up for it and are essentially the reason why you sit in awe in front of the game, finding it hard to believe this isn't in a gallery.
The characters have lost a couple of abilities, and there is no skill tree anymore (as rudimentary as that used to be). Honestly, Trine never felt like an RPG to begin with, so the loss of a couple of features isn't that hard on me. Still, I can see why fans might have felt a little let-down and disappointed at the initial release.
Overall, this is what you can expect from Trine 3: Beautiful graphics and art design, a good tune whenever you need one, and admittedly not that hard puzzles. However, if you're one quick to be frustrated by missing a jump or can't stand navigating levitating boxes around, better keep your distance: You can have a look at Trine 2 if you want to admire similar artwork, and if you find yourself wanting more of the same, you can always come back. I sure hope Frozenbyte will not take the harsher criticism towards the game to heart and continue their great work. 2D, 2.5D or 3D? Doesn't really matter to me.

I like Trine 3. Despite all of the negative reviews, I bought the game because I like Frozenbyte's esthetics, as displayed in Trine 1 & 2, and because while playing 1 & 2, I kept wishing the player characters could move into the scenery instead of staying stuck in 2D.
Looking over the negative reviews, the complaints fall into these categories:
Strangely, the nastiest reviews go on, and on, about how Trine 3 is different than Trine 1 and 2. In other words, because some people expected Trine 3 to be like Trine 1 and 2, they gave bad reviews. In actuality, these 'reviews' are just gripes about personal preferences. Very few negative comments actually describe what the game _is_. Imagine Trine 3 was actually just the first Trine game released. Would reviews saying the game didn't meet someone's personal preferences have any value to anyone?
Too short for the money.
OK, I wish the game was longer too. However, I've paid $20 or so for quite a few games over the years that turned out to be dull or just no fun. I found Trine 3 to be fun and worth the money.
Bugs/technical issues.
Yup, there are some bugs. In multiplayer, one of my group had some strange graphics bugs. The problems went away after restarting the game. I suspect an old graphics driver was the culprit. None of the bugs we encountered prevented completion of the game.
Remember how Frozenbyte said they ran out of money? The game is definitely playable; they should get some credit for achiving that much during a money crisis.
About what the game IS
I found Trine 3 to be graphically beautiful. The puzzles are pretty easy compared to other platform games, but I enjoyed the scenery enough that I didn't mind. Attempting to avoid a spoiler, one section has simulated paper... It is inspired; I hope to see this again in the future.
I enjoyed the 3D environment. Despite being an 'on-a-rail' type of game, there is enough freedom to explore. You can take a break to look around and appreciate the view. You can't get the camera to show every location your player can reach, such as behind buildings, but there is nothing hidden there so it doesn't really matter. You can walk of cliffs and die. So try to avoid it (like in real life). One minor complaint is in multiplayer, when a player dies, the 'ghost' of the player sometimes levitates to a location ahead of the other players, so you might have to wait a bit before another player can reach your ghost to resurrect it.
You can map the commands to the buttons and keys of your choice, which I always appreciate since I don't use the standard WASD mapping.
Using PC keyboard and mice it took my group a few tries to defeat the end game boss. I think a controller would have been easier, especially for jumping in non-cardinal directions. But even one younger player who is typically easily frustrated, didn't even think of giving up. I expect we will replay this again, like we did Trine 1 and 2.
Note to Frozenbyte: You can't please everybody. You took a risk to go to 3D. You learned from it. I hope you don't give up on 3D because I enjoy it and I think you did it right. I bought three copies at full price and we weren't disappointed. If you try again with Kickstarter, I'll be there. Hopefully you'll get enough cash to work out more bugs and avoid some of the negative reviews. Some people complained they didn't like some of the voice acting. After listening to some poor English overdubs of Anime, I had no problems at all with your voice cast.

OneShot is a short game, which is good, because while it does some very interesting things in terms of player engagement (mostly near the end), it is otherwise a pretty unnotable "walk around and find stuff" style RPG. Don't get me wrong, the world building keeps things interesting and the areas are not overly large, there just isn't anything particularly new or exciting going on there.

Unfortunately, if you're reading this before a particular date hinted at in game, you'll also have to wait for what appears to be a content update.
Ultimately, the ending sequence alone is worth the price of admission, but if you're not into wild-mass-guessing style forum speculation and multiple replays.... well you should still play this game at least once.

After playing Undertale I craved a game that paralleled if not outshines it. This is that game and this experience is a devastating one. Unlike Undertale you don't get a happy ending. You're convinced it's you who is going to save the world... yet you don't get the satisfaction. No matter what, in the world you've discovered... it's going to die. Your choice becomes whether or not to let the inhabitants experience happiness before they die, or to kill the world and let the savior go home to his mother. Is this deprived world even worth saving? Or is it the right thing to do to let this world live it's last days in peace?

There've been a lot of comparisons between OneShot and games like Undertale, and I can't exactly disagree with that - they're both meta-games about children falling into mysterious worlds and being given impossible tasks - but I personally feel that comparison doesn't capture the game's greatest strengths. Yes, it's a meta game, and yes, it does all sorts of clever and unique things along those lines, but I'd still be recommending it even if you took all of that out. For me, the game succeeds for the same reasons I still read Calvin & Hobbes 20 years after it ended - both stories do a truly remarkable job of presenting children that act and interact with the world like actual children instead of miniature adults or blithering idiots. Because of that, it's easily able hit whatever tone it wants to - comedy, tragedy, lite horror, etc - without feeling the least bit cheap. It's not the first game to accomplish that, obviously, nor even the first made in RPGMaker, but that's where the meta aspects come in - you'll no doubt have seen parts of OneShot before, but it makes it all feel unique because of how it uses you and your computer as part of the game.
There's a ton I could say about how well all of those mechanics play together, but that'd ruin the surprise. Highly recommended.

If I were to describe Garshasp with one word, it'd be "shameless". Dead Mage's indie title is a near identical copy of Playstation's God of War, from the quick time events straight down to the health shrines. All other differences are purely cosmetic.
Fortunately, the developers did do a few things right. The kill animations are slick and the environments look nice for an indie title. Platforming areas add a nice break from the constant hacking and slashing.
Unfortunately, the cons outweigh the pros. The camera angle is fixed and unadjustable, needlessly making battles with enemies a lot harder than they should be. The controls feel unresponsive, especially the movement keys. Garshasp's moveset is very limited, making combat soon feel repetitive.
Maybe it's good that Garshasp is a short game. Any longer and I might have just given up on it. If you're a fan of hacking and slashing and have a few dollars and hours to spare, then maybe, just maybe, give Garshasp a chance.
Grade: C

For me, the difficulty was just right, and you feel a real sense of achievement when you finally get past a puzzle you've been stuck on for a while. The game gets better and better as it goes on, with a great finale.
I don't think I've played a game quite like this before, and for the price it's great value. For under £5, I don't think you can go wrong with Factotum 90. I thoroughly recommend it and it's well worth your attention.

Aside from the most atrocious UI design ever to be put into a game the gameplay itself is actually very fun. The screenshots might look gaudy and the graphics are but underneath is a rather solid retail store business game.  You can hire maids (janitors), store assistants to help customers, stock clerks to keep shelves stocked and security guards to keep out the thieves. Beyond that you can extend both your parking and your store multiple levels, set discounts on groups of items such as clothing, footwear, electronics, etc and can even charge over 100% provided your customers will pay that much. You have to contract 'transport' or more appropriately delivery contracts to help keep your stocks shelved. Each entity you can hire can be upgrade in several areas to make them better. You can also set the temperature for each floor of your store and you must watch your power usage b/c each upgrade item like vents, registers, lights, etc all require power. You can purchase more power for each floor with the generator on the left side of the floor. The A/C is on the right side and allows you to set the temperatures.
The ugliest part of the game is the UI with fonts that are way too big, windows that blend in with the graphics and scrollbars and menus that are quite honestly very ugly. If this had a better UI I think it would appeal to more people.
The art style is fantastic but b/c everything is essentially the same shade and brightness and b/c it is all 2D everything kind of blends together into one giant convoluted mess. If it used more shading for objects in the background or farther from the camera and then used the brighter colors for objects closer your brain would perceive depth better and the overall look would be much improved.
As it stands now I would give this game a solid 7/10 b/c it is quite fun and engaging and it offers options and areas to tweak that few other business sim games allow. Don't be fooled there really is a lot here and a lot of fun to be had if you can get past some of the shoddy visual design. I found one translation issue on the screen you use to set allowing your workers to rest or not rest. A couple of glitches where stock clerks walk in place and never arrive or customers on the second floor walk right through the wall and disappear. Sound design is solid and believable and the animation of the people is very good .
I recommend this game b/c if you like business sim games at all you will find enjoyment in this one.

The Long Dark is an excellent survival and exploration game. There are four main elements to manage, hunger, thirst, the cold and fatigue. When any of these reach critical levels, your overall condition decreases. If two or more run empty, your condition decreases even faster. If all four reach zero or your condition is fully exhausted, you die. Seems simple enough.
The game has two modes, a story mode which essentially follows a crash landed pilot trekking through the Canadian frozen wilderness in search of his companion (and ex-wife, weird dynamic). This is a great way to introduce the player to the basics of the game as there is no tutorial and minimal interface to explain the surroundings. Playing through both episodes takes around 20 hours.
The real meat of the game is in the Wintermute mode, or a huge sandbox of the campaign maps (plus a few extras unique to this mode) where the player is dropped in a random spot in the world with minimal resources and tasked to survive for as long as possible. In the lower difficulty levels, this is pretty simple. Scavenge for what you need, set up a base, and hunt/fish/trap your way to Bear Gryll's levels of wilderness mastery. As the difficulty increases though, so does the real enjoyment of what this game has to offer. There are times when you will be stumbling through a blizzard with hypothermia setting in, the sun setting, and no cover in sight where real panic starts to take over. Your condition is worsening, your stomach is grumbling and the howling wolves around you start to cloud your judgement. You sprint towards what you think might be a cottage in the distance only to discover its a mirage. You start a fire in the general safety of a cliffside, shivering and hungry surrounded by a starry sky and the dark silhouttes of ancient firs. Lulled by the comfort of your fire, you bravely wander a few yards away in hopes of finding enough firewood to last the night; maybe you'll survive after all you ponder optimistically. Suddenly, a low growl emanates from the dark. You spin around fumbling with your flare, hoping to light it in time to protect yourself from the inevitable. Its too late as two piercing yellow eyes accompany a snarling mouth full of malice as it lunges at you. You stumble backwards, furry death incarnate collapsing on top of you pushing hot breath into your face, while you are desperately grasping at your side for something, anything, that can save your life. You feel the sharp flash of pain but grab something metal and swing at the beasts head. The metal connects and the whimpering beast runs off into the night that birthed it. You're alive. Sort of. The blinding pain in your hand turns to wet heat as blood starts to pool under your shredded gloves. The cold and your empty stomach make you feel light headed as you struggle to your feet. Your blurred vision reveals the glow of your meager fire in the distance and reminds you of the medical supplies you left nearby. Salvation. You stagger forward, barely able to keep yourself vertical through your weakness. One foot in front of the other, adrenaline pumping between your ears. You're close to the fire now. The vertigo takes momentary hold at the last second and you stumble sideways, struggling to keep your balance. Your bloody shredded hand reaching towards the infinity of the night sky is the last thing you see as you fall into your own fire. Peace at last.

Not bad for a one-person mod project, but it suffers badly from ancient game design.
Plus points:
+ Excellent music score. Every bit as good as the original HL, HL2 and Episodes 1 & 2.
+ Some excellent new graphics. The Source engine is really beginning to show it's age but Prospekt pushes it to the limit.
+ Decent sound effects. As per spec for a Half Life game.
+ Decent length for a HL mod. This won't be over in a couple of minutes (lost coast I'm looking at you.)
And now the negatives:
- Quake 1 called, 1995 wants its game design back. Large rooms filled with Combine soldiers. Find button or vent to crawl through. Enter corridor to next room. Fight hordes of Combine soldiers. Find button to enter corridor to next room. Rinse and repeat. Rooms, corridors and crates. This is game play straight out of Quake 1 or even Doom 2. Nothing remotely new or modern here at all.
- Enemy soldiers have vastly increased health levels. Even an enemy grunt is now a massive bullet sponge. Other than making the large-scale fights in rooms pointlessly difficult, I'm not sure what the purpose of making all the enemies very difficult to kill was.
- Lack of direction. Often it's necessary to find a button to push or a vent to crawl through, but what you need to do next is never adequately sign posted. Press-this-button-to-enter-this-room-then-press-this-button-to-enter-the-next-room. Again, game design straight out of the 1990's. Apparently the story in Prospekt is carefully integrated with HL2. Really? What story? How am I supposed to be helping Gordon by killing endless hordes of Combine soldiers?
In all fairness to the developer, Prospekt is far from being the disaster that some have described it as. It's fun for a couple of hours and really showcases the limits of what the Source engine can do, but the truly prehistoric game deisgn ultimately lets it down. Would I have paid for it if I'd have played it before? Yes, but probably only £5.

When I first heard about Prospekt I was pretty excited. Finally, what could be considered a new game in the Half-Life series! Greenlit by Valve themselves and considered to be a sequel to Opposing force! I’ve always been an advocate for paid mods. Some people pour their heart and soul into a mod, and I have no problem with them being paid for that hard work. But with Prospekt, I honestly can't say its worth the price tag.
Where do I begin?
Firstly Il start with the positives. This game looks, and sounds amazing. The environments look incredibly detailed, and work well with the overall atmosphere. I especially like the Combine areas which I honestly think look better than some of the Combine areas in Half-Life 2. The voice acting is also pretty good, which is a rarity with community made mods for Half-Life games. It’s clear to me that the developer knows how to create some beautiful looking environments in the Source Engine.
Unfortunately when we look at the overall level design, this game is pretty poor. I have three major complaints about this game. Firstly, it’s incredibly boring. Pretty much the entire game is just run through corridors and rooms shooting combine. That’s it. I have seen a few people saying that "Well isn't that what Half-Life is anyway?" not really. If you look at Half-Life 2, it has a variety of enemies, environments and different situations that the player has to progress through. Even Half-Life 1 had a more varied cast of enemies which all fought differently. for pretty much 90% of this game you're just shooting combine with the same weapons, in the same situations, in the same poorly designed levels. Which brings me to my next complaint.
The levels are horribly designed. They look pretty don’t get me wrong, but they are so poorly thought out. Most of the firefights are done in big spacious rooms with little to no cover at all. The tactic I had to employ with pretty much every fight was either, fire at will and just hope I kill all the enemies before they pump me with too many bullets, or wait around the corner to bottleneck them into coming at me single file. Which leads me onto the final big issue with Prospekt.
The combine AI. One of the impressive parts of the combine soldiers in Half-Life 2 was how they worked in battle. They would use cover effectively and take turns to pop out and shoot the player. They would try to nudge you out of cover with grenades, and generally worked together as a squad. The combine in Prospekt however, instead decide to just charge straight at you, all guns blazing until either you or they are dead. This leads to some very silly fights where I use my previously mentioned “Bottleneck” tactic where one combine walks around the corner, and gets killed with my shotgun. Then the next soldier walks around the corner and gets a shell to the head as well. So does the next, and the next, and the next, and none of them seem to question “Hmm I wonder if he’s waiting round there to kill us? Maybe we should try a different tactic?” To be honest there isn’t much more you can really do with the combine in these environments. Theres practically no cover for them to utilise and sometimes theres just so many combine piled into one room that they might as well just charge straight at you.
There are a few other niggles I have with the game as well. There are several flashback sequences that happen throughout the game, where we hear some of Adrian’s past in the military. These begin to happen less as the game goes on but, to be honest there doesn’t seem to be much point to them other than at the beginning.
Another gripe I have is that for some reason the developer has changed the skin for the shotgun combine soldier to look either the same or very similar to the regular combine soldier. Half-Life 2 originally had both types of combine look the same, but Valve eventually changed the shotgun wielding ones to have red eyes and wear a slightly different looking uniform. That was done so that the player could differentiate between the different types of soldiers, as the shotgun ones can deal quite a lot of damage. Which makes me wonder why the developer has decided to reverse this decision for what seems like no reason.
The final thing I want to talk about is the final battle. If you don’t want any spoilers then feel free to skip next few paragraphs. The final battle had me so lost and frustrated I had to resort to using god mode and noclip. The whole premise is that you have to overload this reactor thing. I’m not sure what it was exactly because the game didn’t really make it clear to me what it actually was. And to be honest it didn’t really make it clear what I was supposed to do either. There are four buttons spaced out around the core and you have to press all of them to overload it. However combine soldiers begin to flood in and they will try to press the buttons again and turn them back on.
The problem I have with this segment is that, I’m not exactly sure whether I am doing it correctly. I press all of the buttons down and the screen flashes white about 50 times blinding me, but I’m not sure whether the combine have unpressed one yet or not. It seems that when they do, they don’t unpress immediately. They seem to take a few seconds which in that time you can’t go and press it down, until the lights have gone green again. I’m also not sure if you have to keep the combine from unpressing them for a few seconds afterwards, or whether you just have to press all the buttons at once and that’s it. Basically the game didn’t really communicate what I was supposed to be doing very well.
The other issue with the final battle is how ridiculously difficult it is. As the battle goes on, more and more combine flood into the reactor and it eventually gets to a point where theres just too many to fight off. It doesn’t help that there is pretty much no cover at all, and the narrow platforms you have to walk across to get to each button have no hand railings, so one false move and you fall to your death. And the screen flashing white every few seconds doesn’t help either.
In conclusion, Prospekt is not worth the money. I have played much better community mods than this that are free. It makes me start to wonder what Valve is doing with the Half-Life licence because honestly, this is not the kind of game that they should be giving that licence to. Any developer from Valve could see that this game has some serious design issues, but then again considering Steam’s awful lack of quality control, I wouldn’t be too surprised if the only thing Valve looked at in this were the visuals. It just worries me that Steam’s zero quality control is now spilling into Valve’s own licences. Especially Half-Life. I understand that this is developed by one man, and to be honest, he’s done a good job with what he’s clearly good at. Environments. The visuals in this game actually rival Half-Life 2 in a lot of ways. But I think this game would have been considerably better if there was another person on the team who was good with level design, as that seems to be this game’s main flawl. Overall, I cannot recommend.

Two points negative reviews bring up are valid:  1) the game ends right at the beginning of the story (seemingly to lead into DLC?) and 2) it is ridiculously easy and simplified.  NOTE: A few  negative reviews complained of bugs; I played the final release (not early access) and encountered only 1 graphical bug during my entire 100% playthrough which did not affect anything.
Regardless of these two issues, I can still recommend Trine 3 fairly comfortably. It does indeed seem that the developer focused most of their time on the visuals; normally this would be a problem but given that the game launched with a level editor and steamworks support, content should not be an issue.
PROS:
-GORGEOUS
-2.5D environments are breathtaking; I can only imagine what it would look like in 3D
-Wall jump mechanic is easy to perform and forgiving
-Good collectible monitors to avoid time wasted in backtracking
-Several solutions to each puzzle
-Level Editor and Steamworks support
-Annoying mana mechanic removed (but so were abilities!)
NEUTRALS:
-Collecting trineangles is a little too easy. I only had to backtrack for maybe a total of 20 or 25 throughout my entire playthrough (there are 1050 total). I had almost all of them on my first run through each level.
-Essentially infinite respawns make it almost impossible to die.
CONS:
-Due to the 2.5D environments, it can be quite difficult to tell where you are landing.
-No abilities or upgrades (no ice arrows, etc).
-Combat is EXTREMELY simple and virtually impossible to lose.
-"Deflect fireball" or "dash ball" mechanic is heavily underused.
-Several game areas lack proper visual identifiers making it difficult to detect what to move or hit exactly.
-Game ends literally as the story begins. This leaves the player extremely confused and unsatisified and seems to lead into selling more DLC (double negative).

Salt & Sanctuary is Dark Souls 2D with a dash of Castlevania. If you like Dark Souls, I don't see why you wouldn't at least somewhat like Salt & Sanctuary but if you're looking for a pure "Metriodvania" this game will disappoint, because the game is much more Souls than "Vania".
The combat combo system is awesome. Different button combinations produce different attack animations making combat fun and kinda like a "beat-em-up". I would have liked to see multi directional attacks as well, as you can only attack left and right=old castlevania style. I would have also liked weapon and armor drops from enemies like in DS, but its not there, enemies drop loot sometimes, just not weapons and armors.
Overall I do like S&S. Its not near as good as the Souls series and a "Metroidvania" it is not, but it is a wonderful game if you like Souls and 2D side-scrolling action and its unique for that very reason, its 2D Souls! To get the important information out of the way first, Oneshot is an excellent RPG that everyone should experience.
9.5/10
Would buy again if I could. xD
<u>Gameplay</u>
Oneshot's gameplay isn't anything too special. You move around using the arrow keys, Z and X to interact with things, and shift to walk faster. A opens a menu where the player can choose fast travel, have the controls explained, or access sttings. S opens the inventory, where items are managed. Most of the gameplay revolves around finding items in the environment and using them to progress by solving puzzles, either directly or by combining them with other items. Using specific items in certain places progresses the story, and every item has a place.
If I could find anything to nitpick here, it'd be that the method of using items is a little clunky. When you want to use an item, you highlight it your inventory. Whatever you choose remains "active" until you de-select it, and you combine items by selecting one after the other, which often leads to Niko trying to combine the active item with the one you're trying to switch to. To switch active items without doing this, the player has to go to the active item in their inventory, de-select it, then move to the item the want and select it separately. It's not a huge deal, but I found myself doing this a lot, especially when I was starting off.
<u>Story</u>
No spoilers here, but I thought it was incredible. Oneshot's story is very well thought-out and provides plenty of mysteries and plot twists. Plus if Niko doesn't melt your heart, you probably don't have a soul. c:
<u>Difficulty</u>
Oneshot ranks fairly easy in terms of difficulty, and doesn't get much harder if you want to 100% it. The story is the main focus here.
<u>Length</u>
It took me about 4 hours to beat on my first playthrough, but that easily fell to around 2 hours per playthrough once I knew the game a little better and didn't need to stop and read the massive amounts of lore and flavor text.
<u>Conclusion</u>
Awesome game. If you're on the fence about buying, it's well worth the ten dollars.

Con's:
- There are a few bugs

Bugs/glitches I've found:
- Pausing the game in midair makes you lose momentum
- On certain levels if you get max bandwidth and then go to the main menu and then back to the level, you keep your max bandwidth
- If you are in middair (at least after a jump pad) and then you "jump" over an inhibitor, you lose bandwidth without touching the floor

Overall it's a fun game and none of the bugs are really gamebreaking for someone playing to speed run and even if you don't enjoy playing it, it's a free game so all you lose is time.

Now... I guess the best thing I can say about Prospekt is that its concept is well executed, and that there is at least a portion of the game that really ties in with the Half-Life 2 spirit...
BUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUT
1) The game is too hard, even on normal. I couldn't count how many times I double-barrel shot a combine in the head TWICE before he had to die...
2) The level design, is ludicrous. You are being pitched against waves of combine after every door and elevator with NO WAY TO HIDE.
3) The voice-overs, although high in quality, sound too amateur to be convincing and disconnect the original Half-Life spirit from Prospekt.
4) Buttons, buttons and buttons.
5) The story, which each time triggers an incredibly annoying effect as you recall flashbacks from the past, is underdeveloped, but it's not the main part of the game as it focusses heavily on combat, just don't expect a satisfying tale that will move or motivate you in any significant way.

I have to say I really welcome and applaud the additional combine machinery design that can be found across the levels, and the smart use of the cubemaps. My favorite level was the teleport level, even though it just repeated the same button idea all over again.
Soundtrack is excellent, one of the closest things that could absolutely fit in an original Half-Life game, as much as the actual sound design.
I would rate this game a 6/10. Just don't forget that after all, this was made by one person, it's just sad that that really shows in the game.

Salt and Sanctuary is Dark Souls translated to 2D. Full stop. Almost every single design decision is ripped completely from Dark Souls 1 and 2.
There are a few tweaks here and there: boss elemental/damage type weaknesses are emphasized so having a diverse weapon set is handy. Weapon balance is almost as out of whack as Demon Souls. And the lore goes a long way toward writing something that feels more properly fantasy, where the mystery is appopriately fantastical, dense, but has an actual answer, than Souls ever did with its goofy pastiche and dull "all is lost, all valor is pointless" world.
A lot of you are already clicking the buy button, and that's fine. The game does not disappoint. The graphic design has some issues; the world got attacked by the Gears of War color stealing aliens so everything is murky and tough to read, but the core interconnected world, loads of bits to collect, stuff to upgrade, different weapon styles, enemies, bosses, exploration it's all Souls. I recommend it on that measure heartily.
The problem is, we already had this genre in 2D. It was called a metroidvania. The difference here is that the combat borrows more from Souls than anything else in 2D. You seldom really honestly "dodged" anything in a Souls game. You used the dodge ability constantly, of course, but nine times out of ten, you were using the iframes imparted by the dodge to get through the attacks. It's the same way here. Where Metroid or Castlevania will ask you to learn positioning and react to boss attacks, most attacks here are simply handled by dodging through. It dumbs down the combat considerably*, even though the author does his best to throw in "can't dodge must jump" attack patterns every now and again. But, this is the same guy who gave us the quite good Dishwasher games, which are far tougher and more interesting mechanically than any Souls game combat-wise. So to see a simpler product here is a disappointment.
All that aside, don't let me discourage you. Salt and Sanctuary is solid. Everything you loved about Dark Souls is here and it's certainly an enjoyable playthrough. But that we got a PC port of this before Dishwasher Vampire Smile feels like a crime.
To add a couple of more compliments and complaints I had no room for elsewhere: the game is absolutely full of secret nooks, paths, and rooms loaded with shortcuts to other zones and junk to find. There are not a lot of weapons, but there are certainly loads of spells, materials, and clothes to locate. Sadly, the inventory system is a mess, a massive pile of unsortable little icons arranged with no rhyme or reason except kinda in the order you picked them up. No hint on shop vendors as to what you have or how much when you go shopping. Fast travel is convenient and checkpoints and shortcuts are common enough to ensure no boss has a tedious boring long walk a la Dark Souls 1.
*That's not to say that iframe dodging has no place in a side scroller. Shank, Dishwasher, Streets of Fury all make it work, but those are games whose primary focus is on combat depth and variety. Combos, swiftness, flow, etc. Castlevania and Souls don't focus on that aspect. Different subgenres
EDIT: By the way this is a better RPG than Witcher 3.

To get the important information out of the way first, Oneshot is an excellent RPG that everyone should experience.
9.5/10
Would buy again if I could. xD
<u>Gameplay</u>
Oneshot's gameplay isn't anything too special. You move around using the arrow keys, Z and X to interact with things, and shift to walk faster. A opens a menu where the player can choose fast travel, have the controls explained, or access sttings. S opens the inventory, where items are managed. Most of the gameplay revolves around finding items in the environment and using them to progress by solving puzzles, either directly or by combining them with other items. Using specific items in certain places progresses the story, and every item has a place.
If I could find anything to nitpick here, it'd be that the method of using items is a little clunky. When you want to use an item, you highlight it your inventory. Whatever you choose remains "active" until you de-select it, and you combine items by selecting one after the other, which often leads to Niko trying to combine the active item with the one you're trying to switch to. To switch active items without doing this, the player has to go to the active item in their inventory, de-select it, then move to the item the want and select it separately. It's not a huge deal, but I found myself doing this a lot, especially when I was starting off.
<u>Story</u>
No spoilers here, but I thought it was incredible. Oneshot's story is very well thought-out and provides plenty of mysteries and plot twists. Plus if Niko doesn't melt your heart, you probably don't have a soul. c:
<u>Difficulty</u>
Oneshot ranks fairly easy in terms of difficulty, and doesn't get much harder if you want to 100% it. The story is the main focus here.
<u>Length</u>
It took me about 4 hours to beat on my first playthrough, but that easily fell to around 2 hours per playthrough once I knew the game a little better and didn't need to stop and read the massive amounts of lore and flavor text.
<u>Conclusion</u>
Awesome game. If you're on the fence about buying, it's well worth the ten dollars.

Trine 1 was quite difficult in places and very enjoyable
Trine 2 was Fantastic! I can't stress how much I enjoyed it and am still playing in co-op
Trine 3 is completed 100% in 5.7 hours. That includes time spent paused when I went to the shops.
Before I nay-say anything more, Trine 3 upholds the amazing beauty and graphical squee-factor that I have come to expect. The designers have probably moved heaven, hell, earth, water and fire to give us more air in three dimensions.
But that's just about where I run out of nice things to say...
The 3D was... well, different. Cant say there was really any need for it and it honestly brought nothing to the game other than a little more elbow room when dodging two specific enemies.
The puzzles are... well, a bit of a let down.
The storyline seemed bolted on and only needed for an excuse to have the characters* going out again
The bosses were reminicient of old 90s games (nice then, but we have the capacity for so much more now!)
The enemies were easy to kill and not all that challenging.
The characters' abilities have changed a little to handle the new third dimension (and dissapoint anyone who plays as Zoya), Pontius the brave has been overpowered beyond excuse. Amadeus has the ability to WALK while carrying an object, moving it along X and Y axis as he goes (not to mention an actual COMBAT ability now). Zoya... well, she's lost all her abilities and gained the ability to tie things to other things...
Really, if you gave Amadeus a sword, sheild and rope, he could do the whole thing himself!
or gave Pontius the ability to pick up rocks or something and a rope... a whole second or third player just to tie a ledge to the floor?
All characters can grab a ledge and wall jump... WALL JUMP? Pontius is a big, heavy guy. He should need help up those kinds of things and although Amadeus is a dad to three (and husband to 'a firebrand of a woman') there's no way he can keep up with an elf's agility!
Pontius can 'glide' (trine 2), charge (trine 2) break walls (trine 2) and use his shield (trine 1 & 2)
Amadeus can place boxes (Trine 1 & 2) and pick things up (Trine 1 & 2) and now can slam things down on enemies and platforms/puzzles.
Zoya can grapple to well... only rings now (Limited from Trine 1 & 2), shoot basic arrows (Trine 1 & 2) and now attach things to things...
Out of all of them, Zoya has been weakened whereas the other two have had an impressive buff
I played as Zoya all the time but now, I just play as Pontius because he has the simplest combat, the largest range of abilities and nulifies the need to actually work at the puzzles by just stomp, glide and sometimes charge.
Not to mention Zoya's appearance no longer seems mysterious or even elfish... she looks like a miscelanious Gypsy (not that there's anything wrong with the outfit or appearance... but she's a flipping elf people!). The transittion from 'Stealthy theif' to 'discount tomb-raider' was a bit of a let-down.
The characters have not really evolved as such and that's not a problem. but Zoya's change in career seems to be a bit shoe-horned in to say 'She's become a goodie now'. Amadeus is a dad and Pontius is a knight / minuteman. That's been the story since the first trine. There was no need to change Zoya.
There are 8 levels. Side-missions (dreams, pointless arenas and a sorry excuse for a 'how he got there' do not count) and with exception of the sake of completion, there was very little bringing me back to this.
The achievements seem to be 'finish the game and find all the collectibles'.
The leveling-up has been removed in place of meaningless 'just get all the collectibles' items.
Oh, and the last ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on us without the courtesy to call it rain' of this game... IT'S NOT EVEN THE FULL GAME!
They throw a 'to be continued' at the end.
I honestly wonder if they ran out of money or something because after you (SERIOUSLY, SPOILER HERE) get 2/3 of the trine back together, THE GAME ENDS!
There is even a take-the♥♥♥♥♥♥cinematic that reeks of 'buy the next one to see...'

This is quite a game alright, but I feel like if the game were just that little bit more fleshed out, we'd have a real gem here.
Weapon Variety --- A rifle, bow and flare gun are a good start, a chainsaw to scare off wolves and cut logs, a scattergun for bird hunting, and high caliber revolvers would likely be fairly common in rural Canada... and spears should not be discounted, In a true survival situation a sharp stone, some rope and a broompole could score you a buck, let along countless rabbits and a reasonable defence against hostile wildlife.
Wildlife --- Foxes dimishing your rabbits as well as lynx or snow lepard would add some much needed diversity to the number of animals in the game, pelts shouldnt be restricted to specefic slots of clothing either, I'd sure as heck strap deerhide all over rather than leaving the chest for wolf pelts.
Crafting --- Obviously an unacomplished smith would not be able to forge much in the way of fancy tools but I feel the game restricting blacksmithing to specific locations to create such simple things like a shank and arrowheads is really just a grab for "difficulty"... Arrowheads can be made by flintknapping with various types of stone - even glass! And crude smithing such as we see in the game could quite easily be done on an open fire and a large rock, no need for a fancy forge long as you got that temp. up... a lack of options in the cooking department could use some change as well.
Food, Consumables --- I understand that supplies are supposed to be scarce but is it really unreasonable to possibly find a case of soda, or more perishable items such as vegetables? The lack of alchohol is quite dissapointing, with the triple (perhaps not best choice but notheless shouldnt be discounted) use of a temporary warmth or condition boost, antiseptic and as a possible accelerant I do not see why some good ol canadian rye cant be used in a situation like the long dark proposes. The ability to smoke or salt meat and fish should really be an option...
Shelter / base? --- I get that this is supposed to be different from a typical "survival" game but some options to actually build things and make a mark on the world should really be a thing. Making one's own ice fishing holes or in the long term your very own log cabin would be quite the accomplishments as well as being quite useful
Maybe its just me but I really feel like theres quite a bit that could make this into a real quality game.

Alright, I've checked out this game early in November, finished it up to Normal Devil, no Pacifist Grades, nor any Expert Bosses.
Story: Cuphead and Mugman are simply playing outside like normal cupchildren, when they quite figuratively end up on the wrong side of the tracks into the Devil's Casino and into the hands of King Dice and The Devil. Forced into collecting the soul contracts of multiple debtors in parts of Inkwell Isle, Cuphead and Mugman must succeed or the Devil will take their heads. I love the fact that the story is simple, yet it doesn't fret from featuring "adult" concepts akin to the animations of the Depression Era.
Gameplay: Cuphead responds fairly well and each level has a unique feeling with their own obstacles, ranging from a simple forest with the only obstacle being the boss to flying in the air fighting mostly airborne debtors to a nightclub featuring a good ol' fashioned fisticuffs match. Sometimes, however, the bosses, even with the proper gear and trinklets, can be a living Hell on Earth. The biggest example has to be Grim Matchstick of Inkwell Isle 2, whose level takes place up in the air with clouds, where slipping up any of the multitasking can seriously beat your ink right out of you.
Graphics: Seriously, the graphical aspect has to be one of the best portions of the game. Just looking at the hundreds of frames given to every boss to the looping animations of the background characters gives the game such a polished look, it also help accentuate them from the merticulously crafted watercolor backgrounds.
Music/Sound: Also friggin' fantastic. It captures the big band feel of the Roaring 20's, if not the orchestrated feel of most soundless pictures. The instruments can be picked out clearly based on pitch and by how they interact with your ears. Most pieces of music fits snuggily within the level itself and the few that don't clearly fit are so amazing that it barely even maters.
Overall: This has to be one of the better games of 2017, and I seriously hope that Studio MDHR succeeds and doesn't get absorbed into a cesspool company just because of this game. I will give it a 9/10 because out of all the things that I believe could be a problem, the only major turn-off will be the massive difficulty spike against Grim and the Fish Federation and Crustasean Nation.

I don't want to be negative about the game: It's clearly not finished. But for me, it's just the wrong side of not finished to be any fun.
It's a base-builder, colony management game. And that's the problem.
I'll give you an example of the building system, as it stands now:
- To build a surrounding wall you need to lay the foundations - Love it! Brilliant!
- Then you make the wall in sections of stone held between wooden pillars - That's just fine by me.
- But then you finish the wall and you want to add a door. Oh dear.
You can't modify the structure when it's finished. And guess what? You have to destroy the ENTIRE wall surrounding your colony because you can *select* one piece of wall but you can't *remove* just one piece of wall.
Now that's a serious headache but it's made worse by the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI who will seemingly go out of their way to get trapped behind the thing they're building. Whatever you do don't make a tower with a ladder but no door to the inside. Because you will have some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ come along and build a roof over them so they're trapped forever. And you can just make a hole and let them out. You have to knock the whole tower down!
Here's my next serious annoyance with the building system:
- I made a building.
- I decided to move a latern from one place to the side of my new building.
- I changed my mind and (before it had been moved) relocated it somewhere else instead.
- This left a ghost lattern attached to the original position.
- It said do I want to remove it. I said yes. It knocked down my whole damn building. That's not how you cancel moving an object! Thatsanofair!
On top of this majorly hammy building system the AI... Oh man... the AI... It's not the worst I've ever seen but it's not great either. What's the point of archers that won't take advantage of your tower? They'll just wander outside with the knights to die... So what's the point of building a tower? Well there isn't one, is there.
Even with all these problems, after playing it for 10 hours or so, I've completed the tech-tree and become unfeasibly rich. I've only had one person die and that's because I wasn't aware they were dying.
By the way: Don't expect anyone to rescue a downed colonist. Unless YOU explicitly tell them to, they'll leave them to die.  Because screw that guy, right?
Oh and if you ask them to mine something above head height but don't make them a ladder, they won't make one themselves. Which is odd considering they make ladders all over the place when making buildings...
I know... I know... The fanbois will be telling me how wrong I am about everything but trust me: Get Rimworld instead. Yeah. I said it.

Kills me to say it, but Aqua Moto Racing Utopia isn't really worth your money.
It can look stunning at times, but that illusion is shattered by the way your character animates. There's nothing in the actual feel of the racing here to suggest that the rider (or the jet) is actually racing on water, despite everything else on the screen telling you otherwise. Everything is extremely rigid, and has no flow. There's no depth here, despite some valiant attempts at it. The trick system, too, is fundamentally flawed. Not only do the moves lack pizzazz, they're just not satisfying to use at all.
I have a massive, massive soft spot for b-grade arcade racers. Loved them through the 8/16bit generations, and that love was cemented in the Saturn/PSX/64 days. You don't need a massive budget to create a racer that feels right. The surface similarities to Wave Race 64 and Blue Storm do more harm to Utopia than good, as the game really can't match the sublime controls of either title.
I was really, really hoping that Utopia would deliver the goods, but I can't in good conscience recommend the game. Riptide GP 2/Renegade are, right now, the far better option if you have a water racing scratch to itch. And in saying that, I honestly hope the developers go back to the drawing board and re-think their approach to the controls, animation and overall feel. The game has the content, and it's got the glitz, but without the core gameplay, it'll always just be a pale imitation of what's gone before.
I hate writing negative anything, but it's my sincerest wish to see this game evolve and be the game that the devs, and we want it to be.

Overall though these are minor complaints. As you get to learn the tracks the buoy markers won't matter as much.
Aqua Moto Racing Utopia is good for quick bursts of fun. Riptide just feels like the kind of game I would be standing (or sitting) in an old school arcade dumping tokens into.
I'm recommending Aqua Moto Racing Utopia because it IS a solid entry into the genre, it looks pretty, and there are a lot of options and tracks to keep you coming back.

This looks, plays, and sounds exactly like an arcade game from the late 90s. The soundtrack is super cheesy, consisting mainly of really low budget electronic techno-style music (the sort of thing you heard blaring across every arcade centre back then), but whilst I could live with that, the reason I soon refunded this was due to an unforgivably bad UI mixed with one of the worst control schemes I've ever encountered (right up there with Lego Worlds!). It sucked the fun right out of it for me and so I don't recommend this game.
The problem starts with the menu screen UI, which has Xbox controller button prompts hardcoded into it - this is true regardless of whether or not you are actually using an xbox controller, so you're left guessing which keyboard keys are required to access the various parts of the menu.
Once you figure out your way past that and into the tutorial, you're expected to learn the basic ramp jump tricks you need to know in order to progress. No problem - assuming you have an xbox type controller. This is because every on- screen prompt for every trick is hard-coded with 'controller' controls, regardless of what actual control scheme you've set up in the Controls menu. So learning the tricks becomes a guessing game of trying to understand which keyboard control you've set, corresponds with the on-screen controller controls diagrams. It's infuriating, frustrating, and not at all fun.
Even if you have the patience to reconfigure all of the controls and memorize it all, I still believe that the overall control scheme is really bad. For example, one would assume that W = Forward, S = Back, etc, correct? Not this game. WASD refers to rotations in different directions. No problem then, I hear you say - the Arrow keys must then be the standard Forward, Back, Left, Right controls, no? Nope again. In this game, the arrow keys perform stunt/trick modifiers. In order to accelerate, you must use Space bar. Space bar!!! It makes no sense! I've never played a racing game with Accelerate defaulted to Space Bar! So again, you could of course reconfigure all of this and then try to memorize what you've done in relation to what the standard layout would do, but who has the time and patience for that? I just want to race my jetski! Even the Tony Hawk games understood that there needed to be a standard, familiar set of controls for basic movement so that even a beginner could interact with the game in a meaningful way. This game throws all of that right out of the window.
After limping my way through the tutorial, I tried a practice event and hated every moment of it. The issue with the bad control scheme was just too much and I immediately refunded it.
So beware: Even if you have a controller and you're prepared for the madness of the trick button schemes, ensure that you are prepared to deal with late 90s-style graphics and sound effects.

I almost didn't leave a review for Aqua Moto because ultimately I refunded the game due to being dissapointed with it, but I would like to recommend it with certain caveats, as even though I wasn't toally happy it may be what you're after.
If you're looking for a modern WaveRace, then this is the closest thing I have found, by a long shot - don't consider the other options. The controls are tight and arcadey - the water has movement and variation, there are actual waves to contend with. The graphics look decent, nothing impressive but they're certainly 'good enough'. There are several courses to race, all different.
Ultimately though it all feels very low-budget. The audio design, the interface, even some of the models and visuals all feel very early-access - and I don't get the sense that the game will see any active development, which is a shame as it could really do with it. This is what ultimately led me to a refund - it's a game that feels like it has a lot of potential, but just falls a bit flat.
As long as you're able to see past the above, and get the game in a good sale, then there's a good chance you'll enjoy it.

I played this game for about 25 minutes before I decided that enough was enough.
The developer is a beginner and this is very obvious from the structure of the levels and the architechure. Some parts of this seem ripped straight out of Half Life 2. The intro is nauseating and while it looks cool, it does not set the mood.
The game is linear. You solve a puzzle, you go into the next room, rinse and repeat. Many HL games and mods are like this, but there's no going back. You do not have to solve difficult intersecting puzzles in a location as has become so trademark of the game. Instead, you find a switch, and run through a room trying to open each door until you find the one that unlocks. It feels like baby's first sourcemod.
The lighting is absolutely atrocious and is not environment or progress based at all. There were several parts where you are in utter darkness, and many other parts where progress was hindered by the lack of lighting of important objects.
The voice acting is pretty good, but the writing itself doesn't make sense. It doesn't sound like an actual conversation - it is not immersive. The flashbacks are annoying rather than vital to the story. It's like if Amnesia just wasn't scary. Not to mention the GMan jumpscare.
There is no 'purpose' in the design to this game. It is not immersive or atmospheric. The overarching flashback mechanic gets in the way of the gameplay and breaks immersion. The puzzles are simple, yet not apparent that they're even present.
This would be fine as a mod, but it still feels in development. Keep working on it and then maybe rerelease it. But this is not worth paying money for. I will be returning this.

My suggestion to the developer for his next title: get people to play-test it before releasing it. And DON'T CHANGE WHAT MADE HALF-LIFE 2 SO GREAT.
