The only survival game I have managed to kinda get into, even though I still don't really get it.
First the story mode in this is pretty meaty at 12 hours for me on easy, certainly more if you pick an actual difficulty. It's plenty fun to go through and teaches most principles required for the survival mode; the main event of any such game. Now the big problem with story mode is that even though it is lengthy, only 2 chapters of apparently 6 have been released so the story gets going nicely but doesn't actually get anywhere yet.
As far as survival mode is concerned I had a blast doing a couple testing runs and then going for the big one at a proper difficulty. Got some 20ish days into it before dying to a wolf thanks to hubris and kinda boredom. Getting to that point is quite fun and exploring the extremely well made, detailed maps is good. The problem with the Long Dark and other survival games to me is that once you get your footing and check out the upgrade trees and requirements and such the game turns from survival into just kinda doing the thing over and over again without any proper goal in mind. Exploring the world and the mechanics are fun but the thought of just kinda spending dozens upon dozens of hours surviving while doing said exploring doesn't make sense to me. It transforms into monotony, getting anything done takes forever and inventory management is a pain. I'm not going to start a new game just to do all the stuff in the same manner again.
So yeah as said I don't get it, but The Long Dark kept me interested for far longer than any such game before and that does say something for it. I also now feel pretty damn confident that this entire genre just isn't for me; if Long Dark didn't manage it with how much I enjoyed parts of it I doubt any will. And even in the uncomplete form the story mode at least is well worth playing.

I just want to get this out of the way: For a mod created by one person, this is amazing. However, the fact that this mod was made alone shows A LOT.
Let's start with the plot: You take control of Adrian Shepard, the same person tasked to hunt down Gordon Freeman during Half-Life: Opposing Force. After being saved from the G-Man by the Vortiguants, (much like they did for Gordon in Half-Life 2: Episode 1), they give you the rundown on what you've missed since being put into stasis. After giving you your mission, you're dropped into Nova Prospekt. For the record, this game takes place during Half-Life 2, when Gordon is trying to rescue Eli Vance. However, the only problem is that you don't make much of an impact. The only reference you get to Gordon's presence is the destroyed teleporter him and Alyx used to get to Kleiner's Lab. After that, the mod goes nowhere. So the plot isn't that great.
Now the voice acting and gameplay: The voice acting is great. It shines in 4 ways:
1. The Vortiguants when they free you from G-Man at the beggining of the game.
2. The US Marines in Shepard's squad that you have memories of throughout the game. (Think of them as the Cortana cutscenes you see throughout the Halo 3 missions.)
3. The Combine throughout the game.
4. Your Powered Combat Vest. (Yes, it has it's own unique voice)
So in terms of voice acting, in my opinion, is on par with that of an actual VALVe game.
The gameplay is great too, but there are a few gripes. Specifically, the Combine. When the developer says "New AI improvements" he was NOT kidding. They just eat your bullets, even on Easy. And I think Richard Seabrook, the creator of this mod, intended that because you're given extra ammo reserves (Ex. In Half-Life 2, the Pulse Rifle ammo caps at 90 bullets, or 3 clips, with on clip holding 30 bullets. In Prospekt, it caps at 150 bullets, or 5 clips) So he most likely knew this.
This game also has same length as Half-Life 2: Episode 1, so it's a decently large mod.
Now, for the Locations: You visit 3 locations, not counting the areas you're teleported to for a short period of time:
1. Nova Prospekt
2. An Orbital Facility
3: Xen
While the first 2 are done well, the return to Xen was an extreme letdown. You're only there for only 5-6 minutes. You spend more time at Nova Prospekt and the Orbital Facility.
Finally, the Music. Holy Crap, the music in this is amazing. Every track in this mod fits with it's location. I'd buy this off of iTunes if it was avaible.
Overall, this mod is a mixed bag, and isn't really worth the $9.99. Unless you're really thirsty for a new Half-Life game, I'd wait for this to go on sale. Richard, you did a great job and I did have fun playing it; but for your next project, try and get a few more people to help you.
It is a shame to the big studios that one man could make a better game in 2 years then they do over longer periods with more money.

TL;DR: An okay match-X game with addictive mechanics. However, it is techically aged.
Lucid is a matcher game, similar to the match-3 sub-genre. It's a very casual and quite simple game where you aspire for high scores and to survive through a level.
There's a grid of colourful blocks. You can clear them out by drawing over the full length of some colour group, without drawing over the same block twice nor omitting any blocks of the group. Because of this rule some block groups cannot be cleared.
True to the casual genre, there are no time limits so you can device all you want to get the highest score ever. The only limit (and also the winning condition) is that you win the level once you have completed the sequence of cleared blocks of a colour given by the game. Clearing the right colour several times grants a combo multiplier that helps one to reach the high scores.
While I usually prefer "hard" games, Lucid was a surprisingly pleasant experience. Deciding to beat a few levels grew into tens of levels and several hours. The high combos and large streaks are satisfactory to succeed. The reassuring exclamation of "good" every now and then when clearing a large amount of blocks strangely enough helps with the feeling.
In the early and middle levels the game allows any number of blocks for a matching clearing. Later, the levels get more difficult as the requirement becomes at least three blocks per clear.
However, the last few levels had a requirement of a minimum of four blocks that was quite a chore (for me anyway) as it is easy to run yourself into a choke situation where it's impossible to clear a bunch of obstructing blocks. This easily leads to a losing situation, as the only way to lose is to find oneself unable to clear any blocks at all. Fortunately these levels were only few and after a few tries even I could beat them.
As for technical side of things, I experienced almost no bugs. However, while options are simple but adequate (just sound and music), note that
. Also, the resolution options are abysmal: game supports only three fullscreen resolutions (1280x800, 1280x768 and 1280x720) and one windowed (1280x720).
Perhaps the latter issue is an artefact that shows the game's age: it's from 2011, i.e. 5 years ago as of writing this. One thing to note is that the game doesn't come with a colour-blind mode so check the screenshots before buying to see if it affects you.
I completed its 55 levels and 11 achievements (some of which are tricky) in about 6 hours. It's a nice casual game, but because of its age I'd still advice getting it on sale (which are every few months) unless you really dig these match-X types of games.

may be the title for you to pick up.
, offering some mental relaxation as well. There is no story, no bells and whistles or anything of the sort. It’s a matching game where you have to meet certain requirements to clear each level and progress through the game’s fifty-five levels.
Unlike other matching games, this isn’t a match three. You can match two or more colored blocks to have whatever size combo you desire. Using the mouse, you draw lines connecting the blocks you want to erase from the field, something I imagine
. The issue I had with the gameplay was that you had to connect the blocks of the same color together, you couldn’t skip one.  It’s not a huge deal but when the blocks fall randomly it made it harder to set up combos. The game also has “Lucid blocks” which, when used, will clear the board, either helping you out of a tight situation or ruining a set up you had in the works.
Despite the game mechanics trying to be different than other popular matching games,
isn’t really that difficult. You can easily get through half of the game before ever reaching a speed bump. The game also doesn’t offer any other modes of play, once you’ve beaten the main fifty-five levels that’s it. There is also
if you want to go back and replay a level. The game keeps score for you but the score has no effect on the game and there is no leader board so I’m not sure of the purpose. The title does have achievements on Steam if you hunt for those.
The visuals are trippy, the music is trippy as well, it honestly feels like a psychedelic trip the entire time. While not the best game of its kind, it’s
. I would recommend grabbing it on sale or in a bundle, the lack of other features or modes really limits the lifespan of this game. It’s a small fish in a big pond, the matching genre is very saturated and
could do better. But, it does what it can decently enough.

I already just started and it clearly was made for an IOS or Android and not for a person that uses the average PC.
The options are simple, no real configuration settings and manual combat is not really good with a mouse, let alone a trackball mouse or a keyboard, so you're kind of stuck with the very boring auto-combat system just so you don't do anything stupid.
If you ever considered buying this, just buy it on your mobile device. playing this on the PC is just...No.
Just. No.
Edited for additional info: before you say that maybe it was intended with playing a controller, all a controller can apparently do is turn the ship and use the afterburner. Maybe jump as well. It doesn't work when you're inside a station where it requires something to press its buttions. You NEED a mouse or a touchscreen monitor to play effectively or at all.
The map in the game is very...simplistic. That's the kindest description I can give it. Last I saw, it was as if it was drawn with bright red and green crayons.
If you ask why you need the mouse for manual combat, well there's the fact that there's a button for the unguided lasers that you must click once for it to auto-fire. That's right, auto-fire. Which drains your energy bar that also supplies power to your shields and auto-repair systems if you get damaged, which by the way, can have thresholds on how much you can heal and such. If not for the tutorial repair, I would have been dead already in my first fight.
You also need the mouse to turn efficently at the same time as doing it by keyboard is kind of slow and unresponsive and it feels awkward holding a controller with one hand and a mouse in the other to do it. Think about that. No way to effectively dodge in combat normally, if there was any ability to dodge at all let alone aim the manual auto-fire unguided laser, so you must use the auto-combat system to get things done.
Auto combat? It's where you first target an enemy ship, click on a button twice that makes it automatically use whatever turrents and missles you have so you watch and do nothing as either you or the enemy ship dies. You may have to then manually change the enemy and turn it back on again.
Either the developers are pulling a bad prank with shoving the IOS/Android in here as I deleted the game and re-download the game to check and the size was 556MB (Not something that required 2GB of harddrive space that was listed) or this is the real thing.
Seriously, This is not a good choice to buy, let alone try to play at the moment. Until they fix such things, I can't seriously recommend playing this if you enjoy the space genre. I'll hopefully check back in a month or two, but by then I'll probably play some other game worth my time and effort in.

Those familiar with
might understand the dilemna, that an explanation without context both spoils it, yet also falls flat, they're games that need to be experienced firsthand. It's not a hollow comparrison either because both titles are remarkably similar games in many ways; if you liked one you'll probably like the other.
At it's core, OneShot is a character and story-centric adventure game with a surreal twist. It's quite short, clocking in at 4-8 hours depending on how you approach it, but it feels the right length for the story it wants to tell, neither trying to pad itself out, or feeling rushed.

, the modeling was poor, but yet outstanding for an indie title.

You will get angry.  You will give up.  You will be back for more.
This game is hard.  It's wonderfully hard.  Just when you think a puzzle is impossible and you decide to walk away, a little light goes off in the back of your brain and you're sucked back in to give it one more try.  Success is incredibly gratifying - I feel like a genius each time I finish a level for about 7 seconds before being completely stumped by the next challenge. Very interesting logic puzzle game. Worked well on Ubuntu Linux 16.04 (one small video glitch). If you like algorithmic thinking challenges, then you will probably adore SpaceChem. You will learn about chemistry, but this is not exactly realistic chemistry, since SpaceChem molecules are made by connected each atom to another atom, but it is an interesting workflow process game. I thought the gameplay, the tutorials, and the story were all interesting. I am not sure that the music was much of anything, but it was a nice touch, I suppose. I had it all muted within minutes. Overall, I felt like I got a whole lot more than I expected from SpaceChem. I look forward to trying all of the other games that this developer has created.

SpaceChem is a great game for those who seek challenge in problem-solving puzzles. The puzzle objective is to convert the given chemical compound inputs into the wanted outputs in a sequential manner with the available tools on the board. Everything may be confusing at first, but once you understand how the basic things work, the fun starts here.
The puzzles are open-ended, so it allows more than one valid solutions to solve the puzzle. It's up to you if you want to just solve the puzzle or to optimize as best as you can to get an elegant solution. As you progress through the game the more complex the puzzles will be. Also, whenever you reached a new world, the game will introduce a new game elements. The difficulty spike can be really steep at some points of the game, so be prepared to spend a LOT of time to solve a single puzzle.
Beaten the story mode already? Try the 63 Corvi DLC and ResearchNet puzzles for even more challenges. This game also includes the Moustachium level pack that gives you TF2 items upon completion (let's be honest, you are probably getting this game for the TF2 items). It also has a level editor so you can share custom levels with your friends.
There might be a small bug like when you try to copy someone's solution it did not worked as intended, but nothing major. Overall, this game is really solid. 9/10

I really enjoyed the journey and isn't that what a good game is all about - a great experience?
For a one man project Prospekt is an amazing achievement and you can really tell that Richard put in some long hours and hard effort into making it happen.
The "design" in the level design was great, the levels had an awesome level of detail and sense of place and purpose. However, they often came out stale, too symetrical and too perfectly organized to really feel alive - which is probably why the levels felt at it's best during the combine sections of the game where the sterile, lifeless and too well organized really reflected the combine philosophy.
But even though the levels were great to look at, from a gameplay perspective they didn't really provide any sensible props such as covers considering it was an experience focused on hectic battles with waves of enemies.
As far as the Half-Life experience goes Richard made an outstanding job with the feeling and atmosphere.  Outstanding sound design, new voice overs, voice acting and music made the game feel fresh, professionall and intriguing.
The gameplay does however suffer from putting the player far too often right in the crossairs of turrets and multiple machine guns with no cover or escape in sight, forcing the player to press the f9 button just a tad to frequently even on the normal difficulty.
A nice and well polished experience, but a bit too pricey considering the content.
I am however  looking forward to future projects from the developer and would welcome some updates with fresh content and covers thrown into the levels, making the price totally worth it!

But the gameplay's flaws show a game that is out of its era, and sadly it doesn't have a lot to show outside of that. While the environmental storytelling is great and does a great job of showing and not telling, the dialogue sections can be pretty awkward at times, and for me don't add to the lore significantly. But the biggest issue here is the lack of punch: the game doesn't really have that moment that makes it stand out, with no big set pieces and anything new to offer the gameplay. It is a mod, but even mods can have a bite to them, and this one doesn't have any: you'll forget about the game in a couple of days time. That's what it comes down to: it doesn't have the staying power. It's still worth a look at when you get some free time, and the nostalgia trip is fun. It's just more pyrite then gold, but there still is some value here.

I made the mistake of fishing too late one evening, and realised it was already dark outside. I had (stupidly) left my lantern and firewood at my camp to lighten my pack weight. While trying to guess which way was home I got turned around in the dark and subsequently died of cold and tired exhaustion while stumbling around looking for shelter.... This was excellent! I loved how one simple mistake could have such serious consequences.
However... I dislike some of the limitations in the game, you cannot interact with all of your surroundings, you cannot climb or jump so even small rocks or branches can be an impassable obstacle, you cannot chop wood on scavenge bits, you find lots of corpses but cannot remove their clothing to replace your own, you find lots of blankets and material but you cannot use those to warm yourself they can only be broken down into cloth to repair or craft items. The crafting is also very very basic.
Basically, I found myself frustrated and thinking 'why cant I do ........, it is common sense'
From what I have played so far, I can happily say it can be a difficult game with an unforgiving learning curve that offers hours of interesting and challenging game play. BUT it isnt without its frustrating little flaws.

So, I spent just shy of $20.00 to give this game a chance. And after 46 hours of total play time, I think I have seen enough. While there are a few good points to this game, it is clear that its sole function in the gaming world, is to provide ideas and lessons to other indie game developers out there of what not to do.
Lesson 1: 	Have a plan for revenue development before launching a game. This game clearly suffers from lack of funds to be properly developed. And little sign of any significant updates down the pipe. The local diehard community of the game (all 4 or 6 of them) discuss in global chat ‘Go Fund Me’ schemes to be able to provide more content to said small community. Yet the last game news, dates to Nov 7th of 2016.
If you are developing anything at this point. It should be for a wide audience. Not people who have clearly ground the hell out of the game, to be where they are now. Unless your point for having the game, is to have a small group provide you with beer money.
Lesson 2: 	Hooks do not maintain interest, if they are just that. This game advertises 270 Billion stars to explore. If that is your thing, you will be supremely disappointed to discover that the 99.9999825% (that is a real number btw) are completely out of reach. There are only approx. 48 systems available to a new player. 9 are NPC systems, and another 39 or so that have gates to systems presumably built by thos diehard players. You do get a ‘jump drive’ that allows for limited access to stars not yet connected (I was able to get to about 10 other systems, but the galactic map is 'over the top' bad to use). It requires Hydrogen for fuel though, and the only ship it can be fitted on, holds all of 8 units of Hydrogen. Greatly limiting your ability to go forth and explore. Also the only way to get more hydrogen after jumping is to 'scoop' it from gas giant planets. If you land in a system that has none, you can only emergancy warp back to the start system. There are a couple of them like that I found. You also need a certai skill level in gas mining as well to even mine Hydroge. So one more thing (of a HUGE list) to grind.
To get a better ‘jump drive’ and go farther with a higher cargo capacity ship, requires a litany of things and time to accomplish (Did I mention more things to grind yet?). Making the game very cumbersome. Currently I have just ‘researched’ a level 2 one, and after building a large space structure required to manufacture one, I finally got one in production. But a this point I have no interest in bothering to see how far that will take me.  am sure it won't be much farther.
So, while the concept of a tremendous galaxy to explore is intriguing. The fact that it is just a gimmick to get you to spend money and time to get there, is a tremendous letdown.
Lesson 3:	A player based market only works if you have enough players in the first place. It seems simple enough, but if you have to manufacture virtually everything in this game, there should be a working market to trade that stuff. There is attempts by players to do this, but the limited number of them, combined with the lack of a good system in the first place, leaves the new player with a HUGE grinding curve. You can trade from NPC stations, and you can set up your own station with trading in it(If you pay money to maintain something other than the free starbase). But, there is limited ways to find what you are looking for. Also, the game mechanic that is supposed to let you know what is for sale, does not work well at all. Just searching for something simple like Electronics turns up nothing. But you can find plyer stations selling electronics if you look in the right place. It takes a tremendous amount of time however, to find something like that available. If you even know where to look.
Simple solutions would be to 1) provide a better trading system. And 2) seed more items through NPC markets until enough players are building the things themselves. Of the 9 previously mentioned NPC systems, each local market only sells 1 item. And those are items at the lowest part of the production chain, like Iron, or Grain. So, Electronics or Mechanical parts are nowhere to be found. Unless the “Galactic Market” tab happens to work and show you something available.
There are some good ideas here in the game. Going seamlessly from space to planet surface is a good idea. But with little to do on the planet other than setting up a base, makes it unfinished. All you can do is land on a planet, leave your ship, and take a soil sample. That tells you what kind of surface base you can build, and what resources are available (By build btw, I mean queue where in a grid you would like the Factory or whatnot to be built). There is literally nothing else to do. No flora or fauna to explore. You can’t mine it, unless you set up a base (which by the way, requires real money spent to keep and maintain). So, the idea in this game is incomplete. And/or it falls under the hook/gimmick lesson.
Ultimately, while I tried to like it (I did put a work weeks worth of time playing it). The real lack of content, and the promise of what the game coulda, shoulda, woulda been, are too much for me to give it anything but a thumbs down.

Hi all...o/
...I won't add to technical reviews here, because I'm kind of a fleabrain (hence the GT...lol) and I would most likely forget important details. However, I am a long term (since April 2015) member of this community of space farers playing Ascent The Space Game, and I want to post some personal views on this game from my own perspective.
...The Ascent community is hands down the place to be if your looking for cooperative efforts to explore and colonize a galaxy of 270 billion star systems. Yes, I know you have heard that before, but lately we have been discovering the edges of the game galaxy, and it is most likely true that there are over 270 billion stars in this environment...the vastness of this environment, yet the closeness of this community of players, creates an environment that is totally unique to this game, and I wouldn't trade it for any other.
This game, at first glance, seems to be a small cluster of stars called The Apollo Cluster. You are alone in your ship,  and it can seem as if you are actually alone in this game altogether. Look-out! This game is no longer in active development. There are serious bugs and quality-of-play issues that are not being addressed. No updates have been made in the last 10 months.
The whole point of this game is to build and run colonies and space-stations. There are dozens of building/module types that all have to be present and in balanced quantities. You will need to track several dozen resources used in construction and operation of your colonies/space-stations. Be prepared to spend more time building your spreadsheets and working your project-planner than playing. If you fail to account for everything, precisely, you risk causing a cascade of failures that is very difficult/time-consuming/costly to correct.
Colonies can have over million buildings, each one placed by hand, by you, from a spaceship that only turns and goes forward, while being thwarted by the effected of local gravity and having your ship block the view of where you want to build. The process of laying out your colonies/stations is very and unnecessarily, tedious and frustrating.
You are also responsible for moving resources between producing colonies/stations and where they are needed for building, consuming, finishing, or sale. This becomes your ‘chores’ that need to be done everyday, or it will mess-up your production. The amount of time needed increases as you build more colonies and they get larger. The process includes manually loading/unloading the cargo and flying thru multiple ‘gates’. There are the same cut-scenes to watch between having to pick what gate to fly to next. I am at a loss as to explain how boring this is.
There are some resources you will need that can only be found if you mine asteroids. It is the usual; find the right rock, chase it down while your both moving, a long wait while maintaining aim and distance, watch the cut-scene. If you do it right, you are rewarded. Failure gets you nothing. This quickly turns into a tedious and boring ‘have-to’.
The game lacks many quality-of-life features. The type-face and its small size makes reading prone to mistakes. Most of the UI is not movable or sizable. The chat-box is extra difficult to use. There is no mail system for players. Field boxes for typing quantities are not big enough to hold the numbers. Information you need while flying is in the far corners of the screen. While traveling, you can’t select a destination, just the next way-point. There is no compass. You have to visit the actual module/building to see its status or manage it, there is no central facility. The game crashes. And more, a lot more.
The final fail for me was realizing the resource map does not actually tell you where the resources are. The colony map grid, the resource map, and the actual resources placement are not the same grid. I used several days worth of resources to build hundreds of buildings only to find I failed to build my colony the way I expected/wanted.
I did get out an explore with a mid-size ship and only for a few light-years. All the stars I saw except three were already ‘discovered’. The ones with my name on it was hidden behind a larger star in the corner of the sector. It is my understanding that you have to get many jumps out before finding anything new and the needed ship is very expensive. Note that exploring requires a lot of time scooping Hydrogen and there is a limit on how far you can go before your jump-drive wears out. If you are searching for a colony site, you must take the time to manually land on the planet/moon. With hundreds of ‘test’ I found none that were suitable.
The one positive thing I must say about the game is the other established players. There were only a few people on the server with me, but everyone in chat was friendly and helpful. They quickly filled in any information missing from the wiki. Some even make their extra resources available to new players and it helped move the game along for me.
Someday, someone will write a space game that does not require spread-sheets, slay you with time wasters, or club you to death with the ‘space is really big’ thing. Sadly, this is not it.

It amazes me sometimes the amount of devs that make absolute trash constructed from basic, default in-engine assets, sh*t it out on Steam, then have the gall to charge us a ridiculous price for their abomination of a "game" before they take the money and run. But what amazes me even more is when devs release something that's well made, fun, could easily compete with any number of other small scale, indie games, then give it to us in its entirety absolutely free. Thankfully, 404Sight is a shining example of the latter.
This is a 3D runner played from an optional 1st or 3rd person perspective that can be changed at any time. Running though a blocky, white expanse, you can activate a "ping" that makes surfaces appear along the course - green surfaces fill up a boost meter, red slows you down, and purple strips launch you into the air. Try to stay in the green tracks to maximise your boost, deactivate ping to avoid the red surfaces, and time your boost and jumps accordingly to take the optimal route through each of the 14 stages.
I really enjoyed the challenge of managing the boost meter (which also acts as a health bar) to keep it replenished whilst also trying to keep my speed up as much as possible. What can make this tricky are inhibitors, drill-like structures that crash down onto the track and spread out a large area of effect turning everything red, but these can be overcome and destroyed by jumping and boosting into them. There isn't really much else to the game except for the actual layout of the courses, which are very well and interestingly designed with plenty of twists and turns to keep you on your toes and multiple routes for you to navigate.
It was made with the intention of highlighting issues of net neutrality and has some brief story elements relating to it, but I'd have to say it's pretty weak and does a somewhat poor job of actually drawing any real attention to the issue or communicating it effectively to the player in any meaningful way. Those aspects could be removed completely from the game and you honestly wouldn't even notice in the slightest.
I clocked in something like 40-50 minutes to complete it and had little cause to revisit it thereafter, but I still had a lot of fun with that time and would have happily paid a small amount for that privilege. The visuals are clean and appealing, the level structures and geometry a joy to traverse, the music is compelling, and best of all, the whole thing is free. Third-rate, charlatan developers, look at this and feel ashamed of yourselves.

ALPHA REVIEW IN PROGRESS
This simplest way I can describe Stonehearth is that it is a sandboxy, fantasy-medieval themed, town/city-builder and villager sim.  If I had to make comparisons to other games... oh, geez, it has dashes of Minecraft, Warcraft (the old RTS), Harvest Moon, Sims, and maybe a few others.  But, it isn't exactly like any of those, and I am not sure the comparisons due it full justice.
The art style for the world is cheerful and cartoonish, being somehwat block styles a la Minecraft, but with more detail.  I would say that it would be nice if the in-game character graphics were more like they are in the splash screens - a chibi-manga style with soft, rounded lines and a warm, distinctive appeal.  This is sort of my one major disappointment.  The splash screens have characters that seem... well... full of character.  Distinctive, interesting, unique, and full of personality.  In game, they are reduced to a blocky archetypes that visually aren't too striking.  That said, praise should be given to the detail, such as is available, given in customization, with hair, facial hair, skin tone, gender, and name all being customizable, while various traits and skills can be endlessly re-rolled for random personalities, abilities, strengths, and weaknesses.
While there are, depending upon game mode chosen, very likely optimal paths of building, defense (for the regular and hard modes),villager promotions and job assignments, resource gathering, and so on, Stonehearth seems perfectly happy to let you muddle about in whatever fashion you choose.  While some may find a lack of specific development direction dictated to them by the game (via quests or a campaign, as examples) to be a turn-off, I quite enjoy just being able to approach things at my own pace and with my own ideas.
Quests do periodically pop up, but they aren't terribly critical in how you pursue them or even if you pursue them.  They seem more like a bit of variety tossed in should you want to participate in them or progress your village in a certain direction or attain specific achievements and rewards.
There is a lot of customization you can do with how you build and decorate structures.  But, you can also choose from a variety of pre-designed structures for easier village building.  Placement is easy enough, and there are suitable features for facing, editing, and placing your buildings so that you can get the village layout you desire.
Even though various things - job promotion, assigned activies, and crafting for villagers are spread across a handful of menus, navigation of these menus and villager management is fairly intuitive.  One downside, however, is that when building new structures villagers seem completely oblvious to existing items store in stockpile and instead of using those will craft entirely new items to decorate said structures.  This is not a terribly big issue, as any surplus items can easily be sold to merchants.
Given this game is still in alpha (though, amazingly functional none-the-less), I don't have any glaring issues or complaints thus far.  However, it would be nice to see at some point the tutorials fleshed out a lot more.  As it is, figuring out custom buildings and also how various buildings, resources, villager jobs, and so on interact with one another is one part reading every item, job, and resource info pop-up, and one part trial-and-error.  I'm not even sure this is really a bad thing, per se, but it does take some time to becaome proficient and informed on what does what and how.
All in all, I love what has been done so far, and I am hopeful and excited about what comes next for Stonehearth.  Just as it is, I feel like paying for this early access alpha was money well spent.

OneShot is my game of the year.
Obviously, OneShot's most attractive feature is its story, which is positively amazing. It is, by far, the best story-driven game I've ever played. (And, yes, that includes Undertale.) The plot is engaging, tear-bringing, and mysterious, and even once you've seen everything the game has to offer, there's a plethora of enjoyment to be found in trying to put the puzzle pieces together.
The gameplay isn't what many people will want. It's exploration and puzzles; now, they're fantastic exploration and puzzles, but if you're not into that, this game might not be for you. Unless you like story games, because the story makes up for literally any qualms I may have otherwise had about this game (which was really quite few).
The visuals aren't insane, but they're certainly better than 'good'. The pixelart is very well done, and the hand-drawn graphics that appear every so often are stunning.
The music is an interesting case. None of the tracks are anything I'd listen to for pleasure, but despite that, the developers know exactly what kind of music to use to fit the atmosphere. So, despite the mediocrity of the tracks themselves, the music is still done well.
Playing through the game at its lowest level of engagement is probably about three hours worth of playtime. However, I have played and thoroughly enjoyed at least ten hours worth of this game. It truly gives back as much as you put in.
If you even have an inkling of a feeling that you this game might be for you, play it. Trust me, it'll be worth it.

Unfortunately, I can't recommend OneShot with good conscience. It's promising, and certainly does do some innovative things, but a combination of poor characterization, direction, and lack of bugtesting makes it a tough sell. Some people love it for it's 4th wall breaking puzzles and content, and that's fine by me, but I'm just going to be here to point out some mistakes and flaws the game has, so you can be prepared before buying it. If you think you can deal with all the flaws listed here, you might just have a fun time.
First off, the bugs. For context, I played this on the Windows 10 version, and so people on other versions might be fine, but the matter of the fact is that I ran into a good number of bugs. The inherent problem with 4th wall-breaking games like this one is that sometimes (a lot of the time), your non-game ideas don't work on all systems. This is excusable for a free download title (like this game was), but not for something you have to pay 10$ for. I saw numerous 1st day patches and fixes for bugs that wouldn't let you progress, and that's never a good sign. However, if you don't mind your play experience being interrupted by troubleshooting every once in a while, go for it.
Second, the actual game. I will admit, I was intrigued by the world, and the gameplay. It's a varied and vibrant (metaphorically) game, and I commend it for that. However, it doesn't do the best job of guiding you through it. The game very obviously expects you to find certain places and do certain things first, and when you don't, the game loses the charm it has, and becomes a matter of wandering around and trying to find the right place to go or person to talk to. I found that a lot of the time, the solution to the puzzle, or the vital character I needed to talk to was out of the way in some corner I hadn't found yet. And don't get me wrong, searching for things is fine, but not when you're trying to make a fun play experience for this genre of game. There were multiple occasions where I was looking for the one item that I KNEW had to be somewhere, in order to trigger the chain of events to progress, and that is something you NEVER want your players to be doing.
Another issue I had with this game is the characters; or rather the lack of them. It feels like you barely get to know anyone in this place, despite their seemingly interesting surface values. Barely anyone tells you their name, and you might get to milk 10 lines of dialogue out of someone before you get to the end of their unique lines, and they start looping. They're meant to feel like important characters, but they feel more like NPCs; the generic ones that just say a line or two, and then start looping again. The only way I could honestly even TELL who was important was if they had a portrait or not.
[THIS PARAGRAPH IS SUPER SPOILERS]
Continuing off of this, but I don't feel like either I or Niko was interacting with the world. Not really. I honestly thought that my choices, the things that I said, and the people that I talked to, were going to have some effect on the ending. Like, if Niko did x y and z, you'd get this ending, and if you did a b and c instead, you'd get this ending. I can't tell you HOW disappointed I was that it boiled down to a simple "X or Y?" type choice at the very end. It doesn't feel like any of what you did, said, or chose in the game had any consequences, and this is absolutely inexcusable when other games, like Undertale (which is on sale for a similar price), and hell, even free RPG Maker games like Ib and The Witch's House were able to do it.
[END OF SUPER SPOILERS PARAGRAPH]
Finally, the positives. Like I said, the world and story were interesting, and the 4th wall stuff that wasn't bugged was pretty cool, admittedly. Shoutout to Nightmargin, who I know put her soul and heart into this game (and art), and is probably the sole reason I feel guilty ragging on it like this. Anyway, the fact that you can [SPOILERS] talk with Niko directly, and you're treated as separate entities from the beginning was pretty cool, and made for an interesting relationship between you and Niko that I felt could have been explored more. In addition, a lot of times, solving the puzzles was pretty satisfying and as long as you didn't have to look for a lost item, they felt rewarding too. The little easter eggs and extra dialogue (what little there was) was pretty fun as well, and I'll admit that I laughed at some of the jokes. I just wish they didn't have achievements for this game, to make it blatantly obvious whenever you find a cool hidden thing.
And that's it for my complaining. Like I said at the beginning, if you can get past these flaws and play the game, and enjoy it, good on you! I, unfortunately, don't see the sparkling gem that everyone else sees; I see a diamond in the rough. It's got potential, but way too many flaws to consider great, or even good for me. It was solidly Meh.
P.S. If the devs are reading this, here's a list of improvements you could potentially make to this game:
MAP. Oh my god, a map, PLEASE. Your worlds are so huge and labyrinthine that you honestly need a map to get around. The fact that this game doesn't have one is its biggest flaw.
HINT SYSTEM. For idiots like me, and for people who don't feel like wandering around for hours to find the solution to the puzzle, a hint system would be greatly appreciated. Maybe even something as simple as [SPOILERS] The Entity dropping in and giving cryptic advice if you take too long in an area.
MORE DIALOGUE/CHARACTER INTERACTION. This is a must. Your story is heavily focused on these characters, and yet they only say enough for you to take a guess at their personality and past. You have to have them interact with you and the world more if you want them to be believable. Stuff like [SPOILERS] asking the Head Engineer to lift you up so you can reach a gas vent, or other things like that where they feel more a part of the world wouldn't be too hard, and would give them so much more depth.
This one is minor, but CHARACTER NAMES ABOVE THEIR PORTRAITS. You think this one doesn't matter too much, but it can actually help immensely. It's not that hard to do either.
EDIT: As an addendum, I think I might have been a little harsh towards this game, but I'm still not changing my overall rating (for now). I didn't take into consideration that the game would update, and though this, they might be able to improve their problem areas. However, if that is the case, then what the initial buyer base was sold wasn't a fully-finished product, but a work in progress, and even though I am happy it will be improved in the future, I still feel like we should have been told that in the first place.

Really great game.  Puzzles are totally open ended and give tremendous satisfaction from solving them.  The game design is incredibly simple yet very deep.  It’s not just a matter of completing the levels - it’s often more fun to simply watch and improve the solutions you have, and the post-level histograms do a great job of incentivizing this.
The game is really great at being an educational game without being an “educational game”.  It manages to teach complex concepts in a way which are broad enough to be applicable to real world design.  For example, basics of parallel processing are taught in some form or another… you’ll encounter race conditions, synchronization issues, waiting/locking, etc… These lessons are introduced gradually and organically; first by the use of the two waldos on a single job, and later emphasized in levels which you handle multiple reactors.
More generally, the game also does a great job of teaching about design compromises.  It’s almost always impossible to minimize symbol usage, reactor usage, and speed, so you’ll have to choose which to optimize for.
The only downside is that it can feel like “work”.  Granted, it’s a magic version of “work” that’s always leading towards rewarding, lightbulb-over-the-head moments.  But still, I find it kind of mentally wearying to play for extended periods of time, particularly on the more challenging levels.  I do imagine that probably a lot of people might be uninterested in this kind of game, but for those who like it, it provides an incredibly rewarding and deep experience.

This game is a clear example of how one bad design decision can screw up an entire game and ruin the name of an extremely good series.
Dear developers, there is one thing your game did NOT, and I repeat NOT need: It didn't need the possiblity to move in the third dimension. Any ressource invested into that feature was a complete and utter waste of time that did in no way improve the gameplay or the user experience. On the contrary, I feel rather ripped off, because obviously this "new feature" was gained at the expense of half the content that the previous games in the series had to offer. Also the coding for the third dimension is obviously more challening. In fact so challening that with the limited ressources of the project, the latest installment of the Trine series lacks any of the interesting and fun physics of the previous games. The physics in Trine 3 are buggy and glitchy more than anything else.
The third installment does not have any puzzles worth mentioning, it is way too easy and washed down. The story is extremely short and not very engaging.
I recommend anyone to buy Trine 1 and 2 instead, Trine 3 in the current state is too short, not good value and way too easy. In addition, you soon feel like Trine 3 is designed to be monetized by adding several DLCs in the future.
On the positive side:
- Graphics are beautiful
- Artstyle is nice
- Soundtrack is good (although Trine 1 and 2 are better)
On the negative side:
- the game is very short
- physics are buggy
- complete and utter lack of any kind of challenge
- very limited abilities compared to previous games (Amadeus 1 box, Zoya 1 arrow, Pontius only 1 weapon)
- controls are weird, probably because of the many glitches (jumping in mid air or on walls and ledges in an uncontrollable fashion)

)

- You use the crowbar, not the wrench like in Opposing Force.

I actally had a good time playing through this game but, I have more negative things to say about it then not. It definitely

MISSING is a seemingly interesting FMV revival style game. I say "seemingly" because at first glance it appears to be doing everything right. It's got all of the elements necessary to make this a good game. The video quality is top notch. The scenery (what little of it there is) is atmospheric. The brief, teaser of a storyline looks promising. The problem is that despite all of this, the game is unbelievably short - so short that it feels like you're playing an intro to a game. If you used a walkthrough you could complete this in about five minutes.
Turns out that what's missing in MISSING: An Interactive Thriller is the game itself.

The game is good, it is very well made with puzzles that make you think but it is extremely short. I was just getting in to the game and really enjoying it when it suddenly ended which, for me, was frustrating.
I don't think the episodes should be sold seperately because when you buy a game, you expect to buy the whole thing and be able to play to the end, not just part of it.
I would not buy future episodes, no matter how good, if they are as short as this as it was only about 50 minutes gameplay and the episode currently costs £2.79......A bit much for 50 minutes of entertainment.
If you could buy the whole game as one complete game then I would recommend it, but if it is to be split in to 50 minute episodes then I could not recommend it purely because, for me, this does not seem right and causes frustration.
This barely covered any of the plot or story at all.

FMV games are in sorely short supply on Steam and elsewhere, and good ones are even rarer still. So, while MISSING: An Interactive Thriller has some rough edges, may be a bit too unchallenging and remains both short and unfinished, it's still a strong recommendation from the high production value and fun gameplay experience alone and is a must buy for fans of FMV.
One thing that stands out about MISSING: An Interactive Thriller is its great flow and pace. This may seem insignificant, but a title that combines a video game designed from the ground up and a short TV episode also designed by a team from the ground up, into one solid fun experience is no easy feat. The number of things that can go wrong at any stage and detract from the final product are much higher than for each one alone and its a testament to clever design principles that it's all fit together to produce an, albeit short, fantastic interactive video-story game.
The high production value of the video also stands out and while the gameplay graphics are by no means lacking, they do occassionally pale in comparison to the very well shot and editted sequence of video.
On the flip side, the puzzle design is very simple and easy which lends itself to the story rather than the gameplay, which is probably the more sensible priority choice. The puzzle design, while it has some annoyances mentioned below, deserves mention as doing the job well and remaining fun under the restrictions and limitations a title like this produces.
While the puzzles are clearly designed to facilitate the narrative and pace, they nonetheless often feel lacking in terms of challenge and overall satisfaction. The first chapter is by far the most interesting and exciting as it introduces the player to the premise and very smoothly introduces the mechanics, but after learning how to interact it just becomes an, at times, near-tedius matter of finding objects and putting them in the right place, akin to the lacking gameplay of many early Point & Click titles.
I initially felt cheated by the very short playtime of less than an hour, and I concede that the price is very fair for the quality of the production and product and that the future episodes will definitely add to the overall value, but with very little replay value and ultimately one dimensional gameplay it's hard to credit the game for length and this may be a reason to hesitate for some, at least in the early development stages.
Priced at just $3.99/£2.79/3.99€ and clocking in at nearly an hour of interesting and high quality interactive FMV gameplay, MISSING: An Interactive Thriller is hard not to recommend and the only thing that should hold you back is in perhaps waiting to ensure further episodes are developed. The developer has stated they're working on sourcing funding for both the gameplay development and video production and that they hope to aim for longer and higher quality episodes in the future, which are all great things to hear, but with no mention of when or how those things are likely to happen it's ultimately up to the player to decide whether an unfinished story is worth taking part in. Otherwise if you don't mind playing it for the short but unique and interesting gameplay experience, you're not going to be dissappointed.

Lucid is a match-something puzzle game. Like many of its kind, due to the nature of it, I won't recommend playing this on a PC. There's a reason why games like this found a better home on mobile and tablet devices, they're made for bitsize playthroughs to relax with simple controls in mind. Having said that, Lucid is not relaxing nor bitsize, it's more mind numbing and frustrating than anything else.
The game itself is fine for what it is, that is to say it's nothing special. You play through a series of levels with increasing difficulty. Each level starts on a preset board and requires you to clear more and more cubes. To clear cubes you need to draw a path across same-coloured blocks, you cannot clear a set if the path doesn't go across every adjacent same-colored block; this is where the frustration lies.
If a random block drops, breaking your built up combo, you'll just need to hope you get the right randoms to fix it while having other sets to clear bearing in mind that broken combo you built is still there taking up a lot of the board. So the randomness and clearing requirements work completely against each other and make it difficult to plan anything out without risking the entire game.
With nothing else to do but draw paths along blocks, the game eventually becomes repetitive and, other than achievements, there's not much insentive to keep going unless if you like more of the same. There's also no online nor offline leaderboards which is damaging for a game with a point system and a few hours worth of levels.
The music and graphics are also somewhat nauseating at first because of all the effects, especially how everything is bouncy and glowy. This is likely intentional going by the name of the game and you grow used to over time but it's still worth mentioning.
Finally, to nitpick, the menu (just one) in general is a bit weird. For example, there's a large "Delete Save" button which is placed directly under the "Start" button with no confirmation dialogue. So one misclick and your entire save will disappear.  Another option is to "Sign In" which gave me hope for cross-device save syncing, a major convenience in this day and age, but it's just a save selector; not surprising since this game is so old. There's also "Options" which just lets you adjust sound volume, display resolution is limited and picked everytime you launch the game.
So to summarise, Lucid is a simple game with mechanics that work against each other to provide a not so relaxing experience.
Game support is non existent outside the game - Stay clear and save yourself the headache.

After 26 hours of game play I decided to make a review of this game.
This game echoes of EVE online, without the pvp and the rage.  If you have not played games like EVE, you may have a bit of difficulty learning this game, because of the very small tutorial.  There is a wiki for it, and a few youtube vids about this game, which without them,  I would of been lost.  The game is in a full release state, but it is very buggy/glitchy.  Some functions work, then stop and require a restart to gain them back. Restart fixes most problems with this game.
It its an open world space game with little direction or guidance.  Freedom is the watch word for this game.
The focus is on space exploration, mining, space station/settlement/colony construction and operation.  This aspect of the game is very well thought out, and works well.  The game designers vision was for everyone to be able to share everything in this game universe, but the player base decided to change that.  The star bases, settlements, and colonies you build are yours, and yours alone, as designed. The astroid betls throuout the universe are another thing.  The game is designed that any and all astroid belts are for everyone, but the player base has impossed a rule that if you discover an astroid field it is yours, and yours alone.  This player impossed policy is a heated topic on the games official website.  The gaming community will not tell you about this rule, until you accidentally discover said astroid fields and mine them.  Then that community will turn against that player uniformally.  They call this "roid raiding" and consider it theft.
There is a tad of pve, set aside in its own small sector for you combat pilots to play in, but the rewards are minor and not worth the effort.  Pve is not the focus, and its not done well.
All ships are multi-purpose except one of the premium ships, which is strictly for mining/freighter work. You can take just about any ship and make it a combat ship or modify it to hold more cargo to better assist you in your mining/freighter needs.
There is a 3 months premium package that comes with the game, that let you access certain aspects of the game.  To keep your premium status it is very economical, one of the appeals of this online mmo.
Overall, if your looking for a game like EVE, but without the pvp this is it.  If your looking for a space combat pve game, this is not it.
I rate this a thumbs down, purely based on the online community and the unfinished state of the game.

EDIT 2: Recently I was actually able to get in some games and, over the course of a week or so, found that I was able to consistently get in games with minimal issues. There are still some remnants of the connectivity/loading issues mentioned previously, but the rate at which they appear has been diminished significantly. They might even have gone away entirely since the Sunny Side Up patch but I have not played since that patch was released so I can't verify entirely.
But, that said, the bugs have been worked out to a point that I think is very acceptable for an Early Access game so I am changing this review to a positive! The games I was able to play were fantastic and filled with fun and tension. A lot of it depends on the people you play with, and the more talkative players you can get, the better. Playing as a Spaceman is a fun mix of paranoia and tension and the rounds are a good mix of winning and losing, depending on how the monster plays. There are also numerous ways to go about your objectives as the monster so it varies each round, which keeps things fresh. The 15 minute time limit is a perfect amount of time to get objectives done but also keep you constantly moving and preventing the game from stagnating. There are multiple maps, but all anyone ever plays on is Echo. I tried out some of the other maps but people just mostly complained until I changed it to Echo. That is another downside though is that the game doesn't exit back to lobby and there isn't a way to vote for a map change or even force change it yourself as host at the end of a round or set of rounds.
The things I would recommend being aware of if you are a new player are the small playerbase (not a lot of people are on and you need to play in peak hours to find a game). Basically, don't expect to play outside of the hours of 7ish to midnight. Also, there is a bug (again, SSU patch may have fixed this) where servers will only list 1/31 players in the game, regardless of how many players are actually in it. So you have to join the game to see how active it is.
I would also be aware of the crashing/joining/connection issues. They have, for me, almost gone away entirely, but your experience may vary. Also, again, keep in mind that a lot of your fun depends on other players. I have not had any bad experiences with the community, but as it continues to grow, this could change.
Lastly, the pistol damage seems too small. Everyone starts with it though, so I get that it can't be too powerful, and the balance of heavy weapons on the map seems good because you don't want everyone powered up, but I got into a pistol duel with someone and we shot at each other for literally five straight minutes dancing around and neither one of us died and we eventually just ran in opposite directions. If you have just a pistol and are facing down the monster, it is better to just run.
I don't want to end on a negative note so I will say this: this game has, I believe, a terrific future ahead of it. The devs somehow took a horror setting (imo) and, instead of it becoming less frightening with more players, it just gets scarier. That is an achievement in itself. That's not to say that you won't experience some goofy/funny moments, but the overall feeling is very tense and that is a big positive for a game like this. The devs also seem very active in their work on this. I gather from other reviews that there might be some bad blood from a previous project? I can't speak on that, but I can speak on what I've seen with this game and the updates come frequently and they seem to be very aware of the current issues, what needs to be done to fix them, and where the game is heading.
I would definitely recommend buying this game. It is a unique multiplayer game that blends a lot of elements together in a wonderful way. The more people that play, the better the games get, so I would love to see more players involved. I'm typically very wary of Early Access games, but I can say that from what I have seen with this, it is at a point where you should feel safe investing your time and money into it. It is only going to get better. I hope to see a lot more of you Spacemen out there.

EDIT 1: I played the game since the new patch, and while the crashing problem has gone away, it seems to have been replaced with (or maybe this has always been a problem and I never got far enough to try it) connectivity/loading issues. Mainly, when trying to join, I will get to in-game screen and I can see other Spacemen running around, but will get no options to do anything. If it's not that, then I'll get sent to a black screen where it sticks in an infinite loading screen. Anytime this happens, I am forced to ALT+F4 out because there is no other recourse, so basically it went from crashing on its own to forcing me to crash it. I tried joining after the host sent the game back to the lobby, and I still got slammed into the never-loading start screen when the host started the game again.
I managed to get into and play one game, which was fun (mostly bots, but a handful of real people). We lost due to the time limit, but I had a couple tense, close calls with the monster that were exciting. The gameplay is fun on its own, but the true experience seems like it will be heavily dependent on the people you play with. I am glad that my initial thoughts that it would be fun were validated by it actually being fun.
Unfortunately, I have to leave the review as negative. The general instability as a whole is just too much to be able to overlook it, even in Early Access. Getting into one game out of six attempts is just no bueno. It is a good sign that patches seem to be coming out on a pretty quick basis though, and I have no doubt that eventually (and possibly very soon) this review will turn to Positive, but I just can't do it right now. If it were solely based on the gameplay, it'd already be a Positive, but if I can't get to the gameplay, then what's the point?

ORIGINAL: The concept and gameplay look and sound fun from videos I watched from other people, but that is about all you are going to be able to do. It seems like luck of the draw whether or not the game will run for you. At any point, for any reason it feels like, the game will kick you back to the menu, or completely crash. This can happen in menus, in the lobby select, in-game waiting to start, in-game while you spawn, and just at any point in-game, period. This is even if the game will launch in the first place.
There are numerous other bugs, things you would expect from an Early Access game, so I'm not going to list those. But when the game is near-completely unplayable, it should not be released in any form, at all. I have not once been able to complete a whole match, and the most I ever got to play of a match was three minutes.
tl;dr DO NOT BUY THIS GAME. It has the potential to be something great, but that something will never exist in Early Access.

While technically a first person shooter, lovely planet is more of a puzzle platformer that brings in all the manic color and sounds of 'Katamari Damacy' or 'Noby Noby Boy'.

Lovely Planet is a very simple platformer-fps game in which the aim is to reach the end pole after having killed all the enemies. It is a very simple goal and it's a very simple game.
But lovely planet is not without its depth and complexity, the game starts off very simple and quickly ramps up the difficulty, with the later levels (at least in my case) requiring you to learn patterns and make multiple attempts. With my current playtime I've finished 4/5 of the worlds avaliable, with the last world looking like it will take a long time to finish.
The movement is also very simple, but feels very clean and responsive overall. You can rampage through the levels spraying purple pellets across the map, but you won't be able to get the highest rating of three stars. Which reqiures both a quick time and a perfect accuracy rating, overall doing a level with three starts feels very crisp and skillful to pull off, especially on some of the harder and longer levels.
I would strongly reccomend this game to fans of similarily hard platforming games like Super Meat Boy or Dustforce, you are forced to get better quickly in Lovely Planet as you are with these games.
Another thing I didn't see in other reviews is that the game has a good competetive and speedrunning scene if you are the kind of person drawn to that, chasing the perfect indivual level time is also very fun, I found myself going back to the earlier levels which I now find trivial simply to do them better than I did before. The gameplay is just that fun.

What’s Stonehearth?!  You mean Hearthstone? No…
As the last known survivor of Radiant Entertainment, Stonehearth the village simulator has continued to be developed despite their buyout by RIOT Games and the cancellation of Rising Thunder.
In Stonehearth you take the role as a master of your Hearthlings; you’ll select the jobs they hold, where they live, the kind of care they’ll receive, and more.  In some ways, you take the role as a great communist leader, but most people would put it in terms as a “god complex”.  The best way to describe the game: what if The Sims and Minecraft had a baby or in my case, adopted a cat (which by the way, you can do in Stonehearth randomly once you have a Shepard)  The objective is to make your settlement in “survival mode” more prosperous but enables the player to be creative at the same time.
So this is a FULL game right?!  Tons of quality content?  Hold on there buddy…
As of right now, Stonehearth is in development.  The game is available as an early access title, but it’s technically an alpha build.  There are plenty of bugs to go around like AI logic issues (make sure to report them via the game client w/ the ESC key), a lackluster of content currently available (more is planned, like a third human race, dwarves, more jobs, multiplayer, etc), and dead-end UI/clunky inventory management.   (most of the pop-ups don’t connect, causing you to sometimes skip around menus until you remember where to go).  Within 13 hours, I pretty much reached the full content of the game.
Creative Artists that like to express themselves through pixel art, world building, and more will be happy to use the building design tool despite a few current bugs.  I found myself imagining all the art I’ve always wanted to create in Minecraft, but was too lazy to build block by block.  Once you finish designing your building, or placing down one of the default templates, your Hearthlings do all the building your available materials.  This tool is available in a non-creative only mode so it doesn’t feel like you’re cheating.  You can also export your designs by locating the files in the default directory, and share them with friends!
(Steam\steamapps\common\Stonehearth\saved_objects\stonehearth\building_templates).
Feel free to copy the following file of my Slime Pixel Art:
Also, here is a community ran website for shared building plans::
While the mentioned content is lacking, there is still a good all-around vibe of the game, and things to come.  Already there are 16 mostly interesting jobs a Hearthling can work, from the basic “Worker” all the way to a Farmer or Engineer (TURNIP TURRETS!)  At least 50+ placeable items, and 100+ crafting ingredients collectable with the various jobs throughout the biome you pick.  With continuous updates to the community, you can’t help but get excited for the finished product.
It’s hard for me to not recommend any piece of art, which I refer to games as.  However I want to underline, this game is not finished.  Only invest in the game if you’d like to support RIOT’s other endeavours, and a generally exciting game, or if you really want to see what beautiful stuff you could create with the building planner.

Here are a few things Trine 3 does great.
The graphics and art style are phenomenal and awe-inspiring and while the explorable world is not gigantic, it's very detailed and colourful.
Great voice acting, witty dialogue and clever humour.
A variety of environments wich you can explore and while the game is 5-6 hours long I don't think it's overpriced.

A few enemies wich you can encounter, some move slow and are not even dangerous.

Trine 3 is quite a strange little game, taking a completely different direction from the previous games in the series. There are some features that the game retains. The platforming being one of them, the characters being another and of course the beautifully enchanting visuals. Now there are a number of things that sets Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power apart from it's predecessors. The first being that there's no leveling system, all of the skills learnt in the previous games e.g Pontius' shield gliding ability and Zoya's fire arrows, to note two, are now given to you from the very start. Another difference, and quite a major one, is the camera angle(s). No longer are you bound to a 2D plane, you can now wander freely in 3D world. This does make the game more interesting, and puts the puzzling elements through their paces, Although at times it can be hard to judge the distance between certain platforms and how far away enemies are. One quite important thing to note is that this iteration of the game does seems to lack the amount of puzzles that the previous games in the series had. Also, not to mention, the difficulty seems to have been ramped up a little, not helped by the fact that it can't be changed, also unlike the previous two games.
There are a number of moments in the game where it becomes incredibly frustrating, with the scarce number of checkpoints and the fairly annoying, and pointless, side quests that pit you against multiple waves of foes.
Although retaining some of the original traits of the previous games, Trine 3 is sadly a bit of a disappointment. With bugs and glitches scattered around each level and the constant demand to battle enemies in order to progress, this game just feels like it's missing the original charm. The story is fairly well put together, however, and the characters are still as charming as ever. But sadly, for the most part Trine 3 is too lacking in what the series is known for. As a fan of the other two games, it saddens me to have to down vote this game. If you want to play the whole series then you have to play The Artifacts of Power. But if you want a puzzle based platformer that's very much like the previous two in the series, then I suggest looking elsewhere. Good Day!

Art style and presentation is trippy and honestly very interesting.
Gameplay-wise, it’s one of the more terrible puzzle games I’ve played. In this game, you have to clear regions of same-color blocks, like SameGame, but with the baffling restriction that you can only clear a region if you can draw a path through every block. This leaves your options severely limited at all times.
With such limited options for moves, it’s next to impossible to set up any big combos or get out of trouble on purpose (about on par with Bejeweled / Candy Crush), and in the cases you do, the game could drop a Lucid block in the middle of it (which are supposed to be rewards) and force you to reset the board, destroying what you built.
Starting level layouts seem to be hand-designed, but random skyfalls and target colors mean it doesn’t really matter.
Competitively, there are no game mechanics in place to prevent you from playing a level forever for unlimited score, except that getting stuck with no possible moves will zero your score. At about level 48, there’s a sudden difficulty spike as all objectives require regions of 3 or more, so playing through all 55 levels without getting a Game Over is highly unlikely. Oh, and no leaderboards!
For a game that tries to sell itself as relaxing, it’s a bit too far on the frustrating and stressful side, and certainly not something you can zone out to while playing. Achievement hunters should probably grab it on sale, as it’ll be in your 100% trophy case in a few mere hours, but for casual or hardcore puzzle fans, there’s so many better options out there.

I'm not too keen on getting started back up in Ascent since my experence was so bad last time but let me explain why I didn't enjoy it. These problems could all be fixed by now and I could be just unhappy for no reason but let's give it a go anyway.
1. The learning curve.
Sure, a simple game with everything handed to you right from the get go can get boring fast but this game doesn't hand you much of anything at all. I spent alot of my time looking at the community built wiki for instruction on how to actually play the game.
2. The grind.
You need resorces, and lots of them. Those are found in rocks floating though space. Getting those floating rocks to give you valuable stuff takes alot of time since your cargo can only hold so much stuff at once and your equipment for mining also takes up alot of space. (Also there was a glitch where if you mined a rock at the wrong time your laser would stop functioning and you needed to restart the game, this may have been fixed but it was nearly game breaking) Or you can be a galatic taxi service and ferry NPC from port to port. Either way it's the same action over and over again with nothing changing for a few hundred hours. Also you get to watch your ship do the same hyper jump animation a couple thousand times which definattly never gets boring. Another way of getting resorces is though your farms on the 8 or so NPC planets(three unless you pay for premium). But it's also very grindy as you need to collect them yourself and transport them to the bank manually.
3. The Members only area
Most of the game is locked behind a members only screen. Sure you can play for free but you will spend alot more time grinding then you would if you had access to the larger cargo bays and extra NPC planets only members are allowed to have. Since the grind is already unbearable it doesn't make much sense to be a free player for long. The best ships are reserved for players that supported the kick starter and no amount of money (In-game or real) will give you access to them.
4. Setting up a colony
After a few hundred hours of grinding resorces you will have what you need to set up a colony. If it's far out you can fill up your cargo with hydrogen used for hyper jumps and ferry your resorces to your colony little bit at a time. After a few hundred trips you then need to manually calibrate your colonys settings to fit the atmosphere of the planet your colonising. The community written wiki explains how to find the correct setting for your planet by telling you it's very very hard and you should just ask another player for their settings on another already established planet. Also the terrain on the planets is buggy so expect your domes to be clipping though the ground while you piddle around in the eva and try to find the correct camera angle. There is a device to instatly terraform a planet but it's also reserved for kickstarter supporters.
5. Exploring SPACE!
This is one aspect of the game I enjoyed a little. Once you get your fancy new hyper drive and load up on hydrogen from one of the player ran colonys you can jump to systems that are not linked by the player built hyper gates. But you need hydrogen to jump. You can collect hydrogen from gas giants but the collection system is unbearable. You need a large ram scoop to collect it, which takes up alot of cargo space, which leaves very little room for hydrogen since your hyperdrive already takes up alot of space. If your lucky you find a nice gas giant and start scooping away. But it's not as simple as just diving right through the middle. You need to skim along the surface in a 2 foot wide window, The surface is a sphere, your ship flys straight, you can't see where you are, the sphere is lumpy, also you need 1200 hydrogen but only collect 2 hydrogen for every second you are in that sweet spot. Expect to spend an hour or so diving in and out like a dolphin before you get enough fuel to carry on.
6. Hypergates
These are pretty cool, they are player built gateways between systems to remove the need for a hyperdrive. They require a buttload of a special mineral called unobtaniom or something. I spent 30 or so hours mining and never once found the special mineral. This is very much a community thing since everyone needs to pitch in to get it going.
7. The chat system
There is one chat room. Everyone, everywhere is in it. That is seriously it.
The game looks nice, and the community is very nice, everyone I ever interacted with was nothing but helpful and supportive. But after 70 hours I felt sort of like all those people that bought "No mans sky". The game I played and the game I THOUGHT I was going to play, were very different things.
