After over 5000 hours playing, here is my review. I am in no way associated with the company that provides Ascent. I am just a long time player.
What Ascent Is and Is Not
Ascent came on line mid 2013. Since then, there has been many changes and additions. With all those changes, there are still some things at the core of the game that can be highlighted.
Ascent is:
. Similar to Lego, it gives the player pieces to create what each person imagines within the boundaries of the game environment. We are given set pieces and are allowed to put them together as we want.
(Massively Multiplayer Online) game. It allows players to interact, chat, trade, and cooperate in game play and on large projects such as jump gate building and terraforming worlds. At the core of the game is a place to cooperate.
, each explorable with an average of 10 planets/moons in each star system. It is an entire galaxy waiting to be discovered. Each system is procedurally created from random seeds. This means that each system can have a wide variety of differing features, planets, and resources from a base standard set of resources which are available in game. Some are quite common, while a few are quite rare, yet all have been found and can be available to any player within the game.
. We are not forced within a story that limits the players to a defined outcome or role. We are free to create our own story and empire. The dynamics are very easy to work with and after a short time, each player soon becomes a tycoon or master of their realm. There is so much room to play, that one can create an empire and never bump into another player, or create their empire on well established systems and join in on the projects going on within the game. One can switch back and forth between the two easily if mood calls for a day alone, or a day of play and interactions with the community.
. Trade is another core part of the game. Players can trade with NPC Space Stations in the Inner9 systems, or player Stock Markets in the outer systems. Mining asteroids is also a way to get free resources and sell to players or SS Local Markets for high profit trading.
. Because we are given tools of cooperation, not destruction, we are able to assist each other and coordinate our efforts for the good of humanity, not the destruction of it. We get to know each other and enjoy catching up and joking. While we take the game seriously, we can relax and enjoy interacting and relating to each other. The game has a light layer of politics with a few elected positions, so good relations are also a tool within game to further one’s political career. The game waits for the player and is designed for someone to either play heavily, or a few hours a week, if they choose. The few quests in game are more for a tutorial than for locked in play. One can start and stop them at any time and place. Once achieved, the quests are done and allows for a return to relaxed free play. One can even drop into and out of the quests and the storyline waits for the player to want to go to the next step in the quest. The community also puts a lot of time and effort into creating game support. The game wiki pages are supplied and run by the players along with multiple other support tools. While play style can be relaxed, one can do some serious number crunching and documenting. Again, the player gets to choose which way they want to play.
. There are Non Player Character (NPC) pirates that are limited to selected areas. These are the only things players can shoot and attack. They are only in designated areas, so one has to seek them out. This allows to player to choose if they want to fight, or just build your empire. It allows for the relaxed game play. Pirates can be engaged, or ignored. A player can choose to take out some pirates one day and ignore them the next.
. The game is well developed, but not completed. With one developer and many pieces available, like Legos, it can be a never ending play, or one you build a few things, then grow tired. New pieces are added slowly at times and quickly other times. The simple things come fast, but the more complex parts of the game take much more development and come slower. Each piece gives multiple ways of using it, so one piece can just add a little, or change the entire game dynamic. We often do not know until exploring it for a while to see how it effects things. Again, part of the open play that some like, while others do not. Serious bugs are addressed and dealt with, but a few additions are still in process of completion and have small issues that are on the list to be fixed. These issues are not game breaking, but one does need to be patient as they are slowly woven into completed game design. While this can be frustrating to some, remembering that there are some interconnectivity of other features that are coming may be why it is left as is for the present. One developer has to choose what is critical to put time into. Sometimes that time is just running the business and design has to be put on the back burner for a bit. Looking back over the past 4 years, the speed of new game development and additions are quite impressive for one person to have achieved. There is plenty of content for the cost of the game.
. Sandbox games are not for everyone. Some like the tight quests and goals set by a designer. Many enjoy the player to player conflicts. Others enjoy a harsh game environment they must struggle against. Ascent has none of these elements. Those seeking these things will not connect easily.
. It is a place that you can not loose what you have. No one can destroy something you have worked to build or create. The core of the game is construction, not destruction. One player can not negatively affect another player’s game in a major way. No one can own systems, planets, or asteroid fields. They are all open to everyone. While you can not be locked out of anything, you can also not lock out anyone else from anything except your own colonies and starbases. You control those areas and share the rest of the areas of play. If your goal is to cause grief to others, you will find you have little tools to do that. Ascent is not a place to go after others.
. The ultimate goal is to find our way back to Earth. There is so much room and game play left before we can get back to Earth. We are not even sure what is between us and Earth. We suspect some alien influence, but only one encounter of extraterrestrials while progressing through the Neptune Project quest has been revealed. Our fears (really hopes) are there is a large alien force that we much face as we get closer to Earth, but this is all speculation.
. Along with the purchase of the game, the player gets 3 months of premium subscription. This is more than enough time to delve into and build a massive empire. If the player enjoys the community and game play, it is only $3 a month for premium access after the first 3 months.
. The game and welcoming community is always ready for many more new Pilot Citizens (PC). We need those who have the neural pathways (imaginary thing needed in game to use warp and hyperjump drives) which allow their imaginations to determine their game-play. Are you tired of the constant drama and conflict? Are you ready for a totally different way to play a MMO? Are you ready to join us as we work together continuing to expand humanity’s reach into the galaxy on our way home? If you have read this far, we think you may just be one of the ones we are looking for. Come ready to have fun.

This review is for Baldur's Gate 1 and 2.
I come from a generation of rpgs that have held my hand from the beginning and have been simple and comfortable to follow, pick up and play and eventually complete. You cannot go into this series with that mindset, it will chew you up and spit you out. I have only played a few hours of both and I can tell you, you will die very early on and you will be frustrated when you do. It is because of this type of gameplay this is not the type of game for me. The die, reload, die, reload (repeat several times) until the "rolls" are in your favour is very tedious and i've found no measure of enjoyment from it. Even after successfully winning a fight I haven't really felt a sense of accomplishment.
The combat isn't particularly enjoyable as it can either be over in seconds with flawless results on either side (mostly on the enemy side) or they can last upwards of 30 seconds as the character rolls fail completely. Now this may not seem like a long time but when it's the same fight you've been attempting for 5-10 minutes, 30 seconds feels like a lifetime.
Questing is obviously before a time when waypoints and Nav trails weren't a thing so you do get some sense of achievement from that when you figure a quest out and complete that.
All of this being said I do recommend that people try the game so they can get a sense of where we have come from and how easy we have it now. I feel there is a good reason for it though. If you're a glutton for punishment and have a lot of patience then there is a good chance you will enjoy this.

This game is much reviewed and approved by reviewers.  It was the first D&D RPG that fully simulated the (board) game and coined the term "fully immersive" to the RPG world.  By immersive they say: it has graphics that seem to all agree to it's own universe, stereo 3D sound effects (new at the time), story, and art so that the player is pulled into the realm of the game.  Few games have ever repeated that particular quality of BG I/II.
Baldur's Gate II Enhanced is bigger and slightly better (game engine).  However I'd say they are both "must see" and suggest to do I before II.  Note also the BG manual has a good slice of D&D rules in it (i read the orig. rules from an official guide, never sat down for a game tho).
That being said, BG is dated and POE (or DOS2?) is a solid PC SRPG with deeper graphics details.  You need to be in the mood to sacrifice 3d detail for something isometric 2D "that was good enough it started this srpg genre".  It is the original immersive D&D sRPG. Asteroid Bounty Hunter is a 2D side scrolling shoot-em-up taking place in space. Developed by Just1337. Players will adventure across the galaxy fighting off bounty hunters and asteroids.
The gameplay of Asteroid Bounty Hunter consists of dodging projectiles and destroying asteroids and enemy ships. Player will have 3 weapons at their disposal excluding their primary cannon. Each weapon differs from one another, and has their own upsides and downsides. Players can upgrade their ship and weapons to deal with harder levels. Players can play any level on various difficulties, and various modifiers to accumulate more experience.
Asteroid Bounty Hunter does a few things right:
* Extremely easy achievements
* Fun/Simple game
* Entertaining cutsceens
* Varity in level design
Asteroid Bounty Hunter does some things wrong:
* Buggy
* Slow/Basic story
* Lack of variety of weapons
* Not overly replayable
Asteroid Bounty Hunter isn't a bad game, in fact, it's one of those rare small indie games that actually has some substance. At the cost of $3.29CDN, and almost always on sale, it's a fantastic "one and done" game, as well as a great game to 100%.

So I hate to give this a "No," since I'm really into the central conceits of it (FMV puzzle thriller, sign me up). And this episode is fine as a proof-of-concept! But as-is, it's pretty unfulfilling. I'm generally speaking not the sort to complain about games being too short--I want games to be just as long or as short as the story and gameplay require. In this case, however, there's barely any of those two to speak of--the thriller plot is barely established, and the couple of puzzles (and I mean just a couple; not counting hunting for clickable objects, it would be generous to say there's ten puzzles in the game, and at least half of those are "Find something written down in spot X, realize it's to lock Y" variety). There's QTEs that ultimately don't matter (in that there's no fail state), but I find that kind of cute for an FMV game since it means that there's more film to watch if you want to replay.
The bottom line is that I like this as a proof of concept but judged as a game by itself, it's nothing to speak of. I got it on sale for a buck, and if you can do the same, there's no harm in trying it out. But until some more episodes come along with more meat to them, I can't recommend this.

So it's a FMV adventure/puzzle game. The "plot" is basically Saw minus the gore. There really is no plot. The guy wakes up, some detective looks at a car, the guy runs out of a building. The end.
The acting is alright. The video quality is pretty good. It's interesting how they seamlessly keep the FMV look during interactive bits.
So, the meat of the game is the puzzles and I'm juding it on that.
2 sliding tiles puzzles, a newspaper wordsearch, and opening a desk drawrer. That's pretty much it. The rest is just pixel hunting as you move the mouse slowly over the whole screen waiting to see a hotspot. The only time I got stuck was a dimly lit portion where I missed an item and has to backtrack, trailing the mouse over every screen. Never got stuck on a proper puzzle.
So that's it. Only about 3 1/2 puzzles and a lot of tedious pixel hunting. The game is only 30 minutes long, and 5 of those minutes are spent watching a guy walk around a car with a flashlight.
Forget the cheap price, it's just not worth the time.

This game is great. I played through it at least seven or eight times, trying different things and seeing how the game changes in reaction to the chaos level that you achieve in the story. The gameplay is tailored to what you want it to be, with many options to eliminate a target and to move around the venue that you are in. You are able to clear the game with Blink I only, so I think that fact is mighty impressive on the part of the devs and level designers.
However, I personally think that getting the DLC is a must on this game, considering that it could be considered its own game (with both DLCs, that is) and that other elements of the base game were improved in the DLCs. For example, the voice acting in some of the Dishonored base recordings were just plain dreadful, and Corvo's Blink ability is just a simple teleport, nothing more. In the DLCs, Daud (other guy you play as) has a Blink that stops time when you're not moving making for some nice air setups or aiding you to escape a risky situation, and the voice acting in the recordings sounds much better. Not only that, the game fills in a lot of the story behind the base game and it allows you to truly see the base game in an entirely different light.
I also enjoyed the Dunwall City Trials. It just added a challenge mode (think of Batman: Arkham City challenge mode) with stealth, combat, and mystery challenges (whodunnit essentially), although I could go without this. I would recommend picking up the GOTY edition just for Daud's two DLCs, the Knife of Dunwall and the Brigmore Witches. Besides that, the other two DLCs are optional. The Void Walker DLC is meh, it's more for people who want a head start in the game. The Dunwall City Trials are just a challenge mode, but they're enjoyable.
All in all, great base game, but the two Daud DLCs make it so much better.

This is one of my all time favorite games. I've played through it several different times, doing different play styles each time through. Each time I play, I find something new. It's a fun game.

After playing that way, I looked at Corvo differently. Corvo, despite his world getting shattered, and his name ruined, he refuses to become a killer. Corvo, instead, realizes who the real enemy is: those who betrayed him. I like to think of Corvo as the hero who has to do the right thing all while being hated by the public.
Of course, you could elect to be a cold-blooded killer on a war-path, which is also fun. But I would challenge new players, or returning players to try going through the story without killing anybody. Personally, I like the latter playstyle better.
Dishonored's design is great, the gameplay is radical, and the story is rich. I only wish that there was a dialogue system, so I could chat with NPC's and learn more, rather than being the spooky guy in an even spookier mask that just gazes into your soul when you speak.

So you do the final chapter and the Wizard says "Only 2 more pieces to go" and then the game ends. Clearly an incomplete game. There are others problems too.
-Puzzles and stages are easy, requiring minimal amounts of brain activity. There's not much challenge beyond encountering weird physics bugs.
-The 3D setting, while potentially cool, really makes the game frustrating. It's as if the game isn't quite adapted to being in 3D. Trying to shoot arrows at monsters and bosses is simply a non-option given the random result you will get.
-Collecting triangles is what allows you to unlock levels. There seems to be issues with calculation of your total triangles playing multiplayer or single player. Me and my friend kept getting different totals when completing levels together. Stages also wouldn't unlock properly either.
-All the skills you had before in the other games seem to have disappeared. You only get the basics, no planks, no elemental arrows, no hammer...it's disappointing.
-The story just dies when it clearly should not. Otherwise, you had a sense of working towards completing a quest. There are some side chapters that seem like they're just there for the fun and are very superfluous. Wish they had added more to the main story than those flimsy side chapters.
On the plus side, it had good looking graphics. Otherwise, this game is a work in progress and rather unfulfilling.

First thing off the mark, this is a game with great potential.
It is a great game to play, though it has a few limitations that reduce the length of time I will be involved in it.
The background of the game is that a spacefaring human civilisation has collapsed to the point where only a few systems clustered together and linked by stargates survive.
Starting in a small ship, you are now equipped to begin your career as a Civilian Pilot and help to being prosperity to the Inner Systems, and to expand into the greater unknown to colonise and restore humanity to its former position as a sprawling mass of connected systems.
The way to wealth and advancement in the early part of the game is to follow the starter missions which allow you to begin to develop your own plot of land as an Inner Settlement, then expand to your own Inner Starbase.  During the starter narrative and missions, you learn to trade, mine and skim Gas Giants for resources – just to name a few.
It is engaging and there is a lot to discover.
As you progress and, when you activate the Premium subscription you get with the game purchase (3 months of each type of Premium access), you are able to firstly create and develop Settlements on 8 of the Inner Nine (I9) systems, and greatly expand your Inner Starbase.
During this time, your Trading and asteroid Mining skills will increase, as can you Skimming skills if you continue to farm Gas Giants for resources.
Outside of the I9 are the Outer Systems.
Everything here is developed by the players – well, the Jam-1 system is a little different.
So, in the systems that are not part of the starting area, every Stargate and every colony and every Starbase has been built by the player community.  I say player community as the Stargates themselves require so much in the way of resources, it requires a number of players co-operating to complete these projects.
At all times, you are able to pilot your ship to these Outer Systems to buy from players at their Starbases and colonies, and haul resources back to the I9 to increase profit.
That’s the basics and I have mostly enjoyed my experience.
There are a few things that imo are missing, could be better, or could just go…
One of my big questions rattling around in my head has been, if humans got this far into the galaxy, even after a collapse, there should be something left.  But there isn’t.  I don’t get that.  As a player explores new star systems with the intent to colonise and therefore open up new areas, surely there would at least be a remnant of the former civilisation.  As you can EVA on planets, I think it would be great to explore ruins of previous colonies.  Hey, there may even be some active NPC colonies out there???
Research is a bit, well, meh.  You do have to research new buildings for colonies and Starbases but, after that, it is really only improving on current technology.  I would like to see something better implemented here and, if the game incorporated “lost colonies” it would be really cool if you could find “scraps” of past knowledge that might open up new research horizons.
The Political System is a bit raw, and really may not be necessary.  It is really only a system by which to name Planets and Star Systems, and these can change again if a new player is elected to a position of power.  This system has caused some schisms to form and can easily be used as a rather nasty piece pf metagame PVP.  When the Dev had to get involved with a particular dispute on the Forums, he mentioned the Constitutional Rights of the Senators (who can name Star Systems and approve Stargates), but there is no Constitution that I could find…so maybe if there was one, or if System names could only be changed by some sort of consensus, it may avoid the complications of the past.
One thing that I really like about this game is the player community.  They are, in the main, helpful and encouraging every step of the way.  Freely giving advice and helping when you’re stuck or unsure, the community makes this game that much more enjoyable.  There are a couple of nasties, but their impact is easily avoided.
This is a great game and should be experienced to its full.  I only hope that new directions are implemented so that someone like me can be engaged in other areas as well.

As a fan of the previous Trine who's spent many long hours finding all the collectibles and dying countless times to get the host of difficult achievements in both, Trine 3 was a very disappointing new installment. For starters, the achievements alone were dirt-easy compared to its predecessors, requiring a single run without noticeable effort or tactics. Your characters even see downgrades to their abilities from previous games, now with no way to progress them.
I'll admit it was interesting to see a change into more 3D-esque environments, but even that was badly done; it's like they couldn't quite decide whether to keep with their previous style or upgrade, and ended up doing half of both: The maps are very linear with few, if any, branches, next to no secrets, and painfully easy-to-find collectibles, which by the way have no effect on play other than unlocking new stages, which has always been a given before, so now it's just kinda dumb.
On top of it all, the game itself is incomplete. It ends about a third of the way through the plot, very abruptly, with no prior indications aside from the newly-implemented story map simply having no more stages after that one. It is unclear whether the continuation of the story will be presented as another purchaseable game, DLC, or freely, but the fact that the game was released and advertised as a full, complete game at all is infuriating to me, when its predecessors most assuredly were.
In conclusion, if you have fundamental respect for the previous Trine games and are hoping for the same fun out of this one, prepare to be disappointed. Save your money, or at least wait until the game is actually finished first.

Unfortunately now there are some bugs that still haven't been patched.
1) Sometimes (around Ulcaster and the Sword Coast in particular) the action music doesn't stop when the fighting is over, until I reload the save.
2) Aldeth vs Druids quest in Cloakwood is marked as unfinished even though I killed Aldeth. Apparently checking his cabin before completing the quest screws it up, whether you defend the druids or kill them.
3) Couldn't get to Cloakwood after the bandit camp because Chapter 4 didn't trigger. Nothing ruins my experience of a game more than needing to pick at files and lines of code just to get it to progress. I bought this game for a chill little time-waster, but it turned out to be much more than that.
The first thing I wasn't expecting was the difficulty curve.  It started out pathetically easy, but by level 50 the game had become fiendishly difficult (though the occasional checkerboarding seems a bit forced).  As of this review I still haven't beaten the penultimate level.
The line-drawing also adds a surprising amount of depth.  This mechanic lead to me starting to call shapes that couldn't be properly drawn "monstrosities", since if I couldn't somehow settle them into a better shape and eliminate them, they would inevitably begin to catch more of more of their color and spread like a spiky cancer through the board.  You have to be careful not to create them (or feed existing ones) if you can ever help it, but eventually one will slip through.  Often this can spell doom, but every so often you can manage to pull off a win before it gets too bad, which feels great.
The static starting boards are paired with randomized tasks to create the challenge.  On certain late levels it's even advisable to restart until you get better starting tasks, so that you can clear a designed big group and complete a task at the same time for a big head start on the completion meter.  More difficult tasks in the later levels also attempt to ensure that you can't manage to chain them to create a Lucid block, forcing you to deal with the beginning board's complications the whole way through, rather than randomize the board and make things easier on yourself.
My only complaints would be that the "zen" music gets grating rather quickly, and a personal complaint that I did not buy this to get a hard game.  Despite its difficulty it remains fun, though.  It's a pretty good puzzle game.

Some of you may be wary of buying into this game because of the developer's history with the failed game; The Dead Linger. Now luckily, I know the story behind TDL and I understand that sometimes, sh*t happens. The developers have moved on, and so have we. (They've also given previous owners of TDL a 65% discount on this little gem right here, which is more than generous).
NOW. Bring forth, Unfortunate Spacemen. The concept of this game had me interested right off the bat. Think of a multiplayer game version of the movie The Thing. Sounds too good to be true, right? This game aims to make that a reality. Mind you, that's only one of the many inspirations behind this title. Unfortunate Spacemen truly is a unique, new, creative, and most importantly - fun game to play.
Now of course, it's Early Access and that means some issues, some frustrations, some bugs, and some other bullsh*t. "Purchasing" this game is an investment. If you are'nt prepared for some
stuff to happen during development, please don't buy into this. Too many people purchase an EA game so they have something new to b*tch about. Honestly that goes for all games. Right now the only issue I have with Spacemen is the matchmaking. It's very rough, and hopefully is a top priority BUT - it still works. I had a server going with 18 people connected, and it was awesome.
I'm doing it because the developers - so far - are totally rad. For example I had an issue where I was trying to buy my friend a copy, since I have 65% discount that they gave owners of their previous game. It wasn't allowing me to purchase a gift copy, so I made a post, to which a dev replied in a matter of minutes and immediately sent an e-mail to Valve. Valve then revealed that they turned off gifting options for people with a discount because they didn't want people getting multiple copies of the game for cheap. Yet, the developer told them to allow it anyway - that immediately earned my respect. On top of that, these guys are
playing their own game (shoutout to Thunderfist), and they actually communicate with their players.
I love the concept, I'm happy with how they've executed it, and I'm more than pleased with how the developers have presented themselves and treated their fanbase. Honestly if I knew they were gonna' be that cool about things, I probably would have asked to pay full price anyway. As far as I'm concerned, this is already easily worth $15.
Keeping my fingers crossed for the futue of Unfortunate Spacemen!

I love this game a lot.  I don't even know WHY I love it.  I just do.
If you love games that are open world, survival, difficult, slow paced etc...you'll love this.  If you're more into action packed, then perhaps not.  This game is a NARCOTIC.  It's soooo relaxing, from the colors to the actual gameplay.
Don't misunderstand me though: the game isn't necessarily BORING.  You crash in the middle of the Canadian wilderness.
So, it's technical: you have to keep food, water, medical supplies, hunting gear, etc...all the while maintaining the amount of weight you're carrying.  You don't want too much, or else you'll get tired fast.  A lot of activity means a lot of calories burnt, so you have to be mindful of your intake and daily exertion.  You need to rest, stay hydrated, and just keep moving nonstop because where you're comfortable now will end up running low on supplies anyway.  Clothing is another big thing: the condition, the amount of warmth it provides, wind breaking, moisture it retains from the snow.  For some people that could be a chore, but this is a survival game.
Not only that, but the world is HUGE.  And they just keep making it bigger.  I'm not even sure if it's possible to completely play a sandbox mode dry of it's resources, because you're either going to die before that or you can just feed off the land.
For me there's just something totally immersive and relaxing about it.  It's gorgeous, even though it's not designed to capture total realism like other survival crafting games (ARK, 7 Days to Die, etc).  The simplicity of both the art and the theme is just so good for me.  I've had this game on Steam for not very long, but I bought it the moment it went out for the Preview Program on my Xbox One.  And that was about two years ago when it was only a sandbox.
The story is a little dragging at first, but the mystery of it is compelling.  You honestly just want to know more about it.  Why is this all happening?  What even IS happening?  Not only that, but it's all so very challenging.  You can be so close to finishing a Challenge on Sandbox, but then you freeze to death or starve because a wolf decided to nibble your gibblets.
But regardless of how frustrated I get, I always end up coming back.  I never bore or tire of it.  After a long days work of retail, I just want to come home and play this game.  I never thought it would be so breathtaking for me.  Hell, I even have a cabin design to my room now.  I love it that much.

is a very mixed experience.  It's not mediocre -- it has surprising highs and terrible lows.
In its favour,
does a lot of things better than you might expect from a cheap little indie.  Some of the voice acting is quite good (sadly, not all of it).  The lighting on the asteroid models is great.  Planets and nebulae going by in the background look fantastic.  Weapons fire makes spectacular use (possibly overuse) of smoke and particle effects.  There's a music player that allows you to switch songs, and even add your own, and the preloaded music is quite suitable for the game genre.
That's the good.  Much of it noteworthy.
The bad?  Spaceships are ugly flat sprites.  Everything's pretty large, so there's not a lot of room to maneuver.  Gameplay doesn't really change -- you upgrade as you go, but your ship only gains numerical advantages; it does exactly the same stuff in the same way that it does from the beginning.  Gameplay is slow, and rather repetitive.  Boss fights are tedious, not exciting.
In the final analysis,
is not a good game, simply because the bad elements are all gameplay-related, while the points of excellence, which it certainly has, are all stage-dressing and extras.  The poor gameplay weighed against the great features, and gameplay was the more important.

A pretty good game, as "asteroids" variants go.
Breakdown:
Gameplay - 7/10 - Decent. You get several weapons and a sheild, all of which can be upgraded. While the game advertises "unlimited upgrades", be aware that replaying a level only gives you global upgrades (sheilds, cooldowns, and damage), but upgrades to specific weapon and sheild regen only occur the first time you beat a level.
Sound - 10/10 - The music blew me away! Better than many AAA games, not what I was expecting from a simple shmup.
Story - 2/10 - The main character is dislikable. On the other hand, one doesn't play a shooter for the plot... so I'd just skip it.
Graphics - 7.5/10 - The game is pretty. You'll see the same graphics quite a lot, but that's a given for an asteroids clone. The backgrounds are nice, though the occasional oval planet (while perhaps scientifically realistic) has an odd feel to it.
Documentation - 3/10 - Not much in-game, other than during loading screens. However the description on the store page isn't too bad. Mastery points for ships appear to be incorrect, ignore them and just look at "MP to next level". MP is gained from green orbs from killing bounty hunters, and is spent on unlocking new ships. XP appears to be spent on global unlocks, but this may not be obvious, because these are displayed on the same screen as the ship unlocks.
Overall - 7.5/10 - The game has a few flaws, but the core parts work reasonably well.

Didn't know what to expect of this game. A friend of mine recommended it, mostly because the trailer and the art looked amazing, also, both having previously played Undertale, the little we knew and had seen about OneShot reminded us of the former in a strange way. But that's where the comparison, if you thought there was any, ended.
With charming characters full of personality, a mysterious and intriguing story and the constant feeling that there's is something else there, sometimes to the brink of paranoia, OneShot stands on it's own as probably one of the best indie games of 2016, and there's no better way to end the year. Even if it's, relatively a short game (around 4 or 5 hours), every minute of it is worth it.
Dare and give it a try, you won't regret it. Just remember, step carefully with each decision, cause every click, every time you make a decision, it's yours, and yours alone to bear with. Also, you might need some tissues, the flow of feels doesn't stop itself.
Im my personal book, OneShot is a solid 9/10. Wish it were longer.

If you want to experience real excellence in game design and storytelling, have $10 and about 4-5 hours, then PLEASE do yourself a favor and check out OneShot. I have never felt this type of connection with my player character in a game before. Niko is not simply your avatar in this digital world, he is a helpless being who you trusts you to protect him. At one point early on he told me he was scared of this machine and didn't want to get closer to it, but my gaming mind said "yea whatever" and directed him to inspect it closer. When he shrieked in terror and was almost injured by it my mindset completely changed - this game had made me feel bad for doing something to *my own character*.
I could go on and on about the extent of my disappointment and dislike of Undertale, primarily because of its use of numerous critical game design faux pas, but also because it was ultimately completely underwhelming and did not warrant the extent that people lauded it as "groundbreaking storytelling". OneShot is everything I had hoped Undertale would be.

The main hook that separates Lucid from the plethora of countless other falling block puzzle games is the way you remove these blocks. Rather than guiding pieces through mid air to try perfectly filling in empty spaces or position them so they match with their similiars, here the board is already full and you have to use your best judgement to trace a line through blocks of the same colour to remove them from play and send all the pieces above them crashing downwards. Remove the required colour and minimum target number to fill a circular gauge at the side of the screen, the more blocks you remove each turn the greater the amount the gauge will fill up and complete the stage. But there's a catch, as there always is.
While the minimum allowable number of blocks that can be removed in a single action can be as little as two, and with the upper limit only being whatever's actually available, if you want to remove a group of matching blocks then you MUST be able to remove all of the ones that connect to each other in that one action. Also, the line you trace has to be in a single, continuous strand that cannot cross over or repeat back on itself. So, for example, a T-shaped arrangement of blocks could never be removed because, after the starting point, the line you draw would have to move to one side or the other but then could not reach the remaining blocks without going back over itself and therefore could not connect all blocks of the same colour. It sounds kinda complicated, but trust me, it's a lot easier in practice.
There are 55 stages in total, and at first it seems like each one is simply a random collection of mixed colours that you remove with little thought, but you then begin to realise that the field of play isn't as haphazardly laid out as it first appears and there's actually an art to planning ahead and setting up the blocks to maximise your score and finish the stage more quickly. You can still randomly draw away at groups on a whim for the most part, but in later stages you can easily lead yourself into a dead end with no more viable options as the clusters of colours form shapes that are all but impossible to remove.
Unfortunately there's a fly in the ointment, though it isn't so much the way it plays, but rather, everything else. The presentation is mostly passable, but you can't shake the sense that there's something of a cheap or unfinished quality to it, as if nothing about it feels... "solid", like there's a very unsatisfying disconnect between the player and everything you interact with. It's almost like the cursor is hovering over a sheet of glass the entire time and never really touching what's on the other side. This would seem to suggest it started off life as a tablet game (where it would be perfectly suited), but apparently this isn't the case.
This isn't a bad game, by any means, but with its lacklustre feel and complete absence of any additional game modes beyond the 55 stages on offer, what could have been a really great game instead, frustratingly, is only a good one for casual puzzle fans to enjoy.

Really a must-play CRPG at some point in your life if you're interested in computer role-playing games.
Aside from the excellent story spanning 2 huge games (and now the Beamdog-made Siege of Dragonspear expansion. Thanks, Beamdog!), the slow-paced, tabletop-style role-playing, deep Advanced Dungeons & Dragons 2nd Edition rule implementation, tons of lore with decades of real-life development behind it (D&D), more loot, classes, kits, stats, monsters, party members, exploration and dice rolls than you can shake a fistful of dice at, the Beamdog enhancements continue to add a lot of great stuff to the game.
It's the little stuff that Beamdog keeps adding to the game that makes the Enhanced Edition well worth buying. New screens in the inventory, for example, such as the panel that shows visually how much THAC0, Armor Class, etc., you will gain or lose when equipping an item. Or the Advanced AI that actually lets you select finer details with on/off toggles as to how you want your companions to act (do you want them to use items on their own discretion, or spells? Have your Thief always search for traps? Etc..) The high resolution and scaling UI look great and I'm playing on a huge 4K TV several feet away with my Steam Controller profile (the artwork is still beautiful to this day, even if it's going to look dated and lower res.) There's just so many fine details and small aspects they have improved, and with the newest patch as of writing this (2.5 beta), they continue to add more and more to make the experience better.
If you want to know about the game itself, it's a classic BioWare RPG, one of the greatest and most iconic games of all-time. If you're interested in RPGs back before there was endless amounts of hand-holding in games, where you had to explore, think and figure things out without the internet, and don't mind playing an older, slower, different type of RPG that may be more challenging yet also more rewarding for your time invested, then you really have to play the entire Baldur's Gate series at some point. It's really as simple as that. They are the top classics among the classics of computer role-playing games.
It's a boatload of small tweaks that just add up to a much improved total package, and I'm thankful they (Beamdog) do it. Try a second run (or maybe a first, too) with mods like Sword Coast Stratagems for a really wicked excellent experience. The game has a ton of mods, by the way, and years worth of work in that area to explore. There's something for everyone, from Story Mode (already included in the EE) to tactical, difficult challenge mods, companion mods and much more.
Buy it, play it, revere it. They don't make 'em like this anymore.

When I first played this game when it came out originally (back in 1998), I was a wee eight-year-old whose mind couldn't seem to grasp the concepts and logistics behind the rules of 2nd edition Dungeons and Dragons. I was too gung ho and threw my character at enemies with no thought, I didn't know how to properly balance a team or to stock up on useful scrolls and potions, and thought I could just sleep off certain status effects, and made plenty of mistakes.
That said, I could only get so far in this game as a kid, and I never finished it to completion. Regardless of that though, Baldur's Gate was extremely memorable and I loved the characters a lot. They stuck with me over the years.
Fast forward to me recently, years later, where I'm giving this game another go out of curiosity and the desires for a taste of nostalgia. My initial reaction: "Good LORD this game has not aged well..."
Because to be fair, the graphics are far outdated to games that play kinda similarly nowadays (Path of Exile, Divinity: Original Sin, etc.) But I just said to myself "what the heck, I'll give it a go anyway" and gave the game time enough to just outright grow on me. The graphics didn't bother me after just a few hours and I fell completely in love with the characters and story all over again. There's been fixes to a lot of previous game breaking bugs, and I loved how I could use the mouse wheel to zoom in and out of battles to better strategize the placement of my party. Better yet, I knew well enough now how to correct all the things I did wrong as a kid in order to get dozens of hours of gameplay out Baldur's Gate this time around and I got to completely finish the game! It has such a great story, and that is something that hasn't changed at all over the years.
Simply put, Baldur's Gate is a masterpiece. I mean, sure, it's old as hell. Tons of games I grew up with are now. There are probably other CRPGs out there that overshadow this game presently, but you'd be doing yourself a disservice if you claimed to be a fan of CRPGs without even giving this game or its sequel game a chance. Bottom line: if you like Dungeons and Dragons, you're gonna like this game a lot. There's a lot of replayability here. You can make tons of different characters with all sorts of different builds, form all sorts of interesting companion combinations with over 25+ recruitable NPCs throughout your travels, there's tons of side quests and silly easter eggs, lighthearted sometimes outright goofy humor but also morbid realities and life lessons to experience. The list goes on and on.
Also, this was a game made before Bioware was bought out by EA (♥♥♥♥ off EA, you ruin just about everything you guys touch). This was back when Bioware had such damn good writing that they probably made this game and BGII and then decided they had such a blast writing a fantasy story in the Forgotten Realms canon that they wanted to make their own universe and began writing for their Dragon Age series (which turned into one of my fave franchises ever, so thanks Bioware!)
As an added bonus, the developer team that polished this game and optimized it for this Enhanced Edition release (Beamdog) actually made a DLC completely on their own in order to connect the events between Baldur's Gate and Baldur's Gate II together better and I really recommend that too if you decide to go on to play the sequel game. It'll plant the seeds of outright hatred in your heart for the sequel game's villian before that game's events even happen! Good times.

This game is a particularly successful way of making a space game fun to play at least for a few months off gaming.
The universe is full of delightful things to discover and to enjoy.  While there is a lot to learn, it is easily taken on board in incremental steps of discovery.  The Ascent Wiki is fantastic, as are the You Tube demonstrations. There is not shortage of tutoarial materials that you can access that will explain everything to you.  As well as this, there is a very helpful community online that are happy to take the time to answer questions as they are asked.
There is little in the way of major conflict, (unless you choose to go looking for it), as conflict is currently optional at this time. There is no Galactic War going on and I am thankful for this fact.  Having grown tired after years of eternal shoot them ups, I really enjoy this as a hobby style adventure of wonder and discovery.  The online players are working in a collaborative effort to unfold "Space, the Final Frontier" as you read this review.
I read that the developer intends to ultimately make a PVP area for those that are busting to have a fight with their space ships and there is already at this time a PVE area that is optional to go into.
The graphics are reasonable. (There have been major upgrades ongoing and getting better all the time). The personal development is great.  The trading system works OK.  There are tons of things to do that are interesting: such as finding new places to fly and trade, discovering new worlds that get named after you, building bigger and better ships, building and developing colonies / making your own starbases / your own mining operations / researching new technology / building stargates / running for political office ingame / building the community / interacting with some very nice people / learning new strategy to build up your own wealth and prestige and lots of discovery.  There is lots of intricasy in this game.  Enough to keep you interested and occupied for a very long time.  There are lots of incredibly interesting details to learn in producing space stations / colony settlements / automted factories and NPC run trading runs.

Why the hell am I going to write a review of this? It's only a "remastered" release of one of the best RPG's ever made. Perhaps.... to tell people that it is one of the best RPG's ever made? Yeah, lets go with that.
So what did they add to the original game? Well, a few new characters, numerous gameplay elements that were introduced in Baldur's Gate 2, a few new class "kits", and some arena thing I haven't tried yet. The stuff from BG2 could already been modded in with "Baldur's Gate Trilogy" which let you play the whole series in one continuous playthrough. If there is anything this version lacks that  I wish they had done, it is that. With that said character importing into BG2 works fine. As for the (actual) new stuff they added to the game, it is pretty neat. The new characters are interesting, fully voiced, and have their own questlines. Those character questlines are the sort of content that is lacking in BG1 while being the norm in BG2. So to see that stuff in BG1, while cool, really serves to highlight how all the other characters don't have anything like it. Kinda makes the original game look worse. :s
Other than that.... it's Baldur's Gate. What else needs to be said? It was great in the late 90's/early 2000's and it's great now. It stands nearly 20 years later as still one of my top RPG recommendations out there. If you haven't played it yet... then what the hell are you waiting for? :o

Baldur's Gate has since its release set the bar of what can and should be expected from western RPGs - for a good reason.
The writing and overarching story is superb and leaves many role playing options, with a slight inclination towards good/neutral alignments. Though bare in mind that the story is narrated primarily through dialogues composed of text, which while not excessive, requires a great deal of patience from the player. Voiced dialogues are used sparingly throughout the game, but is used selectively for setting the mood. Playable characters are plentiful and of different alignments and personalities, which imbues the player with choice. The music score is equally good and conveys an epic atmosphere of adventure and exploration.
The graphics, which have been bumped to scale for modern resolutions, are perhaps Baldur's Gate weakest aspect and its age is starting to show. Character statistics are derived from early D&D rulesets, which is overly convoluted by today's standards and might require several visits of the wiki to grasp.
Despite these minor flaws, Baldur's Gate still stands the test of time and if you like RPGs in any way, shape or form, you owe it to yourself to play this classic masterpiece.

This is in all honesty nothing but a monetized mod for HL2.f
It lacks in depth. The game, which I speeded through admittedly, took me 82 minutes. An hour and 22 minutes. One of the things I can appreciate in this game is the skins of the Combine soldiers, the level design in the later levels (Specifically past Xen) and the voice acting in the flashbacks.
The Vortigaunts sound like a half-hearted job at replicating Akama from WoW, and sound horribly wheezy. The Combine Soldiers have a strange filter that is nowhere close to the one in HL2, it makes me wonder why he even bothered to add the new ones. They sound like Super-Battle-Droids from Republic Commando, in all honesty. On top of that, some of the gameplay even on Normal is straight up unforgiving.
The Xen chapter, which is I believe a single level, looks quite bad. It is a combination of three to five asteroids that float about in empty space, along with horribly transluscent crystals attached to unexplained Combine apparatuses.
The particle effects, however, are outright beautiful, admittedly.
The viewmodel hands, which should naturally be new, are the same. Nothing different sans the color, which is just desaturated.
There are no new weapons in this game. All of them are the same. There are no new models for the weapons, nor any replacements.
There are no new mechanics in this game either, the only redeeming factor for this point is the end battle, which is pretty satisfying from my standpoint.

You also take roles that resemble a tech tycoon like Steve Jobs, or an Admiral like Chester Nimitz of the US Navy. It also features political roleplay.

The game is PVE focused. Combat is an option. You can choose to gain loot fighting pirates, as well as looking for wrecked ships by buying the location coordinates off the markets. You scan the wreckage & receive blueprints to design your own ship parts. You may choose to build a smuggling operation, by contacting npc’s on starbases & asking them to buy contraband. Once you’ve set up your contacts, you call them when ready to deliver, & bribe or avoid the guards to make the deliveries. &, best of all to me, you explore uncharted stars & they are named after you on the map.
In Ascent, you have a persistent universe that provides a validity to your actions, a sense of player agency, because what you do matters. If you terraform a planet, other players can colonize on your planet also. You’ve created a new world with a breathable environment.
To move around in the universe, you use the autopilot to take jump gates from planet to planet (or moon.) Or, you can use hydrogen & hyperdrives for FTL jumps. It has a few bugs. Nothing that affects enjoyment of the game, but IMHO, it probably was rushed out of EA a little fast (unlike some who flounder there forever.) Usually restarting the game clears any bug. They are regularly introducing new features, & working out the bugs. But, there's lots of info in the community wiki & on Waervyn’s World YouTube.
The game is built upon the premise of a world that has fallen into chaos. Your mission is to reorganize the world by setting up bases of operations in the inner 9 systems, then push outward to explore the stars beyond. The game has incredibly good voice acting & numerous missions that guide you through the story.
The actual flight tutorial doesn’t seem very good, only causing stress to the new player, leaving you confused as to the focus of the game. Just say no to that, open the wiki, & jump right in with the WASD interface. The early Susan Steele Missions function as a de facto tutorial. After you do the few Steele missions, you then have a while to explore & expand before the later missions pop up. A simple & clear guide to the early game missions is Learning to Ascend’ by Max Power
The mechanics let you feel like you are doing more than button pushing. Mining is like a dance with the asteroid. You pilot your ship to within close range of the rock, engage your gravity anchor to slow you down, & maintain a speed that matches the velocity of the asteroid while beaming it with your mining laser. You have to watch the color of the laser to know when you’ve heated it long enough to get the max elements from it. Too long will burn it up & you get nothing. If you are good at playing the market, you can search the stock market for incredible deals on most rare elements, available for you to just pick them up at the seller’s location.
Ascent has simplistic graphics but is very deep technologically. It can be compared to games like Civ V & XCOM: Enemy Within, & fits somewhere in the middle as far as graphics design goes, with Civ V having the flat map, 2D perspective, with overlays for different actions, & popup messages; & XCOM having a 3d map system & voice-acting enrichment. You can really appreciate the fact that 1 man accomplished so much. The graphics are not of a quality you get from larger dev teams, with some flaws. But, they are totally immersive. As a matter of fact, the game ruined No Man’s Sky’s release for me. I got it a week before NMS finally launched, & now today stopped playing long enough to download NMS, only to find myself logging out again & firing back up Ascent.
The maps are composed of a backbone of beautifully designed planetary art that you fly through in real-time within a celestial body’s range of view. These maps are lovely & each system has from 3-30 moons, gas giants, & rocky planets, each with their own design. For an idea of ship art, & to compare sizes, see my screenshots.
The music is played at key moments, keeping distractions to gameplay to a minimum. The avatars are limited by 4, 2 each of male & female; with no choice for personalization. The ships can be painted, with rgb color sliders, so basically you have to mix the colors to get the color you want. It feeds the Science/Sci-fi feel to the game.
It is billed as an MMO simple enough for beginners to be able to get into. &, it does seem to be. The system seems less complex than other MMO's. I think that if there is a good starting place, this may be it. Ascent is the 1st MMO I’ve been able to successfully navigate. Being an older gamer, with a 20+ year gap in my gaming experience, I was thrilled to find an mmo that offers intelligently creative gameplay & still provides an ease of access for the casual gamer. There is a fanatic (& friendly) player base in Ascent. I’ve already clocked over 138 hours as of writing this review, & I’ve had the game about 9 days.
Ascent is underpriced at $20 bucks. I’ve enjoyed it more than Stellaris, because of the gameplay. The premium is unnecessary for those who just want to play normally. You would have to subscribe for a year for the cost to even approach the normal price of games like this. The 2 dlc ships are not only unnecessary to gameplay, since one is a class 1 support ship, & the other is a huge Bowhead too bulky for mining. Rather, they are novelties from the kickstarter reward tiers sold to finance the dev team, keeping the price of the game so cheap for others not interested in novelties. The best ship I’ve found so far for mining is the Mammoth class 10, because of its cargo capacity & maneuverability. I do love flying the different ships.
You are sure to find many hours of your life lost to this game. It comes bundled with 3 free months of the premium access, which is not auto activated when you begin playing. I waited to activate my premium access until I had over 90 hours in the game. I could have waited longer, but I was limited to settlements on only two of the inner 9 planets, & only one ring on my inner starbase, &, I couldn't equip a hyperdrive above class 5 on a ship. (Same goes for ship combat weapons.)
Trading cards for collecting art; as well as a nice artbook & music dlc package would be nice for those of us who like to see the creative process behind the game.

Finally a good survival game without zombies and that throws you out there on your own in an open-world. I love the feeling of being on your own and not having the game telling you where to go and what to do. You have to make the right decisions if you want to even have a chance at surviving the elements. It's yourself against the weather, the animals and even your own condition.
You have to keep moving to find more loot to survive, forcing you to explore new areas. The map is fairly big and even though there's no one else around, it doesn't feel dead at all, which is a good thing but that can also be scary when you hear a wolf in the distance, or even worse, a bear.
Every decision you make can change everything. Every piece of clothing you decide to leave behind might be a mistake. Everywhere you go can lead you to a whole new place that will change your plans, in a good or bad way.
There's also a crafting system giving you the opportunity to make better clothing or tools, and a skills system to get better at different things with time.
The developers are constantly updating the game, adding new stuff and fixing issues, and they are very open. A story mode has been added not too long ago, I have not tried it yet, but I definitely will.
TL;DR version: This is an underrated game and you should buy it.

Didn't know what to expect of this game. A friend of mine recommended it, mostly because the trailer and the art looked amazing, also, both having previously played Undertale, the little we knew and had seen about OneShot reminded us of the former in a strange way. But that's where the comparison, if you thought there was any, ended.
With charming characters full of personality, a mysterious and intriguing story and the constant feeling that there's is something else there, sometimes to the brink of paranoia, OneShot stands on it's own as probably one of the best indie games of 2016, and there's no better way to end the year. Even if it's, relatively a short game (around 4 or 5 hours), every minute of it is worth it.
Dare and give it a try, you won't regret it. Just remember, step carefully with each decision, cause every click, every time you make a decision, it's yours, and yours alone to bear with. Also, you might need some tissues, the flow of feels doesn't stop itself.
Im my personal book, OneShot is a solid 9/10. Wish it were longer.
This game is beyond difficult, but never to the point to where it made me rage quit, but to the point of wanting me to beat the boss so badly that I could not stop until it was done.
It's pretty good!

If you want to experience real excellence in game design and storytelling, have $10 and about 4-5 hours, then PLEASE do yourself a favor and check out OneShot. I have never felt this type of connection with my player character in a game before. Niko is not simply your avatar in this digital world, he is a helpless being who you trusts you to protect him. At one point early on he told me he was scared of this machine and didn't want to get closer to it, but my gaming mind said "yea whatever" and directed him to inspect it closer. When he shrieked in terror and was almost injured by it my mindset completely changed - this game had made me feel bad for doing something to *my own character*.
I could go on and on about the extent of my disappointment and dislike of Undertale, primarily because of its use of numerous critical game design faux pas, but also because it was ultimately completely underwhelming and did not warrant the extent that people lauded it as "groundbreaking storytelling". OneShot is everything I had hoped Undertale would be.

I love Stonehearth's concept and I hope it will expand and keep growing. From time to time I visit development website and you can see that they really are active. They keep their followers up-to-date and post things many times a month, telling what is under development now, what are they planning next etc. Many here say that development has slowed a lot but as I see it from their website, they have reprioritized their stuff. Instead of dumping more and more new stuff into the game they have now turned into improving the gameplay instead of new features. Which in my opinion is good thing because now they have time to fix things instead of bringing in more stuff to fix ^^' The development for big things IS slow but they add small things into it regularly and fix things. Development crew isn't big by my knowledge (even if Riot bought Radiant) so the update pace imo is still pretty good!
About the game itself:
I have started multiple new games through time I have owned it. Eventually I get bored when I have achieved everything there is by the time and stop for some months. And every time I start it again after some time I get hooked again. And every time there's new stuff in game! The game is somewhat buggy but things are getting better after every update and I haven't had anything gamebreaking for a long time. Building in the game is fun, there are problems with it and sometimes hearthlings stop building a house you have designed but I have always found out what "was wrong" with my design and fixing it has helped (e.g. hollow bases seem to be a problem). There isn't much of a story by the time but I have hunch that they are thinking of adding something bigger in the future. By the time there are events that give the player some kind of a picture of a story.
I like the way this game looks and as I said before I love it's concept. Things I'd like to be added to this game are undeground tunnels that can be found and looted after killing it's monsters and then defending your town against creatures you have unleashed from beneath. And of course more playable races.
As the game is by the time, I'd say it prize is too high.. There isn't enough content to have it's prize over 22€ imho but I understand that the development is prizey and that the dev crew need to eat too. I really do hope that they get to finish this game and hopefully Riot gives them more people to work with.
I do recommend that you buy the game... after it has more content in it if it bugs you that things don't happen immediately and that small dev team can't achieve things as fast as big game companies.

TL;DR: Frozenbyte, I am disappoint. I wanted to like this game, and I did have some fun, but it doesn't hold a candle to Trine 2.
I would only recommend Trine 3 when all three of these conditions are met:
* ONLY for diehard fans of the franchise
* ONLY when it's on sale and
* ONLY when it's FINISHED which it currently is not.
Otherwise, get Trine 2 instead.
--- Wall of text begins here ---
What is good about Trine 3?
+ Breathtaking scenery
+ Checkpoints (great improvement from Trine 2)
+ The puzzles are all right, there are some interesting new mechanics
+ The story seemed interesting. If only there'd been more than a half.
What is worse about Trine 3 than either of the previous games?
- 3D platforming. It's horribad. I was willing to give 3D platforming a chance until I ran two characters off the same cliff within ten seconds.
- Control issues stemming from the transition to 3D. I played the first two games with keyboard and mouse, and was familiar with the skills. With Trine 3, I played the first level with keyboard and mouse, thought moving was difficult, played the next two levels with a controller and was frustrated by the extreme unintuitiveness of the skill controls, and then just dealt with moving without an analog stick for the rest of the game.
- THE STORY ISN'T FINISHED. Without giving any spoilers, buying this game now is like buying one half of a book and hoping the author gets around to sending you the other half of the book someday.
- No character progression. There are no skill trees anymore.
- Pontius lost his hammer, Zoya requires a ring to attach her grappling hook to, and Amadeus can only conjure one box at a time. No shield-throwing, no ice or fire arrows nor multiple arrows, no conjured planks (or those triangular floating platforms from the first Trine).
- You need collectibles to unlock actual story levels. Not only that, even if you get every collectible from the story levels, they will not be enough to unlock all the story levels - you have to complete some challenges, as well. Challenges should be a completely optional part of the game.
At least I
+ didn't buy it in early access
+ didn't buy it until it was 75% off

SHORT REVIEW:
+ graphics, soundtrack
+ 3D world/camera
+ individual character challenges
+ easy-to-learn character skills
+ use of physics
+ simple story
+ more ways to solve the problem
+ checkpoints/save system
+ focus on solving puzzle not on fights with enemies
- weak enemies
- slightly lower difficulty
- chapter map (points system)
- little to no graphics/visual options (unnecessary effects which can't be turned off)
- shorter gameplay: 1 or 2 more hours would be enough (longer than Trine 1, shorter than Trine 2)
LONG REVIEW:
I was worried after reading a lot of negative reviews but this game exceeded my expectations. It was an amazing experience, now, in 3D. During my gameplay I've experienced only 2 situations when I couldn't see my character which was fixed by moving a little or waiting for camera to reposition itself. Sometimes I couldn't hit the Trineangles because I wasn't sure where they exactly are in the 3D world but it took me only few attempts. Despite these facts I think the new 3D feature is really well-made and I didn't notice any serious problems with camera during my gameplay. First chapters are designed to learn you how to control your character and how to move within 3D world. The atmosphere is amazing. Graphics in the in the combination with soundtrack in the whole series is a masterpiece. There are a few new visual effects, new challenges where you have to use physics and a lot of ways how to solve problems. Terrible skill points system from Trine 2 is finally gone and possibilities for each one of the 3 characters are very clear, all 3 are needed. Individual challenges are something new because you have only one character (Amadeus/Pontius/Zoya) and you have to solve the problem without help from others. One thing I really didn't enjoy was chapter map (points system). I was missing 45 Trineangles so I had to play one big chapter again to collect more, also, I don't like if I need to choose which level I want to play, it should be clearly defined as progress in the story. Overall feeling from ~8 hours of gameplay is really great and I would recommend this game to every fan of the Trine series and also to every new player who likes Platformer/Indie genre.

This game is a modern classic as far as puzzle games go. It gets significantly challenging fairly quickly, but if you like programming (or are interested in learning), this game is for you. The goal is to take chemical elements coming from input channels, manipulate them in some way (creating compounds), drop them off in the output channels, and repeat (X times). Just like programming, all of this is done through "commands" which are represented by different icons that you place into your manipulation pipeline.
One cool thing in this game is that it is not only about beating levels, but you can also challenge yourself and try to beat the average performance of other players. Performance is measured as the number of commands (i.e., "lines of code"), number of reactors (for creating compounfs),  and number of cycles (i.e., how fast / efficient the code is running; but I'll admit I never got a full grasp of how cycles are computed exactly) used to complete the task. After you beat a level, you see a global distribution of these metrics and where your solution is relative to this distribution. This gives an idea of how much more efficient your code could be, and you can try to see if you can figure out how to make your solution more efficient.  Under such efficience constraints, even a trivial-to-beat level can become very challenging.
If you have a cognitively demanding day job, this game may not be for you, because it can feel like extra work. For this reason I haven't played it for a while now. Nevertheless, it is a deeply rewarding game that I remember fondly despite lacking motivation to go back and finish it. One day, though...
If you like this game, I also highly recommend looking at other games by Zachtronics. They are all similar in spirit, yet unique in their own ways.

Prospekt é um jogo que conta com a participação de Adrian Shepherd, o famigerado marine que deu as caras em Opposing Force, primeira DLC de Half Life lançado em 1999, que mostra a destruição de Black Mesa do ponto de vista de um marine HECU.
Pois bem, a idéia de Prospekt é tentar imaginar o que aconteceu com shepherd e reimaginá-lo em uma história ambientada em Half Life 2, muito interessante se levarmos em conta que o personagem fora "esquecido" pela valve nos ultimos 17 anos.
Bem, existe muita polêmica envolvendo o valor cobrado por Prospekt, será que ele vale 20 reais? nao sei o valor em euros mas enfim, vou falar sobre o que eu achei do jogo e alguns prós e contras:
PRÓS
-Reviver um dos momentos mais icônicos de Half Life 2, a prisão de Nova Porspekt
-Gráficos atualizados, sombras e texturas estão bem agradáveis
-Armas bem familiares de Half Life 2
-ambientação fiel ao universo de Half Life
CONTRAS
-alguns bugs, do tipo nao conseguir entrar num duto de ar e ter que ficar pulando
-inimigos quase indestrutíveis, é preciso descarregar o pente da submachine gun para um soldado morrer
-repetição de salas e abrição de portas
Muitas pessoas reclamam do valor cobrado, lembre se que foi feito por apenas um programador e levou 2 anos para ser feito, o cara dedicou horas e horas e merece algum crédito nao é? eu paguei na pré-venda e nao me arrependo, alguns poderão achar curto, mas lembre-se que tem quase a mesma duração de Episode One.
Não espere que este jogo irá tapar o buraco deixado pelo Half Life 3, este jogo é um spin off e um modo bem divertido de sentir a nostalgia de voltar ao universo de half life, se gosta da série e do personagem adrian shepherd, pode comprar sem medo, se não gosta de jogos curtos e não acha que vale 20 reais, espere as promoções e garanta o seu.

Let me start off by saying that this game is okay. It's not awful, but it's not very good either. It genuinely kept me entertained for the 3 hour game time.
The good parts:
-The music is amazing. It really captures that "Half-Life" style.
-There were some really great parts, such as the beginning and when you see Earth. These parts made me feel like I was playing a Valve game
-The flashbacks to Shepard's friends were cool. They gave him more character.
The Bad Parts:
-It's too short. If the game had more time, then maybe it's parts wouldn't seem so rushed.
-It's very repetitive. All the fights were ambushes and you only fight combine.
-Too much fighting. You never have time to rest and take in what's happening.
-There's not really a story
-The story has no affect on Half-Life 2
-Why was Gordon in trouble and how did the events of this game help him? These are never answered
-It's way too hard. I couldn't finish the final battle without cheating
In the end, this is the work of one man. For one person to make a game like this is admirable, but this game is not as good as I hoped. I hope the developer listens to this feedback and uses it to make his next game even better.

Great little episode that does a fantastic job at blending cinematic moments with gameplay and real life scenes. Unfortunately it is quite short as other reviews state (roughly 45 minutes to an hour) but it is absolutely packed with achievements which I'm sure will seize the appreciation of a lot of players.
You start off chained and unaware of your surroundings and must escape from your newly found prison. Throughout the episode are eerie messages written on the walls akin to the  unforgettable SAW movies that grasped my attention straight away that make me want to delve further into this mystery.
Personally I found that  the puzzles aren't too hard or too simple, but instead is a perfect medium between the two which should accomodate for the majority of potential players. Most comprise of logical steps and the answers can be found around that particular scene, some may be obvious some may be not, but it is not needed to google the answer in order to continue every few minutes or so as they are not exceedingly difficult.
This being said, the story is only just starting to blossom and create immense curiosity in the player with subtle hints as to a serial kidnapper and so on. Unfortunately this curiosity is something that cannot be satisfied.
