I want to start out by saying this game IMO deserves a 9/10. I highly encourage you to pick this game up, upon reading this review! It's a great game, and I loved every second of it!
There really aren't many negative things to say, but I do have a one or two. Let's start with the PROS.

PROS

*Stealth- You can play this game with out much confrontation. Sneak around, sparing the lives of your enemies. (The more blood you  shed, the darker the game's outcomes will be in multiple ways.) Their are many ways to silently, and humanely dispose of your foes, with out shedding too much bodily fluid, but at the same time, you can slit their throats, and leave them choking on their own blood, or send crossbolts into their flesh, unknowingly. Maybe if you're feeling the urge to see your enemies scatter in fear, you can rewire, and turn their own defenses against them, witnessing the cool breeze taking their warm, dry ashes with it. Don't feel like a coward if you need to run away. It is a very huge part of the stealth gameplay. The best part, is that you can not only run, but jump, climb, slide your way into the shadows or roof tops, leaving your pursuers to fumble around in the gnarly, Brined Hagfish scented crop dust you left for them to choke on. Their are many ways to "neutralize your enemies, but I'll let you discover that with your prefered play style.
*Close Combat (When you don't care who hears and sees)- You can always go head on and Destroy your enemies, leaving them in their own puddles of blood and ash. Upgrade your sword, and pistol, to mold them into the killing machines they are meant to be. Nothing like striking down your foe, and thrusting cold, sharp steel in between his shoulder blades. Explosive bolts? Yeah, I'm sure you can imagine how many head will be rolling when you get your hands on those babies.
*Engaging Story- I really enjoyed the story, even though it didn't take me long to complete it. There are many ways to play through it, with loads of choices, allowing you to play the story your way. The game has unique characters, and rewarding side mission's that will have you treking in the direction you so chose to go.
*Runes, and Bone Charms- These are basically items that power up your character, and abilities. They give you the ability to make the Corvo that you want.
*Bethesda- (Nuff said)
CONS (or things I would've liked better)
*Non-Lethal Melee Attacks- The game definitely has it's ways of dealing with enemies once they spot you. (IE.. Sleep darts, Running away, Killing.. ect.) However, I would've liked to be able to bash an enemy with my sword, rendering him unconsious, rather then gutting him like an animal. I just wish that there were some alterative ways to silencing an agro enemy, without killing them, or wasting precious sleep darts. (and they are precious!) There are just those times, when running away may not be an option, and if you don't want to compromise your belief that all life is precious, then that means re-loading a last save. The only alternative, is to be more sneaky, and plan out your takedowns. I'd say it's a way of making the game more challenging, but I think combat was that already, especially when surrounded by multiple enemies, shooting, and stabbing you.
Like I said, not many cons. That's the only one that I had, and it wasn't really a con. More of a reference, really. Anyways, pick up the game and try it out, before #2 comes out! It's going to be awesome, and I hope it lives up to all the hype! Well, Happy slashing!
Sincerely, Deathtoll. (:

Dishonored is an amazing game. Almost everything about it is awesome. The stealth system is good, the combat is simple yet fun, the powers are fantastic, and the story is great. Dishonored takes place in Dunwall where at the beginning of the game the Empress, Empress Jessamine Kaldwin, is assassinated and her daughter, Emily is kidnapped. You play as Corvo Attano, the Royal Protector to the Empress. You are framed for the murder of the Empress and are put in jail awaiting your execution. But, some people are on your side and help you escape. From that point on you take down the men responsable for the Empress's death in a lethal or nonlethal playstyle. What I think is fantastic about this game is the varity you have with the gameplay. You can go through the game without being seen or killing anyone the whole time, or you can go on a bloody rampage and destroy anyone in your path with supernatual abilites and weapons. I have played through the game a total of 5 times, not counting the DLC. There is a new Dishonored coming out soon which I expect will be even better than this. Dishonored easily makes it my personal GOTY of 2012 and one of my most favorite games of all time.

The single most terrifying game ever made. And not cheap terror like a teleporting white guy in a suit that magically kills you no matter what you do. Not random jump scares. Not even with a monster or killer. Your own mind scares you. You're alone. You don't really know why, but everybody is dead, covered in frost and dead. All of the wolves are rabid and deadly, sure, (9/10 deaths will be to wolves) but they arent the scary thing. the cold isnt the scary thing. Nothing in the game is scary, and yet it's terrifying. It's the isolation. You. Are. Alone.
After a few hours in a session if you've got a headset on and no distractions, every bookself becomes a serial killer. The creaks and groans of the old buildings are a monster creeping up on you. You know you are safe yet you are terrified. You set up your sleeping bag in the corner of a building so nothing can be behind you when you wake up. You waste matches or lantern oil to see in a building you've already looted and know the route of because the dark is scary. The isolation is simply torture, and i love to dread it. 10/10 for atmosphere.
As for the game itself... well, you're in northern canada and there's no electricity, and everybody is dead. Don't freeze. Don't starve. Don't get mauled by a wolf. The game is fairly realistic, one killed deer or wolf can sustain you for a long time, their hides are warm, and the wolves aren't zombies. They run if you throw a flare or swing a torch. All the mechanics are solid and they still claim it to be alpha. It's worth a purcase now, and they still regularly add things - just imagine what it could become. If you are any kind of fan of indie games, sandbox survival games, or real psychological terror, then this game is a 100% neccassary purchase. Wishlist it, right now, or better yet buy it.
If you want to see some footage as preview to see if its worth it, i reccomend "Splattercat" he's an ex geologist meaning he knows a lot about how to not die when you're in the wilderness hours from a town, and so he mentions what makes sense and what doesnt. But seriously, toss these devs a bone, let's make them rich, so they can finish the game and go on to make more awesome games. These guys put actual heart into the game, and that's rare lately.

"Normal" is wolves and bears, wolves rabid, bears cool as long as you dont shoot them - and you back off if they stand on hind legs and roar (basically them saying "f*** off") - they're cool and wolves even avoid them, so keeping one near your base isnt an awful idea, although killing one will sustain you for weeks. Hard mode is zombie apocalypse basically. if you want to be mauled to death every five minutes, go ahead. All this review is refering to the "normal" mode, i don't advise either of the others aside from if you think you want a real challenge... of luck (If you find a rifle before you find 60 wolves).

is a really short FMV adventure game, with some basic QTE - quick time events which require you to click on an action indicator within the time limit. This somewhat experimental little game is obviously planned as an episodic adventure, but there has been some time since the arrival of the first episode, and no news of the second yet. As it is, the game has real promise, yet ends out as a glorious demo.
We open our eyes, abandoned, chained and stranded in an old warehouse. The words "Play with me" are painted on a nearby door. All that we know is, that we should escape by any means necessary. Meanwhile, there is an elderly detective who's trying to discover what happened to us, as he vows that "there won't be another one". Curious...
There is literally not a single negative thing to be said about the graphics, since they are real life recordings. It is nearly impossible to say where the cinematic videos end and the gameplay starts. Everything is alive, vibrant and actual. More like watching a short movie rather than playing a game. Ambient, decor and music are excellent. For a FMV, this is one of the best yet. The acting isn't anything miraculous though and I personally think our hero seemed quite dapper for someone who's been locked and missing for some time.
The game consists of 5 really short chapters, weaved around some really basic adventure puzzles, one HOG-ish puzzle and a couple "dodging" sequences. No actual plot given, no character depth displayed, not much of an actual story presented... you spare 40 minutes - an hour if you are an achievement hunter, adore the cinematic immersion and get done with it. There is no replay value at all. Only an endless wait for this to become a meaningful series of events in the future.
I'd be curious about the continuation of the series, if there'd be at least an introduction, or a clue or two about a story! Surely, the game is pregnant with some success, but I really hope it wouldn't end up with a miscarriage, never developing the story furthermore. Take your time, grab it on sale if you are curious. In full-price, I'd only recommend it if you are interested in funding developers.
I do understand that it is a tremendously expensive and tiresome process to fund both game development and real life video recording at the same time for a small development team, thus I refuse to down vote this. I'd like to be hopeful, and wait to see what this may turn into in the future. Thus, I'm recommending the game as an encouragement. It holds promise. Please don't let the promise go in vain.

"Asteroid Bounty Hunter" is the very improved sequel to "Shiplord". Instead of just dodging asteroids now you have to blaster them away to reach your goal. There are also many different enemy ships added which you can bounty hunt for shippoints to buy new ships. Amazing how deep the leveling & upgrading system goes compared to Shiplord. Sure, the graphics quality and controls are almost the same. But actively shooting  things away is more fun than just dodging.
Another feature is the in-game ogg player and a great collection of techno/club tracks. The game is story attended in form of a comic strip. Most bosses are friends/family members which you must beatup. Just to reach shiplevel250 the legit way was a little bit too grindy.

While the game was ok and a decent timekiller, I can't really recommend it because there are plenty of side scrolling shoot 'em ups that are just better than this one. The game was fun for a while but it does get repetitive after a while.
The gameplay boils down to shooting sidescrolling asteroids and then the occasional bounty hunter(s) with a few boss levels thrown in between. There isn't that much in enemy variety and shooting asteroids does get dull after a while. Along with your main gun you have three other abilities that are on cooldowns. You have an ability where you launch three spinning balls, you have an ability that fires a constant laser for a few seconds, and then you have your ultimate which launches a couple volleys of missles from the center of the screen in all directions. I like how you can activate the abilities with both the mouse and the keyboard, although it doesn't tell you the mouse shortcuts (atleast I didn't see it), i just kind of stumbled into it.
The story is pretty lackluster and you shouldn't really expect much from it, but the soundtrack is awesome, probably one of the reasons I stuck with it for so long. Also, there is an option to add your own music, I didn't really try it, but it seems like a nice feature, although why would you want to change the music to anything else?
There are 25 stages with every level just increasing the number of astreoids you need to blow up by 10. There are 2 modifiers that you can put on that will make it more challenging, one makes it where there are constant bounty hunters attacking you and the other makes it where bounty hunters will attack you while there are asteroids around. Every fifth level is a boss stage, which in my opinion take too long and are kind of boring.

I expected this to be another mod that copies existing assets from the Half Life series and compiles them into something else, but this is a bit more. The gameplay, as others have noted, is pretty difficult. Running-and-gunning isn't really an option here and you'll need to take advantage of explosive barrels, carrying obstacles as cover, and simple hauling♥♥♥♥♥to get through. As such, there's a heavy weight on the level design which is often missed by indie developers, but he's done a pretty good job here.
Unfortunately, there's usually just one "good" way to handle a room full of dudes and only a couple ways to do it poorly. I can't imagine anyone getting through an area and thinking "I wonder if it could have been done -this- way." Small gripe, I know, but felt like it should be mentioned. The levels as-is are pretty solid, especially when compared to Half Life's.
Graphically it looks fantastic. The higher-resolution textures really shine through and isn't a huge encumberance on my hardware. Since it's technically (on the hardware level) a re-skin of Half Life 2, SLI support is already in though I had an issue getting VSync to actually stick. I had to force the frame rate to be less than 60 through NVidia Inspector. Can't say for ATI GPUs, though. My only complaint on the visuals is some odd colouring that takes place here and there but it's minor and ends soon.
Audio-wise I can't complain. Custom indie voice-over is usually a guaranteed cringe for me but this isn't that bad. The music is pretty intense during the tougher action areas and really fits the game well. Remembering back to Half Life 2, you'd get that nice pumping music infrequently and when it started, you knew you were in for a rough time. This does it the very same. Not too much music, but when it's there it's good!
Overall, I highly recommend it! For ten bucks you're getting a really unique story in the Half Life world and it's just different enough to make it feel completely new. Definitely can't complain too much here.

Been gaming for 35 years, am a huge RPG enthusiast, and for some reason never played this until a month ago.
For the longest time I told myself it'd be too old to get into at this point. But then playing Divinity left me craving for oldschool storytelling and D&D atmospheres, so I finally decided to give it a try.
No regrets. Yes, the game is dated and often feels clumsy, but I got sucked in the amazing story and atmosphere right from the very beginning.
What I truly love about the game is that it's unapologetic straight up oldschool fantasy, and not many games do that anymore, and none as well as this one. It's not trying to be ironic, or PC, or a reference to a reference. It's just trying it's best to be an immersive epic, and brilliantly succeeds. The often remarkable writing does a lot for that.
Gameplay is dated, and seemed confusing at first. It helped when I started thinking of it as Age of Empire RPG with a pause option to plan your next moves.
Graphics are obviously dated, but are still really charming. The quaint representations of nature and cities actually work really well. It's not trying to be shiny and impressive for the sake of it.
Music is perfect. Mysterious at times, epic at others, melancholic and eerie ... It really completes the overall atmopsheric tone.
The main story, while being far from original, is transcended by it's storytelling. You will often feel like you're in a book.
The world is huge for a game that old, and completely open. It feels alive and breathing. You're free to roam, and to take whichever adventurer you like on the way. Your actions have concequences.
All in all, I'm loving it, and can absolutely see why it's hard to this day to read a RPG review without seeing it mentioned. It is a masterpiece, and I can't wait to play the sequel.
I definitely recommend it to any RPG enthusiast, young or old.

The criticisms I'm leveling at this game are pretty much the same as the majority of people have already stated previously.
The good:
- The game looks gorgeus
- Sound design and voice acting are pretty solid,
- Couple of miscellaneous moments of brilliance (particular puzzle, level style etc.)
The bad:
- Trine 3's 3D gameplay feels more like an afterthought
- Controls feel awkward and sluggish
- Player and platform depth matters even in places where it feels like it shouldn't
- Maps can be quite confusing and unclear to manouver through
- Characters have been simplified way too much
- Very little variety in enemies
- Short game where the plot feels like it hit a brick wall
- The normal price point (21.99€ at the time of writing) is asking way too much
- Progression (even in the main story) depends on collecting "trineangles" - breezing through levels is not an option
The main story and all but two challenge maps took me a bit over 5 hours to complete. If you're looking to completing the game 100%, you're looking at maybe 8-10 hours of effective gameplay, tops. As vibrant as the levels feel, they feel quite clumsy gameplay wise, and replaying them isn't probably going to be a joyful experience. Especially forcing replaying levels if you're missing any golden "trineangels" to unlock challenge maps and even main story levels feels like the developers had to figure out some way to artificially lengthen the game.
Two of the three characters have seen massive simplification, and not really for the better. Zoya (the thief) can now attach two objects together with a rope, but she can now only grapple and swing from pre-placed hooks. She has also lost the different elemental arrows.
Amadeus (the wizard) has the ability to slam levitated objects straight down, but he can only summon one mechanical cube. His levitation now has to happen in 3D space with the mouse controlling height and length and the mouse scroll *slowly* controls depth. Amadeus is practically a forced character in a couple of fights where he has to use his slam attack with precise placement and timing, which is extremely difficult in Trine 3's awkward, half-baked control scheme.
Pontius can float with his shield, and he has a jumping slam attack and a shield charge, but the shield charge controls unpredictably at times. Pontius was mainly a fighting character in the previous games, but now I think I played as him most of the time.
If you absolutely need more Trine after playing the previous two games, buy this only at a hefty sale. Otherwise, don't bother.

Eight years after its release, Serious Sam: The First Encounter got a high-definition upgrade; and let me tell you, it has definitely made a difference to the entire experience. Not only to be known for visual enhancements and remodeling, another upgraded feature is the Serious 3 Level Editor, so that you can make custom levels utilizing the redesigned game engine. There's also a refreshed online multiplayer mode, and an excellent co-op mode that supports up to 16 players at any given time. It's too bad that online is dead, but if you can grab some friends then you will all be in for an amazing, classic FPS online event.
Part of the aesthetic upgrades include more blood and gore, which gives the game a much more mature, less cartoonish approach versus the classic title. The upgraded enemy models are also much more disturbing; the Biomechoids have grotesque, pulsating outer brains, the Aludran Reptiloids are a lot more muscular and ripped, and the trademark Gnaars are more refined and a lot less boxy. When the Beheaded Kamikazie guys explode, they make a huge mess with their blood, and it even splashes on the screen if they explode on you. The maps are as equally upgraded, and their new dynamic lighting makes a world of difference versus the classic edition of the game; bringing out a hundred times more depth to the scenery, leading to a much more diverse experience.
Regardless of whether you're a fan of Serious Sam, it touched your childhood gaming memories, or you're new to the series entirely, you should definitely upgrade to the HD version for Serious Sam: The First Encounter. The new textures, dynamic lighting, additional levels, gore effects, remodeled enemies, and refined audio all contribute to making a massive difference; reviving an otherwise old, tired game. Some people may experience performance issues, and to this I say disable the VSync option. With my GTX 1080 I was getting weird stuttering, even though the title was running at 60 FPS. When I disabled VSync, it ran like a dream.

This review will be aimed at people looking in the reviews section, asking themselves "Should I buy this game?".
To answer that, let me start with asking YOU a question. Are you a you're a fan of fast-paced first-person-shooters, being a one-man-army, decimating literally hundreds of enemies (per map!) using spectacular weapons, and epic one-liners that would be cheesy coming from anyone else? Seriously though, the dialogue can be really funny/awesome sometimes. Anyway, if you answered "yes", then you've come to the right place. Serious Sam is a game about exactly that. You may have heard the phrase "No cover, all man" relating to this game before, and it is a good description.
Before I continue about the game itself though, I want to mention the more important thing. The Developers. Croteam, of Croatia, are my favourite game company of all time. Valve, Bethesda, Ubisoft, EA, and many, MANY other famous (or infamous) developers have checkered reputations. Dodgy or imperfect business practice and the like. But Croteam? None of the sort. They're the type of developers who genuinely want to make a good game. If they find an issue, they fix it. I got an update for my Serious Sam 2 game a few months back, despite the game having been out for a really long time already. I like this, since it means that Croteam, again, want to make their games great. They're not just after quick money like some others you may have heard of, and that, to me, is just as important as the game itself. So trust me when I say that you can't go wrong by getting a Serious Sam game, provided it falls within your gaming tastes, I mean. Even Serious Sam 2 is awesome. Go get it! It's an incredible masterpiece of a game, even if you own the newer Serious Sams. It's different enough for when you still want Serious Sam, but want something different after playing the newer ones for a while.
Anyway, back to the actual game. So, from the get-go, you're pitted against impossible-to-normal-people odds, fighting Mental's (bad guy) alien hordes. You'll start out with a simple and limited weapon setup, and you'll expand your arsenal as you play, finding newer and deadlier tools of destruction as you make it further. The enemies will ramp up too, along with your weapons, in enemy type, and in numbers. So, the fun and challenge is omnipresent. Now you may be asking me, "Is there a reason I shouldn't buy this game?".
If you answered "yes" to my first questions, then my answer to you is "No, there isn't.".
"But what if the game is too hard? You said the enemies ramp up and stuff."
Yes they do. However, YOU control the difficulty you play at. Yes, yes, not exactly a unique concept, but done in a unique way. Tourist, Easy, Medium, Hard, Serious, and finally, Mental. The difficulties aren't just number changes. As-in, you aren't just going to take/deal more/less damage or something. No, all difficulties are hand-tweaked throughout the entire game session to custom-tailer to your preference. To give you an idea, on Easy, your health constantly regenerates slowly (faster on Tourist) and enemies do less damage, and there are tweaks to enemy types, numbers, placement, etc... And on Serious, the same tweaks are made to enemies, except in favour of more dangerous enemy types. There are MANY other changes though, including item placement/availability and such. Even then, every difficulty is playable and fun in its own way. I've checked, and even on Serious, the game is fully winnable and fun, just harder. What I'm trying to say is, if you like this KIND of game, you WILL like this game, regardless of difficulty preference. Thanks go to Croteam for taking the extra time to go through each difficulty and make it an overall enjoyable experience start to finish.
"You said 'deadlier enemy types'. What if I don't like the enemies, weapons, or something else in this game?"
Admittedly, not a question most people would ask pre-purchase. However, I feel I have to address this. The best part!
THERE IS AN EDITOR.
Croteam gives you your copy of the game, and it comes with a free editor in the Tools tab in your Steam Library (If you don't know where that is, Google can help you find it.). This editor allows you to custom-tailor your game to your preferences and tastes, without beforehand knowledge of coding or anything. You just open it, open the thing you want to edit, and it'll list all the variables for you to change through simple number changes. You can also edit your enemies. Basically, everything from weapon damage, fire rate, ammo, and projectile explosion/damage and stuff, to enemies themselves. Don't like that guy's attack? Change it. Think this guy does too little damage? Increase it! You can make the game harder, easier, and just more fun in general. And everyone has this power over their own game. The best part of the best part? If a client joins you, your settings take preference, so you won't have to worry too much about not being able to play with your buddies. You can also make and edit maps, including the existing campaign maps, and there are plenty of tutorials online. Personally, not something I do, but that brings me to my final point.
Lastly, the icing on the cake and the cherry on top, this game comes with a modding Workshop, which turns the already-endless replayability up to an 11. New top-notch guns with new stats, new fan-made maps, new and interesting enemies, new anything! A crowning jewel, cementing this game's place as a game you will be playing and re-playing for years and years to come. :D
Overall, this game is an uncompromising fast-paced first-person-shooter with its entire focus on the player's experience. Seriously, this is my favourite game series of all time, from my absolute favourite developer of all time. And I'm such a serious gamer that I had to think long and hard about putting this at the top of my game list. No, really, I have a favourite game list. And I spent Sheldon Cooper levels of time with internal struggle of whether or not to dethrone Dead Space 2. Long story short and many weeks later, Dead Space 2 now sits in a solidly comfortable 2nd place. :)

Lucid is a casual puzzle game, in a similar style as Bejeweled. There are many blocks on the board, and your goal is to clear areas of two or more to clear them. The catch is that all connected blocks must be cleared at once by drawing a path through them that touches all blocks exactly once. Connecting blocks that match the goal color bring the level closer to completion.
The game tries to be relaxing in aesthetics and in sound, and it succeeds. I don't care much for it, personally.
I'm not a fan of these sorts of puzzle games, since there is little reward for carefully-planned moves. I found this game boring pretty quickly, but I thought the same of Bejeweled, which is quite popular. If you like Bejeweled, then you may alo like Lucid. I don't think I'd recommend it otherwise. Even on sale, there are better ways to spend a few dollars.

A mediocre puzzle game and one of the most boring I've ever played. With almost all of the achievements, I gave it a good shot. Every level is the same in that you draw lines over adjacent jelly cubes of the same color to make them disappear and to fill up a gauge to move on to the next level.
By matching cubes, you score points and there is also a goal color displayed that you should match to increase your score multiplier. In Tetris fashion, you're shown what cube color is coming up next. The only problem is that your score is meaningless since there are no leaderboards. Difficulty never ramps up much and the game remains far too easy and repetitive. Not even a timed mode or any challenges or unlockables. Pick any other puzzle game and you'll have more fun.

Although the music is quite soothing, this is your typical run of the mill block matching game. The goal is to get a specific number of tasked blocks to clear a level. Each task requires you to make color blocks which pushes up your multiplier. If you don't follow the task, the multiplier drops back to zero. Lucid blocks can clear the field, but they are worth crazy points at the end of a level if you don't use them. It's kind of counter intuitive in that the point system is really about pushing up the multiplier rather than going for the largest color blocks. Keep your blocks small and you push up the multiplier to the point where the lucid blocks end up counting for tens of millions of points each.

Let me preface this by saying that yes, this game does run on a premium system, however the pricing is quite reasonable, and the game comes with a generous 3 months of full Premium time already paid up. (The best part about this is that the Premium time from buying on Steam isn't immediately applied to your account, you can activate it whenever you feel you're ready to start using Premium features). After that, Premium is priced on what features you want to use - managing colonies on planets in the Inner Systems, managing large-scale Industry, and taking part in combat are all counted separately, so if, like me, you plan on mostly running a manufacturing operation, you can pay just $1 a month and still enjoy what the game's got to offer for you. Personally speaking, I'm planning on going the full $3 a month anyways, this developer can definitely use the support!
As far as space games go, I've been looking for one that allows me to participate in trade and industry in a non-combative manner, and I've gotta say Ascent so far has pushed all of the right buttons! Think of a large galaxy and a player-run economy like in EVE Online, except entirely PVE, so there's no need to worry about more experienced players rolling by and ruining your fun.
Quite the opposite, the community has been super helpful for me so far, and I've gotta say I appreciate that kind of spirit!
The controls for flight are simple but not overly so - You can navigate between gates and stations using just the mouse, and flying your ship in combat uses the WASD keys to pretty solid effect.
The mining in the game also feels just right - No sitting around like in EVE, and no chasing asteroid chunks like in Elite Dangerous, but you have to match the speed of the asteroid to get a good bead on it, and then use your mining laser to heat it up to just the right temperature to get the best yield out of it.
I'm still just getting started with regards to building colonies and space stations in the game, but I really like what's been done so far! There are still some minor issues regarding framerate and loading screens, but the developers have been super active and engage the playerbase on a frequent basis, so I'd say even if you decide not to buy the game today, definitely keep a close eye on it!

Okay time to get you guys know abit about the game. This is a f2p, but at the time of I'm writing this review, 100 % of the in-game content can be unlocked just by playing the game. What are those content ? Monsters, Hunters, Perk etc
If you are a new player, the game will give you a basic monster Goliath, and a basic hunters, but there are several free 2 play hunters and monster each week. As i mentioned before, everything can be unlocked by playing the game. You will get ingame-currency after each match you've played. The cost of Hunters, perk, Monsters is reasonable. I got 6k Silver  (ingame-currency) after 2 hours played, that's 7 wins and 2 losses. Just a few more matches and i can unlock a new monster which is Kraken, the prices of monsters are around 6-9k Silver. Perk are quites cheap and can be unlocked by leveling your monsters. So that's it, you don't need to worry about unlocking things in this game. It just take time for you to get stuff. I really like the way the they allow players to unlock everything just by using Silver.
About the gameplay. I've played 9 matches. The monsters can kill the hunters at early stage without evolving to stage 2 if the hunters are inexperienced. Yes the game gives you many choices, you want to solo ? you want to be independent ? you don't want to lose just because some random strangers on the internet made mistakes ? Well you just pick the monster. You don't want to be lonely ? you want to heal people ? you want to track that big fat Goliath that hits hard as truck or that sexy Wraith ? Join the hunters, there are 4 roles for you too choose. And every role is matter, the monsters can't win if you work properly together. Well i will update my review later as i experienced more content of the game. But right now, I absolutely recommed this game if you love a competitive game with mixed elements between fps and battle area.

19 years ago, a computer game came out called Baldur's Gate. (Wow... has it really be 19 years?) But 19 years is a long time in the realm of computers and this classic was lost to archaic versions of Windows running on antideluvian hardware. Fortunately, Beamdog have found this lost treasure, re-mastered it and re-released it to our age.
For those wondering what all the fuss is about, Baldur's Gate Enhanced Edition (BGEE) is a remake of a classic role-playing game. The publishers have done a great job of it, retaining the old style, but making it suitable to modern machines with huge displays. Unlike many modern games, it is based on old pen-and-paper role-playing rules (Advanced Dungeons and Dragons / AD&D). These can be a bit quirky at times, for example: the attack stat is called "THAC0" and the defence stat is called "Armour Class". In both cases, lower is better. The rules have also been retained... but that's a good thing. So... should you get it?
Sure, the graphics are bitty, and the sound is rough, but that's part of the charm. Baldur's Gate was an absolute landmark in the fantasy computer game genre. It will have immense appeal for those who are even slightly nostalgic. And for those new to it, it will be an engrossing and compelling story... even if the rules are a bit baffling at times. Either way, I heartily recommend this gem.

NEW AND UPDATED REVIEW, since the game is not in early access anymore.
I picked this game up as soon as I discovered that it was available on Steam because I absolutely love the other two Trine games. A physics puzzle game that I can play with friends because it has a multiplayer mode while relaxing on the couch because it has controller support? Hell yeah.
I have played the first 4 or 5 levels now, together with two friends, the way every Trine game is supposed to be played.
You control one of three characters: The Knight, The Thief, The Mage. Each of them has different capabilities. The Knight has a sword and shield for combat, and can glide through the air while using his shield as a parachute. The Thief can shoot arrows, and use a grappling hook. The Mage can conjure boxes and move objects around.
You can switch characters at any time, although for those of us who played Trine 1 and 2 there is a "classic" mode, in which you can only control one of the three and two friends pick up the other two.
Also, the leveling system has been removed. Every ability for every character is available from the start. I would argue that the leveling system was somewhat arbitrary, but some people will surely miss it.
The Levels are intricate enough to be interesting, with hidden secrets and beautiful design. The general rule is "go right, look left", as it is for every sidescrolling game, but the 3D graphics make for interesting transitions and effects.
The 3D character of this game is the cause of multiple problems though, which include characters going offscreen and getting stuck somewhere, solutions to puzzles or hidden secrets that are not actually hard to find take a lot of time to find because they are simple off screen, and aiming the Thief's bow as well as swinging from her grappling hook get somewhat of a challenge in itself.
Letting the Mage move something can also create some problems, since the camera shows the side view of the landscape while the Mage can actually move objects in 3D space.
Also: Different sized boxes, planks and triangles are missing completely from the Mage's repertoire, which reduces his usefulness by quite a lot.
Controls overall feel slightly wonky, as the goal of puzzles seems to be more of a "wiggle a thing into the right place" more than "let's find an actual solution to a physical problem".
EDIT: I wrote in an earlier review that the game does not support controller for player 1, the issue is now fixed, as I suggested it would be upon release. Good job, guys!
Those of us who have played Trine 1 and 2 will notice immediately: This game is completely 3D. And: The game is beautiful. In terms of graphics, this is definitely a big step up from Trine 1 and a moderate step up from Trine 2. I will ignore the problems with the camera in this section, since they are not strictly graphics related, and just say that I still enjoy the Trine art style. The way the levels are designed (graphically), they sure are some eye candy.
The story is more functional than believable, more meant to drive the gameplay than tell something interesting, but has it's funny moments in almost every piece of storytelling that happens throughout the game. And despite my resentment against games with "functional" story, I did enjoy what Trine 3 showed me so far.
The game is short though. The story is just a couple chapters/levels long.
Works reliable, at least. Pieces of story that were 1-player-only before now spawn in the other two players as well. Characters do not need to be switched awkwardly via respawning. You can request a switch by pressing a button and a player can answer your call. I haven't tried online play yet, since I happen to have people living nearby who also enjoy Trine, but I might suggest trying that out, since it might resolve some camera issues if you have three people on screen who go different directions.
I noticed that there is very little helping each other. Before, players could stand on top of the Knight if he raises his shield for an additional height boost. That is not possible anymore. The Mage can no longer move boxes that players are standing on. The Thief never had an ability to help people, which fit perfectly, because she is the selfish one ;)
I would love to, but I can't wholeheartedly say that Trine 3 is a step up from Trine 2. The controls simply don't feel that smooth yet, and the 3D aspect introduces a whole new set of problems, especially when playing locally with multiple people (Damn you, camera!). If you have played Trine 1 and 2, I would suggest picking this up just to complete the series. If you haven't, playe Trine 1 and 2 first.
Overall, I will give this game a Thumbs Down. It shows potential, and is fun to play in parts. But taking a step in a new direction also means facing new problems that the developers weren't able to solve entirely. The reduced ability pool of the characters, as well as the kind of puzzles that appeared in the game makes me hope that Trine 4 will do better, instead of making me want to play more of Trine 3.
This is Luparax, signing out.

I was quite sure to give a negative review but somehow I don't feel like it anymore.
I do not recommend Trine3 outside of a sale.
I do not recommend Trine3 for someone who has not played Trine1 and Trine2 before.
But I still recommend it as a game for itself.
Visuals:
The game looks great. But the ones before did as well. Exciting and complicated puzzles
should make you blend out the good looks. Intermissions, story moments etc. should get you
back into enjoying them. Sadly Trine3 lacks in the puzzle area. Worse, the great visuals come at a high performance cost. I don't run a perfect gaming system atm but a game like Trine should be able to run with high framerates on any modern computer. (I7, Quadro) Lowest quality, no vsync, reduced resolution and it still feels sluggish.
Takeaway:
- Keep the more flexible and even better looks. (Walking through the pages of a book etc.)
- Make sure the game runs fast enough for extensive puzzling.
Environment:
The engine allows for full 3d movement, the logic however, does not. Input is typically limited to two dimensions with mouse and keyboard. Using WASD and the mousewheel to control 3 dimensions is not a well trained method. It only works as a gimmick in some puzzles when you bring a box closer to the front or back.
Instead of real 3d puzzles Trine3 uses different slices of 2d. In Trine1 and Trine2 you make your way between left and right as well as up and down. Trine3 adds front to back traversal. But most puzzles are reduced to a 2d logic either by walking on the ground plane or by working on a single logical depth layer. Sometimes the logical dimensions are bent and twisted around the 3d environment. Walking a curved balcony still means walking backwards or forwards.
Takeaway:
- Keep the 3d environment as a technical base.
- Slice more strictly into 2d for puzzles, to reduce input back to 2d.
Puzzles:
Mostly disappointing. Most puzzles are not about "Huh? Lets see. How can I solve this?".
Its more like "Urgh. Do I really have to make those jumps and move all those boxes?".
I was rarely amazed by how a puzzle could be solved. Most of them are straightforward. A few combinations with Zoyas ropes were interesting, but I would not see them on par with Amadeus planks and boxes from the former games. They are also less comfortable to experiment with, since the rigid body dynamics of planks and boxes are a lot easier to understand.
Its understandable that the enviroment and selected skills make it hard to build great puzzles. But that is the challenge for a Trine game. Amadeus has been heavily reduced, most likely because controls would be too bothersome with all his flexibility from Trine1 and Trine2. But Zoyas rope trick are not making up for it enough. Mostly its "Tie this, pull here, tie that". There are many single character levels, which I see as a sign that the skills are not that well balanced and in combination make the quality of the puzzles drop.
Takeaway:
- Go for new skills and new combinations. Trine1 and Trine2 are already made.
- Support more variety/experimenting by using simpler to control and better to anticipate skills. Trine needs the "Wait! What if...?" moments.
Story and progress:
To me Trine was never about a great story. It was about great delivery. With that it is very hard to keep the quality up, because repeating things will make them taste shallow. But I am sure Trine3 was a good deal below its possibilities. With the first two games I never felt like "Oh. Thats where the kids are supposed to laugh, right?" Trine3 did not much to entertain me around the puzzles.
The grindable map is nice for backtracking, but backtracking and grinding Trine feels wrong to me. I prefer a more strict separation of story mode and puzzle mode / multiplayer. I do not see much replay value in finding a few pickups that I missed. The former games motivated me, to be thorough because I wanted to buy upgrades. But I also felt like strictly progressing forward through a story. Trine3 lets me replay everything as much as I like. Even parts of a level. But I am neither driven to make progress nor do I care about the pickups. Except for when they stop me from entering another level. A required number of pickups and grinding reduces reduces the gratification from "getting past that spot, so I can move on".
Takeaway:
- Trine is not about the perfect story. Its about delivery and three characters.
- Some people want the linear experience. Some people want to grind puzzles alone or with friends. You should be able to support both.

Prospekt is a Valve approved sequel to the Half-Life: Opposing Force DLC. Unsurprisingly, it takes place in Nova Prospekt, presumably before or around the same time that Gordon Freeman gets their. One of the first things I noticed as I started playing the game was its graphics. They look noticeably better than the other Half-Life games, except Black Mesa of course, and as well as being a welcome improvement, they dont do anything to change that nostalgic feel of existing in the Half-Life universe (looking at you CM13), something which I really appreciate. Another thing that I am glad Richard Seabrook kept in this game is the way the story is presented. Just like every other Half-Life game, for the first 15 minutes or so of playing, you have nothing, and are required to get from A to B by using the surrounding environment, which I personally think is a great game mechanic, as it allows you to take in this games amazing atmosphere, as well as allowing new and old users of the source engine to get used to its controls and mechanics. Another thing I liked about this game was its music. While its certainly isn't to the standard of Kelly Bailey's amazing soundtracks, it definitely makes an epic firefight or nervous crawl through a vent that extra bit more special.
So after these first 15 minutes or so, the game soon turns into the nostalgic and classic FPS that we all know and love, (with a few puzzles here and there to mix up the gameplay), and reminds me of how LITTLE the gaming industry has come with not just FPS, but gaming as a whole since the Half-Life series.
Considering that this game was made completely by one person over the course of 18 months, I am genuinely astonished that Richard Seabrook has managed to make such a well polished game, and there was never a moment in this game where I felt it was tremendously lacking in any form of content. That being said, I managed to finish this game in just over 2 hours, which is far short of the "Episode 1" length we were told, which (for me anyway) took almost 6 hours for me to complete the first time. I also found that the variety of gameplay did become lacking as I continued through the story, from Headcrabs, Barnacles, Zombies, Zombine, and Antlions, to just the Combine...yay. No awesome boss battles against Dropships, Gunships, Striders or Advisors. Whats even weirder is that you get an RPG a long way into the game, hyping up my anticipation that soon there would be an epic boss battle, but...no. I didnt even need to use it, as from the moment I picked it up the only enemies I would continue fighting for the rest of the game were, you guessed it, the Combine. Also, while the return to Xen in this game was certainly cool nostalgia-wise, once again the only enemies you are fighting their are the Combine, no Houndeye, Bullsquid, Alien Grunts, Alien Controllers, Gonarchs or Gargantuas, and you are literally their for 5 F*CKIN MINUTES.
Just incase you think I forgot, I know this game was only made by one person, and the amount of action packed fun, detail and nostalgia inducing atmosphere Richard Seabrook has managed to cram into this game over the course of 18 months is incredible, and for that I can definitely reccomend it to anyone. But... this IS a Half-Life game, so it should be reviewed like one, and in that regard it lacks in certain areas.
In conclusion, if you are craving some more Half-Life, you've come to right place, but don't expect anything more than that.

I've been playing this game for about 2 weeks now. First I want to address the most common complaints:
a) It's pay to win? The DLC Bowhead certainly gives you a lot of cargo space with which to make money, since the game doesn't lock ship size to any player stat other than affordability. But the game has access to bigger ships than the Bowhead, all without the DLC. Making credits is ridiculously easy. I have the next ship in size to the DLC one, the Archon, and could have an even bigger one if that's what I chose to focus on. That's after 2 weeks play.
b) hidden subscription? The game does tell you that the $20 current purchase price includes 3 weeks of premium. Not having premium does restrict what class weapon you can mount (meaning you mount more, smaller weapons) and other restrictions. But the sub price is 1, 2, or 3 dollars a month depending on what you want to do in game. Really, I spend that much daily on coffee. Ever since I've been playing MMO's I've been used to $15 a month subscrptions, and that seems fair.
About the positives- love the depth of the game. The longer you play the more you realize there is a lot out there to do, and to learn, and to build! I even tried combat route, which isn't my forte, and found it interesting. There are updates coming to the UI and the combat system. Me, I love the building starbases and colonies aspect of the game.
It's crazy interactive. Take mining for example. Find the right asteroid, match speed and direction of travel, open up your mining beam and heat it up to the precise temperature- less and you reduce the yield, more and you might explode it. All while moving! Swap out ship modules to optimize the ship to your playstyle, balancing space vs utility.
It's.. huge. At my stage of the game I look at the systems far away waiting for me to investigate... and procedurally generated space means there will be more when I get there, generated as I arrive- named after the discoverer! That is still a month away game wise for me.
The dev is extremely involved, and very positive. Check the game forums, won't cost you anything, and see the bug reports and the actions taken. The community is extremely helpful, in advice as well as hands-up, and will steer you right. They are eager to make the game as good as it can me.
Hey, this is where I spend my free time. IF you like social interaction, building, mining, combat, this is it. If you prefer to play with cooperative players and away from player harrasment, this is definitely the place.
this is the game that star citizen tries to be but never will be.

This is a game that I was very hesitant in purchasing due to all the survival games available. I am here to tell you my scepticism was regrettably uncalled for. From the beginning it draws you in to a conflict that inevitably places you in peril in the middle of a harsh winter setting. From the instant you are given control, you are fighting to stay alive and learn the environment and all that it offers to keep that ticker ticking. The journey through the storyline and map was captivating, thrilling and visually pleasing. The survival aspect of the game is fairly basic in the sense that the valuable items, which there are many, are simple things like sticks, cloth, food, etc. The time acceleration during eating or harvesting is a challenge you have to account for and makes for a good way to pass some time. The graphics are not the greatest you'll see but they aren't supposed to be. It is a basic stylistic approach that takes bright colours with pastels with straight edges and hard angles to create a beautiful backdrop to this winter atmoshphere. The ambience is delightfully erie at times and when paired with the solitary predicament you are in fits smoothly together to create an immersive experience. At times I can't help but feel cold at my desk as I pursue the crows above to my next meal.
I would recommend this game to anyone that is looking for a great survival game that actually feels like you need to prioritize your actions in this first person masterpiece.

I have no hope for this game whatsoever. It wasn't a great game at release and it shows no signs of improving now.
The basic jetpack mechanics feel awkward and floaty. The boosting movement system with awkward wall hugging energy free hover feels unpleasant. Sadly as a hunter you'll spend the vast majority of your game time slowly trudging across the map with this unpleasant movement system.
Because the match revolves around a single monster kill or a single party wipe, combat is all about grinding away at the massive hp sponge monster. Even the players tend to be fairly spongey, though they can sometimes be quickly taken down with a cheezy chain of ability spam.
Overall balance tends to be extremely swingy. My personal experiences:
1. Monster failed to stay away from hunter, gets murdered early on.
2. Player drops from match before game starts, team with AI gets steamrolled.
3. Noob medic fails to heal, monster murders hunters.
4. Team lost track of monster, monster evolves to level 3 and steamrolls team.
5. When the objective comes online, hunters are further from it than hunters, so monster goes straight to it and destroys it with hunters having no chance to stop him.
The extremely strict layout of one hunter of each archtype and one monster means you will frequently be forced to play a role you did not want to. The rigidity of the party makeup also seems to make the game more predictable and boring.
Another personal experience that runied the game for me was the perk system. It was not clearly communicated that you can get all perks, including the high level ones from levelling characters. I spent enough currency to buy several characters on perks before realizing I would get them unlocked eventually from levelling characters.
This game has the full range of chinese mmo style login streak rewards, daily bonuses, timed bonuses, etc. Be warned you will not like this game if you can't put up with free to play reward manipulation. The rewards are structed to try to get you in the habit of playing the game, not designed to be rewarding and let you enjoy the game at your own pace.

Evolve has been made Free 2 Play, in the hopes of selling microtransactions as a last ditch effort to cash out. Turtle Rock Studios has a documented reputation of trying to milk as much money out of Evolve as possible, and this was their final solution. They claim the reason behind this change was to "improve the game" and "raise the playerbase". That is a deliberate lie. Considering that the people who preordered and put their faith in Turtle Rock from the beginning, are the ones who are getting shafted the most. They even try to remedy this with their "founders status" which is essentially just porting over the characters and skins you already paid for. In addition to this, there is content that was cut from the finished product, reports of downgraded quality and an obvious plot to setup microtransactions. These developers and their publisher 2K, have scammed the few players who actually spent money on their game and trusted them to deliver on a premium title. The game will gain popularity for the time being. Because it is a fairly decent game. But overtime the shady business practices that have historically plagued this game since launch will come to light. This game used to be one of my favorites, for what it did differently. Now it has proven to be in the same bucket as all the other F2P trash. Only next time, Turtle Rock Studios wont see a dime from me.

Each level adds more features to the possible manipulation of atoms and molecules.

The voice acting is pretty good, it's quirky and even inspiring sometimes- though more often than not cliché and watered down in to one liners.
The gameplay is essentially Doom 2 with a few new enemy behaviors and more rooms to be locked in until you clear them out entirely of said enemies and much longer and larger levels.
If you think finding secrets and exploring levels is going to benefit you in any way, think again. Exploration and finding secrets is punished abrasively as an artificial difficulty increase. You might get some bonus health, or extra armor, or a new weapon a little early compared to finding it on the beaten path you're seemingly expected to rush through, but you wind up being ambushed by enemies that will more than likely make the collected secret not worth grabbing.
The sound design leaves a lot to your imagination and even more to be desired. You can often hear enemies before you see them, usually you'll hear ones hiding in ambush of you going to secret chambers and stuff, which is sort of a way to know where not to go though it's not always useful since the orientation of where sounds are coming from is not properly given to the player regardless of how you have your audio set up. (Even on a 5.1 you can't audibly tell where an enemy who's ahead and to the left of you is without it being in your direct field of view) which makes for some more awesome "ambushes" from enemies that are around corners and behind walls from you.
The "intense mood music", which plays only when enemies are actively pursuing you, became annoying not even 3 minutes in to semi-active combat.
Overall this game is not ground breaking, it'd be better named as "Frantic Failure". Serious Sam HD: The First Encounter is bold irony and a step back as far as FPS titles are concerned.
If you want to play something similar but actually good check out Rise of the Triad.

A perfect remake where you can kill thousands of enemies in brief amounts of time with awesome weapons. This is a classic FPS game that is meant to be played with over the top action, gore, and little to no thinking involved.

Otherwise:
• it's an 90s style FPS, like DOOM 1&2 or Painkiller
• good antidote to overcomplicated puzzle games
• you'll get bored of staring at indistinguishable Egyptian temples about an hour in; it goes on for a lot longer than that
• level design over-relies on some "cheap" feeling gimmicks like teleporting monsters into the world behind you
• levels feature prominent, genuinely funny booby-traps
• has working, non-mandatory co-op multiplayer
• one technical flaw with the audio: no HRTF. You can't locate sounds by ear very well because the way the game simulates sound isn't detailed enough (it doesn't simulate phase differences caused by sounds arriving at your ears at slightly different times, which is the most accurate mechanism your brain has for working out which direction a sound is coming from)
• some of the monster designs are bad, by which I mean tedious to fight (stupid undead bullet-spongy ponies)
• occasionally the game throws one or two hundred of its most boring monsters at you (ugh so many ponies)
• some of the weapon designs are crap, by which I mean they hit like wiffle bats and that's just boring
• unfortunately, all the voice acting and the sounds… sound like they're from a 90s FPS. Ew.

I think the internet really was too harsh on this one. Savadgely attacking devs who misjudged the cost/time involved in making large changes to their game wasn't deserved. I for one liked most of the changes, the new levels were nice if different than what I was expecting. I think the biggest problem here was unmanaged expectations and early access.
Gamers loved Trine and Trine 2 and I'm positive 90+% of them just wanted what was essentially Trine 2: More Levels. I don't think it was made clear early enough the departures being attempted and how much it was likely to be difficult.  Trine devs should have been a bit more upfront about their difficulties, people understand if told in advance.
I think the other problem was early access and taking people's money before the game was ready. I almost never buy early access because I don't like unfinished products. I think people need to realize that just like Kickstarter, if you pay for something unfinished you are gambling a bit on how it will end up.
All that said, I do hope Frozenbyte continue making cool platformers like Trine. It would be a shame to lose one of the last devs making such games. It is clear to me there was a brilliant game being made here, it just needed more time and money to be made. They just ran out.

Playing as Adrian Shepherd, you come across
(G-Man) who places you in Nova Prospekt, where Gordon Freeman is in need of assistance.
At the beginning the story is commenced as you walk through Nova Prosepkt hearing the sounds of the usual.. combine soldiers dieing, AR shots firing and scary mechanical sounds.
Throughout, you begin to pick up more of what's going on, it's a bit confusing to grasp but it's a game you should really play in long playthroughs.
Taking in that Richard was single-handedly building this game, I respect him for making it a stand-alone game and creating Xen. It's a short play of Xen but definitely looks good in my books for the Source engine.
I don't want to give any of it away but there aren't really any Opposing Force weapons which I won't fault since the gameplay makes up for this.
Ammo is scarce when it needs to be, but when you do have ammo you do find yourself running for cover to try and spare those last rounds. This created a really great combat experience.
There are recycled materials from Half-Life 2 but when you reach the whole Combine base you come across really really futuristic stuff.. I mean like
stuff. Some combines are reskinned but you have to wait til' later in the game to experience some of the new things.
No bugs were found in my experienced gameplay. Just headcrabs, manhacks and hunters.
Overall I would definitely say give this game a try if you do not want a mod, it's a stand-alone game that gives you a really good Half-Life 2 reboot experience, but in an Opposing Force point of view.

It is NOT a mod- it is standalone and does not require Half Life 2
The first chapter is very atmospheric and eerie- it reminded me of the feeling I got playing Ravenholm in HL2 for the first time.
The second has a lot of combat. The combat is okay but on normal difficulty I found the marines hard to kill with the SMG especially when they often have mounted machine guns. In HL2 you kill Cps first and by the time you are mass killing marines you have lots of ammo.
The chapters were also quite dark and the flashbacks whilst interesting did sometimes get annoying.
Steam achievements might be a nice addition.
Also the subtititles were either no always correct, didnt appear etc.
Overall it has potential and is well worth buying to support similar creations being brought to steam!
so far 7/10 :D
EDIT:
I have almost finished the game- it has taken around two and a half hours which is not really comparable to HL2  Ep 2 like the dev said but I guess no one plays quite the same.
The next chapters got better.
The combat was more enjoyable as I got further and ammo/health was given out more.
The Xen level was great- I love jumping from one island to the next and it was nice to see Xen under combine control. I hope the dev will expand this level more in the future, include some of the xen creatures- there was only combine which is a slight disappointment, and perhaps feature the caves and bounce pads from xen we all loved in half life one.
The darkness hasn't got much better and I feel that certain areas of the game need brightening up. In contrast many need reducing in their blinding flashes. You may note that I said that I have only nearly finished the game as I am unable to beat the last level. That may just be my skil but I had to turn the difficulty down to easy and that didn't help. The light is blinding and most of the time you can see next to nothing. The screen is also shaking too much. A bit adds to the atmosphere but the dev has gone a little to overboard to the point where the last level is virtually unplayable. It is also made worse by the fact that there are TONS of combine and very little health.
It would also be nice to see in the future some of the unique opposing force weapons.

You know those Ads for ♥♥♥♥♥♥ games on Youtube where they say you can "Build your own civilization from the ground up, customize your buildings, defend your civilization from creatures and monsters"
But then you play it and its really just a 2D map manager.
This ISNT one of those games.
THIS GAME, allows you to ACTUALLY build your own customized civilization from the ground up. Although Stonehearth is in its Alpha stage this game is full of stuff to do. First you start by picking your People's backstory, where they came from, they're attitudes, aspirations and appearances. Then you decide where in the randomly generated map you would like to start your little caravan off. First after gathering some supplies you craft little shacks with beds to shelter your "Hearthlings", then soon your building your next Knight's watch tower, or your building another giant farm plot to feed the next wave of Hearthlings you need to expand your now City. After your Hearthlings are safe in their town ou can send them off to fight the monsters of the land and claim rewards and treasures.
I've only just started playing Stonehearth and I see a lot of potential for it and i hope the Devs keep up with it. It's a really unique experience and i hope i interested some of you enough to give it a try.

Serious Sam HD: The First Encounter is remastered version of a rather old game from 2001. Back then it got good reviews and earned popularity among pc gamers. But how does it hold up today?
Pros:
Neutral:
Cons:
Great game, loveeeeeeeeee thissssssssssssssssss <3

First Encounter is waaaayyy Harder than the second encounter, Mental is actually mental in terms of how he uses his minions, In the second one he learns that I am just gonna kill them all the same way.

I find the 2nd Encounter better than the 1st SS, but it's up to you to decide. Anyway, 1st of all HD version is beautiful but old gnarled non-HD version for me way better (+ its easier to find secrets :) ).
+Visuals - HD-rework looks beautiful - very high quality, very well done.
+Sound - amazing soundwork, OST is simply the best, last levels songs providing goosebumps in huge amounts. Weapons sounds are great as well.
+Gameplay - run and gun as is, huge amounts of enemies (especially if you are playing multi because a number of enemies increases with each guy). A Huge amount of secrets, an enormous amount of the jokes, and Sam is just brutal. Your mom sized monsters, your willy sized monsters, flying monsters, fish monsters, monster monsters, and a lot of deadly traps.
+Multiplayer - Co-op for campaign, or PvP arenas, both very fun :)
+Various difficulties - actually difficulties heavily affect the gameplay in this game - harder the difficulty - worse guns you find on levels, less ammo, lower amount hp healed by medkits, the amount of the enemies and their hp increased, they even become invisible, like all of them.
+Lore - huge wiki describing all the enemies and weapons you face in your pocket, very fun and interesting to read
+-Steam achievements - HD version includes steam achievements but they have 2 problems, 1st of all sometimes they just refuse to trigger, and 2nd there are a lot of multiplayer achievements that hard to get.
-Lacks of Chainsaw, Sniper Rifle, Flamethrower and Serious Bomb.
This game is the best, try both versions old and new and compare yourself, personally I like the Second Encounter way more than the 1st, but I can be wrong here, 1st Encounter is not that bad after all. Buy this game for yourself and your friends for a better experience, good thing that SS often put to the 90% discount, but actually it worth every penny.

I really enjoyed this game for the most part, but had some issues with the difficulty curve, and the various stats of the cars.
Most of the time, the opponents range from too easy to just about right in terms of ability, but every now and then, a series of races would feature a racer that would obliterate me - I'd be half a lap ahead of 3rd place, and the car beating me would be a lap ahead of me. So for a couple of cups, I'd basically be rolling the dice that that one particular racer wouldn't show up for the race, or they'd somehow get jammed in behind the other racers.
Besides that, the various stat bars for the vehicles didn't seem to correlate to one another. For instance, I maxed out the speed stat on the racing truck, but it isn't as fast as the Countach with speed at three quarters. Given how long it takes to save up for the top end upgrades, it's frustrating to sink a bunch of money into a car, only to realise it will never be as good as another car, despite what the stats look like.

It's just an awesome little game. I played it on Android for a while before I found it on Steam. All normal cars are unlocked from the beginning as opposed to having to buy like the mobile app. There are still unlockable cars for completing each championship and there are some cross overs with TF2 & Portal and Fruit Ninja by Halfbrick.
What I like the most is how car upgrades make a noticeable difference in performance. I would strongly suggest sticking with one or two cars that match your driving style. One for the beginner championship and about halfway intermediate, and a better one for Expert and Master. At least for me that's all I needed. The $16,000 upgrades are worth it, trust me.
One of the downsides to this game is that the AI doesn't actually get "tougher" with higher difficulties. They are significantly faster, but that's it. They still make the same stupid mistakes, bump into walls and each other, use nitro when they approach corners etc. Cars are VERY easy to push away, no matter the size or "weight" (realistically, how could a Ferrari push away a truck).
It also gets a bit repetitive once you reach Master, because then they'll unlock 20 pages of tracks for you to finish instead of individual cups. Found that very demotivating.
Overall a great little game, fun tracks, fun music, dumb and annoying AI, reasonably priced car upgrades and enough variety.
A neat little racing game to enjoy.

It's game which shouldn't have left early access in my opinion, its unfinished. The story is half a story, I was amazed when it finished how it did, as early as it did.
I sincerely struggle to believe that the team which developed this would place it alongside Trine or Trine 2 in terms of quality, in terms of strength of puzzles, charm, the flexibility which you have in tackling puzzles, level design, length of game and general overall completeness of the product. It isn't there.
Trine 1 & 2 are classics, on any system. Two of the best games ever made. Trine 3 takes what made the previous games and strips the game back to almost barebones. Amongst the changes are that Amadeus can't cast planks at all or multiple crates or cage enemies, Pontius' hammer / magnetic shield is gone, Zoya's grav / fire / freeze arrows and multiple arrows are gone, the rope swing also seems to have been nerfed meaning less scope for acrobatics - its changes like that in my opinion which limit the puzzles and overall fun of the game. The puzzles are weak and the new 3D engine is more psuedo 3D in my eyes. The new ability which Zoya has to attach rope to rope points works well, the boss fights are a marked improvement but it isn't enough.
Its the weakest game in the series by far from a developer which should know better. Such a let down.

I have mixed feelings about Frozenbyte's jump to a 3D environment. On one hand, I appreciate when a game developer tries something new and ultra-ambitious. On the other hand, I loved the aesthetic and gameplay of Trine 1 and 2, so I sort of feel like why fix what wasn't broken.
This game is beautiful, absolutely beautiful. There were more than a few moments where I paused and appreciated the artwork. But there were even more occasions where the 3D movement made puzzles confusing or frustrating, and that's not to mention the occasional clunky/glitchy 3D behavior (Zoya's swinging in particular). None of these things made the game unplayable, they just took me out of the moment.
The most startling aspect of the game is the 'cliffhanger,' where you are made to think they are just about to continue their quest, but then the credits start rolling. Actually, I wouldn't even mind the cliffhanger, if I knew they were continuing the story. But I've read, because of overly negative feedback, they are questioning whether or not they should. I really don't think that's fair, though, and I strongly feel that they (or anyone in their position) should finish what you've started.
It was, in the end, a fun game. Not the best in the series, but still fun. I would recommend it, especially if doing so meant they would finish the darn story.

You know, I only bought into the series after seeing Trine 3 and thinking of how great this seemed. Maybe I'm one of the select few who looked at this and thought it was amazing. I've started the trilogy at the third game and even with the stupid and menial bugs/glitches I have seen, I would have to say that I really enjoy this game. I have enjoyed the concept and even though I have started at the last installment, I plan to venture into the previous games of the series. If, according to the reviews, this is the worst game of the trilogy, I look forward into heading backwards into the previous games. All in all, after seeing the value just in watching the trailer video for Trine 3, I bought into this series. It didn't take but a few minutes into this game that I have enjoyed the concept of Trine and looked forward to the depth and intrigue into this game. I can understand the feeling that there may have been a rush to push this third sequence, but for what it's worth I appreciate all aspects of this game. I would not rate this game a 10/10 in any means. but for the value of buying this trilogy on sale I feel the money is well spent. Even if you invest time into one of the games in this trilogy, it is money well spent.
Long story short, do not over look this game due to the negative reviews. It's a great pick up for the sale value. Today 12/1/15 the trilogy is $15 of which I think Trine 3 is worth the value. Watch a let's play or a walkthrough before you count this game out for the mixed reviews. You wont be disappointed, unless you highly detest the type of game, not the story or value as a whole. It has been one of the few steam games that has kept my attention for longer than 5 minutes.

Imagine a little kid comes up to you (not yours, but maybe your friend's or neighbour's), holds up a picture that they have just drawn in your face, and asks "is it pwetty?!" all the while beaming with pride. And you have an urge to respond with the truth - "NO IT SUCKS" - but that would be wrong, maybe even socially inappropriate. This metaphor accurately describes the dynamic in play between me and this game.
From a distance it looks like a typical indie horizontal scroller, maybe even a bit above-average if you're as gullible as me when it comes to Store descriptions. The 3D spinning asteroids look pretty cool in the video preview, the ships made from simple geometric shapes don't look
bad and the abilities are shiny. The first real hints of trouble appear when you boot up the game for the first time; cheap-sounding vocal trance hits you in the main menu, the lettering on buttons is pixelated and when you click Exit, the confirmation prompt reads "Do you really wanna quit the game?"
The game... the game itself is what it says on the tin, surprisingly. You fly a ship, you shoot asteroids, enemies ("bounty hunters") and bosses, you upgrade your stuff. It's solid, if mediocre. It never crashed for me (or maybe once)! The crux of the issue here, is that this core gameplay is packaged in layers upon layers of unprofessional... everything. Here are a few examples; viewed together, as a common denominator of sorts, they portray the overall quality of this game:
Okay, I needed that. So why, pray tell, is there a thumbs up here? Because I can see how much love and effort went into this. Not the best effort, admittedly, if we ended up with
, but still. There are some horrible design decisions here, yet the conviction with which they're implemented gave me pause. The creator had a very particular vision and chose to stick by it, even if they had to poop all over modern game design tenets in the process (defined as "what sells and what doesn't on iTunes"). This resulted in a bizarre, mostly negative product that I find a bit inspiring at the same time. And over the past week three updates were pushed that improved the game significantly, fixed some things and added some other things, so they're still trying. And I tend to believe that trying is more valuable than winning.

Ah, Baldur's Gate... I first played this gem back in '98 when it first came out. Man, those were the days... Now, I know what you're thinking, Why should you buy a game that came out nearly two decades ago? I'll tell you, because it holds up.
There was a time when the market was over saturated by games based on D&D, or at least inspired by it. Some of these are still great to play now days, others not so much, and I can say for a fact that Baldur's Gate lands in the former catagory. Really the only limiting factor that could potentially stop any D&D fan from enjoying this game is the rule set. 2nd Edition AD&D is... well, it's a mess. A fun mess that wears a silly hat, but a mess none the less. The game can be quite restrictive due to the rule set, but it makes up for that by being a fun experiance with a cast of intersting and fun characters. Take Minsc for example, a human ranger who at some point suffered a sever head injury that leaves him little more than a blithering idiot with a "miniature giant space hamster" as his animal companion... it's name is Boo. If that isn't memorable, then sir/madame, I don't know what is.
The story is also a good selling point and paved the way for what Bioware would later do with the Mass Effect series of games, specifically being able to transfer your save file into the sequel and carry over several features. Granted, they weren't able to carry over story elements such as any party members that may have died during your adventure, but it was a new idea at the time.
At the end of the day though, take my opinion of the game with a grain of salt. While I love the game, you may not. It's also entirely possible that I am blinded by nostalgia goggles, but what can I say... I love this game.
