The MOBA/ARTS genre has exploded over the last few years. With Heroes of the Newerth, the original DotA, League of Legends and Dota 2. Now Monolith and Warner Brothers have decided to get in the fray, with Guardians of Middle-earth, a Lord of the Rings themed MOBA/ARTS game for Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3(and now PC...) If you were ever afraid that a DotA style game would be dumbed down when brought to a console, I can say that your fears are unfounded. Guardians of Middle Earth is anything but dumb, in fact it's quite deep.
In Guardians, you get the typical 3-lane 6-tower map setup from a top down perspective. Exactly what you’d expect in any MOBA. A mix of upgrades for towers and buff shrines in the jungle area, between the lanes, that your team can capture. Each shrine increases a teams health regen, allowing you to stay in lanes longer, which you need to do to gain XP. While there is a single lane map I’d advise against playing it. It devolves into rage quits quite often, which ruins the experience.
There are no item or gold mechanics in the individual matches, nor is there any last hitting required. These meta game elements are Call of Duty style loadouts and unlocks from experience and gold gained for completing matches. The amount of individual loadouts are gated by your account level. The items used within are gated by gold. You buy gems, potions, and relics from the in-game shop using gold. This is a way of specializing your loadouts to meet certain needs across any character. This whole area of the game is way too large to go over extensively in a review. Suffice to say, the depth and variety in loadouts is immense.
The in-match skill mechanics are more to do with team work and map awareness than twitch reflexes. Movement controls with the left thumbstick. Attacks control with the right thumbstick for directional aim. Your characters face around a 360 degree axis. Your facing will also change with your movement. Holding the right stick will override the left stick’s facing controls. Allowing you to strafe and backpedal. A ring is drawn around your character showing your attack range, area of attack(usually a cone), and directional facing. It works well most of the time, but there are situations where you can’t tell if you’re hitting your target or not.
Using abilities can be frustrating. You get the same ring shaped hud element for each targeted skill. These skills assign to the face buttons. I don’t know about you but I don’t have the dexterity to hit the A-button and use the right stick at the same time. You will usually end up having to aim with your movement and be careful enough not to run too far while attacking. It’s not ideal but there is a certain level of acquired skill in doing it.
One nifty feature borrowed from Monday Night Combat is upgrading towers. Towers are upgraded by all players so long as they are a certain in-match level. Each of the 4 upgrade types need different minimum levels in order to apply. The creep waves are altered in the same fashion by upgrading a barracks found behind each lane’s second tower. These barracks are immune to attack until the towers in front of them are destroyed. Upgrading the barracks allows the creep wave to concentrate on different styles of pushing. Heavy siege units break enemy towers or front line fighters hold the enemy from being able to push to your base. It’s a great strategic mechanic that more games in the genre could enjoy.
The Guardians are ripped straight from the pages of Tolkien's classic. They range from the bastion of good himself, Gandalf the Grey. To the epitome of evil, Sauron. And a few other notable characters like Gollum and Legolas. Each Guardian fits a different archetype and role, that create what could be a diverse meta-game. Only time and community will decide how competitive the game becomes.
As for the community and player interaction: there doesn’t seem to be a lot going on in that department, at least within the game. Most players don’t seem to wear their headsets, which is a blessing and a curse at the same time. My time spent with the game has been rage and troll free, but just about every match has had someone disconnect or leave. It’s unfortunate, and I’ve yet to win a game short handed or lose a game with a numbers advantage. Luckily, queue times were short and lasted only about 2-3 minutes.
There isn’t much else to say. The character design is great and borrows from the films and the sound is pretty top notch too. The graphics are as good as you’ll find on current-gen systems, if not a bit muddied. The gameplay though is the core of the experience. If you’re looking for an easy way to get yourself into the genre, Guardians of Middle-earth is one of the best chances you have.

Tentative recommendation. If you're willing to overlook the exceedingly long dev time, Stonehearth is a decent builder game with some light action.
You start off with very little as either a desert-peoples or a feudal-peoples,and can pick a location to match. I've always liked city builder games and Stonehearth really scratches that complete control over the process. Well, sorta. You draw up blueprints that you can make from templates or design completely yourself (my favourite part) and then give your workers orders to build them. The AI is a lot better than it was, and now will only never finish a building 1/15th of the time.
Occasionally you'll be distracted by goblins and kobold attacks, which you'll fight with an archer, footman and cleric and go back to building. The content noticeably peters out as you play and you're left with very little to do apart from expand and beautify your city. That said, watching things get built is like a drug, it's very easy to just watch and watch and watch. I do like this game, I really do - there's just not enough content for a 4yr old game with a sizeable dev team.
If you like building games and your favourite part of Emperor: Rise of the Middle Kingdom was building wonders, you should get this game. If you're looking for Dwarf Fortress, probably not for you.

I have no hope for this game whatsoever. It wasn't a great game at release and it shows no signs of improving now.
The basic jetpack mechanics feel awkward and floaty. The boosting movement system with awkward wall hugging energy free hover feels unpleasant. Sadly as a hunter you'll spend the vast majority of your game time slowly trudging across the map with this unpleasant movement system.
Because the match revolves around a single monster kill or a single party wipe, combat is all about grinding away at the massive hp sponge monster. Even the players tend to be fairly spongey, though they can sometimes be quickly taken down with a cheezy chain of ability spam.
Overall balance tends to be extremely swingy. My personal experiences:
1. Monster failed to stay away from hunter, gets murdered early on.
2. Player drops from match before game starts, team with AI gets steamrolled.
3. Noob medic fails to heal, monster murders hunters.
4. Team lost track of monster, monster evolves to level 3 and steamrolls team.
5. When the objective comes online, hunters are further from it than hunters, so monster goes straight to it and destroys it with hunters having no chance to stop him.
The extremely strict layout of one hunter of each archtype and one monster means you will frequently be forced to play a role you did not want to. The rigidity of the party makeup also seems to make the game more predictable and boring.
Another personal experience that runied the game for me was the perk system. It was not clearly communicated that you can get all perks, including the high level ones from levelling characters. I spent enough currency to buy several characters on perks before realizing I would get them unlocked eventually from levelling characters.
This game has the full range of chinese mmo style login streak rewards, daily bonuses, timed bonuses, etc. Be warned you will not like this game if you can't put up with free to play reward manipulation. The rewards are structed to try to get you in the habit of playing the game, not designed to be rewarding and let you enjoy the game at your own pace.

One of the best puzzle games I've ever played.

A brutally difficult but immensely satisfying chemistry-themed puzzle game about designing complex automated systems. Not for everyone, but Zachtronics' games all tickle that algorithm-building code-writing part of my brain in a way no other games have.

Less daunting than it seems and very fun if you like logic puzzles. The game subtly pushes you towards making elegant solutions by having leaderboards that show your friends' metrics (how many cycles/steps their solution took, how many reactors they used, how many logic symbols it took), which adds another layer to the challenge. It's the kind of game where I'll be stumped by a problem and will walk away, think about it over the course of the day, and then come back and try out some of the solutions that I'd thought about. A lot of trying and failing and refining until you come up with something that works.
In a sense it's a primer for Zachtronics' later programming and engineering games, as it was where they first developed the underlying programming-esque gameplay that drives them. I guess what I'm saying is that if you like or think you might like programming, you'll probably like this.

Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power is the third in the Trine trilogy and the first in its series to enter the Early Access market but I'm sad to say it is the weakest in the Trine series
The graphics are simply amazing! The environments are beautiful and have improved greatly from its predecessors, traditionally Trine and Trine 2 had the 2.5D prespective with the camera, Trine 3 on the other hand sticks with the 2.5D perspective but also delves into the 3D aspect where the camera moves freely
Many Trine fans were not happy with this transistion, personally I am okay with it, the camera now shows more of the beautiful environments which I am not complaining. However, the camera is annoying and sometimes where I try to reach a certain platform, the camera makes me think I can reach the platform but when I jump to the platform, I fall and die... which can be really frustrating!
The story is okay not as brilliant as the previous two Trine games, but I'll come back to this later in the review...
The controls are okay but Trine 3 really plays better with a controller rather than the previous games where you can easily play with a keyboard
The missions, the game now introduces a hub where you can freely move around and play around with the missions, there are also side missions where you can collect additional shards. I hate this new system, Trine and Trine 2 were heavily narrativally driven and never had this type of hub. Trine 3 on the other hand you have to play these additional side missions as well as replay the main missions to collect the required amount of shards to unlock the next mission
The side missions are incredibly annoying and I hated every single one, I have the feeling that the developers just added these side missions so that they can extend the length of the story, and I'll come to the length of the story very shortly
The voice acting is still as brilliant as the previous two games and the same voice actors from Trine and Trine 2 make a return which made me really happy! The music is okay, its not as amazing as Trine and Trine 2's music was, Trine 3 it just feels like rinse and repeat the same music, over and over again...
In Trine and Trine 2, there was a lot of character development with the three characters; Pontius - a knight, Zoya - an archer, Amadeus - a wizard, and in Trine and Trine 2 you had more abilities to use that in Trine 3. Amadeus had more wizard abilites than in Trine 3! In Trine 3, you just make one box with one control... in Trine and Trine 2 you had the ability to make movements with your mouse and either a box or a plank would be created, Trine 3 doesn't have that ability, very dissapointed...
Now, to the length... I cannot understand why it is this short... and with a cliffhanger ending too!? The boss battle is one of the weakest I have seen in the Trine series and the cliffhanger ending made me feel like the developers said, "Yeah, we want to tell you the rest, but that's it for today...", the ending is so ridiculous that I am going to ruin it for you without adding a spoiler cover over it... the Trine was split into four pieces and scattered across the world that the Trine series takes place in
You manage to find one piece in one of the chapters then you find the last piece after defeating the most stupidist boss battle possible, then the three characters say that they have two more pieces to find, they walk off and... THAT'S IT! My mouth was left wide open when the credits started rolling, I was astonished and amazed at how short this game is! Thank god I did not pay full price for it...
I cannot understand what Frozenbyte were doing with Trine 3, they literally made a copy and paste of the previous Trine games, add a few bits here and there and not improve on the other gameplay elements. I am very upset that Trine 3 was not as good as previous Trine games, and this is the first Trine game in which I am not going to recommend... its difficult as I love the Trine series but sadly, they ruined my hype for it with Trine 3
If you are a fan of the Trine series, then I would say buy this at a very heavily discounted price. If you haven't played the previous Trine games and you are interested in playing the Trine series, play the previous two and don't even bother touching this game... they are heavily discounted anyway
A real shame...

Do not buy this game. Very disappointing sequel to an otherwise excellent franchise. Trine 3 attempts to a third dimension to a 2D platformer, which is so poorly implemented as to make the game frustratingly unplayable. The difficulty of the game is not in the intricacy of the puzzles, or clever level layout, but rather through gimicky, flimsy controls which leads to monotonous repitition.
- Previously it was possibly to aim the assassin's arrow because the environment only had two dimensions, now the game will automatically select a target based roughly on the character's heading.
- The same problem happens with the wizard, where you cannot tell which object is going to be affected by the levitation power until you press the button. You can no longer select objects with a cursor, instead game selects whatever arbitrary object is nearby to manipulate, or require you to toggle between multiple selectable objects if more than one exists on screen at a time. Once selected, manipulating objects in 3D space is ludicrously difficult, especially with a gamepad.
- Many obstacles need to be solved by placing objects ot jumping "into" the screen (along the Z axis), but without depth cues this is mostly just random guesswork.
- When characters die a blue ghost avatar floats to a random location in the world. The character is resurrected by standing in or near the blue avatar for some time. Sometimes this is in an impossible to reach location (eg. a location requiring the assassin, who is dead), or in the middle of an infinitely spawning battle (eg. requiring the knight, who is dead). Invariably this means forcibly killing the remaining characters and rewinding the game to a previous checkpoint, which are far and few between. In the earlier versions of the game, characters would be resurrected immediately when passing a checkpoint.

Looks nice and controlling the characters so far feels quite direct. Pontius the Knight does not feel as fat and sluggish compared to earlier titles, which makes sense given that he can use his shield for gliding in the air ;)
The third dimension is a bit overwhelming for somebody who has played quite a bit of time into Trine 1 and 2 but I guess it's just a matter of getting used to it, I see it as a welcome addition.
Also runs really well on Linux, just the gamepad configuration needed a bit of tweaking (inverse axis for right thumb stick on a Logitech F710).

This game has a good share of problems:
The worst for me is the lack of optimization - the game has no business sucking up well over 2 GB of RAM and having load times >5 seconds between missions. Yes, I dialed down on the graphical settings, which is why I'm not complaining about it using over 3 GB.
The upgrade progression system is tacky - it's not really that meaningful. Just a poor excuse to navigate through some extra menus between missions.
The enemy variety isn't all that great, but the few that do exist are well designed and fun to fight against - also a big thumbs up to the boss battles as well.
With all of the specific details I point to, I ought to flag this review as negative, but Asteroid Bounty Hunter does have an undeniable factor - I want to go back to playing it and play more. In spite of its flaws, it's fun.

This is another entry into the Space Flying Sidescroller brought to you by Just 1337 Studios. Having already reviewed their other game Ship Lord, I'll start out by saying, they have a lot of similarities.
You are in a small spaceship with space rocks flying at you and bounty hunters trying to kill you. Unlike Ship Lord, however, you actually get to shoot back this time. Your ship, Karma has four weapons capable of blasting those pesky chunks of dirt into pieces, which is pretty much the entirety of the gameplay aspect. Along the way you will encounter bounty hunters who want to kill your alcoholic pilot and bosses who have odd mechanics to make themselves more annoying.
You can upgrade your ship components and your ship itself through the completion of levels, the annihilation of bounty hunters (culminating in the collection of Mastery Points) and by leveling up through killing every asteroid you come across. There are three difficulty ranks per level, easy, medium, and hard, each of which modifies the maximum HP and Experience granted by asteroid kills, and two multipliers, Bullet Hell, and Bounty Hunters.
Bullet Hell modifies the level so that there is no longer a break between the asteroid waves and the bounty hunter waves, effectively upping the difficulty. Bounty Hunters modifies the game so that bounty hunters will spawn endlessly, asteroids or not, this can snowball quickly.
All in all it is a great addition to the space shooter genre. The controls are smooth and easy even on keyboard and I had a lot of fun playing through the game. Video Review Below.

This game is sooo good! The mechanics are complex but not so much so to the point where they're convoluted. Every action you take has meaning and consequence, so you can't just sprint everywhere and expect to survive for very long. The atmosphere and sound design are great as well. You can really feel the desperation creeping in when you're low on food or water. If you're new to the game like me or haven't watched any Let's Plays I recommend doing the story mode. It's still a challenge but it eases you into the game mechanics. As well, this game is on Humble Bundle right now for 12 $, it's a steal for this game alone.
EDIT: Thought I would share the best experience I've had with this game so far.
It's the dead of night and I'm slowly freezing. I found a secluded alcove out of the storm, use up the last of my kindling in a desperate bid to warm up. Eat, drink, even manage to get a bit of sleep. Sitting by the fire as the last of the embers die down, I resume my trek into the unknown. Checking all the abandoned cars in the area for food or supplies, I hear a noise behind me. I turn around to see a wolf bearing down on me. I climb back inside the car just in time. He sits outside, watching and waiting, so I do the only thing I can do as I'm horribly unprepared for the harsh wilderness; I wait too. Eventually he leaves, and after a bit more time has passed, I head out. The cold has started to creep back into my bones. Now I have no kindling left, and nowhere to get out of the storm. The only way to survive is to push onwards. In the midst of a blizzard, I can only hope there are no more wolves or I'll certainly be an easy meal. I make my way into a forest, finding some much needed sticks strewn about the forest floor. I'm now able to build a fire, albeit one that won't last long enough to provide much warmth. I decide to make a torch instead. The light from the torch is enough to illuminate a path forward. My torch begins to dwindle down, and I'm on the verge of hypothermia. I know in the back of my mind I won't last much longer, but I have to keep going. Practically falling down a snowbank, I realize I've come to the edge of the forest. I see signs of civilization again. Then I hear it... a howl in the distance. It's not quite morning yet, and my torch is all but burnt out. Out of the corner of my eye I see something rushing towards me. As it draws near, I can make out by fading torchlight the largest wolf I've ever seen. With an actual yell from me I hurl the dying torch at it as a last deseprate attempt to scare it off, and miraculously the torch finds its mark. With a whimper, the wolf scampers off into the forest. I breathe a sigh of relief as I know I've survived for at least one more night.

God, this must be how Star Wars fans felt when Episode 1 came out, incredible improved graphics and a rich detailed world stripped of most of its fun and charm. Like so many of us, I loved Trine, and when Trine 2 came out it brought improved graphics, a longer main gameplay and story and some fantastic multiplayer/co-op additions which all added to the original formula and gave more value to me. So why oh why would you want to throw all your money at the styling and art only to ditch the core values that made the first two games so successful Frozenbyte? Yes, the 3D is an interesting addition and the graphical improvements and design have not gone unnoticed, but when they result in emptying out all the challenge, cutting the playtime in half and doubling the price, you have know you're making a bad choice somewhere in development.
It feels as though the majority of Trine 3s' development has been focused around the new 3D Engine and the graphical artefacts and objects therein and at least to a small degree, it's paid off. It's fantastic to traverse a world where the same intricate level of detail from the first two games has remained, and due to the textures, resolutions, and most of all the lighting effects, the world and environments look even better. There's been a lot of time and effort spent on making most of the objects and art interactable or responsive in some way, and the world (though probably not the story and characters) truly feels a little more immersive than in the prior 2 titles.
The other thing that I really liked was the side objectives, though I felt due to the short length of the game they'd been forced into main content (you actively need to complete them to progress with the story now) which is a shame, but doesn't stop them from being great side-stories and fun in their own ways. They even have jokes and references to other games and they helped break up some of the issues the game has.
The single biggest player complaint on this title is the short length and/or the unfinished story/abrupt ending. While I felt the levels themselves were too short, there were more than enough of them to make up a full game here and it honestly doesn't feel that much shorter than the first title, especially considering the love and attention that has been put into making them so beautiful to look at, I think we've just been spoiled from the length and amount of content put into the second title. However, as Frozenbyte have confirmed, they simply ran out of funding and released what they had with a rather short, flat and emotionless ending, which truly is a shame when the happy comradery and whimsicle story were the fun backdrop upon the last two titles shone. Ultimately the gameplay and game itself are what count most and the ending with the comparatively short 5 hour play-time aren't what bother me most since 5 hours of a good title is, in my experience, worth more than 10 hours of a less enjoyable title. Instead it's the other failings and choices that make me very concerned and cautious about recommending Trine 3 and so ultimately the price is my single biggest complaint. Twice the price of the other titles when it's the least challenging, least engaging and most buggy of the three is simply an outright joke.
The 3D Engine is the cause of a few of those problems, particularly the lack of precision and accuracy seen in the prior two games. It a regular thing to jump past an area or over a platform only to fall or die because the controls or leap felt impinged by the engine, and even more annoying when it happens because you can't see what's around the corner. This has clearly been addressed somewhat by removing some of the challenge and slowing down the game a little, which I would normally be fine with, but when it's overdone so far as that it makes the entire game unchallenging, removes the progression system where you can unlock new skills and abilities and simply replaces them with collectibles, it feels cheap, flat, bland and worst of all, boring.
Currently available on the Steam store for £31.99/44.99€/$44.99, Trine 3 is flat out overpriced. It's not a bad game, and while it lacks the challenge, complexity and some of the fun of the first two, it definitely still has a great world and environment to explore if you keep your expectations on level, but given the lack of improvement and the large price it just isn't worth the cost for most of us. If you want to pick it up, do yourself a favour and wait until it's less than the price you got the prior two titles, as that's the only price at which I'm comfortable recommending it to most, especially when you take into account that the developer have mentioned the story and game will not be updated or extended in the future.

What happened?
I was one of the many that originally bought Trine 3 during Early Access, and all I can ask is "what happened?". This game is just so unfinished! All this final version of the game is is the Early Access build with 1 or 2 tweaks and a couple more main levels and a bunch of boring side "challenges."
For the positives, like it's predecessors, this game is so damn beautiful. If anything, Frozenbyte's engine can really pump out great graphics at a smooth framerate. Other than that, new puzzles with Zoya's rope mechanics are a great addition to the game.
For the negatives, the combat is still the same from the Early Access build, which basically consists of having Pontius run around and mash X and Y to kill things, or spam RT with Zoya. And since there's no alternate weapons or upgrades for the characters, it gets old FAST. You'll basically end up just knocking enemies off cliffs as Pontius and going on your merry way. Enemies will also only spawn in on combat arena sections of each level, which makes every encounter even more monotonous and predictable.
When you're not locked in the simple combat, you're stuck in a platforming collectathon for "Trineangles". I don't mind collectathons much, but it's almost all you do in Trine 3 and it's extremely dull. And this is MANDATORY to unlock all levels in the final build, which is insane. Puzzles are generally ultra simple and nonexistent.
Often times while hunting Trineangles and progressing through a level, you'll be trying to judge where you'll land or where you are in relation to other objects, as the new 3D element of Trine 3 makes it hard to orientate yourself. To be honest, the 3D aspect doesn't even add anything to the experience, rather than detract enjoyment from it. This probably wouldn't be an issue if Trine 3 didn't hold onto the right analog as its crutch and gave players full 3D camera control with it instead, though of course the levels weren't designed with this in mind.
To make things even worse, issues from the Early Access that should have been polished up STILL persist, e.g. object collision (I literally ran through an object within 1 minute of the first level in the final build). Hell, even the story feels unfinished as there's NO resolution. The last level leaves you with a massive cliffhanger and nothing else, as if the rest of the game had to be cut short.
In short, do not buy this game unless you want a glorified tech demo. If curosity grips you, wait until a sale at the very least. You'll be done and fed up with this game in 4 hours and want your money back.

It pains me to say this but I'm not going to recommend Mini Motor Racing EVO basically down to the game having really bad physics.  Most of my play time was spent racing with a friend in 1v1 races which were generally decided by how the physics treated the player.  In some occasions a vehicle could get flipped on its side seemingly randomly and on a lot  of occasions an agressive side-swipe at my opponent would leave me in a worse off situation than him!  There seemed to be no realism or accuracy in the physics therefore removing any type of skill factor in the driving and racing.
Now the game looks really nice and fun.  It almost seems criminal to me to make a top-down racing game appear so nice and colorful to look at but then get let down by such a major game-breaking factor!
There's a large array of cars to choose from and an even more impressive track selection with day and night variants.  I learned today that the game also has Steam Workshop for creating and sharing your own track designs!!
You have an option of two different systems to control your vehicle.  The first type is the more conventional method of rotate/steer the car clockwise/anti-clockwise and the second type is to push in the direction you want to travel.  Now the second method of pusing in the desired direction of travel sounds awful to me but I actually found it a more efficient way to play this game.  You still have to accelerate and brake the same with both methods.  It's worth testing them both out with an open mind and seeing which works best for you.
There is no local co-op feature but the online multiplayer works fine.  I'm not sure about the playerbase but I managed to find my steam friend to play with without any problems and our games ran smoothly.
So many positive points about this game let down by a lack of fine-tuning in the physics.  The game boasts "cross-platform multiplayer" so possibly the physics were acceptable on a mobile platform.  I think on the PC platform we expect a bit more from our game.
If you can put up with the clunky physics and have a friend or three to play with then you could have some fun for sure.  For me though, it removed almost all competiveness and thus removed the fun and motivation to race further.

OneShot is a game about life, life that's in a very troubled spot that may not ever recover, but life all the same. Someone very fresh is pulled into a life that's on its way out, one way or another. In any case, it's a game that has you be as important as a role as the absolutely adorable main character as a majority of the game's puzzles require you to think outside of the box. And I do mean this literally. I won't spoil anymore as it is one of those kinds of games you really need to go into with as little information as possible. It helps that the game is also really short so if you have three hours to kill then you probably can and should finish it all in one sitting for the maximum impact. And speaking of as little information as possible, there's a lot of analysis to be done, though I hope there's enough speculation and information available to accomplish this. We'll see.
I can't say I felt myself really drawn into this world though, despite how lively it is I can't say it generated the sort of impact and emotional response that I probably should have gotten. But it did draw me in, to which I'm happy to have given it a play.
Recommended at full price since it's only 10 bucks anyways, why not, right?
ALSO, to any of you on Windows 7 and higher operating systems are going to need to do something very important: make sure the game file (inside the SteamApps Common folder) and the other very important file which I'm sure you'll figure out how it works when the time is right, are both in compatibility mode for Windows Vista. Otherwise the game will just crash when it should otherwise do something pretty dang cool.
Edit for Solstice Update: Well, now the game has a full complete ending! Not to say the original game doesn't have one. Simply play along with the game's desires after finishing the first run and on your second run things will be a little different as long as you know where to go. Anyways I won't spoil more than that. The update does make the game feel a little more complete and is enough to again recommend it at full price.

This is one of those games that if I tell you all the reasons its great, it will ruin the experience for others. Overall it is very well written with interesting characters you get attached to, has a lovely soundtrack with well chosen sound effects (click all those sheep!), a simple art style that doesn't get boring as you travel the world, and all these elements combine to create a wonderful experience. OneShot is a game that doesn't shy away from breaking the fourth wall. It harnesses my love for games that mess with your head and play with the conventions of game design. Games like The Charnel House Trilogy or Richard & Alice are clear examples of these types of game.  Unlike those titles though, OneShot takes it to a whole other level.  To say the least, OneShot has some really innovative ideas that go outside the window, literally.
OneShot plays with deep concepts such as life, sacrifice, morality, and the environment. It's easy to see why the rabid fan base is quick to compare this to a game like Undertale, especially given the childlike innocence with which these topics are approached. It hits the heart in just all the right places. While I don't want to get spoiler heavy, as the games primary enjoyment comes from its story, I will outline the basics.
In the game you help Niko after he mysteriously wakes up in a world with no sun. Niko doesn't know how he got there but he does manage to find a light-bulb that magically illuminates in his hands. This begins his long journey. A journey that will take him all across the world. If there was a way to describe this journey it would be like a Miyazaki film. The entire adventure feels unnerving but beautiful all in one breath. It propels you to an ending that leaves you questioning more about the world, more about yourself and the decisions you made.
Mechanically OneShot is simple, there is no battle system to speak of or anything really all that fancy. This is mostly a straight forward narrative game. There is an inventory system that lets you combine items to move the story along. You've seen similar systems in point & click games. The real interesting part comes when the game suddenly jumps into windowed mode. Once in a while you will come upon a puzzle that requires you to, "think outside the box."
These puzzles usually involve some sort of outside factor that actually isn't in the game itself. One puzzle might have you hunt down a file for instance. One of my favorites is the one that has you matching symbols to progress in a maze. It's very cleverly done and its something you have to experience to fully understand. Explaining it doesn't really do it justice. That sums up how I feel about OneShot in general. The experience is what makes it great.
If you are looking for extremely difficult puzzles, this isn't the game. It will make you think logically, but I didn't find it to be mind blowing in difficulty.
To back up the storytelling and puzzles, the game has an equally unique art style. Now keep in mind this is an RPGMaker game so it's pixel graphics, but that never holds the game back. At key moments the game also has these beautiful cut scenes that really draw you into the moment.
As you travel, each area has its own color palette and theme ranging from factories, forests, and the city. The world is dying, so OneShot has to balance its dreary setting but maintain a level of pleasing aesthetics. It accomplishes this with bright colors contrasting very dark backgrounds. It's quite effective at building the mood of the game. One area that does deserve mention is the characters sprites, which are fantastic!
The music of OneShot is also exceptional as well. Again, all playing into that creation of atmosphere that this title is based around. I personally enjoyed it but didn't find any particular track that piqued my interest. It got the job done, which is all that matters. Same with sound design. If you find that you love it, then FYI, the developer is releasing the OST soon for purchase.
The game can take anywhere from two to four hours on your first play through. If you read every scrap of lore, book, and investigate every nook and cranny. Once you do beat the game, there is a new game plus mode that unlocks. This area is the one I have the an issue with. Certain things were not finished in the first playthrough and are left unanswered no matter what you do. The new game plus practically tells you that things are going to be different and tells you to play again. This is sadly a bit of smoke and mirrors. My second playthrough was an hour long and I counted about five things being all that different.
The content isn't, as of when this was written, in the game yet. So hence the minor gripe I have. The end more or less leads you on. It could be far worse as certain players have gone as far to play three or four times looking for anything, to no avail. Despite that, the game is very enjoyable, the first playthrough is by far going to be the best. The puzzles don't change so the challenge is eliminated at the second playthrough.
Of course the developer is still actively adding things to the game so this is bound to change and I am very curious as to what awaits behind certain doors. Perhaps forgotten heroes? You know what I am talking about OneShot fans.
To wrap up, games like OneShot are what make Indie games so vitally important and amazing. They innovate, they have creative stories, and we need more games like it. I really enjoyed OneShot and hope the developers only grow from this and make bigger better games. Coming in at the low price of $9.99 this game is worth every single penny.
I gladly recommend this game and if you love narrative driven games then you need this in your library.

This is a special little game conceived originally as an entry to an RPGMaker contest a couple of years ago.
You guide a little creature called Niko to put the sun back on top of the Tower, in order to restore light to a dying world. It's a short little game, but that's okay, because it nails the characterizations, atmosphere, and worldbuilding down to a T.
As much as the game gets right, the best part about it is Niko herself. I found it really charming that Niko talks directly to you through the screen, in first person, but it's her personality that truly shines. This is not Niko's world, nor is it yours. Niko is lost and cannot do this without you, but you start out just as clueless as she is, so the two of you start out on an uncertain journey and learn about one another. I was surprised how quickly and how deeply it made you care - it's like you know the character personally after a while.
Your relationship with Niko and the world are also not what it seems; let Niko take a nap and the game will close. Start it up again and you'll be in Niko's dream... You'd even need to 'think outside the box' a couple of times to find answers to problems that present themselves in game, or even after the game is finished, because the answer 'no longer exists in this world'.
Much of this is eventually explained, but to talk any further would be doing the game and you a great disservice. If you view games as an experience, this is the little gem of 2016.
N.B. If you do pick up the game, keep an eye out for a future content drop on a date revealed in-game. If you're lost, the keyword is
:3
The game does some of the cool things it does through the Windows API. I didn't have any problems at all on Windows 10, but at launch time, it had some compatibility issues with some versions of Windows, so check the forums if you do run into trouble.

Asteroid Bounty Hunter
Arcade Bullet-Hell
Just1337 Studio
Kupi Key
is an arcade bullet-hell game developed by Just1337 Studio and published by Kupi Key, the same guys behind
.
You play as John, a veteran who is trying to do amends in his screw up life and he only has his space ship AI, who still cares about him. You will fight bad guys and destroy asterodis. The end.
Okay, the story is slightly more complicated, but unlike ShipLord it is more fun and interesting, and I kind dug the cutscenes. But it still isn't that great.
The engine is the same one of ShipLord: pretty background, good-looking asteroids and a good variety of bounty hunters that you fight. The enemy projectiles are also clearer, and they hardly blend into the environment.
This time you can actually shoot! You have a basic laser attack and other special attacks with cooldowns: fire balls that damage the asteroids, a straight-line of power that constantly delivers constant damage, and a phoenix that shoots missiles in all directions for a couple of seconds which deal a lot of damage.
Your main goal is to destroy a certain amount of asteroids. The longer you play, the stronger they get, giving you a tough time to blow them up. And between waves of asteroids, some bounty hunters appear, trying to kill you, so you need to kill them or avoid their projectiles. At the end of each round, you get XP points to use to lower the cooldown lenght, improve the power of your abilities and so on. It is very entertaining and way more fun than ShipLord, delivering a more complete experience.
You have a health bar that recharges over time, but the game is still pretty tough on the higher difficulties. However, replaying a level multiple times will give some XP points to spend in order to improve your abilities and manage to sustain more damage.
The sound effects are really solid, and the soundtrack is pretty good. A welcome addition is the possibility to skip the track you are listening and to add your own music to the game's library.
You have 25 levels, three difficulty modes and different modifiers that will greatly improve the lenght of the game.
Overall, this is a very damn good game about blowing up asteroids and bounty hunters. If you enjoy arcade-y games like this, you must play it right now. Otherwise, pick it up on sale.

I have never been a big fan of Space Shooters, but Asteroid Bounty Hunter really helped me to find some comfort and liking in this genre. What ABH does especially well is create some tense battle moments that make you almost fall off your chair as you make it in the slip of the moment (or not). Don't get me wrong, I have not seen many space shooters that actually give a damn aside from smashing the gunbuttons, so the effort is appreciated and should serve as an example for other space shooters. It cannot be helped, however, that the story is non-existant, with mediocre quality voice-acting and merely serves as small intermezzo's to keep a certain line of interest among the levels (which succeeded in that very small aspect). In short:
+ Excellent combat
+ Excellent powers, they all have their devastating effect and none of them are too OP or worthless
+ Moderatly good upgrade system, allowing you to choose early-on what's most important for your ship

+ Multiple ships to choose from

The price is solid for the amount of gameplay and the quality of the difficulty progression. You won't regret it even at full price.

Imagine if you will, the year is 2569 (because anytime the year ends in 69 it's going to rock), the human race has developed the ability to travel through space at light speed.  The Milky Way is the Galaxy we used to call home, Earth was destroyed in the year 2150, a huge asteroid stuck and destroyed the Earth laying to waste millions of years of human civilizations.  The left over remnants of Earth's population have taken up residency in Andromeda galaxy.  On a nearly Earth sized planet where life was sustainable.  Since an Asteroid was the root cause of Earth's destruction, the governing body of New Earth have been paying adventurers to pilot their ships into the vast ocean of space and destroy all the Astroids before they can endanger New Earth..
You take on the role of John, a down on his luck alcoholic who enjoys drinking, forgetting to feed his dog and owing people money... lots and lots of money..  Can you help save New Earth while at the same time killing off the bounty hunters looking to cash in on your death..  (as an Alcoholic who borrows money I can't afford to pay back I can assure you this game is top notch, and really helps put you in the shoes of John)
Gameplay - you're typical shmup fair, you control a ship, asteroids of various size fly toward your ship, occasional breaks in action see Bounty Hunter ships try to attack you using various forms of attack..  The game has 25 stages, each stage gets progressively harder.  After every fourth stage you fight a boss.  The five bosses have unique attack patterns and can prove to be quite difficult.  Memorization of their attacks is key to beating them.  Look for the pattern, exploit that pattern and bask in all the glory and riches that should follow our hero John.
The ship has four main weapons/attacks..  the basic attack, the laser, the spinning balls of death (Photon Swarm), and the Bird of flying missles.. otherwise known as the Final Blast  (no we're not talking about the money shot).  As you kill asteroids, you gain experience which can be used to boost up various skills your individual ship has.  Furthermore you can upgrade your global ship states which act independently of the ship skills.   You can unlock a total of 5 unique ships, each ship gets slightly improved stats over the one before it.  You should also learn how to dodge, probably the most important aspect of any shmup.
Pros'
fun factor is through the roof.
Awesome music (and you can add your own songs!!!!  Fight for your right to Party, blaring in your ears while you blow up asteroids... yes please)
Easy achievements that for the most part don't feel like a grind (for those times when you want to tell someone your opinion is more right by showing off your e-peen)
Some amazing looking hand drawn art work for the cut scenes (I think they are hand drawn.. either way the art style is unique in a good way.
The asteroids are varied enough that you won't find yourself looking at the same ones over and over again.
Con's
The game crashed a few times after exiting a stage.  In 2 hours of playing I had about 3 or 4 crashes.  Nothing a Ctl, Atl, DEL couldn't fix, but for a game this simplistic I'd expect little to no crashes
The background could have given the appearance of movement, as it stands now it looks like it's a static background, although some of the plants move around.
So do I recommend this game?  I'd say yes, if you're a fan of shoot em up's spaceship flying or having a game which is nice laid back experience, this very well could be that game.  Keep in mind this game isn't all bells and whistles, it's not your traditional bullet hell game, but the option exist to make the game resemble other classic shmup's, on the easier settings you may very well find yourself wanting more action.

Serious Sam HD: The First Encounter is a game developed by Croteam and published by the wonderful peeps at Devolver Digital. The First Encounter is the first part of two parts, known as The First Enocunter and The Second Encounter. The first two games in the Serious Sam series have been faithfully recreated in HD with a brand new engine and shiner graphics while still retaining the original game (now known as Serious Sam Classic)
The story follows Sam "Serious" Stone as he is employed to travel back to Ancient Egypt after aliens take over the world in the near distant future to put a stop to the invasion in the first place. As Serious Sam, you get to travel across old Egyptian ruins and fighting against creatures of all shapes and sizes
The gameplay is like that of old classic games, such as DOOM and Wolfenstein where you shoot enemies non-stop in huge arenas whilst getting keys, objects, health and ammo
Since this is an HD remake, we expect the game to be nicer than the original and with that it manages. The game runs on Croteam's very own engine, Serious Engine 3 and I must say the graphics were really nice. The arenas are huge and sprawling, full of Egyptian scenery
The music and sound effects are faithfully brought back from the original, so nothing new there. The sound effects are good but you can hear the difference in sound quality, sometimes poor to sub-par. Music too was the same, the music quality varied from poor to sub-par but this is understandable
The only thing that bugged me was the enemies, they were annoying to say the least. Always running towards, knocking down your health like there no tomorrow and Serious Sam runs so slow that even my late grandmother could run faster than him. The game doesn't feel as face paced as other arena shooter games I've played
Serious Sam HD: The First Encounter was a good first part into the introduction into the Serious Sam series and I cannot wait to play the second part of Serious Sam HD: The Second Encounter. If I had to recommend either the classic versions or the HD remakes, I would go for the HD remakes. Although I would still recommend the classic versions of Serious Sam, I think the HD remakes still hold up

So nearing the amount of in game time that equates to 10 actual rotations of the Earth (228.6 hours at the time of this review), I feel as though I have a proper understanding of this game, and my input will be valued.
Short version: This game is superb. You'd have to be an absolute fool to neglect this purchase.
Long version: My roommate suggested me this game after learning that I was looking for games to speedrun. I purchased it, fired it up, and not a moment later, fell in love with it. That kind of love you feel that just warms your whole body. My initial reaction was, "Wow, this soundtrack is incredible! And these graphics! It's so simple, yet so capturing and quirky!"
I started on 1-1. The first level in the first world. As the music changed from the Menu music to City, I got swept away in a feeling of bliss I hadn't felt in years. The controls were simple, the enemies were clear, and the objective straightforeward. Use the keyboard to move and jump, use the mouse to look and shoot. Reduce the enemy count to 0, and walk into the purple pillar. So simple! Why aren't more games like this?
As you reach the goal, a new window shows up, displaying information such as how quickly you completed that level, how quickly other people completed the level (a leaderboard), as well as how quickly the fastest person completed that level. Just like that, you already have a new way to enjoy the game, as if the gameplay itself weren't enough. Now you can not only compete against your own times, but other people too? Game on.
As you try to get top 15 times on the leaderboards, you start to try new things. Push the routes you used to take, or plan entirely new ones, hoping that they're faster. As you inevitably burn through all the levels in City, you move on to world 2, named Village. With each new world, new levels, obstacles, and enemies stand between you and those sweet sweet top 15 times. Can you hack it?
This game is designed in a way that the player doesn't feel coddled, but at the same time, it's not impossible to win. It's designed to be challenging, but not unwinable. New enemies are revealed in open, contained areas that let you see how they function, before throwing them just around a corner in the last levels of that world.
227 in game hours ago, I had the biggest, stupidest grin on my face. The joy of this game hasn't left me, even 227 hours later. If you're looking for a fun casual game, then you've found one. If you're looking for an speedrunning game that puts your skill to the test, then you've found one. Buy. This. Game. It's worth every penny.
Note to potential speedrunners: This game contains little RNG. The only RNG it DOES contain, bears no effect on how the game is run, or how it affects you or enemies. The only RNG occurs when an enemy dies, or your bullet registers as a hit, your gun will be showered in stars, providing a visual cue so the player can continue without having to watch the shots connect. I can find no pattern to where the stars appear. This is the RNG. That's it. This is an extremely skill and execution based game.

I really love puzzle games. They stuck me in, and usually don't let me go until I solved them. However, I haven't found a good one until recently.
When I first bought this game I didn't have the time to play, not even on my mobile. I recently installed it and gave it a try. I logged out 6 hours later.
This puzzle is the rare kind that have a relatable backstory. You don't have to read it to advance in the game, and it's not forced down your throat. It's nice and relatable, especially for people who worked at a high tech firm before.
The tutorials could be a bit more interactive, or at least animated. Some controls are well hidden, and never explained throughout the game.
The graphics are… OK, it's not beautiful. Well, it is, if you are into retro gaming, but given it's 2017 and you are playing as an employee of a space age high tech firm, it's pretty low. However, you spend most of your time on the reactor screen, which is pretty good.
Controls are OKish. You can't customise the keys, though, so unless you like to play dragging and dropping, prepare for the standard WASD keys (and you still need your mouse). Oh, you are using Dvorak or Colemak, or another esoteric layout? Then you should stick to your mouse.
The puzzles, however, are really nice. You occasionally get an easy one, that can be solved in minutes. But then you get an insane one you spend hours to figure out, without finding a solution. Oh, did I mention there is no easy way to start over? I really miss a reset button.
All in all, this is a very good game. I can spend countless hours without even realising it. You should definitely try it.

* Research Assignments (the 'simplest' type, which all takes place in a single chemical reactor).

Well worth 15 dollars.
-Pros
- Works with xbox controller under pinnacle game profiler flawlessly
- A newtonian colonization sci fi experience that you could easily spend 100-1000 hours on
- Only one developer, but is extremely active, releases patches regularly and can be spoken with in-game easily
- A friendly community that doesn't care to help noobs
- Nearly 3 billion star systems, and ones you discover are named after you forever
- Good newtonian physics
- Awesome ship diversity - i'd guess there are 20-30 ships in the game but they are very robust and more are being added
- NPC auto trade system
- Smuggler system
- Extremely complex colony and starbase system that can be customized
- Good soundtrack and atmosphere, in-game AI SAM 5000 is based on HAL from 2001 a space odyssey he's very amusing
- Minimalist gfx, but still a pretty game
- Stargates are developed by a team effort of players
- Planets are terraformed by a team effort of players and it takes like a year
- Advanced gravity and atmosphere based on real newtonian physics
- Skim gas giants for fuel
- Finally a game with interesting asteroid mechanics. you have to chase rocks down manually, point them to a certain temperature to get the best yield results. It also has some cool rare asteroids that feel rewarding when you find them
- Cons
- Confusing monthly fee that is based on tiers and is kind of hidden from you until after you buy what appears to be an online-only client - game is free to play after you buy the client but at a steep cost in the form of restricted features
- Fifteen bucks for no singleplayer
- Doesn't work on Linux even despite being developed in unity
- Ran like garbage on my Macbook even despite being developed in unity
- Playerbase is only 30 to 40 players in the absolute best case scenario, community could die at any moment
- Like most sandbox games, this is only for players who can entertain themselves in a sandbox
- Repetitive trading expected with most space games, but this game is worse because some galaxies have dozens of player colonies so jumping into said system causes extreme lag
- Making colonies and planting domes sounds good and all, but there's alot of research required to get into this game and you need to know that setting up your colonies requires actual console commands and some math skills
- Game rewards players who are the most intelligent and spend the most time, this is a good or a bad thing depending on your perspective
- Combat sucks in this game so bad but it is early access. nobody does combat in this game right now because it is a painfully frustrating experience
- Game is basically a singleplayer experience with an MMO gimmick. There's no function that allows you to team up with other players, and interaction with other players is limited to financial transactions
- Can explore unknown star systems, but all are empty and generic. some planets have no textures whatsoever and look lame. stars only come in three types. some systems might have an asteroid belt with rare spawns but that's about it. you wouldn't want to colonize these unknown stars systems as they are so far away so exploring them is mostly pointless
- No npc missions aside from courier runs (trading) and most aren't worth doing. not much to do in this game if you're not building a colony or a starbase
Should note that the game does have a premium option, you get three months with the purchase and after that it's 1.00 per month per tier to a maximum of 3.00 per month. Premium features include being able to fly class 13+ ships, mount class 13+ weapons, and to have 8 free newbie colonies in the NPC populated core systems.
IMO, having the starting newbie systems for a dollar a month isn't really worth it, except for the fact that without it you can't build more than six rings on your newbie starbase (you get the first starbase free). It's a significant disadvantage as starbases cap out at 100 rings. The newbie colonies are not as robust as the outer colony system and are extremely limited - one can only expect yields of 10,000 resources per colony per half day or day depending on colony efficiency whereas the outer colony systems can yield MILLIONS or even BILLIONS per day as they are huge, and furthermore can yield more than one resource. They can also act as player controlled trade hubs.

Ascent the Space Game is a wonderful find, I've been playing for months and am not tired of it yet in the least.
The concept behind the game is that you begin piloting a basic ship, and make your way into the universe.  Tutorial missions will guide you at first, and it's definitely worth it to complete these as they will give you access to a plot of land to place some mines on, a Star Base in which you can construct components necessary to colonize worlds, build ships, etc.
The game universe consists of a small core of 9 NPC run inner planets.  Each planet is in a system, and you travel between them using gates.
Outside of that is when the game really begins... as there are millions of unexplored star systems out there.  Players can explore, colonize worlds and build colonies producing minerals, food, alcohol, etc.  Construction of Gates between these systems are large cooperative projects, but there are many already in place and more planned.
Which brings me to the community.  The player community in Ascent is fantastic.  I've rarely felt at home in a game like I do in Ascent.  Certainly one of the big selling points to me.
Another positive for me is that PVP is not really an issue.  Roughly a quarter of the Galaxy is designated for the "Red Zone", which is the only place PvP can take place (it wasn't in effect at the time of this review).
The game is still in development... changes come often.  New ships, new asteroids to mine, new things to build with new minerals, smuggling is soon to be added, and PvE combat will be a priority after that.
For the price, I don't think you can go wrong.  Yes there is a small (and I do mean small) monthly fee for advanced features, but the game comes with three months for free which you can activate when you want.
So if the thought of getting into a ship and exploring, mining, colonizing untamed worlds, etc... while interacting with an outstanding gaming community, appeals to you... then you just can't go wrong with Ascent the Space Game.

This is the second game I randomly found on Steam that I've never heard about but is actually fantastic. My ship's on board computer has a commandline that allows us to set parameters (quite frankly this was totally unexpected for me, and it adds to the cool factor for me).
There is trade, there is massive exploration opportunities, probably more starsystems than will ever possibly be explored even if this game is around for 20 years.  100s of billiions of stars out there, and we can set up a colony and our own space station eventually.  I'm impressed.
This game appears to have all the features I've always wanted in a space game, and I was shocked at how easy it is to get the hang of.  Although I heard from others using the interstellar communications that the further along we are in the game the more complex it gets.  So I asked them that even if it gets complex can I just still choose to explore, and be mellow.  They said yes this is a sandbox.  They said we could just do the tutorial and take it as slow as we want.
Also it was a nice suprise that ships do not expend energy unless you use hyperdrive to travel to stars without a jump gate.  I also couldn't wreck my ship by crashing into the space station (which was nice since I didn't realize all I had to do was use autopilot to dock my ship).  In any case this is totally up my alley since I don't like micromanaging fuel while still learning a game.  We can keep flying from station to sation, mine, land on planets explore without fear of crashing and blowing up, or running out of fuel until we are ready to go out and take on more deadly stuff.
I don't know folks but this game seems like it is like a real universe.  I read all that stuff on the website about the graphics needing to be better and stuff, but I'm impressed at how immersive this game is and the graphics aren't an issue with me at all.  It also said they were working on improving combat (I honestly haven't tried combat yet, but the list of controlls seem simple enough).  This is still just early access so I totally don't expect this to be feature complete, but my goodness I'm glad I got this game!  I definitely recommend, and I'm not some long term fan boy that is biased about this game.  I really think this is a good find.

In my previous review of Asteroid Bounty Hunter, I said that the game suffered from too many issues to be worth a recommendation. A couple days later, the developer issued a patch that fixed...well...everything! Now this is a fine shootemup with several good ideas, plenty of content, and solid controls.
This is one of those games where everything you need to know, is spelled out in the title. Your job is to destroy asteroids, but apparently there's a price on your head, and bounty hunters from all over the galaxy are looking to collect. Karma, your ship, is armed with four weapons, three of which operate on cool-down timers. The strategy is in using these weapons at the right moments to avoid getting crushed by asteroids or blasted by hunters. As you complete stages and acquire experience, you can level up your weapons and shields.
Each stage plays out in the same manner. Your mission is to destroy x number of asteroids, and you're frequently attacked by bounty hunters. In my opinion, these stages are implemented in too rigid a fashion. When hunters appear, rocks stop flying at the player. By the end of the game, there are five types of hunters, but it gets pretty dull just fighting them.
However, in this version of Asteroid Bounty Hunter, two new modifiers were added, and they dramatically increase the fun-factor of this game. When you turn on the
setting, hunters continously spawn every few seconds. If you can't keep up with them, you're liable to get overwhelmed. The
setting causes asteroids to continually assault the player, no matter how many hunters are onscreen. While it's very nice that toggling these modifiers adds a significant boost to your experience, I like them simply because they make the game a lot more dynamic and entertaining.
To really explain just how much these additions improve the game, I'll provide a couple examples. Some hunters prefer to stay on the far right side of the screen, so that they can pelt you with bullets. Since asteroids are continually flying around, they're going to block most of your shots. This means that you'll have to work harder to find openings, or focus entirely on dodging until the enemy ship flies off. There are other enemies that fire giant lasers and spin around, you can move in a circle to avoid the lasers, but that isn't always possible with everything else flying around. You either have to unload your powerful weapons to destroy these foes quickly, or trust in your shields and take the damage. As new enemy-types are introduced, the game becomes even deeper. You really have to be considerate of your options, in order to survive these dangerous challenges.
It's important to also keep in mind that if these modifiers prove to be too much for you, then turn them off. Even with my level 180+ ship, I tend to get crushed when I play the latter stages on the harder difficulties. Sometimes you'll need to grind a little and bring your weapon levels up. Being able to destroy asteroids and aliens quickly is paramount to your survival. The difficulty can become a little unbalanced when hunters are constantly pouring into the chaos, but that's the trade-off if you want the exp. multiplier bonus.
The bosses provide a nice break from the other stages. Each of the five rivals has their own arsenal of weapons, and there are other factors to consider like black-holes and laser-walls. If you want an added challenge, you can choose to have bounty hunters attack, while you're fighting the boss. This is an especially risky decision, because there's so much that can go wrong. The bosses are large targets, and it's very easy for hunters to hide behind the boss, all the while firing away at you. Certain boss-attacks will also "funnel" you, leaving very little maneuverability. If hunters start firing at these few safe-spots available to you... Too bad! Again, these modifiers are optional, but who can turn down the added challenge and triple the experience?
Alongside the substantially improved controls and mechanics, Asteroid Bounty Hunter also provides a great soundtrack, a rather charming storyline, and more than enough action to earn your money and time.

I was approached by someone on my friends list (Whoracle) and asked if I would take a look at this game and maybe review it. I'm not sure if Whoracle is the dev or not. He says in his own (glowing) review that he got the game from a friend, yet it was Whoracle who sent me 2 keys for the game via steam PM. [edit: apparently whoracle is a friend of the dev who the dev got to help out by giving them keys to distribute and does not work for the dev. I'm just stating that as what the dev told me in PM, with no editorial]
This is a very simple and somewhat amateur game. Basically it boils down to thirty something stages. Each stage is a horizontally scrolling shmup that features asteroids followed by spaceships bullet hell followed by asteroids... repeat. Every few stages there is a boss fight with more extreme bullet hell mechanics and some story in the form of amateur art with amateur voice acting. The music is of a better quality than the other assets in the game, probably because it's all by other people (it's all cc by attribution).
The weapons are upgradable and there's some limited tactics to when you decide to use them rather than just spamming them and there's ship ugrades which amount to stats of shield or damage, and then there's different ships that I didn't get to see because I didn't get that far.
It's not utterly terrible and it can be challenging but it's so repetitive! I only played as long as I did because I was reviewing it: I would have given up a lot sooner if I got this game in a bundle say. In fact I doubt I would have installed it based on the screenshots.
Here are the reasons my review is negative:
1. Price: The game is £5.59. This is too expensive. It should be £1.99 in my opinion, considering the repetition and simplicity.
2. The store page seems to go out of its way to make the game seem more interesting than it is:
"defend the nearby planets from vicious asteroids attacks " = shoot asteroids while planets appear in the background
"Your job is to save planets from incoming asteroids, while taking care of your affairs with other bounty hunters. " = shoot asteroids while planets appear in the background for most levels, while every few levels the level is a boss fight.
3. There's also little annoyances like the default option when you press return at the end of a successful level is to repeat the level, rather than continue.
4. The extremely high number of positive reviews and the fact that the most glowing review is by the guy who gave me the keys for the game makes me extremely suspicious. [edit: I am not claiming, nor do I wish to imply that they bought reviews in any way, merely that I believe they contacted people and gave them free keys with a suggestion that they might review the game]

This game reminds me of the old FMV games from the 90s, which is the angle I think they were going for.  But there are a few differences.
Firstly, the game looks pretty good.  It switches between high-quality, movie like cutscenes, to a slightly low quality interactive "find the hidden object" scene.  Overall the graphics look rather nice.
There are three main things you do in this game.  Firstly, there are a few puzzles.  The puzzles are rather easy, and will take you a few minutes tops.  Secondly, there is the point and click "find the hidden object" sections.  Most of the things you need are fairly easy to spot, but there are a few you might miss at first glance.  Lastly, there are a few quick time events.  While I'm not a fan of QTEs, there are only a few in this game, and they are pretty easy to get (as long as you have your hand on the mouse).  All around I liked the gameplay.
This is around the part where I would normally give a bit of insight into the story of the game, but there really isn't much to talk about. I will say that while I've never seen any of the films in the "Saw" franchise, I have a feeling the creators might have been somewhat inspired by it.

I would suggest waiting for this game to go on sale.  I bought it for $1, and I wouldnn't really recommend paying more than that, unless you just want to support the devs (who I'm assuming are an indie company, but I may be wrong).

Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power was released by Frozenbyte, late 2015. Common themes found in Trine games are: fantasy graphics and locations, story book tale telling, and puzzles.
Once again our Hero's Zolya, Amadeus, and Pontius are brought together to assist the Trine
in yet another adventure. However, this time the Hero's are growing weary of always helping the Trine and they are starting to become quite discontent.
The biggest change in Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power, is that Trine3 is in 3D. By that, I mean the game is played in a 3D plane unlike the past games which are played on a 2D plane and emulate classic side-scrolling gameplay, but with fancy fantasy graphics.
There is now a "World Map" that you can select the level/zone you want to play, with the addition of the world map there are side mission which you can do to unlock more story missions
The characters have new abilities or changes to past abilities. As in past Trine Games you switch between three characters: Zolya, Amadeus, and Pontius. To help you remember these different characters I've taken the liberty of giving them nicknames.
Zolya (Aka "Assassin's Creed Woman") can use a grappling hook, and shoot arrows. Unfortunately her skills have been severely downgraded from past games, she can only grapple hook on specific environment objects.
Amadeus (Aka "The Boxer"), he too, has been downgraded from his past skills. Now he can only conjure boxes and move most objects you see on the screen. In past games Amadeus could create platforms as well, but Trine 3 has given Amadeus a new ability! He can now smash his enemies with boxes, which is quite hilarious and very fun to do.
Pontius (aka "Meat Shield"), I'm happy to report I haven't changed what I use Pontius for since the previous two Trine games: I switch to him for combat, or if I need to walk through some spikes. He has lost his magnet shield ability, but now he can ground pound.
All in all, some of these changes are a game-breaking to some people, others get turned off by the random glitches that occur to the physics
.
There are two kinds of achievements right now: Beat the level achievements, and collect all the things achievements. I have little doubt there will be more achievements added to the game later on.
The past two games had much more difficult achievements and achievements based on the character you're playing. specific actions within the story, completing the game on the hardest difficulty
Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power is priced at $21.99. I judge games by how much they cost verse how much time I spent playing the game, I only spent 6 hours playing Trine 3. After those 6 hours I had all the achievements unlocked.
To quickly recap, Story: enjoyable, I always love Trine's story telling style. Gameplay: This will make or break your feelings for the game. Achievements: At this time, Trine 3 is an easy 100% completion, I would be shocked if that didn't change in an update eventually. Price: Too high, but it was extremely good quality and fun to play.
You can tell the designers focused most of their attention of making Trine 3 3D
, unfortunately with the high emphasis on 3D levels/zones, it looks like the story, puzzle complexity and length of the game was severely cut back.
I recommend this game to people who enjoyed the Trine series for their style and story telling aspect. If you really liked the puzzles or any of the "perks" systems in the old games, this game will disappoint you.
For anyone who hasn't played a Trine Game yet... I suggest trying out Trine Enchanted Edition, and/or Trine 2: Complete Story. While it's not needed to understand the story in Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power... you will experience a far more 'complete' game in the previous installments.

404Sight is a free and quirky little game from the people at retro Yeti Games.
You play as Alice (I think) and your job is to deliver a data package to a server (I think). The story is simple, told to you the moment you open the game and nothing else is said of it until the very end of the game. The game has a focus on gameplay.
Speaking of, 404Sight is a Third Person Platformer in the same vein as Mirrors Edge. It's alot less detailed, alot shorter, alot easier but hey you get what you pay for. There are a few wgameplay elements to stop the game from being tedious. You have a Bandwidth Bar (which is like a health) bar that fills up as you go over "Fast Lanes" (green lanes that when you run over them, they speed you up). The bar is depeleted by entering "Slow Lanes". They are less like lanes and more like red patches on the ground you shouldn't run over.
Another feature are the inhibitors, which are basically drills that come from the sky and land in front of you producing an area of slow lane that, if you run over, your health disappeares entirely. The last are bouncy pads that when you run on they, they bounce you in a certain direction. You do not choose the direction.
The last unique feature is the "Ping". Left Clicking activates Ping which allows you to actually see the fast/slow lanes, bounce pads etc. You have to turn it on and off at specified times but generally you have it on at all times and just turn it off when coming up to any red areas, then turning it back on.
The game is VERY linear. Sure, there are numerous paths but everything leads to the same destination. You have a time counter but it really doesn't seem to matter how fast you go as no achievement is tied directly to this.
Speaking of achievements, they are VERY easy. You can not only beat the game, but also earn every achievement within 1 hour. Seeing how the game is free, there's no opportunity to pass this up. Free, easy achievements. There's really no better.
However, there are ALOT of glitches in this game. Infact, most of the time the glitches popped up in the first level. Here they are, in the order they happened:
1. After dying in the first level, upon repsawn the characters feet were stuck in the ground. I couldn't move. This happened numerous times throughout the game and the only fix is to quit the game entirely and retsrat.
2. Upon getting to the exit, after running through a small tunnel I fell dowwn. As this was the first time I reached the end I thought it was what I had to do but it just turns out I fell through the world. When I respawned, problem 1 happened.
3. Upon getting to the exit a second time, it was completely blocked by a wall. Had to exit the game and try again.
4. Sometimes Ping does not reveal any of the lanes.
5. Moving the mouse sometimes does not change the camera direction.
Overall the game is short and sweet with easy achievements but can prove to be very annoying  if you have a short fuse.
