SpaceChem is basically its own genre of puzzle game. Each level requires you to program the "waldos" (the red and blue circles) to move input molecules around a screen and create different molecules as output. As you progress in the game, more commands are introduced which allow you to use the waldos in more interesting or more efficient ways. I played this game for 92 hours, more than any other game in my account, to beat every level and obtain the 20 achievements. It has remained challenging and engaging throughout, and I have never played a game quite like it.
What really distinguishes SpaceChem from puzzle games in general is that it is open-ended. It feels like you are inventing a solution, not finding it. For any given puzzle you will find people who have implemented a solution and optimized it in dozens of conceptually different ways. Speaking of optimization, it's important to mention that the creators made optimization totally optional. Yet, I have found that some of my most satisfying moments playing the game were getting some highly optimized solution to work (e.g. with just one reactor, or with a tiny number of symbols) after hours of effort.
As far as programming games go, a major strength of the game (over, for instance, TIS-100) is how visually intuitive it is. Everything is executed by the waldos moving around the screen; nothing is hidden from you. Debugging your program is simply a matter of watching what happens when you click "run". You don't really have to read what the rules are, as you just learn them by experimenting.
I do have some negative things to say. I am not alone in complaining that the boss fights are not as enjoyable; especially the very last level, which was made difficult in a number of annoyingly artifical ways and ultimately made me take a few months away from the game. Having beat it, I appreciate it a bit more, but the limited space for the reactors was just unnecessary. In general, I think that I enjoy small, elegant puzzles a lot more (which I can then go and optimize), rather than these 5- or 6-reactor messy puzzles where the solution is to put a whole bunh of easy pieces together into a working contraption, and debug it.

I'm still dumbfounded. Not exactly by this game, but by the fact that this game, a B-movie equivalent (zombies in space with bad voice actors) and a friggin' port from mobile, has a better PC port than many high-profile titles I played. Mouse acceleration? Turn it off in the options menu! Same with mouse smoothing. And the FOV goes up to 90 vertical. VERTICAL!
Enough rambling. What is this game? Gameplay-wise, it's a sort of a first-person-looter. You go through levels, kill stuff in first-person with your weapons (not all of them are guns, there are viable meele bulds as well), go back to base, spend money earned on upgrades, spend skill points earned on upgrades, you get the idea. There are main missions you can select from a map, there are side missions and loads of them. And you can play them with friends cooperatively. Nice, eh?
Replayability is legions. You have tons of side-missions, you can replay everything, assuming you amass enough money, you can try out many different weapons with many different character builds. Don't need to level up endlessly, you can respec as often as you want, assuming you have enough money.
Don't get me wrong, there are some donwsides. Hit detection could be better, for example. The general art style makes enemies hard to detect sometimes as they blend with the environment and why you only get one primary weapon to play with is beyond me. At least, that one makes me cherish a newly found gun more.
Atmosphere-wise, it's the video game equivalent of a B-movie. Zombies & mutants in space, evil soldiers trying to take you down, a "dramatic" plot about experiments gone wrong, nothing groundbreaking, but it serves the purpose. The gameplay isn't as polished as let's say Shadow Warrior 2 (my 1st favorite first-person-looter but I've played through it 2 times already), but fun nontheless. Considering this game here is pretty cheap, get it!
PS: I should add that while this was originally a mobile game and it features "premium" in-game purchasables, they're all purchasable with in-game money. Unlike some high-profile titles (Shadow of War, Battlefront 2), there are no real-money transactions at all. You can only buy stuff with in-game money you earn from playing the game. Again, another thing this cheap B-game does better, than A-games ("AAA" is dumb, let's stick with one "A").

So I remember getting the first game a couple of years back for about 79p and it was rough as hell. Enemies were bullet sponges, weapons underwhelming, level design - well, a big corridor and the plot/voice work was pretty atrocious. How it got a sequel I'll never know, but you know what - it wasn't half bad.
It's overloaded with superfluous stuff - you have gear, implants, weapons (which you can upgrade), skills, gear augmentations and weapon augmentations. You also have story missions plus 4 other game types, side missions (which are really tasks - i.e. kill a number of a certain enemy or collect various gear), online availability of all game modes (which add to your loot) and an XP system. Far too much, with too little value in most of the stuff you get; loot for the sake of loot.
Further issues are that the level design and aesthetics are still pretty dull, the voice work is still awful, the story just stops really abruptly (you get a screen saying 'Congratulation [sic] - to be continued!') and let's be polite and say that the graphics were kept modest to ensure a smooth frame rate (or something.)
But in spite of all that, I had a reasonable amount of fun with it. The gunplay is pretty satisfying and, within reason, the upgrading and tinkering with gear is okay and I even enjoyed a few online games too. The lack of an ending annoyed me somewhat but for the £1-odd I paid I definitely got good value (about 7 hours or so).
I'll probably buy the third game (it's been announced but no release date, I think) when it's down to a quid, at any rate.

the many hours I've been in it.
In spite of that my opinion about it is utterly negative.
This isn't because of the community, one of the best I've encountered
so far, or the idea behind the game.
The reasons I've come to dislike this game are the following ones:
1) the developer is too slow in implementing new features and doesn't
fix many existing bugs for very long times. He's a one man team, true,
but if he doesn't have much time why does he waste time in implementing
nonsense like "Cargo now ejects into crates - these can't be re-captured but
they're fun to kick around". This nonsense while there are lack of many
fundamental functions like a decent in game chat or the ability to change
the game login password!!!
2) the developer is too self centered in developing features he likes
the way he wants without listening to the community.
Take as an example the npc traders: they trade whatever they like at
the price they like and get only half of the goods you've in a stock market.
Not to mention the stock markets are opened to anyone and you cannot implement
your own close loops.
This kind of implementation is nice only in the developer's mind!
3) the game learning curve is scary! Forget to log in the game and have
evreything you need to learn or to do right in one place: in the game itself!
You have to read pages and pages of wiki and forum and even after that you
will need plenty of help from many experienced players.
If you don't have too much time you play OR you spend hours reading poems
about learning HOW to play.
4) the in game chat is a joke... there is only one global room and nothing more.
No trade chat, no private chats, no personal chats, no messaging system between
players. Something you would expect from day 1 from any game developed in this age.
There is barely an ignore feature, too bad it gets reset evrey time you log out.
VERY useful!!!
5) The interface is ugly and ludicrous. There are tons of textbooks explaining how
to properly develop a nice basic game interface, but the developer is too busy
developing useless features like the cargo crates mentioned in point 1).
6) The game is gradually becoming a pay2win kind of game. Recently the developer added
two addons to the game: the bowhead and the hawk. If you don't pay you can't have them
and they cost more than the game itself, which is utterly ludicrous.
7) The game mechanics are grind galore. To make money there are basically two ways:
keeping hauling goods from point A to point B or to mine asteroids. The hauling part
is especially boring because doing the same set of actions hundreds of times per day
evrey day cause alienation in one's mind.
8) the game is open ended, but in the sense it doesn't have any purpose after a certain
stage. At the beginning you keep grinding to become bigger and bigger. After you have
reached the top, meaning biggest ship and some colonies, you don't have nothing to do
basically. I don't like games which tell me what to do in a strict way, but mechanics
to keep me busy at evrey stage of my gameplay are essential to keep my interest up.
9) To extend further point 8) one of the best game mechanics would be npc space pirates
attacking colonies and/or trading ships. Too bad the developer will implement this feature
in his usual self-centered way: the npc pirates will be enabled/disabled using a checkbox...
Who in the hell would enable such checkbox is beyond me!
10) When there is too much noise about the way a feature is implemented the developer just
closes the threads in forum telling "this isn't up for debate" and that's it. What's the point
of having a forum? To exploit experienced players' knowledge to compensate the lack of any kind
of decent tutorial/help in the game itself of course.
Conclusion: Stay away from this game. There are much better options out there, better priced too!

Trine 3 is a great game but is very different from the first 2 games.
As always, Frozenbyte delivers a great game in both visuals and audio. But to my regret, it's a lesser title than it's predecessors.
The collectables are no longer experience points, but will count toward unlocking new levels. This also means you'll have all available skills at the start.
They made the move from 2.5D to full 3D.  Full being a bit much said. It still behaves like the sidescroller this franchise has been know as. And with 3D, the problem of depth arises, most present with floating objects and enemies.
This game is quite shorter than what the franchise is know for, with the ending demanding a followup.
But this doesn't mean other new things are bad. Amadeus finally has a decent combat ability, and being able to move while levitating is a nice addition too, even though his abilities have been reduced to a single box. Zoya can now tie her rope to objects. In both I see possibility to be used in the old 2.5D style. In addition, all characters can perform walljumps, which I'm fairly ok with.
In the end, would I be willing to pay full price? Not in it's current state I'm afraid. What would I consider a good price? Well, I bought it at 50% off, and what I got was well worth the price. Frozenbyte titles are known for their insanely deep discounts. Trine 1 and 2 have seen 85-90% cuts, and it hurst me to see such great games go so deep. So yeah, I would definitely recommend buying at -50%, perhaps a bit more.

This game is 100% reliant on luck. Skill is secondary.
This game seems designed to be condescending as well. Perhaps you're a better player than I am, but I've never beaten Easy mode + I have about a 70% win rate w/ Too Easy mode.
There is also an "unlockable" ship - in quotes because I don't think its actually possible. To do so, you have to complete the game w/out your crystal taking any damage. I say impossible - because of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ number of enemies that spawn + a large number of those enemies designed to beeline it - ignoring defenses/heros.
The devs have released quite a few free updates that came w/ characters + ships - which was nice.
If only they play-tested and realized a bunch of the heros are absolute trash. Either they die way too quickly - attack very slowly - or have terrible skills.
The buildable turrets are also - incredibly weak - even at rank IV.
This game might be enjoyable if easy/too easy mode - actually was easy/too easy mode, but they aren't.
And the difficulty of the game really isn't fun. It doesn't feel like a hard fight - it feels like - you got lucky w/ floor exit placement - if you win. Or you got lucky to find a dust box item.
Floor 8+ is pure luck based. You won't find enough resources to keep enough rooms lit - so each time you open a door - there is a large chance of an absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ number of enemies spawning from each unlit room. I'm talking wave sizes of 6+ per unlit room. It gets stupid quickly. Compounded by you having to split up your heroes - To cover all the paths to your crystal. Since - like I said - the buildable turrets are absolute trash.
Most enjoyable time I had w/ the game, was when I threw pretense of giving a crap about the other heroes out the window - and min-maxed the armory ship. This gave me 4 reliable - powerful heroes. Thats the closest this game gets to an easy mode. The armory ship makes each indiv. hero significantly more powerful - removes some starting tech - and doesn't allow you to research or build attack turrets.
You do have to unlock that ship, but if you want to have any fun w/ this game, I recommend you do so ASAP.

I was very excited to play this game, I love resource management and I have enjoyed tower defense in the past too, but sadly it missed the mark for me.
Without going into all that is good about this game (there is plenty), I just think the RNG factor is too high.
Your ability to power rooms is random.
Your ability to find the exit is random.
Your unpowered rooms can spawn waves randomly.
This combination makes can make for some very high swings in difficulty and lead me to some bitter moments.
This one factor seemed to be the biggest differentiator of winning and losing.
I didn’t see any dramatic successes due to upgrading modules, upgrading heroes.
I can only optimise my micro management of my 4 heros so much to prevent waves spawning.
So again, all of this lead to bitterness in my case.
On the flip side, unfortunately the game is too slow and long term for me to simply shrug it off as ‘dying is half the fun’ like other roguelikes.
At the end of the day I see a lot of other people enjoying this game and I am super glad they do… I just couldn’t.

This game is truly a thinking game.  There are many tough puzzles with a progressive learning curve to them.  The puzzles are a challenge that remind me of robotic programming, and are fulfilling to see a comparison between you and others based on a global statistic shown at the completion of the puzzle.  The puzzles are complex due the simplicity of the inputs.

This game is incredibly difficult. The learning curve is steeper than perhaps any game I've ever seen, and you're expected to pay close attention whenever the game teaches you something new. Oftentimes just looking up the solution for a puzzle online won't be enough to help because it requires a thorough understanding of how things work in order to progress. However, once you get the hang of the mechanics and are into the rhythm of the puzzles, it is one of the most rewarding puzzle games I have ever played. The complexity of the game means that there are millions of creative solutions for a single puzzle, and I've even gone back to previous puzzles to improve on an old design after learning a new trick or two. The room for improvement is almost infinite; I could see playing for hundreds of hours and still getting better.
So if you're a puzzle aficionado willing to get past the first two hours of struggling to understand what the hell is going on, it's easy to lose yourself in this game for hours at a time. An instant favorite in my puzzle game collection!

This isn't a racing simulator, it's a racing arcade game.   It has a cutesy theme, with the cars in the game being a little squishy, this is part of the design intent.  The gameplay is viewed from an overhead perspective, and is thematically very close to the 1980's arcade machine game, Super Sprint.
One big warning, this game is a console port and thus has clunky control schemes compared to what PC gamers are used to.   The arcadeyness and control schemes are certainly drawbacks for people who aren't fans of the genre.
However, credit where it is due.
The game is polished, technically solid (runs fine with full settings on a 4K rig), with clean graphics and UI and a smooth interface.
There's a big variety of cars with different attributes all of which are relevant to various races.
Upgrades let you improve cars as you go along.
Quite a few interestingly themed maps with tight corners, rough terrain and hazards infusing a lot of variety into each race.
All in all, Mini Motor Racing Evo is a well put together game, fun to play (because of the attention to look and feel, slick interfaces and smooth yet detailed graphics. and despite the console throwbacks) and would be quite suitable for families, kids, and fans of the ancient arcade game, Super Sprint, which this game shares more than one point of similarity with, and captures the same spirit.

Mini Motor Racing EVO is an overhead racing game that's a kin to the single screen arcade racers of the 80s. The title is apt and descriptive, because you're driving around in miniature vehicles. Its a beautiful game with a lot of diverse locales, fitting music, fun and challenge all rolled into one. Its tough to get anything more into this package, but Mini Motor goes the extra mile with a map editor and online or network multiplayer. Its also a game that uses its licenses admirably from games like Team Fortress 2, Portal 2 and to my amazement Fruit Ninja.
The game has two major control schemes, both of which play excellent with a controller or keyboard and mouse. The first controller feels alien, yet its so right. Point the analog stick the way you want to go, much like non racing games. They still have a more typical control scheme of left and right to steer, but pointing the stick plays a lot better, there's no overshooting your vehicle's angle.
The driving does take a bit of time to get used to. Your vehicle can turn on a dime, and often you're going so fast that you'll leave skid marks with every turn. Letting off the accelerator will put you at a dead stop almost immediately. There is no momentum in this game, unless you're pushing the gas. There's also no reverse, but that's the side effect of being able to turn your car without hitting the gas.
Like the majority of racing games, you also have a nitro button and in this game, it feels a lot different. You have blocks of nitro. Press the nitro button once to use a block and this nitro cannons you forward at a reckless pace. Its total risk or reward with this nitro boost and you'll need it to overtake other vehicles that outmatch yours. Nitro canisters always appear on the track at random to give you an extra nitro block as long as you're under your maximum. You can also pick up cash on the track as well.
Mini Motor Racing has three difficulty campaigns. You start on easy and then after a few cups, you'll unlock the next difficulty. These difficulties have a series of cups, each cup has four races. When you come in third place or higher of all races in the cup, it will unlock the next cup for you. Of course some cups can last twelve races, so its not limited to four. The cups transition smooth from one to the next and you can play any previous race.
As for the races themselves, they're brief on closed circuit courses that are only around a minute for three or four laps. I say brief, because they're still a quick shot of fun and never overstays its welcome. The races do get longer as you proceed further into what feels like it could be a long game. At two hours in, I haven't completed all of the easy beginners championship races. You race against five other cars for most of the game, but you do start out against one, two then three competitors and so on. With more aggressive racers, it can become hazardous to even start a race. Faster vehicles can ram into you and turn you around before the first turn.
The cars feel heavy, you can ram someone and push them around. While the game hardly has realistic physics, the dirty play physics are great.  Ramming someone out of your way or spinning them with such tight quarters is always a joy that other racing games have forgotten about. With the racers being mini, it becomes a feat to spin someone around rather than just pushing them. That can come back to haunt you. Any pile of cars becomes dangerous as they push right into you rather than dodge you. This is geared for the arcade, rather than realism. Its tough to avoid pile ups at the first turn.
These races all have themed environments and music. Vernice city streets near waterways. A port full of shipping containers. The wilds of Africa through a river next to hippos. Racing on a Mayan temple. At a yellow sand beach across a bridge that dips into the water. Its all bright, colorful, eye catching and makes the game more fun.The soundtrack is diverse and good even if its generic, its all still fitting. Its rare, but tracks can go indoors or under bridges where the overlying areas become transparent. The developers made the game dynamic, eclectic and shows the effort put in.
To get longevity out of the courses, you will be racing on a lot of the courses a few times, but with a twist. Some races reverse the track. Other events are at night, or at dusk. The largest twist when you do the same race in a different cup is a literal one. The game will shift the perspective of the track. It helps to keep things interesting on what would otherwise be the same race for the forth time. The mini map stays the same, so what is north on the mini map could be southeast on the track itself. There are a few objects to bump into on each track. You can run down cones, knock over tire stacks and it all feels good to interact and mess up the course a little.
Team Fortress 2 and Portal 2 tracks are a big appeal of the game and they do make good uses of their respective franchises. You have Helen's voice in the Team Fortress 2 and the sentries voice from Portal 2. Portal 2's level has a big portal at the end to bridge a gap from the end to the finish. The Team Fortress 2 map has a lot of indoor areas and I can best describe it as the race version of Badlands. I only encountered each track once, but the Fruit Ninja track is everywhere.
There is a large variety of vehicles. I keep calling them vehicles, because there are more than typical stock cars, derby cars, muscle cars and race cars, because in Mini Motor, you can drive as a police car, school bus, jeep and even an ambulance. The big buses can be dangerous with their top speed. It gives the game a lot of character and flare to be driving what you want.You'll find plenty of vehicles unlocked from the start and they're all free. The vehicles all have different skins to chose from, so you can even play as Herby the Love Bug.
Each of the vehicles has their own stats for acceleration, top speed, nitro and handling. These stats can be upgraded to a certain extent by purchasing upgrades with your race winnings. The higher the tier of upgrade, the more it will cost and you'll need these upgrades to keep competing with higher levels of competition. The unfortunate part is that if you switch vehicles to one that you haven't spent thousands on upgrading, there's no way to be competitive in further races. At least you can take your cash earned from one vehicle and carry it over to a new vehicle. You can downgrade as well if you need to.
Upgrading never felt like I could instantly win, it always felt like a competitive challenge. Sure there are races where some cars are just geared toward that terrain and those curves, but for the most part everything was good enjoyable, neck and neck fun once I was past the first initial races.
There are quick race modes with all of the tracks you've unlocked and ones from Steam Workshop. You even have a track designer. I never expect much from a budget game's level designers, but this is easy to use and you can create something good to play in a short amount of time, albeit dull and lacking from the main game. Clicking your mouse on angles and dragging the road to make the precise curve or angle you want. Investing more time would probably yield great results if you spend the time to place props down.
You can download tracks from the Steam Workshop, but what I really want is entire cups worth of tracks or the ability to make my own cups on top of tracks. A single racetrack is just too quick. Its the bread stick rather than a complete meal.
Mini Motor Racing EVO is a fantastic game for a dirt cheap price. Its a game for any fan of the overhead racing genre and a fun, enjoyable experience with challenge. At $5 its tough to argue with the price for a game with so much fun and content.

Easily my favourite game ever produced so far. Ontop of every other stealth/combat game, this manages to exceed itself in every way possible. If your a fan of stealth as an option, this is easily a top choice when chosing a game, Dishonoured gives you the options of many paths within each misison. Whether it is to sprint and jump across the rooftops, dropping down on your enemies like tomorrow, you can go complete stealth without having to ever use your blade. However as many other games propose, is when playing something heavily integrated with stealth, it is often pointless to try and face the enemy head on when playing on the hardest difficulty, Dishonoured still gives you that option as it is still completely possible to face them head on. It still is extremely hard to do, I find after much practice of combining teleporting and agility together it becomes a non-stop intense fight until someone is left standing and the other taken apart by rats or sliced to peices. This takes me onto the next point of a concept, the use of this "steampunk" world ran by whale oil is made completely believable through the realistic-appocalyptic setting. The world becomes a part of the way you play through each mission, after my personal 7th playthough of the game, I still find things I have never discovered before, purely basing my knowledge off the way I had previously encountered similar structures within the world of Dunwall. Whether you choose to kill everything in your path and lead to a particularly destructive conclusion, or whether you remain to become unseen throughout the whole entire game remains to be your choice. Finally, the DLC. Out of all games this remains to one of the best DLC-integrated games where it is 100% worth buying after you finish the game, whether it is to play as Daud who had just an equally as good story as Corvo where more secrets of the city are unveiled, or to play in time trials and challenges, rating yourself against the rest of the world.
All in all my favourite game above Skyrim, Far Cry 3 and 4, Hitman Absoloution and Shadow Of Mordor.

TL;DR: Wonderfully made, incredibly short.
For a throwback to the good old days of FMV games, MISSING is very well-made.  The interactive elements look natural in the environment, the actors do an adequate job, the puzzles (such as they are) are immediately apparent (no time spent wondering what to do with a puzzle).  The gameplay is engaging, the story (so far) is intriguing, though the use of jump-cuts from one area to another can feel disjointed, but it is a satisfying puzzle experience.  There is, however, a lack of "adventure" elements--you essentially move in a linear fashion from one puzzle room to the next, solve the puzzles you're presented with, and move to the next puzzle room.  In each area, there's investigation for clues or keys to the various puzzles, but little more in the way of it being interactive.  There are QTEs, and some of them feel out of place.
In any case, it's important to note that this is a short episode.  Very short.  As in, took me less than 45 minutes short, and a total of about 75 minutes to 100% the achievements.  All-in-all, though, MISSING comes across as something special, and I look forward to the next episode.

Bought this game a while back, thinking the concept was interesting and I liked the more close-up style of management as compared to other similar games. I can't remember exactly how my first few play-throughs went, but they were bad enough I deleted the game for a long time without reinstalling it until very recently this last week. I played the game slightly obsessively for the first few hours, working to maintain my colony and not be overtaken by the Golbins trying to kill us all. However I quickly encounter many problems that just annoy me to the point I don't want to play anymore...
My first two setups things were going fine, until one big raid of Goblins came and killed everyone. I watched helplessly as all my villagers slowly died and then restarted. Same thing happens again, even though I had tried to focus more on the military aspect of the game. However, with a meager 20 max villagers my military was really lacking.
I decide to quit the game and come back to it with a stronger military force later the next day. It goes well, I pass the raid and huzzah! There's pretty much nothing interesting after that, other than my game freezing constantly,  my villagers getting confused and breaking, or an engine error popping up and forcing me to restart the game. I tried both the unstable latest patch and the offically release stable patches. Both failed me...and also after enabling the unstable patch just to see if there were any updates at all, which really there aren't  (then disabling after it crashed even faster than before) all my custom buildings broke and if I tried to place them the game crashed once again. Had to delete them all and start over. Fun stuff!
Pretty much the game is exactly the same as when I bought it, and it's just as unplayable and annoying as before. Pawns will stop building things mid-build, people will starve in holes instead of building a ladder to get out, and the village numbers are so meager you'll never really have fun with masses of items or pawns. Also, there's a 3000 item limit on the game, this includes buildings and inventory. You will quickly fill your inventory and quit the game like I did on my third play-through. I regret thinking it might get better and not getting a refund...
UPDATED 9/28/17 - Decided to give the game another try...figured with all the updates there might be something interesting. I also increased the item/person cap to 50 hearthlings, wanted to see how many my computer could handle since this is such a hungry game. I finally got through the entire "Quest for Township" and managed to build a decent town, and for a while I was thinking "Wow, I might really need to change my review to a positive one."
But! And it's a big one...there's literally nothing after you construct the (3) gongs other than getting your♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ed repeatedly. I survived through all the trials, with a population of 27 hearthlings. 15 of them were dedicated to round-the-clock security, because after you defeat the Tribe Masters that come to challenge you (or whatever they are called) the♥♥♥♥♥rape just DOES NOT STOP. I was clicking R *RUN TO SAFETY* every 5 seconds. Seriously. It got to the point that my hearthlings couldn't even farm...plants were dying in the fields because I had to call them to safety points so often. Things on the map could no longer be gathered or created because if my hearthlings went two feet from the troop of guards, BAM, here come the goblins + kobolds + ogres to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥up. Also couldn't change their job or turn off the "job" cue to just make them haul, because then...BAM! Goblins come. So there was loot just littered around the map that was essentially untouchable for my hearthlings. When the guards cue for job was paused...they don't defend. Everyone dies, nothing gets hauled. Yay! Multiple invader groups would often show up at once as well, with mutliple Ogres in each troop along with archers and clerics and some swordsmen. Because of these large scale invades happening all at once I ran into another massive problem...
Broken doors. Ogres can smash through them, and that's about all they do. I had one structure in particular...just finished, four doors. Almost instantly, three Ogres show up to smash all four doors (instead of fighting the troop that is right next to them. Makes sense, right?) This doesn't seem like a huge problem...until you realize they don't get replaced. Ever. Never ever. Not unless you remove the whole building. This is such a huge flaw for me, that lead to me entirely abandoning the town...I cannot deal with a thousand doors around the colony with tiny little hearts next to them - or worse, entire buildings with shadow blueprints for doors that will never be replaced...On top of this, I was being invaded so often (I timed it, about every minute n 25 seconds) that I had no hope of completely removing and rebuilding the structures without everyone dying in the process. It was  a nightmare late-game to say the least.
The 20 hearthling slow-down is still very much so a thing. Unless you have some series power and ram, don't expect to get over 20 hearthlings. I have 16gb ram with an I7 6700K 4.00GHZ processor, and the game ate it up and spit it out like it was a joke once I hit my 27 hearthling mark (but it was already well slowing by the 20th hearthling). I also noticed the prereqs for getting more hearthlings becomes obscene in the way of foods. I can handle accumlating large wealth, that's easy and it makes sense. But large masses of foods makes less sense to me...yea I should have enough to feed all of them but, why do I need 2500 stacks of foods along with 13,000 wealth for a single new colonist? Seems a little...impossible when half your food goes bad in the pile before your three cooks can even touch it because you're being invaded again (and the cycle continues...).
I would say I enjoy the building aspect of the game, which is the main reason I would tell anyone to try it out at all. It's very rewarding to see some of the structures come to life and to really get a feel for how you want your town laid out. However, this is also flawed in that you can't delete walls after they are placed (sometimes.) I don't understand why it happens, but during building planning the walls won't undo or erase...just super frustrating when you are halfway through a building and you misplace a wall.
Overall, I would say the game in it's current start is a solid...5/10? Worth buying/playing but only if you REALLY like building things with super limited items and being able to see how happy/sad your colonists are.
(Honestly, I would just go with Rimworld. It's not 3D, no, but it's so much more playable at the moment.)

The single player experience is a little short, clocking in at around 6 hours for me. However, everything else about this game is thoroughly enjoyable. I play games on GNU/Linux exclusively and the performance for this game on my OS is great. The art direction is top notch, as in the last two games. Everything about this entry feels like a worthy addition to the Trine franchise.
There are some things different in this game, most notably the lack of skill progression. I know former Trine fans might really miss that, but honestly I felt rather ambivalent about it myself. I mean... does it really make much sense anymore anyways? For me, I love Trine for its light-hearted storybook-style fairy tale setting and story. It actually kind of bugged me that if you played the first Trine you started off in Trine 2 without some of the skills you gained in the first one, and some don't even exist in Trine 2 that existed in the first Trine. Likewise when people complain that Amadeus can no longer conjure more than 1 box at a time in Trine 3, I have only to remind everyone about the lack of floating platforms in Trine 2, other player abilities, equipment in chests, etc. So, it's not without precedent.
I actually think it's good to see Frozenbyte trying to stretch out and experiment. Accordingly, having the freedom to move along the Z axis in 3D is a great addition. At first I was skeptical and thought it might be too confusing or change up the core gameplay mechanic. But, how it's implemented is done really well. It's different enough to be interesting, but subtle enough to keep things familiar and intuitive.
Really, the biggest thing for me (as I mentioned earlier) is the story, and Trine 3 presents something very intriguing that recontextualizes the two prior entries in the franchise. I don't want to give any spoilers away, but suffice it to say the game goes back to its roots and sets out to answer a question I hadn't really thought to ask before: what is the Trine in the first place? What is *its* origin?
It's not just this new revelation either. The game also goes back to its roots in bringing back skeletons and other darker elements seen in the first Trine. I actually played Trine 2 first, so going back to the first Trine felt a bit disjointed at first, since the story seemed more epic and a little darker. Trine 3 manages to keep the light-hearted fun tone of Trine 2 while telling a story more on par with the first Trine.
Sadly, it looks like the devs were shooting for a story scope that would fit the epic premise of Trine 3. I say sadly, because the game ends rather abruptly on a cliffhanger. Maybe in the future with a DLC or two the story presented can be properly finished. I know some players could look at this as some kind of money grab, since in the past with Trine 2 its DLC expansion was truly an expansion, with the original story relatively standing alone.
But, y'know, even there there's precedent. Plenty of films have ended on cliffhangers, and $8 for a 2 hour film at the theatre is still more expensive than $22 for a 6 hour game--especially when said game also includes multiplayer.  (Disclaimer: I actually only purchased the game while it was on sale here recently, but mainly that's because I was waiting to get the game once the Linux version exited Beta).
All in all, I would definitely recommend getting this game if you like the Trine series. It's definitely different than the prior entries, but if you go into it with an open mind you might just be pleasantly surprised.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Asteroid Bounty Hunter is a two-dimensional side-scrolling shoot-em-up (shmup) rendered in 3D, with great music, pretty graphics, ship upgrades, a cliché story played out in weirdly drawn and partly animated comic-style cutscenes, and lots and lots of asteroids.
Graphics - The graphics are a bit mixed. The 3D asteroids come in an assortment of textures, colours, shapes, and sizes, and are rendered well, although some of them seem a bit too realistic for the rest of the game. The backgrounds are for the most part very pretty and different enough so as to not get boring. The player ships are a bit unimpressive and samey -- the typical enemy ships even more so -- but the weapons are mostly nice and bright and colourful, giving you a pretty satisfying feeling of power and destruction. Boss enemies are unique. I've only seen two of them so far and they're also a bit uninspiring, although their weapon effects are mostly pretty good.
I haven't experienced any slowdown on my aging gaming laptop (I7, Nvidia 485m graphics) playing at 1920x1080 and with all of the (fairly limited) bell-and-whistle selections enabled, even when there are enough missiles, lazers, swirly flamey things, and exploding asteroids to all but cover the screen. Overall the game looks pretty good, and moves smoothly.
Sound - Music is terrific: absolutely excellent. I haven't looked into where it came from, but the game comes with a selection of electronic music tracks in a number of genres, and I've liked every one that I've heard. If it's not to your taste, though, don't worry: just add some .ogg files to the relevant folder and you can listen to your own music instead. Sound effects are okay -- what you'd expect for the game -- and voiceovers are very variable, but a welcome inclusion regardless.
Gameplay - The plot is introduced through a very slow cutscene. The style is interesting, like a black-and-white sketched comic with some portions coloured and some small parts animated, but the subtitles are terribly written and full of extremely bad grammar and spelling errors. I also don't know if it's bugged, but there was no sound for me, and screen fades that took many seconds to move between scenes. Anyway, you play the titled bounty hunter, destroying asteroids for money to protect endangered planets. You're also a terrible booze-hound and quickly manage to get other bounty hunters coming after you. The plot is quite thin and you've mostly seen it all before, but it's fun nonetheless, and later cutscenes are much better, with voiceovers that range from really quite good (Karma) to rather awful (Nix). Oh, and the terrible grammar doesn't get any better!
The game itself is divided into 25 stages, each of which can be played at one of three difficulty levels, although there seems to be no way to track which ones you've completed at which difficulty levels (and there's also only one achievement based on difficulty, so there's not that much reason to replay them).
The first four stages of each group of five are all the same: progressively more difficult waves of randomised asteroids that you need to try to destroy, interspersed with short waves of enemy ships that move to set patterns. On each stage you need to destroy an increasing number of asteroids without losing all of your ship's health and exploding. Destroying some asteroids breaks them into smaller ones, and often causes massive speed-up and ricocheting of these smaller asteroids, presumably through some simulated conservation of momentum. From stage four and beyond you have four weapons available to you at any time, each with a varying cooldown timer. Each level thus requires some strategic thinking to work out when best to fire each weapon.
The fifth stage in each group of five is a boss fight, which I believe is against a different bounty hunter out for your blood each time. I've only completed the first ten levels so far (after playing for more than two hours), so there's a fair bit of time required to get through the whole game. I'd guess that you'd gain most of the included achievements, if not all, through a single play through.
Completing a stage awards points to upgrade your ship's weapons and shields, as well as different points to upgrade your ship itself. There are five ships to choose from, but they're really all much the same, with each new ship simply having bonuses to various attributes. Still, together with the sort-of interesting cutscenes and the achievements, this gives you something to keep playing for if the goal of shmup frenzy fun itself isn't enough for you.
I've only played with keyboard, although it's a bit annoying having to navigate menus with the mouse. The game apparently 'partially supports' controllers, too. A controller would probably be a better option.
Pros:
+ Addictive and fun
+ Excellent included music with an option to play your own instead (including simple 'radio' controls to change the track that's currently playing in game)
+ Pretty graphics
+ Weird cutscene style that grows on you
+ A good number of achievements and ship upgrades to keep you playing
+ Runs well with a lot of action on screen like a good shmup should
+ The four weapons with different cooldowns works quite well as a strategic consideration, making it more than just bullet hell
+ Trading cards
Cons:
- Cliché story with very poor writing. It could have at least been run through a spell checker!
- Upgrades and new ships are just stronger versions of the starting ones; at level four you've seen everything your ship will be able to do -- it'll just get better at those things as you upgrade it
- No visual representation of weapon powerups
- A bit repetitive, but not too bad for a shmup
Asteroid Bounty Hunter is addictive and quite fun. It has its bad points, but in my opinion the good points far outweigh them. There's currently an announcement on the Steam game page regarding co-op play and further graphics improvements coming soon, which will make it even better! If you're into side scrolling shmups then I'd recommend you give it a try.

The premise of the game is excellent, and with additional work on graphics, a better tutorial, contract management it could be a great game. The UI is poor, some of the text boxes have a black background so you can read them, and the rest have transparent backgrounds making them almost impossible to read at some of the space stations - especially if another ship happens to be docked in that view area.
You can get as many contracts as you want, but some mysteriously disappear in transit. I have been using a spreadsheet that has the various resources and specials listed in the rows and the stations listed for the columns. Each can show 9 contracts, who supplies what, and shows passengers and packages. At every station that I dock at, I go through the scrolling window and verify which contracts were fullfilled or just disappeared so I know exactly how much I need to get and deliver. For instance I know Elysium is the supplier of Titanium, and on my spreadsheet I see that I have a contract to deliver 56 units to Orion, three contracts with Mica (52, 44, and 34 units) and 34 units to Solaris. I have color coded the space stations so I know which warplines they are on. So I know I have to jump to Mica first, in order to continue down that warpline to Solaris.
I have been able to upgrade ships quickly, so I am in a class 5 now and almost ready to buy a class 6. Unfortunately, I am not able to hire a pilot to run the old ships even though in the manage ship section there are text buttons for pilot and crew. You can sell your old ships on the galactic market, but you can not get back to your listed ship to change price or take it off the market. I have never received a notification of a listed ship being sold so there could be my class 1, 2, 3, and 4 ships still up for sale.
A recent update gave us the option of turning off the white screen that shows during a warp. Unfortunately, we do not have any control over the rest of the psychedelic warp screens which show for way too long. There are no controls to set up a transit route or a trade route. If I had 58 iron, 42 grain, and 60 fruit in the hold and I am going from Andromeda to Plato to deliver the iron contract, then to Archon for the grain delivery, and finally to Solaris to deliver the fruit I have to manually select each warp gate and each station. So it would 12 warp segments to accomplish those deliveries. Each individual segment has to be done separately after sitting through another long viewing of the same psychedelic warp scene. Even cheap GPS units today allow you to do a trip plan with intermediate stops. Surely a civilization that has the technology to build warp gates and space stations could concieve of a better trip planner.
At some warp gates a fuzzy red blob will come flying at you then execute a 90 degree turn and fly off into the heavens. Since the ship or shields have never been damaged, I have to assume that it is not someone attacking me.
I have bought blueprints for each of the bays in the private space station and for a farm on the surface of Ceres. Building will not commence though until you deliver all of the raw materials needed for each section. I have tried to deliver the farm robots and some material to the surface, but could not offload anything. I ended up stuffing everything in the hanger with the hope that it will become clearer with more gameplay on how to actually initiate building and delivering of goods.
It is in early release and the developers are steadily working on the bugs and player feedback so I am hopeful that the UI, trip planning, building, and overall look and feel will steadily improve. Right now it is just rote grinding, upgrading ships, and slowly assembling the parts to have a private space station and surface farm.

Ascent - The Space Game Review
First of all, this game is not suited for every single age group. If you were born in the 80's or 90's, they you should probably like it due to the nostalgia level graphics of a AAA game made in that time period. Also, for fans of outer space, space ships, mining ,farming, ect, then this game is going to be a great idea to buy during a sale.
You can: farm, sell items, buy items, mine, get destoryed by Enemies, get more ships, upgrade your ship/s in many ways, destroy enemies, explore 270,000,000,000 (270 billion) star systems worth of:  exploration, colonization, starbase construction, research and technology, mining and farming, trading and combat.  Also, outside the first sector, everything in game is made by real players. There's some spects of 'City simulation' involved, but I didn't discover completely yet. The game is so much cheaper than EVE or Elite: Dangerous, while it also having some fast developement speed, awesome and trutworthy community plus many of hundreds of hours making the game play for you, make it what you want! If you want a City simulator, then so be it. Like mining? Do that then.
Oh boy, where to start. The tutorial is a bit floaty and hard, especially the part  where you need to fight a weak drone. You spend ages just aiming at it since the ship is so light and moves so fast while also sliding too far. Then, once it is in sight, you can spend ages shooting at it, after quite literally 30-90 minutes, you have finished the drone part, which is where I quit the tutorial and went onto the game itself. After the tutorial is done, spend a lot of time finding the icon for the Autopliot (which is transparent until you hover above it), and then spending around 10 minsutes doing the firs fex missions. Then the real fun part is trying to find out what to do on your own. Farming? No, can't conolize a planet yet. Destroy ships? Nah, can't find any. Destroy Asteroid and meteorites? Yes, then sell it all for cash. After the first 60 mins of gaming, you should have around 10K cash, which you can do quite a lot with.
The graphics might not look like much, but they are still quite pretty, also, it keeps the loading times less than 5 seconds! So that right there is a giant point to the finalized score. Anyway, moving on. The graphics are what you would expect from an Early Access game midway-nearly finished developement. Anyway, these are still some pretty graphics and are satisfactory for my needs and, hopefully, the majourity of the audience can agree with me on this topic.
This is where beauty truly met the eye. As I already said in the overview and gameplay topics, this game has some of the .ost in-depth systems ever to be in a video game. So think of EVE + Elite Dangerous, a game based around space and becoming a high rank withing the community by upgrading ships, colonizing your soon-to-be empire and so, so much more to come. The developers are awesome, they listen to feedback, do Kickstarters to help out with lots of different subjects (one of the most recent one was for the games graphic improvements), but, in my opinion, the HuD is very ugly. the Chat has its own HuD, most things do, but it's a try-hard at doing a futuristic orange 6th grade art project

Well it's exactly as advertised. An HD remake of the first encounter. Unless your computer can't handle it it's the best version of Serious Sam. There's nothing new here, but nothing has been removed either. It's literally the same game as the classic TFE but looks AMAZING. If you don't already have the games the Hd versions are the ones to get (unless like I said your pc can't handle it). If you already own the games there wouldn't be a point in getting these unless you want better visuals(I have all versions of the games on steam because I love them).
If you've never played the games before it's basically an FPS where you fight massive groups of enemies in large, open, arenas, shooting, strafing, and jumping like a cracked-out spidermonkey with an unquenchable thirst for mass murder and an warrant for death. You will hear people compare it to quake/ DOOM and while it is closer to that side of the spectrum it doesn't really play like them at all. The ID games were designed more like mazes, while SS has more straightforward level design and is focused solely on combat. Not to say that SS has poor level design (it's quite good!) it's just a different style.
The only real issue I could see anyone having with the game is the fact that the entire encounter takes place in Eygpt, but they do a really good job of incorporating variety into the levels, and sure the setting of the game stays the same, all the levels feel different. They are all really well designed and interesting/fun to go through. Some people might also whine about plot development, but I'm pretty sure if your'e playing a game for a narrative you are looking at the wrong form of entertainment. Go read a book. Punk...

SpaceChem Review - Raymond KT
Summary: Zachtronics Industries is back with an ambitious new design-based puzzle game. Take on the role of a Reactor Engineer working for SpaceChem, the leading chemical synthesizer for frontier colonies. Construct elaborate factories to transform raw materials into valuable chemical products! Streamline your designs to meet production quotas and survive encounters with the sinister threats that plague SpaceChem.
Before we start this review, the first thing you need to do, right now, is ditch any preconceptions you’ve made off the back of SpaceChem’s chemistry-related imagery, or the fact that the screenshots look, at worst, like educational software. I can guarantee that you will learn almost nothing of any value, scientific or otherwise, playing this game. Your leisure hours are safe. If I have any chemists reading this, I can also guarantee that you’ll suck at SpaceChem as much as the rest of us. Sorry, chemists.
In SpaceChem you play a new employee of a profoundly sinister interstellar chemical company (called SpaceChem), with the story of your career being told throughout the game through well-written text vignettes. The actual game of SpaceChem is, quite simply, building circuits. Using an intuitive and satisfying interface, you whip up tracks for chemicals to travel down with the objective of carrying an entirely different chemical to the level’s ultimate destination.
If you like those kind of games, it's probably the best of the last 25 years. It's a game of extremes, the graphics are simply annoying, but it can keep you playing one level for a whole day.

Pixel perfect dungeon explorer trash with interesting but flawed, annoying design.
You basically command a team of up to four characters that unlock a room after another in a random dungeon of 13 levels, when they have enough 'gold' to power any room.
The idea is that you unlock rooms and decide what to build inside them, between resources, science, food or defenses, to increase your chances of survival. Point is, the 'gold' to unlock the rooms is a random drop by itself, and non powered rooms spawn monsters. This is equally randomly possible in level 1 and in level 13 without the least ability to influence it. Just because of this, this game should never have existed as it's the typical worthless piece of garbage that sells artificial difficulty for skill.
Sadly though, as is typical in these half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥piece of **** pixel games, difficulty is entirely artificial: you can literally waste 2 hours on a perfect run to the last level, and get literally defeated by an entirely casual room that disables all your facilities in a random number of already visited rooms.
Of all the annoying rubbish that the game throws at you, this is so frequent that it -will- be dealt to you in any playthrough in one level or the other, even multiple times in a playthrough.
Difficulty is so stupidly and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly badly calibrated, that you'll easily lose in "very easy" difficulty, especially later in the game, just because the game decides that out of 13 rooms, only two of them drop any dust.
To be honest, it quite looks like the game is -designed- to **** you over for a certain number of hours to boost its replayability. For this very reason, anybody with a sound mind should steer away from this randomly generated vomit.

It's a nice distraction. Gunplay is clunky, upgrade system is kinda samey and there's not much variety, and it's a bit arcadey in that as your weapons get more powerful, so do zombies. On the other hand, it's just easy enough to suck you in with the "just one more upgrade" routine that keeps you occupied until you reach max level. Boss fights are _really_ disappointing, but the rest of it is pretty fun.
The biggest issue i have with the game is that it is kind of repetitive. So you start the game, you have a crap gun, and you shoot a zombie in the head, and he dies. You'd think that by reaching level 20, you'd be mowing down hordes of zombies with your powerful weapons, or at least would be fighting more powerful zombies more often, but no - you're still able to kill about the same amount of same zombies you could kill on level 1. It's not like Serious Sam, where you simply get more powerful weapons to mow down more powerful enemies - the enemies are the same, they look the same, they do the same stuff, and they take about the same amount of damage from your guns, as long as you're keeping your gun up to date.
It also has a "failed Doom/Quake clone" vibe to it in that the levels kinda feel like they're designed for futuristic Doom-esque deathmatch, and there's plenty of multiplayer modes and some of the game modes (e.g. Biohazard) are basically implemented as "multiplayer with bots". It's clear that the developers aspired for this game to be a fun multiplayer zombie shooter, but since gunplay is really clunky and frustrating at times, i don't think it would succeed in that capacity. Never tried, tho.
All in all, it's not the best game in the world, but it's decent fun.

Overall it seems very clear why Get Off My Lawn is free and even with that price tag I'd like my time back.

Quite a lot of fun once you figure out a few of the quirks of the game, namely:
1) Controls: I've been using a Xbox 360 controller and could not get used to the thumb stick for driving.  Basically your car moves in the direction of the stick; left and right are not relative to how your car is pointing.  Thankfully the digital pad works in a more traditional manner and once I realized this it was a total joy to play.
2) Physics: You have to play the tracks a bit to get the hang of where the walls are and where you can shortcut.  Your car rotates on it's center (not the front) meaning you can turn on a dime and spin out if you aren't a bit gentle with the controls during turns.  The physics are also wonky when your in midair and turn your tires prematurely before you land; instant wipeout.
3) Tracks: So EVERY racing game reuses tracks, makes it a differnt type of day, reverses the driving direction; no big deal.  However, this game added the challenge of also changing the orientation of the camera on repeat use of a track.  This actually makes it super challenging to revisit a track as your brain says "this turn is here" but on screen the turn is actually THIS OTHER WAY since the camera is now in a different position.
Other things of note:
1) Graphics: Very pretty.  I love the feel of the game and how smooth it flows on the screen.
2) Sound/Music: Very enjoyable.
3) Difficulty: Starts off easy enough; you learn when to use your 'nitro' to boost away from the pack of crazy cars and they become a non-issue.  By the 20th or so track however, the AI is competant and WILL whoop your butt.  Car upgrades are a must!
Overall I've enjoyed it quite a bit and plan on treking to the end of the game.

Got the game during the Warner Bros Bundle. At that time i wasn't into MOBAs so i gave it a pass.
Now that i got fully acquainted with MOBAs, i decided to try it out. After all, this game was created by Monolith, the creators of No One Lives Forever, Blood and FEAR, and was the first MOBA (and the last) to hit consoles.
You have a selection of 36 heroes, in a 5v5 mode with either a solo or trilane map. One thing i would like to clear out that all the heroes are actually purchasable with ingame cash (5000 gold). The DLCs give you instant access to those heroes, along with unique skins and extra gold. To be honest, i could bear with it, since you can earn gold by just playing.
When you first start the game, one thing you realize - there is no shop. Yes, last hitting doesn't matter. There are no items for you to buy. Instead they have this "belt" system. You create a belt out of 7 gems. The max level cap is 14, and every 2 levels one of your gems will activate. That's pretty much how you add stats to your heroes. Lifesteal, extra damage, crits, extra health etc ...
That's the ugly part of the game. 5k for a hero i can understand. but the gems cost gold too, and their prices range from 200-5000. We are speaking about items that can make a hard carry out of you. That's unacceptable.
Additionally, your belt has 4 slots for potions, which cost gold too.
Finally, you have 4 slots for commands (which are all free). They are basically extra abilities, and you can choose 4 out of 16, but using 1 will put all of them on cooldown.
There is no mana. Yes, abilities can pretty much be spammed, since the cooldown isn't very lengthy either.
All heroes have a "free teleport scroll". Yes, they can teleport to the base. The ability has no cooldown. It cancels if you get attacked though, but still, there isn't even a cooldown.
To be honest, going back to base isn't even required because each lane has healing item pick ups somewhere on the side (they look like tangos to be honest), and they heal pretty damn fast.
You can upgrade towers and barracks. When you reach lvl 6, 9 and 12, you get to choose from 4 different types of barracks that will spawn different units, and 4 different towers. The building can only have 1 upgrade, so if another upgrade is applied the first one is removed.
Shrines - there are 4 points on the map, that when controlled give your team extra health regeneration and damage resistance.
Defeating neutrals in the forest gives you buffs, some of which last 2 mins (kind of like runes in dota).
Also, i noticed that the skin of the map changes. During my first match it looked like Osgiliath and during the second, it was Hobbiton. It practically wields no difference, but it's a nice thing to have.
Other than the normal 5v5 mode, there is also a Survival mode aka Horde Mode, which is pretty good. It allows up to 5 players.
Even if you were to look down on all those problems - there is one major problem.
To earn gold, you must play matches, but how would you do it if Steam db says that only 3 people are currently playing the game (one of them might have been me).
You do get gold for bot matches, but it's so small (i got about 500 per match).
The game costs money, and it has heavy elements of pay 2 win.
Overall, it's a poor use of the license. It's very softcore and lacks a lot of elements that make a MOBA.
But hey, at least you can play it with a controller!!!
No kidding, the game is pretty good with a controller. No as good as a mouse, but overall they managed it.

If you're a D&D player, I don't see how you could dislike that game.
If you're not a D&D player, like me, you'll have to spend a lot of time reading the manual or looking up online how the game works and how to build your character (turns out putting points in two handed swords sucks if you're planning on dual classing Fighter/Cleric). I've serioulsy disliked the 10 first hours because I had no idea what THAC0 and Armor Class meant, how valuable were Arrows +1 compared to Arrows, how a lot of spells worked, and I basically hit a wall at the end of Chapter 2 after starting the game without any advice (turns out I was very underpowered for this stage of the game). I had to do a lot of research and start a new game in order to finally enjoy the game. If you're not ready to spend time learning the rules or if you despise RNG based games, don't bother.
Overall I liked the game and the main story, you definitely fell more powerful as time goes on, and there's a lot of possibilities to explore. Some items really change the way you're playing the game (looking at you, Boots of Speed), and even though the game lacks in character depth, the world felt more lively than some more recent RPGs like Skyrim for example. I'm definitely going to try BG2.
Still, even though I enjoyed it, it still had a lot of issues and hasn't aged very well. Pathfiding is pretty bad, having to move your character every 4 or 5 seconds because you can't set a destination in the fog of war is very annoying. 80% of the sidequests are absurd ("Someone stole my belt/ring/wine/boots, go get them and bring them to me"), bringing neither satisfaction nor good rewards (but you still "have to" complete them to get the exp). Fighting every time you can is way more rewarding than trying to find more interesting possibilities. And the worst of all has to be the traps and the "finding trap" system. I get why they would place traps in a dungeon but walking and stopping every 2 seconds with your thief in order to find them, only to get hit by an arrow because you had to put him/her in front of your tanks, is NOT fun (let's not talk about the fact that you activate the traps but the ennemies don't, so if they are standing on one of them and you go in melee range, you're ***). Savescumming and resting when you're not supposed to are the rules, but it is often the case in RPGs so it shouldn't bother you if you're into the genre. Also, no range and AOE indicators so prepare to hurt yourself a lot with fireballs and such.

This game was single-handedly the most emotional experience I have ever had in my enitre gaming history. More so than Journey, Undertale, or any others. It roped me in within minutes, and kept me going for hours.
It is a game that makes everything within it feel... Real. Genuine. The connection I had to the main character felt intricate and intimate, and just... real. I didn't want to quit the game. And in fact, I never once did. Not only was the game so charming and emotional that I felt I could not put it down... It had a very substantial sense of dread to it all that made me scared to put it down.
From the very start, it broke rules that should not be broken. The game reached out in ways I did not think possible of a game made within such a simple engine. (RPGMaker may be surprisingly powerful, but this blew me out of the water.)
Because of this... Just as with the positive emotions, there were very heavy and very REAL negative emotions that wracked my heart from start to finish. That innate and unnerving sense of dread is a fear that no other game has instilled in me. And yet I want more.
Be careful playing this game. There are consequences where you think there may be none. Emotions coming from unexpected places. And the constant threat of only having one shot... This terrifying and heartwarming experience is one that nobody should pass up.

OneShot is a weird and lovely game. If you've got 4 hours to burn, I'd really recommend it. It's adorable, funny, kind of dark and sometimes downright chilling, with plenty of surprises and great characters in store. The music and art are fantasticly charming, and it feels like a lot of love went into this game and it's humor and delivery. If you know absolutely nothing about it, it makes this game ten times better.
Honestly, you should really play OneShot. If you have the money and are even slighty interested, buy it. Play it. You won't regret it.
It has a few flaws, sure. It's puzzles are sometimes obtuse, and the lack of direction can be really frustrating at times. The menu and item system takes a little while to get used to, and there's only one bed per level, which is how to safe quit the game. And digging through some of the more- involved puzzles, if you will- can sometimes be a little bizzare.
But this game is charming and lovely.

The original OneShot back in 2014 was, and still is, one of my favorite indie titles of all time. In a pre-Undertale world a game that works with a meta-narrative was not a brand new concept, but my experience with the freeware title was after that other game’s release. Even with experience of fourth-wall breaking mechanics and a game that had knowledge of you as a player, the original OneShot still stuck with me long after finishing it and inspired me in its tone and characters in a way that most games are unable. The game also had permanent choices that left me nervous every time the game was launched, but it was well worth its short playtime. After hearing about the Steam release, all I hoped for was a few touch-ups in areas and a few more places to explore.
This enhanced version of OneShot goes far beyond the scope of the original, expanding areas that in the original were tiny yet sweet, and is chock full of interesting characters and narrative that wasn’t present in the free version. The way the game works with your computer to solve different puzzles inside and outside the game environment was clever and interesting, relying on your knowledge of your computer in order to solve various puzzles.  The updated art and sprite work is fantastic as well as the updated soundtrack that was filled with old and new songs alike. The main character, Niko, is as adorable as ever, and the journey you and them take still feels harrowing and charming as you traverse the dying world.
When I played the original I couldn’t ask for much more out of it, but the amount that has been added shows real care from the developers and is well worth your time. Even if you haven’t played the original, you should definitely give it a shot.
…Remember, you only have one.

//EXTREMELY MINOR SPOILERS BELOW, LEARNED IN THE FIRST FIVE MINUTES//
I have never played a game like this before.
When you play a good game, you often feel as if your screen is a window to another world, where the events of the game actually take place. In OneShot, this happens LITERALLY. The character you play is from another world, yes, but neither your world OR the game world. You guide him through the world as an observer from beyond, a guardian spirit helping him to save the world.
Because elements from that world communicate with you in YOUR world. Files on YOUR computer give you the knowledge you need to guide this child. The immersion that this creates, along with several other mechanics, is absolutely staggering.
OneShot is both a game and an experience because of this. One of the most poignant memories I have is running through the first area of the game and suddenly releasing the "run" key because I was worried the character would get exhausted. THAT is how immersed I was in this game. THAT is how much you begin to care for the protagonist.
And the ending... the last twist of the game is one that you WILL see coming a mile away, but it is still one that you will sit at for a long, long while. I have never in my life wanted more to just reach into a game and hug the main character.
I don't care that this is an RPG-Maker game. I don't care that there is no combat or epic fight scenes or any of that. I don't even care that this game is a remake. As far as I'm concerned, this game is a modern-day Alice in Wonderland.
OneShot is an experience that will linger with me for a long time. And I'm happy that it will.
TL;DR
Buy this game and hop on the feels train, we're going for a wonderful ride.

Ascent is a fantastic concept, a PvE version of EVE Online without the real time skill training. It is still early access, but it is my opinion that the direction of the game is going in such a way that a negative review was needed as a warning for future purchasers. If there was a "neutral" button for the review I would have used it.
User Interface
The game’s user interface is horrid.  You will notice it the minute you hit the startup screen.  Instead of a login and character selection screen it has a button series that looks like a single player game, up to and including a “LOAD” button.  Fitting ship modules is a complex and clucky text selector box maneuver.
Community
The community is friendly, and will answer basic questions in game chat. There is only one “global” game chat, and no in-game guilds or other such mmo “norms”.
Graphics
The game uses stock Unity graphics for the most part. The ships and starbases may have been a unity resource pack purchase. The game had a kickstarter specifically to add ship graphics, but everything else is very simplistic.  Planets are little more than a multicolored globe and your character avatar is a guy in a tee shirt and jeans. Still early access.
Player Cooperation
The game might as well be single player. Your “cooperation” with other players will be limited to buying stuff from them off a market board.  Even such grand ventures such as building a new jump gate basically boils down to hauling loads of minerals.  There is no “grouping” for combat, no sharing ownership or access to buildings, no real reason for other players to be in the game aside from a chat based social and game-economy aspect.
Ship Design
Each ship “class” is just a different skin.  The only technical difference between the base ship “skins”  is that each class increase basically doubles the cargo space. There is a marginal difference in turning, but basically the only real game mechanic-based difference in the ships would be cargo space.  A higher level ship can equip higher level modules, such as a better mining laser.
Grindy and Repetative
Ascent is extremely grindy. You will buy and sell resources via NPC contracts, or buy and sell resources for other players, or mine.  Your ships cargo is the only limiter, when you purchase a new ship you gain more cargo space, thus the grind starts anew for the next ship.  You will also need to grind to purchase blueprints, planet plot deeds, and a hyperdrive.
Exploration
This seems like a fun concept, and the developer brags about 300 billion star systems; however, you need cargo space to carry fuel for the hyperjump so you will need to grind a lot of money to purchase a decent sized ship and hyperdrive (ships on the NPC market do not come with them).  The ship’s hyperdrive allows you to explore and discover new star systems; however, they get more expensive the larger your ship is (almost always being the same price as the ship itself).
For a game that brags about exploration, they sure do make it hard.
Also, you get a star system named after you just for being the first person to jump to it. No real planet exploration is required.  Basically, you are getting credit for a "discovery" that was already made by some guy with a telescope years before.
Pay To Win
You can skip the grind and buy a bowhead, one of the largest ships in the game.
Complex
The game has a steep learning curve. I did not mind this too much, but it is worth mentioning.  You will be doing a lot of wiki research and youtube video watching.

As many people say, yes, the game is short. However, it is a great game. Yes, you can see they miscalculated the cost/complexity of going full 3D and this cost them to have to release a game that's much shorter than they envisioned. Remember this isn't Ubisoft, EA or Activision with infinite pockets and market researchers crunching numbers. Frozenbyte is a very small studio consisting of a bunch of dedicated gamers/designers.
That said, would you rather them give us a short piece of fun, learn from the experience and make a better Trine 4; or go broke and never again see another Trine? With the recent %50 discount (when I bought it) this game is now priced right, as it definitely feels like half the game it should have been.
Buy it and play it, specially now that's $11. It's fun, it's absolutely GORGEOUS - production values were seriously increased in this third game. I say buy it because for nearly ten bucks, the half game we got is certainly worth it. Another reason is that I want Frozenbyte to get money out of this, because they surely learned their lesson and will apply this knowledge to Trine 4.
I want Trine to keep happening. Frozenbyte got too ambitious and messed up a few things this time around, don't be a vengeful person and boycott them. They're a tiny studio made of people who put so much of their life and money into this. Some cite their 5 million budget as a reason why they *should* have been able to make the full game. Those people have no idea how much making a game costs, 5 million is nothing. Games cost easily triple and quadruple that price to make.
Enjoy the short experience and support this studio. They'll only be better in the future.

MISSING is exactly what it wants to be, an interactive thriller that takes about as long as the episode of a tv show. The only thing it lacks is the plot a tv show would go through in all of that time. Sure, it does have a story that can easily be followed, but I found it a bit lacking (especially since the protagonist doesn't say a whole lot of words) and would have preferred to see it all in go.
The gameplay is totally fine, however. It's seamlessly integrated into the live action experience and none of the puzzles should be too hard. The crossword puzzle was unnecessarily complex, though. Could have been a lot smaller while achieving the same result. The Quick Time Events were really easy, though.
Therefore, I'd tentatively recommend the game. Seeing the entire story from start to finish would be more satisfying, however.

I used to love playing FMV games back in the day. So it was very exciting to see a new game utilizing full motion video. It's very well done in terms of professionalism but the episode itself was incredibly short. The puzzles were all very easy to solve as well, not requiring much thought at all. The only reason to replay it would be to get some achievements you may have missed the first time. Hopefully the episodes after this one will be a bit longer and more immersive. I also hope the "hidden object" and puzzle aspect of the gameplay will become more challenging as well. This episode felt more like a demo, showing you the potential of what it can do. The QTE's seemed very similar to Until Dawn, and the way they were presented sort of took away from the action in some scenes. Nothing major.
I guess another thought would be...why is it done in FMV, anyway? It's a seemingly realistic game about realistic things. It could have been presented just as well in another way. But that's probably just me, because when I think of FMV, I think of games like Harvester and Phantasmagoria; games that were so fantastical that the added "realism" of FMV just made them all the more creepy and enjoyable. This game, on the other hand, just sort of feels like I am playing an episode of CSI or something. Again, this could all change over the course of the next episode(s).
