Lovely Planet is a FPS platformer in a surreal and cute world. However do not let the cuteness fool you, this game is brutally hard.
The graphics remind me of the Nintendo 64 games with crude 3D shapes mixed with occasional simple 2D textures to give character. I know this is a bit far-fetched, but I find it cute in Lovely Planet.
The gameplay is swift and responsive, the only weird part being sliding off some ledges that look like it would be possible to land on them. Framerate is perfect and the game runs well. However the FOV cannot be changed.
The idea is to get across a short level while jumping on platforms and shooting baddies. Simple enough, so there are leaderboards to compete, and stars given according to accuracy and speed. At first I kept trying to go faster and faster without understanding why my impressive runs didn't get rewarded by the game, until I learned that the third star was only given for 100% accuracy. I like a good challenge, so I worked on finishing all levels 100% with three stars.
At the start the levels were pretty straight-forward and it was fun. But then... then the apple fell too far from the tree. Literally, because falling apples is the one game mechanic that ruined the game for me. Any single apple hitting the ground triggers a game over. The early ones are thrown at the player, which is fine. However after a bit the apples are shot in the sky from a different place in the level, and just fall right where they are, whether the player is around or not.
Let me explain better how this is infuriating. You are in a part of the level, merrily shooting and platforming your way. And then, suddenly, you cross an invisible line and hear the dreaded sound of an apple been released. And now, the only thing that you can do is rush forward in the level to reach the part where the apple is located, and start shooting from afar (because the bullets take time to travel), without a target nor a crosshair, where you predict that the apple is going to fall . And then you realize that three apples were triggered, and you need to pre-shoot three different locations with pinpoint pre-accuracy and timing. So, basically, you have no choice but to quickly shoot in several directions and hope for the best, and do it again and again until you are a robot that has complete muscle memory of the right way to deal with this nonsense. And let's not talk about the moment where you have to jump on a jump-pad, and while in the air, shoot where an apple is going to land BEHIND you, then quickly turn back forward and shoot where an apple is falling in FRONT of you. I managed to do it. I did all of this. I had three stars in these levels, so 100% accuracy. But instead of being happy at my achievement, I was thinking "why? why so much time wasted being a robot and not having any fun?". Then I started the 4th world, and noticed that the levels were engulfed in fog. Superman 64 level of fog and fun. With the nerve-wrecking treat that I also had to pre-shoot apples that I couldn't even see, and it was made even more obvious that completing the levels would be a tedious chore of memorizing every single move and shot.
No, thanks, I like a good challenge, but this is just a waste of time, and the cute graphics are hidden in fog anyway, so why bother. Goodbye Lovely Planet, I only recommend you at a very cheap price to fool around in the early levels, otherwise I do not think that you are a good game worth investing my time and sanity to complete.

The Long Dark is a well thought out, well paced and extremely difficult game to master. Take a step back from all the open world survival games that have been thrown at us and this game hones in on just a single aspect of it: the survival part. Everything in this game matters, and it varies based on the difficulty level you set before you begin the game.
To get into specifics would ruin the most enjoyable part of the game for me, which was the discovery aspect of it. There are not very many things we're allowed to craft, and the lootable items are permanent and do not respawn with every playthrough. What that means is the first time you pick up that knife off the ground, it won't come back. Does this also mean that you're going to hold onto that knife once it's at 0% durability or are you going to throw it away hoping another one will come your way soon? But to repair it you need scrap metal, which can be had from harvesting equipment or metal parts found all over the map. But because resources are limited, and knives aren't the only things you can repair that you'll need, you're always in this state of inventory management (much like in real life). You find yourself pausing to think about the decision you're about to make regarding equipping/looting/dropping loot you come across, and it's not as simple as leaving it and coming back for it either because items naturally decay over time. This is very much so with food, and you will always be looking for food in this game. Will you sacrifice the precious calories depend on so you can chop that firewood that will keep you from freezing? Is it worth weighing yourself down with firewood when you have to outrun a pack of wolves?
Dying is a one time affair. You don't respawn. Everything you accumulated in game dies with you. This is why the game transcends other games in the survival genre, because it focuses on only surviving and it does it so well. It matters where you stand, what path you take, what time of the day it is, if the wind is against you when you walk, standing in areas that will block the wind as you take care of something else, positioning yourself so you're not seen by the predatory wildlife, making sure you have enough supplies to make it through the night, etc.
Basically this game simulates what would really happen to us if we were stuck in the Canadian wilderness in winter. There are no zombies, no other players to worry about, just you against mother nature. And mother nature is a ♥♥♥♥♥.

So far i've been playing the episodic sections of the game and my god does this game challenge you! i died within 2 and a half minutes of playing this game on my first go at it but thankfully Episodic sandbox has checkpoints. You won't be so fortunate in standard sandbox, you get one life and that's it!
the long dark isn't stupid, it's also not big into handholding either. anything you think you would do if you were lost in the canadian wilderness is pretty much what you do in this game. Loot abandoned houses, learn how to make fires, camp out in caves if you have to. manage supplies in your backpack. make difficult decisions (will i bring a hatchet so i can get some firewood to keep warm, or will i bring medicine in case i get attacked by wolves?). depending on the way you'd like to play these are examples of choices you gotta make. the Episodic sandbox is very good for practise and has a more casual feel to it than the standard sandbox. It teaches you the ropes of what the game has too offer but doesn't give all the nucks and crannies away. ( it keeps secrets from you!) So far there are 2 episodes, the first being definitely nothing more than a Tutorial and the second one introduces a lot harsher mechanics but also gives you access to more "cool" things.
The episodes like to drip feed you enjoyment, instead of shoving a cake in front of your face really easily like some survival games this one is very good at rewarding progress and you playing with common sense and smarts.
For instance, i go to an abandoned shop for food, i bring a crowbar, just in case, turns out i did need it and i am rewarded with some nice loot inside a few lockers!
or i go out to this new area i've never been to before i make sure to pack my hunting knife and some medicine just in case and i get mauled by a wolf when i get there, but i'm prepared for that!
However it is at the end of the day a "walking simulator". you're very iscolated and for the few humans that you get in contact with in story mode they don't actively contribute anything to you, so for the most part you're on your own.
Overall if you enjoy having your metal really tested i'd recommend this game because is so close to real life but not so much so that it makes the experience dull and unpleasent to experience. i wouldn't recommend it to people who actually lives in the canadian tundra, you might find it too easy.

Let me start off with saying, I LOVE THIS GAME and I highly recommend it! The story is simple, but compelling. So is the premise (You must survive in the Canadian wilderness), even if that is easier said than done! The game is also visually beautiful, with a charming character design, beautiful wild vistas, and breathtaking nighttime scenes.
That being said, there's a few drawbacks, which don't lessen my approval of this game really. But they're still annoying.
1. Your pack. As of so far, I haven't found any way to upgrade your backpack so the amount you can carry is higher. I know it's supposed to be a challenge to utilize what matters most, but it becomes unncessarily burdensome later in the game when you have to carry multiple quest items along with even your most basic but necessary gear. Hell, even when I had bare bones basics in supplies, my pack could still very easily become overburdened and would slow down my movement speed or disable my ability to sprint. It's incredibly tedious. A little too tedious for a video game.
2. Wildlife glitches. I've had several instances where wildlife, as I am hunting them, would get into places I was physically incapable of reaching. For example, I shot a deer and I was following it while it bled out. But the damned thing went up onto a cliff side, glitched, and I was completely incapable of reaching it no matter what I did. Bullets wasted. Meat wasted. Time wasted. Wildlife you are hunting should not be able to reach places you as the player character cannot also reach.
3. You can't jump. This is pretty self-explanatory. Some basic issues with some of the aforementioned unreachable places would be solved if you could simply jump.
4. Hunting and following blood trails. It's very useful to follow animal tracks and blood trails once you've shot and hit your target. But the blood trail is so damned tiny! Itty bitty little droplets of blood that can be very difficult to see even if you are right on top of them. I've mistaken small rocks for blood spatter and it's entirely disrupted my tracking. They also fade in and out of view, graphics-wise, very quickly unless you are right on top of them. And I say this as someone who's graphics are turned up as high as they can go. This also makes hunting frustrating, as I've lost whole kills because I couldn't find the blood trail correctly.
Are these things annoying? Yes. Do I wish they would get fixed? DOUBLE yes. Does that mean I don't recommend this game, however? Hell no. Play this game. It is FUN AS HELL and I cannot put it down! It really is a testament to the concept that you don't need an overly complex story, details, flash or premise to make a good game. Sometimes all you need is that simple motivation to push forward. Because otherwise you will die.

What an incredibly pleasant surprise.
So when I tried the demo, and I loved the gameplay, the gunplay felt fantastic, the game was incredibly gory, and there were zombies in it, which at the time of trying it (earlier in the day) I wanted, for one reason or another, a game with those exact characteristics, and thankfully, this game fullfilled them.
I was just worried about a couple of things:
1.- The upgrade system, How does it work? Does it even work when playing the game offline by yourself?
I didn't play far enough into the demo to know about this, and the internet didn't say much.
Turns out you CAN earn upgrades offline, they're not tied in to any online aspect from what i've seen, nor any commercial one neither, which in this day an age, I applaud practices like this one being implemented in games.
2.- How was the game structured single-player, and multi-player wise?
The game pretty much has two starting missions in which you need to complete some very simple objectives as you obtain a very limited selection of weapons, a gun, and an assault rifle, you interact with objects that usually require you to complete very basic, yet entretaining, and fun, minigames, in order to either progress to the game, or alternatively, gain access into lockers, which can have ammo, or health kits, that you can use by opening your inventory, and clicking on them.
After you complete both missions you unlock something of a "hub area" in which you can talk with two characters in order to upgrade, your character, or buy, upgrade, sell, and "optimize" your weapons.
The characters are incredibly silly, yet not to the point in which they end up being dislikable, if anything they retain a certain amount of personality within its terrible, and banal appereance, or strange 3D modelling, and terrible voice acting.
The character that you play as can also speak, and he, or she, will, for most of the time, a series of cheesy, and nonsensical, but funny conversations, think of Duke Nukem, or Serious Sam.
Even then the game its not really about the story, or about the characters.
In the "hub-area" you can partake in story missions, survival missions, and plenty of others that are endless, and replayable, so the ammount of replayability that the game has, it's frankly, flawless to say the least.
Just a bunch of content, a bunch of weapons, a bunch of upgrades, a really straightfoward, but enjoyable, and replayable campaign, that despite its linearity mantains a very clear sense of progression, thanks to very clear objectives.
Paired with a satisfying, and rewarding, gunplay, that makes everything blow up into a much of blood, and gore.

I bought Dead Effect 2 as part of a bundle of other games. I didn't know much about the game prior to buying it, but had heard the name before and figured it couldn't be too terrible.
Ultimately, the best phrase I can use to describe this game is "mindless". It's a fairly direct port of a mobile game, and it shows in some of its quirks (no jumping, lots of recycled maps, only a few enemy models, ammo refills for a tiny amount of normal currency), but I'm not really broken up about it since I paid hardly anything for it. The game is superficially similar to a Borderlands-type FPS-RPG hybrid, but your choice of character/class is actually almost completely meaningless. The only real differences between the three classes that I can see are their voice actors (which is one of the major weaknesses of the game; I play with the music and voices turned off since they're so distractingly... eeh) and their initial choices of class ability. The class abilities are almost all useless; you won't need most of the ability unlock points that you have at max level. However, if you like being nearly omnipotent and invincible because of all the health/ammo/energy regen items you'll quickly accumulate if you're good at the first story missions, you'll enjoy this game. I've taken a single character to max level, and am currently grinding for the last few achievements while upgrading every weapon's Mythical variant to level 24 (on that note, if you come across a good Legendary or Mythical Vulcan machine gun, that weapon will carry you for more levels than much of anything else).
I could go into a lot of detail about individual weapons and levels, because if you really get into it there's a not insignificant amount of depth to the game's items, but suffice it to say that if you get this game on a heavy sale, and don't think too hard about the plot or the premise or pretty much anything other than shooting zombies and soldiers, this isn't a bad game to spend time with.

//EXTREMELY MINOR SPOILERS BELOW, LEARNED IN THE FIRST FIVE MINUTES//
I have never played a game like this before.
When you play a good game, you often feel as if your screen is a window to another world, where the events of the game actually take place. In OneShot, this happens LITERALLY. The character you play is from another world, yes, but neither your world OR the game world. You guide him through the world as an observer from beyond, a guardian spirit helping him to save the world.
Because elements from that world communicate with you in YOUR world. Files on YOUR computer give you the knowledge you need to guide this child. The immersion that this creates, along with several other mechanics, is absolutely staggering.
OneShot is both a game and an experience because of this. One of the most poignant memories I have is running through the first area of the game and suddenly releasing the "run" key because I was worried the character would get exhausted. THAT is how immersed I was in this game. THAT is how much you begin to care for the protagonist.
And the ending... the last twist of the game is one that you WILL see coming a mile away, but it is still one that you will sit at for a long, long while. I have never in my life wanted more to just reach into a game and hug the main character.
I don't care that this is an RPG-Maker game. I don't care that there is no combat or epic fight scenes or any of that. I don't even care that this game is a remake. As far as I'm concerned, this game is a modern-day Alice in Wonderland.
OneShot is an experience that will linger with me for a long time. And I'm happy that it will.
TL;DR
Buy this game and hop on the feels train, we're going for a wonderful ride.

Starting off as an RPG Maker 2003 game in 2014, and now re-released from a RPG Maker XP build, OneShot brings a lot of the heart and pure story telling. You follow Niko, a cat "person" being that has been tasked to saving the world.
As you adventure through the world you'll learn a lot about its history, a lot about its inhabitants, but most of all, a lot about Niko.
The graphics are top notch for an RPG Maker game, nothing looks stock, and the overall system has been tweaked to give OneShot a unique feel and presentation.
The dialog is a joy to read, with simple videogame text rules adhered to like - screen wide text should never be more than two pages long, characters should speak with personality but also be concise, talking to someone more than once usually gives you slightly different dialouge, etc.
The puzzles in the game are not nard, but they usually require a bit of investigation to figure out what the goal of the puzzle is. Once that is accomplished things have a tendency to fall into place. Nothing is too hard in the game, pray perhaps the first puzzle in the game, and once you get into the groove of the game, you'll know what to look for.
The storyline is very well layed out and information is clearly laid out to your in a structure way that follows the path of the character. From the very get go, you know the path Niko will take, and the story is molded to that journey. I know that sounds kind of cryptic, but it is a very well directed way to telling a story and keeping it well paced.
Overall, OneShot threw some surprises at me that I didn't expect at all from an RPG Maker game, and absolutely endeared me to Niko. This game gives you One Shot at guiding Niko through this world. Enjoy the time you have with Niko. I know I did.
Overall - 8 / 10

I'll say this-- the game has a good few original ideas that make the game interesting. I'd say that the game was worth the time that it took to play, and don't feel too sour about how much I spent to play it. However, the game seems to be missing a lot of what it would need to make it complete, in my opinion.
The majority of characters are bland distributors of text, existing solely to help the player move forwards with the game. Gameplay is 'trapped in a room' esque, almost to the point of being a keyboard-controlled point and click puzzle game. Player choice affects nothing. The ending is incredibly predictable.
Overall, the game feels rushed-- like it had the right idea, but had only a week or so to write the story/characters. There are points of interest that seem to have been scrapped from the game; areas that are hinted on being accessible and yet prove to be nothing but red herrings. There are characters who seem to have resolvable issues and sidequests, but none of which can ever really be resolved. Even one of the major plotlines of 'the world is decaying', and the mysterious appearance of dead pixels on the screen-- mentioned, investigated, and then drops off the face of the earth to never be mentioned again.
That being said, I was bored one Saturday night and gave the game a try. It might not've rocked my world, but it kept me mildly entertained for the few hours that I played it. So hey, go ahead-- just don't expect anything too memorable and/or impressive.

A boy falls in love with a girl.
Unable to confess, he is gifted with by a deus ex machina with the girl’s phone number. Never minding the strange area code, he immediately calls her, and is overjoyed to find out that she has a crush on him as well.

Even with mods and third party programs, the original Baldur's Gate does not work very well on newer systems at higher resolutions. You can get the game to work well enough with DXwnd but every time you talk to someone the screen will have to scroll to centre the characters in the top left of the screen.
If it wasn't for this, I wouldn't recommend the Enhanced Edition. Instead of just updating the game to run properly on newer systems and adding some quality of life tweaks (they did do this and a good job they have done in this area) they also saw fit to replace and add many things to the detrement of the overall package.
The new cinematics are not only less numerous than in the original, they also brush over important details found in the original FMVs. The ending cinematic in particular is almost incomprehensible and you'll want to look up the original on youtube once you complete the game as the replacement will leave you absolutely puzzled as to what has happened.
The majority of new content and characters are poorly written and even more poorly voice acted with no option to remove it if you want the vanilla experience. Most of it is easily ignored and I do wonder if it only sticks out to me because I'm so familiar with the original game.
The new UI is uglier and feels like it has had much less love put into it than the vanilla game, tool tips no longer have a nice scroll opening animation and instead you just get a fairly ugly flat scroll texture with text in it. The journal looks unfinished but I will concede that it is better organised in the enhanced edition.
Other graphical changes like sprite outlines, sprite smoothing and character selection circles are painfully ugly and turned on by default. Some people may like these but to have them on by default is going to give some people a very bad first impression, especially people who have played the original game.
**
I recommend turning off sprite outlines and filtering in the graphics options, and in the feedback menu turning on classic character selection circles. This will go a long way to making the game look like it once did.
**
A further odd choice is a filter that is placed over the background art, making it look blurrier than it should. Zooming out one click and zooming in actually removes this and it looks much nicer. Clicking the middle mouse button to reset zoom will reintroduce the filter. It's very odd. I found that zooming out three clicks on the scroll wheel resulted in the cleanest look and luckily the game will save your zoom level so it's not a huge deal.
For new players there are difficulty options to make the game easier which you can ramp up on the fly once you get the hang of things and veteran players will like the higher difficulty modes that are available.
So, in conclusion this is probably the best way to play Baldur's Gate on a modern computer but it will take a bit of digging around in the options menus to get everything to your liking. The new content is not very good but can mostly be ignored and in the end, it's still Baldur's Gate, one of the best CRPGs ever made. I wish Beamdog had been more respectful of the original developers intentions when adding content but the core game still shines through.

Easily my favourite game ever produced so far. Ontop of every other stealth/combat game, this manages to exceed itself in every way possible. If your a fan of stealth as an option, this is easily a top choice when chosing a game, Dishonoured gives you the options of many paths within each misison. Whether it is to sprint and jump across the rooftops, dropping down on your enemies like tomorrow, you can go complete stealth without having to ever use your blade. However as many other games propose, is when playing something heavily integrated with stealth, it is often pointless to try and face the enemy head on when playing on the hardest difficulty, Dishonoured still gives you that option as it is still completely possible to face them head on. It still is extremely hard to do, I find after much practice of combining teleporting and agility together it becomes a non-stop intense fight until someone is left standing and the other taken apart by rats or sliced to peices. This takes me onto the next point of a concept, the use of this "steampunk" world ran by whale oil is made completely believable through the realistic-appocalyptic setting. The world becomes a part of the way you play through each mission, after my personal 7th playthough of the game, I still find things I have never discovered before, purely basing my knowledge off the way I had previously encountered similar structures within the world of Dunwall. Whether you choose to kill everything in your path and lead to a particularly destructive conclusion, or whether you remain to become unseen throughout the whole entire game remains to be your choice. Finally, the DLC. Out of all games this remains to one of the best DLC-integrated games where it is 100% worth buying after you finish the game, whether it is to play as Daud who had just an equally as good story as Corvo where more secrets of the city are unveiled, or to play in time trials and challenges, rating yourself against the rest of the world.
All in all my favourite game above Skyrim, Far Cry 3 and 4, Hitman Absoloution and Shadow Of Mordor.

Just finished playing through Trine 3. I've put off purchasing this due to the many "helpful" nagative reviews. However, it was half price, and I love the Trine series too much to pass it up.
I wholeheartedly enjoyed this game.
The graphics are as lovely as it's predecessors'. The gameplay is smooth. The story is on par with the series. The collectables are fun to collect. I feel cool when I do cool stuff.
To address the common critiques.
-The game is short.
Yeah it is. I started it yesterday afternoon and finished it this morning. However... I could play through the previous Trines in that time as well... You know what you're in for. At the $12 I paid for it... well worth it! At $24, maybe a bit much. But now knowing how much I enjoyed it, I would tell past me to go ahead and buy it full price.
-3D is weird. Graphics are glitchy. Controls are hard.
Maybe. Rarely. Not really. The 3D looks lovely. Do I think it really adds anything? No. I think most of the levels could be easily redone as sidescrollers. But at the same time, the game rarely forces you into a super 3D enviroment. I would describe it as a sidescroller with a bit of depth here and there. Glitches? Only when I tried to climb the background scenery I had no reason to climb. I had almost no issues/glitches during any critical gameplay. The controls were fine. Once in a while, object depth combined with weird lighting shadows, made thigns a little unclear. However this was only a couple spots, and I'd like to think of them as learning moments in gameplay.
-Ripoff ending
It's clearly chapter 1... and aparently money may keep us from the rest of the story... But I'd like to encourage you all to buy it and support the devs if you hope to see the rest.
Stuff I liked
-3D has it's moments
It really adds to the previously monotonous combat. One more thing to pay attention to. The worlds are gorgeous. Object interaction is 3D is cool. While I would have been happy with another 2D Trine, I have no bad feeling about 3D after playing it trhough.
-Combat is cool
The Knight finally has his moments in combat with all sorts of knockback. The Wizard is given a box smash attack which keeps him combat non-optimal, but not totally useless. The Rogue's attack is insanely well controlled for how difficult it must have been to program. Her range, the areas combat occurs, and the speed and movement of the minions strikes a good balance to keep you switching between characters.
-Game looks so good.
In case I haven't already made it clear... This game was as stunning as the first two. Character models, level design, textures, effects... all lovely. The whole playthrough was lovely.
My point is... buy the game. By comparison to the first two, it's clear where people are pulling critism from, but viewed on it's own I think it's a great game. And I think most Trine players will appreciate the new experience.

Trine 3 is an interesting addition to the series.  The transition from 2D to 3D is actually handled reasonably well, and I had a good time playing through with different mechanics from the Trine 1+2 platforming.  Fortunately, the game retains Trine's lush visuals, so it's still a treat to look at, and the newer mechanics made possible by the move to 3D are fun (though I missed the more fluid rope-swinging that Zoya was capable of in Trine 1+2).
The transition to 3D is helped out somewhat by the level design, which for the most part allows you to play individual setpieces as if they were still a 2D puzzle.  It's true that sometimes player positioning becomes an issue, and occasionally you'll end up misjudging where you are in relation to where you're jumping, but overall I didn't have any problems with it really.  I did have a few unintentional deaths due to my character not being where I thought she was, but since death is only a minor inconvenience in the game, it never bothered me.
Character abilities are restricted compared to previous Trine games, to account for the increased complexity of dealing with them in a 3D environment, but it's nice that the characters start out with all of their abilities intact.  The "trineangles" you collect in Trine 3 no longer count towards character upgrades, but to unlocking levels.  This could've been problematic, but the Trineangles aren't super hidden, and when you select a level section from the menu, it'll tell you from which sections you're missing Trineangles, so it's much easier to hunt down missing ones.  Unlike with previous Trine games, I'd very often finish up a level to discover that I'd gotten all of them first time around, so I did far less replaying than I'd done in previous installments.
The biggest drawback, of course, is that it's definitely a shame that Frozenbyte wasn't able to create the full-length Trine 3 that they'd set out to create.  The ending is certainly abrupt and leaves the storyline hanging, and anyone not prepared for that is likely to be quite disappointed.  It helps, certainly, to go into the game knowing that it's a truncated storyline.  It's also shorter than the other Trine installments, for the same reason, but I got a good eight hours of gameplay to get through all the content, which I was happy enough with for the price.
So yeah: certainly not a perfect product, but IMO it's a worthy addition to the series.

I picked up SpaceChem during a sale for around $1 or $2. While I got my money's worth for what I paid, I believe the full price is not justified for anyone but the most hardcore puzzle game fans.
EDIT: I realize from the reactions to this rating that I have not explained my rating well enough to be of any help to potential buyers. While the puzzle aspect is creative as always and may appeal to fans of other Zachtronics games, I suppose I found it too restrictive at times, and tedious at others. While I understand that the game wasn't aiming for realism, it seems too abstract to uphold its theme. In any case, I found the difficulty curve to be a bit steep after the tutorial is over. The game could have perhaps benefitted from some amount of player progression between levels, or even something of an upgrade system in each level. Perhaps the player could have a limited amount of currency at the start of a level that they could spend on reactor upgrades (more bonders, waldos, inputs, outputs, etc.). This could possibly taint the nature of the game as a puzzler, so I'd understand a reluctance to add such a feature.
As for some positives that the game has, I must say that the game does have a solid control scheme. The reactor UI is clean, if perhaps overly abstract, while the building UI is more detailed. Furthermore, I do appreciate that the game makes some attempt to alleviate tedium with reactor templates. The story seems interesting too, although there was not much of it to experience considering how far I was able to make it.
I should also mention that even though I am a developer, the game did not appeal to me as much as some of Zachtronics other games. I enjoyed The Codex of Alchemical Engineering and found some merit in The Bureau of Steam Engineering, but SpaceChem fell short for reasons I've described above. Just know that even if you are a programmer or enjoy the style of "Zachlikes," you are not guaranteed to like this game.

The Long Dark doesn't look like much. A first person shooter without weapons, and not a hyper-realistic survival game either, but there's a lot of tension and strategy. There are so many things threatening to kill you at the same time - mainly hunger and hypothermia, but thirst, infections, injuries, and wild animals can take you out too, that you have to think carefully about how to invest your time and energy and where to search for useful items. When do you choose to light a fire? How much effort should you use to find firewood vs seeking out abandoned houses and the like, which mean more food?
The one thing I don't like is that when you first start, you can be dropped randomly anywhere on the map, at any time of day or night, in any weather. As a novice player, if I'm dropped outside at night in a snowstorm, then the situation is absolutely hopeless. You can also be dropped pretty far from any structures, which means that finding food is next to impossible unless you've played enough to be very familar with the map. My last two characters couldn't find any shelter whatsoever before freezing to death, which is kind of a drag.
But overall it's a good strategically oriented game. I haven't played story mode - the idea doesn't interest me. But the survival mode has been fun enough.

Lovely Planet is a FPS platformer in a surreal and cute world. However do not let the cuteness fool you, this game is brutally hard.
The graphics remind me of the Nintendo 64 games with crude 3D shapes mixed with occasional simple 2D textures to give character. I know this is a bit far-fetched, but I find it cute in Lovely Planet.
The gameplay is swift and responsive, the only weird part being sliding off some ledges that look like it would be possible to land on them. Framerate is perfect and the game runs well. However the FOV cannot be changed.
The idea is to get across a short level while jumping on platforms and shooting baddies. Simple enough, so there are leaderboards to compete, and stars given according to accuracy and speed. At first I kept trying to go faster and faster without understanding why my impressive runs didn't get rewarded by the game, until I learned that the third star was only given for 100% accuracy. I like a good challenge, so I worked on finishing all levels 100% with three stars.
At the start the levels were pretty straight-forward and it was fun. But then... then the apple fell too far from the tree. Literally, because falling apples is the one game mechanic that ruined the game for me. Any single apple hitting the ground triggers a game over. The early ones are thrown at the player, which is fine. However after a bit the apples are shot in the sky from a different place in the level, and just fall right where they are, whether the player is around or not.
Let me explain better how this is infuriating. You are in a part of the level, merrily shooting and platforming your way. And then, suddenly, you cross an invisible line and hear the dreaded sound of an apple been released. And now, the only thing that you can do is rush forward in the level to reach the part where the apple is located, and start shooting from afar (because the bullets take time to travel), without a target nor a crosshair, where you predict that the apple is going to fall . And then you realize that three apples were triggered, and you need to pre-shoot three different locations with pinpoint pre-accuracy and timing. So, basically, you have no choice but to quickly shoot in several directions and hope for the best, and do it again and again until you are a robot that has complete muscle memory of the right way to deal with this nonsense. And let's not talk about the moment where you have to jump on a jump-pad, and while in the air, shoot where an apple is going to land BEHIND you, then quickly turn back forward and shoot where an apple is falling in FRONT of you. I managed to do it. I did all of this. I had three stars in these levels, so 100% accuracy. But instead of being happy at my achievement, I was thinking "why? why so much time wasted being a robot and not having any fun?". Then I started the 4th world, and noticed that the levels were engulfed in fog. Superman 64 level of fog and fun. With the nerve-wrecking treat that I also had to pre-shoot apples that I couldn't even see, and it was made even more obvious that completing the levels would be a tedious chore of memorizing every single move and shot.
No, thanks, I like a good challenge, but this is just a waste of time, and the cute graphics are hidden in fog anyway, so why bother. Goodbye Lovely Planet, I only recommend you at a very cheap price to fool around in the early levels, otherwise I do not think that you are a good game worth investing my time and sanity to complete.
I'm not sure if I can recommend this or not, but there is one certain thing:  this game will make you hate apples, tomatoes or WHATEVER THE HELL THOSE DAMN BOMBS ARE.

You have to shoot all the targets and run to the finish of the level, which takes about 15 seconds when you succeed. This game starts off easy but gets really difficult. Your projectiles are slow so you have to lead moving targets, and you fail the level if you let some targets hit the ground or get hit by an enemy projectile. The gameplay is very trial-and-error. You have to figure out a sequence of shots and moves and execute them close to perfectly, or you'll fail. To give you an idea: often you have to jump into a teleporter after which you are greeted by three projectiles flying at you from different directions, so you have to shoot them to not get hit, but at the same time jump on a disappearing platform and reach around the corner just in time to hit two tomatoes before they hit the ground. Very difficult. For enthousiasts, there are achievements for being fast and for 100% accuracy in each level.
If you like difficult/trial-and-error games with instant restart (such as Super Meat Boy), get this game. But don't expect a lot of variety. There are about a hundred levels and they all look similar.
Delightfully charming, deceptively difficult, but not in a bad way. Definitely worth checking out.

An incredibly well done mix of Tower Defense, Strategy, Survival and Action. I had incredible fun playing through it and even almost made it to Floor 12 before the game decided to crash with no savegame to load from.
It is very similar to a Tower Defense game that also has heroes and resource management for power. Very often you will run into situations where your Crystal will be exposed from all sides, or situations where you don't have enough power to supply all rooms to the exit, resulting in very stressful but rewarding floors. The floors are also well designed, even if a bit randomized. Important things are near the Crystal in the beginning and then the higher floor you get go further away, until you might not even want to use them.
Personally I'd either recommend a Controller or using the Keyboard and Mouse. The game does not handle multi-monitor systems very well, which is one negative aspect of it, as it doesn't lock your mouse to the play area either.
After a while, the game tends to repeat itself, giving you the same stuff, the same layouts, the same enemies. The biggest variety is in how you tackle the problem that is infront of you and which heroes you take along for the ride - because there's a few standard and DLC characters and a lot of unlockable characters.
The game has some kind of modding support and is based on the Unity engine. For some the Unity engine might be a huge sign to turn away, but for this game it works fairly well. There are rare crashes, bugs and even straight up rendering errors (which I'm pretty sure I've also seen in Golf With Friends a long time ago, possibly due to an older Unity engine).
I recommend this game, purely because it is fun to play with friends and alone.

Games like this, games like Monster Hunter (specifically for me, Tri:3), games with an identity of being unique, boy do I wish games like this would be more popular in our infested gaming industry.
When I first found this game, I was looking for a dungeon crawler. Simple, go down into depths, kill stuff, get loot, move on. However, I didn't expect to find this. I saw this, and watched the trailer. The music is what hooked me first. I started to listen to the soundtrack, and before I know it, I'm counting down the days for the Winter Sale, and boom. This game (and the bundle) gets marked down to a great price. So I look at it, about to purchase it, and I second guess myself.
I could've boughten many games in trade for this, but I decided, 'Hey, why not? It looks fun,' and I made the purchase. This game is a gem, and has a unique flavor that will keep me coming back (I'd say something more unique like, It's kept me coming back for ages, but I haven't played that long). The micromanagement, the characters, it all leads to a sense of survival, and getting as far as possible without killing everyone in your team. It takes skill, and as a guy in a video once said, no one can say they are 'Good' at this game, and I like that. This game is challenging, even on Too Easy, and it will keep you thinking and figuring out the best possible stradegies. No amount of videos will ever truly tell you how to survive the depths, for it is up to you to decide your best play style.
One thing though that I will say I haven't tried, and leave it up to you to decide is multiplayer. I don't have anyone to play with, and I haven't even attempted to make contact with someone random. So that part to me is vague, but the Singleplayer experience is a deffinite must try.
EDIT: So one big thing I have noticed is the amount of emotion you'll feel when a player you started with dies. Not only that feeling of losing their progress (such as levels and stuff), but the fact that they have (more than likely) been a vital part of the team, whether that is tanking damage or dealing it, or being the main repair man/lady, It is a unique experience I haven't felt in a game were losing a squad member really matters, as you can't save scum, which means, they won't be coming back.

While this game is probably worth what I paid for it, it's nothing to call home about.
The game touts full range controls yet is limited to arrow keys, which still doesn't allow the precision needed for weaving through bullet patterns.
Multiple spelling and grammar errors grated my nerves, both in the story segments and in the documentation/hint screens.
Graphics are pretty, and the soundtrack isn't half bad.
I might come back to this game if/when I upgrade this computer to see if the controls get any tighter.
--Addendum with version 1.4:
The controls are a bit more responsive now, and the ship's inertia is removed.  Previously, I thought it was an artifact of my four-year-old compy, but, no, it was a feature.  I think performance has improved since last time I played;  refighting a boss showed much less slowdown than the first time.
Documentation is cleaned up (though the typeface might benefit from lower-case letters) and I haven't seen more loading screen errors.
The addition of two game modes helps to alleviate the level monotony somewhat, and paradoxically makes them more passable.  Normal mode has about a dozen rocks hurtling towards you, after which one or more enemy ships crawl in and shoot, asteroid-free.  This runs up the level timer, which has the effect of multiplying asteroid hp and xp... but you hit a wall where you can't output enough damage to any single asteroid before it runs past you... and there's more ships to shoot again.  Bounty hunter mode keeps the asteroids coming when ships show, or perhaps makes the ships show when the asteroids are coming.  This way, you can keep accomplishing something while the ships crawl in invincibly.
Overall, it's better than when I first played, but still don't think it's a must-buy.  Fans of the genre might enjoy it, the graphics guys know what they're doing (calling it merely "pretty" isn't fair, I suppose), but I can't get more enthusiastic about it.

OneShot is an environmental exploration game with memorable characters and soul crushing dilemmas. It features a young not-cat child named Niko exploring an unfamiliar, desolate landscape in a world on the brink of destruction. It is soon apparent that it is Niko's task to save the world and it's the player's job to protect Niko.
The Steam version of OneShot greatly expands on the original while bringing freshness to familiar characters, environments, and puzzles. The artwork and sound design combine to create a wonderful nostalgic environment. The maps have been heavily reworked to fit the extra content.
OneShot forces the player to make tough decisions in a way that most other games only hope to. It’s hard to know what the right answers are, if any.  The game and its inhabitants call on you to decide their fates. Good luck.
I would recommend OneShot to anyone looking for a unique gaming experience, or any fans of exploration games like Yume Nikki.
Pros:
OneShot has beautiful characters, art, music, and environments.
Meticulous exploration is heavily rewarded as is creative problem solving.
Veterans of the original will find plenty of new content.
Niko is perfect.
Cons:
Some segments went on for longer than I would like between beds. While closing the game doesn't kill Niko, I was determined to play it like the original.
In the original the consequences of failure, and any results of the player's decisions are *permanent*. Because you only have one shot, this added a lot of pressure and made The Entity, and the world much more hostile. The remake loses some of that tension if you are aware of certain things.

A great book that brings out the child in you.
A interactive storybook that is great for even the youngest children, or the young at heart. It might be more fun if a parent where to read the "scary" parts in a deep bellowing voice when reading it.  This is not a game, it is more similiar to a visual novel. There are many visual novels on steam, but hardly any interactive books that are age appropriate to children.
SO WHAT IS A INTERACTIVE STORYBOOK?
`A book you can move around the page with your mouse on your computer and look at the details.
WHAT IS DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A VISUAL NOVEL AND A INTERACTIVE BOOK?
`The big difference is that in a visual novel, you can choose responses to the NPC (Non-Playable Characters) and interact with the storyline. In a interactive book, you only can look at the pages of the book, interact with the pictures on the page, and not interact with the actual storyline.
IS THE BOOK ANY GOOD?
`Yea. It is geared for young childen from 6 years old to 11 years old, but anyone who chooses to can read this book. The book is about overcoming fear and lonliness. Suffering from my own form of lonliness due to my conditions, I am very familiar with the lonesome fog in real life. The best thing you can do is ignore it and move on.
IS IT SAFE FOR MY CHILD?
`This is not a violent book, nor does it show death, blood, or other things found in violent games. This is probably one of the few "interactive books" on steam i recommend for a young child learning to read, or someone learning english language. This is a really great company that made this game, and you should check out their other games they made, like Meadow, the non-communicating social interaction game.
Recommended for being clean, safe, fun for children, and great for a inspirational bedtime story.
NOTE: I suggest as i posted below, use different voices for the characters. It makes the book more fun when reading to yourself or to a child.

Trine 3 is overall, a fun, beautiful game. You don't have to play the first two to enjoy the third one. Also, local multiplayer is an option!
The upsides: The graphics are stunningly beautiful. The co-op works great, and the puzzles are well designed. Some of the bonus levels are quite challenging. The story is also interesting, and the dialog is witty; you'll smile and laugh often as the characters interact. A huge improvement over the previous installments is that the level select screen gives you hints as to where the missing collectable 'Trineangles' are in the levels. This really increased replayablility, and decreased frustration.
The downsides: Frozenbyte was only able to complete the first half of the game, so it ends abruptly at a cliffhanger. They did say they would produce the rest when they had enough in their budget to finish the game. Occasionally, the 3d is difficult to navigate, and occasionally there are bugs - every once in awhile the 'trineangles' would only collect for one person in multiplayer. This wasn't a major issue, more a minor annoyance.
Overall, I strongly recommend this game. It's tons of fun, with great multiplayer, and a beautiful world to explore.

+ The graphics are breathtaking

I don't normally write reviews, but after finishing this wonderful game, I can't help but try to convince others to give it a try. To start, Lovely Planet is a game about shooting angry red guys. In order to get all 3 stars for a level, you must kill every enemy, beat the level fast enough, and not miss a single shot. With the low shot speed of your bullets, this last one can be a pain, but all of the game's enemies are stationary (except for apples, which can hardly be considered enemies) and you'll get used to the gun.
The game has great visuals and music, especially if you enjoyed the katamari series. Even after hearing the same song for a few hours, you shouldn't get sick of it unless you really hate jpop.
For me, the game really shines in its wonderful level design and difficulty curve. The first world is quite easy and will introduce you to the mechanics without being too punishing. As the game progresses, however, you'll find that every new level is just slightly outside of your skill level - not easy but never impossible. As someone who never plays first person shooters, I never felt that a level was too difficult to complete with all 3 stars. As far as the level design, there were multiple occasions where I saw what the level wanted me to do and got giddy with excitement, completely in love with the elegance of the design.
I can't recommend this game enough. This is a game that I will always remember fondly, and I'll probably play it again in a few years when I've forgotten the specifics of the levels.

Intensely engaging and above all frustratingly, keyboard-smashingly, wall-punchingly difficult.

Cons:
-Nonexistant community means you can only play practice against bots and training mode.

-Tons of DLC (character packs, skins, etc.) which are useless because you can't play multiplayer.

Final Verdict: Yeah, don't get this game. I did it.
I beat this game.
It only took me 6 years.
Look at my time spent. That's how thorough this game forces you to be for just the campaign.
The game is based around very basic programming and chemical principles, and involves you taking chemicals as inputs and transforming them into desired outputs. More difficult puzzles involve you using multiple sequences like this in tandem to power different devices to defeat some kind of boss.
It may start out simple, but by the end it gets obscenely complex
The level of catharsis is proportional to the elegance of your solution, but even a brute-forced, less elegant approach will still warrant a satisfying sigh of relief for a job
done.
All in all a great and very challenging puzzle game. While it may help a bit, you don't need a high level of mastery over chemistry to understand the game--that said it'll help teach you some basic principles. Buy if you're looking for a challenge.

The Lonesome Fog shows how a cub has a lot of fears--ones that she can't seem get over--and shows how when met with the right conditions, everyone can get over their fears. The cub grew to be fearless, just like how everyone can be if they wanted to...atleast, that's the vibe I got from it.
Anywho, while it was a tiny bit short, it was truly a masterpeice. The visuals are stunning, and the story is fantastic, besides a few grammar mistakes here and there.
If the Shelter games are something you really enjoyed, I recommend that you read The Lonesome Fog. It's an amazing add-on to the story, and shows off some about how the Blob works. It's a truly stunning experiance.

I know the Lonesome Fog is more about fears and doubts in general, but it really speaks to my depression.
Especially one of the last lines where it speaks about her (the cub who I believe is Inna) facing the “Lonesome Fog” head on each time it came to pass before returning to her family.
I think it speaks not to let your depression, or simple fears and doubts in general consume you but at the same time, not to just run away each time they act up.
Face your insecurities and learn to resolve them, grow braver with each time they whisper doubts in your ears.
You will be fine. The fog will come to pass, even if it takes hours, days- perhaps even years -everything will pass on.
That’s the Circle.

The criticism regarding the story is, unfortunately, valid. The story already in the game is quite good and fun to follow, but it ends very prematurely. Why this is I can only guess. Maybe because of limited funds or time. What should have been the transition between "chapters", is now the end of the game.
Though I do not agree with the criticism regarding the removed features such as the different skills from the heroes. The 3D aspect of the game, more than makes up for this. The 3D made the navigation through the world much more fun, and the boss fights, though few, were very interesting.
I do no think it is worth its full price as it is way to short, but I would recommend buying this game during a sale, as playing it for a few hours with friends was still very fun.

Alright- I'll be the devil's advocate here. Lovely Planet is a Quake-esque first person platformer and bullet hell shooter. People are comparing this game to Super Meat Boy, but I disagree completely. Not only that, but I think this game is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Here are my points:
Super Meat Boy is about precision, and tight controls. Meat Boy himself is basically a walking hitbox- he's a tiny cube that dies if he touches any enemy or any environmental obstacle, and while that insta-death aspect is true in this game, really nothing else is even close to similar to Meat Boy.
Unline Meat Boy, LP is in first-person, which is a challenge for bullet hell-style insta-death games, because traditionally the idea of a bullet hell is that you can see what's going to hit you and be able to dodge it based on your hitbox, whether it be that glwing dot on the back of your spaceship or Meat Boy's tiny, but rigidly defined body. In an FPS, however, you lose that precision. When a bullet is flying toward you, you have no clue how far you need to dodge to actually have it not hit you, which makes a lot of deaths in this game a result of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ design rather than lack of skill. First-person view also restricts your vision- in a 2D shooter or platformer, you have all the information right in front of you, but in an FPS, you have to be constantly swiveling around, trying to see everything around you, and that restriction of your vision can be frustrating.
The same goes for the platforming- very few FPS games ever do precision platforming because it's just so ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to pull off: in a game where you can't see your own legs and can't see your own hitbox, jumping into obstacles and getting a death can often be the result of hazy game design rather than being bad at the game, and people don't like that. People want to die because they're ♥♥♥♥♥♥ players, not because not enough thought went into the design of the game.
Yet again, the shooting suffers from similar falling-off points: lack of clarity being the main one. I find it hard to even call this game "precision" when it doesn't even have a crosshair, and if, say, the weapon you're holding came out of your character's midsection Quake-style, then that would have been a little bit better, but no- it actually shoots at an angle to the left, making it incredibly unprecise.
Soundtrack's good enough, though- I get that what they were going for was kind of an ironic, disingenuously quirky theme to contrast with the hard gameplay, but it really just didn't do it for me.
As you can see, I haven't even played very much of this game yet- I'll admit, I've tried the first level of the second world maybe 200 times and no matter what I do, I die seemingly at complete random when I'm not close to even touching any obstacle. I'm sure it's something that the game just hasn't explained to me, and for ♥♥♥♥s sake I don't need a completely hamfisted tutorial to understand it, but holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ I literally just die every time I move in any direction in the first level of the second world, and I can't get past it. And I'm not terrible at FPSes, either- the game is just so unclear that it's not fun for me at all.
(sigh)... if everything I just said made you leap to your feet and think, "finally! a game just for me!", then for ♥♥♥♥s sake buy it, it's only six dollars. But I think it's a prime example of when a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game gets acclaim just because of the unique visuals and concept, instead of quality gameplay, and for a game that really does lean incredibly heavily on its gameplay, that's a very bad sign.

This week marks my first month in Ascent, The Space Game. What a ride! First off, everyone has a different reason for playing these types of games, and for the most part this game should satisfy an itch whether it's in trading, crafting/production, economies, exploring, discoveries, colony building, and much more.  The emphasis is PVE, but there will be a PvP component in the future.  But I really want to discuss my play this past month.
I am one of those guys that enjoy the journey, rather then the destination.  And this game hits my spot.  Yes, the beginning is tough when you start on a small ship and 1,000 credits and you hear people on chat talking about millions and billions of credits.  But I decided at the very start that I would invest on a foundation to support future play.  I did the early quests, and settled on the inner 8 planets.  As I did this I slowly raised my ship level.  In my style of play I did not use chat to beg and cajole people to give me ships or money to move along quickly.  I had watched Sinstrite's videos before playing and then looked a little at the wiki, so I had an idea what to expect.  After my 8 settlements I built my ISB (Inner Starbase).  It has 100 rings but I found that I only needed 60 or so to be productive.  I scanned dozens and dozens of wrecks and claimed many blueprint fragments for higher level ships.
So where am I today?  I am still in a Mammoth, and not a Seraph, which is a much bigger ship, but I am fine with that.  Amazingly, I have already built 5 Mammoths in my shipyard which I sell to other players.  I have built my first colony and outside starbase (OSB) so now I have two shipyards working, increasing my production effort.  My colony is growing, and I am looking through the 100 new systems I discovered myself to find a suitable second colony.
The game keeps going.  It is what you make of it.  The people in the game are extremely helpful.  Hey, if you want someone to give you a leg up with a better ship and credits you could probably fine someone, and there is nothing wrong with that.  This game has something for everyone. This economy is player driver for the most part.
I heartily recommend this game.  If you see me, wabasco, in game.. give a shout!
Hard to explain my thoughts, the game is definitely 10/10 though... I haven't said this about any game I have ever played lol look at my reviews. Enjoy.

To anyone who has ever played Eve online but disliked the PVP aspect of the game... I recommend that you try this game.
When you buy the game via steam you get 3 months premium bundled with your purchase.  This "premium" enables you to  build a colony outside the "inner 9" which is what the central hub of the game is called.  And several other things.
My suggestion is to not activate your premium untill you have played a while, as it is not required untill you get into the later stages of the game.
The game is under constant development.  Jam, the dev is constantly updating the game. (I think he never takes a break.)  Most patches are small, in the 8mb size range.
The graphics are really good and constantly being updated and expanded.
The Gameplay... It is so extensive that I probably have not experienced 20% of what you can achieve.  My experience has so far been mining, trading and doing contracts.  There are colonies and settlements, but I only have a single Settlement from the tutorial missions.
The gameplay is progressive.  As you get a bigger ship the contracts and items available to you also increase.
I am someone who likes to read about the bad points of a game as well as the good points of a game...  So i will try and point out some bad things as well. :P
Cons :
There are bugs still in the game.
- Some contracts do not accept correctly.
- Changing ships means you have to undock and dock again to update the ship info.
- The start of the game is slow to get yourself some money...  The first mission outside the "inner 9" takes an age to earn the money for.
- Purchasing your first few ships takes forever. :)
- sometimes the autopilot button might not work, possibly requires a restart.
- complex command system for computers.  (some may not get the hang of it easily.)
But even the few cons are minor things, that Jam the dev is working on to fix.
Overall this game is well worth purchasing.  It has alot of potential.

I was not expecting much here after the first Dead Effect. The stiff animations, clunky action, and constrained upgrade system all turned me off to more zombie shooting in space, which is exactly what this one promises. But Dead Effect 2 also promises a much broader progression system, filled with randomized loot and upgradable powers and an open mission structure. This, it turns out, was enough to hook me, and the minor tweaks and improvements made elsewhere in the game were enough to keep me mowing down space zombies despite my misgivings.
I don’t know how Dead Effect The First ended on account of how miserable it was to play, but the second picks up there and catches you up right quick. You can choose to play the same shootman or shootlady as before, or a third ninja-ish fellow if you’re feeling less shooty. The evil scientist antagonist is dead but the giant colony ship you’re on is still filled with zombies, you’re still stuck on it, and now there are soldiers gunning for you. A mysterious lady with mysteriously pert nipples rushes to your aid and helps you set up a base of operations, from which you recruit other survivors, work to take back the ship, and learn more about your own unusual past.
The hub is at the heart of the key changes to the formula, offering you a place between missions to talk with characters, buy and upgrade equipment, and pick what kind of zombie-mashing you’d like to partake of next. The open mission structure is a huge boon here, doing away with the stock standard linear progression of the first game in favor of story missions, repeatable missions, survival, wave assaults, and other modes that can be attempted at any time. You can tune the experience through mode selections and difficulty options to exactly what you want to be doing, and make progress doing it by scoring more experience, items, and money that can be used to help you advance in other areas.
In terms of character progression, the two games are barely comparable. The first Dead Effect offered you different weapons at exorbitant prices and small upgrades to each. Dead Effect 2 has character levels, skill trees, randomized weapons, armor sets, cybernetic upgrades, and a crafting system. Leveling up gets you points to unlock new powers, both active ones that function like Mass Effect biotic powers and passive ones that let you carry more ammo or switch weapons faster. These powers give some much-needed variety to the combat, allowing you to ragdoll zombies en masse or shield yourself from annoying commandos. They also feel tuned to address some of the complaints I had about the first game, such as the slow pace of your actions.
As for the rest, this is very much an ARPG-style loot game now. Gear drops in different color grades and has its own levels, which can be raised in weapons by purchasing upgrades for that weapon. There’s a wide variety of guns and melee options now, everything from chainsaws to flamethrowers to railguns to revolvers. They drop like candy in missions and can also be purchased with your giant stacks of currency, if you don’t need to spend them on other upgrades. Codex items can be slotted into gear to provide additional effects like improved accuracy or movement speed. Effects like that are also found on armor pieces and cybernetic upgrades, which are their own vast realms of randomized, color-coded loot.
You may have noticed I haven’t even gotten to the actual gameplay yet, and that’s because it honestly feels secondary to all the customizing and collecting you can do. Dead Effect 2 is built around essentially the same core as the first, which means gunning down shambling zombies in samey sci-fi corridors. Enemy variety and animations have been punched up a little, but it still feels like a low-budget shooter that’s lacking in variety. That variety is supplied this time by the loot you get and the mission options you have, and that’s enough to make me look past the actual combat but it might not be enough for you. Definitely don’t come for the story either, because three hours in very little has happened and the voice acting is terrible in a way that fails to wrap back around to funny. At this point all I really want to know is why Danette is so conspicuously cold all the time.
Dead Effect 2 is an absolutely fascinating way to do a sequel, because it sticks closely to what (little) worked in the first game and went far afield for everything else. While not everything has grown by the same leaps and bounds the important parts have, and they keep me coming back for more gore and goodies. The character progression is the star of the show here and only gets better as you find more exotic guns to upgrade and more armor sets to collect. It all still feels very low-rent and unpolished but it doesn’t try to hide what it is, a zombie grinder that constantly rewards you with new trinkets to play with. And if you don’t ask more of it than that, you definitely won’t be disappointed.

SpaceChem is an extremely difficult puzzle game that has players think like programmers in designing "reactors" that turn chemicals into others on an atomic scale. Two "waldos" move along tracks you design and execute commands on those tracks. There are several different commands and new mechanics that are implemented as you play.
There are three game "modes" in the main story: "Research", where you work within one reactor; "Production", where you use multiple reactors; and "Defense", essentially "Production", but with added commands and boss fights. Throughout the main game, the player is told a story of a protagonist who joins SpaceChem, a company that produces chemicals, as they learn of its dark secrets.
The game is simple at first, even up to the third world, but then one hits this game's learning cliff. Where it seems the puzzles can't possibly get more difficult, they do. Exponentially. It took me over a year to beat this game (though I played on and off times), and that was just the main story.
SpaceChem has loads of user-created puzzles (I believe over 100) that further test your knowledge of the game. Your solve times are also ranked against other players on histograms. SpaceChem also has a full and powerful level editor and ways to upload your own puzzles. The community is great too, although it has been less active.
There's just so much to do in this game - you'll find yourself spending hours just solving or optimising single puzzles. Nothing beats the euphoria you'll get from finally beating a puzzle you've been stuck on.
Overall, SpaceChem is worth the full asking price as an excellent design-oriented puzzle game. It even has large discounts on it and its DLC very often, and trading cards to go with it. If you're a programmer or enjoy programming, or you just want to get into Zachtronics games, SpaceChem is definitely the way to go.

Spacechem is a puzzle game. Unlike many such games, these puzzles have countless solutions. Your job is to build one.
The puzzles involve geometry and threaded programming. The difficulty ramps up quickly, but there's plenty of opportunity to learn by refining solutions to earlier puzzles. Rather than lines of code, the two "waldos" follow symbolic instructions placed along their track.
Pilarbox aside, the game has aged well on Windows. Not so well on Mac and iOS. If you're playing on a Mac, you'll need to download an additional tool to fix your installation. (Why the developer can't distribute that fix through Steam remains unclear.)
If you've ever written multithreaded code (and enjoyed it), you'll love this game. One of the most important instructions is "sync," which works just like a cyclic barrier. Both waldos must reach a "sync" instruction before either can continue past one. Spacechem was the first puzzle game to exercise this part of my brain. The games that have followed all lack a simple synchronization primitive like "sync."

So here's the thing, Guardians of Middle Earth is an awesome game, and why? I know it's a lot like League of Legends (or Dota, if anyone plays that..) And I like it because it's easy to learn your heroes and strategies like a boss. I also had a problem with all the suggestive materiel in League. and I don't have to worry about the curse words or the pornography in Guardians, and that makes a world of difference to me. I also love to use the Xbox controllers when I play, and thy are not accessible to League, but thy are in Guardians. And its a peace of cake (figuratively speaking, I'm not Gladus or anything) to level up and earn heroes. The only down side to this game is that their is only a very small community, but that's why I am writing this review. It's a great game, and oh so fun to play for all LOTR lovers. And I hope you enjoy it as much as I do.

Guardians of Middle-Earth, is not a solo-playable game, instead it consists of Player versus player in match sets, as well as co-op mode versus the CPU. You can manage your character inventory, equipment and commands, giving you control over your character and the ability to personalize it based on your play style. The wait times for co-op matches can be annoying, but the real-time action makes gameplay fun, and the graphics are pleasant to look at. I personally do not care for games where I am forced to play with or against other players, unless it is something I choose to do, so I would not play a game like this normally; However, for it's genre and given the quality of the game, I would recommend it for players who enjoy the pvp, or co-op gameplay.

I beileve Stonehearth is completely worth it's money if that is holding you back from buying this game. I honestly think that this could be an incredible game once it is released. I do have very minor issues but nothing that would make me regret purchasing Stonehearth in any way.

The controls were a bit different than the other games I've played but like I said, I was able to get past it and afterwards the controls weren't an issue at all.
I also wish there were a more variety in craftables that were available to the crafting career paths. The herbalist (if you are viewing for the first tim they craft wth herbs found in the world) is very limited to what they are able to create and therefore are challenging to level up. I also don't beileve that the cook has nearly enough food to be able to cook. I personally believe that the chef should have the most to craft over any other job but instead it has almost as little as the herbalists.
I also wish that there were multiple biomes and yes I am aware of mods. But I wish that there were more than the Desert and Temperate biomes. I actually have mods that allow more than two biomes but I wish that there were more available to anyone that doesn't mod and just plays the basegame so they too can get a better experience without having add any specifications to their games.
I think this game really needs some more plants and animals other than the raccons and foxes and the brighbell and frostsnap herbs to make the world seem a bit less barren. Although there are the three domesticated animals including the sheep, rabbit, and poyos (chickens) I wish there were more to make the world seem a bit more lively to make the voxel world a bit less barren.
The only issues I have with Stonehearth are just the lack of variety in general but like I said earlier they don't make this game unplayable. But I also have very positive thoughts on this game. I love what they recently added in Alpha 21 with the traits that your hearthlings have and earlier (I think Alpha 20) where you can personlize their looks rather than just randomizing and hoping they don't look too out of whack.
Even though it is voxel the shading and how clear the graphics are really impress me. I think especially for a voxel that the game looks good as well (better graphics option in settings). The music also is very soothing and I feel enhances the mood rather than the audio previously set to damage you ears.
I would reccomend this game to anyone to love city builders, farming simualtors, or even history since the game is based upon a group of seven Hearthlings that come to settle and make discoveries.
This game is only in Alpha 21 so there is always going to be more until the final verison will be published. I really hope that if anyone happens to read this at all that you find my suggestions helpful to you and that I had a positive impact on your thoughts to Stonehearth. I have found Stonehearth to be a game where the devolopers are constantly prorgressing and able to give us something new each time. Thanks for reading to the very end of my long review. :)

Short of it:
Trine 3's story does end in a cliff hanger fashion after about 7-8 hours of play time. That said, if you liked Trine 1 and 2, you will probably like 3 and the changes it introduced.
Long of it:
Trine 3 was, unfortunatly, released early due to budgeting issues. It is still a fairly well polished game however. There are 8 major levels, with a good mix of mini-challenge levels. Other than the first 3 tutorial levels, the main levels are pretty long. Story-wise, it feels as though this was intended to be the first third or fourth of the full story. Game-wise, it took me just over 8 hours to complete and it was fun the entire time.
Upgrades have been removed, so there are no more fire arrows or additional platforms in this game. I beleive this would have been added if the funds did not run out. The new 3D element was used pretty well with the puzzles but can sometimes lead you to miss a platform while jumping. (Depending on the exact camera angle, it can be hard to tell if you are properly aligned with a platform). The 3D element was not overdone however, which is awesome. It is still a mostly linear puzzle platformer. The 3D aspect is only used to enhance that game style, not replace it.
All in all, it was definently a fun game. I hope Frozenbyte can eventually continue the story through DLC or something.

REGARDING MY TIME PLAYED - I don't know why Steam is saying I only spent an hour playing this game, I finished it completely and easily spent 20 hours playing it. Something weird has happened with the calculation or logins but believe me - I played this game start to finish for a LOT longer than one hour, as I also completely finished Trine 1 and 2.
I'm a huge fan of the Trine series but I just cannot recommend Trine 3. If I could only use two words to describe this game they would be:
Beautiful and FRUSTRATING!!!
Seriously it's like this game wasn't even tested by average players. Most of the quests are side quests are too hard, and most aggrivating of all - if you die you have to start ALL over again including the loading screens! The skill required to complete even some of the main questline makes it seem to me like the game was only ever playtested by the actual developers.
So, constructive criticism for the Trine team because you guys are awesome and you deserve constructive feedback for Trine 4.
GOOD THINGS ABOUT TRINE 3
--------------------------------------
* Breathtakingly beautiful colors and graphics
* Fun, well-loved characters
* Witty dialogue and a decent enough storyline
* Good puzzles (just too hard)
* Very good controller support (thank you!)
* Lovely soundtrack
* An enchanting world to play in, as with all the Trine adventures
HORRIFYING THINGS ABOUT TRINE 3
---------------------------------------
* The semi-3D approach to platformers, argh this was so innacurate and so NOT fun to play please don't do it again. The Trine series loses absolutely nothing by being a pure 2D platformer, that is part of it's charm!
* The clear lack of playtesting by non-hardcore gamers.
* How utterly useless both Zoya and Amadeus are in combat (especially Zoya's shooting arc - way too limited)
* Biggest bugbear - The way side quests had to be started over (and over and over) when you died in them. Surely resurrection points could have been included in the side quests as well?
I hope this helps, and I'm looking forward to seeing how Trine 4 is developed.
