There is very, very little for the Hunters to do as they are searching for the Monster. Sure, you will occasionally get a match where you might fight the Monster within 60 seconds, and even then, you're bound to just have to run around the map indefinitely. The only incentive you have as a Hunter to actually kill the monster, aside from ranking up and gaining Keys (currency), is killing the damn thing before it levels up so that you don't have to run around looking for it for ten more minutes.
The game is really, really rough on the wrist.
I played the Open Beta back when the game was first launched and I, along with many other people, noticed this problem then as well. Don't ask me how they could sufficiently remedy the problem, because I don't think I could supply any significant ideas, but all I know is that the lack of actual fighting makes this game a chore to play. A very beautiful and good-looking chore, but a chore nonetheless.
I do, however, appreciate the speed at which you gain sufficient currency to purchase roles, skins, and perks. I haven't played much of the game because of the reasons stated above, but I can tell by how much currency you recieve, win or lose, it doesn't take an absolutely inordinate amount of time to unlock and purchase things. Which, again, I really appreciate.
Turtle Rock I love you guys, but just..... Do something about the running around, yeah? Give the Hunters more things to do while Hunting. Let us use animals that we capture as bait. Give us more ways of luring the monster in to fight us instead of waiting until IT is ready to fight. This game can be great, and in many ways it is great. It's just that there's no evolution or incremental changes or upgrades on the Hunters' side.
To end, I'll simply restate what I feel is the summary of the game's main problem.
The only incentive I had to kill the monster was to kill it before it leveled up so that I didn't have to look for it more. And I don't feel that's a healthy attitude to have towards the game.

I played a lot on PS4 but as the playerbase got smaller and updates stayed infrequent I got tired of it. But after f2p I'm seeing a lot of new faces and a much more active community. The balance changes make teamplay a little bit easier while still leaving a lot of space for skill to take over. It seems like there's a bit less to worry about for newer players since support's situational cloak was replaced with a straightforward shield tool and the mobile arena is now usable to all players. The dome also never goes up unless the monster is caught, which might take away from the "hardcore" side of the game but was definitely a necessary change to pick up the pace of the game, especially for beginners who don't yet understand the map layouts and aren't that good at cutting off the monster.
Yet again though, the game still does not teach enough about your roles. It makes the game look much shallower than it actually is from the outside. Yeah you're the trapper, so you find the monster, but you have a responsibility to use your tools (slow grenades, harpoons etc.) to slow down the monster during the fight. Yeah you're an assault, you shoot the monster up and all that, but you also need to be using your mines or toxic grenades to force the monster away from your allies in a pinch. So what you find is a bunch of hunters only doing one job when they generally should be doing two, and playing a really boring messy version of evolve because the game doesn't go out of its way to teaach you the fundamentals. It's no wonder a lot of people thought it was a simple repetitive game for this reason. It's a great game, but only if you can invest some time and watch a couple of beginner's guides to a couple classes to understand the real role each character has, because it's the first step to actually enjoying the game.
You might have to work a little to understand the nuances at first, but it becomes a GREAT game once you understand the fundamentals. It's free, and can be very rewarding for some people, so what is there to lose?

FIRST IMPRESSIONS
I was kind of on board with this game at the start. It was free, so I was going into it with a bit of skepticism. Right off the bat I can see, whether it is or not, it looks like a mobile port. I'm not finicky about graphics, but the menu itself was confusing. The screen was mostly empty space with icons in the corners. What do these icons do? You can't find out without trying them.
VISUALS AND SOUND
I won't dwell on this for very long, because its simply bad. Firstly your character doesn't move, he teleports between the lanes. Okay the graphics are kind of decent otherwise by free to play standards, but the sound design. The music is generic and repetetive, the guns are far too loud, and the ship sounds like the teleporter from Star Trek: TOS (that's kinda cool at first, but like the game, gets annoying).
GAMEPLAY
I'll admit I enjoyed the first half hour or so. Then it grew tedious, to the point that from then on I'd only play while listening to a podcast. There are two ways I can think to describe it. Its either Plants vs. Zombies without plants or Galaga with lanes. That's all there is to say really. There are also gun upgrades and power-ups, which are obtained by spending orbs earned by killing, but they don't seem to really do all that much.
MICROTRANSACTIONS
If you're still with me I'll go on and say that I hate these with a passion. Especially when they can rack up to cost more than the game could possibly be sold for. You can buy the aforementioned orbs with real money. Except I don't see why you would. Even if you enjoy the game, the upgrades are basically what kept me going for as long as it did. What other motivation do you have? Well, I suppose there is one thing...
ACHIEVEMENTS
There are loads! But they're all really grindy. Now, you may be wondering what that ending of the last section was about. Well, there's a microtransaction achievement. Yeah. In order to "complete" this free game, you have to buy something in it. If you weren't already sure about whether you should or shouldn't get this, that should be enough.
FINAL THOUGHTS
Okay maybe its not all bad. It just needs some serious polish, but it would appear the devs have cast it aside. Its free, so you might as well pick it up just to try assuming you have the spare bandwidth.

Some of the puzzles are a little tricky (like the drawer puzzle) but most of them are pretty straight-forward and the answers are given to you simply by playing the game. Plus, there aren't any variations in endings. Even if you mess up on pressing cinematic buttons during cutscenes. there are only minor changes. In all honesty this game should have been great, and a long time ago when it was first released this game was actually great.  Released on the Consoles in 2012, this game was a well polished and much needed intorduction to the MOBA gameplay concept to console players.
The developers were fast and transparent.  The community was alive and everyone was happy.  Somehow the development team slowly changed from being fast and transparent to being non existent and deceitful..
It started with the release of one character, Snaga, he spelled the downfall of this glorious game.  Somehow his release saw a magnitute of glitches and bugs which made the game unplayable, and until that point hadn't existed.  Speed bugs, and gold mode bugs and everything imbetween.
The developers spent the next few months trying and failing to find a fix for the issues caused by Snaga's release.  They released the remaining DLC characters and then went into hibernation mode.
This brings us to the PC release, a new Developer at the helm Zombie studios..  promises were made of fixing all the issues which plagued the Console release and and saw the once great community decimated.
Fast forward almost 2 years later and the PC game is a virtual graveyard.  The game priced at 19.99 is unappealing to new gamers, and the gamers who already own it just flat out have no reason to play it.  If you could write a book on missed potential GOME would be it.
The gameplay itself is really nice, the characters counter each other fairly well, no one character is super OP, the controls and movements are smooth.  The learning curve isn't bad at all, and last but not least you can play as the well known Middle Earth characters..   With that said, I would avoid this game like the plague, if you already own it, idle those cards and remove it from your harddrive, if you don't own it, consider yourself lucky.

Ah, Trine 3...you had the opportunity to be a truly great game, but you turned out to be...just average.
When I first heard that the 3rd Trine game would be 3D, it was essentially an instant buy. The whole concept sounded great and I was very excited to play the finished game.
In practice, the 3D works pretty well now (a lot of the negative reviews seem to be of the beta, before it was all sorted). It's a logical continuation of the 2.5D gameplay and the character's abilities have been adapted to work in a 3D environment very well (though it is worth noting that the change in controls that this necessitates is confusing at first). The graphics have been updated again and the lighting, backgrounds and environments in general are just as beautiful as in the first two.
So where does it fall down? Gameplay length. Making it 3D tripled the production budget, meaning that the gameplay itself had to be shorter - or the game cost more. Frozenbyte chose the former, and unfortunately, that means there's only about 4-6 hrs of gameplay, and it ends on a cliffhanger. This has attracted the ire of a lot of people, and admittedly disappointed me. Nevertheless, what there is is solid gameplay, and Frozenbyte have said they are open to continuing the series after they have reviewed all the criticism.
So...down to a 7/10 or so from me. Really solid gameplay and a great continuation of Trine 1 and 2. The length issue isn't enough to stop me from recommending it, but it still knocks a few points off.

Baldur's Gate: EE is what it says it is: a quick and easy way to get Baldur's Gate running on modern PCs. Beamdog has done an excellent job providing us exactly that, and for folks who have never experienced this seminal CRPG, there is no better way to start. It's not as long as a lot of more recent RPGs like Skyrim--I did a basic runthrough in a little over 35 hours--but it makes up for that in quality. Yes, it's not in 3D and doesn't make use of godrays or post-processing effects, but who cares? The story is intriguing and the NPC companions are some of the best in the genre (and some of the most annoying too). I've always been of the opinion that isometric 2.5D games look great when done well, and this one is no exception. Beamdog's additions, The Black Pit horde mode and new NPCs, are fine but not essential. Where this version really shines is as being a simple way for new players or veterans to visit or revisit this corner of Faerun. Having said that, the $20 asking price is a bit stiff for a 20-year-old game, so you should grab it on sale or in a bundle with Beamdog's other EEs.
And that brings me to Siege of Dragonspear. Bearing in mind that this is Baldur's Gate 1.5, right off the bat, Beamdog made some interesting decisions--Imoen is not given to you as an optional party member but acts as an info-dump character in the beginning and later is said to be training so she can't accompany you on this adventure. I don't know whether there was some behind-the-scenes reason for that, but as a fan of Imoen, I still couldn't disagree with it. In BG II, she was a very handy companion; in BG I, she was pretty weak and useless and had a tendency to gripe a lot. The expansion picks up almost immediately after the end of BG I, in medias res, as it were, with you and some of your old companions hunting down the last remaining followers of Sarevok. This was also a good choice, as it almost immediately gave me this nostalgic sense of "hey, I'm playing brand-new Baldur's Gate!" Once that's wrapped up, you get caught up in the region's battle against a mysterious woman leading a movement to journey to the Nine Hells and release the souls of the victims of two past conflicts. If that sounds weird, it gets weirder. And harder. This is still Baldur's Gate, which means the combat tends to be challenging if not occasionally very difficult on normal settings.
I need to address THAT controversy--the brou-ha-ha surrounding Mizhena, the transgender character in the game. This struck me as an odd controversy years ago and now that I've actually played the expansion, it's a serious tempest-in-a-teapot situation. Mizhena is a cleric who was born a boy and now identifies as a woman. She mentions this, without a significant amount of prompting, when you meet her in the siege camp, where she provides clerical healing services and sells priest scrolls, et cetera. And, that's it. There's no gender-bending-related character sidequest arc because she isn't available as a party member. Unless I'm missing something huge, that's the whole root of the controversy. I have to assume that the people who were upset about this are the same ones who are freaked out by same-sex romances in BioWare RPGs, in which case all I can say is "grow up, losers."
The bigger controversy, in my mind, is the ending. I'm not going to spoil the game here, but suffice it to say that after the big battle is won, your PC ends up with a price on his head and flees the area. This starts to look like a well-developed epilogue to the main story and then the game just abruptly ends. It's really off-putting and genuinely the first time I can remember that a game's ending bothered me in this way. It almost makes it look like the dev just ran out of money and said, "Okay, let's roll credits here." I get that this is a setup for BG II, but it seems hard to believe that it really needed to happen in quite this way.
Dragonspear is worth playing, but, again,  I'd wait for a sale.
Oh, I should also note that Beamdog released a portrait pack last month as a $2 DLC. This seems like something that should have been released for free or included in the main game. It's these kinds of low-content DLC releases that give modern DLCs a bad name.

Some cult classics are timeless. Take Fallout, for example. Every couple years I feel the need to install it again and relive the journey of the Vault Dweller.
Some cult classics don't age well. In its day and age, Baldur's Gate was a breakthrough, an epic journey that brought the magic of a pen-and-paper RPG campaign to the computer screen. But revisiting it after two decades made me realize that, unless you are a game designer, journalist or scholar, there's no reason to play it today. It's not about its age alone: it's about the fact that everything this game did, other games have since did better. There is a whole genre of games that do Baldur's Gate better than Baldur's game itself!
By modern standards, it's very poorly written. The story is a mediocre political thriller with zero depth -- nothing remotely like, say, Planescape: Torment. All the events you see in the wild are simplistic, and do not affect anything later in game. The companions are shallow, with little dialogue -- don't expect deep and nuanced characters like in Dragon Age. And let's not even start talking about the game's mechanics and combat system -- by modern standards, the rules based on D&D 2 edition are horribly archaic and just barely more playable than SSI's Gold Box mathfest.
In short: the game was incredible for its time. But today, whatever you liked about it -- story, combat, exploration, companions -- there are games that do it much better.

My first introduction to RPGs in general was Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn and I never got round to playing the original Baldur's Gate until the Enhanced Edition.
Simply put, if you enjoy classic RPGs, it's fantastic. The interface and resolutions are all updated and modernised for larger screens and work beautifully, the game runs extremely well and the gameplay remains as compelling as ever. It still allows modding so any other perceived failings can potentially be addressed through this route and all told the game is a fantastic package and well worth the money when you consider the vanilla game requires a certain amount of modding to be brought to the same level.
That all said, there are some downsides - the EE NPCs are a little inconsistent, where their quests or personality don't quite fit in, or they're compelling and interesting but mechanically fall short (looking at you, Rasaad). The voice work is top notch, but the writing could be better.
Still, even just as an updated and modernised Baldur's Gate the Enhanced Edition is well worth it and I've now played this more than I have BG2.

The Long Dark is a magnificent survival game with a great exploration experience. In the first attempts to survival you will only explore the nearby areas and you will die really fast. With more experience of the area (you can make a map) you will go further and further. In every step you do you can feel the surrounding rough world. Unlike in other games of this genre you cannot build any houses or other stuff in the world. Everything you find is only there to keep you warm and defend against nature. Furthermore, you have to find food to satisfy your hunger. Therefore you can shoot animals, if you have found a rifle, otherwise you have to live with small amounts of food that you can find in houses or shacks. In every step to find more food you will notice the cold in your back and wolves surrounding you. Its a great experience and the best survival game I've ever played.
I can recommend this game for everyone who likes survival with a good immersion and exploration part.

Dead Effect 2 is a mix of zombies & soliders that are on a space ship. Experiments broke out yada yada you get the jist of it.
You the player get to pick three different type of characters. A heavey gunner, assault or light. Each character has their own names and specific start weapons. You later on can use any type of weapon that is in the game for your character as long your the right level.
Missions- there 15 story mission & 5 Generic missions. You can gain weapons, money, gear & power ups during each mission. You have side quests you gain more money & better rewards.
Other Missions - Biohazard mode, survival mode, lone wolf missions & Infestations offer more play time after you beat the story. The developer has also fixed the online requirement issue so now those who play solo can stay solo. The only issue I have is during survival missions, there are way to many crawlers.
Items- you can get items as rewards or buy them. You can buy medkits, ammo pack ect ect. Hotkeys would have been nice since using items pauses the game.
Gear- gear is basically helmit, chest plate, legs armor & arm armor. These are what helps upgrades your health, stamina and special. Better the gear, better stats. Only issue is when you add a perk, you can't remove it.
Implants- these are upgrades that help with movment speed, aim, stabalization & energy. Same as gear, the higher the better. Still can't remove a perk.
Equip & Unequip- Weapons you get you can equip them to specific slots on your character. Primary weapons ( assault, shot guns, bows ect ect). Secondarys (pistols, mini shotguns & melee) are on your side.
Hacking- the hacking is very cool & fun to do but it would ne nice to have seen a few different ones other then the counting down and lock matching.
Respawning- you can respawn if you die but doing so requires credits (money). You will pick up money during that mission, so its not hurrting your saved money unless you didn't pick up the full amount. If you don't want to lose any moeny then restarting the game is an option you can do.
Weapon Upgrading- you can upgrade every weapon you aquire. You can upgrade the damage, accuacey, magazine, codex and reload. The issues I have with the upgrading is the percentage of the accuacey and reload. A 100% should be almost instant and anything beyond 100% is god like. Heck you accuecy being 150% it like shooting from the other side of the universe and still hitting your target or reloading speed being 120% happens so fast its like you never did it. I was alway told there is no 110% just 100%. Also when adding a codex upgrade, you can't remove it.
Weapons- there are good weapons in the game but after a while its the same weapons just different colors and different stats. Heck I would pay DLC to have weapons from different games being in here.
Zombies- there are different verity of zombies. Some easy & some hard to kill. Its seems headshots are still almost 1 hit kill unless a blood spiter, acid spitter, armor zombies or a dog. Although when killing a TNT, Hungry or Spacer zombie, they will still throw their ability at you even if you quickly kill them.
Soliders are tough to kill but do provide a challeneg. Soliders are more of a threat then the zombies so it's nice to encounter soliders lesser.
Trophies- the game does have trophies you can try to get. I think 177 of them, not to sure.

For a $19.99 game you are getting more, its actually a steal at $19.99. It's VR version is the same but you don't have to worry about some upgrades and you get 2 extra weapon slots. The game does get a 8/10 from me. If you don't have this yet I recommend you go and buy this game right now. If the developer decides to make a Dead Effect 3, I will buy it 1,000%

Don't let this game fool you with it's name and graphics -- after playing it for an hour, you'll be furious, because you won't be able to complete some level in the 2nd zone. You'll be screaming at the game, most likely sluring a lot, yet you'll get weird feeling of a satisfaction after completing the level you've been grinding for the past 15 minutes.
There's really not much to tell about it: it's basically a fast-paced puzzle platformer with weird Japanese graphics and j-pop to pair with. As of the level design, you usually have to grind as hard as you did in Super Meat Boy to complete each zone -- you have to memorize the maneuvers and timings, time your shots and watch your step carefully; hell, late levels are a lot more hardcore than Super Meat Boy, I tell you!
Shooting 4 apples in the air simultaneously, then landing a few inches from spikes, dodging 2 shooters (shooting off their bullets with yours, then shooting them) and jumping from the disappearing platform -- all of that happening in a timespan of 1.5 seconds; that's the harsh reality of this game.
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
Is it worth buying? Hard to say. I'm not a fan of the genre, so I'd rather pass on it if it wasn't in a bundle. But hardcore die-a-lot puzzle platformer fans might find it interesting. So yeah, I'd recommend this game to them.

I got this in a humble bundle, mainly for this game. I was kind of interested in the MOBA genre, but I've always hated how hack and slash dungeon crawlers (diablo) or MOBAs (LoL/Dota) make you move by clicking. I alway say that using WASD would make if for a more engaging experience.
Unfortunately, this game wasn't the one to prove that. as it is mired with a TON of other problems.
-nobody plays it, so expect huge queues to be stuck with 1 or 2 others, and the rest bots
-you level up as other MOBAs, and can level up your abilities like other ones (3 normal abilities and an ultimate 4th). Unfortunately the abilities are TERRIBLE. Basically you want to play as a damage dealing character and you will rule the game. If you play any sort of support, CC, tank, ETC your abilities are just stupid.
- instead of going the awesomenauts route and letting you augment your abilities, or the ever other MOBA route and letting you pick from an array of items in game, you have to use the in game currency outside of combat to put "crystals" on your belt. as the game progresses a bar that is your belt starts to fill up and you unlock the crystals. The problem is you not only decide what crystals, but also the order of the crystals, AHEAD of the game. That would be like picking what items you have in LoL before it starts and what order you will buy them, and then jumping in a game and seeing the enemy has something you didn expect. Ascent - The Space Game is a PvE "sandbox" MMOG which features you in a spaceship so you can mine or fight your way to economic prosperity and the ability to colonize planets anywhere in the galaxy.
For the TL;DR set, some brief highlights, both positive and negative. I've deliberately not attached these labels to these highlights so -you- can decide for yourself what they are.
Overall I recommend this game because I like it.
However, this game may not be for everyone, and I encourage you to read on past the TL;DR point to understand my perspective better.
I've been playing a short time (46 hours over two weeks) and wanted to start a review before the repetitive nature of what I'm doing casts the game in a more negative light than I'd like.  So this is more of a stream of consciousness description for those that want more information or to see where I'm coming from. Note well that I'm not a veteran player, and that my perspective will more closely match a new player's perspective...I feel this kind of perspective is more valuable because a veteran has usually overlooked things that are annoyances and/or game-breakers to most people. These issues obviously don't game break for the vets since....they are still playing
My draw to this game is this: I've learned there is a set of what look like awesome colonization mechanics that appear to make it worth grinding to get to. In studying these mechanics, it seems there's a lot of interesting engineering to be done just to find a spot to colonizxe, let alone manage and maintain your colonies. It seems you have to build and manage environmental domes (unless the atmosphere is perfect) and supply them with the atmospheric gases you need to maintain a habitable environment for your colonists. You have to do this before you can get to any of the good stuff (e.g. growing food, mining resources) that a colony will help you with.
The caveat here is that I can't do any of this neat gameplay yet. I need to make at least a billion or two before I can afford it, plus I need to research a few key factory blueprints and get more settlements up producing goods.
This brings me to my pet peeve of this game...Research.
Researching anything: 24 hours. Increasing the level of something: level * 24 hours. ("Class" is a synonym for "level" in this game). Class 12 gear is what you'll need for the top tier ship that you can get. It will take you over two months (78 days) just to research ONE key ship module to that level. Examples of key modules: weapons, hyperdrives, mining beams, and ram scoops. This means I'm mostly forced to buy these modules from players if I want to make faster progress. (You can argue that I could spend the better part of the year just logging in long enough to cycle my research to the next class. That's ludicrious to me, but technically true.)
This is not game breaking for me, but see above...I have a draw that I want to explore. There have been a couple of discussions in chat about this issue where frustration was expressed and I'm sure new players will find this frustrating. Be ye warned if you want to play. I still think it's worth it, but that's me.
If you are going to research, you'll want to build your starbase quickly. This is going to require cash for blueprints (available via the contracts board) and resources (available from space stations and players). If you want a steady stream of resources (income), you can start building settlements. Settlements, set up correctly, allow one a certain amount of resource income per day. Both settlements and starbases take a bit of work to setup; it's going to take many trips for you if your ship's cargo hold is small. I waited until I had a big enough ship.
Yes, there's repetitive content.
Making money for me was initially about buying low to fill my cargo holds and selling high between space stations, easily reached by the autopilot menu.  Once I had enough money, I could buy the next tier of ship which holds more cargo. This allowed me to make money even faster. If you are new, please discover the "stock market search" in the map screen; this will allow you to find places to buy trade goods even cheaper. At some point, for me this was when I was flying a class 6 ship, trading becomes less lucrative than mining asteroids. I was able to get a relatively inexpensive class 5 mining beam and suddenly I was swimming in lucrative resources. I was able to use contracts (available at space stations) and the previously mentioned stock market search to turn the resources into credits.
So...at the moment, when I want more cash, I go farm asteroids. Repeatedly. I do vary where I do this, and because my cargo hold isn't uber huge (I'm in a hammer atm) I do have to break and go drop off/sell my cargo. It's not bad at all for me, and I -am- what people call "ADD" so I do need lots of stimulus to not be bored.  But this is me.
So, if you like space games, resource factories, economics, and science...this game is definately for you.
I may revisit this review after I've been playing a lot longer.

Great idea for a game,..A very sandboxy PvE universe to explore and build your own little (or big) space empire in.  I honestly really like it and will keep playing, but it has at least a couple big problems that I will deal with for the moment considering it's still early access but it would be a joke if they weren't addressed before the official launch.  It pains me to give a thumbs-down but I will definitely change it if they work on these areas.
1.  The Starship Computers:
Holy Carap!  I don't know if it is meant to be somehow more gritty and "realistic" or if it is just a placeholder until someone gets around to making a menu and/or GUI interface.
The current situation involves a command console type interface (think DOS or UNIX) to interrogate the computer for a lot of important information and functions especially when it comes to exploration.  It takes like 40 keystrokes to do what should be done in 4.  In terms of gritty it doesn't get much better than this but in terms of realism I think in an age of faster than light travel they would have a post-Apollo interface for their computer systems.  Getting to the point of making your own probes and figuring out what all the data means is hard enough...having to beat the info out of the computer is just plain unnecessary.  They certainly don't have to dump the console for people who want to think they are computer scientists, but a more user friendly option should be available for the rest of us living in the 21st century.
2.  Chat Channel:
...as in singular chat channel for the whole universe.
No trade chat, no private chat...group or otherwise, no in game e-mail system....Wow!  You'd think that kind of stuff would be in any MMO on day 1.
3.  Galactic Market (player auction house)
Apparently the galactic market computer system is much more advanced than the on board ship computers because at least you don't have to shop via command console LOL.
...but...
The only way to search items is by keyword, quantity, and price point.  Also, only 1 page can be displayed so if there are more results that you want to see you have to narrow your search to get them on the first page.
The Good:
1.   Friendly Community
2.  Working Economy
3.  Not overly buggy or crashy
4. Generally playable and fun
5.  Freemium model at $3/month is reasonable

One of the best and most interesting puzzle-type games I've ever played. It starts off quite simple and naturally builds a lot of depth as more elements are added and as you discover more creative ways to use what you already have. The levels have no fixed solution and the amount of flexibility and freedom you have is staggering, so you're left to just find the best solution you can, without being railroaded into some design the developer thought of, like in so many other games.

This games rewards the best possible thing: ingenuity. Many games put their emphasis on reflexes, accuracy, muscle memory or memorized patterns, SpaceChem concentrates on just using your brain. The puzzles may seem impossible on the first glance but little by little, step by step, you start to unravel it and the solution starts to become clearer or clearer. There is no one way to handle the problem: there are time efficient solutions, there are resource efficient solutions and there are creative solutions. You never think that, "Oh, this is what the designer wanted me to think!"-moments but every solution feels like an accomplishment be it created with ruthless efficiency in mind or if you just want to see those atoms move elegantly in the reactor.
This game is a diamond. It looks rough and it concentrates on one thing but it does so damn well.

Despite having a decent PC, the load times were irritating, but quickly forgotten in the very well-done story missions. The side missions punctuate every failure with a load screen, which quickly drained my patience. The fluid visuals and witty use of space throughout every level is something to be proud of, but the game left me wanting more. Seriously, this game cuts off so abruptly that I went back to check for anything I might have missed, thinking that I might find the other half of the game. Nope. None to be found. Trine 3 is fantastic while it lasts, then ends with a drunken stumble rather than a big finale. This is an understandable budget problem, but I can't help but grade the material that was provided, and this was all I got.

For those who have played the original Baldur's Gate:
- Graphics now fit full-screen without looking stretched (as much as possible in a nearly twenty year old game)
- Includes both Baldur's Gate and Tales of the Sword Coast
- New area: The Black Pits (focuses on arena-style combat rounds, with a plot line)
- New DLC as of 2016: Siege of Dragonspear (takes place between BG1 and BG2)
- Some improvements carried back from BG2 (but I would just be quoting from the game description)
- Big selling point for me? You can organize your journal to track quests properly! I hated having to scroll through the entire journal in the original game in order to remember what I was supposed to be doing (and I'm sure I'm not the only one), especially if I had left the game for more than a week.
For those who have never played the original:
- CRPG (pen and paper adaptation to computer game)
- Utilizes Dungeons and Dragons 2nd Edition classes, lore, and rules (option to display 'rolls' in scrolling text window)
- A lot of dialogue to read, no voice acting beyond the narrator between chapters and click/movement activation (I know many now prefer hearing instead of reading when long bits of dialogue are dropped on you).
- Pick-and-choose up to five party members to join as you meet them (it is possible for choices and dialogue interactions to cause them to leave you permanently, so keep alignment in mind)
- Can control the level up and skill distribution of all party members, or set it to automate (good for new players or those unfamiliar with D&D system)
- Perma Death is optional, may set it so characters only faints in battle
- Much steeper difficulty curve than present day RPGs
- Requires strategic thinking over brute strength (dodging traps, exploiting weaknesses, spell conservation, etc.)
- Gives minimal guidance in terms of plot/solving the quests; you will need to pay attention to dialogue and your journal entries to track them (although the journal is much more useful/specific than in the original game)
My positive recommendation comes from the fact that I'm a huge fan of this genre, and this company's adaptations of D&D lore and rulesets is very well done. If you liked games such as Pillars of Eternity or Divinity:Original Sin, this is where the inspiration came from. While simpler than their modern counter-parts, this is a classic game that challenges the player to use more than brute-strength and puts emphasis on exploring to find or solve quests.

Baldur's Gate remains the best RPG I have ever played.  Honestly, coming back to this game was like coming home.  I had the hardest time just picking a party.  I wanted to play with every character: experience the familiar ones, try out the 'new' ones, see if I could enjoy the 'useless' ones I never bothered much with before.  In the end: Imoen, Khalid, Minsc and Jaheira, because, yeah.  Irenicus.
Sure, playing it again, as a slightly more mature adult, the writing isn't the ultimate essense of perfect perfection I once thought, but it's clear to see that this is the game that set the mold so many less-clever developers have tried to fit into in the years since.
True, I see some things that I would have changed with the Enhanced Edition (Minsc is still a Ranger, even though Barbarian and Berserker were added to the class lineup, and at 15 constitution he's whining about needing rest before his witch and has a pretty meh stat-line in all), but that's okay though Minsc.  You just hold onto Boo and keep breaking every single two-handed sword I find 6 to 24 seconds into combat.  Love you.  Love this game.
A classic in every sense of the word.
What you need to know if you're a new player:
I'm running the game on Windows 10 (64 bit?  Did they even release it in 32?  Whatever) -NO WORKAROUNDS NEEDED.  That's right: a classic game that can run on a modern machine without having to dig up some old .dll file referenced in a forum archive from six years ago.  Just download and play.
The rules are an old form of D&D, and confusing as hell: -6 AC is good?  1/2 attack a round?  Speed factor?  There are some good, free guides out there though, and most of them are relatively well-written by people who love the game.  I'd read up on some basics, at least get a good sense of what spells are useful before trying to play as a sorceror.  Just don't pay attention to their absolute dictation about which classes are 'best' and which are 'worst' unless you get your joy out of power gaming.  Without doubt, some are more usefull than others, but you CAN play the game as a Bard, if you want to.
There is a lot to read.  And what I mean is, there is very little voice narration to the game.  If you can't read a block of well-written dialogue text and enjoy it, you may as well steer clear.  I'd recommend you give it a shot anyway -broaden your horizons, but who am I kidding, right?
The combat starts out slow.  Painfully slow.  Until you level up a few times (or power game), you'll spend a lot of time watching characters swing weapons and hit nothing but air.  It's a bit off-putting.  Despite being older and more patient, I found myself turning on story-mode just to speed the action up a bit (until I discovered how ridiculously over powered the Ranger-Archer subclass is in BGEE).
Last but not least: grab a back-up weapon.  Dat iron do.

Years later and I'm still amazed at how much I love this game. Someone I know was playing it and I took mild interest in it, bought it for myself, then was swept away almost immediately.
-Gameplay
The basis for the game is simple to learn, more difficult to master. If you have played a "tower defense" style game before, you will already be ahead in what to expect. There are different difficulties and different modes of play (shown as different ships). There is enough variety to keep you coming back, especially with the "roguelite" elements.
-Story
There isn't much of a story going on. Depending on which characters you bring along, you may find out more about certain relationships as you try to escape the depths of your ship. Despite being a choose-your-own-involvement level of story, they did a good job of making me interested in it. I found myself wondering if the other Endless games had clues to why we crashed, or what happened after we escape.
-Graphics
Now we are getting to where Dungeon of the Endless really shines. In an age full of people trying to pass off lazy pixel art as an homage to retro graphics, it is lovely to see people who put actual care into their art. From the characters, to the layouts, the logbook, to the backgrounds, everything feels well loved. My favorite parts are the different ambient elements inside he different ship sections. It is easy to lose sight of such things in the middle of the fray, but when you have a moment, you can see just how much atmosphere is in the air.
-Music
The best part about this game, hands down. I mentioned the atmosphere before, how the visual artists packed plenty of it into every pixel. Now what really sets it off: The soundtrack. FlyByNo has composed a soundtrack that has rocketed its way into my top 5 (possibly even top 3) video game soundtracks of all time. This is incredible to me, as my tastes tend to stick with nostalgia. It is easy to rank FlyByNo alongside other contemporary greats such as Darren Korb of Bastion fame, with his beautiful soundscaping, or Simon Viklund, a man who can weave loops and tracks into a game seemlessly. If the game doesn't sell you, try the soundtrack anyway.
-Downsides
This game is not without flaws:
*The biggest one would be difficulty. Personally, I find the difficulty to be spot on. "Easy" mode is "Hard" in this game and "Too Easy" is "Normal". If you are a fan of strategy, "Easy" will be fine. If you just want to get through and experience the game "Too Easy" may still pose a formidable challenge, but you have more resources to start, more per turn, and other small perks to help you through. With enough effort and attention paid, the game shouldn't bar less skilled players from completing it. Listing this anyway because not everyone shares the same views on difficulty.
*Multiplayer. The online multiplayer must've been added as an afterthought. There are certain bugs that are only present in multiplayer and they can be doozies. Finding other players is difficult if you do not have a friend in mind to play with either. I would suggest making sure you and your friend can play for the entire duration of one game, as there are some saving quirks as well. If you go into multiplayer knowing these things, it should be less frustrating but far from stellar.
*Variety. Earlier I said the game can keep you coming back due to the variesty, but no matter how many characters or how many ships there are, the core gameplay can be repetitive. After solving some of the best winning strategies, I found myself planning new games around "How can I best reach this same sort of winning state with what I currently have?" Some of the structures you can make seem essential, while a select few seem nearly useless. Don't go into this game expecting the gameplay to drastically evolve on repeated playthroughs.
I give this game a solid 8 out of 10. It could be a 9 if there was a bit more polish in the programming department, but I don't think it could ever hit a 10 due to many runs feelign the same. A game I would recommend to anyone while also knowing it will not be everyone's cup of tea.

I'd turned up my nose to so many "classic" PC games in the past, stupidly thinking that modern graphics were the be-all end-all. Funny, considering my all-time most memorable gaming moments happened in games like Call of Duty 1, Battlefield 1942, and Guild Wars 1.
Not being a DnD player, and thoroughly despising the vast majority of ARPGs and MMOs, the entire combat system in Baldur's Gate is a huge breath of fresh air. It's gotten me so interested in DnD that I'm going to my first ever DnD night, all because of BG!
This game has also piqued my curiosity for a whole generation of PC gaming classics, some of which I know I can play through Steam, and some of which I'll have to find alternate means of playing. Who the hell needs so-called AAA gaming when so much of it is rubbish, and "retro" games like the BG series can keep you hooked for hours and hours.
In-game, I haven't even reached the city of Baldur's Gate, and yet I feel like this game has more than paid for itself a dozen times. I'm already planning how to roll my next character - a lawful evil Elvish mage. Would be nice to not have Dorn leave my party on account of my heroic rep.
TL;DR: Thank you Baldur's Gate for opening my eyes to a whole generation of classic games that will provide me years of gaming joy.

This is a fantastic game. It can simultaneously be beautiful, awe inspiring, terrifying, and gripping.
For the longest time, this game was built around a sandbox survival mode experience, which is very fun. The difficulty ranges from tricky to impossible. While the large number of survival tactics and mechanics will take time to learn, once you have an idea of how to play, the survival mode becomes a whole lot of fun. Be aware though, this game will give you an unstoppable fear of wolves.
The recent addition of an episodic story mode is also fantastic. The progression of the story trains you in the various mechanics the game has to offer, and provides  you with familiarity of the different maps in the game. While many missions can get tedious, gathering X kg of wood/food/meat/fish for the current NPC you're interracting with, the steady depletion of resources and beautiful atmosphere makes the grind manageable if not fun.
Beyond the gameplay elements, the artistic style of the game is on point. The graphics are simplified, yet they capture the beauty of the wintery north. The almost oil paint like asthetic meshes well with the theme. The music is another fantastic element. While not in your face, the score is beautifully sad and creeps in at just the right times to be especially meaningful.
While the harder modes for the sandbox might not be for non-masochists, the story mode and some of the easier difficulties are well worth the price of admission.

I stopped playing after like two weeks. Also, the game is officially no longer receiving updates. Old review below.
I played a lot on PS4 but as the playerbase got smaller and updates stayed infrequent I got tired of it. But after f2p I'm seeing a lot of new faces and a much more active community. The balance changes make teamplay a little bit easier while still leaving a lot of space for skill to take over. It seems like there's a bit less to worry about for newer players since support's situational cloak was replaced with a straightforward shield tool and the mobile arena is now usable to all players. The dome also never goes up unless the monster is caught, which might take away from the "hardcore" side of the game but was definitely a necessary change to pick up the pace of the game, especially for beginners who don't yet understand the map layouts and aren't that good at cutting off the monster.
Yet again though, the game still does not teach enough about your roles. It makes the game look much shallower than it actually is from the outside. Yeah you're the trapper, so you find the monster, but you have a responsibility to use your tools (slow grenades, harpoons etc.) to slow down the monster during the fight. Yeah you're an assault, you shoot the monster up and all that, but you also need to be using your mines or toxic grenades to force the monster away from your allies in a pinch. So what you find is a bunch of hunters only doing one job when they generally should be doing two, and playing a really boring messy version of evolve because the game doesn't go out of its way to teaach you the fundamentals. It's no wonder a lot of people thought it was a simple repetitive game for this reason. It's a great game, but only if you can invest some time and watch a couple of beginner's guides to a couple classes to understand the real role each character has, because it's the first step to actually enjoying the game.
You might have to work a little to understand the nuances at first, but it becomes a GREAT game once you understand the fundamentals. It's free, and can be very rewarding for some people, so what is there to lose?

Lovely Planet is a game that literally takes the phrase "Don't judge a book by its cover" to a whole new level.
On the surface the game looks cute, innocent, forgiving and would probably only be enjoyable for kids under 8.
But that's just what the developers want you to think...
This game requires a good amount of trial and error, memorization, patience, quick reflexes... and did I say patience?
Lovely Planet has one goal, you have to reach the pink beam at the end of the stage without dying or killing innocent jelly people (that also shoot back at you occasionally).
Got it? Good, because there's more to it then just that!
The game features five worlds and about 16~23 stages in each of them. When you first start out, the game's just telling you to go from point A to point B with almost no resistance in-between.
Quickly it goes from being hilariously easy to 'moderately' difficult as they introduce:
-Jelly people that shoot back (some of them you can't actually hit or you will instantly lose).
-Apples that can't hit the ground.
-Timed mines.
-Homing bullets.
-Fog that limits your vision.
-Ice that freezes you in place for a couple seconds.
-A lot of restarting....
Once you start getting into the groove of things though the game does actually get really enjoyable. Restarting will become second nature and you will probably be getting used to not knowing what's around every corner, or where every apple is falling in the stage at any given moment.
Lovely Planet gets compared a lot to games like Quake/Serious Sam with its fast-paced fps nature, Beautiful Katamari with its aesthetics, and Super Meat Boy with its emphasis on speedrunning.
The game has a beautiful soundtrack that during the frantic, heart-pounding gameplay tries to keep you calm and relaxed. All the while you're fighting back the urge to not break your mouse/keyboard (or controller) over that shot you missed that was ever-so slightly off mark on the last thing before the stage was about to end...
I'd highly recommend Lovely Planet but it is a short game, so unless you know you're going to be replaying stages for better times/stars or going for some of the achievements then just wait for a decent sale.

Missing: An Interactive Thriller is an episodic Full Motion Video. I’ve never played an FMV before so Missing popped my FMV cherry on that regard and boy was it a great experience.
We start the game with David, a seemingly innocent man, who is kidnapped for reasons undetermined as of yet. He is thrown into an abandoned building where he must use his wits to solve the obstacles that bar his way. All the while, taunting words and pictures of his family are littered all around him as he traversed through the corridors of his prison. Is his family captured as well? Where are they?
Curiously enough, I believe his captor is leaving these breadcrumbs, a trail of clues that actually aids David rather than hinder him on his quest and we are shown that perhaps this is some kind of twisted test that he must passed in order to continue and see his family.
While this is happening to David, in the outside world, we delve into the role of Lambert, a detective who might be in charge of the case involving David’s disappearance. There seems to be a string of cases like David’s and Lambert is determined to find him.
I wasn’t expecting much so it surprised me that I actually liked it. I beat Episode 1 in an hour or so but game time will vary, depending on how fast you solve the puzzles (which are fair and I thought some were clever). Most of the time, puzzles consists of searching for items and inserting them to their correct spot. They’re self-explanatory.
There are QTEs but all are pretty simple, achievable with just a click of a mouse so all hope is not lost. Perhaps this is just me but I was getting this Heavy Rain vibe. I won’t spoil that game for anyone but essentially, David’s kidnapping seems very personal to his captor. That’s just me and we shall see on the next episode.
For the base price of 4.99, it may not be worth it to some because of the game’s short length, so it might be best to wait for a sale or at least wait for the full package because all the episodes will probably be bundled together. However, if you’re a fan of FMVs, I highly recommend it.
Anyways, here’s my video of me fooling around in the game. If you also need help with the puzzles (which I doubt you will) the solutions are in the video description.

Spacechem has one of the worst tutorials ever. It doesn't really help much in terms of teaching you the controls or how to play the game or the concepts that you need to think about to solve the puzzles. It even unintentionally teaches you some bad habits that unnecessarily clutter up your solutions and make things harder on yourself.
However it's still an amazing puzzle game if you're willing to put the effort into it. While many puzzle games are designed to require a very specific order of steps to solve them, Spacechem is more of a sandbox. You work on your own to learn new mechanics hands on through experimentation, then you can try to think about how best to apply the concepts with meticulous planning or just try to work through it with trial and error and  gradually refining your solution until you find something that works. And as long as it works, it doesn't really matter how efficient your solution is (though you can always try to improve your work). So maybe the tutorial being bad isn't as big a deal as it might seem at first (assuming it doesn't turn you off the game completely).

Game is Good for its current early access state. It combines an open universe, resource manangement, exploration, and a little combat. The free content in the game is limited though.
The universe is a PVE environment so there is no worry about end gamers getting board and one shotting the little newbe's, like happons in EVE online a good deal. The non-hostile world is very relaxing, you travel, mine astroids, manage your holdings, make money, spend more money, make upgrades with little to stress you out.
You can do anything in game you want, although you really can't get away from mining, at least not until later in the game when you own a lot of production, and even then the late game is when mining is most productive.
Making money can be be easy most of the time, you can take contracts to buy and sell goods, deliver people to other places, but mining tends to best for time verses money.  There are 2 main astroid belts in the core systems, the roid respawn rate is good but there is usually an over abundence of people in the belts competing for the good ones.  Its best to get out of the core systems to make mining less crowded, though early game your mining with suck too much to make the long hauls worth while. You will be able to buy plots of land on the core planets and set up resource gathering, each core planet supports a different resource type. These plots take a lot of time, money, resources, and planning to get set up. Its best to reseach this aspect of the game before blindly dropping buildings down. Same applys to your first space station, early game the only thing your spacestation dose i suck you dry of money and materials. One day mine will make things but for now i have spent a weekend marathon gathering what i need to make the 6 buildings its supports, it will likly be another week or so before it produces anything.
The combat is clunky early game, later when you have access to turrets and broadsides it might be better but i am not there yet. There is only 1 location at this time where you can fight, and have to start missions to get the enemys to spawn. There are no hostile forces anywhere except that one system, and you cannot run into them accidentally. So thats nice in many ways, though i would not mind a couple of pirate systems where there is more combat to be had.
The game is a grind, its take a good deal of time and resources to get anything done, but your ability to procure stuff tends to scale with you as you progress in the game. For example early game the idea of mining 1000 ore for a project is brutal but later in the game you can mine that and more off 1 astroid.
The community does not seem overly large but is generally helpful. At this time there tends to be a good amount of "help the new guys" mentalitly out there, it's not uncommon for someone to sell you their ship cheaply when they get a new one. The market however is driven by the players and in the week i have been playing has been driving to rather insane levels. In the first few days of the game for me one of the ships i wanted was running around 100k, a good grind for my skill level and equipment. Now after only a week the average price for the same ship is hovering around 1mil. The ship is not worth half that but thats the nature of these games.  You have to be patient when buying and wait for good deals or just suck it up and pay ripeoff prices. Late game vehicles are a different story, the price tag can hit the billions mark but for the time and resources thay take its understandable.
You must watch ship your buying, there are real A-holes out there who can ripe you off, a ship must have every peice of equipment on it to leave space dock, (with the exception of weapons and hyperdrives). There are people out there who will look at the average price of the ships of that type and put one up for sale very cheaply, many people seeing the low cost buy it up quickly thinking they got a good deal. When you click on a ship in the galactic market watch out for a red warning at the bottom of the ship data, the warning will tell you and ship cannot fly becuase its missing a piece or peices of equipment. If it something like a mining laser or armor its no big deal and you can take those off your current ship. if the item is a ship teir specific item like a reactor the ship is junk. Most of the ships systems have to match the level of that ship, so you cannot take stuff form a smaller ship to put on it. At this time you cannot sell ships to the AI only to other players, so once you upgrade you leave your old ship where ever you picked up the new one at. There is not a way to bring all your ships to one location so a common tactic, once you have a space station running, is to part at your station, build a shuttle and take the shuttle to pick up your new baby.
There are a number of things that annoy new players, the tutorials can be a little vague and do not explain what to do clearly much of the time, those of us to game a lot get through them fine but many flood chat with the same questions over and over. You are frequently told to go to the Wiki or check online, i find both those lacking. Much of the time you will not find the information you need online or on the wiki.....(least not on google seachs anyway)(anyone know of a real seach engine so i can stop the google uselessness).
The game is only arond $20, it also offers a subscription. If your going to play this game seriously your going to need to pay.  For Non-prem players you can own anyship you can buy or build, but are limited to Class 5 equipment (Equipment goes to class 12 i think). You can buy and use higher class equipment but it will only function as class 5. Mining at class 5 is good for early to mid game but for end game needs will not cut it. Your starbase is limited to 6 buildings without premium, once again good enough for early game but not acceptable for late game unless you like projects taking several real world months to complete. You cannot make colonies in the outer systems unless you have premium. So there is a lot of pay to get anywhere in this game.  At this time there are no micro transactions though, you can't buy ships, resourced and such with real money, all has to be aquired in-game with in-game money. I guess this game is larger an MMO of sorts.
I like the game but have already started making spreadsheet and such to manage my small and pathentic empire, so yes the game is already becoming work. I have not decided if i want to pay the subscription or not and thus contiune playing. But at the point i am at in game the lack of premuim is not hurting me yet, one more ship upgrade and i will have to make the money decision though.

Ascent is a truly wonderful game, offering the most pure fun I’ve had with any game in a very long time. I enjoy building slowly to develop self-sufficiency, but, in the four months I’ve played, I have been the recipient of much kind advice and an occasional helping hand. I have to echo what so many others have said, this game has a great, caring community.
Jam is an incredibly talented developer. I am grateful that he has kept true to his own vision which, I think, has produced the coherence and scale we see already in this relatively early stage of the game. Yet he is very responsive to player experience and ideas. That makes it much easier to be patient when glitches arise, as they must, during the development process. We know Jam will address them.
As to gameplay, I am able to immerse myself in the game’s premise, that we are struggling to recover and rebuild the high civilization we’ve lost. As a number of other players have done, I have developed my own tools, primarily spreadsheets, catalogs and calculators, to record my own exploration and production data. What has been for some an inconvenience has been for others an element of realism.
At the same time, I am able to engage the community’s meta-game, expressed on the forum and wiki, in the lively chat flow, and now, perhaps, here in the Steam forum.
Finally, Ascent is the kind of game that allows me to step back when RL demands. When I return, I’ve suffered no loss.  Jam has added new features. My colonies have kept producing. My fellow players have devised new plans and projects, all of which enhance my game.
It’s just pure fun.

Serious Sam HD: The First Encounter is a remake of Serious Sam: The First Encounter, as you could guess. It was released in 2009 by Croteam and was also known as the first game to use Serious Engine 3. And yep, as serious as ever.
It also came out on X360 through Xbox Live service. The only difference that I am aware of is that it had multiplayer only up to 4 players and aim assist.
Multiplayer community seems to be dead. Okay, maybe not completely, I did get into some match once at one day. But in other times server list is completely empty. And it makes sense, since Serious Sam HD: The Second Encounter has Fusion feature which means that owners of SSHD:TFE get to have Egypt levels to be ported into that game. So instead most of people play in SSHD:TSE.
Premise of original Serious Sam is that Sam Stone is sent into past into Egypt to try to stop the Mental forces before they destroy the Earth. And to do this he would need to pass many levels that have sections designed to serve as arenas to lock players inside. You didn't have as much exploration as in Doom or whatever Quake clone game. Instead it was more focused in pacing and tactical choices during combat itself, with encounters lasting few waves, as enemies keep pressuring you to move around. There were a lot of different enemy types and you had a lot of different specialized weapons, so you would have to choose correct gun for each sitatuation, prioritize targets and avoid all the different attacks. It's a classic!
HD is surprisingly faithful to the original. I kinda expected it to change a lot of core gameplay, but Croteam is just a honest indie company and gave a game just a nice graphics upgrade. Gameplay is almost same and the awesome soundtrack is completely identical. It's quite nice! And yep, even included Karnak from demo version, just like original. No technology test though.
And yea, it looks excellent, with much more natural looking desert and canyons. And if you take a careful look then you will see that some details that was just part of texture is now actual geometry, for example. Though, environment feels not fully finished, as inner places didn't get any additional details and some models seemed to have same textures quality, like statues, despite having more destruction phases. Just good nice new rendering with new light. Though I do wonder about some changes. For example, Alley of Spinxh levels is always at night and the third level of tomb has a fog changed from nice blue color to some dusty brown. As if Egypt doesn't have enough brown color with all sand.
But hey, look at all those great shiny weapons. And look at all the remade enemy models, now with ragdolls. Gore and weapons effects just got sexier, as you can now even gib part of enemies bodies, dismembering them, splitting apart, blowing head off with shotgun. It's awesome. Just look at the bull's death, where it would still slide around after being shot, leaving a trail of blood! And heavier enemies now can even be gibbed with a cannon, the heaviest weapon you have. The only strange thing is that Skeleton Kleers and Harpies are always gibbed upon death. For skeletons it looks good. But for harpies it looks strange, even gibs looks like just a few tiny chunks.
It also got some nice editing on gameplay. Some beheaded have a saw on their heads, giving them a melee attack. Bomberman looks fancy with that head on a spike, even. And heavy biomechanoids only shoot a single rocket when close to player, to let him have it easier, while it almost always was a certain death being very close to one in original. Kamikazes also seem to have smaller radius of explosion too. Flying gnaars seem to be more dangerous, not stopping when attacking. And weapons switch was made faster, which I approve. Though for some reason you can't walk anymore. Not that it ever was needed, just fancy.
If there is one thing I am most thankful the most is that new Netricsa messages notification is put somewhere to the side of a screen and doesn't grab your attention so you can ignore it easily. It was freaking annoying to be visually nagged by it everytime I killed each enemy types while playing custom maps in original.
Though, not everything is going perfect and some cuts had to be made. Most noticeably is that some of obscure engine features of Serious Engine 1 weren't implented in Serious Engine 3. Due to this, all the gravity-changing shenagians had to be cut. To be honest, I don't miss them too much, in Serious Sam 1 they were used only as funny thing in a bunch of a secrets, plus once non-secret usage in a secret level. It probably costed more time to reimplent them for something so small. I mean, at least when Croteam was making the first Serious Sam they had plans to make it much bigger game, with futurustic levels which would abuse gravity features. Once they cut it all to be Egypt-only, well, it was pretty much funky leftover.
It also doesn't have mirror and sliding surface, which I remember used only once.
They also seemed to screw up weapon balance slightly. You see, minigun was made to shoot two times slower, but each bullet does two times damage and is supposed to consume two ammo. But it only consumes one. Result: There is no more reason to use Thompson and you effectively have two times more ammo for minigun than in original. Oh well.
But hey, at least Laser gun isn't glitched in HD. It would sometimes start shooting only at half-speed in original. So flaw taken, flaw given.
And multiplayer is still awesome. Didn't get to cooperative, but I bet it's same spam, with same cutscene-skipping. And competetive part is awesome, still fast-paced. Although I noticed that rocket-jumping got nerfed and jumping off the slope doesn't give you additional height. But you are supposed to use knife to run fast and it still gets you in many places. And yep, still awesome arena-shooter which proves that you don't need some fancy strafejumping to be balanced and fast-paced.
Oh yea, and double shotgun in original was shooting at double speed. In HD it's same as in single-player/coop. Not sure what I think of it, but I think I like it this way. But maybe I need more experience with both ways.
Oh yea, and did you know that original The First Encounter was particulary embaressing due to having only a single DM level? Thankfully, HD added a bunch of them, even including Little Trouble from The Second Encounter. Hm, though HD multiplayer doesn't have scorematch mode, only fragmatch. But no one, absolutely no one, was playing scorematch in original anyway, so nah.
Overall, not perfect, but damn excellent HD remake with a bit of balance editing, untouched core gameplay, some environment upgrade and great gore system.
And yes, those who want to play Egypt levels in Serious Sam HD: The Second Encounter have to have this game purchased.

DISCLAIMER:  I played Serious Sam HD: TFE inside of Serious Sam HD: TSE, so I've logged more time than Steam would suggest.
The first two Serious Sam games were pretty novel when they were first released.  As Sam, players ran through massive levels, fighting similarly massive groups of (often massive) enemies.  It wasn't exactly the most radical idea on paper, but it was executed on a
that was previously unheard of in FPS games.  Levels often had over a thousand enemies, with fights pitting hundreds of opponents against the player simultaneously; a few enemies were even larger than
in other FPS games.
Since then, several of the games Serious Sam has (inevitably) been compared to have caught up to Sam's scope--for instance, there are countless Doom "slaughter" WADs that will throw hundreds or thousands of enemies at you.  But whereas most of Doom's arsenal was never really intended to contend with thousands of enemies, Sam's was built from the ground up with mass extinction in mind, and its bestiary was designed for enormous arena battles.
Weapons are your primary means of interacting with the world in an FPS and, in the case of Serious Sam, the arsenal is especially rock solid.  You begin with the typical pistol(s) and combat knife, but it isn't long before you're fielding double-barreled shotguns, miniguns, laser rifles, and even an enormous cannon.  Virtually every firearm fills a niche and will find ample usage--especially on higher difficulties.  Rockets might travel further to snipe distant stationary targets, but the grenade launcher can charge up significantly faster projectiles and shoot around corners; the laser gun doles out tremendous damage up front, but its projectiles take time to travel through the air; the minigun's hitscan shots can mow down faraway crowds, but its ever-so-slight wind-up is a liability in close quarters.
The guns generally feel great to use, as well.  With an appropriate thunderclap, the double-barreled shotgun reduces Kleer to bone fragments; the SBC Cannon's VW Bug-sized shots blast through enemies like so many bowling pins and wipe swathes of the battlefield clean.
Enemies are well-designed, too.  Unlike later installments in the Serious Sam series, TFE and TSE don't make the mistake of having numerous hitscan enemies.  Rather, most opponents produce a variety of physical projectiles--some follow you, some scatter, some cut through the air in small volleys, and some lazily fly towards their target--that can be
and
.  That one factor is crucial because it means that dodging can keep you alive even when fighting a hundred foes.  Indeed, Serious Sam almost feels like a sort of "bullethell"-FPS at times, and by encouraging fancy footwork over taking cover, the game maintains a higher degree of momentum than many modern FPS games.  The sheer variety of enemies can be a refreshing change of pace from the standard/heavy/sniper trifecta that so many FPS games like to focus on nowadays.
Then there are the levels:  They're huge, and they're especially gorgeous in the HD versions.  While TFE focuses exclusively on an Egyptian-themed mapset, it still includes some beautful setpieces including sprawling palaces, moody moonlit stretches, and Oases.  It certainly doesn't hold a candle to TSE's greater variety, but it does its best.  The maps are
full of secrets--some obvious and some devious--as well as easter eggs and entire hidden levels.  If you're a completionist, be prepared to spend a lot of time hunting down some of these secrets.
Given the size and scale of eveything, one of Serious Sam's biggest selling points is (perhaps unsurprsingly) its co-op support.  Up to 16 players can take on the campaign(s) in TFE and TSE, with a wide variety of player skins to choose from.  You've never really experienced everything a classic FPS has to offer until you're bunnyhopping across massive sand dunes, gunning down waves with half a dozen other players who look like cyborgs, neon cowboys, and Santa Claus.  In fact, there are several different co-op modes including a "Coin-Op Co-Op" arcade-style points/lives system that helps strike a nice balance between players having infinite lives and the level being over for a player the moment they die.
Honestly, I played countless hours of the original TFE and TSE years ago and I still feel that I got my money's worth with the HD remakes.  While they run on earlier versions of the Serious Sam 3 engine than Serious Sam: BFE, they're still perfectly capable of squeezing out some fantastic graphics.  And if you're planning to run TFE HD on an older computer, the sheer number of graphics options will let you tweak everything until it's just right.
In conclusion, I'd happily recommend TFE HD to anybody who has enjoyed Serious Sam in the past, who is interested in taking a breather from modern FPS's, or who is simply interested in exploring what is now widely considered a "Classic FPS".

I like Trine 3.  Despite all of the negative reviews, I bought the game because I like Frozenbyte's esthetics, as displayed in Trine 1 & 2, and because while playing 1 & 2, I kept wishing the player characters could move into the scenery instead of staying stuck in 2D.
Looking over the negative reviews, the complaints fall into these categories:
I found Trine 3 to be graphically beautiful.  The puzzles are pretty easy compared to other platform games, but I enjoyed the scenery enough that I didn't mind.  Attempting to avoid a spoiler, one section has simulated paper...  It is inspired; I hope to see this again in the future.
I enjoyed the 3D environment. Despite being an 'on-a-rail' type of game, there is enough freedom to explore. You can take a break to look around and appreciate the view.  You can't get the camera to show every location your player can reach, such as behind buildings, but there is nothing hidden there so it doesn't really matter. You can walk of cliffs and die. So try to avoid it (like in real life).  One minor complaint is in multiplayer, when a player dies, the 'ghost' of the player sometimes levitates to a location ahead of the other players, so you might have to wait a bit before another player can reach your ghost to resurrect it.
You can map the commands to the buttons and keys of your choice, which I always appreciate since I don't use the standard WASD mapping.
Using PC keyboard and mice it took my group a few tries to defeat the end game boss. I think a controller would have been easier, especially for jumping in non-cardinal directions.  But even one younger player who is typically easily frustrated, didn't even think of giving up.  I expect we will replay this again, like we did Trine 1 and 2.
Note to Frozenbyte: You can't please everybody. You took a risk to go to 3D. You learned from it. I hope you don't give up on 3D because I enjoy it and I think you did it right.  I bought three copies at full price and we weren't disappointed.  If you try again with Kickstarter, I'll be there.  Hopefully you'll get enough cash to work out more bugs and avoid some of the negative reviews.  Some people complained they didn't like some of the voice acting.  After listening to some poor English overdubs of Anime, I had no problems at all with your voice cast.

Here we have a game that offers you a deep and complex gameplay where your choices matter. Do you explore an extra room in the same direction for a chance to get that sweet loot for your character? Should you spend your valuble food now to level up your character or save it later for the potenially great character for hire? Do I focus on building more industry or do I build more turrets?
You will keep asking yourself if you made the right choice and this is a game best played with one or more friends. It combines the turn based element of some strategy games giving you plenty of time to think things through. At the same time, when you have decided it's time to move on by either entering a new unexplored room or to simply start hauling that crystal, well you better be prepared. Things go into real time then. It has a procedurally generated maps and what you find after you open a door is quite heavy on the RNG. But it does not feel like the game is badly balanced as it gives you plenty of room for control. It grants a unique blend of RNG and decionmaking. It has left me and my friend wondering what WE did wrong and not that the game was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t on the RNG.
It has of course been ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t but those are the exception. Still, I love this game quite a lot as it's really exciting to play as you make desicions based on either "go get 'em" attitude or calculated moves. No matter your palystyle this game suits both.

Mini Moter Racing Evo is a pretty good racing game, that I enjoyed playing.  In this game you drive smaller versions of bigger cars on small tracks, kind of like child sized. There are quite a variety of cars to choose from, each somewhat different than the other.  The game has 40 tracks as it says on the store page, and there are night and day versions of each.  Each version also has their own song.
The point of the game is to go through championships, and gain money to upgrade your car.  Now each car can be upgraded, but be careful where you spend your money as early on it is hard to make money.  Swapping from car to car giving each of them upgrades would cause you to have no money and bad cars.  The unlockable cars are pretty nice, you get one for completing a championship and completing certain races for the portal team fortress and fruit ninja cars.  Though I never used them because I wouldn't be able to afford to upgrade them.
The Achievements in this game are rather easy to get except the last achievement which is the money bags one.  It requires you to have 100,000$ cash on hand at once, which is impossible because you upgrade your cars, and that costs a lot of money.
One downfall of the game is the repetitiveness.  Each track is recycled over and over again, so by the time you finish the game you've played each track 20 times both day and night, so it does get boring after a while.  The AI is absolutely idiotic and does not improve over time, all that makes the game harder later on is that all the AI's cars are upgraded, and the races are more laps.  Near the end the races are so long and take nearly 2 minutes each, and since there is a 100 races in the master cup it's insanely time consuming, and unfortunately it becomes boring.  The controls for me were quite easy to figure out but they might cause a problem for some people.
Overall I did enjoy the game because of the music mostly, the tracks were ok, and AI annoyed me at times.  For 5$ I'd say there are better games but it's ok.
