This game is good looking and the new 3D engine is cool, even if uncomfortable at times, but it isn't worth the money.
I usually never pre-purchase games, but I really wanted to play it with my girlfriend so I bought TWO copies of this garbage.
Now, don't get me wrong, I bought the early access and we had fun.
The game got out and it was fun, but it's a rushed game full of bugs and glitches that doesn't hold up against the first two games in length, puzzle depth and storywriting.
So, 22€ each copy for less than 7 hours of content. The developers knew they were running out of money (they spent it all on the 3D engine...) so they did the whole Early Access thing to cash in what they could, without warning their players the game was ♥♥♥♥ing short and the story wasn't finished.
They even cut out the skill tree and the characters' levels, so now you just get the same skills the whole game. Zoya lost the various types of arrows, Amadeus only has one box and no planks, Pontius can't charge his shield to interact with objects.
It's just a bland, short, 3D copy of Trine 1 and 2.
We had to close the game and reopen it while playing multiplayer because the client would often desync, making cooperation impossible, as a desynced trap would hit you even if you saw the blade on the other side.
It's cool Frozenbyte wrote a post explaining why they did such a mess, but it's a mess nonetheless.
Wait for sales, when it'll sell for 5€ then go for it. It's almost a scam, and if the time wasn't up (because I played it in Early Access, while waiting for the "full" game) I'd be asking a refund right now.

First of all, I love Trine and Trine 2. I have played them many times and still find them enjoyable.
The problem with Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power is that it took away almost everything the previous games had, like an experience system, different weapons or Amadeus' stackable conjurations. The new 3D enviroment is great but makes the console clumsy at times. The 'trineangles' that replaced experience points from previous games serve nothing more than a means to unlock pointless challenges, although the small story levels as the individual heroes are quite fun.
But those are not the worst thing about this game. The worst is the length. I played it for 4.2 hours (according to Steam) and in that time I managed to complete the story and side levels as well as collect all the trineangles. The story, in spite of being enjoyable, feels incomplete, whereas the previous games were both finite stories of Amadeus, Pontius and Zoya.
All in all, this game shouldn't have been released as complete in this state. An episodic format would make much more sense.

This is the first game in the series I played, and I played it with some friends who played and loved Trine 2.
Personally I love the design, the gameplay and the 3D thing (although a lot of fans dislike it, but I actually enjoyed it).
However there are 2 things for which this game shouldn't be priced this much:
- Bugs and glitches: Seriously, I would be ashamed to release a game this bugged. It looks like it didn't go through a beta-testing phase. Bridges getting stuck, boxes or stones disappearing, falling through the floor and dying...
These bugs don't really ruin the game that badly tho, and sometimes they are even fun, but what really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off was...
- Length and ending: I won't spoil the ending, also because...IT'S NOT THERE! The game is not finished, it has no ending: what was supposed to be a cliffhanger is not an ending at all, we have no way to see how the main characters will complete their quest, if they even manage to do so that is. We actually beat the game in less than 4 hours, hanging around and wasting a lot of time. I suppose a normal player would be able to finish this easily within 3.5 hrs. I don't mind a game being this short, but I would never ever pay 20+ € for merely 4 hrs of gameplay.
TL:DR The game is fun as long as it lasts, but ends too fast, without a real ending and is so buggy overall that looks like an indie game.

Solid gameplay. Expertly written storyline. This game still holds great competition to even some of the most recent D&D RPG games to date. With a new graphics overhaul and its added key features, this game will send your nostalia nerve tingling all the way through to the end. Ready your party, Baldur's Gate awaits.

Simply put one of the best CRPGs ever made. If you're into isometric RPGs, get it. If you're into immersive environments and stories, get it. If you're into great and rewarding exploration, get it. If you're into interesting characters, quests, and even items, get it. If you're into... You get the point. It's an oldie but a goldie, and well worth your money.

Baldur's Gate has you living as an orphan to a old wizard named Gorion who has taken you away from your usual child labor job to send you away on a mysterious journey. After unfortunate events you're left with no friends or idea of what to do, so you investigate why the iron coming from the mines is brittle and unable to smelt properly quickly getting involved into a larger plot involving who you really are. Nothing mind blowing amazing about the games story, serves it's purpose and had me marginally interested through out the game. The real meat comes from the story you make as you live life on the sword coast.
Baldur's Gate makes D&D dice rolls really fun actually, its real-time but has a pause button for managing items or deciding tactics. Gameplay is challening but highly rewarding, unlike a lot of games now you really feel the sense of progression from fighting tasloi and wolves to bandits all the way up to the big bads like invisible stalkers or powerful wizards. Absolutely brutal on higher difficulties but its really satifying to finally kill something thats been giving you problems for the last couple levels.
Enhanced Edition has some nice upgrades from the original Baldur's Gate but overall doesn't make a massive overhaul, its no show pony but it doesnt need to be and still looks quite nice for an almost 20 year old game. what it lacks in the looks it makes up for in gameplay.
The writing is a little goofy at times but is still top notch for what an RPG should be. Pretty much all the NPCs are great and there are some awesome friends to make for your journey. Beamdog added a few new characters and some people may say they dont fit the game I never personally thought of them in a bad way. I mostly only used Neera personally and she's great fun but her voice is a little lackluster plus her quest is a let down with no real conclusion. The game has happy, sad, good and evil with a bit of goofy moments like a talking chicken or a guy with some bedroom problems.
Baldur's Gate is one of those come along every 10 years or so games that makes a big (or little) splash and is on plently of top 5 games of all times list or favorite games. If I had to pick a second favorite game it'd be this one right here. It's kind of sad Bioware was able to making something of this quality and to do it again for years then make a sudden drop off in quality. If you're a fan of D&D (even if it uses the awful 2nd edition rules) a fan of CRPGS or just good games in general. You can't go wrong with this one.

The best part about this game is that the story is completely believable, unlike many other great RPGs, where you are epic and/or special fairly early on in the game. This game has a SLOW pace, much like a real D&D game, the main quest line is NOT epic for most of the game, and you get to be a lowly nobody for quite some time. By the end, you have earned your reputation.
The main story, while it has dire consequences should you fail, is not really a far-stretch for the imagination. It's mundane enough through most of the game, that when big surprises do happen (and they do!), you're in awe!

For such a simple game (like Mirror's Edge), it was well done. I only had a few problems with it, well three. It has an enhanced view mode, the problem with is, is that the  game doesn’t tell you that using it is how the game is meant to be played. That fixed a lot of the unknowns about the game and most total problems with the game. The next problem was after multiple paths were introduced. I often went down all of them (since they joined up at certain points) and later on I was actually stuck after going though all paths three times. This was fixed by looking at the plentiful number of arrows all over the place, there’s just that many that they seamed to be apart of the background or by enabling the enhanced mode.
The last major problem was when there was nothing but jump pads to get though an area. There was arrows but with out knowing how to get though there they weren’t as helpful as the earlier arrows. On the plus side that was the final area, which explained why it was so hard and the solution was once found easy to understand.
I did have a few minor problems. At first no controls worked for some reason but I was using an xb360 controller and after resetting it some how everything worked. Another properly controller related problem was that the mouse stayed on screen while I was in game. Which was properly because you control the mouse with the controller instead of moving between options. Which brings me to the graphics options. Which since this was a game made by a group in a game development course were limited, but the problem for me was the lack of resolutions. As somehow my monitor (TV!) can't show the full screen at sanded TV resolutions (720P/1080P/anything else changed to that). It always cut off a HUD size section off the bottom of the screen and sometimes the right side. As of when I played it, it only had; 1080P (1920x1080), 720P (1280x720) and 1600x900 (very wide screen?).
In conclusion:
If you liked Mirror's Edge but can't play (for veracious reseons) or want to try out a demo of the game. Well this game is just what you've been looking for and its third-person!
Apart from the problems listed upove, which are minor it is a fairly okay game and its free. The devs even had time to make bug fixes for the game. They have tryed to be a bit funny to lighten the mood, of an otherwise boring thing.  Two examples would be always putting a joke like phrase in the updates and saying that nausea is a bug to be fixed.
Which is good to me at least for there future as most triple A companies and many below them [other famous companies that are not big] have gotten way too serious over the years.

Bethany's VA did a very good job, as did the VA for the main character, but there were some lines that sounded more hollow for want of a better word.
Though, despite the bugginess of the late game, I did like several aspects of the game:
- The plot, as mentioned before, was competant at least. I rather liked the handling of the MC's amnesia as such a cliche is easily butchered.
- The concept of the powers in the hand was a novel one that I really rather enjoyed.

This pixel art traditional roguelike is soaked in blood and bathed in light, where you tip toe on a thread between vampire and vampire hunter, where lighting or the lack of it dynamically alters your tactical decisions, and illuminates or shades your path through the Golden Krone Hotel.
The shifting perspective between the lightbringer Human adventurer and the desperately needy Vampiric survivor, really plays out in the mechanics and provides a strong thematic foundation for the action to be lifted beyond the "usual" roguelike adventuring.
It's very accessible to newcomers to the genre, particularly from player who have enjoyed roguelites but want to dip their toe into the world of more classic/traditional roguelikes. The light mechanic is really innovative and keeps you in a state of constantly shifting priorities. Lighting torches when Human, dousing them for safety when Vampiric. Luring enemies into their destructive beams, or seeking the stealhty safety of the darkness to pounce and bite.
GKH herals a new breed of more accessible traditional roguelikes, to hopefully entice the unsuspecting rogueliter into the darkness and bleed them into a euphoric state, turning them into roguelikers.

This is the work of someone who understands not only why roguelikes are such a long-lasting genre but also why they've been mostly stuck in a niche for nearly forty years: by identifying what actually works and separating it from what is just tolerated by inertia, Golden Krone Hotel is all gameplay and no busywork. A bit like DCSS in how it doesn't want to bullsh*t the player or let the player bullsh*t it... if DCSS took place in a cozy little Romanian castle (read: spooky, poorly lit, broken windows, not really
little, vampires everywhere) instead of in a sprawling Australian underground dungeon.
As a vampire hunter turned vampire, or maybe a vampire turned vampire hunter, or possibly even a hunter vampire, you spend roughly half your time as a spell-casting, sword-swinging, revolver-shooting, lore-reading, human-looking, slowly regenerating BATTLEMAGE, and the other half as a slowly decaying monstrous bloodthirsty nightvision predator who probably can't sign his own name or even properly grasp a pen with those massive claws to begin with, and who also spontaneously combusts if exposed to the scorching sunlight of a gloomy Romanian afternoon; mind those broken windows and keep aware of the time of the day unless you want your vampiric self to develop instant atomic skin cancer. The Hotel has some very spacious rooms so I'd recommend just exploring the opposite side of the floor while the sun impersonates Auric Goldfinger's laser cannon.
Or, you know, just drink one of those Soul Elixirs that turn you back into a human. This is what the game is about, in the end; managing your time and abilities as both a spellcasting human and a faceshredding vampire. NPCs from the opposite faction will attack you, and different areas have different predominant populations; resources are generally limited just enough to be comfortable for a whole game as you alternate between forms, but to make it not really convenient to try to spend all the time as one of the two. All in all, an extremely solid game that knows exactly what it wants to do. It is rewarding on account of how differently the same character might play as human and vampire; not only the way you approach each fight changes, but you also need to reevaluate constantly whether you should really be in a particular room, floor or even branch of the castle around the time you transform.
While a lot of roguelikes both old and new take pride in their unstoppable feature creep and unwillingness to let players play the game, instead clobbering them with infinite menus and inventory screens and cooking recipes and fetch quests and all other kinds of bloat that just get in the way of the moment-to-moment gameplay that made the genre, it's refreshing to see a game that presents no more than a few novel core mechanics and builds a fair, balanced and distinctive experience out of it.

The lighting gimmick sounded neat, but I can't say it works for me so far. Light comes from a different direction depending on the time of day, but the time of day changes very rapidly which produces an encircling effect on more open areas of the level and if you're stuck in the vampire form this is gonna block you completely from moving until the (short) night comes. At that point "gameplay" seems to be reduced to hiding behind pillars and waiting for the light to go away, in a game where waiting means dying.
Even though I imagine that with experience you could look at the minimap, clock and enemy placement to plan your every step, this sounds utterly tedious and not fun at all. At least regroup all info needed for movement decisions in a single place. To be honest I think the light would work much better as a static or very slowly changing feature rather than a bewildering whirlwind, given appropriate mechanics changes so that vampires can traverse these areas if they use the correct tools.
I also got stuck in a situation where a cave was the only place I could safely go (I was a vampire on low life and the level above was very bright), but the way was blocked by water which meant insta-death. Means of changing from one form to the other are limited, and this seems to easily create gameplay dead-ends like this one.
So it saddens me to give a bad review to a traditional roguelike, but the flagship mechanic is really unintuitive and bothersome. I'll update my review if I revisit the game and it turns out to be actually fun.
(For the record, I like some of the other innovations, such as giving you three possibilities for each potion instead of completely removing the ID system like some boring roguelikes do. Nice compromise between push-your-luck and predictable strategy. The game seems otherwise solid in its RPG and item mechanics.)

Golden Krone Hotel has this incredibly jaunty tune that plays when you die, and I cannot get enough of it. Seriously, it’s like a little festival breaks out as your character fades away and the restart options rise into view. It’s such a little thing but it takes nearly all the sting out of dying, which is huge in a game where you die as much as you will here. It’s also an excellent example of the care and attention put into crafting this roguelike adventure, and you can expect to find plenty more as you work your way through its twisting halls.
You are Sorina Arobase, a renowned general and famed vampire killer. She’s on a mission of revenge against exiled vampire prince Fane, probably having something to do with how she tends to turn into a vampire from time to time. Her quest has brought her to the vast and looming Golden Krone Hotel, a mighty structure of many floors, chambers, and deadly inhabitants. Only by scrounging for gear and picking her battles will she eventually reach the dark object of her journey.
So yeah, she turns into a vampire sometimes. Golden Krone Hotel is very much a classic roguelike with its turn-based grid-based bump-based combat, but adorned with clever mechanics like bouts of vampirism. You generally start off in human form, with a meter that slowly fills over time. Once it’s full you turn pale and ravenous, changing not only your looks but your stats, your skills, and how you interact with enemies and the environment. The floors are full of humans and vampires alike, and when in a particular form you’ll only be attacked by those of the opposite species. Sunlight will burn you as a vampire and darkness will hide you, but as a human dark places limit your sight. And blood heals vampires, of course, but as a human you’ll need to find time to rest.
The duality of your character is a major reason this title feels so fresh every time you start up a new character. You’ve always got to mind the meter as a human so that you don’t change while bathed in sunlight or surrounded by soldiers. And as a vampire you need to be lapping up blood whenever possible and carefully considering when to use your potions that restore you to human form. There’s a lot of strategy wrapped up in this system, enough to make floors feel completely different depending on which form you approach them in.
As if that wasn’t enough to consider, there are also twelve unlockable classes (disguises, they call them here) that start you off with different stats, skills, and forms. Skills can be learned from books you find but only in human form, and they provide powerful effects like invisibility and knockback. There’s also a unique potion system that starts with every vial you find unidentified, but shows three possibilities of what it could be. For once this makes IDing items fun because you almost always  have to test them to tell, which will land you in situations where you really needed an antidote and gulped a face-full of noodles instead.
The rest of the structure is quite streamlined, with basic tiers of equipment that auto-equip if better than what you have and a simple leveling system with three familiar stats. This allows you to focus most of your attention on the unique systems and, of course, the challenge. Golden Krone Hotel is balanced around individual enemies being plenty deadly if you’re unprepared, and groups nearly impossible to overcome. You’ll need to make the most of your forms and your skills to survive more than just a few floors because the difficulty curve can feel like a brick wall until you really grok the strategy. The game has easy and normal difficulty modes but I’m still beating my head against the early stages of easy here.
It’s an unusual mix to be sure, a game with simple, unique systems and precipitous challenge. You would think the winning strategy would be obvious but it really isn’t, being heavily dependent on enemy composition and your form and conditions and the environment around you. The design gives you fresh new tools to overcome traditional roguelike challenges, and it produces a title that feels like a classic without becoming boring or familiar. It’s good for short sessions and silly deaths, or long marathons and serious focus, and manages to be fun either way.
The crunchy pixel art is perfect for a retro-styled roguelike, and there’s even an option included to set it all the way back to ASCII. You already know what I think about the soundtrack but the effects and ambiance is top-notch as well, selling the gothic decay of the grand structure you find yourself in. It’s a little harder to hang with than most roguelikes you’ll find on Steam now, but the unique elements stand out more than enough to make it worth it. Golden Crone Hotel has the charm to keep me fighting its hordes of beasts and blood-suckers, and I don’t expect the uphill battle to get boring anytime soon.

tl;dr: Very fun classic FPS that should be played Co-op.
This is "Serious Sam: the first encounter" with an HD polish, I'm unsure what else has changed other then that, but the game definitly felt easier after all these years. Anyway... Do you like FPS where you mindlessly kill hundreds of silly and random enemies? This is the game for you. Serious Sam HD also supports co-op and is much more enjoyable with friends (like most things), in fact this game is a blast to play with other people in general. Single player is there if you need it, but Co-op is the way to go.
Keep in mind this is a classic FPS. It's all about running and gunning, no hiding, no regening health, lots of big and cool weapons, enemies that defy logic for the sake of being fun to fight.
Strengths:
-Classic FPS as stated above (This style of FPS was dead for quite a while, but is starting to come back.)
-Lots of shooting, lots of cool weapons, lots of enemies, and the gameplay is seriously great and polished.
-Awesome and mindless Co-op action for you and your friends
-Secrets! Despite the lackluster level design, there are a lot of very clever and fun secrets to find.
-Silly, pointless, and old school story (It's there if you want it, and doesn't get in the way when you don't)
-Stupid one liners (You either love them or you don't)
-Good difficulty settings, there is literally something for everybody here.
Weaknesses:
-Early stages are pretty boring, Serious Sam games generally take a bit of time to ramp up the serious.
-Level design is very very basic and nothing to get excited about.
-Graphically still a bit aged, but who plays sam for that?
-The game is repetitive in general. (I don't really tire of it, but I could see some people not liking it.)

Totally worth trying. I feel i'm going to get stuck in this game for a while.
EDIT: Now that i've been playing for a while and i'm starting to get the hang of it, I feel like I can make a nice review summing up the main points for this game.
KEEP IN MIND that I didn't play the game before F2P.
PROS:
-Visually attractive, extremely polished graphics for what a free to play usually is.
-Really smooth gameplay (Running in an intel i7-2600 and nvidia GeForce GTX 960, 16 GB of RAM), I haven't experienced a single frame drop in my whole playtime.
-As you start playing, you feel like you need to git gud one way or another, or else you are going to be loosing in every match. My recommendation if you are new is to not play with the monster as it's the hardest role in the game, and focus in learning first how every hunter works and what works best for you, and only then start trying to learn about the monsters (play to learn, not to win, as you are really prone to get massively wrecked even after playing a bit of each role).
-As I just implied, the gameplay has many layers of depth in which you can focus to keep getting better and better, I could really see this becoming a popular E-sport if they added some more variety (more characters, more monsters, and maybe more roles?).
-Incredibly fun to play with friends, playing as any role (but specially monster) usually makes you stay on your nerves the whole match, as a single ♥♥♥♥-up can lead to a defeat in the majority of cases.
-At the moment EVERYTHING can be unlocked either by playing or buying with silver keys (the game currency), which there is no other way to earn than playing as well. I personally don't see where the profit for turtle rock is made here, as I haven't found a single way to spend real money in the game.
-Teamplay is as essential for hunters as being swift and quick with the monster in the stage 1, as if any of those two fail, it is going to be an easy win for one of the two sides. I specially like this point because it feels like the mechanics, once you get the hang of them are easy but not really as "casualized" as some people seem to point out. You can not win a match if you are not decent as a hunter or really know what you are doing with the monster.
-Playerbase is skyrocketing and matches don't take more than 30 secs to find, (seriously, take a look at
, this game has never had as many players as it has now).
-Key contents (like maps) are available to all players, which is nice because this way the playerbase isn't divided unlike in some other games like Cod, battlefield, etc.
CONS:
-I feel like the game needs a little bit more variety in the gameplay, role-wise, as once you get the hang of a specific role, you kinda know how the rest of characters are going to be played, (medic heals, assault tanks, trapper tracks, and support shields other players and calls in♥♥♥♥♥♥to fall from the sky; monster is kind of the same, stage 1: you run and eat, stage 2: you run some more and you eat some more till they trap you, [in which case you fight back and you can either: 1- wreck their asses and win, 2-manage to escape and keep feeding till third stage,  3- get caught in a downwards spiral where you can't run away from them (this is massively influenced by what monster you are using and what map you are playing it in) and die miserably], stage 3: here you normally are really good or the hunters are not playing that well (if you don't have a single scratch on you), you can die but it's complicated.
Don't even try to go for the relay, as it's lifespan is HUMONGOUS and you are never going to destroy it in time. My recommendation here is to wait for the hunters in a nice fighting arena where they suffer (like an acid pool or something like that, and then be accurate with your attacks and stay close to those who die)).
so yeah, more variation, turtle rock!
OVERALL:
TRY THIS IF YOU HAVEN'T ALREADY, TRY IT NOW!
The game offers many hours of fun just till you get the hang of it, and many more once you find a role you really like.

If you're new to the game its probably worth trying out if you know two major things:

Not all hunters and monsters are available to you off the bat, don't expect perfectly fair games since many players have all the characters since they owned the game. This while debatably isn't a big disadvantage, still will probably bother new players. Unlocking things with in game currency is what you would expect, 5-10 rounds nets you what you need depending on if you win or lose.

This game has a pretty cemented meta, even with all the changes a monster with feeding speed and move speed will avoid you like the plague, and as long as they know to get domed in areas where they can hide they will avoid you there too. If you go in against the legacy players you will probably feel pretty lost, and since they reset all progression, you WILL get matched with players much more experienced than you.

If neither of those are deal breaking then the game could be a good fir for you, ive played periodically since beta, and you eventually come to realize that the pros outweigh the cons. but the flaws tend to be the first thing new players encounter so evolve tends to be a love or hate game depending on how patient you can be.

As for returning players who are already familiar with the game, they have changed a lot.

Perks have undergone a (needed) rework but I still find myself going for the same perks, I just can combine them now.
This is actually big for hunters, you can play to a hunters strengths easier this way, rather than having to take jetpack recharge most of the time.

The dome was also reworked, for the better as far as I could tell from what I played. as the monster I prefer it this way since many games were decided on weather or not I was domed at stage 1, and if I wasn't id snowball to stage 3 and win without a fight. the new dome promotes skirmishes along the way which is just more fun for both sides. this also reduces the impact of one bad teammate.

I don't disagree with any in game changes, however I did notice one really upsetting thing as a returning player.

they removed all my elites. I don't feel good about the majority of my progress being wiped away, eliting monsters and hunters was the only thing to do really, aside from ranked which just split up the playerbase...

not only did they remove the icon next to your name, they took away the skins as well.

Sure founders get some extra skins, but most of us already picked up a boat load of free skins from the weekend events.
The elite symbol was cool, and the elite hunter skins were some of the best.

Its worth a try if you dont mind the disadvantage of not having all the characters, if you do you probably only play Dota 2 anyway.

Played through BG1 and Siege of Dragonspear. This is a spoiler-free review of Siege of Dragonspear.
I am, however, going to spoil the review and say up front that I would probably have given this one a "neutral" score if I could.
SMALL PREAMBLE
I'm aware of the "controversy", but the game has been updated to alter the content in question since then, and I've only played this version. Nothing really struck me as too overly political, which I think is what was at the heart of the matter.
PROS
- The writing fits the (kind of weird) tone of BG1 very well, but is more concise. This is great.
- Some of the new companion characters and side stories with the old companions, are actually pretty fun.
- I think the tie-ins with the mini-campaign "The Black Pits" will work really well if you play Black Pits after Dragonspear.
- The combat encounters are generally a little more focused than they were in BG1 (or Icewind Dale), with smarter enemy scripts for some battles (using potions or alchemical grenades, or setting up ambushes with magic for example,) and fewer "time waster" encounters (though there are a still a couple of those teleporting spiders here and there.)
- Some of the voice actors do a really good job, hamming it up and chewing scenery in ways that really do feel like Baldur's Gate.
- A lot of the environments look rather nice, especially compared to BG1. We also never ran into any very badly designed dungeon corridors or other places that completely obscured the party (like there are many of in BG1)
- If you're willing to deal with some pretty serious bugs, the co-op actually mostly works, which is more than I honestly dared hope.
- The tie-in between BG1 Imoen and BG2 Imoen works fairly well.
CONS
- The co-op is much buggier than BG1, (and BG1 was already much buggier than Icewind Dale.)
- Some of the voices are a complete trainwreck. There are a few truly terrible voice actors in the game (as in "this is probably someone from the dev team" level of acting). Some just desperately need a pop filter or a microphone that records in higher fidelity than a WW2-era radio broadcast. The quality whiplash from the best to the worst is staggering.
- Story bugs. There are several, but here's one example: there's a bug where a certain NPC you need to talk to simply leaves, disappearing from the game. The only way to get around it is to do a seemingly unrelated and nonsensical thing where you "change your mind" when talking to your questgiver a few times - then you can turn in the quest with another NPC who hasn't left (the same NPC who previously insisted that you needed to talk to Mr Absent).
- Very minor/early spoiler;
- My biggest peeve with this game is this: you're able to break the sequence of the main story so that you know important plot information early. This also happens occasionally in BG1/IWD, but in this case it's a huge and crucially important piece of information about what's happening that would change everything if you could act upon it. But alas, your character behaves as if it never happened and can't mention it in dialogue or act upon it, until much later. In other words, a huge gaping flaw in the game's narrative that undermines the game's storytelling efforts more or less completely, depending on who you are. I was not immersed; I was exasperated.
BOTTOM LINE: If you think you'll feel differently about the way the story is written, then I can probably recommend it to you, if you like Baldur's Gate.

It's a 3d dwarf fortress-lite game. There's not much more to say about it. It's quite fun, the technology tree is pretty interesting, and the economy, while static, adds another neat mechanic to the game. This is definitely what's good about this game. These are the best parts.
However, it's not wholely good. There are problems with it. The building template system is obtuse and workers will get confused and be unable to complete buildings quite often if not given very, very generous space. The way that special potions work, and how the Herablist works are both hard to understand, and not taught to you whatsoever.
Workers also have a hivemind kind of thing, they'll all clump onto a single task instead of spreading themselves amoungst it, I understand that this may be to lessen computing power needed, but it also has some less desireable effect. For example, farmers will harvest one field at a time, which can cause you to lose crops or just simple be stuck harvesting carrots forever if you have enough of them planted. Same thing happens with mining, hauling, etc. This doesn't happen with crafters, as they'll split they're work in a more intelligent way, but you're still constrained by the queueing system.
As far as enemies go, there is a point around day 20 where you get hit with a large wave of enemies, if you're not prepared then it is game over. That's not so great, but honestly it's a neat way to game over people that are trying to be as peaceful as possible, and who ignore their military.
There are also serious performance issues. Every villager seems to have their own mindset and their own tasklist and their own traits, etc, etc. They perform relatively independently, outside of gathering/hauling jobs, like I noted above. This brings about performance problems though, as they probably are not wholely optimized quite yet, as this game is still in alpha, and your CPU will get a thrashing.
Something in the game is also stored poorly, or at least that's my best guess. The game uses mountains of RAM after you've been playing for a few hours, like crash your computer amounts of RAM. Restarting it helps this, but it builds back up to insane RAM usage after another hour or so. It seems the further I go into the game, the faster the RAM builds up. I doubt that it's a memory leak, and I'm convinced that it's because of how the game stores it's voxels or how it stores the player-made buildings. This is a serious problem, and I doubt it'll be fixed anytime soon, as it's been around for months now.
However once the game is feature complete, I'm sure the devs will devote tons of time to optimization, as they should.
So, to sum up this rambling, if you like indie and alpha games, and you like Dwarf Fortress, and don't mind tehcnical problems, then this is a definite buy.
If you can't stand that stuff, want a professionaly complete game, or just don't like dealing with technical issues, then it's probalby wise to take a pass on this game, but you really should check in on this game again when it's finally released, or at least in beta.

Stonehearth is a game about building a small town, with the help of a group of 'hearthlings' who build, mine, farm and craft their way to victory (sometimes) over ever-stronger groups of enemies. You have an amazing amount of control over the appearance of your town, and you can custom build every house, road and wall. There are a variety of decorations and tools to place around your village, and there are two main storylines to follow (if you aren't playing on peaceful) - fighting the enemies, and becoming a township. You also get to pick one of two types of hearthling: The Ascendancy, who live in the forest, or Rayya's Children, who live in the desert. They have slightly different skill trees, so the gameplay is a little different.
The hearthlings in the game have basic personalities, and the newest update (Alpha 21) brings likes and dislikes. They have attributes too, which make them more or less suited to certain jobs. It's easy to pick up which attributes make a good soldier, for example, but some of the other classes are more complicated. This makes for an immersive town, where new arrivals' talents can mean the difference between life and death for your people.
Crafting in the game is simple, and you have the (amazing!) ability to easily queue multiple items, and even request that you always have four beds in storage, for example, so you don't have to intimately micromanage every item crafted. Items placed in houses you design will also automatically queue to be produced by your crafters and placed, which enables the game to run smoothly. Even if you don't have the ingredients to make the chair you want, if you place one when you design a house it will be built and placed as soon as the ingredients are ready. There are a variety of crafters, from the carpenter to the herbalist, and every town will require a different approach (as each map and every hearthling is random). You can farm a variety of foods, including animals, and mine the hills around your town for ore. Traders will visit, and you can sell them products or buy goods.
The only downside I can think of to this game is that it is not complete yet. However, I've loved watching it develop over the last 565 hours that I have played, and I can't wait to see the finished game in the future. I am excited for the new types of hearthlings planned for the future, in particular. (And if anyone on the development team ever sees this: I'd love to have some of those pet fighting wolves for my hearthlings, please!) I really feel like the development team listen to their audience, and I have been very impressed with the quantity and quality of the work they are putting into this game.
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys minecraft, terraria, the sims, simcity, cities skylines, stardew valley or animal crossing. It has beautiful scenery, and great animations. You do not need a powerful setup: the game runs smoothly on my ACER Aspire F 15, which does have a dedicated graphics card (NVIDIA GeForce) but which is not a gaming laptop. I have minor lag when my town reaches 25+ hearthlings, as the candles flickering at night make my computer slower. I find that toggling the walls down on my buildings at night solves this entirely, and it's really not an issue.

You might be expecting, as I was, that this one takes place in some kind of theater. Well it doesn't, unless the kinds of theaters you frequent are hewn from the bones of giants, have multi-story crypts attached, or are built over mysterious Egyptian ruins situated in a remote, snow-capped mountain range. There's no performance here, aside from a struggle against a gangly demon for the soul of a small girl trapped in an enchanted bell tower. Although as I type all this out, I suppose the Absurd part of the title is at least accurate.
Did any of that make sense? I bet it didn't, and part of Theatre of the Absurd's charm is that it rather gleefully doesn't. You play the auspiciously-named Scarlett Frost, a visitor to Dr. Corvus' remote Castlevanian abode where he resides with his golden eye and arcane cube and daughter. In a sudden (and much, much later explained) fit of rage he destroys the cube, releasing a demon and imperiling his daughter. It's up to you to reassemble the enchanted bell that can somehow drive away the demon wandering the bizarre halls.
That's just the tip of the iceberg, because the story has some twists in store that can barely be justified and it's kind of great how earnestly it leans into them. Everything about the game, from the ridiculous plot to the insane setting to the ill-fitting name give Theatre of the Absurd the sensation of being unstuck from logic, existing in some kind of pocket dimension where all theaters have skull motifs and adjoining necropolises. It's a fever-dream of a game capped off with an oddly dark conclusion that only makes the journey that much more odd.
Luckily the puzzles and item searches don't follow the same lunacy that guided the rest of the game's design. They're quite easy for the most part, the hidden object scenes in particular because they have no gimmick and just twelve fairly large and obvious items to find. I got through most of the scenes just blindly clicking, they're so large. The puzzles are bound to be quite familiar to old hands at HOGs, with a few extra steps taken out to make them even easier. You'd have to completely forget where you've been or what you're doing to get stuck, but there's a helpful hint system in the form of a cursed forearm that straight tells you what to do, and handles a few puzzles for you as well.
The graphics are on the higher end of the genre, though don't expect the resolution to meet modern standards. There are some decent effects and even a few genuine spooks thanks to some unnerving design on your nemesis. Sound design is also plenty solid, with a moody soundtrack, rich effects, and a few inspired choices for environmental sounds. Your adventure should only take about two hours and then there's 20-30 minutes of bonus material that really just muddies the story even more. But that's what you should be here for, a solid hidden object game with a story so absurd, they named the game after one of the least important parts of it. Luckily for us, that was really the only mark they missed here.

Besides, we human beings love a mystery and a HOG provides the perfect opportunity to break out the magnifying glass. Playing HOGs may be an acquired taste but beside the entertainment value, I think there are cerebral benefits and cognitive gains to be had from virtual detective work, especially for “seasoned gamers.” The developers at Gogii Games have done a masterful job with “Theatre.” If I ever escape the manse, I’ll try another of their offerings. This, this right here, this is an amazing game. I've seen a lot of comparisons to Mirror's Edge, which I haven't played yet, but 404Sight is a 3D platformer/runner where your objective is to ... actually, I'm not entirely sure. Deliver a file, I think? In any case, you control an avatar who must go through the interwebs, dodging slow lanes and inhibitors while staying on the fast lanes and conserving bandwidth to make it to the end as fast as possible.
The graphics are simultaneously the best and worst part of the game. Everything looks vibrant, and it's easy to tell fast lanes from slow lanes. Simplistic at its best in play. Unfortunately, I think the game might have some sort of optimization issues; when I played this on my desktop, it wasn't running well at all unless I toned the graphics way down, and at that point it looked more like a bad Flash game than anything else. I mean, I could still see where I was going and it looked beautiful for what it was, but it's a shame I couldn't run it well unless it looked worse than it could.
The sound effects are superb. Speed boosts, inhibitors crashing into the landscape, bounce pads, ping, it all sounds beautiful. There's a bit of a disco feel as well, which is perpetuated by the music that sounds so upbeat. I am definitely downloading the soundtrack after posting this, it's really amazing.
Gameplay itself is phenomenal, and a good statement at that! I didn't realize the bandwidth was a health meter, but you have to stay on the fast lanes to regenerate bandwidth while avoiding the slow lanes and inhibitors that will suck out your bandwidth. You can use some bandwidth for a speed boost, which also destroys inhibitors, but other than that your goal is to get to the end as fast as possible through 3D platforming. It's very, VERY well executed and a job well done.
The fact that this game is free means there's no excuse to not pick it up and give it a go. I highly recommend it - it's fun, it's engaging, and it's intriguing. Loved it.

This game is a gem of a traditional roguelike. It has all of the featured beloved to veterans of this genre: it is turn based, played on a tile grid, procedurally generated maps, a hunger clock, inventory management and character sheets. On top of all of this it has some really fun and innovative mechanics, including play modes based on vampirism, lycanthropy and being human.  Sun- and moonlight shine through windows burning vampires and invigorating werewolves, allowing you to use them as weapons or forcing you to hide from them, depending on your form.  Like the best games of its genre, it is simple to learn, hard to master, and every playthrough brings its own unique challenges.  I have barely begun to explore this game, but I am hooked!

WIth a decent amount of play into this game before the release of Stage 2 [Free to Play] I must say that I have always enjoyed this game, even through some of the grueling downsides.
Let me start off by saying that these grueling downsides are the obvious sore spots that the game has had, mentioned in every review with a thumbs down [and even most of the thumbs up], which include A.) Terrible pay structure system for DLC, and B.) Terrible que times.  With release of Free to Play, I imagine both of these major issues are going to be resolved, due to content being obtainable through JUST playing, and also free to play almost always equates to larger player base meaning shorter que times.
With those two things aside the game play is as follows:
A team of 4 hunters vs 1 Monster, Hunters have an early advantage due to their numbers against the weak monster.
Monsters CAN make early plays but only IF Hunters are playing sloppy and not sticking together.  Monster is trying to sneak and remain hidden as much as possible while leveling up through consuming wildlife to get stronger.  This happens ideally until Monster can reach stage 3 and can then attack a generator that Hunters must defend.  At this point in the game, Monster is a major force to be reckoned with.
My opinion of the gameplay, is that at the time of release, this was fresh as hell.  It was something different for the FPS genre.  Now with Dead by Daylight out, there is another game that fits this niche.
As far as balance goes, I can't say much for the balance since the game was JUST updated with balance tweaks, but one would assume that these changes are either an improvement as is, or will be further improved upon after Stage 2 beta ends.  As it was when I played it, playing Hunters could be difficult if coordination was not happening.  Same goes for Monster though, it was really hard to get away from GOOD hunters.  At the time, I felt the pace was set by the Hunters, but I did not climb very high in ranks so it could have just been my lack of skill.  None the less, I had fun every game I played.
Graphics and Audio, are beyond immersive IMO.  I always play this game with my audio cranked up, so I can hear the monster running around, giving me clues as to which direction he came from, or whether or not he might be trying to sneak up on me.  The soundtrack I think is suitable, not amazing, but still immersive.
All in all, I am very very hopeful for the future of this game.  The developers heard the cries of the dead dog being beaten , the community NEEDED this to be free to play.  Those of us who enjoyed the game, had to enjoy it through very big sore spots.  But now with a larger player base on the horizon, and a free to play model that seems appropriate, there is no reason not to give this game a fair chance.

Ventured out to explore and gather more materials to make arrows and fire, only to sprain my ankle fleeing from a pack of wolves. The limp slowed me enough to have them tearing at my backside by time I got home, and the injuries left me bedridden for days. The Long Dark is a refreshing change from the kill everything you encounter in many adventure games. There are no zombies out to get you. Rather the game plays out as a real adventure. You must carefully monitor four areas in order to survive the unrelenting hardships of being stranded in the desolate North. Hunger, thirst, disease and most of all heat are your main concerns. The episodic part of the game has an abundance of supplies lying around for you to find. I like the daily goals being specified for you. Achieve these, and you move on to the next day. Fail, and you will be replaying that day. At least you don’t have to go back to the beginning.  It took a while for me to get accustomed to the game play. There is no actual tutorial. You are dropped into the frozen North and are immediately looking for heat. Some non-specific hints do pop up trying to point you in the right direction. They are in fact very useful if you are already familiar with how to play. It would have been helpful to be told hold down the space bar in order to pull up the radial dial of instructions. All in all, I have had many hours of game play and a lot more are ahead of me just in this episodic part. The game also has a couple of other modes, which will provide even more game play. Sitting in my nice warm room and listening to that cold wind blowing across the screen sends a shiver of cold running through me. This real life adventure game is definitely worth trying out.

I've never been a huge fan of FMV games, but I gotta say... Missing is probably one of my favorites so far. This first episode leaves you on a cliffhanger, but the devs are nice enough to give a short sneak peak at episode two.
Jazzy, relaxed noir style music and minimalistic dialogue leaves it up to the camera angles and acting to create an intense, immersive experience. The puzzles are simple, yet enjoyable. While it's nice to be presented with a challenge in most games, the casual game style of Missing really offers players the advantage of relaxing and enjoying the full motion video, atmosphere, and story rather than worrying about completing complex puzzles.
The ride only lasts about an hour, and it's well worth the asking price even when it isn't on sale. I seriously can't wait for the next episode. Not much of the story is explained within the first episode of Missing: An Interactive Thriller, but the atmospheric set-up and the effective capture of intense emotions from the main character are solid foundations to build from.

The biggest problem with this MOBA is that it doesn't have a clean feel to it, smooth movement, easily explained abilities, fluid auto attacks, and super OP/Nerfed to hell characters.  I'll go through each of these, but first, I'd like to state one of the cool things about this MOBA:
The system for upgrading your minions/upgrading towers is A: Easy to understand, B: actually worth using, and C: works.
Now, onto the problems:
The game feels like it wasn't polished or cleaned, just thrown out to the public because of deadlines.  It would be like if you took LoL from Season 1, and compared it as an equal MOBA to Season 4 LoL.  Season 1 feels gritty and awkward compared to season 4, and it's becaused it's been cleaned and polished since then.  This game needs that cleaning and polishing badly.
Movement in this game is unresponsive and delayed.  You'll be trying to dodge a skill shot, or just move in random ways to fool your opponent.  Well, unfortunately, even in offline mode, it takes about half a second for your character to respond.
The abilities are convoluted and stated in weird ways that don't just say "roots your enemy for 1.5 seconds" or so on.  It takes up 3-4 sentences describing it, and not really telling you exactly what it does.
They had an interesting idea for the auto attacks, having melee auto attacks cleave an area in front of them, while ranged attacks will hit the first enemy in front of them.  The problem is that auto attacks are delayed, like the movement.  So by the time you auto attack, your enemy has probably killed you.
Some characters in this game are just extremely powerful and others just pointless to use.  Gandalf the Grey, his E ability deals massive amounts of True damage, and it scales.  It also roots the enemy till after the damage hits.  It's insane.  Whereas Gollum/Smeagol is supposed to be an assassin who leaps in, stuns and silences, getting resets on his ultimate, but he deals 0 damage with any of his abilities.  Those are just 2 examples.
If the devs were to really focus on making this game work, I think it could be something great.  However, it seems they've given up, and nothing is getting fixed.

Alpha 21 Review:
I backed this game on kick starter (2012) because it looked like a neat take on dwarf fortress or towns.  The cute little 3d voxel guys with destructable 3d voxel terrain and customizable voxel 3d buildings and forts, I was sold.  I have played the Alpha on and off for years, and I have waited patiently for a working voxel based town simulator that allows me to create neat buildings with little 3d voxels.  So here is my review, because the game should have been finished back in 2014, according to the kick starter page.
Is it like Dwarf Fortress?  -No.  You have much more control over your people in SH, and you only get 20 people...
Is it like Gnomoria? -No.  Gnomoria is closer to DF, and SH is nowhere near the oh crap feeling of running out of food and everyone dies.
Is it like Towns? -Similar, but watered down.  Less jobs, promoting is painfully slow and the level up system is annoying.  SH doesn't have the dungeon diving that Towns has.  SH more or less keeps you on the surface and you are raided just about every day by very annoying enemies.  Dang near have to keep an army on hand to repel attackers, or build a giant wall around your settlement with a simple door...yes, a door, keeps enemies out.  The devs haven't added the ability for AI to bash or bipass doors in..years.
Pros: It's cute, stable enough on common alpha builds to play for a time with little to no serious issues, save the occasional CTD, annoying debug error popups, or the dreaded slowing down of the game when you have 20 peasants all moving around.  Though I have a good rig, so it isn't too bad.  The building of towns or forts can be fun, but it's also tedious and frustrating at times.
Some things have improved, like AI path finding, which was terrible in early alpha versions, UI / presentation, stability, and overall performance, which used to be terrible but isn't too bad until late game.  However, many other key aspects of the game have actually gotten WORSE over the course of development.  Primarily, the very feature that got me to back it in the first place, designing and building custom buildings.
CONS:
This is one of the few titles that has seemed to go one step forward, and two steps back.  What's more, the developer continuously makes excuses and dumps money in useless quests, presentation, and blatantly feminist artwork.  Most every picture features a woman being in the position of authority or strength and the male is subservient, but that's just personal taste, I don't appreciate feminism or cultural marxism in my games, and feel with the times, it's necessary to warn people that do not want to support such things, or support it, your choice.
I was furious when one of the Cannon brothers made the comment to me that not everyone agrees that the editor is a key feature, so it isn't a priority, back in 2014.  Yet over the years, I have seen hundreds of people complain about the editor's bugs and features being removed, not fixed, from the game.  Many of the original promised goals have yet to be implemented in the game, which has been in development for over 5 years now.  With each new Alpha build, a few new tweaks are added, but nothing mind boggling, or remotely close to what was promised ever surfaces.  Like multiplayer, seasons, or a building editor that allows you to modify completed structures or delete walls.
Funny that you used to be able to disassemble houses, even re-design houses or erase features.  The feature was bugged, like workers get stuck, are unable to get all the blocks, or AI can't pathfind and the project sits idle and is ignored.  Instead of fixing these things, it was just scrapped in order to add cool things (sarcasm) like, leveling up your workers, constantly being wiped out by hordes of annoying goblins on day four, or re-arranging the UI for the 18,000th time. Come to think of it, I still haven't received my kick starter backer pet reward.
Overall, this game could have been really really awesome.  But progress has been really slow going.  So I will not recommend this game to friends unless I see significant improvement.

Trine 3 is an absolutely stunning game, one that keeps true to the Trine roots but unfortunately fell prey to the sin of ambition. The artwork, soundtrack and cinematography are still top notch, showcasing production values that I’ve come to expect from the series. The core mechanics and gameplay are still there, just streamlined a bit in order to reduce friction. However the game is clearly only a third of the creator’s original vision, with numerous levels and story left undeveloped, never to be explored by us gamers. It’s really quite unfortunate as parts of Trine 3 we’ve got are just incredible but that quality has obviously come at a cost. Hopefully this isn’t the death of the series as it would be a real shame to see it go just as Frozenbyte was reaching its peak.
Read my full review here:

: Frozenbyte
: Frozenbyte
: A key for this game was provided by the developer for the purpose of writing an unbiased informative review. No other compensation was given.
==========
Very few games actually feel like they are magic. In fact, the only games I have ever had a magical vibe from were from this series. Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power is the 3rd title in the Trine series, and is every bit as magical as its predecessors. A few shifts in its core design were made to make it a bit different from the other titles, but it's still a magical experience. An extremely beautiful 3D puzzle-platformer, Trine 3 absolutely shines in nearly all aspects.
==========
Like in the first two games, Trine 3 is a puzzle platformer, but the biggest change to the game is that it is now in full 3D. You can literally move in all 3 dimensions. Trine 3 focuses on three specific heroes: Pontius the Knight, Zoya the Thief, and Amadeus the Wizard. You are able to switch between all 3 heroes at anytime, allowing you to tackle any situation that presents itself. Each hero has their own unique abilities, which you have complete access to from the start of the game. This is something that was changed from Trine and Trine 2. Using their abilities in tandem, you will traverse wonderous environments on your quest for the Artifacts of Power to restore things to the way they should be so our heroes can go home and live their lives peacefully. Understanding each character's strengths and abilities is the key to playing the game, so I will be going over each of them in the next few sections.
Pontius the Knight is the first character you are introduced to. His abilities include being able to attack enemies with his sword, as well as a powerful charge attack with his shield raised high. This can be used to knock around objects in each stage. Using his shield, Pontius is able to reflect projectiles in any given direction, such as fireballs and rocks. This technique is great in certain portions of the game. He can also use his shield to slow his descent from a jump, allowing him to glide long distances, covering more ground than the other two characters. Lastly, Pontius is able to use his considerable size to perform a stomp attack, which dazes nearby foes and can be used in certain puzzles.
Zoya the Thief has a few special talents that make her absolutely vital to our band of heroes. First, she has a grappling hook, which can be used to latch onto many objects. Some such objects include rings placed in key locations, which Zoya can grapple from and swing between platforms, or other objects such as block which can be used in solving puzzles. She can also latch both ends of her rope to anchor the line--which I completely forgot you could do for quite awhile, and is a key point for a few puzzles! Zoya can also perform a dodge roll to avoid enemy attacks until you are able to get into a safer position to shoot them with her bow and arrows. One thing changed about Zoya is she now auto-aims her bow. You used to have to aim manually in previous games. You still can, however, but the game will automatically fire towards targets of interest.
The last character you can control is Amadeus the Wizard. Amadeus specilizes in conjuring arcane cubes that can be used as platforms to get to areas that are out of reach.  He can also hurl them at other objects or foes. Most objects in the environment can be picked up as well, and this actually serves as a key for some puzzles. When holding a cube or object you are able to rotate it and move it in any direction, which is useful for situating them for puzzle solving purposes.
The general gameplay of the game is simply amazing for a platformer. As you adventure through different environments, you simply switch to whichever character is best suited for the task at hand. A horde of monsters is coming your way? Pontius the Brave will make quick work of them with his sword. Giant gap to cross? Zoya will get you across with her grappling hook in no time. That button's out of reach? No problem, Amadeus can use an arcane cube as a platform to reach it. The key to the game is understanding each character's abilities, so familiarize yourself with them so that when you come upon certain puzzles, you are able to tackle them with no issues.
Scattered around each level are what's called "trineangles": small golden pyramids that are hidden everywhere. Collecting these unlocks extra playable chapters to further extend the game. Each stage has a set amount of them, and you are able to replay stages to find these hidden trineangles.
Co-op is also available for you and up to 2 friends, each controller a character.
==========
I literally have no idea how they were able to improve Trine 2's graphic style for Trine 3, but they somehow pulled it off! This game is absolutely gorgeous. And I mean GORGEOUS. The overall look, the colors, the lights and shadows...everything looks outstanding. Trine has always been know as a series that looks very impressive, but Trine 3 takes the cake! If you look at this game and aren't impressed, then you have a serious problem that you need to get checked out.
Each character has gotten a considerable upgrade to their model since Trine 2 and it shows in the game's various cutscenes. Everything is so vivid and colorful, which makes everything stand out. It's very difficult to miss many details in the game's environments when they all stand out due to looking so amazing. You will find yourself taking a lot of screenshots and simply admiring every environment you explore. From dark castles, to bright, lush forestland, Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power is one of the most beautiful games I have ever played. And this isn't something I ever say lightly.
==========
Another great area of detail for Trine 3, the music is very upbeat and addicting. Bright, cheery tunes abound all over the game, even in some of the most perilous areas. When enemies appear the music shifts to a more serious tone, but once they are defeated it returns to normal. Great little detail, in my opinion.
A sfar as the sound effects, everything is as it should be. Sword slashes, running, objects knocking together...all of it is spot on. I like how Amadeus' cubes sound when they pop into existence!
==========
Like a charm is how Trine 3 runs. The only issue I had was when first booting it up to play it took a couple of minutes to load, but after that it's smooth sailing. There is a short loading screen inbetween each area, but it is much shorter than the main menu loading.
A controller is the way to go, honestly. But the keyboard controls work pretty well by default. I was just a lot more confortable with a controller, as the game requires some precise platformer in some stages.
The game ran at a smooth 60FPS most of the time, and aside from the menu screen loading there was no slowdown, stuttering, lag, or framerate drops. It ran as smooth as silk, which honestly surprised me considering how amazing the game looks.
==========
Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power is very much a worthy successor to the Trine series. If you enjoyed the first two titles, you pretty much have to play this one. It continues our three heroes' adventures and is an incredibly fun and balanced puzzle platformer. Not too easy, not too hard, Trine 3 will appeal to audiences of all ages. The only downside to it is that it's short, as it only requires a handful of hours to beat.
==========

The game is a very quirky and cute RC car racer.  The AI isn't as bad as everyone seems to be saying it is.  Playing on anything higher than easy greatly improves the AI experience, and makes the game a real challenge.  The bumper car-style gameplay goes away once you ramp up the difficulty.
The graphics are that of a very high end mobile game, and it shows that it is actually a mobile game.  The controls are actually a very good port of touch based controls, from the mobile game.  It includes all the DLC mobile maps that you originally had to shell out money for, and does so in style.  It's a true proper mobile to PC port, removing all the bad bits of mobile ports and keeping the good.  The good being very fun 15 minutes at a time game sessions.
Racing wise, the handling can get a little sloppy on a few maps.  There are some bumps that just shouldn't exist, and can cause you to fly off the map.  However some might say those are simply skill challenges and you need to slow down.  Outside of getting air handling is very tight and well done.  You don't drive on ice like in GTA, instead you drive tight turns when you mean to, and wide turns when you mean to.  It's very easy to control, probably due to it's extremely sloppy control background on mobile games.  Seriously, touch racing is impossible.
There is a variety of maps, and quite a lot of cars.  A truly endless amount if you include the workshop.  There is also a map editor for you to make maps for your friends, or to upload to the workshop.
Which leads to the next thing...  Multiplayer.  It's very well implemented and not at all laggy.  It's very fun to race and bash you're buddies, just like in any other game.
I picked the game up on a whim of liking cute RC racers, and I don't regret it one bit.  If you're the same, go ahead and grab it.  If you're looking for a captivating, serious racer, look elsewhere.

☺ Easy to play.

☺ Brilliantly realised Portal and Team Fortress 2 maps.
☹ Unchallenging.
☹ Wonky physics.

(Note: This game was played with a controller).
Mini Motor Racing EVO is a casual top down racer suitable for most ages, with easy to grasp controls and an aesthetic that greatly reminds me of playing with toy cars as a youngster.
While there is a decent selection of maps (and most notably the Portal and Team Fortress 2 maps are brilliantly realised), they quickly become repetitive as you play them again and again through the championships - in forward, reverse and with the camera on a slightly different angle (which is a surprisingly clever way of making the same track play a little differently). There is also an ingame editor linked to the Steam Workshop to create, share and download other tracks which is very simple to do.
While enjoyable to zip around the tracks and drift around corners, the AI opposition rarely put up any challenge at all (the exception being a couple of maps where you could do with a speed upgrade, that is easily passed the moment you have acquired it or a higher top speed vehicle). It also appears the AI Drivers have been drinking...while it's nice that they don't always perform the perfect lap, they will frequently slam into corners or boost directly into a wall.
The physics in the game can cause frustration, as you slap to a halt after performing a jump or snag on a slightly uphill piece of track.  There is also an oddity that before a race gets underway you get a glimpse of the tablet UI for the game, but that doesn't impact the experience in any meaningful way.
At the time of writing, there were no active multiplayer servers.
It's very hard to recommend Mini Motor Racing EVO except for the extremely casual gamer who's unfamiliar with racing titles and just wants a little fun zipping around a track.

Mini Motor Racing Evo plays like a cross between MicroMachines, Rock'n'Roll Racing and Skidmarks, all of which I spent a great many hours playing in my youth.
The Isometric viewpoint gives you a good look at the nicely realised themed tracks, and it adds to the challenge in much the same way as it did in Rock'n'Roll Racing - by not letting you see too far ahead.
Physics are good, with the cars generally feeling well connected with the road. The road surface affects grip and some adaptation of driving style is required to succeed.
There is a decent roster of cars to choose from and unlock - and they can be upgraded as you proceed through career mode. I've only really used one, though (Gulf liveried sports racer), and I suspect that using one of the others now (in career mode) would mean starting from base-specs and having to grind my way through leveling up again - a shame you can't port your progress over to a different vehicle.
As with the three games I referenced, the AI is pretty wild. They basically do their own thing, and if you are in their way they try to drive through you. I've seen a number of reviewers suggest that the AI tries to "take out" the player, but I've seen no evidence of this.
Overall, a fun game - though no classic.
