First things first. If you bought the game prior to it transitioning to free to play, that stinks, sorry. But get the ♥♥♥♥ over it. Game prices fall with age and if you want you could keep the game at 60 and have fun playing with empty lobbies. It going free to play seems like the only reasonable (and expected and suggested by the community) choice.
That out of the way, let me clarify Ive only begun playing since it went f2p. I intend to review the f2p game as it is in its current state rather than complain about what it used to be.
SO HOW FREE IS IT? Instead of most games having a premium and in game currency, this one only has one single currency that works for everything from skins to new hunters. As far as I can tell you start off with only the weekly free rotation hunters (a la league of legends style). MAJOR TIP: if you go find a steam key from some provider (which is pretty easy) and valued somewhere between 5-15 dollars, you get about 2/3 of all the characters unlocked along with skins and currency. In terms of how easy it is to aquire currency, by the time ive reached rank 11 with about 4 hours in and subtracting the currency I got from buying a steam key online for 5 dollars, ive had enough to buy a top tier hunter of my choice along with perks and skins for said hunters weapons. They have a lot of challenges and level up rewards to make it easy to progress. Like i said if you just get a steam key for dirt cheap, you'll already have more than enough content to keep you preoccupied for hours.
COMMUNITY? I have no idea, its the first day and right now theres more than enough players online to find a game instantly. All have been friendly and reasonably skilled at my level. I actually managed to land in a quick match with the dev team my first hour. They were extremely polite, cooperative, and forgiving. They seemed to really want to enjoy the game with the new community.
GRAPHICS? there are some performance issues all around from what i hear but its a god damn beuatiful game.
GAMEPLAY? This is one of the most unique pvp games ive seen in ages. UNIQUE. As in it will be wonderful for others but horrible for some. Your enjoyment is completely based on how competent your enemy and allies are though. If you have a teamate who fails at their role it makes it significantly harder as a hunter. If you have a handicapped monster, the game can end in under a minute. Pacing is weird. Not bad... Weird. It goes back and forth from quite semi boring chasing and strategic hunting where you have to plan how to corner the monster to full on♥♥♥♥♥♥hitting the fan. Its fun and transitions fast. Some rounds have more action than others.
STORY? Pretty much nonexistent. Its a game about shooting giant monsters with giant♥♥♥♥♥cool guns. Get the ♥♥♥♥ over it. While waiting in the drop ship, your teams selected hunters will discuss and give some insight into their characters which is great fun and interesting but wont change your world. like i said, at 4 hours in i have yet to hear dialogue repeat itself.
WARNING / CONCLUSION!!!! give the game a chance. I personally hated it my first few rounds until i figured out all the basics and im still learning about environmental buffs and proper tracking techniques. Theres a large learning curve. If you seem to be having trouble finding competent players to surpass the basic learning curve, grab some friends or make some. It helps garuntee a fun play environment. I get it, a lot of people are mad that the content they paid for (or did not and simply complained about it in previous reviews) was essentialy scrapped for a fair free to play model. At the same time though this is clearly the best thing that could happen to the game. It is not for everyone but the bottom line comes down to the fact that its is a unique game with tripple A development and a fair pricing model for no barrier to entry. Try it (AND CONSIDER SNAGGING A STEAM KEY AS MENTIONED ABOVE!!!)
Finally, some change to a game that had so much potential.  I hope this brings new, sustained life to evolve and games like it.

Dungeon of the endless is one of the most unique games ive ever played. At first i was a bit shaken by the games approach, but after playing it more, I was able to get a grasp of everything this game throws at you (which is a ton). DOTE rolls up many genres into an incredbily well done presenation that becomes addicting as all hell. Perma-death makes every decision that you make extremenly important to the outcome of every level in the dungeon. If you have a rough start, you will have to figure out a way to make it work to escape. Not planning your resources properlly may have drastic effects for you as you process to the next level. All of the characters are super cool looking and useful in different ways. The ability to level them up over time is awesome as you will start to love many of the characters you have in your party. If you are a fan of rpgs, rouge-likes, or tower defence games, DOTE takes the best parts of these types of games and creates something thats highly strategic, tense, and super fun to play. 9/10.

Simply a fantastic game. A rogue-like with real time strategy elements. Personally, not a fan of RTS games, but some of the elements I enjoy, and DotE does it well. The atmosphere fits very well, making you feel that resources really are limited and finding new people is fresh and rewarding. The different game ‘modes’ (or rules) based upon what landing ship you choose adds a great replayability element. You can also find ‘hidden’ dialog with certain paired up characters between floors. Unlocking their entire conversation grants them a future permanent buff. My favorite aspect is how you can set up traps or characters in however much time you want, until you open a door. Once the door opens resources are harvested and baddies begin to hunt you down. Here’s my favorite part: at any time the game is ‘moving’ you can pause it, look around and issue commends or begin building defenses. Nothing happens until you unpause it, giving you all the time you need to prepare you troops, even if the battlefield changes. The game is built around this, so there’s no unfair advantage, but I really like it because it means if I miss something or forget something, I have a chance to redeem myself rather than have too severe of a punishment. For me, that’s the fun. Make no mistake, however, the harder difficulties will require your best tactics, trying to pause and make up for mistakes will simply not cut it as your resources are more limited and the waves of baddies are more difficult. This is a great JRPG/turn-based feeling game, all the while letting you choose the pace of dynamically. You can choose to get everything unlocked with the rogue-like elements on the easiest settings, with a really slow, relaxing pace. Or you can let it all flow as you zip from map to room-view frantically trying to keep everyone safe/alive while defeating enemies as they come.

1. Find hidden things in a picture

This game is pretty fun and has a lot of potential. It's a village building simulator with custom building options and RPG elements all rolled into one! Sadly, since the game is still in development, you will encounter bugs. I have not had any game breaking issues at 30 hours in, but certain glitches are common.
You start off with 7 hearthlings who need to be fed and sheltered, and it's up to you to build their town and assign them with jobs. Design your town how you want with custom buildings, or use templates for quick builds. Craft furniture and decorations, build roads and gate houses, etc. You control what jobs your hearthlings do, from Cook to Knight you decide how to distribute classes to achieve your town's goals. As they work they level, opening up more options and skills. Play in Peaceful mode to focus on town building, add some danger with the regular mode in which you will have to defend your town from monsters, or challenge yourself with Hard mode. You can also choose two races and two climate types to play in, from the typical Medieval European style villagers to the new races which is more desert oriented. Each race has their own outfits, building styles, music, and some craft items specific to them. I enjoy the blocky, cute graphics as well. It's sort of like Minecraft, visually, but with more detail.
The main drawback of this game, currently, is the glitches. The one I get most often is issues with builds not finishing. It's not uncommon to have to destroy and rebuild several times to get a building to finish. I also have problems with placing items inside a house, sometimes it seems to add this to the build Queue for the building even if the building is supposedly finished, and then causes it to glitch finishing building so the item never goes down. I've also encountered hearthlings getting stuck in strange places they shouldn't have been able to get to, and nearly starving until I told them to build a ladder, and ladders (or scaffolding) from builds being left floating in the air and impossible to remove. Issues with lag due to lack of optimization is sometimes a problem as well, though they have already made some improvements in this area.
If you enjoy this genre of games and you're adventurous when it comes to glitches, then you may find this game worth the $25 even pre-release. If you are intolerant of glitches, stay clear until the game is officially released!

SpaceChem is quite possibly my favorite puzzle game, ever.
Its best aspect is that there is no clear-cut, one solution to each puzzle. Instead you're given some starting materials, and it's up to you to make the products. You can make each solution as elegant or convoluted as you want.
Puzzles range from dead easy to brain-melting in the later game. I've been stuck on certain puzzles for days. Some are one screen only, while others require you to manage different reactors with inputs and outputs. It's really awesome to work out a solution using the bare minimum number of reactors possible.
The only part I wish had been done differently are the "boss battles", where sometimes it's difficult to tell exactly what you're supposed to be feeding into reactors and when.
If you enjoy HARD puzzle games, and enjoy optimizing your solutions to beat others on the leaderboards, you owe it to yourself to play SpaceChem. It's fantastic.

"A bit too simple, is this really fun?"

The only problem is it might bore you before you "get" this game.
When I just got into this game, I've no idea how certain arrangements are possible---like multiple entries within 1 run, or overlapping pipelines, so it takes a long time to arrive at the solution---outside the box thinking takes a bit of wrestling.
It's challenging. It's getting addictive. If I beat a level but my solution isn't exactly neat, I'll replay the level.
The game also starts showing more variations in gameplay.
I'm not there yet. I'll see if it loses me anywhere, or if it'd be both brain-wracking and fulfilling fun at the same time.

The difficulty curve is perfect, and there are enough levels for everyone to enjoy the game even if you don't make it to the end (the last couple of levels are pretty hard).
Because there's no fixed solution to any problem, the replay value is huge. It becomes staggering when you take in consideration the different leaderboards and how getting a good score in each category requires a completely different approach each time.

Okay, serious review time
This game is pretty cool, though I don't play it as often as I should. It's a randomly generated driving horror game. I've personally don't think I've seen anything like it (and if I did, I forgot it) It's attempts to recreate a PS1-era game have succeeded, resulting in a terrifying, surreal experience. Horrors await you all along the road, and all you can hope for is that you maintain your car and sanity long enough to get the book, bell, and candle the witch needs to break your curse.
The scares in this game are actually quite effective. So far, I have accidentally run over a pedestrian while hallucinating, seen a stranger in my backseat who caused me to crash my vehicle, had a severed head land on the hood of my car, and drove through a tunnel of flesh.
Along the way there are shops to upgrade your car, items to restore your sanity, and a chance to replenish some of your depleted cash through scratch tickets or checking out a dark alley. If you do the second one, something bad COULD happen.
The game does have a permadeath system, encouraging you to take your playthroughs seriously.
The only problem I can see with this game is no save feature. Got to get up early tomorrow? TOO BAD! DID WE FORGET TO MENTION THE DEMONS!? BREAK THE CURSE! DRIVE! DRIVE! DRIVE! DRIVE! DRIVE!

I got the game as part of a recent humblebundle and would highly recommend the game to anyone who is a fan of the age old Katamari Damacy series, as any fan of the Katamari Damacy series can see that Lovely Planet takes a huge artistic inspiration from those games.
Lovely Planet is essentially a merciless speedrunner with Japanese undertones (although it should be noted that the Developer QuickTequila is located and based in New Delhi as stated in their twitter) and a cute art style, and a nice upbeat kind of music score (created by Calum Bowen whose soundcloud and bandcamp you should check out if you enjoy the game's music). The game boils down to shooting anything that is red and/or has an angry face while navagating through a labyrinth like map that can range from easy to hard all while being timed as you compete against a leaderboard of other players who have beat the game in a certain amount of time. What makes the game difficult, enjoyable, and challenging is that the gun does not have cross hairs and that the movement of your character is enhanced (in the sense that you move fast, you jump far, and you just have an overall snappy and springy movement). The time aspect makes the game addicting as you constantly try to compete with others (the closest I've gotten is roughly 5.45 seconds to complete a map where the #10 rank for that map was 5.25 and goes down to almost 2.20 seconds for rank #1).
This has been repeated quite a few times in the reviews I've read below, but I would like to repeat them once more as they are a very accurate description of the game. Lovely Planet takes the speedrunning aspects of Supermeatboy, the springy mechanics of the Super Sam series, and the aesthetics of Katmary Damacy to create an enjoyable game for the price that is offered of $5.99. I myself bought the game in a recent humblebundle for roughly $5 with other games, but would recommend it to anyone who finds themself debating if $5.99 (or the regional equivalent) is worth the investment. If you are someone who enjoys speed running and some nostalgia from old Japanese-esque aesthetic PS2 games then Lovely Planet is worth the price.

Sometimes it looks like there's a wall next to the platform you're on when in reality it's floating above the abyss twenty yards away. Other than that, I have no real gripe with the level designs, there are plenty ways to diverge and go about reaching point B on the maps, enough to keep me going back.
The controls are tight and feel great, never once did I feel cheated out of a jump, roll or my bandwith due to bad control or level design. In this regard my only real gripe lands in first person mode, while it is rather cool to run in this mode and I would much prefer it to 3rd person, the rolling and leaps of faith often leave me disoriented and sometimes send me tumbling to my doom. It's hard to accurately pinpoint how to fix that issue. Also, I'd like to mention that the jump pads need to send me flying a bit faster, it breaks the flow of the game and gets tedious when you mess up a jump, especially on the final level.
In a full release or summat later down the line, there's a lot that you could add to it. More environmental interaction, both good and bad. Ledges to grab hold of, wall running, variation in jump pads, leeches that grab onto you and suck away your bandwith until you roll them off of you, making gravity pull you down from a jump a bit quicker, those kinds of quick fixes.
Lastly, bugs. There are a few, mostly the cursor getting unlocked from the game and it not showing up at all after you beat the game and go back to the main menu. Other than that, it's a great little F2P game.

404Sight found its way into my recommended list and got a quick download because it was colorful, and at the glorious price of FREE, I decided it was probably worth the money.
You can tell immediately that the game has some rough edges but it's simple enough and has the familiar feel of an old-school platformer, re-envisioned for a 3D environment. Obstacles and pathways are marked in vibrant colors as you might expect in a cyber-punky type world which is also simplistic and easy to look at. 404Sight's integration of the "Ping" and "Bandwidth" systems is easily the most impressive part of the experience and show potential for a much more ambitious project.
My only real gripe is that it claims to be based on the fight for net neutrality but has very little to say on the subject. What could have been a very interesting way to raise awareness on this very relevant subject falls flat where it should have highlighted the importance of this struggle and showcased ways to make a real life impact.
All things considered, this was a fun game that Retro Yeti Games generously gave to the public for free. I hope to see more from them in the future as 404Sight left me feeling like it could be an early demo for something very exciting.

Trine 3. What can I say? This is a great adventure, and a worthy successor to the first two Trine games. The graphics are beautiful, the puzzles are challenging the the combat isn't too arduous. Overall I am enjoying the game, though I suspect I'd get more from it with a second player joining in. However the game is frustrating at times. The 3d perspective can be tricky to get the hang of, and the controls have strange glitches. For example, when Pontius jumps onto the ground to break objects or damage opponents, occasionally he will go charging off in a random direction when he hits the ground. While normally harmless, sometimes it means he goes sailing off into the abyss and dies! This is especially irritating on the bonus levels, when after 1 death you are sent back to the beginning. Developers, PLEASE, PLEASE! put some sort of checkpoint system in those levels! Yes they are short, but it gets incredibly frustrating doing the same bits of the puzzle over and over again so you can get those much-needed Trine-angles.
I would recommend that you play through the tutorial levels more than once. I didn't get the hang of all the controls the first time round, so a second play-through was most beneficial. Plus that sheep is adorable! :3
In conclusion, if you enjoyed Trine 1 and 2, get this! You will love it, but it will have you tearing your hair out at times!

It's a great game, but not exactly a Trine game. Do I recommend it? Absolutely, it has 5 hours of co-op fun and an awesome fantasy-bursting story that ties into the first Trine game.
So what do I mean by "it's not a Trine game?" Well, it's barebones. There are no difficulty settings like the first two Trines, instead however hard it's supposed to be is as hard as it is, which isn't very hard at all. Every little enemy dies in 2 fully charged shots of Zoya's bow or in a few hits from Pontius' sword or one hit of Amadaeus' box - speaking of which the wizard now gets an attack. While useful in bad situations, it feels weird since the wizard was almost useless for combat in the last two Trines, except (again) in special situations. The larger enemies just fly around and cast spells at you until you hit them with Zoya about 6 or 8 times and they aren't a big threat either. There's also no health jars, instead you regenerate health automatically after a certain time of taking no damage.
There's a lack of collectibles. Throughout the game you'll find Trineangles, and that's it. Each major level (of which there are about 8) has 150 Trine angles, except for the final boss, and all the other little chapters have 25. What's disappointing is the only purpose to collect these Trineangles is to get enough to unlock the next chapter as your characters can't level up anymore. You won't be getting a fire sword, triple arrows, or the capability to place five boxes and two planks in this game. Also why do I have to collect Trineangles to unlock the next chapter? This is something to expect in a free phone game, not a paid for Indie (is Trine still indie?) game, much less Trine. If you ever have to go back to collect more Trine angles you don't have to finish the entire level again for the game to recognize you collected them. This is good because some levels are 30 minutes long.
Back to the difficulty - there are checkpoints EVERYWHERE, and they make a ridiculous amount of noise. For the one or two puzzles I got stuck at it was really obnoxious hearing their sounds for the 5-10 minutes it took me to figure it out, but that's also a testament to the puzzles... They aren't that hard. In Trine 1 and 2 I still get stuck on a few of them, but I walked straight through 90% of Trine 3's.
The smaller chapters don't have checkpoints, and as a result are rather difficult sometimes. One with a big swirly platform mess took me 20 tries and had me raging, which was a good thing. I wouldn't want there to be checkpoints in those levels, it would ruin what difficulty it has.
Also, it's no longer a sidescroller, which makes some jumps harder than the puzzles themselves. It's hard to tell where you are on the ground, and where you're going to land, and I often found myself falling to my death. At least reviving dead people is easy, but you only get one per checkpoint which was never a problem with me. If someone required to finish a puzzle dies then that person will always be revived.
Despite these Trine negatives, it's a good game. For $20 you get more time out of it than you do on a $60 Call of Duty single player, and the story goes much deeper into the history of the Trine and, as stated before, ties well into the first game. If you're a Trine fan then this is clearly a must buy, but don't expect a Trine game... expect a different Trine game.

This thing right here is surprisingly good, I'd suggest trying it with friends though. That way you get the full Dead Effect experience. For a ported mobile game it's pretty damn good, I had low expectations that jumped higher as I progressed.

The relationship between platformers and cartoons is one goes deeper than realised. The original Donkey Kong arcade was originally meant to be a Popeye video game, and most platformers from Banjo Kazooie to Rayman have a cartoonish essence. Perhaps that's why Cuphead's design feels so natural; It is a genre's tribute to its roots.
Many have heaped praise on the visuals of Cuphead, and rightfully so, it has stunning animation, incredible character design that can be attributed to the emphasis on boss fights and its ability to both appear accurate. But what is really great about the game is that it has a streak of sincerity to it. Whilst it is ultimately a parody of the slightly insensitive yet overly moralistic cartoons, it does not feel forced or out of place. You are instantly immersed into the game from the very beginning, and like the cartoons of the past, it is instantly relatable.
The soundtrack is incredible, a jazz band performing bespoke themes for each level and boss that perfectly fit their personalities and the intensity of the fight. Often the music may be grinding as you attempt to repeat the same level over and over again, but once you take a moment to sit back and listen you really begin to appreciate how much time and effort went into every facet of the game.
The gameplay is challenging, yes, but I am surprised by how many people claim the game is 'too hard', whilst I definitely struggled at times, I never felt out of my depth or unable to continue, and when you finally kick the devil's♥♥♥♥♥♥ there is a genuine feeling of accomplishment, which is what a game should be making you feel. By trying to reduce that difficulty, people are not able to gain the full experience of the game. Likewise, I found that Cuphead offered enough perks and weaponry to give you a solution to a tough fight. A weapon that may have been incredibly useless in one level could be the key to beating that boss which has given you so much trouble.
If I were to give the game a downside, it would be the fact that the fights, whilst incredibly fun and enjoyable, are far from perfect. I found a few glitches that ruined my chances in a fight (Getting randomly hit for no reason on the final boss for example), and sometimes the way that the boss fights apply RNG means that you are often forced into a position where you are going to take damage regardless of your skill. Another issue is that sometimes the fights themselves feel wildly inconsistent, the progress bar is useful for seeing how 'close' you are to beating a level or a boss, but at times it feels like one 'stage' is incredibly time consuming, whilst another one takes barely any time at all. Likewise, whilst some bosses are incredibly challenging for certain reasons, others are perhaps a bit more predictable and feel far less of a 'challenge' (Sally Stageplay and Werner Werman for instance were far easier than Captain Brineybeard or the Phantom Express, mostly because of the RNG element) but the experiences fighting each boss seem to vary between player to player. I found Grim Matchstick to be very easy, whilst others really struggled with him.
Overall, the game is incredible and absolutely worth every penny. Even if you find platformers difficult, this game's charm and execution seems to have an appeal that is almost universal.

The high definition remake of the original Serious Sam: TFE turned out to breathe some serious new life into the game.  One of the original kings of the FPS genre, Serious Sam does a lot of things right, with a few things wrong, and suffers a tad from being a bit of an old title.
On the upside, the map sizes in this game are huge, providing a great open-world, fast-paced FPS adventure.  The voice-acting is nicely done with the expected humour and satirical remarks.  The design and layout of the levels are great, and very well-planned and make the game flow very well, but the downside to this game thing, is that if you manage to play for a long stint of time, the game manages to blend it's levels together and it starts to feel a little stale.
Nothing about this game is really amazing or innovative compared to todays FPS games, but it does manage to create an atmosphere of non-stop action from start to finish.  There's always something to shoot around every corner, some new tactic to come up with, new enemies to fight and new weapons to pick up.  The old-school secret areas are also a great touch to the game providing secret weapons, armor, health pickups or maybe getting a weapon earlier than you would otherwise.
The boss fights are pretty fun and in general the game is still really fun, the added benefit of the HD remaster in graphical fidelity and a few new features (autosave, etc...) really gets Sam back in the game.
I would recommend this game to anyone who likes new or old FPS games, just give it a try, you might like it.

You get some games like this that are a blast for the first hour or two but then start to wear thin as you realize its just a shallow, super simple arcade racer but this game seems to be pressing all the right buttons after a good 5+ hours in.
First off, the driving is somewhat physics based, with air time, tires and cones that you can hit that'll go flying or get you snagged up, banked turns that improve cornering... it DOES take skill to make the fastest turns and cuts and a good player will totally rock the socks off a bad one. Then you get the whole Nitro mechanic that can make or break a race if you know when and where to fire one of those off.
Second, the graphics are actually quite good, with reflections, dynamic lights and some nice textures for the most part. Some tracks look damn nifty.
The tracks combine fun themes, good looks, and good racing gamplay which is pretty much the holy grail. Around 20 tracks with day/night variants as well as backwards/forwards runs. Got a good mix of real fast, short tracks and some longer ones where skillful steering adds up. Really are some pretty cool and fun tracks like Turnpike, Cliffs, Fortress, Aperture Labs, Alpine and Downtown - my favs.
I do have to say that'd I'd appreciate some more loooonger tracks as well as off road ones. Think Turnpike but with mud puddles, ramps... like WARIOS STADIUM from Mario Kart 64, haha
The cars are simple in appearance but that more or less fits the game - not super silly but not realistic either. Cars have 4 stats that you can upgrade and each car has a different distribution when fully maxed out so they perform differently as well. Some might have really high top speed and nitros but lack in the handleing and acceleration department as an example.
Multiplayer works well as I've played a good 40 races that were smooth and fun. There are a few kinks to work out but an actual Developer was racing with us from time to time and he said there was gonna be a patch soon that'll help smooth a lot of it out. Could use a few more features like a 5-6 track points tally game where after the cup is over the player with the most points wins, though.
All in all defs worth the 8 bucks I paid for it!

First things first. If you bought the game prior to it transitioning to free to play, that stinks, sorry. But get the ♥♥♥♥ over it. Game prices fall with age and if you want you could keep the game at 60 and have fun playing with empty lobbies. It going free to play seems like the only reasonable (and expected and suggested by the community) choice.
That out of the way, let me clarify Ive only begun playing since it went f2p. I intend to review the f2p game as it is in its current state rather than complain about what it used to be.
SO HOW FREE IS IT? Instead of most games having a premium and in game currency, this one only has one single currency that works for everything from skins to new hunters. As far as I can tell you start off with only the weekly free rotation hunters (a la league of legends style). MAJOR TIP: if you go find a steam key from some provider (which is pretty easy) and valued somewhere between 5-15 dollars, you get about 2/3 of all the characters unlocked along with skins and currency. In terms of how easy it is to aquire currency, by the time ive reached rank 11 with about 4 hours in and subtracting the currency I got from buying a steam key online for 5 dollars, ive had enough to buy a top tier hunter of my choice along with perks and skins for said hunters weapons. They have a lot of challenges and level up rewards to make it easy to progress. Like i said if you just get a steam key for dirt cheap, you'll already have more than enough content to keep you preoccupied for hours.
COMMUNITY? I have no idea, its the first day and right now theres more than enough players online to find a game instantly. All have been friendly and reasonably skilled at my level. I actually managed to land in a quick match with the dev team my first hour. They were extremely polite, cooperative, and forgiving. They seemed to really want to enjoy the game with the new community.
GRAPHICS? there are some performance issues all around from what i hear but its a god damn beuatiful game.
GAMEPLAY? This is one of the most unique pvp games ive seen in ages. UNIQUE. As in it will be wonderful for others but horrible for some. Your enjoyment is completely based on how competent your enemy and allies are though. If you have a teamate who fails at their role it makes it significantly harder as a hunter. If you have a handicapped monster, the game can end in under a minute. Pacing is weird. Not bad... Weird. It goes back and forth from quite semi boring chasing and strategic hunting where you have to plan how to corner the monster to full on♥♥♥♥♥♥hitting the fan. Its fun and transitions fast. Some rounds have more action than others.
STORY? Pretty much nonexistent. Its a game about shooting giant monsters with giant♥♥♥♥♥cool guns. Get the ♥♥♥♥ over it. While waiting in the drop ship, your teams selected hunters will discuss and give some insight into their characters which is great fun and interesting but wont change your world. like i said, at 4 hours in i have yet to hear dialogue repeat itself.
WARNING / CONCLUSION!!!! give the game a chance. I personally hated it my first few rounds until i figured out all the basics and im still learning about environmental buffs and proper tracking techniques. Theres a large learning curve. If you seem to be having trouble finding competent players to surpass the basic learning curve, grab some friends or make some. It helps garuntee a fun play environment. I get it, a lot of people are mad that the content they paid for (or did not and simply complained about it in previous reviews) was essentialy scrapped for a fair free to play model. At the same time though this is clearly the best thing that could happen to the game. It is not for everyone but the bottom line comes down to the fact that its is a unique game with tripple A development and a fair pricing model for no barrier to entry. Try it (AND CONSIDER SNAGGING A STEAM KEY AS MENTIONED ABOVE!!!)
Finally, some change to a game that had so much potential.  I hope this brings new, sustained life to evolve and games like it.

"Roguelike."
The word alone calls to mind so many gaming archetypes and settings as to be an almost irrelevant descriptor, and yet we all know the basis of the procedurally generated game with randomized elements.
"Tower Defense."
Again, a genre so permeated with varying degrees of micro-management and strategy archetypes that the picture in each person's mind could almost be a different game.
DotE is an amazing offering in that it takes both of these genres and combines them in a way that makes a single player experience on a short campaign almost a multiplayer game... and turns a multiplayer game into a uniquely individual experience even for a group of four players working together.  Or
working together - because this game can be both of those things, as well as several degrees of in-between.
First, this is a resource-driven game.  If you haven't the luck of the draw to find good research early on, you have to play with what you get, and that can be very challenging when you can't build any defenses and the heroes alone have to do all the fighting.  It's possible to win early levels this way easily, but after 2 or 3 levels the monsters are just too big or fast.  If you find all the weapon technology you can use, it still doesn't help you mine resources, and that leads you to starting new levels without anything with which to build.
Second, because of the many characters playable and the size of the group involved at varying stages of the game, as well as the randomness of spawn and how players deal with the baddies, playing the same strategy several games through will more than likely be an exercise in frustration.  If you don't find rooms with any place to build gathering modules, you don't get much for resources, but if you have rooms that allow ONLY for a gathering module, then they are not defended when a horde spawns in the next room over.
"Turns" take place every time you open a door; every door you open has a chance to spawn enemy waves, which will appear in rooms that are uninhabited and unpowered, and there's no such thing as hallways in the typical Rogue/nethack sense, only "rooms" that are longer, where you can build... or not.  As a result, the dungeon is more like... a house layout, or an open-concept office building than the old, twisty corridors of the ascii game from which the genre takes its name.
Starting a single player game, you'll have 2 characters (choose from a pool of 10 or so, depending on DLC - see note about DLC, below) and (may) meet more in the "dungeon" that can be hired for food - which is also the currency used to advance character levels.
You'll immediately be faced with the decision to build 1 of 3 resource generators (or not, but you should ASAP), and then move to the next room.
Gather resources, build new gathering module, defend crossroads spawn points, move heroes to operate gear... open door, get mobbed, run fervently around the revealed level to battle spawn, go find the last, hidden, door-breaking baddie out there - and don't forget to heal your lone operator out on the fringe!  It sounds repetitive (and it can be so) but it doesn't get old,
when you're voiced with friends.
Unlocks of new characters and ships happen as a result of ingame recruitment, mission successes, and other factors related solely to game play, excepting one annual event where a character unavailable for 361 days per year becomes available in the middle of January, if you can find him.  Recruit him and make it through 3 levels, and he's another unlock.
There are two notes worthy of mention, if this is going to be a good and thorough review:
While most games I've played that have been hung like that
I think 1 of around 16 or 17 games  were unrecoverable.  That said, I've never lost a solo game to any kind of malf, and I wonder if the multiplayer games where it has happened could have been caused by some players having/lacking the DLC.  If for example, a player without the DLC is host, and some dialogue option is supposed to occur with a DLC character another player is using, perhaps this can cause a conflict resulting in a hung game... but that's only conjecture.
Of all the Rogue-like and TD games I've played, this one by far has the highest replay value
is the best one to play with friends... but I'd suggest being voiced when you play: two or three doors opening at once and losing a high-level game to such an error can get old after the first two laughs.

- Puzzles can be solved by an average user. These don't require a savant or prodigy to solve.
- Ambient effects and animation keep it from looking like still frames.
- Hints and a complete "Strategy Guide" (walkthrough) are built-in if you do get stuck.
- Sparkles to indicate when something in a location can be interacted with. This is especially helpful with all of the backtracking.
Cons:
- Somewhat cheesy story and voice acting.
- Lots of backtracking and re-use of previous scenes for Hidden Objects during the course of the story.
- Use of shadows as objects.
- The lighting effects in Hidden Object scenes can make it difficult to see certain objects. Sometimes I had to wait for the light to change in order to see something.
- Fixed 4:3 aspect ratio. The in-game copyright says 2012, well past widescreen adoption, yet they didn't at least put in a decorative border.

Lovely Planet is an enigma.
On the surface, the game is cute, bright, colorful, and has one of the best produced soundtracks I've ever heard, taking major influence from J-pop and various production styles like it. It looks adorable, it feels adorable, it is adorable.
Then you start playing it.
This game is a first person shooter that is essentially a very cute target practice sim. You need to haul it as fast as you can through various obstacles to the ending pole, shooting any and every red enemy that you see, while avoiding shooting at the blue ones. You run pretty fast, you jump very high, and you have infinite ammo in your block shooting gun. No enemies take more than one hit to kill, and only one type will shoot back at you; shooting the bullets they shoot kills them as well as stops the bullet. You have three objectives to get stars at the end of the game; beat the level (duh), beat a minimum time they give you, and have 100% accuracy on all of your shots. Sounds decently straightforward, right? That's because it is, in theory.
The first world is decently easy. However, even in this world expectations are quite high; a lot of the levels I beat the minimum time by few milliseconds, just because it's so fast paced. This might just be me being bad at the game and not being fast enough, because a lot of the world records are half the average speed. However, as angry and frustrated at both yourself and the game you get, you're never genuinely mad, because of how cute and fun the world around you is. Beat a 10 second minimum level in 9.997 seconds? That sucks, but holy sh*t this soundtrack!
The second world adds a new mechanic into the game; you need to shoot apples (tomatoes? large red bean bags?) before they hit the ground. Now, this would be very easy if your bullets had normal bullet physics; however, they move at a consist speed, about the same speed you run. So, if you need to shoot one of these things from a good distance as it's falling down, you need to aim your bullet down just above the ground so it'll collide into it. This is not as easy as it sounds, and I've had amazing runs destroyed because the apple hit the ground a few frames before the bullet hit. However, as all this difficulty stacks up and starts to become extremely frustrating, the amazing soundtrack just slowly washes it all away.
Is this game relaxing, fun, and a good takeaway from stress and other more violent and dark games? Absolutely.
Is this game frustrating, rage-inducing, and the bane of speedrunners everywhere? Absolutely.

I have just cleared the first world on normal difficulty and therefore I might not be well suited for an in-depth game review on gameplay issues and level design. Hell, this is my first review and I did not even bother to review or comment games I love and have nearly 100h+ on. So If you expect a full and detailed review, there is plenty of those out there!
This game is a blast. I feel reminiscent of my Jump and Run childhood and the good old "pass the controller once you die" memories come to mind a lot when I play this game (although I don't think it is too hard, prepare to die a lot!). The key difference, I don't even need to have a friend around to be grinning at my own failures. I thrive in malicious joy and it is because of the three core aspects of the game, of which I feel only capable of handling two accordingly (art style and music).
The gameplay feels really rewarding once you beat those bosses and I will definitely come back getting those P- and S-grades once I got time to finish this (although I might turn out to be like the onion in this game by attempting this).
As musician, I really rejoice hearing those jazzy big band tunes! 56 tracks, according to the Spotify-Playlist, is way more than any Blockbuster movie would ever get. The themed tracks are marvelous and bring a level of immersion and style to the game I thoroughly enjoyed. I miss this with all those realistic AAA pieces of garbage that came out recently. I can only imagine the effort and work that is required to compose, rehearse and record/edit such a massive soundtrack. The music itself is worth your money and I definitely will buy the soundtrack, although I might be listening to it via streaming services.
It is a vital part that activated my masochistic side, quite frankly enjoying myself in this perpetual cycle of dying and getting pumped for the retry (f**k the slot machine).
I am not an artist but even for an art-style illiterate like me, I was blown away by the level of detail and thus the amount of work and effort put into this game, I applaud you! Every attack animation and boss "transformation", indicating the corresponding boss phases, feels unique and refreshing and I always keep wondering what kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t (in a positive, challenging way) I will be facing, after I reach a certain "phasepoint". Really creative stuff you put out there and fairly well executed as well!
This synthesis of great music, fantastic artstyle, a comic and cheerfully vile world and a challenging but rewarding and addictive gameplay let this game stand out and literally force me to throw out my initial impressions on this matter, even though I spent so little time on it (bought it yesterday night).
We need more games like this in the current wake of AAA "games as  service" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and microtransactions shenanigans and I strongly recommend to buy it if any of the aforementioned appealed to you! And please, please, please stop comparing every game to the Souls-series. This game is not a game as a service, but a service to the gamers!

Lets start:
Core Gameplay 5/5:
The base gameplay is revolved around opening doors in a randomly generated dungeon and trying to defend the crystal and any other modules (structures), while looking for the exit. Each room can contain anything from enemies, to equipment, to merchants, special resources and even additional heroes for your party. Each room, as well as any defeated enemies, will contain dust which the crystal will use to power explored rooms, which will in-turn power modules and keep enemies from spawning in them. Enemies will spawn in two ways, the first being when you open a door and they're just waiting behind, and the second being spawning in rooms that are both unpowered and don't have any heroes in them; If you have any rooms like that, each time a door is opened a horde of monsters will spawn there. Finally we get to getting to the exit: Each floor will require you to find an exit room and then have one hero carry the extremely heavy crystal to said room; Once the crystal is picked up all unopened doors will open and enemies will infinitely spawn from those unpowered rooms, and if the hero carrying the crystal dies then its an instant gameover. While the gameplay may sound like it'd become tedious very quickly, theres something about opening those doors that keeps you on edge.
Story 3/5:
I won't go into the story of how the heroes crash landed on Auriga Prime, but instead say this: Every hero has thier own story to tell, when they're paired up with specific characters. Each story is rather short, but not only do they expand the character's lore, but the lore of the Endless Space universe, though only a little.
Heroes 4/5:
Not including DLC, there are currently 16 heroes available to unlock/play, and including DLC there are 26. You both recruit and level up heroes using your food resources, expectaly giving them higher stats and new abilities. Heroes have four stats they use, most of which the hero is already geared toward. These stats are Strength, Speed, Stamina and Wit; each of these stats do what you'd expect them to, though those who are defaultly higher in one stat will be more likely to have skills related to that stat.
Multiplayer 4/5:
Multiplayer is supported and in my opinon improves the game, its much funner to run around with someone to talk to, then by yourself; It should be noted that some aspects of escape pods (gamemodes) are disabled, such as starting with four heroes in the armory pod while playing with two people (it could've been each player controls two heroes). Each player also has thier own individual resource pool, instead of a team resource pool like you'd expect; but this means that if you can get your teammates to give you all thier resources (for say a research project), you'd be getting 2x/3x/4x the normal amount. But if you intend to play multiplayer you should arrange for someone to play with you, since multiplayer is non-existant.
Music 3/5:
Some catchy background music, though you probably won't remember any of it until you boot up the game.
Graphics 3.5/5:
The acutal models and portraits look rather good, though almost all of the hud's icons are either heavily based on or flatout ripped from Endless Space, and I'm torn on rather they should've made new icons or keep the old ones like they did. On one hand I feel that a new game needs new icons, but on the other I feel that it has a more Endless Space feel by using those icons.
Overall 4/5:
Admittedly, I purchased this game just for the bonus race in Endless Space, but I've enjoyed playing it; From the opening of doors, to the short stories, I sincerely enjoyed myself, Its got an addictive element to it!

If this were released on its own rather than as a third installment in a so-far solid series then it would undoubtedly garner a huge amount of praise, despite its very short length - I finished the main storyline in a single sitting of around 4-5 hours and there are only a handful of optional levels I have left to finish. Unfortunately, as the third part in a trilogy, it would be reasonable to have a certain degree of expectation for this release. So overall I was disappointed, but I am still recommending this game on its individual merits.
So why does it compare so unfavourably? Well, firstly, I'll discuss what it does right. The environments themselves are absolutely gorgeous and extremely detailed, even more so than the first two. The continuation of the story is compelling and the writing and voices are as excellent as ever, and it is good to see the background stories of the main characters and the Trine itself fleshed out further. The move to full 3D exploration is a bold and refreshing change and the new game mechanics, both as a reult of this and some other new additions, are certainly very interesting. Unfortunately where this falls flat is that these mechanics do not feel exploited to maximum capacity and most of the puzzles are very run-of-the-mill. Many of the more interesting puzzles and uses of the mechanics appear to be in the optional levels rather than the main quest.
Additionally these changes produce some undesirable side effects. Only being able to use the rope on specific hoops rather than on lots of surfaces feels somewhat like a step backwards. The different character abilities also feel quite redundant now since a lot of puzzles can now be completed with any character - any of them can move objects around which seems to be the solution to a ton of the puzzles.
And sadly, the introduction of 3D environments which, as I said, was potentially a very interesting change, in the end doesn't really add anything new and is in fact even detrimental to gameplay. Exploration can be very confusing at times, and the camera angles frequently obscure the player and other things that you want to be able to see. The controls are more awkward since there is an extra axis to think about, it is slightly strange because sometimes "up" means "up" and sometimes it means "forwards". For the large part it is just a cosmetic change rather than adding anything deep in terms of gameplay, or remixing the classical gameplay elememts with this new paradigm. Mostly it feels like it's still a 2D platformer so the 3D controls just get in the way.
Another quibble is that respawning seems to have been made worse, especially on the optional single-character levels. If all your characters die you restart at the last checkpoint and sometimes there aren't enough of them. But on the single-character levels there are no checkpoints at all so you have to restart the entire map - the main reason why I haven't completed many of those levels and I'm not sure if I really want to go through and finish them all.
Finally the story just doesn't wrap up in a satisfying way, due to the short length. Such a shame!
So overall, this is still a very fun game, just lacking in content, and certainly doesn't stand anywhere close to the first two. If you go in with the right expectations then hopefully you will still enjoy it.

Just finished the game in 8.6 logged hours. If you look at the discussions here on steam, you will see that many complain about its length. I don't. The Trine series was never meant to be a series of lengthy games. It's meant to be casual fun for the casual gamer. And it is! Don't be silly and expect 20-50 hour gameplay. I see a lot of reviews by people who have finished the game in half the time I took and then give it a negative score. Why are you in such a hurry? My playthrough wasn't plagued by deaths or full level retries. When I was done with a level I took an extra ten minutes going over each area (not the full level) where I missed some Trineangles (yes, that's what they're called) and then moved on. The chalenge levels I all completed 100% on the first try. Why people feel the need to rush through games I will never understand.
Trine 1 was great. Trine 2 added new mechanisms and, in my opinion, ended up being too fiddly, repetitive and tedious as you fought the physics engine more than the game. Trine 3 simplifies the experience and provides smooth progression (some say too easy). The levels are creative and enjoyable. New ideas are well implemented.
Frozenbyte does a good job of balancing the characters and constructing puzzles that utilizes all character powers. Zoya still suffers a bit from being nerfed from the first game and Pontius is still a bit too powerful in combat after being buffed in the 2nd game. But I won't complain about that. They're all good and you'll need them all regularly to finish the game in singleplayer.
The new thing in Trine 3 is the departure from a 2D platformer to a 3D platformer. To be honest, I think it still feels like 2D but "enhanced" to the 3rd dimension by allowing depth movement of both characters and objects. You still don't controll the camera. It's still fixed as in the same way as the previous games. I think Frozenbyte did a great job evolving the game further in doing this. Thumbs up!
As others have mentioned, the character progression is gone. No skills to level up or abilities to unlock. This is the only thing I missed in this third installment. But I wasn't bothered by it considering how fun the game was from start to finish.
All in all a great sequel in the Trine series! I loved it!

I loved Trine 1 and 2, but Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power really disappointed me on some levels. While the 3D, level design, voice acting, and soundtrack are top notch, the overall game is just the opposite, a very lackluster finish. The game is ridiculously short, and it drops an enormous cliffhanger ending that is unlike other cliffhangers that are suspenseful, this one just made me angry. It stops directly when you feel like you're about to gain momentum and kick off the story, I felt like the map would extend and then we would continue our journey with finding the other parts of the story, but no, I was greeted with a credits screen...? It frustrated me to say the least. I love the Trine games, don't get me wrong at all, but this one just kind of dropped the ball. I understand they ran out of money, but an uncompleted game is never a winner.

Firstly in taskmanager this program looks somewhat dodgy. The actual exe is named NetNeutrality-Win32-Shipping.exe and uses around 300mb of ram, while a background exe named 404Sight.exe runs at 2mb. Might just be how the game is coded, but this looks awful suspicious.
Also of note, there are no audio options what so ever and the firstperson view has no adjustable fov. The actual graphics menu is very non-descript, with everything getting a low-ultra prefix.
The framerate is very choppy and drops anytime a particle effect is on screen, despite the game looking quite visually undemanding (although it has a nice artstyle) and me running a pretty medium tier rig.
Jumping is very floaty and odd. You can steer left and right (something you can't really do in real life) but can't pull back and forth (something you can do in real life by shifting your centre of mass.)
There is no score-screen, inter-level screen or even heads up to tell you that you're on the next level. As a result, I exited out and then selected the latest level on the level select screen, which was 14. I had never even started this level, nor had I completed or started the previous one.
The core gameplay is actually a cool 3d platformer with a lot of glaring ui/menu issues that hamper your enjoyment of the game. If the dev can get this, and the dual exe thing, fixed, I will definetely recommend this to any fan of the platformers or timetrail type gameds.

This review will also be discussing Siege of Dragonspear as well
Baldur's Gate is a game that when it came out, was revolutionary for it's time. I actually owned (and still have) the orignal five disk game that came out back in 1998. Put out by Black Isle (under the developmental eye of the three original founders of Bioware), it is a game that takes place set in the Forgotten Realms. In this game, you're basically playing Dungeons and Dragons, but for those of you out there that are familiar with nothing older than 3rd Edition, you may find the mechanics for the classes a bit odd. Baldur's Gate uses the old AD&D 2nd Edition rules set and it is still quick to pick up.
Character generation is rather straightforward, allowing you to roll and re-roll your stats as much as you'd like until you're happy with them. Compared to the original, the Enhanced Edition shows you the total point number that your stats total to. This is helpful when trying to shoot for a total number. You are able to store a rolled set that you like, but can only store one set at a time. Regarding character creation, you have a variety of races to pick from, but only humans can be any class. The trade-off to this is that non-human races can go above an 18 during character creation, and in AD&D, that is rather huge, since unlike later versions of D&D, your stats will not improve. Beamdog brought the kits from Shadows of Amn (the sequel) to the base game, allowing you to get a feel for the kit right away. This is something I wish the original game had when it was released. They also added a couple of new ones from 3rd Edition, such as the Shadowdancer for Rogues and the Dwarven Defender for dwarf Fighters. Due to the nature of the game engine, there is an experience cap for classes, which is 169,000 XP (most classes will hit level 8, wizards will hit 9, and rogues will hit 10).
The story is rather intriguing, and keeps you wondering what is going on in true, classic D&D style right up until the 5th chapter, when you finally see the whole picture. Then it becomes a “race against the clock” (not literally) to save the day. Unlike it's sequel, Baldur's Gate assumes by default that you are playing the hero, or at least an anti-hero (not a villain). You can be evil, but if you become too evil, you won't be able to ever complete the game, since you won't be allowed to enter cities (the guards will literally come, tell you there's no entry for you, and attack you). There is also two optional missions, thanks to the game's original expansion – Tales of the Sword Coast – Durlag's Tower and Balduran's Isle. It also added a new area called Ulgoth's Beard, a small village with some new items for sale and some missions. These have been included in the base game from Beamdog. Durlag's Tower is a classic dungeon crawl, with deathtraps and monsters, as well as rewards and a climatic battle at the end of the quest line. Balduran's Isle is a tale that has you follow the final voyage of the great hero Balduran (whom the city Baldur's Gate is named after). While the tower is difficult, it is still much more enjoyable than Balduran's Isle is. This was one area I felt that Black Isle fell short on, and quickly jumps up in difficulty.
Speaking of difficulty, Beamdog has added an option for “Story Mode”, for those that just want to play through the story. Think of it as “super easy mode”, where you can't die, and nothing harmful can affect you. While I think this is not a bad idea for those that are not fond of the old school AD&D rules, I didn't like using it. I experimented with it a little, and never went back after trying it. The game has been mostly untouched, which is smart by Beamdog – it has just been tweaked, bringing back a lot of things they added in Shadows of Amn. As for the new NPCs that have been added, I have already heard from many how they feel “forced”. But my only argument against this is this – this game is nearly 20 years old. How else are new characters supposed to feel like without feeling like they're mod NPCs? I think they are a nice addition, each with a voice actor that did a great job on them (Rasaad is actually voiced by Mark Meer – Male Shepard from Mass Effect).
Siege of Dragonspear was the massively new expansion put out by Beamdog for this game. They managed to bring back just about everyone from the first game that had a character in it, such as Jennifer Hale, Jim Cummings, and Melissa Disney. The expansion is very well done! While at times, it felt a bit rushed in sections (going through a underground cavern to Dragonspear Castle), the expansion is still very well made, and does an excellent job covering the massive gap between Baldur's Gate and Shadows of Amn. Those that played Shadows of Amn back in the day will easily recognize who the hooded man is. Siege of Dragonspear increases the XP cap, letting you get a little higher (I believe I ended at level 10 or 11 with my mage). This is handy because you're that much higher when porting over your character to Shadows of Amn.
While I'm sure there are reasons for all the poor reviews by “the old guard” about Siege of Dragonspear, they do not speak for all of us. I only speak for me, and being part of that “old guard”, I absolutely loved this expansion, and consider it to be part of the entire game experience now. While I was a bit sad at who they brought over from the first game (Safana? Garric? REALLY?) they still managed to bring over a few fan favorites. Hats off to Beamdog for Glint, the gnome cleric/rogue; a very well written character, and a likable personality. He slid right into the slot of both cleric and rogue in my good party, and part of me wishes Beamdog would have added him into the base game. M'Khiin (goblin shaman) is a neat idea and something I actually thought was creative to do for this series. There's also an optional battle pit called the Black Pits (but I have not experimented with that much, so forgive me if I don't feel knowledgeable enough to discuss it in this review). If you are looking for a D&D game that has a great story and good characters, I do recommend checking it out.
Siege of Dragonspear is a journey full of nostalgia, but is a worthy journey. It is actually a bit refined Baldur' Gate original experience.

It is sad that I am doing this, but Trine 3 did not live up to the other 2 games.
They should have kept it 2D. Perhaps they could have kept in a couple 3D transition parts, which gave some spectacular vistas etc. It would have significantly reduced the scope on a lot of levels and allowed for much longer game and more complete story. They even mentioned in the forum that they had a better game and story written, but the 3D made it too expensive and unwieldy.
They also put in a bit too many destructible items. Sure it is nice, but having a fence that can break just makes it easier to fall off the map. It must have also taken more production time as a result. The levels, however were incredibly detailed and goorgious. The models were amazing to look at. However, due to its length, it did not have the variety of Trine 2.
The 3D also reduced the capabilities of the characters and barely added to the puzzles. They took so much away, like the leveling system and most of the character abilities.
The game is a bit buggy too. I often could climb up a wall that you should not have been able to and walk up above the map. There was a bit of animation stuttering and a lot of clipping too. None of this happened in the previous titles.
I, personally, had no big problems using a keyboard and mouse and traversed the game seldom dying. Most of my deaths was me running off the map due to bad camera angles.
The game's length and abrubt end is the most disappointing part. I finished it in just over 6 hours. That is getting all the achievements while I slowly traversed the levels looking at every nook and crany there was. I love to look at these games at a detailed level. Most will probably finish it in 4 hours. You might think that would lead the story to be rushed. Quite the opposite, however. We literally got half of the story, and they leave you on a cliff-hanger. Plus, some of the levels had little to no story narration and acted mearly as transition levels. All the side missions literally had no story elements at all and acted is basic horde modes for those to unlock further levels. Of the 8 levels, the first 3 were to introduce each character and brought them into the story. Another 1 or 2 were transitions. That leads to 3 or 4 story missions, of which 1 specific level had the majority of the entire story.
It is really sad. I hope they make enough money to make another Trine. It is - hands down - the most beautiful series of games of all time. They have charming and entertaining stories, and I would hate to see it go away.
They even said that this cost them nearly $5.5 million to make and their original scope would have cost over $15 million. They could not afford to finish it and if they were a bigger developer or had more money, we would have seen an amazing game. You often see other developers with budgets orders of magnitudes higher still make worse games. I wish Frozenbyte had the same opportunities.
They need another go at it.

Trine 3 is a fun and quirky puzzle adventure with the cheeky charm that I have come to love since the first installment. If you are a fan of the series, I can heartily recommend this sequel, you will not regret picking it up. If you did not enjoy its predecessors, then you will not find that much different in the third game and should probably pass it by.
A few more detailed remarks:
- The artwork and soundtrack are once again lovely. Game world and characters have become even more detailed than in the previous game.
- The new 3D movement adds a lot of depth to the levels and puzzles. Unfortunately the controls feel a bit clunky at times and the fixed camera can get in the way. There were a few instances where I died simply because I couldn't even see my character.
- There are a few interesting new gameplay mechanics. Most notably, Zoya can now pull objects around with her grappling hook and tie them to other objects / surfaces. This makes for very cool solutions to some of the more challenging puzzles.
- The game feels a bit short. My boyfriend and I went through it in about 7 hours, and that includes all possible bonus missions / challenges. The story ends at a point where you'd expect it to finally kick off properly (the rest is really just lots of exposition and prologue) and it's obvious that there is at least one addon/sequel planned, probably more. Of course you can't expect a full 200h fantasy RPG for this price and Trine 3 certainly isn't designed to fill that format, but I still would've liked a bit more content for my money.
- I can't say much about the singleplayer and local multiplayer modes, but we've had a few issues with the online multiplayer mode. Our games seemed to get out of sync with each other fairly often, symptoms of which include inconsistent state (obstacle destroyed on one screen vs. still intact on the other), flickering or random teleportation of characters and maneauvers failing simply because the other player is not exactly where you see him on your screen. None of these things are gamebreaking, but they can be quite annoying. We also had a very strange bug in the final level, where the flaming lava projectiles needed to defeat the end boss would only spawn when one player was tabbed out of the game. It took us several minutes of frantically trying to figure out what we were supposed to be doing (we even tried to fling the Knight character at the thing with a sort of catapult contraption) before discovering the solution by accident when one of us tabbed out to check a walkthrough.
- The new physics and rope engine, while being a central part of the gameplay, can also be quite buggy. Ropes snap for no apparent reason, the Thief character sometimes gets thrown around wildly instead of pulling an object towards herself, and once my partner was killed by a thrashing rope bridge gone berserk at the slightest nudge. Again, nothing gamebreaking as such, but it can be annoying.
- The puzzles in general feel a bit weakly defined. Obviously there are always multiple solutions to most problems to accomodate the different characters / amounts of players present, but sometimes it seemed like there were maybe too many solutions, to the point where we couldn't figure out what we were supposed to be doing. We often ended up cheating our way through a level by boosting each other up with the wizard character or just building big stacks of crates to the exit, instead of finding a "proper" solution.
Despite all of this, Trine 3 is good game. I think it would have had the potential for being a lot better, e.g. if the gameplay were a more polished and it had a bit more content, but it's still good value for its price.

If you started with this game and liked it i dare you to try the second game on the series.
