When this game first arrived in my inbox, I was hesitant to play. it had been years since I played any games (past 2006), and I've grown up a console kid, so I was unsure if I could enjoy the game with a keyboard and mouse. I grew to love the game so much that I decided to purchase a usb controller to enjoy it more comfortably (hours of mouse use can cause wrist strain, which shows how long I've played this game in a single sitting).
Another one of my doubts was this being a Kickstarter game. I've heard some bad tales of Kickstarter games, so initially I had a bad attitude towards it. Story mode may fall short, but Survival mode is where this game shines.
The game is littered with bugs still, so expect frequent crashes if your computer is not up to par. However, the creators humbly admitted that the official release didn't go as smooth as they had hoped; and rather than try to push out a half-finished game before the holidays they notified that they will be working on a major update to be released in 2018. I was very impressed by this move. The game is still playable as of now, so you don't need to wait for an update to start enjoying this game now. Just brace yourself for the occasional hiccups.
Now, as you might have understood by now I'm a casual gamer: not by any means striving for achievements or high scores. I play games to relax from my day jobs and take a break from 'adult' life. This game has been part of my routine of relaxation. While the wolves do tear into your patience a bit, hunting, scavenging, and exploring are serene moments. Ever seen the Northern Lights? While it's a far cry from the real thing, it's wonderful to see it and it's effects on the in-game world.
If you are looking for a game away from people, this is that game.

That said, the events are sometimes too inconsitent with what you can do in game. For example, I got an event that told me how Christopher Columbus  sailed across the ocean to found colonies. The game gives me an explorer, Christopher Columbus, but not any conquistadors, which is a unit necessary to explore uncharted land. In this situation, I'm just sailing the sea discovering new waters, but I can't get on any new land and found any colonies. It really negates the selling point of this game and I'm afraid I can't recommend it becase of this.
Also, although this game supports modern resolutions, the text scale way too small and you'll likely find yourself playing on a 4:3 resolution anyway.

Short Version: Europa Universalis II: But with the bugs ironed out and better mod compatibility so it's VIP QUALITY from that alone.
I liked Vanilla EU2, I did not like the occasional CTDs and complexities with using mods. For the Glory irons out both issues, so it's that experience but better. My one issue was lacking the original OST, but I copied that over and solved it on my own.

This is an absolutely excellent 1/4 of a game.

The puzzles are relatively simplistic, but what do you expect from the first levels of a game?  Things are going great, the story is beginning to pick up, and then.... it's over.  The game essentially ends after Act 1 of the story.  In 5.6 hours (while multitasking!) I was able to complete this game to 100%, including all collectables.
Now, not all short games are bad!  The original Portal, for example, can be finished in much less time than Trine 3.  But in Portal, they present the "final test", and then the game opens up.  In Trine 3, they present the game opening up, and then roll the credits.
I *love* the Trine series, and I *love* Frozenbyte, but as it stands I cannot recommend this game.

Dishonored is a first-person stealth action-adventure game set in the fictional plague ridden city of Dunwall. You play as Corvo Attano, body guard to the Empress and friend to her young daughter Emily. Framed for murder, you are forced to become an assassin and spend the majority of the game seeking those who wronged you.
Gameplay for a single campaign can last anywhere from 15 to 40 hours, depending on how you go about accomplishing your objectives.
Because of the games steam punk inspired art style the graphics still look great, despite it being almost four years old.
This game boasts a quality soundtrack, gameplay that can be tailored to a wide range of styles, good artistic direction and a compelling story, but my favorite aspect of Dishonored is what a big emphasis it puts on players choice.
The game allows you to complete each mission in a variety of ways. The more you explore your environment the more options become available to you. Because of this, how you chose to reach and accomplish objectives impacts the environment and the way the story progresses. You can do ‘low chaos’ or ‘high chaos’ runs - deciding to use stealth, weapons, or magic to move forward.
Creating panic and leaving dead bodies spreads disease, increasing the number of rats and weepers roaming Dunwall city streets. Operating under stealth and choosing to spare people usually takes takes more effort, but will make the ending to your story a happier one. Making different choices vastly alters your environment and how NPCs react to you in the game, giving it good replay value.
The DLCs included in the GOTY addition are worth playing. They do a good job of continuing and complementing the story but are not necessary for it to feel complete, which is how downloadable content should be.

Basic key rebinding, doesn't detect Mouse 4/5 (Thumb Buttons). Controller has no mapping, and while it has cute icons in the environment to go with it, I wouldn't at all recommend using it because of the difficulty. Graphics options are minimal (AA, Vsync, Adjustable Frame Cap incl. Unlimited). Supports multi-monitor and all common aspect ratios if not everything. No FOV Adjustment (default is okay enough for average PC user), No Crosshair even optionally. No performance issues.
This game is amazing, but not for the feint of heart, or for those with even average dexterity. Beyond the middle of the 3rd world, out of a total of 5, the game becomes extremely difficult, and that's even with an on-screen crosshair (built into my Asus Display), which the game completely lacks by default. Up through the 3rd world I was able to complete the 2 bonus stars for time and 100% accuracy, but beyond that point more and more levels become an immense challenge just to finish at all. In other games, if you aren't good you can beat things, but you just wont get all the points or whatever. In this, if you aren't exceptionally good, you literally will not beat the game.
More enemies, mechanics, and obstacles are added as you progress, and while most aren't portal levels of brilliant, they do a good job of mixing up how you think about different situations. Though because of the difficulty near the end, it makes it a challenge to experiment with various timings, as it puts you in situations with very little time to react and execute, though retrying from the beginning of each level is nearly instantaneous.
The controls are extremely responsive (they really need to be for the end-game), and there's more variety than you'd initially expect. Though again, you need to be good enough to even see all of it. However, once you unlock a new world, ALL of the levels are open to you instantly. You're not completely stuck if you find a level right in the middle that gives you trouble, you can come back to it later, or never at all as you only need a certain amount of stars to progress.
The visuals are very minimal, but extremely charming in combination with the music. The game is frustrating, but the amazing music by Calum Bowen forces a smile onto your face for most of the experience. The soundtrack was free around the release of the game, and I've listened to it a considerable amount. The only thing I'd wish for, is more variety in the environments. There's definitely some there, but ones with drastically different color palettes or even nighttime levels would be a treat.
I completely and totally recommend it for fans of shooters both old and new. It's extremely responsive and the music and visuals just make you smile. The beginning levels are a joy and they're worth experiencing for it's common sale price. Just don't plan on seeing everything unless you're already skilled in twitch shooters, or you're willing to work at it. This was clearly made by a fan of shooters and PC gaming, and other than some small adjustments, I tremendously appreciate it.

Get Off My Lawn is a free-to-play vertical lane shooter. Your role is to take control of a old age pensioner with a liking for guns and defend your home from alien invaders.  Enemies descend vertically from the top of a 7x7 grid in waves, which become progressively harder to defeat.  Gameplay consists of moving the character left and right across each lane while shooting the advancing aliens before they can reach and damage your house.  If they are not killed before they reach your home, it takes damage until it is destroyed.  Then its game over!
Your armory consists of three guns: musket, shotgun and ray gun. Each has its own advantages and disadvantages; i.e. the ray gun shoots through all ranks of aliens in a lane but has a delayed firing time, while the shotgun shoots across three lanes but only at a shorter distance. Orbs are dropped when aliens die.  These can be used to upgrade the house, weapons and to buy boosters.  There is a combo counter which maxes out at 10x.  Keep this going to increase your score faster.  There is only one life but if you die you can spend 1000 orbs to continue.  There are three weapons: musket, shotgun and ray gun which have their own characteristics and should be used at particular moments of gameplay.
+ Its free.
+ Its a space invader variant with Tele-Tubbiesque alien enemies.
+ Can start at levels 1, 5, 10, 15 or 20 depending on the challenge you feel like facing.
- Too few enemy types.  Only four exist: grunts, dodgers, behemoths and tanks.  Even if each possesses different behaviour and strengths/weaknesses.
- Non-transferrable MTs.  Limited to the PC purchased on.  I.e. the orb-doubler and orbs wont appear on another devices that they were purchased on.  Why wasnt a profile system added!?
- Gameplay while very easy is very, very repetitve.
- Scaled for free-to-play model.  Orb collection is painfully slow without the orb-doubler.
- 100% achievement requires at least one purchase.
* It has micro-transactions. But these are not needed to complete the game.  They just make progress faster and give some income to the dev(s).  Well it is free!
* Basic, functional graphics.  Look alot like stock assets.
* Fairly well balanced.  Its pretty easy to get to level 20 (if you play alot).  However even with maxed weapons you can die quickly afterwards.  Almost always needing a booster to avoid damage to the house during some waves.
* Well conceived weapons, upgrades and boosters to help progress.
* Most of the achievements are a variation on a theme and are fairly easy to get.  Endgame achievements are very grindy.  Maybe taking 100+ hours, depending on your ability.
Get Off My Lawn is what it is.  Its nothing great.  Its adequately made.  It plays okay and the gameplay is very, very simple and very, very repetitive.  Most gamers will likely get bored quickly and move on.  However if you are after a casual space invader type shooter to kill a few minutes here and there, then it could be what youre looking for.  Dont expect much more given its mobile origins.
I have only two gripes.  First its scaled to make you purchase the orb-doubler in order to make gameplay bareable.  If you dont, then dont expect to complete the game (read obtain 100% achievements) in less than 100 hours.  Or you could look at it as given £1/$1 to support the developer's effort.  Second, the inability to take MT purchases across devices is unforgiveable. Let me start off by saying I might consider changing my vote to a tentative recommendation if the rest of the story isn't paid DLC when it's finally done.
I'm not complaining that the game is too short (it is, but a short game can still be enjoyable). My main gripe is that the "ending" is a terrible place to leave off in this adventure. Imagine playing Ocarina of Time and the game ends after you get two-out-of-three spiritual stones. That's how I felt when I beat the last level here. I actually had to check and make sure I just didn't see the "Early Access" label.
I didn't notice much for bugs outside the occasional 3D physics hiccup, but I'm usually lucky at avoiding that sort of thing. Note how I didn't say the game was bugfree.
They didn't just streamline the characters—they gutted their skills and abilities to pretty much the bare minimum. Where is Pontius's Hammer of Satisfying Thumping Noises? There is no upgrading or equipment of any kind. What you start with is what you get for the entire game. The puzzles are incredibly simplistic too, like they're trying to make the game accessible to pre-K kids.
All least it looks like a Trine game. And it's in 3D... but that's about it.

Yet again Frozenbyte delivers another beautiful Trine game. This time they implemented 3d! Being use to using the WSAD keys in most of my games, this was easy for me to get use to, unlike some of my friends. Now there is a level choosing system in a game board-esque styled start point. Here you can choose what levels you want to play, as long as you have enough Trineangles to unlock it. You can also play through certain parts of that level if you haven't collected all of the Trineangles first time (it will show you what part of the map you missed them and how many you missed).
With a new 3D Trine comes new controls. You can no longer draw with the mouse to conjure boxes from Amadeus (F is an instant box while Q and E moves the box further/closer from you). Levitating a fellow player on a conjured box in co-op is not possible any more(and if you can I can't seem to find the option). Using the W and S key for Zoyas rope to go up and down won't let her swing in certain directions (it is now the middle scroll wheel). Pontius can scale walls like a professional rock climber so you barely need to play any other character (is this a glitch?). Respawning a friend is really slow.
Overall it is still a great game to play with friends. There are some bugs including the Zoya co-op floating stasis in her intro, boxes spazzing out, characters becoming stuck in weird places, characters falling through objects, respawns being placed under objects in dangerous water, and Trineangles appearing orange even though you've collected them. There are probably more, but these are what I have personally witnessed. I will always be a Trine fan and will continue to be one, but I have to admit I think Trine 2 is the best so far.

Although the game itself is very short (Took me about 4-5 hours long on my first playthrough), the game itself is very fun. The 3D envirement adds more depth to the game, but it still feels like Trine 1 or 2. Although the lack of upgrades does take from the replay value of the game, since I already got all the Trineangles and all the achievement with that as well, there isn't really any replay value, unless I'll do a co-op playthrough as well. DLC is probably gonna happen, especially after seeing the game's ending. Overall, I really enjoyed the game, but the game was too short for a $20 game, and the lack of replay vslue that was in the other two Trines is gone from this game.

I will reccomend it, because in the end it is still a fun game. Although the transition to 3D has resulted in a few quirks in the controls it still plays like a Trine game, complete with wonderous visuals and fairytale story. There are few complaints; namely the puzzles aren't really solvable in as many ways as previous games and the wizard isn't quite as versatile as he once was. The big one is the length. Far too short. At time of completion, I feel as though the story has been only half told. Aside from these gripes, I'm loving the rope mechanics implemented with Zoya and the resultant puzzles; as well as the epic, beautiful environments Trine is so well known for, extended in 3D with more interesting backdrops.
All in all, a bit short, but still fun. Maybe wait until more content is added or it's on special to pick it up.

Serious Sam is a weird game and there's reasons why it's still considered fondly to this day, and it's all about identity.
Serious Sam looked at the more serious FPSes and went "pppffft, they're GOOD but they're not serious enough". And then decided to make a game with incredibly serious enemies with a seriously smoking arsenal of serious weaponry. And while part of this is a joke, I'm also completely serious. It's a seriously solid game.
Each enemy behaves differently (with there being a couple pallete swap enemies) and there's enough of them so that you'll be killing every non-boss enemy at least 50 times before the end of the game, so you'll know how they act, how to avoid their attacks, and how to kill them. This game counts on that because as time goes on, levels start getting longer and enemies become increasingly numerous and unforgiving. It reaches points where you're killing hundreds of enemies every level and they are literally everywhere. It's pretty awesome. Well, to a point.
The first half of the game is great, your weaponry slowly expands as do your rogue's gallery. You learn the purpose of how each weapon can be used effectively while exploring the scenary to get your hands on much needed ammo, health, and secret weaponry. But by the time you get to the Dunes about seven levels in, it starts becoming apparent that this game relishes in sending waves after waves after you. It's fun, but only for a while.
Levels become larger and less confined to give you more space to work in and fit in more enemies, but repition also hits pretty hard with it. Serious Sam is definately the kind of game where you want to take breaks or risk tiring yourself out because once you make it to the Metropolis, the game starts becoming increasingly stale, despite the various landscapes and obstacles.
Don't get me wrong, this is still a fun carthatic hectic game (and you better save often...) but it just becomes really repetitive in a hurry and soon even amazingly fun things like spamming Cannonballs becomes the norm and your best bet for survival in battlefields that take minutes to cross.

I'd like to start off saying that it takes a lot of a game to make me want to write a review for a game. Portal (It was a very short review, yes, I know, I did not write it, but another person who has played it did) and Terraria being the only other games I have written reviews for. So why this game?
Early Access - Can be very undependable, but not for Stonehearth
This game has a very interactive community. With weekly streams where sometimes viewers can contribute their ideas (Check the lore for Rayya's Children on the Unfired Pot and the Clay Bed) and where viewers can easily ask questions and learn about where the game is going and it's current projects. They also provide an option to play their most recent update that isn't fully released, to test for bugs. This way you aren't forced to play a very buggy version, but you can still help test. But this doesn't mean there won't be bugs, but for an Early Access, the more stable versions are pretty good. This means there are also constant updates, usually one every one to three months. The developing team also provides a road map and progress on their official website.
Freedom to Express Creativity
Stonehearth has a variety of ways where you can really call your settlement yours. From easy custom design on buildings to decorative furniture, you can make a wide range of areas from a park to some outlandish building that defies physics. If you want to have a more peaceful play through, so you only have to worry about the resources instead of the intruders, there is a Peaceful option to play with your settlement.
Relaxing Game
As your hearthlings will say frequently, I can't believe the tranquility. Even with those pesky, annoying, ugly, well-named goblins being cowardly thieves, you can't say this game isn't relaxing. Even the goblin chief has a soft spot for Bluebell! With starting off in a beautiful forest or arid desert, it is just breath-taking. The music just adds to it. It only gets stressful when you get two goblin raiding parties at the same time with two defending footmen who just got out of a battle... with a giant wolf. Atlanta will be remembered.
Stories
This game also already has so much history and lore! But it also has freedom to make more. There is no more to be said.
More
There are many more smaller categories I could hit, but with these main points, it should help you decide if you want to buy it. I would suggest watching some of it if you are still on the fence.

Ah, Guardians of Middle-Earth... the LotR under the MOBAs.
This game is a fairly bad MOBA, really. Commands and abilities often don't work, timing is an issue, and the game contains quite some random bugs every now and then. It is enjoyable and playable though, and can be a lot of fun! In fact, the game itself is not bad. It just has its issues. It is a bad MOBA however, if you look at the fact that there are quite some MOBAs out there that are way and way better, like League of Legends, DOTA 2 or SMITE. Yet... I'm going to have to give this a positive recommendation.
First off... this has been the first actual MOBA I have played. I know that LoL and DOTA 2 players will disagree with this, but for a first time MOBA this is quite an awesome game. The genre just works well and if you are not used to the superb features the other MOBAs offer, this game is a very enjoyable experience. Additionally, I started playing this with a friend due to our great love for Tolkien's Lord of the Rings and its franchise, and though maybe in a way that could have been better both graphically and gameplay-wise... it succeeds in enjoyably allowing you to play as a lot of well-known and less well-known LotR characters with good voice lines, matching characteristics and extremely well-matching lore, abilities and playstyle.
Therefore, I recommend this to everyone who enjoys the Lord of the Rings universe, and in case you have never played a MOBA before, this game is a good way to start off with the genre.

Because it's free, I have no reason not to recommend this game. Gameplay wise, however, I'll say that it's got a few unique features, such as choosing to activate your ping to speed up, but also needing to know when to deactivate it so you can avoid having your bandwidth/health drained, which you incedentally also use to fuel your speed boosts to break through the tougher barriers.
As it stands, the game is fun but also can be buggy at times. On more than one occasion I found myself confused as to why the booster pad didn't launch me, and at other times the track felt like it was pulling me to the side like a magnet. The jumping mechanics for the game are a little wonky, and I found myself mostly relying on the launch pads to get me where I needed to go.
Graphically this game is interesting, as it's obviously supposed to have a minimalistic feel to it, but at the same time it's right on the border of unfinished. The assets are all well designed, but once you turn your ping off everything loses its color and you're left looking at blocky grey pathways that seem like the base of a novice graphic designer's good intentions. The Tron-esque feel to it all is nicely done though, and in first person it really does feel like a spiritual, technological successor to Mirror's Edge.
The best thing I can say about this game is that the music is extremely well done. All of the tracks are interesting and nonrepeating, and you can tell that someone put time and effort into creating them. If there were a way to listen to the music by itself, like as an option in the main menu, I feel that this game would be a little higher on my list.
So all in all, a good game if you'd had to pay around five bucks for it, but since it's free I'd call it a great game instead.

Probably one of my most frustrating gaming experiences.
This game is amazing. Truly, it had the potential to be a shining gem out there. If you play the solo campaign, it is great and fun and totally worth it. Get it on sale and you should have no regrets.
Yet, I do not feel like I can recommend it because in multiplayer it is ridden with bugs and glitches that are not just game-breaking but can also ruin a good 5h+ run.
And this is such a shame because the multiplayer experience has almost everything to be amazing. Until your game crashes after 10 floors and a corrupted save file keeps you from recovering it. Or the game decides to act as though you did not kill all monsters, and thus prevents you from healing, although you did. Or some mechanics do not work as intended (plenty of bugs including the Mechanic Pal module). And quite a handful others including syncing issues where what players see on their end differs from the other players' experience. I had my friend's character dying to a monster although he had moved his character back to a safe room. On my end it only looked like he was still in the monster's room, getting beaten down, and thus died. But then his items spawned in the safe room, showing that he was not lying when he said he had moved back. And he was the host, so his "version", if not properly synced with mine, should have had precedence.
tl;dr, I love the game, it has amazing potential, but if you want to play in multiplayer, too many game-breaking bugs can really ruin your experience, especially in a roguelilke that can prove tough and requires micromanagement where small mistakes can end you. And when the game has been out for a while and even issued DLCs but did not fix these major bugs, this really saddens me and I cannot honestly recommend the game.

Dishonored is a first-person stealth action-adventure game set in the fictional plague ridden city of Dunwall. You play as Corvo Attano, body guard to the Empress and friend to her young daughter Emily. Framed for murder, you are forced to become an assassin and spend the majority of the game seeking those who wronged you.
Gameplay for a single campaign can last anywhere from 15 to 40 hours, depending on how you go about accomplishing your objectives.
Because of the games steam punk inspired art style the graphics still look great, despite it being almost four years old.
This game boasts a quality soundtrack, gameplay that can be tailored to a wide range of styles, good artistic direction and a compelling story, but my favorite aspect of Dishonored is what a big emphasis it puts on players choice.
The game allows you to complete each mission in a variety of ways. The more you explore your environment the more options become available to you. Because of this, how you chose to reach and accomplish objectives impacts the environment and the way the story progresses. You can do ‘low chaos’ or ‘high chaos’ runs - deciding to use stealth, weapons, or magic to move forward.
Creating panic and leaving dead bodies spreads disease, increasing the number of rats and weepers roaming Dunwall city streets. Operating under stealth and choosing to spare people usually takes takes more effort, but will make the ending to your story a happier one. Making different choices vastly alters your environment and how NPCs react to you in the game, giving it good replay value.
The DLCs included in the GOTY addition are worth playing. They do a good job of continuing and complementing the story but are not necessary for it to feel complete, which is how downloadable content should be.

After trying out EU4 for a free weekend on steam and my being unable to purchase a 40 dollar game, i was starving for some Europa Universalis action... And then i found this for only 2 dollars...
And while i made this purchase on somwhat of a whim i do not regret it (not just because of the price i got it at, which is practically nothing). For the Glory is a pretty good spin-off game and it has a few mods built in which you can enable or disable. It's a bit slow on new systems. It also tends to crash every so often SO SAVE EVERY CHANCE YOU GET, MULTIPLE SAVE FILES ARE YOUR FRIENDS!
I think the reason it tends to crash for me is because i'm playing on Windows 7. I'm told this game works best on a machine with Windows XP, but the game still manages to run fine despite the occasional crash. When it does get crash-happy though (something i've only encountered once as of this original posting of this review), that's probably a sign from the universe telling you to stop playing and go back to sleep, though on average, the same only crashes once or twice and my game-session is usually smooth the rest of the way (and i play my games without mods). According to the small community for this game, it's almost impossible to run on Windows 8 which is a real shame. I'm also unsure of what'll happen to you Windows 10 users who buy this game and may not be able to run it. Then again, modding is a thing so you may be able to run it with some help from the community, so if you have a newer operating system don't be afraid to ask around on the forums first.
Compared to the new EU4 i find For The Glory a lot easier in comparison. It doesn't have as many menus as EU4 and it's pretty simple, especially if you're new to Europa Universalis. It's the same level of addicting (you'll spend hours and lose sleep over your nation expanding and surviving the test of time), the graphics are a little dummied down compared to the newer games because this was a game made for XP afterall, but it's nothing too bad to look at. The game also has a number of cheats and mods that can be used in the game if you feel like giving yourself an advantage.
The only flaws i really have to complain about with the game is the crashing and that it doesn't have any steam interface built in (so if you want to talk to your friends while you play, that's out of the question because you don't get any pings to indicate that your friends are trying to talk to you). You have in front of you the final update and ultimate achievement of the Europa Universalis I/II formula.
You see, when in 2007 EU3 came out, it was... bad. I mean, REALLY bad. It was broken. Featureless. A big step back from EU2, that came out in 2001. The first big expansion of EU3 came out THREE MONTHS later. And even after another one in 2008 (when the game was repackaged under the "EU3 Complete" name) it was a disappointing game, coming after the historical flavour of EU2.
So in 2009, 8 years after EU2, the team behind the AGCEEP mod for EU2 released this "sidequel" to EU2: it had widescreen resolution, it had 10,000 historical events, it had major tweaks to the rules and the AI, it had a better, more streamlined UI, it had better mod support. It was, in that particular context, the "real" EU3 (more like a EU2.5).
So, it's a great grand strategy game. But.
BUT.
But in 2010, EU3 saw the release of another TWO expansions, and the game became good at first, and excellent after the last one (now it was repackaged again under the "EU3 Chronicles" monicker). Yes, the historical flavour was still lacking compared to For The Glory, but in every other aspect, it was now a superior game.
So I still recommend For The Glory in 2014, when even Europa Universalis IV exists? Yes, even just for a trip into history of strategy gaming. If you want to try Europa UNiversalis I or II, skip those and get For The Glory instead.

If you've ever played the later games (x-com or x-com 2) but not this, you are missing out. The game is split up in two sections, "geoscape" and "battlescape".
In geoscape you maintain your bases (yes multiple). You construct base-sections, select research and manifacturing projects, and buy and store supplies (such as ammo, grenades...). I enjoy the latter part but understand why some people wouldn't. Make sure to store ammo or else you'll have to go on missions without! When your radars find UFOs send out your interceptors to shoot them down.
When you attack a crashed or landed UFO you enter the battlescape. The feeling of fear and excitement on the mission
hasn't been captured since. Shots actually has consequence due to a couple of things: friendly fire is on, a "missed" shot can actually hit another alien (no better feeling than that) and scenery destruction.

What to say about this game? Purely based on my childhood experience, it is 17/10! I still remember hanging out with my mate (as I didn't have a computer at the time). He managed to name each soldier after one of his family members (we were like 10) only for the vast majority to die in a single mission leaving only his distant uncle alive and killin'.
Push forward 20 years, nostalgia aside, I still feel that this game is appealing. Clearly graphics have been outdated by about 45 years, but the gameplay is clever for what it is. I loved the 2012 remake, I really did, but it just lacked that 'something' that this game had.
Overall, my favourite things about this game was that it was and is immersive. When you are on a mission to save a city from an invasion, (whilst the AI is terrible) the game actually felt like you were part of the team. Another thing that I liked was careful planning and base building. The thing I liked the MOST about this game was the fact that it had so many elements to it. No game to date, for me, has been able to replicate this.
So here is my final analogy. XCOM UFO Defense is a game that covers so many facets. All the games that try to mimic (even the brilliant XCOM Enemy Unknown) this game are like the The Expendables movies; full of money, ideas, time, developers, researchers, hype - only to fall short on the main thing - plot (and if you are not following my analogy - immersion).

The whole is packaged with minimalistic graphics which suite the games just perfect. Any more eye-candy would have been a distraction. The puzzel interface is also well made, with shortcut keys allowing for quick restructuring. What remains is the 'storyline' which  is surely rather minimalistic but still motivating to 'move on' to the next level and see what happens. If you like training your brain with novel ideas, this game is a must-have. Just don't be too hard on yourself if you get stuck over a puzzle for a long time  - finally cracking it is so rewarding! Though in early access, the game can be fully played and is quite enjoyable. Think of it as a more accessible alternative to dwarf Fortress with 3D voxel graphics, and a bias towards above-ground building.
Some rough edges remain obviously – it is an alpha version after all – but even the rolling-release version is stable. In dozens of hours of play over the last two weeks I had only one or two crashes, which is far less than many AAA games.
I am running it on a Geforce GT640M (2GB). It works at around 30fps, with occasional drops depending on the cluttering of the village, though I have to significantly reduce some settings (e.g. player-built local light-sources).
Some pointers for the beginner:
- Look through the options menu. There is an experimental "super speed" option, which has to be enabled from the main menu and is quite useful to accelerate construction projects. Further options like "automatically queue parts needed by buildings" or "autoloot fallen enemies" allow reducing micromanagement if so desired.
- Some tools, including prebuilt house templates, seem to favor odd-sized structures, but the work is built from 4x4x5 blocks; The tunnel mining tool also operates on those, so aligning everything to these helps.
- The building tool works well, but has some notable limitations – sometimes undo doesn't work, walls and roofs can only be placed but not removed and thus you have to cancel and start over. Using user-defined templates allows saving intermediate steps for large buildings, or generally creating larger structure from reusable components (e.g. city walls).
- Careful about path-finding! In some situations you need to manually rescue you citizens ("hearthlings") with a ladder from starvation on battlements of a building they just built, or from a hole they just dug.
- There is currently no way to hide upper floors of buildings when using the available indoor-views, though this rarely becomes an issue.
- You CAN emulate dwarf-fortress and build a subterranean city, but inside the building-tool will only be good for creating nicer floors; You can create two-floor high caves capable of holding structures with walls and roofs, but it requires additional effort, as the citizens cannot dig upward.
- When designing a building, make sure that there are no inside-compartments without doors. Hearthlings may get walled in and starve (unless you tear down the building.)
- Normal-mode is sufficiently peaceful to concentrate on building, but later on enemies will become a problem unless you have good fortifications.
- Monsters spawn outdoors, where no citizens walk. Unused buildings don't help.
- When overproduction becomes a problem, try building a merchants stall.

Set in a fictional world, inspired by the previous Thief game(s) Dishonored is here.
What a true masterpiece of the stealth / cyberpunk genre.
Dishonored is one of those games you expect a lot out of (since it has so many positive reviews) and trust me it deserves every penni you spend and it is one game you might get stuck with until you really finish it (i.e. all the achievements including the dls) or just give it a try and see what it is like. Now to give you a short review of every aspect.
Story: (7,5/10)
Plain and simple, Dishonored story isn't anything new or unique in the Game industry, however, since it is a stealth game and like (almost) every stealth game the point is to drag in with the top edge art and cunning gameplay along with the dark and silent atmosphere. When you take those points into though and compare it with other so called
stealth/cyberpunk games like Deus Ex human revolution you will see it has quite a furfilling story.
Art: (9/10)
The art for the date it was realesed was good hands down, and even after 4 years you can't really say it's bad. Resembling a cartoonish like pattern along with a correct mixture of sharp and blurry art alike, it brings you just the colour that this sort of game needs, never mentioning that the art playes a quite role
in making you realise the consquences of your actions in game
Sound: (7-8/10)
While being to absorbed in the game you will not really listen to the sound or music BUT for those that do, the sound effects are sharp and clear that give you a good sence of distance and drag in further more into the game.
Gameplay: (10/10)
Probably being on of the very best games I ever played, Dishonored provides you with so many opportunities to complete a level, with so many upgrades and skill sets and so many different ways to finish a chapter that I cannot put it into words. Anything from the abilities to the routes that you can take to reach your target to the alert level of the guards, the "chaos" meter and the surroundings (i.e. weepers (zombie like creatures) rats, fish, civilians etc.) it is simply amazing!
In sort, buy the game or pirate it and then buy it, it will be worth your time even for those that are not so keen on stealth games.

So, after a good amount of play time in this amazing title, I'm going to leave you folks my honest opinion of a review.
This game is rewarding in several ways. Are you the type of person that loves to explore, even the dangerous places not meant for the average beginner? You might just find yourself that toasty warm piece of clothing that'll save your life. How about trying to take down that bear just because? Yea, he was tough, but now you have more than enough food to worry about hunger. Like crafting? There's a whole lot of that in here too, you don't have a sharpener and your knife just broke... You've got some of that plentiful scrap metal right? Go craft another! Want to go fishing but no hooks or line? Use your hunting prowess to gain the materials for fishing.
The game has a whole lot of options and choices, so beyond the survival aspect, you do have a lot of freedom, and you can get hours upon hours of rewarding gameplay out of this. The $34.99 tag is worth it. If it's on sale? It's a steal. The developers? Very aware of player issues and comments, and are definately spending their time to make this as enjoyable an experience as possible. Free roam, story mode, and challenges. Many ways to play, all very interesting.

In general:
It's a very good exploratory game, where you wander around the beatiful world, take in the atmosphere and try to survive.
Kinda like "Dear Esther" or "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter", but with enough interesting gameplay mechanics to be engaging.
The Story mode so far is excellent, with interesting characters, exciting mystical plot and good delivery of the lore (meaning, it's all very compact, delivered to you in small cutscenes and tiny written articles, that you only read if you want to, no wikipedia-worth-of-cutscenes shoved down your throat on game launch).
And there's the Sandbox mode, which just lets you go out in to the world and survive the hell out of it, as long as you want/can.
Also, the voice actor cast is great. If you want to hear Solid Snake teach Commander Shepard how to survive in the wild, this is the game for you.
However, it SUPER IMPORTANT to note, that this is NOT a shooter game.
It is, technically, an FPS, but the pace of the game is totally different from a typical shooter.
You don't butcher a thousand nazis in the first hour of gameplay, things don't explode in your face and you don't install cyber-augmentations on your character.
Instead, you navigate your way through a blizzard before you freeze to death, get spooked by wolves at night, creep in on a deer to shoot it and harvest it for meat and crafting materials, get impressed/depressed by the characters you meet in the world, cook a can of beans over your campfire, while watching the sun set. And so on.
It's a very meditative game. So, if you're looking for an action packed, hign octane thriller, probably best you keep looking.
On the last note, I feel like this game is quite an original one, as it avoids most movie/game tropes and finds other ways of being very impressive. The night is scary without the jump-scares (and really atmospheric), the dynamic hunger/hydration/temperature/fatigue system makes you always aware of the passing of time, as you need to feed yourself and not get caught without shelter in the stormy night.
I got mesmerized many a time, while looking at the snow falling from the night sky, or the orange sun above the pine trees at dusk, or the white and blue snowy landscape I saw from a hign vantage point.

I sooo wanted to love this game.  It looks great, it's reviewed well, and the gameplay looks like a ton of roguelike/tower defense mashup fun.  This should have been up my alley in a hard way.
Buuuut...
The UI is just awful:
- You can't get a good, comprehensive view of a level all at once, so when enemies spawn each turn, they can wreck all your off-screen stuff without you even knowing it.
- Controls are absolutely clunky.  Since it's also an RPG, this game has a lot of different commands, which are hard to map naturally to the keyboard, especially when the main action is mouse-controlled.
- With the pixel-styled graphics, more than a few characters in a single room become impossible to manage.  During a fight, everybody's sprites and health bars turn into a big jumble, leaving no way to manage your individual characters.  Healing or fleeing in the middle of a brawl are crucial, but often impossible because of all the action.
- Every problem above is compounded by permadeath - totally fair in a lot of circumstances, and in a lot of games I play (Don't Starve, Minecraft, X-Com, Binding of Isaac, etc.) but with all the cheap shots this game throws, it brings the fun to a screeching halt.
Sorry if it seems I'm nitpicking; as I said, I really wanted to like this game.  Everybody says you have to give it a chance, get used to the lousy controls, and eventually get over the learning curve. This game, this series, is a lot to take in. Grand strategy games can be a ton of fun, but you have to be willing to put in the time to learn how to play the game before you can truly enjoy the game.  Europa Universalis basically allows you to reshape history, starting from somewhere in the 1400's up to the early 1800's (Although mods can make it so you can go on indefinately). My first game I tried to take over the world starting as England. I ended up getting conqured by France and whoever that is at the northern border of England at the time within a few years.  And that's how learning in this game works. You're gonna get a basic tutorial, to give you the general gist of how to do things so you're not going in completely blind, and then you've got to go in and get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you learning. I spent four games trying to figure out what to do when you're at war(♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ portugul, taking the land for my work...) and how to annex or gain land.  The game can provide alot of fun for those who have the apptitude to learn, adapt and conquer. I'd say this is one of the good Paradox titles to try out if you're looking to get into the Grand Strategy genre, mainly cause it's the cheapest in the main series of thier games.  But despite it's age, it's still a really good game.  So if you're looking for a good, deep strategy game, and you've got the time and patience to learn, this is a game you should consider.

This is an updated version of Europa Universalis 2, and is unfortunately not in serious development any more. The most recent beta patch is from December 31st, 2013. While this is an update to the predecessor game to EU3/EU4, they are quite dissimilar. Paradox had a distinct vision when creating EU2 compared to EU3/EU4. A lot of time was spent on trying to model historic events in EU2(FTG) and this is enhanced with the included AGC-EEP mod. While EU3/EU4 are designed from the ground up to be mostly dynamic, FTG has a lot of reliability built into what will generally happen. Specific events that mirror history will pop up and a lot of times history will repeat itself. That is not to say that the game is not dynamic and that everything happens the same way, as the AI has some freedom of choice and the player is limited only by their own skill. However, if you play as Russia, be prepared to face the Time of Troubles, as a German a radical Reformation, as an indigenous American tribe a lot of technological disparity, etc. While the engine does not have anywhere near the polish of later EU games, it is fun and has a separate appeal of its own.
An amazing strategy game. Not as complex as the newer Europa Universalis games but still very deep and fun. I totally recommend this game to any paradox fan.

It is a own nich of the EU series, but it lake many of the functionality that the later expansions of EU II and III introduced, not to mentioned EU 4.
When it came as a mod to EU II this was an improvement but its improvements has been adapted and improved by the expansions to EU II and III.
If you don't have a really limited computer capacity buy the later series in the EU series with expansions.

This game is amazing, and if you're love turn-based strategy, this one is definitely a reccomendation.
However, a quick disclaimer for you guys:
Keep in mind that this game is from 1994 and you will be playing this on DOS box. Because this is such an old game, you will find it to be slow at times, so that means the game will take some time (not forever) to acknowledge that you clicked your mouse on a menu button or on the battlefield map. If you're very patient, this should be no problem. Just keep this in mind, though.
On to the actual review:
Compared to the new Xcom, I'd say this one is much more challenging, but it's also very rewarding, because the AI makes you fight real hard for victory. Your Xcom agents, if wearing no armor, tend to die in as little as one hit, so you have be very careful early on in the game before unlocking armor.
Also, this game has features that Enemy Unknown does not, such as:
-The ability to create more than one base.
-You can put in way more than just 6 agents in a skyranger.
-You can also use more than one skyranger per base, and assign different squads to that skyranger.
And of course it has the familliar features that the new Xcom borrowed from it as well, such as researching alien technology, capturing aliens, etc.
What I love the most about this game is simply the fact that Xcom feels more like an elite, small, but specialized army that functions on a far bigger scale, unlike Enemy Unknown. In Enemy Unknown, you just have one skyranger, one base, and only get to assign 6 agents per mission.
So yes, while I still love the new Xcom, I definitely appreciate this old classic as well. I've only started playing it now recently and I do have to say I'm impressed.
One last reminder:
This game can be confusing at first because the logistics and resource management is a bit more complex. Also, keep in mind that there's more options in both the Geoscape menu AND the battlefield map, so it would be wise to understand how the menu and the combat system works by experimenting. Also, ask advice if you need to.

It's not a bad game, but you should think carefully about whether or not you are the target audience.
On paper, SpaceChem sounds exactly like my kind of game. It's a playful take on concurrent programming, and on top of that, it's themed around chemistry.
I like puzzle games. I like programming. I like chemistry. Surely I will like SpaceChem then, right?
Unfortunately not. I tried really hard to enjoy this game, but each time I play, a very distinctly nagging feeling hit me: I could just be programming. The game isn't bad in any notable way, and I actually had some fun playing it. But I just have so much
fun actually programming.
This will be a "buyers beware" to the kind of people that get irritable during handhold-y tutorials and on-rails games.
SpaceChem is a game. Not a sandbox. This game boils programming down to two concepts: Solving the problem, and optimizing your solution. There is going to be one single "best" solution to the problem at hand, and your solution is going to be either optimal or sub-optimal. End of story.
If you need someone to tell you what your immediate goal is, if you feel uncomfortable with just being dropped in the deep end with no milestones or objectives,
Intimidating as it may seem, this game does a wonderful job at providing the player with a controlled environment, clear goals, instructions and rules.
This game does its own thing, and it does it well, but it is neither chemistry nor computer science in any way. It is a game with a theme. At most, it is about repeatedly improving on solutions to the same problem. Hence, neither "because programming" nor "because chemistry" should be your reason for purchasing this title.
If you have a fascination with chemistry, have done any programming in the past, or just generally prefer sandbox games,
not for anybody (not for me)

Dead Effect 2 is a surprisingly well crafted Indie shooter to the point that I've got little doubt that it would've been truly ground breaking if it had an AAA budget. Now that doesn't mean Dead Effect 2 is not without its flaws but then again even AAA games have those.
The question is do those flaws totally out do the pros and ruin the game? Well for me they thankfully didn't but we're all different so I can't say they won't for some.
Its a solid game for the money asked and probably a steal if you get it on sale for even cheaper.
TLDR
Lets dive into more details.
Pros:
+ The Sci-Fi setting puts a slightly new spin on well used Zombie FPS genre.
+ Flexible play style (no matter which of the 3 characters you chose you can ultimately use whatever weapon types you want).
+ A impressive amount of weapons and weapon types (Katanas, Chainsaws, Broadswords, Compact Bows, Plasma rifles, Miniguns, Gernade Launchers, pump-action and double barrel shotguns, Magnums, Axes, Baseball bats, Semi auto pistols, Explosive Crossbows, Sniper Rifles, Assault Rifles, Arc Guns, Machetes, Saw Blade Launchers, Gatling Lasers, Thor's Hammer, Chemical Launchers, The huge battle hammer from Halo, and thats just what I've come across so far there might even more that I've yet to come accross).
+ Various stat boosting armor pieces and implants for your cybernetic body.
+ A item rarity system no doubt inspired by Borderlands, which makes looting and item purchasing all the more fun.
+ All armor, implants and weapons can be upgraded and have bonus stats installed into them for extra awesomeness.
+ Enemies scale with you so game is always a challange even when you rerun older levels.
+ A healthy selection of abilities that you can unlock as you level up. You can switch and swap them out as you please to give you give you whatever special edge in combat you like, be it bullet time, mind control, stasis fields, massive area attacks, etc.
+ Fair amount of story missions (for a Indie game) along with a respectable amount of side modes ranging from clearing out Zombie hordes from certian maps survivng a set amount of waves to name a few. Almost all of the modes can be played Co-op.
+ A decent amount of various enemy types, ranging from your standard shuffling Zombies to hulking mutants with heavy weapons. On top of the Zombies and monster types you also have to deal with human foes ranging from your standard assualt rifle grunt to fast stealth ninjas.
+ Hidden items that can make exploring each map fully more worth while.
+ The music is surprisingly well done and is set up masterfully to seem perfectly in place for areas and events.
+ Has controler support.
Cons
- If you play the story only, don't back track and take no detours to level up or farm for more items the game can rather short. (Though keep in mind this is a indie game not a huge budget project so you shouldn't be expecting some epic 100+ hour saga anyway)
- If you're not a loot fiend the game might get dull and the need to sporadically get newer gear might get annoying.
- Enemy AI isn't best, even human enemies can be some what predictable. (once again this is a Indie game so you shouldn't expect top tier right off the bat).
- Missions some times feel repetitive.
- Not being able to detect Gernades tossed by Zombies till they are about to blow can get annoying, and can lead to game essentially getting some cheap deaths out of you.
Neutral
-+ The voice acting isn't gonna win any awards and the dialog can be cheesy at times but its not nearly as bad as some of the reviews are making it out to be. Some of its actually rather witty (in a B-movie sort of way) Though to be fair I play as Kay (he sounds like a gruff, grumpy Jet-Li with sarcastic tendancies, priceless imo) not Davis (the supposid legit main character) so maybe Davis's voice actor was just horrid, I can't say.
-+ The plot is a bit cliche but not enough to ruin the game.
All and all its good game, I've sunk 20 hours into the game and haven't even beaten it yet, mainly due to loot and side modes being so much fun. Dead Effect 2 is a great time killer and you'd be hard pressed to find a more deverse Co-op Zombie Shooter with as many weapons and skills as it offers.

I stumbled upon this game while looking through steam decided to give it a shot
Having gone to college for 3D animation and personally knowing many game design majors, I can honestly say this game seems like a college capstone project.
The overall quality of the player character is nice, but really stands out awkwardly in the game as it's the only thing in the game with any detail. Might want to get some environment modelers guys; or match your character better with it's surroundings. The design overall is just really boring and simple, nothing unique or particularly relating to "net neutrality" or whatever message that was pushed under the rug for gameplay.
Controls pretty well, although with the automated jumping I got pretty bored as I felt the game was playing it self most of the time.
Overall it's OKAY, I honestly don't think it's really that interesting. I enjoyed the music, even though it was a bit skippy when you changed levels.
The game overall feels like it's trying really hard to be Distance and Mirrors Edge pushed together, and I found that is fails in both respects. neither being that good in platforming like mirrors edge, nor excitingly fast and atmospheric as Distance.
It's sub par, but I honestly wasn't expecting more than that from a free game that has a really gimmicky "story" to it.
The "Dome" that follows you as you progress through the level makes it extremely hard to see obstacles when you're going really really fast, again, a problem that would be remedied with having the "dome" much larger.
Lastly the game just gives you free achievements for playing the game, pass two levels and you'll have nearly all of them just to playing the game. I don't get it, that sounds pretty stupid to me.
Tips to make it better?
-I'd reccomend deciding on a style that works well, the current one doesn't really have much of a focus.
-Make the platforming harder, and that doesn't mean adding more and more of those stupid loud red drill things.
-most importantly, if you're going to push the important message of net neutrality, you might want to actually make it relevent to what is going on. I honestly just felt like that was some excuse to have a "story" to all the linear gameplay.

**UPDATED 1/25/17**
Welp, with Alpha 20 just releasing, I think it's about time to re-review this game! Let's get into this!
Stonehearth shows what good can come out of Steam Greenlight! With developers that update the players every week and stay in close contact with the fans, to alpha releases nearly every month! Radiant Entertainment, the fine developers of this game, are the shining example of what game studios should be to their fans. A large amount of things you see in the game today are based from player recommendations. How do they keep in contact with fans? Well, they have a stream every Thursday, and on their website,
, they  have updates on development every Tuesday!
Stonehearth is a game about helping a small band of 'Hearthlings' carve out a town in the middle of nowhere. You'll need to harvest, craft, build, and more to survive in this fleshed out world! Using special tools, you can turn some Hearthlings into carpenters, trappers, farmers, and more (There are already a large amount of classes, but more are still being added!). Things won't always be sunshine and rainbows though, because as you progress, monsters of many types will come after you to halt your growing town! Monsters like Goblins, Ents, Necromancers, Zombies, Skeletons, Cobalts, and a lot more (Radiant Entertaiment is always adding new baddies to fight!)! You'll have to combat them with your own army, and luckily you can have your Heathlings become archerss, knights, footmen, and clerics! Hopefully then you'll be able to best these monsters and keep your town going!
Stonehearth has a very indepth building system to it. You can build whatever your heart desires with it! Houses, castles, watchtowers, dining halls! Anything you want! You'll have to harvest resources like wood and stone to be able to construct these buildings though! Also in this game you'll have to supply your Hearthlings' needs or they will become very unhappy. Many things will make them upset like being in cramped areas for long periods of time, or eating the same type of food all the time. Many things will make them happy though, like being in spacious areas, sleeping in beds, eating cooked meals, and more!
There are some problems in this game though, with it being still in Alpha. Sometimes the enemies can seem overpowered. Sometimes Hearthlings have trouble building complicated structures. Sometimes performance can drop at seemingly random times. Sometimes the AI will become confused and stop working. There are more problems in this game, as is in any game, but I fear not about them, because Radiant Entertainment is always working with players to find and eleminate these nasty bugs.
Overall, I give Stonehearth an 7/10 for very amusing and enjoyable gameplay, but it is sometimes lacking content wise and has a lot of bugs,
I wish the best to Radiant Entertainment as they continue this great game, and I cannot wait to see what comes from Stonehearth in the future

What if Age of Empires, The Sims, and Minecraft had a baby? Look no farther for the proverbial answer, my dear reader, this is that game.
Stonehearth could be easily dismissed among the ocean of voxel sandbox titles. Upon seeing a few screenshots, I had initially confused it with Cube World, a defunct adventure game that died after its foray into early access alpha a few years ago. Games that employ this simplistic art style are a dime a dozen nowadays... however, Cube World this is not.
The premise is as follows: make a village and survive against invaders, mine and collect resources, slay bosses, and construct buildings. You are given a starting set of "Hearthlings" (think 'Sims') and can name them, assign them classes based on their strengths, build them homes and view their thoughts through the town journal. Naming them after real people made me feel more invested and attached to them. I'm really excited to see if they'll add more procedural interactivity between Hearthlings in the future because there's a very solid base for a great role playing sim here.
From the moment I started making my first village, it was clear that Stonehearth is very different -- for better and for worse. Because there aren't other games quite like this out there, there's somewhat of a learning curve. There are different camera views, zoning tools, a custom building mode, mining/gathering/looting modes, managing classes, placing items... it's all quite confusing and somewhat daunting at first. I think I accidentally skipped the tutorial when changing the game settings to fullscreen (it made me restart the game and the tutorial was nowhere to be found).
After becoming mostly aquainted with the systems, I began to appreciate how there are some wicked smart minds working on this game. The custom building tool -- while clearly an alpha product due to general wonkiness and a surprising pechant for not letting you delete misplaced things -- is surprisingly robust. It's pretty clear that their goal is "If you can imagine it, you can build it." It isn't as time consuming as Minecraft to make a fully custom house, as you can lay the floorplans and everything can be queued up for you, and soon enough you'll watch your little Hearthlings get to work building your masterpieces. On the fastest speed setting (which can only be enabled in the settings), it feels like watching a time lapse. Very fun to see them work.
In my experience, I'm left believing that the AI runs on magic. I have no idea how they managed to program pathing, gathering, build-queuing this good... all while running quite well on my 6 years old system. Your workers will always be productive getting done the chores and tasks you've set up for them to do. Of course, they'll stop and tend to their needs from time to time (which only includes taking a lunch break and sleeping... we don't have room for lazy slaves in this kingdom).
The team have laid out their broad goals for 2017, which sounds refinement heavy. I've been impressed with their progress thus-far, and updates are frequent.
If you have interest in this game: stop hesitating. Once it gets multiplayer in 2018 (my prediction based on their roadmap), this game is going to get a serious cult following. Very impressive alpha.

For The Glory A Europa Universalis Game is a very aptly named game. It is, essentially, a collection of advances made in the Europa Universalis II modding scene bundled together and sold as a full game. And while For The Glory is a great experience it is also an experience you can get from playing regular Europa Universalis II and installing a bunch of mods.
From the standpoint of an un-modded Europa Universalis II all the advances in For The Glory will look tremendous. A massive increase in the number of events you will receive, both as a historical player or as someone that thinks the Reconquista should be going in reverse. The AI is smarter, focusing it's forces much better, new map modes makes conquests much easier to plan and a ton of general balance changes makes everything feel sharper and better. Even graphically there is some improvements.
One place it goes backwards however is in the multi-player department however as without Valkyrie-Net it is horribly unstable and neigh unplayable.
As much as For The Glory advances the regular Europa Universalis II game it does very little to advance the modded gameplay. If you have the choice between buying this or Europa Universalis II then I'd recommend getting this every time. If you already own Europa Universalis II however then there is absolutely no reason you need to own this.

As a rule, I prefer my roguelikes to be turn-based.  If one mistake is going to ruin things, I'd like the opportunity to think about it.  For that reason, I was initially not keen on Dungeon of the Endless's mixed turn based-real time system.  I certainly had a lot of frustrating deaths early on where I didn't react to a bad situation quickly enough.
But I eventually got past that and found an enjoyable challenge with lots of possible strategies where each run lasts the right length of time.  A big part was realising that proper preparation in the turn-based parts of the game are the key; the difficulty is in setting your defences up correctly.  Another was appreciating the different approaches that become available with different characters.  A third was that the different starting pods offer surprisingly different gameplay within the same basic framework.
One criticism I do still have is that while there is some nice art for the dungeon rooms, I often found myself playing in the zoomed-out view where this is invisible.  Another is that the story implementation is rather weak.  I only learnt that there was any story beyond the short opening cinematic when reading the wiki.  With the DLC characters I think you'd have to play a lot of games to get a story combination by chance.  And then, once you look it up and jump through the necessary hoops, what's left isn't all that exciting and in some cases can be quite annoying.
But despite these issues the gameplay itself is solid, with plenty of replay value, so I do recommend.

Dungeon of the Endless could almost be a tabletop game. Substitute randomly generated content for a dungeon master and you're almost there. As the dungeon unfolds, as each room is discovered, it adds a piece to the game board, and each piece is a potential threat until it can be lit up. Dark rooms spawn monsters, and new rooms are always dark. Light it up and that's when the newly discovered game piece, a room in a dungeon, falls into your hands and becomes a tool. It's the sheer amount of number crunching that goes on in Dungeon of the Endless that necessitates it being a PC game, as hundreds of enemies spill towards you through tight corridors.
It's also got those core RPG elements backing up the gameplay. There is loot to collect. There's a leveling system with accompanying leveling stats. It's turn-based, with each door you open starting the next turn. There is a colourful cast of characters given personality through their outstanding sprite design and a spattering mediocre flavour text. There are tower defense elements, but when Dungeon of the Endless feels the most like a tower defense game is when your back's against the wall, the cards are stacked against you and your run is about to end. You scramble to your most fortified room and try to hold out. When the game gives you what you need, and you use it well, it feels like a dungeon crawler. When it gives you the middle finger, that's when it feels exactly like tower defense.
This is an insanely difficult game. Difficulty is a feature, not a bug, and the level of challenge is compelling, but it has issues with difficulty scaling. Sometimes you'll open the first door on the first floor of the dungeon, and two enemies will pop out. Sometimes you'll open the first door of the dungeon and five enemies will pop out. Within a floor this scaling is consistent, as each time you open a door hoping to uncover better equipement and collect more resources the potential wave of enemies that could appear is bigger than the last. You generally have a sense if opening one more door would put you in a bad spot and can weigh your options from there. It's possible to escape a floor early and leave doors unopened. But it's between floors that it gets wonky. Just like the number of enemies on the first floor isn't fixed, sometimes you'll encounter a difficult mob type on the fourth floor and sometimes you won't encounter it until the ninth floor. How this is determined is a complete mystery. Part of it seems to be your hero selection, as using more powerful heroes seems to generate more difficult dungeons. It could be tied to your heroes levels, but if it is, the game doesn't tell you so. You never know exactly what you're getting yourself into and planning ahead is impossible. You take what the game gives you and you work with it. This game has little to do with chemistry. It's an automata programming game.
I remembered the first time I see such a game when I was in high school. It's called
. You are literally programming Turing Machines there. And I think SpaceChem is quite similar: the semantics of and the interactions between the elements are simple, but with these simple elements, you can do infinitely complex jobs.
It's hard, but not all that hard. I completed all the puzzles in the story line except for the optional ones and the final boss fight in a little more than 20 hours. You do need to focus on the most specific things like the placement of the bounders and routing the two waldos through the array of symbols, and some times these problems are solved with ugly ad-hoc tricks, but you definitely should go beyond that level. Once you discovered how to do a recurring task like moving around a cross-shaped array of bounders to assemble or disassemble a methane molecule or arranging several flip-flops to perform a sequence of commands a desired amount of times, the puzzles starts to get easier. You quickly figure out similar structures in the input and output and decide what should go where. Then you adjust your known structures to solve each step and the job is done.
Every time when you see in the statistics that your dashed yellow line is way to the left of the peak of the bar chart, you feel clever.
Those at the right end of the chart are not stupid either. Everyone who progressed to the later part of the game must be clever.
But some people are just more clever than others. The research net is the difficult part. It is organized into volumes and issues, just like real scientific journals. Amusing. But the puzzles there are seriously difficult. Most of the time you stare at the puzzles and think, "How is that even possible? The author must be insane!"
When you finally solved a difficult problem and see your efficient and elegant (or not so mush so) production pipeline running, see those materials flowing in and products flowing out after some arcane transformation, you start getting fascinated, even though you are the one who built those things. Sometimes I am amazed at how good us humans are at discovering patterns and constructing increasingly complex structures from simpler ones. Maybe that is central to our intelligence.
No...... Just...no.

The incredible depth and learning curve held up until the last few levels got a bit sketchy, your answers to the problems can be honed and optimised for endless replayabilty. However be careful of those strange recurring dreams of Waldos and Bonding Reactors, the efficient preparation of the dinner table each night and the complete dissociation with the outside world when piping reactors.

What I can say is Trine's transition from a 2D scroller to a fully-fledged, more or less, 3D world is not as successful as one would have hoped. In fact, it brings to mind Oddworld Inhabitant's decision to take Abe from 2D to 3D with patchy results.
That's because in Trine 3, much like Munch's Oddysee, the puzzles which were so intrinsic to the success and charm of the previous games, are sadly lacking in this latest outing. Gone are the carefully upgradable skill trees so beautifully crafted onto each character creating sublime puzzles and a genuine sense of progression, in favour of what is essentially an overly physics-based assault course - with more emphasis on grinding than puzzle solving. The transition to 3D adding very little to the player experience.
Whilst I could recommend Trine 3 to gamers who've played and enjoyed similar games, I find it quite difficult to recommend to those, like me, who've grown to love Trine 1 & 2.

Disappointing, short, buggy mess - meet Trine 3.
I loved Trine (including Enhanced Edition) and Trine 2. Really, I did. And I can honestly say I enjoyed Trine 3 during the Early Access period, hoping to see much more content in the final game. Sadly, there is not too much new content. As many said before me, Trine 3 is incredibly short. 3 introduction levels focused on each hero, 5 standard levels. These 8 levels can't last more than 3 hours. Of course there are some side missions, but they are merely a bonus challange, a desperate attempt to do something about the short gametime.
Another significant problem? Bugs. Almost every aspect of the game, every feature is bugged and full of errors. Camera, physics, animations, controls, cooperation elements, Steam achievements... simply put, the whole game is incredible bugfest. It certainly doesn't seem like finished product, more like a beta. Playable content is there, but it's not polished and it needs a lot of testing. Bugs can ruin everything, from some interesting puzzle to basic things like selection of already unlocked and completed levels.
But wait. In fact, playable content is not there, at least it seems. Remember that awesome character development combined with slight RPG features in Trine 2? It's missing. Treasure chests? Missing. More weapons and abilities for each hero? Missing. Some really interesting story? As you may probably guess, it's missing, too. It feels like too many features were sacrificed during the attempt to transfer the whole Trine experience from 2D to 3D. By the way, the story and especially its ending is another problem. All I could say about the "ending" was simple: "What the hell was that?" Not to mention the final boss. Every so-called boss in the game is not really entertaining or challanging, but the last one is a joke. Really strange and poorly executed joke.
I certainly see some potential in Trine 3. Conversion to 3D is interesting, graphics combined with art style and level design is really beautiful and the soundtrack is simply awesome. Basic gameplay is fine and I am also grateful for Steam Workshop support and good optimisation (at least on my hardware). But that's not enough. There are too many bugs and other errors, too few levels. This is NOT the Trine 3 I was waiting for and I can't reccomend it to anyone.
Maybe one day, if the developers properly eliminate all the bugs, add new levels and really release something which could be called a "finished game", I will change my mind and recommend the game to my friends, just as I did during the times of Trine 2. But right now, it's a mess. And it's really painful to see that the trend of unfinished sequels with lack of important content has come to indie sphere. Maybe it's not fair to compare indie and AAA titles, but current state of Trine 3 is very similar to the initial state of games such as Assassin's Creed: Unity, F1 2015 or Batman: Arkham Knight. And that's simply wrong.

The actual gameplay is miserable.  It's a pretty bog-standard first person shooter set on a space station or ship or something.  I didn't pay much attention to the horible story.
