Like the first game, Dead Effect 2 is a first person zombie shooter set aboard a large spaceship. It fails to shed the B-movie persona of its precursor, but believes it does, making the story-based campaign oddly unsatisfying. Gameplay is good, though, and cooperative campaign, online multiplayer modes and some decent weapons & armor leveling means there is quite a bit of fun to be had. A good effort by Badfly Interactive, but stops well short of becoming a classic.
Total size on my hard drive: 10.7 GB
+ Guns are great. Not Battlefield level of gun design, but whoever designed and animated them did a great job. Badfly must have made this a priority when developing Dead Effect 2, and it shows.
+ Weapon upgrades are great. While there is no attachments system, there are a number of things that can be purchased to make your weapon of choice more powerful. The weapon does not change visually, but the damage progression is very noticeable.
+ Same for armor. There are dozens of varieties of armors available. Each suit is divided into feet, legs, chest, arms, and helmet parts, allowing mixing and matching. And each part has one or sometimes two slots for additional components.
+ Graphics are decent. Bluish light and black shadow splash across the screen often, leaving a cold and dark feeling.
+ Decently optimized. I had to reduce shadows (to medium) and bloom (I have an R7 260X), but after that I had no trouble playing the game @1080p 60fps.
+ Drop in / Drop out coop works well. Not too many random matches to be found, but they work well when they’re there.
+ Decent soundtrack (which is included as MP3 files).
+/- Headshots are OP as hell. The length of your longest killstreak in multiplayer translates directly into the post-mission bonus multiplier (a kill-streak of 50 will result in a multiplier of 50). It can be very easy for a skilled player to earn a ton of credits fast. Aim and accuracy modifications to the armor can help even more.
+/- The armor customization does demand focused specialization. If you try to create a “good at everything” build, the bonuses will be too small to make much difference.
+/- The story is actually half-way decent. Wake up in a ship, have to survive while a classy English voice tells you what to do. Do a few missions, then discover that you, the player-character, are considered the result of an experiment, and if the “relief ship” (containing lots of soldiers) catches up with the Meridian, you will be taken captive and disposed of as just another of Wagner’s clones. Danette, she of the classy English voice, has an interesting story that could have delved into all kinds of ethical concerns – but doesn’t. Not that Dead Effect 2 needed to be like The Walking Dead, but there is potential for additional depth which isn’t explored at all. Disappointing.
- The story ends too soon. You fight some creature, then – “Surprise! That was actually the final boss! To be continued!…”
- The voice acting, with the exception of Danette, is poor. Dr. Bielik sounds like a highly exaggerated Chekov (from the original Star Trek) and is annoying as heck any time he opens his mouth. And if you choose Jane as your player-character, well… Some of the worst “voice-acting” I’ve heard in a long time.
- Level design is small. It’s tight, confined and claustrophobic – so tight that there isn’t always room for two players to run past each other in a corridor. If never feels like we’re on a huge spaceship.
- Few enemy varieties. Your standard zombie, puking zombie, grenade zombie, and giant zombie. There are some good-looking bosses, but unless you’re playing a shotgun build (which risks getting close to the boss for maximum damage), it’s easy to keep them at a distance.
- There is a huge amount of loot. And I mean HUGE. I would barely get my character upgraded (which cost some serious credits) before some really epic loot would drop, making all my careful upgrading seem worthless. I expect this to happen once or twice in a loot-based game, but here it happened 4 or 5 times (more frequently as my character’s level was higher).
- Character appearance never changes, despite equipping some awesome armors.
There are definitely some talented people working at Badfly Interactive, and while Dead Effect 2 improves in many ways over the first game, it’s not the masterpiece that will launch them into the mainstream. Hopefully their next game in the series, Tau Ceti, is already under development and they make it as big and B-movie as possible. If they want to go the "serious" route, get better voice actors, open up the levels. and don't be afraid to tackle some serious issues with the story.

A very poor portfolio piece, cunningly disguised as supporting a cause to promote itself further.
Virtually nothing about this game links back to it's story or message.
The gameplay is agonisingly clunky and clearly has not been playtested correctly, and if it has, then none of the glaringly obvious problems were addressed from those sessions.
The optimisation is beyond bad, with the frame rate dropping below 15FPS when many effects are on the screen.
Large parts of the interface and design are clearly stock UDK components (the Area Complete 3D text being a glaringly obvious example).
The interface otherwise is mediocre at best.
Many elements of the game are not explained (bandwidth is your health, not your speed, boosting takes up bandwidth).
The game's story desperately needs fleshing out, as currently it feels more slapped on than Rihanna.
The soundtrack starts strong but quickly gets repetitive, which really disappointed me. I really expected to enjoy the OST throughout but I was actually grinding my teeth by the end, fed up of hearing the same song rehashed a million times.
Mechanically, this game is a mess. The ping-toggling system is not even useless, it actually hinders the game in my opinion. You should NEVER reward the player for doing something that isn't fun, and turning off pinging, and your access to boosters through that, is agonisingly un-fun.
Nobody wants to gently walk around traps; they want to blast through them or avoid them at blazing speed. Pity that 80% of the traps REQUIRE either ping toggling or boosting (which drains your life, penalising the player for doing something fun is poor design). The other 20% of traps, which can simply be avoided, are painfully easy to avoid.
The game could have been incredible, with only a little more polish.
Put it back in the oven for another month or two, University of Utah.

As many of the other reviewers are saying: Quake(FPS and movement) +Super Meat Boy (Speed and platforming) + Katamari (visuals). It's a cutesy but challenging game which will test your reflexes and memorization of patterns. Deceptively simple in the beginning, it adds more and more content as you progress, and what was simply a "bounce forward through the level shooting static enemies" experience becomes: Immediate 180 turn, forward and left past moving blob of death, bunny hop gap, shoot blob blocking landing then instantly shoot dude right in front of you, then jump onto bounce pad, then shoot a falling apple in midair, then quickly jump across three dissapearing platforms, hop over spikes, dodge shots and kill two more guys around corners, then shoot an apple with unhittable targets behind it, and finish. Then they intoduce homing projectiles and flying enemies and stuff, and the content gets really frantic. The level design retains the same aesthetics, but with small changes on each particular level, and more stage hazards as you progress. There's also a couple possible paths on most levels, and there are secrets hidden throughout the game as well. There's not a ton of motivation to find them in my opinion, but if you're an explorer then you can poke around for the achievements. The game is arcadey, and scores you based on your performance. Getting three stars for a par time and perfect accuracy for your bullet ballet feels great, although don't expect to do that past the 2nd or 3rd world. It's a good example of a videogame that comes out of left field to provide a neat experience I didn't know I was missing. It's not perfect, but it's certainly worth a look. 7.5/10

This review is mainly for the Siege of Dragonspear expansion, rather than the base game.  I felt I had to share my two cents on it because of how much hate it was getting.  The people who are shouting all the nonsense about the writing being poor in SoD are either insane, or are just doing all they can to trash Amber Scott.  There's simply no other explanation than that.
I myself am 34 years old, and the fact of the matter is, Baldur's Gate 1 is an old game.  It's a VERY old game.  And lets face it - while the writing and play mechanics were "decent" for its time, unmodded it doesn't hold a candle to the writing in most RPG's, let alone modern Bioware titles.  If you think otherwise, you're not being honest with yourself.  It's the nostalgia talking.
Beamdog did the best they could with the material they were given, and the honest truth of the matter is, their product turned out to be more impressive than the original title.  Let's not kid ourselves: If this expansion had been released 15 years ago back when the Infinity engine was still popular, it would have received awards.  They took BG1, and bumped it up as close to a modern standard as they possibly could.  The story and presentation are far more intelligently designed than the original, while still staying perfectly true to the established lore - not an easy feat, yet they accomplished it in spades.
I can only surmise that all the backlash is coming from social media troll armies - no more, no less.  It's a good expansion with good writing - made for a game that I'm willing to admit is past its prime.

I'm a big fan of Baldur's Gate 2 so i decided to finally try this one. To say i was dissapointed is an understatement. I seriously question the wisdom of starting at level 1. A level one character in 2nd edition dies quicker than a mayfly with progeria. You're basically shoehorned into playing a fighter or cleric, as thieves have so little HP a swift breeze will kill them, and mages have the same problem with worse AC but have the insignificant bonus of a single 1st level spell.
The combat is pretty bad because of this. becuase of your lack of strategic options, battles are decided by the most lopsided RNG I have ever seen. You cant use cleric spells because you need to use all of your slots for heals as taking more than one hit is certain death, and your mages cant cast more than one spell per rest, and stealth characters are near worthless becuase if you fail a roll, and you absolutely will four out of five times, getting discovered means instant death every enemy is instantaneously and perfectly aware and has already fired seventeen trillion arrows into each of  your orifices. Im not joking. I tried to use Imoen to scout ahead and find traps she got found by kobolds and thunk thunk thunk she was dead in less than half a second.
BG2 was certainly difficult and in many areas downright cheap, but you had options. you could try different spells or different buffs, different weapons and equipment, Here no such luck if those wild dogs mysteriously all made a save against your sleep spell prepare for melee and probably reload after agonizing reload until you have suffered long enough for the dice roller to reach ♥♥♥♥♥♥, then you will finally survive losing half your party and be allowed some paltry amount of progress, only to have your party wiped out by a bear that is clearly constructed from adamantium.
I wanted to like this game, but it is simply not fun to play. The dialogue and character development that i loved in Baldur's Gate 2 are not present here, but the plot was interesting enough. however the tedious combat with fighters who could not hit the broad side of a barn from inside the barn with a barn of equal size,  thieves who couldn't sneak their way around a deaf bat, and wizards who cannot do more than fart in the general direction of an enemy without needing an 8 hour nap afterwards. Though this was unplayable for me at release and remained so for almost a year, Beamdog have redeemed themselves by creating the best and most playable version of the Baldur's Gate Saga to date. The recent patches, v2.3, have added so many quality of life changes that the game feels modern and slick, though a change to the inventory system would have been welcome too, or at least more inventory slots.
The game looks amazing. The graphic tweaks make this already beautiful game really shine and feel new again, and I can't think of a better way to introduce yourself to the series. Even by todays standards, Baldur's Gate is still ahead of it's time. It's beautifully simple premise hides a suprising about of depth and sophistication. Unlike many RPGs that followed, exploring the world feels rewarding and fresh everytime I play. The game doesn't throw treasure at you in every nightside table, but thouroughly searching every container and reading flavor text is always rewarding. My view on BG may be tinted with nostalgia, but I think this game, with the modernizations of the Enhanced Edition, still holds up to anything out now and is worth a try.

The fact that I just sunk 100 hrs into a game that launched 15 years ago is worth a recomendation for that alone. Not many games can age well over a 10th of that time.

The graphics, even with the upgrade are low grade (but ccome on it launched 15 yrs ago!), although the scenery itself is gorgeous in a early-2000 way. The mechanics are a little clunky, and the story could be a little faster paced.
BUT if you enjoy old school style RPGs, battles that are every bit as difficult all the way through, where clever tactics and correct leveling of your character matter, where choices matter, where you can choose to do pretty much anything (you can kill any char if you are able. I got a "game over" screen because I killed a char essential for the main quest), where you will find yourself rerolling different characters to play the game in a different way as the vastly different tonnes of classes - coupled with some great narrative and memorable companions then Baldurs Gate is still very much worthy of your time.
Just remember, the game wont hold your hand, but you wont want it to - although, Quick save is you friend.

This game is stressful in a good way, and by that I mean it's thought-provoking, which plenty of "strategy" games fail to achieve these days. The pace is as fast or as slow as you want it to be, and the game certainly teaches you how to be frugal with your supplies.
Will you take the risk and open that next door, even when you've already found the exit? Do you have enough industries for the next map? Have you saved enough sciences to upgrade a module?
The game is fun up until the point in which you learn that filling a room with 2 Neurostuns and a bunch of prisoner prods or KIP Cannons(and a tear gas, if you have an empty slot) carries/saves runs from disaster.
I'm too lazy to write a more detailed review, so i'll mention the reasons why you should and shouldn't get Dungeon of the Endless:
+ Ever wanted 2~6 hours to fly by without you noticing? This game is just for you.
+ Thought-provoking, a single mistake can and will be punished, and you will regret your actions.
+ Glorious pixel art. You have cameos and references to characters and/or people.
+ Fun with friends, fun alone, multiplayer has the added boon of giving you more resources to work with if each player is delegated a role(who handles industries, who opens doors, etc.)
+ Soundtrack is relaxing, which is good contrast for the amount of stress the game places on you when deciding to open doors past door 20 on the higher difficulty.
* Don't have time for 2~6 hour games? Sure, you can save your run and resume progress later, even in multiplayer.
- Each run takes 2~6 hours, maybe a bit less if you're really fast.
- Like any roguelike, mistakes are heavily punished, and losing your best hero can result in being unable to complete a run.
- Somewhat steep learning curve-- there isn't really a tutorial, and there are some things a player might not ever figure out without being told.
In short, just buy it. Jump in and play, no regrets. If you like randomized runs//roguelikes, then Dungeon of the Endless is just for you. Just make sure you take care of your health while playing, and don't neglect food, water, or sleep, because this game is incredibly distracting.

Ingredients
Serves: 24
225g (8 oz) butter, softened
200g (7 oz) caster sugar
225g (8 oz) dark brown soft sugar
2 eggs
1 dessertspoon vanilla essence
375g (13 oz) plain flour
1 teaspoon bicarbonate of soda
1 dessertspoon hot water
1/2 teaspoon salt
350g (12 oz) dark chocolate chips
125g (4¼ oz) chopped walnuts
Method
Prep:20min  ›  Cook:10min  ›  Ready in:30min
Preheat oven to 180 C / Gas mark 4.
Cream together the butter, caster sugar and brown sugar until smooth. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then stir in the vanilla. Dissolve bicarbonate of soda in hot water. Add to batter along with salt. Stir in flour, chocolate chips and nuts. Drop by large spoonfuls onto ungreased baking trays.
Bake for about 10 minutes in the preheated oven, or until edges are nicely browned.

I've played a lot of programming puzzle games before. As a general rule, if you're teaching an aspect of computer science, it usually turns out fairly good, and if you're just teaching people how to bash directions into a small space, it usually sucks.
And then you've got stuff like SpaceChem, RoboZZle, and Jahooma's LogicBox, which are a bit of both. And they turn out amazing.
(There are other categories, although Hack 'n' Slash gets its own special category for pretending to teach you how to hack but you have to go through some cumbersome chores first and you get bored before you finish them. Avoid.)
SpaceChem, from a computer science perspective, is a game about multithreading, and avoiding race conditions. Or something like that.
From a non-compsci perspective, it's about moving atoms around, binding them together, and hoping you get the right results and also hoping they don't smash into each other.
Either way, it's a puzzle game that holds your hand for a few tutorial levels and basically gives you the "standard" answer, and then leaves you to it. It has a rather sharp difficulty curve, but even if you're stumped on a later level, you can always go back to an earlier one and look at just how bad the "standard" solution you were given on a silver platter was, and improve on it.
You can also

against your friends to see who can solve a puzzle in the fewest number of cycles, or use the fewest number of symbols... or the fewest number of reactors for some of the later puzzles that are still early enough to be in the demo version.
Did I mention there's a demo version? You should play it, and then if you like it (and I will make you like it) then you can throw your money at Zachtronics and get the full version.
In short, SpaceChem is a really good programming puzzle game that teaches you the fun of dealing with race conditions, and there's more than one way to do each puzzle.

RPGMaker Games are always like scratch cards. You stumble upon wasted money and time most of the time, but you encounter small gems sometimes. It is my version of gambling, if you may call. This time, it's a puzzle game, wrapped in a 3rd rate high schooler story with worse rated anime humor. Nope, we definitely don't have a winner this time. As you can get the clue from my description,
wasn't among the best of my experiences within the genre. Sure it is cheap, but for a one dollar puzzle game, you can get something better here around.
Our protagonist is a boy named James, looking forward to the start of his summer vacation. Unfortunately, he has finals to deal with first. On his way out, he convinces a suicidal girl (?) that life is worth living and goes on with his life. As he crams for the finals, he falls asleep and meets the Goddess of Mathematics, Seshat - who is no other than the nameless suicidal girl from school. From there on, he is to enter the Godly Olympics of Science as the Champion of Seshat. He is to overcome challenges, compete against champions of other deities and snatch the winning prize. What would be the prize? Something, anything he can wish for...
Well, the story seems curious enough, but there is a truckload that would declare this game simply unsatisfactory in a moment. To begin with, the game is exceedingly short. You have 2 trials + 3 competitions against other participants, and that's it. You are at the end of the game. Considering its length, there is no room for either decent story progression or character development. It's all cheesy, superficial and dry in all departments. The dialogue feels completely artificial, social interactions are synthetic like public service ads and the narrative is riddled with typos. Display qualities couldn't be considered amongst the best either, with simplistic soundtrack and amateur artwork.
The game? Well, from all puzzles that you'll encounter, only the first one is a mathematics puzzle. Next is a card matching memory game, then "lighting pillars in the proper order" game - repeated twice, only change for the second time is you gotta do it while running away from an opponent - and pulling stones from bags, so you gotta be the one to pull the last stone for the last challenge. I must say that final "puzzle" is completely luck related rather than being brain-scratching. You lose, you lose, you lose and huh? You win? How? Yeah, that kinda thing. Only the first puzzle is even remotely challenging which would ask for you to "calculate" anything. The rest? Garbage if you ask me.
You can play the game in 4 different difficulties, in which only the numbers involved will augment to raise the frustration, not the challenge. If you complete the game in either hard or expert difficulty, you are allowed to watch an epilogue - which is the sorriest, nearly the most cliché gag ever. That's it.
Can I recommend it? Maybe if you have stumbled upon it free, but then again it is still more frustrating and cringe worthy rather than being entertaining. Sorry guys, nothing to do here.

Unfortunate to be writing a negative review of this game as ive loved the previous titles of the series.
But this game simply does have way too much negative things as people have pointed out.
To sum up the game shortly.
First positive things
+The game looks great, the art designers have been doing quite good job in this one as in the previous ones
+Soundtrack. While this is matter of taste, i have enjoyed the work of Ari Pulkkinen in previous games and he did do good in this title as well
And thats about it unfortanetly, to move to negative sides then
-Length. the game is ridiculously short in comparision to previous titles. I played it trough with friends in 4 hours. If you were to skip side missions in the game, which hold no real value. Theyre just mini levels or an arena where youre locked to single character. also if you were not to fool around alot like we did. You could finish this game under 2 hours easily
-Character progression. unlike in previous tittles, this one has none of it. no talent trees, no new weapons, no new skills or spells. instead youve actually been reduced at amount abilities in this game in comparision to others. wizard can do only a box, knight has only sword and shield and the thief has only one type of arrow.
- 3d. While it did have some interesting usage in the game, with thiefs rope and such. over all i would say it came with negative impact to the game. the camera angle can get very awkward at times, especially if youre intending to backtrack. It also glitches the knight somewhat where youre actually capable of wall jumping of the side walls and the back walls, if you glide while youre doing so. you are capable of reaching infinite height and pretty much can skip all the puzzles if you so desire.
-Price. For a game this short, the pricing is way too steep. 20/22€ for a 2-4h game is way too much in my books.
I do feel like ive made a mistake for buying the game this early, as for me that is too high price for the content im getting.
-Bugs. There is quite alot of those, the earlier mentioned knight wall jumping i imagine being one, others being objects going crazy randomly, your ghost after death going out of level, in air or just simply disappearing so you cannot be ressurrected. Also the online multiplayer having quite a few bugs tied to it too. only host being able to destroy some of the boxes containing triangles, there being laggy things and what not.
Over all it felt like i did get 25% of trine game i were expecting.
As extra notion, i can say vaguely that the ending is a cliffhanger and very abrupt. which does tell they're intending to adding dlc to the game most likely or a sequel. But untill they do and if its free or changes the game drastically, I simply cannot recommend this game.

hodiny. A ne, bohužel si nedělám srandu.
Vemte si všechno co jste milovali na prvním a druhém Trinu. Pěknou grafiku, zajímavou hratelnost, zajímavý a pohádkový příběh, vtipné dialogy, originální hádanky... Máte? Tak jo, teď to všechno zahoďte, protože Trine 3: The Artfacts of Power nenabízí vůbec nic z toho. Hádanky jsou buď naprosto jednoduché, nebo jsou tak šíleně pos**né, že vás začnou frustrovat. Nepočítám do toho bugy, šílenou fyziku, vlastně nulové RPG prvky (postavy už nemají žádné dovednosti co si můžete vylepšovat). A ten příběh? Neskutečná kravina, opravdu. Napsáno suše, podáno stroze a celkově je to opravdu nezajímavé a neoriginální.
Občas se objeví něco zajímavého, to hře nechám. Má občas pár zajímavých nápadů, (např. 5. kapitola je obzvlášť pěkná - především její výtvarný styl), ale jinak? Pokud jste fanoušky série, od tohohle se opravdu držet zatím dál. Dohrajete to za naprosto příšerné tři hodiny, sbírání Trineanglů (trojrozměrných trojuhelníků, které nahradily XP body) je úplně na nic, kromě odemykání dalších úrovní (všechny si stejně odemknete snadno), kooperace občas funguje a občas ne. Soudě dle otevřeného konce se dá očekávat, že tvůrci plánují přidávat další kapitoly. Netroufám si říct, jestli zdarma nebo ve formě placených DLC. Ale tak či onak je aktuálně Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power
opravdu velmi bídnou hrou, kterou nedoporučuji ani ve slevě. Po perfektním druhém dílu jde o obrovské zklamání, které nedoporučuji ani fanouškům série. Resp. obzvlášť těm.

If you're a run and gun COD fan or the hack and slash away at the Orc hordes, then this game is not for you.  Sure I have spent only 75 hrs so far, but every minute was spent surviving in a well done harsh enviroment, where every minute counts. Instead of running 10km to find a heli crash or that player that justr KOSd ya for the 5th time, the Long Dark has a funny way of punishing you and rewarding you all at once. For example, my last playthrough I was holed up in my repurposed camp office and just finished crafting up some fishing line. I went to head out onto the lake to try some fishing.  As I got to the door I could hear the wind gusts getting stronger.  As I exited the building all I could see was snow. Snow on the ground, snow in the air, Snow going sideways.  Yay! Being from Maine, I have a deep love/hate relationship with sideways snow, and the Long Dark brought those fellings in me on that day.  Knowing my semi tattered clothes would not keep me warm for that long.  I went to plan B, I decided to hang around my shelter and gather other supplies, sticks, CATTAILs (good to eat and start fires), Melt and boil water etc...  That storm lasted all day.  So by the end of it I had plenty of sticks for fires, about 10L of water, and enough stones to actually hit a wabbit with.  Yeah, it took me ten tries to actually hit the wabbit with the stone.  I saw it on Youtube and wanted to try. :9 That is one reason why I love this game.  Its not just a start running to nearest mili posts to loot up game. Its a game where you have to plan your every  move, and then come up with plan B,C, and D (sometimes on the fly) just incase.  It still needs work, story mode and such, but right now I think its well worth it. A solid 4 out of 5 from me.

I adored the original

I got this game planning to give it a thumbs up without even playing it (and many others have done just that.) But above all else, I must be honest in my reviews. I can't imagine actually playing through this game today, with its clumsy, backward design.
But I'm not rating this game while living in the time
was originally released. It's been over twenty years,
. We've learned a lot about UI and "User Experience" since then, and to charge more than a few dollars without doing some serious reconstructive work is asking too much.
The "enhancements" are only the absolute bare minimum required to make the game acceptable by today's standards, and those are the standards I'm obliged to use since the game is for sale
. The superficial changes (such as being able to choose higher resolutions) don't impress me. At $40 (the asking price at the time of writing), I would expect at a minimum for the game to have a redesigned UI.
It may have been state-of-the-art when I was a lad, but ultimately sweet nostalgia is all I could wring from this game - a game that had its day long ago. The sun has set on that day, and nostalgia is free. So do yourself a favor and spring for something newer.

Stonehearth is, by far, my favorite city builder. It's still in Early Access, so there's a few bugs here and there, but as long as you remember to save often (especially before creating a custom-made building), they won't detract too much from your enjoyment of the game. You get to customize your own little town while managing every villager, assigning them jobs in which they can progress and advance. Every job plays an important role in your city's growth. The game also features invasions by hostile creatures, not to mention goblin camps that can form near your town, demand tributes and declare war on you if you refuse.
Pros:
- Lovely graphics. Everything, from your villagers to the critters prancing about is just so goshdarn adorable.
- Quality music/sounds.
- Good building customization. There are plenty of blocks to choose from in order to create something that feels unique.
- Interesting combat system. Simple, straightforward and works well.
- Good job advancement/progression system. Every level your character gains unlocks perks and you can advance them into a more specialized job once they meet the requirements.
- Great developpers. They are active, communicate with/listen to the players and update the game fairly regularly.
Cons:
- Buggy building system. Custom-made buildings will sometimes bug, either during the editing process or while it is being built. There are console commands to fix some of the errors, but make sure to always save before making a new building.
- Unfinished game. while it certainly is enjoyeable in its current state, Stonehearth remains an unfinished game at the moment. Keep that in mind when making the purchase.
Overall, Stonehearth is a game that I keep coming back to every now and then to see how it's growing and it never disappoints. This game really deserves more attention. It has a lovely community, great developpers and so much potential. Worth a buy for sure!

This game is a huge disappointment. I really like the core gameplay loop, and I would enjoy playing a similar game with meaningful progression, maybe a story, maybe checkpoints, things like that. This game should not be a roguelike. A single run takes hours, and everything must go perfect the entire time. Are you 2 hours into a run and clicked to send one of your characters one room further than you meant and took 1.5 seconds to realize it? Or did you get complacent in your boredom and didn't notice the huge difficulty spike in terms of monster waves until 2 seconds too late? Did none of the rooms on this floor have any dust and now you can't power any rooms and are getting huge waves every door? There go those two hours. That run is over, and AT MOST you might unlock a new character if you found them early enough by luck. That's the only persistent progress unless you beat the entire dungeon. Enjoy playing through hours of boring, challenge-free early game to get back to the part you're dying to try again.
The game also explains nothing. You will rely entirely on fan wikis and forum threads to teach you even the most basic mechanics. The tooltips are unclear when they are present at all.
For example, all the game tells you about the Wit stat is that it affects the bonus from operating modules. What does that mean? How do you do it? The game does not tell you. The answer is that if a character has the Operate skill (Who gets it? Alt-tab and Google it.), and you go into a room with a major module (minor modules don't count), a white gear appears next to them. This does nothing. But if you then have a different character open a door, the gear will turn green. Now something happens depending on the module. What happens? Alt-tab and Google it. Also, the Mechanical Pal minor module can operate major modules in its room. Two characters with Operate skill do not stack, but Mechanical Pals do stack with a character or with each other. How do I know this? I Googled it.
Here's another: there's a major module you can research called a Shop. Now, there are shops you can find throughout the game in random places. The shops allow you to buy things. You might think that the Shop research allows you to build a shop of your own whenever you want to buy something, which would be handy! Nope. The Shop module is not a shop and will never buy or sell things. In fact, it doesn't do anything. But if you find a shop, you can build the Shop module and the merchant will then man that shop. This still does nothing. But if you Operate the Shop module WHILE a merchant is in it, you will generate a resource called Dust, which is not money, but in fact your source of electrical power to run your machines! Make sense? Oh, and don't worry if the merchant is in an inconvenient place. Once you find him, he will teleport to the Shop module anywhere you build it. Guess how much of this information the game tells you. If you guessed, "It tells you that there is such a module as the Shop," congratulations.
Pros:
-Fun basic gameplay, once you find the right fan-made guides
-Possibly a lot of content? Most of it is gated behind beating the game repeatedly.
-Some cool character designs that create interesting alternate play styles.
Cons:
-Each run takes way too long for a roguelike
-Complete lack of explanation of anything
-Extremely long, easy, and boring early game. You must play for an hour or more to get back to the surprise difficulty spike that killed you so you can try it again.
-Very little persistent progress.
-Too much RNG affecting the difficulty factor
-Absolutely tiny mistakes snowball instantly to an unwinnable game state
I wanted very badly to like this game, and I put in a significant amount of time in hopes that it would "hit its stride," but it simply doesn't. The absurdly long runs, sudden difficulty spikes, RNG challenge factor even very late into the run, lack of anything to show for a failed run, and extremely boring early game just combine to make me feel like my time is being disrespected. I'm sure I could play the game for 20 hours or watch a 2-hour Youtube video and learn to beat it, but there are lots of games out there that don't make me work nearly this hard to find the fun.

This is weird game. Seriously. It was also bundled bunch of times, so you can grab it, if you so desire, for almost nothing. TL;DR (regarding gameplay itself) at the end.
But what it's all about? I wouldn't say "chemistry" like others (and whats funny - also title) says. In chemistry, at least for now, you have to use reagents to get specific products (for example Na + Cl2 -> 2 NaCl). Here, you can operate on atomic level to manipulate what are you getting.
You have something in your inputs and there is requirment to get something specific to output. Sounds easy? At first it is, only thing you need is to "spawn" molecule, grab it (with weird looking circle-like thing), drop it, "despawn" it and do it periodically. After that? Get 2 molecules, bound them and send them out. Next? While having only single H (hydrogen) and single C (carbon) make not CH but CH4 (methan) instead. And you can't simply spawn 4 H's (they appear in the same spot - causing an error), grab every one of them (only one atom with its bindings can be taken at the time) bind them with carbon...
I would say playing this game literally using YT to pass levels is pointless (and I saw it in leaderboards that its common practice) because difficulty level grows quite quickly, you will need those YT clips to pass next level... and next one, and next and so on - which will become boring very quickly, you won't enjoy it as much etc. It is logical game for a reason. It took me good hour to do one level, but it was so good feeling I did it MYSELF without external help.
(almost)TL;DR:

Cons:

My first review was just stating that the game is good and that you shoul buy it. It is ood and you should buy it, but I'd like to elaborate, to expand upon, what my original review was.
I have done a total of 3 playthroughs of the game, one stealth/lethal (my first), one kill everything (my second), and finally the no kill/ghost playthrough (my third).
Out of all the playthroughs, the kill everything run was the shortest, but also the most entertaining. It allowed me the most freedom in my playstyle, for I had no limits. If I wished to use a grenade to kamikaze I could (I would usually survive due to increased health). I would say that this should be either your first or second run of the game. I chose the darkest ending of the game, the "everything is fxcked" ending. It truely was a fun, quick run of the game.
My first playthrough was where I attempted to play the game like any other stealth game. Kill people who are in your way, hide in shadows, you get the drill. I started that run a few years ago, so I was rather inexperienced (I have gotten better at games since then). I didn't even know how to quicksave! I played the game how I wanted to, but keeping to the stealth playstyle (something I would do in any game that had the option of stealth). It was by far my longest playthrough, since I only finished it recently. I took my time to explore every level, tried to get every bone charm and rune, things like that. Admittedly, while I had a lot of fun playing the game like that, I would personally want to replay the game in that style and specialize in certain powers, because by the end of the game, I had unlocked most of the powers without upgrading them. It was a mistake on my part. Speaking of end game, towards the final mission, I started feeling guilt. That I had made a big mistake in killing all those people. However, in games with morality, this usually happens to me when I take the bad route.
My final playthrough was surprisingly fun. I had heard from friends and the internet that no kill runs were boring and while it certainly isn't as fun as a kill everything run, it was still entertaining none the less. I focused less on knocking out my enemies and more on avoiding them. Keeping in the shadows, using Bend TIme when needed, Blinking around the level unseen. In terms of difficulty, I played on the hardest, but it was rather easy. After all, if you're caught you simply slam F9 to go back to your quicksave. If you do wish to do this kind of run, learn that F5 and F9 are your best friends. As for powers, focus on Blink and Bend TIme. It will do wonders for you. You don't even need to collect that much money, since all you'll be buy is sleep darts and crossbow upgrades. Now, by the time I finished the game, I felt satisfied having gone through the entire game without being noticed. The ending was a nice resolution, though knowing there was a sequel around the corner diminished some of its impact.
Now, I look towards the DLC, and the adventures of Daud the assassin. I plan on doing the same 3 playhtough style with those, and I cross my fingers that the sequel will allow us to continue to explore the interesting world of Dishonored.

Dishonored is not:
- An open world Bioshock
- Assassin's Creed with Powers
Those were my initial impressions going in. While Dishonored shares similarities with Bioshock and Assassin's Creed the end experience is not the same.
Stealth is one of the main factors in the game and you can choose to operate through violence or non-violence. Violence makes it easier to stealth around since guards won't eventually wake up from choke holds or tranquilizers but the plague in the game is fueled by the number of corpses lying around. Even if your morality compass doesn't lean towards non-violence there is a legitimate reason to want to keep the body count as low as possible.
Through the gadgets and powers available, the game gives you several different ways of achieving your goal. Take the high road, the low road, stealth your way past enemies, teleport, assassinate or set traps remove enemies from your path. With several different ways of doing things, you could probably get some decent replayability out of Dishonored.
A major downside in my experience is that the characters are dull and uninteresting. The world is dull and uninteresting as well, despite the inclusion of steampunk elements. I wanted to enjoy my playthrough but just couldn't get the thrill I'd get from doing the same thing in other games. That isn't to say that the game has no appeal, or can't be fun, but its not a joyride the whole way through.

Poor controls, terrible networking, and an overall flawed design prevent what would have been an amaing entry in the MOBA genre from truly succeeding.
The game is designed to be used with controllers and has very poor PC optimization for mouse and keyboard. Skill activation latency when using a mouse and keyboard gives a distinct disadvantage when instant skill/item use is necessary in sudden skirmishes.
Bot games are hosted server side and are plagued with the same issues.
Between champion design and the LOTR namesake this game could have been a success. However, there is no late game scaling and no items to buy. The game requires a very high degree of teamwork and any player(s) who can work with one another will dominate those used to a more free style of "Champion" building that comes from games like DOTA, League, or Infinite Crisis.
I obtained my copy through a Humble Bundle so I will not remark on initial cost. However, the game certainly would have been a wash for me if I HAD paid the $15 MSRP. There is also a VERY high degree of pay-to-win with in-game activated consumables that boost damage, resistance, and other useful stats. These can be purchased with currency obtained from playing games, but if you have used all your currency then you better get to the shop to acquire more, lest you lose your matches because of a disadvantage in stats.
Avoid this like the plague until they fix some of the issues. Players have been complaining for months about problems and Monolith just doesn't seem to be listening. Either that or they don't know how to fix it and can't outsource a solution to save their product.
If they ever fix the issues plaguing the game then I can say that in my own opinion this game could be a great success; very far down the line, mind you.

Dark Angles has an interesting balance for a hidden object game. Its first half excels in storytelling but lacks in interesting gameplay mechanics, whereas the second half does the exact opposite.
An all-female quasi-mystical group of warriors fighting the good fight against the ancient forces of evil is a favoured topic in modern action fantasy settings. Dark Angels: Masquerade falls into this line, following the adventures of the newest initiate to an order of leather-clad women, who has to take her mother’s mystical chakram to combat a bunch of clandestine monsters. Said monsters not only invaded every levels of society, but also manage to muster an attack against our heroes on more than one time planes.
From this setup, one would expect some third-person action/adventure, maybe a hack & slash, but Dark Angels is a humble hidden object game. Granted, a very action-packed one for its genre.
Still, a HOG has to include the usual elements, so after the climactic attack, the story mostly takes a backseat to add most of the hidden object scenes and some traditional puzzles expected by its audience. Ironically, this is probably the game’s biggest issue, since the premise does not really fit the adventure game nature of HOGs. It should not keep away any HOG player though, especially if they like awesome soundtracks.

But I'm not rating this game while living in the time
was originally released. It's been over twenty years,
. We've learned a lot about UI and "User Experience" since then, and to charge more than a few dollars without doing some serious reconstructive work is asking too much.
The "enhancements" are only the absolute bare minimum required to make the game acceptable by today's standards, and those are the standards I'm obliged to use since the game is for sale
. The superficial changes (such as being able to choose higher resolutions) don't impress me. At $40 (the asking price at the time of writing), I would expect at a minimum for the game to have a redesigned UI.
It may have been state-of-the-art when I was a lad, but ultimately sweet nostalgia is all I could wring from this game - a game that had its day long ago. The sun has set on that day, and nostalgia is free. So do yourself a favor and spring for something newer.

Stonehearth. Not to be confused with the card game Hearthstone nor the novel Stone Heart by Charlie Fletcher.
It's a medieval town building game where you control what your settlers, also known as Hearthlings, do, somewhat.
It has a Sims-esque overhead view where you can position the camera to watch settlers eat, sleep, mourn over the fact they ate a turnip raw, or plant the camera into a nearby mountain and see how fast you can scroll out of the mountain.
Enough about the camera, what about the gameplay?
It does have strong points, the Hearthlings can farm, mine, deforest an ecosystem for a chair, or be threatened by goblins about 1/3 of their height. Hearthlings don't fight back when attacked by monsters. Oh, sorry, they do. They just have to have another Hearthling be killed in order to do 1/4 a heart of damage. Sort of a human shield metaphor going on.
The only ones who will fight back before wimping out because they were attacked are footmen, knights, archers, and walking bandages- whoops. I meant clerics. I thought this supposed to be a town building game, not a DnD set up.
Before I continue, I'd just like to point out that the "heart" I speak of serve as a HP bar, when there is only one heart.
The combat is interesting, albeit unforgiving if you are outnumbered. Enemies will group up if Hearthlings don't kill them fast enough and they will chop at their health like a chef to a carrot.
Speaking of carrots, there's farming. It is quite smart to have a rot system on raw ingredients, but from what I know, cooking the food will eliminate rotting and make it an MRE, essentially. But before your Hearthlings can have a nice serving of cold soup, you must have a cook because it seems like the Hearthlings were spoonfed and never learned how to roast a carrot over the campfire you are given from the very start. Oh yeah, there are levels for jobs as well, still leaning to the DnD metaphor, since the Hearthlings get buffs and skills from leveling up. Extra damage, more recipes, being able to herd sheep you pulled from your bum.
"Ok, it looks like I need an archer and a knight since these footmen are getting destroyed by a sentient stump."
"Hold on there! Your footmen are only level 2! They need to be level 3 before you can promote them! Just have them walk in circles around that small farm plot for 4 hours!"
"That seems easy, 4 hours ingame isn't that long, it's 4 minutes."
"No, I meant 4 hours in real time."
So I may have exaggerated there about leveling up. The Hearthlings level up their job by, er, doing their job. Farmers farm, Blacksmiths smith, Soldiers stare at dirt.
Some Hearthlings level up faster than others because of their special buffs. There are 3, but based on value, the only ones worth having are Body and Mind. Body (health) is pretty straight forward. Mind makes your Hearthlings level faster and create better versions of items.
I didn't really understand that. How does a carpenter take the materials to make 1 chair and create 2, while one chair is of higher quality?
The higher quality furniture doesn't have any other use other than having a nicer look and a higher gold value. Trading in this game is similar to other games; Vender sells item at a fixed price, you can sell the same item for half. Sometimes you can get specialty deals from wandering traders. While some are good, the others are asinine. Some come along the line of "I'll give you one twig for your 54 baskets of pumpkins!" or "I'll give you 40 steel bars if you show me a smile, you heartless being!" Before you can make this transaction, you must wait a period because, I don't know, the trader has to preform a broadway play or something. Which makes sense, they make a deal which can be done in a minute or in 5 days. Sometimes you can get a trade for something from the other band of Hearthlings, which is nice if you hate seeing the same stalks of yellow vegetables. I couldn't say it WORKS yet, let me find out later, I got an offer for watermellon seeds and it just seems like it took my corn.
Deforestation is also an issue. They fixed that by adding farmable saplings. "What? Now it's both DnD AND Minecraft?! It's just a rip!" And that is why those who point out things like that shouldn't make reviews. Wait... Anyway, be prepared to either have a sapling farm that makes 1 sapling every harvest, which isn't a lot, or 200 every harvest, which is just a tad too much.

The first time I started to try to get into this game I found it frustratingly difficult and I couldn't seem to get very far at all or understand exactly all the mechanics taking place but after a bit of perseverance this gem easily became on of my favourite games ever.
The art-style compliments this very fun mixture of tower defence, party-based RPG, and classic perma-death rougue-liteness which in my opinion has been tried a variety of places and never quite got the right balance for me to keep coming back for more. I have turned this game on so many times for a quick run and something to pass a bit of time away then in quickly turning into my whole night. Rarely does the game feel too overwhelming, it always seems to give you just enough randomness so that your skill still feels like the main factor in victory. It burns a little slow at first, takes some time to unlock the characters and ships, which open up quite a variety of play-styles and stategies.
The complaints I have of this game are minimal - so insignificant to the overall quality of the game that putting them in this review for people who haven't already played it are pointless. I came in with zero expectations when I booted up Dead Effect 2 which allowed the game to surprise me on many levels despite its mobile influences. I’m not saying it’s a good game. I’m not sure if I can say it’s even an okay game. It’s has B-movie levels of quality when it comes to the writing, voice acting, animations, and overall production value, but there’s just something about it which kept me going until I reached the end of my 9-hour journey. Having functional co-op was also a major factor in my enjoyment of this ARPG FPS.
You start off the game being rescued by a woman in a future where bras don’t seem to exist. You work with her to survive and recruit new members for your cause as you make progress in the story by shooting zombies, robot mutants, and soldiers. You can select missions from the hub that you return to every time you complete one. You can also experience some diversions with the other modes – Generic Missions, Biohazard, Survival, Lone Wolf, and Infestation – if you want a break from the story mode or want to focus more on finding loot. There’s a surprising amount of things to do if you don’t mind plenty of repetition when it comes to the environments due to them being repurposed for the other modes.
Loot and upgrades are how you become stronger in this FPS game. You will find plenty of weapons, armor, implants, and consumable items. They all have varying qualities with Mythical being the best of the best. Every piece of equipment can be socketed with codices which can add an effect or simply provide more stats. Weapons can also gain levels if you buy them enough upgrades (damage, magazine size, accuracy, codex slots, and reload speed) which usually results in a huge damage increase. You’ll want to stay on top of it all if you want to keep playing on Hard or above, otherwise just select Normal for your missions. If you’re not finding good loot, you can pick up some from the vendors in the hub or even buy a consumable loot booster. It’s also worth noting that this game has some kind of special love affair with Norse mythology since many of the item names are borrowed from there.
Oh right, you can also give the game’s four skill trees a gander. One of those skill trees will change depending on the character you select; the other three are accessible by all characters. You can only have two active abilities equipped, so choose wisely or purchase a skill reset if you have regrets. I just went with two that I liked once I reached a high enough level and purchased any of the passives once they were available. Skills have levels too and can have their damage, range, or passive effect increased.
The game has a bunch of numbers that like going up, but how does it actually play? Well, the melee combat isn’t that satisfying with most weapons. However, my favorite melee experience has been with the bladed fists. They have better animations, a decent knock back chance for ragdolling pleasure, and the right click is an uppercut. The gunplay is better overall, but some choices aren’t great. Shotguns and explosive crossbows reign supreme while the charge up plasma beam is a very acquired taste and the handguns feel underpowered. There’s a fairly large selection of weapons available, but you’ll probably gravitate to only a couple types until you’re rolling in dough since upgrades do cost a pretty penny. Adding a friend to the mix only makes it better, especially if you combine abilities and loadouts intelligently.
I want to be very clear, this game is a mindless shooter. The abilities can spice things up by letting you slow down time, turn everything within a certain radius into gibs, knock down baddies in a line, and more. You also have grenades at your disposal. What’s weird is that you can’t jump and there are some strange mini-games for opening doors or interacting with panels. Some stuff is obviously mobile such as holding down LMB while drawing a circle to turn a valve while others will be frequency matching or solving a number problem.
It’s a somewhat nice looking game. The flashlight is terrible with its bloom, but the weapon details are quite good. The text you can see around the levels on the screens and everything else beat a bunch of modern games when comparing legibility. It has some kind of filter on it that probably helps with making the rest of the game look okay for what it is. Some areas will have framerate drops for an unknown reason. There might be a graphics setting that’s not optimized well, but it’s been a mostly 60 frames experience for me. Uh, the UI for the shops can be clunky too.
The game does have a story if you want to pay attention to it. Your character is trying to figure out why everyone is trying to kill him/her despite saving the universe from Dr. Wagner, the antagonist of the first game. There are a couple interesting story bits when it comes to figuring out who’s on your side, but the ending is very abrupt and doesn’t tie up any loose ends. Instead, it sets up the sequel scheduled to come out next year according to the pre-rendered cutscene. Classy. In addition to all the dialogue, there are plenty of tablets to be found that provide some flavor text which are later stored in a terminal in the hub. You’ll also receive emails from the main characters which provides more background on them. It’s all there if you want it, but the real star is the voice acting of Dr. Bielik and Minikin.
Minikin is a character with some form of brain damage to his speech center when he came out of cryostasis, causing him to refer to himself in the third-person with some Hulk speak. Every time he greeted me with a “Minikin.” I thought of Matt Damon in Team America. Bielik’s voice actor did a Russian accent on a level so bad that it could reignite the cold war era. It was as if he combined a Russian accent with a German one and some other stuff that I can’t understand. Some people might become aurally annoyed, but I was fascinated and was usually laughing at what I was hearing.
I believe Dead Effect 2 falls under the “So Bad It’s Good” category. It has some things going for it such as completely functional gameplay and co-op which makes it much better than it is since you can enjoy the bad VA and other questionable things with a friend or two. It could be worth a go with a nice sale price, but definitely check out the gameplay first to determine if it’s a good fit for you. The Mixed rating on Steam is well deserved and there are better games out there.

You can develop your character in many ways with many moves / powers; together with many weapons (and their respectable upgrades) you can develop your own strategy style.  Like push off the feet w force ability then melee bash mostly, then nade / rocket big clusters of zeds or stronger ones, or pistol then main weapon combo, or put up shield field ability / bullet time + chain / mg the horde and such.
Pros - reflexes, sharp humor (if you get Conan at least), more social w char's n coop, level up / develop char, more weaps = much richer variety of tactics.

Other thoughs - was free for my cell, but unplayable/not fun, $6.99 for PC, now its 11.99; interesting, I guess more people are bying it.  Oh - and Unity engine is implemented  just fine here, no fps spikes; 2 year old PC w GTX 970, i5 DDR3.

As somebody who's owned Evolve since launch, I've had no problem expressing my regret towards ever taking interest in the game.  It was a great game but had balancing problems, a crapload (metric unit: 10 arbitrary measurements) of bugs and balancing problems, and its DLC policies were terrible.  It didn't stand a chance; redownloading the game months later showed me a nice game of "play against the four people who are now Gold Destroyer rank and know everything about the game.  Its community died slowly and painfully.
I read the news about Evolve being taken down with the big TU9 "#stageup" hype train they tried to get going, and thought to myself "The game's already done for.  Why bother?"  As with many others, I'd completely given up on the game.
Yet, Turtle Rock is taking it and making this thing work.  I genuinely like the changes made, where all DLC can now be obtained freely and new players can jump in and get the hang of it soon enough.  It goes far beyond a simple business model change, though; the game is more action-oriented with shorter match times, redesigned maps, streamlined hunting mechanics, rebalances to remove the "Flee 'till 3" elements of Monster gameplay, and turned it into a chase rather than a slow and annoying hide-and-seek game.  It went from a huge letdown to my favorite game on Steam practically overnight.
As for people whining that they paid for the game: look, I feel your pain, but if I had to pick between a $60 game being dead forever, and a $60 game going F2P and being fun again, I think you damn well know which one I'd like to pick.  This was a great update and revival, but advertise your games for once!  Nobody cares about your Bioshock Remastered ads, 2K, Bioshock can sell itself on name alone.  Take your fledgling IPs and stop dropping them the moment they hit shelves!

-When you start playing the Campaign mode of the game and you are ready to select a character......READ THE BIOS OF ALL THE CHARACTERS!!! The Bios are the best part of the game!!!
I'm joking of course, but please read them.
They are the most wtf, weird, unbelievable, hilarious, background stories I ever read!!!! Pure gold!!!
-You start the game with a special perk for your character. I wanted to say all the perks are good, but..........select the Vampire perk right away. Killing millions of zombie/mutants hordes and getting health for each kill is the best way playing this game [for me at least].
-The gameplay is a pure action shooter with some RPG elements on it. You get levels after you killed enough enemies and you can update your character by putting point in different skills.
Also you can change the weapons/items you are using depend how useful/powerfull is for you.
-The weapons are indeed the biggest part of the game. Nearly all the weapons you are using in the game are perfect and enjoyable murdering the endless waves of enemies you meet. Also they are so many of them that I finished the Campaign mode without using them all!!!
Every single time I found or bought a weapon, I acted like a little kid trying my new awesome toy.
-Many secrets you can find in the game and gladly nearly all of them are actually worth find. Find a secret a get a powerfull armor/weapon is always welcome.
-Big Variety of enemies to fight from a simple zombie rat to giant mutants with rocket launchers!!! My favourite enemy are the wing naked ladies you fight :3
-The story is hilarious, classic ,cliche B-Movie style and ridiculous. Even the dialogs are cliche as f*ck.
-The enjoyment of killing thousands or enemies in a sigle room after a hard day at work......Aaaaaaaaa the feeling is good.
I suggest you to buy the Minigun and a giant Multi-Rocket Launcher as soon as possible.
-Controlling a Tank and a FlameThrower Robot is a nice break and relax a little for worring about dying.
[Cons]
-The graphics are VERY outdated and look indeed like a 10 years old game, but let face it, they serve their purpose and the gore look good. Personalty not a con for me, but for others it might be.
-Before start playing, go in the Graphics options and turn of three things:
Film Effect, Vsync and Bw/Color.
Two reasons why:
1.If the Vsync is on, the game surprisingly lag REALLY bad. I hope this not happen to others, but test it first to be 100% sure.
2.The Film Effect and Bw/Color make the game look like a black n' white Horror B-movie. However this didn't worked for me....
I prefer to see the things as it is in this case.
-Problem with the screen resolution. I tried many times to fix it for a 16:9 monitor, but again the screen doesn't fit.
-The unpleasant feeling when you try to move around to small places and get stuck from small objects.
-At some point you will drive a car with a giant gun on top of it. Sound great but sadly the driving is terrible...
-It is a Zombie game. Yes, in our days the Zombie Theme is a negative and I will admit, I am sick of it as well a little myself.
Final Thought
If you want to have a relaxing day by killing a massive hord of zombies with a giant variety of weapons, this game is for you.
However I suggest you to seek for guidance on Forums if you have technicals problems with the game.
Also if you are sick of Zombies, then this game isn't for you.

This sequel manages to be worse in every game play aspect. The graphics, models, sounds, and music appear to be the same, so you should expect a very cheap presentation and overall quality. This is very low budget even on a 1990s standard. The voice acting is absolutely terrible, which made me actually laugh a few times in the beginning, and the game gives you the chance to cringe because of it quite often. The AI has not been improved over the first game, and this is made obvious from the very first zombie you face. They have a tendency of spinning in place and being stuck, with conjunction of terrible path finding abilities. The developers decided to make the display grainy and purposely of lower quality than it would already naturally be, as well as using a very small amount of color throughout the game. There are spelling errors throughout the bleak mission briefings, as well as many bugs and glitches that manifest themselves as menu issues and clicking problems. The game play mechanics have stayed about the same as the original, where you simply move and shoot at any zombies coming your way, but also with the addition of operating a turret from a moving car that you have no control over. Zombie Shooter 2 looks and feels like an extremely low-end development, with all of its facets being obviously rushed, poorly designed, badly implemented, and generally deprived of creativity and any true enjoyment. The original Zombie Shooter provided the player with mindless and lackluster game play, but at the very least it had its few game play merits of running and gunning with the occasional smile or smirk. The sequel fails in the continuation of the series, and carries on lousily while adding many other problems that did not exist in the original. The character's movement is sluggish and sometimes not very responsive to control. It feels like Zombie Shooter 2 was a junior college computer programming project that was barely finished. It lacks polish, imagination, and game development technical skills. The folks at Sigma Team have showcased how limited they truly are. The game's description boasts RPG elements that do not actually exist in any way, shape, or form. There is simply nothing there to make any such absurd claim. You are able to make weapon and ammunition purchases, as well as some other items that may aid you through each of the levels, but there are no RPG mechanics or elements whatsoever. This claim is basically not true. Upgrading health, speed, and accuracy do not equate role playing mechanics. The difficulty levels are not programmed properly, in addition to some of the stronger zombies being extremely overpowered and with an unreasonably large amount of life. Sadly, there is just too much wrong with Zombie Shooter 2. It is almost entirely crippled, unbalanced, and limited in every describable way. The music is also rather poor and of low production value, but thankfully, you are allowed to turn down its volume or to mute it completely. The loading times are atrocious for such a low quality game run from a modern computer. The vehicle levels where you are able to control direction while shooting can be slightly satisfying, yet short lived. The save system is nothing short of idiotic. It does not use checkpoints, and it does not allow you to save mid level, or any time you so desire. What it does instead, is that it saves it for you at the end of each level only. This means that if you die during a level, or near the end of a level, you will be forced to do it all over again from the beginning; meaning that you may waste another 30 minutes or longer attempting to beat certain levels again and again. The unbalanced and overpowered enemies makes this bad design decision much worse. If you have enough patience for an extremely poor, low budget title, there is some small amounts of fun to be had with Zombie Shooter 2. There is really not much to enjoy in it.
Zombie Shooter 2 is bad.

Wanted to wait a while before I posted this review, make sure I gave the game every oppourtunity before I made up my mind.
WHY I BOUGHT THIS GAME
This game stuck out for me. Saw it in my queue during a steam sale about 2 years ago.  Its 8 bit graphics and unique style and story made me consider paying full price for it as I didn't get it during the sale. I thought "This feels like one of the old sierra games but with a better story and lots more engrossing action,  it could be something I'll play over and over and not get bored"

WHY YOU SHOULD NOT BUY THIS GAME
Fast forward to 2 years later and I've all but lost interest. I have tried on several occasions to get into this title.  The biggest problem is, despite being very well put together, it doesn't know what it wants to be. Part of me wonders if it was passed to 3 or 4 different DEV teams during production, and each team wanted to make a different game.  Is it a resource management rpg? is it a tower defense game? its it an side scroller? An exploration adventure?  The answer is yes.  The problem is that it doesn't do any of these things well enough to compensate for the ones it does poorly. With that kinda confusion it doesn’t really know what audience its selling to.  I wish they had just focused on two of these elements, the game would have been fantastic.  Add to that, you can be phenomenal at setting up your defenses, picking your characters, managing your resources, and you will still lose, and have to start all over again. There is no saving.  So much of what determines the win here is pure Luck. Save up your resources to level 11 but misspend them by taking a wrong turn, you lose.  There is no way to recoup or recover from a mistake. Alternatively, You can spend no resources at all and still manage to win if you get lucky with which doors lead to exit rooms. Which are also totally RNG generated.

Multiplayer is Bugged.
Something is wrong with the multiplayer in this game. Not sure what, sometimes it will let you form a group , other times it just kicks you and sends you into game on your own or back to starting menu.  This is not my PC, firewall,  or connection, have investigated and ruled both of those out. Devs were supposed to offer a fix, it never happened.

PROS
Retro graphics
Cool premise
Lots of things that seem like fun
Fun multiplayer (when it works)

CONS
Things that seem like fun, turn out to be tedious and frustrating
No ability to save you game
Luck of the draw to Win
Broken Multiplayer (for the most part)
Game tries to be all things to everyone with only average results
CONCLUSION
It called Dungeon of the ENDLESS, but dungeon of the EXITS would have been more fitting.  The strategy the player has to adapt is to hord as much resources as possible, which means (not building cool items during the levels, so you are encouraged not to use those mechanics and also running for the level exits as fast as possible.  To win, you are actively encouraged not to explore the endless doors or tunnels, not to seek adventure in the levels but just find the exits as soon as possible and then get off the level.

A great opportunity has been lost.

Dungeon of the Endless was a surprise for me.  I had only heard some basic information about it, but the concept and the aesthetic immediately appealed to me, so I decided to pick it up.  It quickly sucked me in and had me determined to complete the game and escape to the surface.  Though it took a good number of failed attempts and did drain a little of my will to continue playing, I managed to make my way to the end at least a couple of times before I moved on to other games.  Yet I still feel like I’d be more than happy to head back in and try for an even tougher run.
This game is a unique mix of elements from a few genres.  It has the core of an RPG where you’re managing a party, gaining new equipment, leveling up and enhancing stats, and finding new members to join.  There are also a few roguelite qualities in that each run is an independent experience where losing a party member is permanent and certain starting members can be unlocked over time as you find them in the dungeon.  It also features procedurally generated dungeons and certain modifiers that you can add to each game session making it potentially easier or more difficult.  All of that is the standard for many roguelite RPGs, but on top of that, you have a twist on a tower defense game.
The premise of the Dungeon of the Endless has you ejecting from a prison ship in a pod (which serves as one of the modifiers for the game, changing some mechanics and stats) with a party consisting of members you’ve selected from the pool you’ve unlocked.  Each character has unique traits and abilities and will use particular types of equipment.  The escape pod plunges into a planet and deep into the levels of a dungeon, where you’re tasked with finding several elevators and carrying your escape pod’s power generator up to the next level and enough times to finally make it out.  The challenge is that every door you open (often) spawns various angry creatures that want to take out you and/or your generator, spawning in any room you’ve opened that isn’t powered up by the Dust you’ve gathered.  Dust is somewhat rare and most of the time you won’t have enough to power every room in your search for the elevator, so you’re required to build defensive structures in the rooms you’ve unlocked to slow or kill these enemies in the path behind your party.  All of this is managed through a resource system and ground nodes that add another layer to the general effort to survive each opening door and finding your way out.
While it seems complicated, especially in writing, I will say it is at first.  However, as you get used to the mechanics you’ll start seeing the strategies and resource management necessary to get through the game.  The challenge is there from the start and only increases as the game progresses, so often it’s just as important to clear out an entire level of the dungeon to gain resources, potentially risking your party and generator, as it is to rush your way toward the latter parts of the game.  Getting close to the exit ill-prepared can lead to defeat much faster than taking risks early on for additional gear, party members, or resources.
Dungeon of the Endless is a bit old now, but age doesn’t slow it down – yet it does make it quite a bit cheaper.  As of this review it’s only $2.99 in the Steam sale and $4.99 for the whole collection with DLC.  I fully recommend this game, with or without the DLC, because I found it kept me thoroughly entertained for many more hours than your average indie game.  A fan of any of the many genres Dungeon borrows could find it enjoyable, and a fan of all of them has a major obligation to pick this up if you’ve somehow missed it.

Serious Sam throws so much insanity, anger and general chaos at you that you're missing out if you don't have someone else to act as a human shield. Boss battles that'll catch you off guard and don't always make sense initially. (Trust me on this.)

So, that being said, I'd say get the game. Great with friends. Unless you don't have friends, in which case find some you sad, lonely depressant.

The cRPG market is flooded these days, but cast your mind back to the mid-90's - past the heyday of the AD&D Gold Box era, when traditional RPGs were represented by Fallout and very little else. Baldur's Gate was released with little fanfare or anticipation, but a solid engine (if not state-of-the-art) with eye-catching art design and some solid writing with fleshed-out characters with distinct possibilities elevated the genre and set a standard imitators weren't able to copy. Sure, the story seems cliched now and the creators at Bioware went on to bigger projects (including the incredible Baldur's Gate 2), but this was a game that created the cliches in the first place, and if characters and writing have more depth today, it's because the bar was set pretty high to begin with. Baldur's Gate will always have a place on my hard drive, and the Enhanced Edition isa  great way to just install and play it on current hardware. Highly recommended.
