is a hidden object adventure game that focuses on Kate Evans, a young modern day woman who becomes entangled in a world of demons and freedom fighters. It’s a fun game filled with action, fun puzzles and hidden object scenes, it also has great music and visuals. While it’s certainly not a perfect game having an outlandish plot, some irritating puzzles and audio issues, for the price tag I enjoyed playing it and was able to look past its flaws. Though it may not be the best hidden object game on the market it’s still a good gaming experience.

Kate is a young fashion designer haunted by the memories of her mother’s death though she soon finds out the beings responsible for this murder are now after her. Her mother was part of a secret organization that fights demons, one that dates back hundreds of years and has notable members like Jeanne d’Arc and, I kid you not, Marilyn Monroe. Things get even more complicated as the dark forces have built a time machine and use it to erase the organization from existence, prompting Kate and a few survivors to commandeer it and go back in time themselves.

The plot is just all over the place and while I’ve played hidden object games with weaker storylines, this one could have been better. It’s completely unrealistic that Kate went from a fashion designer worrying about clothing one moment and then becomes the saviour of an entire guild of demon hunters. She has little to no training but that doesn’t stop her from wielding her weapon like a pro, granted it’s mainly due to the player controlling her. While I know she is the main character and thus has to be the hero, it sort of hurts the validity of the game that such a novice outshines women who have much more experience.

This is a point-and-click hidden object game so all you need is a mouse to play. You can interact with people and objects, collecting useful ones along the way. Items are stored in your inventory and some can be combined to make a new item though the game does this automatically for you. One note about the inventory is that you can lock it in place so it always minimizes when not in use, this is a pet peeve of mine. You only have a fast travel map when you’re time traveling though you don’t really need one in the present day since there isn’t much backtracking involved. I enjoyed the variety of hidden object puzzles, while there are your basic list of items to find there are also ones where you’re given a shadow of an item and have to find in a scene as well as other types. While there is also a nice variety of puzzles, some are rather frustrating and some are often just pointless. Putting a puzzle on the side of a truck is pretty silly.

This game is riddled with annoying item fetch-quests for problems that could be solved in a much easier way. One example would be when Kate has to find a shard of glass despite having a very sharp weapon always on hand. Another odd feature is that of dialogue choice, while I do think this can be fun it really has no effect whatsoever on the gameplay or story at all, thus proving to be pointless. Kate can also use special potions to grant her super strength, special sight and slow down time. An interesting feature but a needless add -on. Also, the only way to get these potions is to find figurines and add them to what seems to be a checker board that Kate somehow always carries around. Adding a new figure grants Kate a potion which is always conveniently the exact one she’ll need for her next problem.

On the plus side, this game has very nice graphics with attractive character models and good animation. The colors are vibrant and nothing is too dark or hard to see. This game also has its own theme song which sounds beautiful. The lyrics are touching and the melody is very soothing but very catchy. I’ve never played a hidden object game that had its own song, I actually sat through the credits a few times just to hear the full song. Sadly, the rest of the game’s audio is hit or miss. While the background music and sound effects are fine, the voice acting is the issue. It’s fully voice-acted but some actors aren’t very good and Kate herself sometimes overacts her lines. Also, there are some problems with audio quality, as some characters sound louder than others.

While it might seem like I’m picking apart
, in the end I really enjoyed playing it. It was fun and had great hidden object scenes, plus I did like Kate for the most part as a main character though they could have fleshed her out more. The good part about this game is that it’s cheap so even if it’s not the best hidden object game, for its price point it’s a really good one. The game also has Steam trading cards and achievements which are not too hard to collect. I recommend this game to fans of the genre, it’s a good game for a good price.

When I started playing
I was certain that I would give it a thumbs up.  The graphics are top-notch for the genre, and the music exceeds anything I would expect to hear in a HOG. The plot, though an absurd mash-up of
and
with ridiculous gaping plot holes, is still rather fun.  The cutscenes are unusually long and well done.  The whole thing seems carefully polished.
However, for all the prettiness of it, I don't think I have ever sworn in frustration at a HOG so many times as I did at
.  The more I played, the more I hated it.
The issue that kept infuriating me, over and over, relates to the nature of the progress barriers.  That's how the overworld in a HOG functions, of course -- an array of progress barriers, functionally doors in disguise, requiring a variety of objects that act as keys, which you must obtain by finding them, solving puzzles or playing minigames.  Here, however, the progress barriers were all so
and
At one point, for instance, my character needs to open a container, but it is tied shut with a piece of string.  She is carrying no less than
sharp objects, but she can't cut the string until she finds a piece of broken glass, because apparently none of the much better cutting implements
will do!
At another point, there's an object I want lying in the dirt.  It's right there.  I can see it.  But my character won't pick it up until I find a glove for her, because she doesn't want to get her hand dirty.
My constant refrain to this game was "Just ^&#*ing
, already!  What's stopping you???"
I click on a cart, and the character helpfully tells me that she could push the cart.  "I
you can push the cart," I scream. "I want you to do it!  Stop telling me that you can do it, and just do it!  What is your problem???  Is it that wheel chock?  It's a single little block of wood!  Just kick it out of the way like a normal person!  Do you really need a corkscrew and an electric toothbrush just to remove a #%^$ing wheel chock???"
Over and over, the biggest challenge in the game is figuring out precisely what dumb object your character wants in order to overcome some silly problem that should be trivial to handle in any number of ways.  Even though progress barriers like these are an inherent element of the game, the ridiculously contrived nature of those barriers, along with the sole means of passing them, just overwhelmed my ability to suspend disbelief.
It doesn't help that the means of giving you the "keys" is often just as baldly contrived as the problems that require them.  At least a half-dozen times in the game, something that you achieve will result in a character saying some form of "It's dangerous to go alone. Take this," and then handing you some bizarre object that no sane person would possibly expect you to need, but that is, of course, exactly what you need to pass another barrier.  As if that wasn't enough, you also drag around a magic checkerboard whose role is to dole out key items at exactly the time you need them and not before.
I don't expect realism from a HOG, but please, at least work with me a little!  Make the impediments to progress plausible!  Ensure that the expected means of solving those problems is the most logical one!  Present key objects in a way that isn't blatantly handing them to me!
Add a few localization errors and a touchy UI just to add spice to an already infuriating stew.  I've never before given the thumbs down to a HOG that is, on the surface, so technically meritorious, but, similarly, I've never had such an unpleasant time playing one, either.

This game. . . Lord have mercy, this game!! I am a big Xcom fan, being introduced to the games via Enemy Unknown. Let me tell you here and now, UFO Defense gets my brain chugging and my heart pumping like little else and leaves me with a good taste in my mouth after a session.
I'm a man who likes to steadily push his limits. Not going to fast, but hardly stagnating, and UFO Defense really tests my mental metle in the best of ways. Your soldiers feel vulnerable and easy to kill, the aliens feel like they're everywhere and nowhere, and you never feel liek you've wrested full control on the situation. The aliens feel truly like skulking, deadly extraterrestrial creatures form a horror film.
I've never been a big fan of horror, but this is more of a horror you feel like you can combat effectively, should you play your cards right.
However, with this, the game isn't always intuitive. The UI isn't the best and the game doesn't exactly tell you what you need to know, but what game from the 90's did? There are mods to make the game a bit more user-friendly, a few of whom I may try out. Alas, aliens also feel like they come out of nowhere without giving you a chance to react before a good chunk of your men are dead, but I suppose that adds to the terror and unfamiliarity of the situation.
I havne't gotten very far in the game as it's pretty difficult, even at earlier stages, but the more tactics you learn and the better you adapt, you'll be left with a satusfied sense when you down an alien craft, kill any remaining crew with minimal casualties, and still come home with the power core intact.
You will come home with several stories of how your men beat the odds and came home with the gold, and just as many stories of how half the men were killed and your one legless soldier made it home with nothign more to his name that a shattered ego and half a hand... Where he will later die.
You'll be chewed up, torn a tsunder, browbeat, curbstomped and tazed six ways form Sunday, but when you backhand the aliens across the face in the end, you'll feel like a king.
If you like a challenge, a selection of tense moments and an engaging defense of Earth, Xcom: UFO Defense is for you. This is a must-have for any turn-based strategy fan in my book.

I've decided to review Evolve since it's no longer pay to play (I bought the game on release last year).
Evolve is a great, addictive game, but flawed because of its company moves and bad DLC practices. As a full AAA game, it lacked content and was way above the asked priced tag. Further on, myriads of DLCs with no substantial content, a pricy Season Pass and limited content made it die too soon. Don't get me wrong, making Evolve go F2P was the best move they could've done for this game, and also, people who already owned Evolve and its Season Pass are going to receive bonuses. Remember, no one was playing this game. What's the point of keeping it P2P if you couldn't find a match?
To sum up, I rather have an alive, good F2P game sitting on my Steam library than a dead P2P. Therefore, if you're pi$$ed by this transition, remember that now, at least you'll be able to enjoy Evolve without having to wait 20 minutes to find a match.

I love testing serious games. I mean, everything that can contribute to a learning process is something interesting. Calcu-Late seems at first sight to contribute to that, even if it's in English. But in the end, it's a disappointement.
Calcu-Late puts you in the shoes of James, a young boy that falls asleep while he was studying for his math exam. But Seshat, the godess of Mathematics, choose him as her champion, in a competition where Gods and Godesses are fighting each other in a sort of Olympic games... with a champion in a series of trials and non-violent fights.
You solve a puzzle then you're fighting against someone else. You have several difficulties and I choose the easy one. The first enigma was easy: create two equations to make sure that their sum is making a certain number. Next, it was a memory game. After that, nothing around mathematics was present: you had a puzzle that will be your next fight but with an opponent ready to hit you and finally the mighty final where the champion of Dolos should be the player that would get no stone if you wanted to beat him.
And it's called the easy difficulty. Not only I had an hard time with the second part but that last fight was really hard as I was under the impression that the AI was programmed to make sure you loose everytime. I managed to win but after I don't know how many tries and despite trying to find the right strategy. However, I still don't know how I won. The problem is that I was always the beginning player and the number of stones you can pick from a pot is unlimited...
However, in Easy, you don't have the epilogue. I started in Normal and I'm since stuck in the first enigma. I don't know if it's because the game is in English and that it's not my maternal language, but I'm pretty skilled in the language, else I wouldn't be writing reviews in it or contributing to Neoseeker. However, the first enigma is mysterious because I don't understand anything and there is no real hint to help you. I see elements, I'm pretty sure that I need to make a code with that, however, I don't know how to crack it apart making random numbers (and as you have six of them, welcome to make sure that you did every combination). Is Calcu-Late made only for geniuses or was it just done like that, without any consideration for people that may overanalyze stuffs or struggling with logic?
I wanted easy enigmas, calculus (after all the title is the verb calculate), I found myself very lost, thinking about kids or teenagers that would think that they're stupid as they can't even pass an enigma in normal. I found myself thinking that the AI was coded to make sure you can't win (unless you have a stroke of luck) and that it was to prove that you're just not adapted for this kind of challenge.
If the gameplay is really... well... frustrating, the scenario was good: James, despite having difficulties in maths, shows himself as a good boy, trying to help the others or to comfort them: he managed to stop a young suicidal girl, to show to someone that is mesmerizing everything that dreams are also important, etc..
But no, I can't quite recommend Calcu-Late despite the nice visuals (yeah, I know, kinda RPG Maker, he?) and soundtrack and story. The enigmas are just there to frustrate you, even in Easy. The last fight is just hard for a low difficulty and nothing can be done apart loosing and loosing and loosing and hoooo, a win - but how did I do that?
Now, I'm trying to grab the cards but none seems to be coming. It's perhaps the only thing worthy for 1 buck.

I have to say I liked Zombie Shooter 2 more than the Alien Shooters, but I think that is personal preference.
Is it much different from Alien Shooter 2? Not really, the music is the same, the graphics (and environments) are the same, the characters you can play are the same- same for the gameplay. The three survival missions are the same as in the other games, too.
Only difference- you shoot zombies instead of aliens.

I also like the "storyline" more- although you won't get any Shakespearian plots here.  The campaign and missions are different from Alien Shooter 2,so you are playing through different levels- although the environments are basically the same as in Alien Shooter 2.
Oh, and this time round you have also the option to play the game in black and white- with only the blood as red (or green). Quite atmospheric.
Should you buy this?
If you liked Alien Shooter 2 and like more of the same, I can recommend this, I had quite some fun with this one.

There is no way to edit the land once you have mined it. If you make a mistake...oh well...i hope you are not OCD like me. I currently have the grass layer near my village floating in the sky because either i made a mistake or my workers did not do as they were told.
Finally, once food starts going bad in your storage it is a nightmare. Your workers do not remove this rotten food on their own accord. You must manually delete each basket of rotten food. Im at the point now where I literally spend a quarter of my day scoping out the food storage to remove these rotten baskets.
This game is definitley on the right track but I would still wait until release to see if these kinks will be worked out. If they are this would likely become one of my favorite games in this genre on steam.

- AI needs work
- Need an option to turn off rotting food or make workers remove it on their own
- Need a few more land editing options in case you make a mistake (or your workers)

Dungeon of the Endless was a surprise for me.  I had only heard some basic information about it, but the concept and the aesthetic immediately appealed to me, so I decided to pick it up.  It quickly sucked me in and had me determined to complete the game and escape to the surface.  Though it took a good number of failed attempts and did drain a little of my will to continue playing, I managed to make my way to the end at least a couple of times before I moved on to other games.  Yet I still feel like I’d be more than happy to head back in and try for an even tougher run.
This game is a unique mix of elements from a few genres.  It has the core of an RPG where you’re managing a party, gaining new equipment, leveling up and enhancing stats, and finding new members to join.  There are also a few roguelite qualities in that each run is an independent experience where losing a party member is permanent and certain starting members can be unlocked over time as you find them in the dungeon.  It also features procedurally generated dungeons and certain modifiers that you can add to each game session making it potentially easier or more difficult.  All of that is the standard for many roguelite RPGs, but on top of that, you have a twist on a tower defense game.
The premise of the Dungeon of the Endless has you ejecting from a prison ship in a pod (which serves as one of the modifiers for the game, changing some mechanics and stats) with a party consisting of members you’ve selected from the pool you’ve unlocked.  Each character has unique traits and abilities and will use particular types of equipment.  The escape pod plunges into a planet and deep into the levels of a dungeon, where you’re tasked with finding several elevators and carrying your escape pod’s power generator up to the next level and enough times to finally make it out.  The challenge is that every door you open (often) spawns various angry creatures that want to take out you and/or your generator, spawning in any room you’ve opened that isn’t powered up by the Dust you’ve gathered.  Dust is somewhat rare and most of the time you won’t have enough to power every room in your search for the elevator, so you’re required to build defensive structures in the rooms you’ve unlocked to slow or kill these enemies in the path behind your party.  All of this is managed through a resource system and ground nodes that add another layer to the general effort to survive each opening door and finding your way out.
While it seems complicated, especially in writing, I will say it is at first.  However, as you get used to the mechanics you’ll start seeing the strategies and resource management necessary to get through the game.  The challenge is there from the start and only increases as the game progresses, so often it’s just as important to clear out an entire level of the dungeon to gain resources, potentially risking your party and generator, as it is to rush your way toward the latter parts of the game.  Getting close to the exit ill-prepared can lead to defeat much faster than taking risks early on for additional gear, party members, or resources.
Dungeon of the Endless is a bit old now, but age doesn’t slow it down – yet it does make it quite a bit cheaper.  As of this review it’s only $2.99 in the Steam sale and $4.99 for the whole collection with DLC.  I fully recommend this game, with or without the DLC, because I found it kept me thoroughly entertained for many more hours than your average indie game.  A fan of any of the many genres Dungeon borrows could find it enjoyable, and a fan of all of them has a major obligation to pick this up if you’ve somehow missed it.

A unique retro graphics style game with a mature storyline about the Spanish Civil War. As far as 2.5D games go, this one's unique design is one of its highlights. The 8 bit / pixelated look of the characters and some of the environment provide an interesting juxtaposition between the colorful graphics and the more abrasive thematic content of navigating a war-torn city while scoring headshots or knife stabs against enemy infantry. As a fan of For Whom the Bell Tolls, I find the game to be an interesting parallel to that universe somewhat. Full controller support including aiming with the analog sticks to score headshots as you dash between cover to evade enemy fire (think Alien Hominid style..) is practically applied, while the music and sound effects are both well done.
The game could use more abilities or unlockables to take it to the next level, and backtracking through previously tread areas can become cumbersome and disorienting (especially when you don't realize there is a path you can press "UP" on to move through the 2D space on a Z axis to traverse a separate X plane, for example..) however what is present is enjoyable if you are into either retro style graphics OR unique military storylines in games, and I would recommend it primarily to fans of either of those tropes. I would suggest looking up unedited gameplay footage of the game as well before pulling the trigger on a purchase, as that should give a quick indication of what to expect. The gameplay is not very complex, but if you find the setting and graphical style appealing, I think you may enjoy your time with it.

BugZy's Review: Vaccine War - Experience a brand new platformer/sidescroller experience!
The following is my opinion.
Vaccine War is a brilliant little game set in the 1930’s where you play a Prussian war veteran named Daniel. The general gist of the story is that Daniel tries to escape the terrors of war by settling down in a farm in Spain to live a peaceful and harmonious life, only for it to break out where he lives. His main goal is to find and take back his daughter from whoever took her (whoops, spoiler alert) and find out why whoever invaded his farm attempted to kill him (whoops, again!)
Trying my best not to spoil what I have already spoiled about the game lore, the above paragraph is about the whole backstory. You must fight the bandits and different armies within the country to get to your objectives around the map and ultimately, try to live in peace and harmony again. There is game dialogue that you can read if you want to which adds to the feel and emotion of the game. If you aren’t interested in that sort of thing, however, you can skip it easily. I recommend reading it though!
The game has its own unique play style, where you move between the ‘layers’ of the map. Daniel is such a good citizen that he literally can’t jaywalk. The reason for that is because there are preset paths that guide you around the map and you cannot move outside of them. This can sometimes be tedious and slightly annoying, but also makes the game different from other games of the genre, a new experience definitely worth trying.
The combat system Vaccine War uses is new to me and as a new experience, I enjoy it a lot. Hiding behind the cover of a crate or rock and peeking out with your loaded gun or grenade to attack your enemies with whilst utilising an angle-based aiming method is a big plus for me! You must take down riflemen, grenadiers and CQB experts with guns, grenades and knives before they take you down, or you die. Not for good, though, as long as you interact with a mailbox every time you see one you should be fine.
The bosses of Vaccine War are a good challenge as each of them have their own combat style (one throws barrels, one throws grenades and I won’t spoil the rest) but can be easily defeated if you get your timing right and find their weaknesses!
The visuals are also unique, 2D and pixel-based with a healthy amount of 3D models involved (like houses, fancy awnings, fences, bridges, etc.) The different parts of the map introduce different colour palettes and objects such as cover for you to hide behind in a combat situation (as stated above) and enemies controlling different parts of the map.
The game features some nice acoustic music which turns hardcore if you find yourself in a standoff with an enemy and sound effects that you would expect from a game with guns and grenades. The music that plays is different for the different parts of the map but also plays on a loop so it can sometimes get repetitive. If it does get on your nerves you can turn it down in the settings and turn on some music, maybe hip hop or electro, whatever floats your boat!
All in all, Vaccine War is a new experience and something I would definitely recommend to people who enjoy platformers/sidescrollers and/or wish to try something new!
Vaccine war has earned a score of 8/10 dingos.

Games for Tutti is a Valencia, Spain based development company. Vaccine War is their first game but what is most impressive is that it is also the first game to use their specialized tool that saves time animating pixelart. This tool is called the Magic Pixelator. They claim that with this tool they can create animations of 20 frames in just a few minutes rather than being forced to spending significant time drawing each and every pixel. The characters within the game demonstrate that they were able to create fantastic character animations that feature particle effects such as fire and smoke as well as the game’s environments. This is a great achievement for a small studio that is made up of just four full time employees and a collaborative team of two others.
Their game, War Vaccine is set during the Spanish Civil War but is a completely fictional tale. This is a setting that doesn’t often get portrayed in video games and as such it gave me a reason to be interested in the game before I began as well as checking out their new software tool. I can tell you that although I am yet to complete the game that I am thoroughly impressed with my exposure to the game. It uses the Unity engine but it’s so much more than your standard indie throwaway game made with it. There is solid production value throughout the entirety of what I have experienced thus far and I have yet to run into any bugs. That’s not to say there aren’t weaknesses with the game because there are but rather that I appreciated the game as its whole.
What I will pinpoint as the primary weakness in the game is the combat. The combat system has a lot of potential but it needs work. It’s simply not as precise as what it needed to be. Your attacks will have the appearance that they should be connecting but for some reason they do not. This is generally with the melee weapons but can extend through to guns and range weapons. This makes the cool abilities such as running attacks and jumping attacks very frustrating to use as you’re just never sure if or when the attacks will actually land and play as intended.
I would also dearly like to see the dev team add achievements to the game. It’s a game that would do well with achievements for reaching certain points in the game and maybe arbitrary ones such as number of enemies killed, etc. Trading cards would also make for a nice addition to the game.
But it’s really the artistic flair that shines through here. It’s a perfect prototype game that demonstrates to other studios that their software tool has tremendous value moving forward. I would like to see what the team can develop next and whether or not other developers consider purchasing the right to utilize the Magic Pixelator in order to give their games a big boost in the quality of its animated pixel graphics.

There's a lot to like about casual point-and-click adventure: diverse locales, exciting story, great graphics, and a few fun hidden-object scenes, as well as easy mini-games. There's even a cheesy “goth” theme song. Fans of the genre would enjoy this.
There are some stand-out elements. First of all, it's, like, the girliest of the girliest of themes. We already know these games target a female audience, but having you play as a stunning fashion designer is laying it on a bit thick... hope you enjoy arranging fashion collections and refusing to get dirty. And obviously all the women-warrior-heroes look like supermodels. There are also some nice ideas for mechanics involving combat and magic, which unfortunately are barely used.
There are two problems: one is that it's too short and easy. The other is that there's a major production blunder for the English voice acting. It's usually fine, but once in a while the protagonist's voice is replaced with this bizarre shrill
voice that I imagine was a placeholder during development. Either they forget to replace those audio clips, or they just didn't finish the production. It ends up being quite jarring, but also funny.

Here's one reason this is one of the greatest Video games ever made. I was on a alien base mission with a full complement of varied skilled soldiers(about 14). Everything was going well. I had taken out a few aliens with no casualties. Then it happened.  A misplaced blaster bomb trajectory trail (my fault). The bomb took out about 7 of my soldiers. Most of them were my high ranking soldiers. Panic ensues. Half of the remaining soldiers panic (when soldiers panic they either drop their weapon and run around using up all their movement points leaving them completly vulnerable or they shoot wildly and use up all their movement points again usless and vulnerable.) The aliens take full advantage of this situation. They crawl out of the woodwork and start picking off the panicked soldiers which in turn starts to panic the remaining soldiers. The panic snowball is rolling down hill at full speed now. I have lost control of my whole team at this point. Soldiers are running around aimlessly getting picked  off by aliens. The death screams still haunt me. By a miracle I regain control of one of my soldiers who has holed up in a 3 by 3 elevator room. He had a high bravery rating. I just kept him in that room while I heard the alien footsteps all around. One by one the aliens would come into the elevator room where my guy would blast them with a Heavy Plasma gun. He killed about 8 of them that way  and went on to complete the mission. He and one other survived the botched mission. Even though the mission was a success it was a devasting blow to my barracks. It was an amazing come back that never happened again like that. I'm sure there are a lot of stories about crazy things that happen in this game. Even with the cheap price, it's hard to recommend this game.  There are only 5 puzzles in the entire game, and 2 of them are pretty much identical.  One of them is very easy, and the other 2 deal more with luck, it seems, than anything else.
The music and graphics aren't bad for an RPGMaker game, but there isn't much of either of them.  The story is nothing worth mentioning, since it's practically non-existent, other than a small token of it.  And what is there has poor spelling and grammar, but that's hardly a dealbreaker.
I personally beat the game reading the entire story in around 45 minutes, and then had to idle a bit past that to finish getting my cards.
At 75% off, you're paying 5 cents a puzzle, it's probably worth it, especially if you sell the cards and make around 15 cents of that back.  Really, though, there's probably better things to occupy an hour or less of your time than this game.

Here's the short of it:
-The story is pointless. It's obvious that there should be more in it, and that it wasn't done or it was blatantly cut.
-The characters are pretty dumb
-The puzzles are either basic or matters of luck.
-You can claim that it's just pixel art, but it's still low-res, and the drawn images should be higher quality.
-Playing higher difficulties does not offer more of a challenge, just more frustration on chance-based puzzles.
-It's not worth the time. If you have cards you want to get, just open it and go play your Xbox for a couple hours.
There are only a couple basic puzzles. The first one is always a variant sudoku. The second one is just a memory game. Flip cards over and get the most matches. The third one is that one minigame you find in all the action-exploration games, like Bioshock. The one where flicking a switch causes certain lights to turn on, and others to turn off, and you have to turn them all on. The fourth is the same thing, but now somebody is trying to hit you, so it's kinda a race?
The last one is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, especially on the higher diffuculties. You have three buckets with a random number of stones in each one. You have to take stones out of each bucket, one bucket per turn and as many stones as you want. Your goal is to be the last one to take any stone. While the concept is simple, the random numbers is what ruins it. You always have to go first, and unless you get an amount of stones that fits sequentially, then you lose. You have to retry over and over until you get the sequence you need to win. It can take you several tries before you have what you need. So it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t because there it's impossible until you have one with an actual solution that works in your favor. It took me 13 retries on Expert to get one that actually worked.
Yeah, let's talk about the difficulties. So, if you finish on Easy or Normal, you get the basic ending, woopee-♥♥♥♥ing-doo. BUT, if you complete on Hard or Expert, you get the BONUS SCENE! It's not great. Even if you want to feel something for the characters, there's no reason to care about any of them. It'd be interesting if there were more challenges, more puzzles, and ones that didn't require listening to the asinine MC over and over. Excuse me, skipping the text of the asinine MC over and over. I just hit the retry button, I was just here, I don't need the instructions for the 6th time. Just take me to a "Do you want to hear the instructions again?" and I'll decide if that's what I want.
Now, as seems to be the case with a lot of RPGMaker games, there's a lot of grammar errors. The one puzzle that I hate? One of the most common lines from your opponent is "Can you win againts me?" I mean, one or two typos will make it into any game, but I have to look at this line over and over! I guess I'm a stickler for good grammar, but it's apparent that this wasn't proofread by someone proficient in english.
Also, WHO THE ♥♥♥♥ IS THE LADY BEHIND SESHAT ON THE EXPERT ENDING?

My buddies and I bought this back during the Holiday Sale 2015, and we all put roughly 25-40 hours each into it together.  We always had fun with it, and our having people to play with skews our experience as opposed to people who bought it to play solo.
We were lucky enough to enjoy Evolve as it was mostly meant to be enjoyed, balancing issues and some bugs aside.  We never once thought "that was a waste of money."
Now I see that they are giving Evolve a massive update and turning it Free-to-Play and giving all previous owners the Founder's Pack and I couldn't be happier.  Hopefully this will help others experience what my friends and I did, and hopefully the changes to the maps, hunters, and monsters increase the fun, rather than destroying it.
Now, let's look at some of the changes and I'll throw my two cents in:
You can find the full patch notes
Good change, being the Trapper required (along with medic) the most skill, and was always singled out by the monster during PvP.  It also sucked whenever your Trapper was new and couldn't keep up with the rest of the party
In my opinion, this is a good thing.  Sometimes you think you're going the right way as hunters, you're 100% sure of it - the tracks lead this way, there are dead animals everywhere... then birds get spooked 400 meters in the opposite direction, and you hear the roar of the monster as it reaches Stage 2.  The Scanner will narrow the location and point you in the general direction of the monster without spoiling the actual position, and the Dash ability makes it so the Trapper class still has the best chance in the party of securing a Mobile Arena around the Monster.  Overall, smart move.
I like the idea, it will lessen the Doc's work after a battle and having those eager hunters run away from your healing weapons.  It also means that after a Dome Fight or ambush that the Hunters can keep on with the chase rather than having to wait those important 10-15 seconds healing before continuing the pursuit.
The mobile arena collapses too quickly, most of the time falling only after finally breaking through the armor of the Monster.  This would not be such a problem if it were not for the fact that the Monster now has passive (and fast) armor regeneration, and doesn't even need to stop to feed while being chased to get its armor back.  I lost two matches due to the fact that the monster could kite us around the map and make back the armor it lost during the Mobile Arena fights.  If Turtle Rock could either decrease the time effects of certain combat milestones during Mobile Arena fights, or halve or completely remove passive armor regen then I feel it would be fairer.
This is possibly the most frustrating mechanic I have endured in Evolve.  In four of the twelve or so matches I played in, the Monster was able to evolve despite eating next to nothing becase we were on its heels and breathing down its neck basically the entire match.  We let it (all four times a Meteor Goliath) out of our sight for less than twenty seconds, and then we hear the roar and "Monster has reached Stage 2."  My friends and I were absolutely dumbfounded.  Half of the point of the chase is to prevent the monster from eating and gaining enough biomass to evolve.  I was able to play the Elder Kraken in one match and despite only having eaten a few beasts, was surprised when running away that the "Evolve - Press V" appeared on the left of the screen.  I did very little but run away from the very mobile Hunter party, and almost never got the chance to eat any wildlife because they were always behind me.  They were doing great, and despite their efforts, I was able to evolve and then turn around and completely wipe them as a freshly-evolved Stage 2.  This needs rebalanced.
"The match lobby is full."  Umm... Why would matchmaking kick people out of my party just so it could place me in a match with four randoms?  I have friends that wish to play so we can coordinate and have a medic or assault that does their job (No offense to the newcomers, but it gets frustrating seeing Caira or Markov every game and never seeing a heal grenade come my way or the Arc Mines being placed and having nothing aside from your Assault Rifle being used).
My friend mains EMET as his medic, and when we play we were surprised to find out that the only textures for his model that render now are his arms and face.  Even when being outlined behind structures, the only outlines are face and arms.
I will continue to update this review as my experience with Evolve Stage 2 increases.

attempts to improve the first game force a nosedive in quality. the first zombie shooter was entertaining for its lighthearted feel and solid gameplay. zombie shooter 2 tries to hamfist a story and nigh desecrates its pacing with heavier and uneeded rpg elements. not a single person on earth is going to take this game's story seriously. I say that because I'm not either. the difference between an excuseplot of the original to the sequel's full-on b-movie feel isn't very enjoyable because the game's artstyle and music do not coincide with the scenario. this would only be a minor complaint if the game delivered on its gameplay but sadly it does not
on the positive side, stats and perks actually matter. on the negative side, because now they do matter, it is possible to have a character that really isn't equipped to face the final levels (I recommend cash perk if you're going to play). cash is MUCH more important so save for the bigger weapons and only the big weapons. you see, instead of having fps weapon bar with everything at your disposal, you have only 3 weapon slots: small, medium, and large. this more or less means you use a pistol, machine gun, and rocket launcher... the whole game. being that the enemies are generally idiots the lack of interesting guns until very far in contrasts with the pacing of the original. the insistance on rpg elements makes the early half of the game a sort of a grind and, really, I just wanted to shoot zombies, not deal with half-arsed progression
so there is equipment now, but it is just armor that functions like old fps (and the previous game) and implants that raise your stats. changing implants for your situation can supply depth, but it is marginal. sometimes I wanted more hp, sometimes I wanted to move faster. the OPTIONS! anyway it's stupid expensive to repair armor so you're further punished for just playing the game. if you take damage in a level run through then you're digging yourself into a hole unless you're wearing cheap or no armor - and then why is there even armor? ammo for powerful weapons is also expensive, so yeah. have fun with your pea shooters
the game is an exercise in poor resource management. the enemies and environments are varied enough to warrant a good time, but instead of being a jump-in action game, it's some kind of frustrating survival shooter. hordes of zombies with rediculous amounts of life aren't really how survival games operate. the inventory system, story, and rpg progression are a step back from the original, basically. I must praise the game's so-called film filter though, it gives the game a unique feel that was somewhat lacking from the original. I'd turn off the black&white option though - what's so fun about black blood. the soundtrack is on par with what sigma puts out, so play your own music gents.
or don't play this game, it's not worth the aggravation. did I mention there are points in the game where you can get stuck in the environment? totally stuck, movement will get you walking into the walls. it's possible to leave the way you came out, but it may take minutes to figure out the precise angle, and many people find that they need to restart the levels. if you, for some godawful reason, really need more zombie shooter, try alien shooter. if you have to play this game, give easy mode a shot. I did not play on easy mode but I wish I did. the modal difficulty does not excuse the game's flaws

Tips for campaign mode:
Just buy weapons for slot 3 as slot 1 & 2 becomes useless on latter part, and choose ones based on its price, the more expensive the better.
A rocket launcher with higher damage and wider blast range is enough to clear the path.
Most of newly added weapons are useless so try to save your money.
Remember to buy missile-intercept drone, it's one of indispensable items on latter part!

The good:
- it's Baldur's Gate
- it runs like a charm on modern machines and as digital version I have no hassle with ejecting discs
- the easy transition to BG2
- quality of life upgrades and addition of BG2 classes makes the first game even more enjoyable
The "who cares":
- quite a few upgrades to interface, shortcut and character targeting are unwelcome. Luckily most of these are voluntary and can be deactivated in the options menu.
The bad:
- not being safe of possible future fiascos of corporate greed or social justice warrioring trashing on a beloved IP
All in all, if you were a Baldur's Gate fan, make sure to read up on what changes were made, but definately keep an eye on this title. Unfortunately, since Beamdog bought the rights to BG, the only new legal versions one can aquire are the EE ones. I personally don't mind (I do own the originals still if it ever should become a problem) but some people might be anoyed.

In an age of explosions, fighting, and looking-over-your-shoulder styles of survival games, there exists a rare gem - The Long Dark. I spent years looking for a quiet, yet challenging survival, but to no avail... until this.
The Long Dark does not ask you to fight the undead, it asks you to sneak past a lone wolf as it is focused on it's own survival. It does not expect you to build a giant castle on a hill, it expects you to use existing shelter to escape the raging blizzard. It is not a game to eat popcorn to during a party; it is something deeply personal. (Not that a Long Dark popcorn-party isn't something to aspire to. That would be awesome.)
There is something compelling about finding your way through a bleak, white forest listening for the crows and watching for bear tracks; finding the stories hidden within an abandoned cabin.
This is a very special game that requires you to think about where you're going and where you came from. There is no way to survive if you cannot mark your surroundings in your mind (or the newly updated mapping system that is primative enough to not affect my original statement. Well done, Hinterland!)
In conclusion, if you crave the hollywood definition of excitement, move along. This is a thoughtful exploration of a winter wasteland that is well worth your time and effort to explore.
P.S. Did I mention that you can organize your belongings? I love spending blizzards filling my shelves with oil cans and water bottles. The only downside is the lack of stacking, so I end up dumping piles of sticks in the corner. After Hinterland finishes their massive plans for development; I plan to start bugging them for wood-stacking. It's important for firewood. *nods sagely*

XCOM is a wonderful game! I love being able to name your bases and Soldiers (I name mine after Mobile Suits), I love the base management, The Research, and the random Missions. The Turn based combat is well designed and I'd love to see more games that use it.
However, there is one thing I'd like to point out, something that may be bad for gamers with bad tempers: The mind control. Aliens such as Sectoids and Etherials use Mind Control and this ability is vastly overpowered. For one thing, they can use it on soldiers of yours that they can't even see (something you can't do when you gain access to it). And second, they use it so frequently, sometimes like 3 times on one soldier. And since you may not have access to technology that can prevent Mind Control, it can turn most missions with these enemies into certain failure. And even when your character has high mental resistance, they can still get Mind Controlled.
Personally, I wish they'd remove this ability entirely, as the game can still be challenging without it. Aside from this one issue, the game is perfect.

This game was a great nostalgic blast to the past for me. XCOM: UFO Defense was my favorite game of all time from the first time I played it all the way up to the release of XCOM: Enemy Unknown. Everything from the terror-inspiring fog-of-war, to the antiquated screaming and gunfire sounds, to the green plasma bolts lancing out of the darkness at your beloved squad makes the game ooze atmosphere. There is also a ton of freedom of base management and you juggle your finances down to the last dollar.
This game has some problems though that honestly makes the Enemy Unknown (in my opinion) the superior game. First off, the game is about as intuitive as any high-realism game from its era. Which is to say, not at all. There is no tutorial of any kind and very little indication as to how well you're actually doing. Prepare for your entire first playthrough to be thrown in the garbage when you encounter Ethereals for the first time and find out you're nowhere near where you need to be to fight them. Even when put on super-easy-wimpy mode (I think the game calls it "Beginner") prepare to lose the game more than once.
Frustration aside, the game rewards you for success. What other tactics game can get you blood racing and sweat beading on your forehead as you have your team prepare to breach into a crashed alien ship? Or cheer as the Commander that you've had since the beginning of the game makes a last-second shot to bring down a charging crysalid before it turns a group of helpless civilians into zombies?
This is a Microprose strategy game, pure and simple. It expects a lot out of the player and really challenges them to be their best. If what you tried doesn't work, dust yourself off and try something new. I've been playing this game on and off for almost 25 years and I've never beaten it, and yet this game is still one of my favorite games. Definitely worth a playthrough if you're interested in very challenging tactics games.

404Sight is a fun game with cool effects, milkshake smooth gameplay, and it's free!
The game's special stunts can be wonky in first person mode, the sensitivity is too low, and there are a few bugs. The game is also very short.
As a free indie game, 404Sight is worth trying out. It's guaranteed to entertain you for a while, as you attempt to beat your high score or replay levels all in first-person. The game is fun, beautiful, and a bargain at just $0.00.
Overall, this game is great! The gameplay is smooth, looks great, and includes tons of visual org*sms.
This game incorporates three of my favorite things: cyberpunk (Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon for the win!, parkour (I'm a huge Mirror's Edge fan), and 404 Errors (no prizes for those who guess why that is).
There are only a couple of downsides to the game. First, I personally don't agree with the game's message (net nuetrality), but that's just my little opinion.
The second downside is that when you perform a special stunt in first-person mode after leaping of off a bounce pad, the camera often is at a wierd angle, causing you to fall to your demise. Also the initial mouse sensitivity is low, but that isn't really an issue, since it can be easily adjusted from the "Options" menu.
But there are upsides as well. The game looks great, the effects such as the "Ping" special ability looks fantastic when activated (surges of energy pulse throughout the map, and looks quite badass). I also like the camera shake effect when enemy weapons rain from above and explode. The special parkour stunts are great in third-person (not in first, as I said above). Also, when you take damage, the screen becomes pixelated, which is a nice touch.
The game is pretty short (it's only 14 levels). Hopefully the developers will add more content in the future. :D
In the end, 404Sight is a great
indie game.

Was a fun game but a bit disappointing to be completely honest. I've been looking forward to this game for a month or so now due mainly to it's premise, and unfortunately the net neutrality theme to me actually seems like a gimmick of all things.
Before I go over that though, I do actually recommend the game itself. I finished all the levels in a little over half an hour, and it was an enjoyable enough time. It's basically an unbounded runner (Think Temple Run without movement restrictions and with actual levels rather than being endless), akin to Mirror's Edge but with a bit more emphasis on speed rather than parkour. From the little time I had with it, it was fun and definitely worth my time. The soundtrack is nice too.
However for the game claiming to be in support of net neutrality and based around it, it's surprisingly shallow in that aspect. Outside of a short intro of "OH NOEEZZ GOVERMENTZ ARE SHUTTING DOWN MY INTERNETZ HELP ME ADA!" and an outro of *spoiler I guess* "YOU DID IT YOU SAVED ME BUT YOU CAN'T DO IT ALONE! (Even though you kind of did)" there isn't really any mention of net neutrality at all. It pretty much assumes the player knows the current issues behind net neutrality and even then hardly touches upon the subject. Even the gameplay outside of naming has nothing to do with net neutrality. I mean I didn't expect them to get really creative and create a full blown story regarding what would happen without net neutrality (although I was hoping they would, it would have been nice), but at the very least giving some background knowledge on the issue would have been nice, I highly doubt players will go seek out info on their own initiative after playing this.
Overall though, it was a fun game and since it's free I guess I can't rant too much. Give it a shot!

6/10
+Fun system, pleasing to look for secrets and loot
+Updated graphics, but still has that old feel. If I didn't know it, I'd say my enemies were flat. (That's a good thing, trust me.)
+Runs 60 FPS on every system I've tested on, no matter what the graphics settings were
+Lots of customization in settings (Basically, you have the options to change what color/kind of blood you see, and how the atmosphere of the game looks like.)
+Database system encourages researching enemies, and quickly identifies the foe you are fighting
x Level design, it can be really good at times (Puzzles, mild parkour), but otherwise, it's straight and forward or it's an arena
x Lots of difficulty settings, but they feel really poorly designed (I'm playing at normal, and it seems way harder than normal. I've played easy, and it's way too easy. There's at least 6 different difficulty setings. :B)
x Saving! You can save, great right! Not really. So, in the game, you can press F6 to quickly save your game. Otherwise, if you die, you are set back to the start of the level. This sucks when you forget to save or are too busy getting blown up to save.
x Sound quality. First off, Sam is hilarious. He says some super-generic puns that'd you'd expect from a cheesy action movie or Duke Nukem. But, the enemies sounds... Well, you got the Kamikaze who screams his a** off when he charges, Scorpion bosses sound like someone taking a sh**, and the Bone Horse-thingies are too loud. The game's music isn't that great, but you can't really mute it, because sounds play such an important role in knowing when you're going to be attacked
-SUPER REPETITIVE, I kid you not. Combat doesn't change, it just gets harder because the enemies have more health, fire more bullets, or are more plenty in numbers. The combat is basically just jumping and shooting, avoiding enemy charges, or tearing down hoardes.
-LEVEL DESIGN! (I know I said this already, but...) There's this one level that was just agony. You start off with your pistols and shotgun (Only the shotgun does good damage) and you have to go into a large field with enemies. Once you kill them all, you have to fight another wave. Then, another wave of harder enemies come. Then , you fight a boss. Then, another boss, and then another, much larger boss. Again, this all takes place in the SAME FIELD.
-Plot doesn't justify the game. Why am I fighting? How did I get here? Why are these enemies spawning? Why are there so many? Why do they look the same? What am I looking for? Isn't there a much easier way? What do you mean I have to read about it? It'd be so much easier to explain if it took place in hell.

You're probably like, "Dude, stop talking about Dwarf Fortress. This is Stonehearth", and you're right, I shouldn't bring up past relationships, but Stonehearth scratches the same itch that kept me interested in playing Dwarf Fortress, and it looks perfectly adorable on top of it all.
Stonehearth isn't as in depth as Dwarf Fortress, but it is most definitely a Dwarf Fortress-like.  If you're like me, and you enjoyed Dwarf Fortress, but maybe the graphics bothered you or maybe you're looking for Dwarf Fortress Lite, Stonehearth may be worth buying.

The basic game still stands the test of time well. Obviously not competing with the graphics of modern titles, but visuals are never the most important thing with RPGs particularly - it's all about the story, sense of adventure, the NPCs you interact with, and developing your character(s) - all of which this game has in high quality spades. It set the solid foundations upon which practically a whole genre was then successfully developed, which still has a strong following today with the success of Pillars of Eternity. Many of those subsequent games may be considered better in one way or another (e.g. character development in Planescape Torment), but the original still brings me back for simple, good clean fun (or dirty if you want to play evil)! The Enhanced Edition's new characters and Black Pits 'dungeon crawl' are a bit of additional fun, but it's the original game that's really a classic for my generation of RPGers.

Baldur's Gate is a RPG that was originally released back in 1998.
Since then it has inspired a tidal wave of RPG games and reinkindled a belived to be dead genre. So it was just a matter of time before this classic game got an overhaul which resulted in Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition.
The game tells a rather intriguing story about two rivaling nations that are on the brink of war. But not all is what it seems to be and the true reasons behind the potential outbreak of war lie hidden in a double and triple layered web of treason and lust for power. In addition to that the player is also concered with his own heritage and what this could have to do with the events that are laid out in the game.
Before starting the game, the player has to create his character, which will be of course, the main character of the game. In addition to the main character the player can control a group of up to six characters (including the main character) which can be recruited over the course of the game.  There are quite a lot of companions available to recruit for your party which differ a lot in terms of personality. This is a key factor the game, because it adss a lot of replayablity to it. Also this allows you to play the game in different ways. You can be the shining hero, that is beloved by the inhabitans of the Sword Coast, or you can be the dark villain that only thrives to satiate his own lust for conquest. Due to the alignment system in Dungeons & Dragons (the pen & paper system which Baldur's gate is based upon), you will find good and evil companions which support the correspondet playstyle. So it would be a bad idea to recruid only evil characters and then play the shining hero because there is a possibilty that those companions would leave the party if your reputation which the inhabitants of the Sword Coast gets to good. The same thing goes for recruiting only good aligned characters and accomplishing evil deeds.
The gameplay itself is based upon a pausable real time combat system. So your orders to your party members will be executed in real time and you can pause and any time to get a overview of whats going on. Does someone need a heal? Can you stun a certain enemy? Which opponent should you attack next? Should you focus your attacks on one enemey or split up to keep certain enemies occupied? The Combat system evolvers a lot around tactical choices, which makes it fun and challenging. While melee and ranged combat is pretty straight foward and self explanatory, some players might find the spell system weird, because you have no casting resource such as mana or other form of energy. Instead you have a spellbook with a limited number of spells per page that you can write into your spellbook. Now you can choose a few spells that you would like to memorize. Spells get memorized after you rest at an inn or via the rest function in the wilderness. You can only use spells that you have memorized. There are some exceptions to this, for instance the sorcerer class does not need to memorize spells. So the player to equip his mages with a good mixture of utility and damage spells in order to maximize their potential.
Beside the main story there are a lot of side quests that reach from the simple "go there, bring me back this" to rather complex and story rich side quests. The game does no handholding with quests. You sometimes get a vague direction (or none at all) where to go for a certain quest. But in general you have to explore the areas that you go to. Because often you will stumble upon your quests targets in the wilderness. Talking about side quests Beamdog added 3 new companions to the game and each of them brings a new quest with them.
Also you have to read a lot. There is a lot of text in this game. And you have to read carefully, otherwise you might lose your direction. There are nor questmarkers or markings on the map.
The developers from Beamdog made a few changes to the Dungeons & Dragons ruleset that the game uses. Also they introcued some class and race options which were only available in the original Baldur's Gate 2. But in general these are good changes because they add some more variety to the game.
The not so good changes are some to the UI. I Personally liked the old quest journal a bit more than the new one. And they changed the character sprites a lot. The old ones looked better. Gladfully this can turned off in the options menu.
All in all the Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition is a worthy overhaul, it runs smoothly on new systems and still works fine. Sure it is not a remake. But it brings a classic game to modern era pc gaming and despite the changes that are not liked by everyone, the game itself is still fun and intruiging ans the original from 1998. So I totally reccommend this game for anyone who is interested in old-school party based RPGs.

As a person who is not at all familiar with FPSes and barely plays them, I am most certainly the best candidate for writing a review on this hardcore twitch-FPS game.
I am just absolutely in love with this game.
I expected to enjoy it at least in the easier parts of the game, but I was not ready for how much bloody fun this little game is to play, and I did not expect how INSANE it could get. Even more insane is the fact that... yeah, I *can* deal with this. Somehow. (At least, up through world 4 as of writing)
This may be because, secretly, this game is identical to precision platformers in every way other than the basic gameplay style. Steep but smooth difficulty curve? Check. Short, but challenging and tightly-designed levels that never drag on too long? Check. Scoring system that focuses on optimization and speed? Check. Instant restarts? Check. Heavy trial-and-error based gameplay? Check. Lives counter? Haha, not in the slightest.
It really *is* right in the same vein as precision platformers. Yet it's not the least bit frustrating. At all. I have not found myself raging at the game even once in nearly 10 hours of play (as of writing). There are a few minor instances of somewhat questionable level design (mostly in the form of apples that you have to blindly shoot in world 4, but there are only a few of those) that annoyed me, but every obstacle is overcomeable with enough practice and there's never too long of an iteration time to get back to where you messed up. The more challenging/precise a level tends to be, the shorter, too, so you don't have sudden difficulty spikes in the form of longer, mind-numbingly fast-paced levels that come out of nowhere. Everything feels smooth and natural. You approach a new level with a feeling of "how the hell am I ever going to do this" and then you beat it and have the same experience with the next level. Going back and replaying the easier levels after completing the harder levels only makes them better, too; you can completely annihlate them and feel like a champion for doing so.
Also, did I mention how gorgeous the game is all around? Absolutely wonderful art style, fantastic soundtrack, very polished controls. It's presented wonderfully, and the cutesy wrapping hides one hell of a hardcore experience. For $6 this is a steal, I cannot think of a single negative thing to say about it and it's certainly in contention for game of the year for me.
I also wouldn't be surprised to find that I am better at FPS games than 90% of the people who've been playing triple-A titles for the past 5 years, because I doubt any of them give as intense of a training course as this game.
Now for world 5 to kick my posterior mercilessly... help...
EDIT: Post world-5 update.
So... the game gets incredibly quirky... and even more amazing... some of these levels are among my all-time favorites in any game I've ever played, haha, and the difficulty never lets up, only getting crazier. And yet... no frustration. At all. Nearly 18 hours to perfect every level and I did not get the slightest bit mad at the game. It's just... perfect, I don't know what else to say.
EDIT: I'm editing this for the steam awards thing, but, I have to say. This game is just marvellous, even two years later. I think about this game frequently, I've played it more than most any other game in my steam library, and it's the only game I've ever seriously attempted speedrunning. It's just great.

We all have played the games were you are the lone hero, constantly growing in strenght and overcoming all obstacles...
This games ticks of a lot of those but in very diffirent ways.
You are alone, but not by choice and it does not make you stronger.
You do not grow in strenght but rather fight endlessly to not become slowly weaker and weaker.
You will have to overcome obstacles but it will always be at a cost, and you will constantly question yourself "Was it worth it?".
If you are looking for a hardcore survival game this is it.
Some developers goes out of their way in stacking the odds against the player, alluding that evidently bad design was a part in "intentional" difficulty.
on the other hand has managed to almost perfect the indifference of nature. Indeed, while the core mechanic of the game is to punish any "mistake" done by the player, it never feels unfair.
Sleep outside in the woods and you might have an encounter with hungry wildlife, try to save time during a windy day by cutting across a frozen lake might lead to hypotermia, not drinking will lead to dehydration and so on but despite all this, as a player one rather feels that
gave you all the tools to succeed.
There are plenty of places to sleep safely, it was just the player who decided to ignore the setting sun. Exploring on the other side of the lake could have waited a day and gathering twigs and setting a fire to melt snow is propably the first thing a player is taught. Failure is caused by the player, not by bad controls or design.
provides a good introduction in the basics and necessities of survival(gameplay) without feeling to slow, bolted on or convoluted and gives the player a good grasp of the "real" part of the game,

The game that practically created a genre, or at least many sequels and even more copycats.
UFO: Enemy Unknown (as I knew this game back when it was first released in Europe) came out more or less when I started getting into the joys of PC gaming. Some of my fondest memories of my early gaming days come from this, up there with the first Civilization game.
The tactical missions are the highlight, with you leading a small group of soldiers to take on a downed ship, or abduction site, or whatever. What really grabbed me though was the additional blend of base building and having to manage your funds and threat level, keeping other countries happy to avoid them withdrawing support. It was this blend that was the key to X-Com's success for me, and allowed this game to stand the test of time for many years. None of the sequels or copycat games really captured the magic of the original, and best.
It would be remiss of me to review this game without mentioning the remake / successor by Firaxis, XCOM: Enemy Unknown. As of writing this review I have admittedly not completed the game yet, though from the 15 or so hours I have put in so far I have to say that it is an excellent remake: It keeps what worked, updates the graphics and changes what needs to be changed to make the game more accessible for today's market.
Honestly, this is a great game, however if you are new to the game I would play XCOM: Enemy Unknown instead. This does serve as a great nostalgia piece though, which, for the money Steam are asking for, is great value. I would even say that getting the Complete Pack is worth it for the added value.

I have played less than two hours of this game and can affirm that it is golden. On the surface, it looks like some kind of strange puzzle game that requires you to know a thing or two about chemistry, and while it does actually kind of touch on and teach really basic chemistry topics, it has nothing to do with it otherwise.
No disguising the fact that it is a puzzle game, though, and a very logic heavy one at that. Every level tasks you to get a certain output from a set of inputs, and the mental gymnastics you have to perform to get some of those outputs are astonishing. Like most truly good puzzle games, the way you solve it will probably be different from the way the developers thought to solve it, your best friend will think to solve it, your dog will think to solve it; the whole chain of command. At the end of every level, you're given a graph showing the best and worst scores for the puzzle, and you can hit tab to see how you compare to your friends, and eventually see where your friends gave up. The rankings gauge you in three areas - how fast your solution performs, how many reactors your solution uses (efficiency part 1) and how many commands your solution uses (efficiency part 2). I tend to get all of my high scores in fast solutions, and I find myself replaying the same levels over and over to try and create a more efficient, speedy solution. I'm sure the novelty of that will wear off... probably.
Certainly the best game I've purchased for a dollar, and it really outshines some that I've payed more for. For the amount of content and replay value in this, I'd say its normal price tag of ten dollars is a fair price. If you're a puzzle game enthusiast, or someone who wants to keep the logical part of their brain in tip top shape, buy it, it's good fun.

I basically never write reviews, but I feel that this is well deserving of one.
There were three things I loved so much about the Half-Life series. First, the story is incredibly immersive and the sequence of events makes sense logically, game-wise and story-wise. Second, and this is one of the major defining points of Half-Life series, is the fact that it is entirely 1st person. Thirdly, is that it is one man against all odds.
For Dishonored, the story is incredible, and I've only seen an hour of it. You have been wrongfully accused and you are driven by vengeance. This is a type of story I personally love. Gordon Freeman's goal was to defeat the combine and free Earth. In Dishonored, you must free the city of Dunwall from control by the Lords who assassinated the queen. But what I love is that it takes its own unique twist on it. It adds in the factor of vengeance which Half-Life never really had. And I love it.
The fully-immersive 1st person is lovely too. It's almost the same as Half-Life. What I liked about Half-Life, however, is that even between loading screens, you wouldn't leave the 1st person view. And during cutscenes, your view would sometimes shrink in the game. That's the only issue I have with it. It's fantastic anyway.
My recommendation:
If you like Half-Life, buy it.
If you like Half-Life 2, buy it.
If you like any Half-Life game, buy it.
If you like 1st person shooters, buy it.
Hate any of them? Still buy it.

I played the beta of the game ages ago. It was a super fun game and I was really hyped for it. I almost even pre-ordered it. It was also one of the most anticipated games at the time!
But then, sometime before launch, like really close to launch, the game was suddenly filled with microtransactions and DLC totalling hundreds of $. To make it worse, the content already in the game without the DLC wasn't even worth the original $60 price tag!
Due to that suddenly happening, the game became a "DLC & Microtransaction Simulator" for $60. Many people cancelled their pre-orders, and people who really wanted to buy it (like me) decided not to buy it. The game died (player base was almost nothing) like a month or so after release.
Now, since the game has had a F2P (free 2 play) model since launch, it's officially going F2P. It's mainly to cash in on people dumb enough to buy the in-game microtransactions/purchases, and to revive the player-base for those who have already owned/bought the game.
So, should you get this game? Ofcourse! It's a very fun game and is worth trying since it's free. But as of writing this review, I do not know if the microtransactions make the game Pay 2 Win (P2W) or ruin the experience.
Now, would I recommend this game? NO! Because the practices and marketing that the developers chose for this game should be looked down upon and not supported. The dev's have learned their lesson hopefully, and hopefully other developers learn from their huge mistake.

Those who try to build a game of one genre, using a toolset intended for another, very seldom meet success.  The result is typically clumsy and clunky, built of parts not really meant for the purpose.
So it is with
.
While my impression from the store page suggested that this would be an educational math game, it turned out to be more of a generic puzzler, built in RPGMaker.  Though it's interesting to see RPGMaker pushed to create something other than still another formulaic SNES-era RPG, the outcome is more tiresome than fun.  Clicking through dull, badly-written dialogue in order to provide a patina of context for the puzzles proved even less enjoyable than clicking through them to establish the clichéd, half-hearted romances and shopworn revenge motivations of the typical RPG.
Similarly, solving puzzles by plodding around with the overworld controls was slow and frustrating, when compared with the mouse interface of a normal puzzler.  I don't know whether the developer chose this path as a personal challenge, or simply had only RPGMaker available to work with, but this was an endeavour more noble in conception than in execution.

A young guy was flipping through a book of recreational math puzzles while a shonen anime aimed at guys just a bit younger than him played in the background.  He started to wonder how to make a successful game that he could proudly show to the world.  It filled him with immense hope and ambition, but the struggle to translate nerdy challenges to far-reaching entertainment tried him mightily.  Hours had already turned into days, then weeks, then months; he now knew the end was coming and he would have to pay his rent somehow.  In a fit of frustration and exhaustion, he attempted a cram session of programming and passed out on the keyboard.
In a dream, the guy encountered a mysterious and very powerful force that coalesced into a beautiful and imposing figure, a woman of mystery known only as LSD.  LSD invited the guy to explore the realms beyond light and time--a land of wild and supernaturally useful code snippets, with which even the lousiest hack could easily generate interest beyond their imagination.  But to reach the realms, he would have to exceed the greatest foes of his own mind at the very riddles he wanted to use as gameplay material for his star project.  After many tries, with LSD's constant guidance, he surpassed the dangers of Desperation; he conquered Past Failures more easily.  Nearing the realms, Inability almost forced his hand in defeat; but he found a sly detour by simply ignoring it until it ceased to exist.  At the realm's precipice awaited the final foe: a half-naked toddler with a gazeless stare, drool all over his face and body, and torn chocolate-and-crayon-stained papers crumpled messily in his sticky fingers.  Though he struggled mightily, he could not beat the toddler, who always seemed to know his riddling moves better than he did himself.  For what seemed like an eternity, the two waged a mental war until finally one finally exhausted and gave up.
When he woke up, the guy's mother picked him up by the trainer-pants and put him back in the playpen.  She did not recognize the crumpled papers in his hands, though some of the handwriting clearly belonged to his father.  She thought nothing of the tatters of math puzzles and story problems upon them.  But when the father returned to his computer that evening, he panicked to himself that his hidden drug stash in the dusty old notebook by the monitor was suddenly gone!  And even more strangely, his Steam program now contained links to something he had never seen: the Steamworks API.  Therein, he found that his account had somehow published a game and posted it on Greenlight without his ever knowing.  He tried the game himself, but quickly gave up in frustration.  Somewhat amazed but mostly confused by the whole series of events, he decided to let the Greenlight process go on its own; when the game was actually published, he didn't even know how to take credit.  In truth, no one would.
That game, by the way, was called Jesus Christ RPG, and it's still better than this piece of crap.  In fact, you probably had more fun reading this than you would with this game.  In fact, I spent longer writing this review than beating this game.

I can only recommend this game if it's free.
